And he foresaw for Pharaoh seven years of abundance in livestock and grain, and just as many of scarcity and famine, because he had seen in his sleep seven fat cows grazing in the marshlands, and seven other thin ones on the riverbank devouring the very fat ones. And he saw seven ears of grain sprouting from a stalk, full, and just as many empty and scorched by the wind, the former devouring the beautiful ones. And because Joseph himself had dreamed that his own sheaf rose and stood upright, and the sheaves of his brothers stood around and bowed down to his sheaf; and that the Sun, the Moon, and eleven stars bowed down to him, it was interpreted that his eleven brothers, father, and mother would bow and revere him. 

Again, from the cake of bread baked in the ashes <note>original: "subcineritio pane"; refers to the dream of the Midianite soldier in Judges 7:13</note>, which a Midianite had dreamed rolled into the camp of Midian, reaching the tent, overturning it, and leveling it to the ground, it was interpreted that the sword of Gideon would utterly destroy the camp and capture Midian. 

The statue that Nebuchadnezzar had dreamed of had a golden head, silver arms and chest, a bronze belly and thighs, iron legs, and a foot that was partly clay and partly bronze; and a stone cut from a mountain struck and broke the statue, and the statue vanished, and the stone became a mountain and filled the earth. Daniel, by God’s power, interpreted the golden head to be the great Nebuchadnezzar, and the silver foot <note>The text says "silver foot," though the biblical Daniel 2:32-33 describes silver arms and chest</note> to be the kingdom to come; the bronze part signifies that it will rule the whole earth, and the iron part that all these things will be crushed. The iron part of the toes signifies the division of the kingdom. The broken part and the solid part—iron mixed with muddy clay—which are mixed by human seed but do not adhere, just as iron does not mix with pottery. 

So too the tree in the middle of the earth, whose height was so great it filled the sky, beautiful in form and fruitful; beneath it were beasts, and in its branches birds. A Holy One calls from heaven: "Cut down the tree, destroy the fruit, and scatter the beasts and birds; leave the roots, and let them be bound with a band of bronze and iron among the wild herbs, and let it be wet with the dew of heaven; let the human heart be changed so that it becomes like a beast’s, and let its duration be for seven times." Daniel interpreted this from God to mean the tree was Nebuchadnezzar, whose power ruled over all the earth. But the Angel announces to the son <note>original: "filioque"; the text here may be conflating Nebuchadnezzar with his lineage or using "son" as a generic title</note> that you shall be cast out from men for seven years, and you shall be a beast, and eat grass like an ox, and be sprinkled with dew, until you recognize your Lord. But after you have recognized that the kingdom comes from God, it shall remain for you; this is the sprout of its roots.

But let us digress to the histories of the Greeks. An eagle portends misfortune because it is predatory and bloody. Penelope dreamed of an eagle killing the geese she raised at home, from the nineteenth book of Homer’s *Odyssey* <note>The Latin text says "vni decimo" (eleventh), but the dream occurs in Book 19</note>, from which it is interpreted that Ulysses would kill the suitors who were destroying his goods. 

Philip, King of Macedonia, after his marriage, appeared to have fixed a seal of a Lion upon his wife in a dream; Aristander of Telmessus, the dream-interpreter, affirmed she was pregnant, for seals are not usually fixed to empty things, and that she would give birth to an infant with the nature of a lion. Alexander dreamed that he lay with his mother; it was interpreted that he would possess the rule of the entire earth, for "to lie with" is to lay someone low, and the "mother" is interpreted as the Earth, because the Earth is the universal mother. Hecuba, while pregnant, saw in her sleep that she gave birth to a torch by which the kingdom would be burned; she gave birth to Paris, because of whom Troy was burned and reduced to ash. 

The things read in the works of Artemidorus Daldianus <note>A 2nd-century professional dream interpreter and author of the 'Oneirocritica,' the first manual of its kind</note> are all taken from the similarity of things. Forests designate sadness and disturbance of the soul. For forests are full of confusion; they portend lashings for slaves, because the rods with which they are beaten are cut from forests. Planting trees is an excellent omen for those getting married, for they will procreate children. The woman is the field, and children are planted in her like trunks in a plowed field. 

Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician of the 5th century BC</note> said that budding trees, laden with fruit, portend that the body is in good health; if they are sterile, it signifies the corruption of human seed. If the leaves have fallen, the body is harmed by moist and cold humors. If they bud without fruit, it is harmed by hot and dry humors. In the case of olive trees, to cast out waste <note>original: "excrementa eijcere"; likely referring to manure or organic fertilizer</note> is prosperous, because olives delight in such fertilizer. Likewise, to be anointed with oil signifies joy. Sweet and ripe apples are good, especially for the married and for lovers, for apples are friendly to Venus because of their sweetness; sour ones, however, signify strife and contentions. Mulberries and pomegranates signify wounds because of their color and likeness to blood. The pear signifies prosperity because it lasts a long time. White figs are good; black ones at an inopportune time signify calumnies and detractions. Nuts, and whatever...

...they are broken, they signify noise and disturbances. Laurel <note>original: "Laurus"</note> is good for women because of its evergreen nature and beauty, but for those who are hoping for something, it is bad because of its bitterness. The Pine is related to sailors because of the timber from which ships are built, as well as its pitch and resin. To wear a crown made of tree branches anywhere other than the head is noted to be a sign of disaster, since the proper seat of a crown is the head. Zoilus saw his sons crowned with olive branches around their ankles in competitions; they died before they could enter the contest, since the ankles are not far from the ground. Xerxes dreamed that his head was bound with an olive crown, and that all of Greece was shaded by its branches; because of this omen—and because Athens was the discoverer of the olive—he set out for Greece, even though many advised against it. The Palm tree grants freedom to slaves, since it is the right of free men to wear crowns. Thorns and briers are signs of fertility, since hedges are made from them. 

You may read more in Plato, and in Cicero’s book *On Divination* and *On the Nature of the Gods*, and in Valerius Maximus. Both Aristides and Iamblichus, in their writings on the secrets of the Egyptians, record that the sick were accustomed to receive cures in their sleep through similarities; and Strabo says that those staying overnight in the temple of Aesculapius at Epidaurus received counsel regarding their health through such means. In Haruspicy <note>the ancient practice of divining the future by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals</note> the same principle of similarity is observed, of which we shall collect some examples from the writings of the ancients—not so that we may place our faith in them, but to show that in such matters, and in all things, similarity was observed. In the discipline of Augury <note>divination through the flight or behavior of birds and animals</note>, a horse always signifies empire and war. In the time of Gaius Julius Caesar, a horse was born with almost human feet, having hooves divided in the manner of fingers; the Haruspices responded that it portended the empire of the world for its owner, and Caesar raised it with great care. That the horse also signifies war is shown by the clear testimony of Virgil:

->For war, horses are armed; these herds threaten war.<-
<note>original: "Bello armantur equi, bellum hæc armenta minantur." — Virgil, Aeneid, Book 3</note>

The chickens predicted an unhappy conflict for Mancinus against the Numantines when they refused their feed and flew out of their cage. In Homer, Jupiter signified with a great crash of thunder at night that Ulysses would avenge the insults of the suitors. And when the battle lines of the Greeks and Trojans stood ready for combat on both sides, it rained blood, signifying a great slaughter of the Greeks. While the Greeks were sacrificing in Homer’s account, a serpent crawled from the altar to a nearby plane tree, in which there were eight sparrow chicks; Calchas interpreted this to mean that the war against the Trojans would be prolonged into its ninth year.

### BY THEIR OWN SIMILARITY, PLANTS DEMONSTRATE
### *the cultivation suitable for them.* Chapter XI.

<image-desc>A decorative square drop cap frame containing a large letter 'N' set against a background of scrolling floral and foliate patterns.</image-desc>

No less divinely than clearly, that supreme overseer of the world has shown through Agriculture how each plant rejoices in the specific cultivation it has adopted, according to the character it displays. For individual plants demand a peculiar kind of care, not only under different soils, climates, and locations in the world, but even under the same sky; with only a short distance intervening, everything is varied and diverse, so that nothing can be prescribed for them universally or perpetually. For this reason, we have always considered the diligence of the ancients in establishing rules for them to be vain and even ridiculous. 

But because Agriculture is so necessary for the daily and long-term survival of men that the lot of mortals could not persist without it, it has been brought about by the industry of nature that every plant demonstrates its own suitable cultivation and timing through its form, similarity, and way of living, so that it can be gathered through simple inspection and observation. We shall reveal the matter in a few clear words. From the inspection of wild plants which grow by the impulse of nature, one may observe: a single root, creeping forth in a simple stalk, demands deep soil, such as the cypress, the pine, the pear, and the Italian oak <term>esculus: a species of oak with edible acorns</term>; for as much as they rise up in the body, so much do they descend in the root. However, a root that is short, twisted, and wandering through the surface of the turf is content with little soil, such as the olive, the plum, and the pomegranate. A plant that rests upon more slender fibers, so that it ends in hairs, threads, or the thinnest filaments, requires loose and thin earth, so that it may more easily...

BOOK ONE.

...can be handled, such as orache <note>original: "atriplex"</note> and blite <note>original: "blitum"; these are soft-leaved potherbs</note>. But those that are hard and solid seek a hard and solid environment. A plant that spreads broad from its stem and tapers to a sharp point, so that it resembles a pointed wedge, seeks out stone walls and ruined buildings, living packed between the gaps in rocks; it is therefore called **saxifrage** <note>literally "stone-breaker"</note>. Trees that hasten to sprout, such as the **almond**, **peach**, and **apricot** <note>original: "præcox, & armeniaca"</note>, which bloom in January, should be planted during the first summer rains. Those that bloom late, like the **mulberry**, we can sow later, as we do with the **vine** and the **apple**; for it is necessary that they lie beneath the earth for a little while so they may unite with the soil and conceive. Those that sprout in the intermediate time can be planted between autumn and spring. **Cereal crops** <note>original: "Frumentacea"</note>, which have a hungry and thin appearance, rejoice in rich fallow land and fertile manure. Hungry things desire more food, and dry bodies long for abundant and rich nourishment; they draw no benefit from what is dry and lean. Just as hungry and thin men delight in rich food so they may improve in color and strength, the same is truly seen in trees. A plant demonstrates it must be warded off when it is a vice and a troublesome companion to the crop. Drooping vine-shoots which take root as soon as they touch the ground and are born again—filling everything unless they are restrained—clearly show they wish to propagate themselves. Those plants that show aborted and degenerate fruits are demanding lower ground. 

In **grafting** <term>infitio: the practice of joining a part of one plant onto another so they grow together</term>, those things unite which have the same nature of bark and which bloom equally at the same hour, having a shared timing for sprouting and for the union of their shoots. For whenever dry things are resisted by wet ones, or hard barks by soft ones, they conceive with great difficulty. Trees clothed in a thicker bark, because they suck up copious moisture from the earth, require **foliage-grafting** <term>emphyllismon: a method where a shoot is inserted under the bark</term>, such as the fig, olive, and cherry; otherwise, when the shoot is driven between the bark and the wood, the bandage of the bark is burst asunder. Those joined by a thin bark, being dry on the outside and content with less moisture—as if the moisture had retreated from the bark into the inner marrow—such as the vine and the citron, require **cleft-grafting** <term>encentrismon: inserting a wedge-shaped scion into a cleft in the host's wood</term>, and they nourish the foreign shoot in the nurturing lap of the parent. For those whose bark wavers with too much moisture and possesses a rich sap beneath, **budding** <term>enophtalmismon: from the Greek for "eye" (bud); inserting a single bud into a slit in the bark</term> is appropriate: for they enclose a bud taken from another plant, receiving it gently in the soft beds of the bark and joining it in a living bond. For those whose lopped-off branches do not regrow, grafting is denied; never have farmers seen a **cypress**, **spruce**, or **pine** that nourished the offspring of another. Those that "weep" resin and pitch scorn the fellowship of other inoculations and graftings; a grafted branch never takes hold in the spruce or pine. 

Those trees require **pruning** which are exhausted by excessive fertility, like the vine, for its luxury is restrained by pruning; in the same way, those that grow wild with a wanton boldness of branches, like the olives, need it. But for those that are harmed by clipping, we advise that nothing be taken away. Those that produce watery and large fruits in a short interval of time rejoice in marshy and shady places, like the **melon**, **cucumber**, and **gourd**. Those swelling with a large, heavy fruit over a longer time, like **quinces**, **citrons**, and **apples**, prefer moist places or those that can be irrigated. Those with tiny fruits, like the **jujube** <note>original: "lotus"</note>, **dogwood**, and **palm**, prefer mountains and sterile places. Flowers of a cheerful appearance and charming elegance, like **roses**, delight in basking in the sun; those of a sad and pale look seek out shady places, like the **boxwood**, **cypress**, **nightshade** <note>original: "solanus"</note>, and the like. Because we have treated these matters copiously in the work dedicated to this task, we will omit them here; let it suffice to have tasted a few examples to show that through similarity and the form of the thing itself, all things demonstrate their internal gifts.

This is so that memory may be aided by a brief compendium, and we may arrange the matter into a more elegant series with few and clear words. Therefore, the hidden properties of plants are demonstrated by similarity: first to living creatures, then to inanimate things. We shall speak first of living creatures—namely man, quadrupeds, birds, fish, and reptiles. For Man...

BOOK TWO OF PHYTOGNOMONICS

...not only through their similarities to human limbs, which they heal, but also to diseases. This occurs not only through their parts—such as the root, trunk, foliage, flower, fruit, and seed—but also through their actions and habits, such as whether they retain or shed their leaves, their offspring, their number, their beauty, or their deformity; and likewise, they mirror the habits and actions of animals. Even the qualities of stars, metals, gems, and stones are found within them. First, we shall review those that bear a resemblance to the limbs of the human body, including not just the primary parts but even the smaller components of those parts.

The humors of plants, when consumed as food, increase those same humors in the body; for instance, phlegmatic plants increase phlegm <note>original: "pituita," one of the four bodily humors, associated with coldness and moisture</note>, and bilious plants increase bile. When these same plants are received as medicines, they have a designated power to draw out those same fluids. **Orache** <note>original: "atriplex"</note>, **cumin**, and **bishop’s weed** <note>original: "ammi"</note> turn yellow or leaden in their juice; with continuous eating and use, they increase bile and induce "the royal disease" <note>jaundice</note> and paleness. Yet these same plants—orache, cumin, and the like—by their own nature expel yellow bile and cure jaundice.

The dark colors of plants increase "choler" <note>black bile</note> to such an extent that men appear demonic—such as **cabbage** <note>original: "brassica"</note>, **thyme**, **poppy**, and **henbane** <note>original: "hyoscyamus"</note>—and they induce diseases born of black bile. However, the juices of these same herbs, such as cabbage, **dodder of thyme** <note>original: "epithymus"</note>, **black hellebore**, and **mandrake**, work to expel those humors. White-flowered plants, such as **basil** <note>original: "ocymum"</note>, **white hellebore**, **elder**, and **flax-leaved daphne** <note>original: "daphnoides"</note>, induce and draw out white phlegm. Those that drip with blood-red juice purge the blood, such as the **rose**, **centaury**, and **rhubarb**. The **mulberry**, **pomegranate**, **rock-rose** <note>original: "cisthus"</note>, and **knotgrass** <note>original: "polygonon"</note> suppress the menses and are used for wounds. 

Thus, plants of mixed color remove mixed humors; for example, **feverfew** <note>original: "parthenium"</note>, with its yellow flower surrounded by white, draws out both phlegm and bile. **Red cassia**, with its blackish pulp, purges the blood of scorched bile, or yellow bile that has degenerated into black. **Lettuce**, **sow-thistle**, and **spurge** <note>original: "tithymalus"</note> are "milky"; they provoke the flow of milk and increase the seed of generation. Hairy plants, such as **maidenhair fern** <note>original: "adiantum"</note>, **wall-rue**, and the **maidenhair** of Apuleius, are effective against mange <note>original: "alopecia," or hair loss</note>. Fleshy, woody, and fibrous plants, such as **bulbs**, **southernwood**, and **poterium**, increase and heal the flesh, bones, and nerves.

Those plants that resemble external limbs, such as **orchids** <note>original: "orchides"</note> which display the appearance of testicles, are incentives for love. **Hermodactyls** <note>literally "fingers of Hermes," likely meadow saffron</note>, which are finger-shaped, heal the fingers. Those that resemble internal organs are effective for the heart, such as the **citron**, **mountain nard**, and **wolfsbane** <note>original: "antitora"</note>, and they restore failing senses. For the spleen, there is **spleenwort** <note>original: "asplenium"</note>, since it consumes it; for ulcers of the lung, **lungwort**; for the windpipe, **cassia**; for a woman’s uterus, **birthwort** <note>original: "aristolochia"</note>; for the bladder, **alkekengi** <note>winter cherry</note> and others which are contained in the third book.

### THAT PLANTS WHICH REPRESENT THE SIMILARITY OF ANIMAL PARTS POSSESS THE SAME POWERS.

->Chapter XIII.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' with floral and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>

There are also plants that represent the form of animal members rather than human ones, so that they may be understood to possess the virtues of those animals. Here it is fitting to bestow more accurate care, for from this more hidden storehouse of nature, the properties and riches of plants are brought forth. We said in our previous work on **Physiognomy** <note>The study of judging character from physical features</note> that just as man alone possessed the habits of all animals—brave as a lion, changeable as a fox, lustful as a deer, or quarrelsome as a dog—so too does he suffer the diseases of all living creatures. For he suffers from quartan fever like a lion, from hair loss <note>term: "alopecia" (from the Greek 'alopex' for fox)</note> like a fox, from lust like a deer, and from madness like a dog. For this reason, craftsman Nature displayed the shapes of animal members in herbs, so that man—the most miserable of all creatures—might learn how to bring help to his own illnesses.

In this work on **Phytognomonics** <note>The study of plant signatures</note>, we shall follow the pure and true dogma that we used in our works on Physiognomy. We have said that specific signs claim the primary role in investigation; these specific signs are drawn from animals. These signs correspond directly to passions <note>afflictions or conditions</note> and are mutually interchangeable: he to whom the sign applies also experiences the effect, and he who has the affliction likewise possesses the sign. Those who lack the signs lack the effects. We have provided an example: to investigate the proper sign of courage, we considered the genus of animals in which that passion exists universally, such as the genus of Lions, and then other genera of animals which might suffer that same passion not universally, but specifically...

# BOOK ONE

...they experience, such as the horse, the bull, the boar, and the bear. Next, a sign must be considered that is never absent from the lion kind, and is found in others specifically; those that are strong possess it, while the weak lack it. That sign consists of having **large extremities** <note>original: "extrema magna," referring to large paws, hands, or feet</note>, which is inherent to the entire genus of lions; and the lion, the bull, and the strong bear also have large extremities, while those who lack this sign are flabby. This shall be the true sign of strength, especially since strength is exercised through those very limbs. From these observations we argue: *Every creature possessing large extremities shall be strong.* 

Returning to our rule <note>the "canon" or system of Phytognomonics</note>, one must track down the plant that offers protection against the poisonous bites of serpents. First, one must consider within the family of plants which one possesses the primary gift of healing the ailments caused by serpents; and since no worthier example comes to mind at present, let it be the **species of brambles** <note>original: "ruborum species," such as blackberries or raspberries</note>. Soon, other kinds must be tracked which are protected by that virtue not universally, but particularly, such as the **pear** and the **olive**. Next, the "mark" must be observed in the bramble which the entire genus possesses and which is present in others that have that same virtue: that mark shall be the possession of **hooked and curved thorns**, which mirror the teeth of vipers and other serpents with which they inflict venom by biting. 

The bramble is exceedingly thorny; the pear and the olive lack thorns, yet they work diligently against venom; however, the wild olive and the wild pear are more thorny and more powerful in their action. Indeed, many thorny herbs work against poisons, such as the **puncture vine** <note>original: "tribulus"</note>, **Christ’s thorn** <note>original: "paliurus"</note>, **buckthorn** <note>original: "rhamnus"</note>, **white-thorn**, **white chamomile**, **rough bindweed** <note>original: "smilax aspera"</note>, **sea holly** <note>original: "eringium"</note>, and **blessed thistle** <note>original: "carduus benedicta"</note>, which are effective not only against the bites of serpents, but also of rabid dogs, scorpions, spiders, and others. 

Yet, lest we be deceived in the selection of signs, if a double disposition and a twin sign should exist in one genus of animals, let us teach which indication fits which disposition. We previously brought forward the example of the lion, who is endowed with a double disposition—namely, strength and liberality—and displayed a double sign: large extremities and a broad forehead. Will the raised forehead be a specific mark of magnificence or of strength? We advised there that this rule must be used: it is necessary to consider animals like the bull, the horse, and the bear, and other robust creatures. If we know they have large extremities but are not munificent <note>generous or noble</note> nor have a raised forehead, then the raised forehead is understood to be a primary argument for **liberality** rather than strength. Other animals must also be looked at which are munificent and walk with a raised forehead. 

We shall use this same method in our **Phytognomonics** <note>term: the art of knowing a plant's nature from its appearance</note>. We know that the **deer** <note>original: "ceruum"</note> heals fevers and venom. Lest the minds of those investigating be distorted or a wavering soul be delayed, should **Hart’s-tongue fern** <note>original: "phyllitis," which translates to "leafy" but is historically "deer's tongue"</note>—which represents the image of a deer’s tongue—be used against the sharp bites of venomous creatures, or against the cycles of fevers? We shall contemplate other parts of the deer, and we will see among other parts the **antlers**, which are much branched and seen with a remarkable rarity. We shall consider whether there is another herb that imitates the antlers of deer and heals those whom a serpent has bitten or whom fevers have invaded, especially since the horns of the deer are considered a remedy against venoms. 

Into our hands comes **cumin**, which has leaves that are dissected, branched, hair-like, and sharp, rising in an alternating position in an orderly series and branched at the tips; it possesses gifts against venoms that are not to be despised. From this, we conclude that cumin prevails as an antidote to venom, while the Hart’s-tongue fern prevails against the rounds of fevers. We see that not only cumin, but all **fennel-like plants** <note>original: "ferulacea"</note> imitate the horns of deer by the same habit of their leaves, such as **fennel**, **giant fennel** <note>original: "ferula"</note>, **hog's fennel** <note>original: "peucedanum"</note>, **galbanum**, and **euphorbia**; nor does **wild nigella** <note>original: "melanthium syluestre"</note> shrink from this form, performing the same uses.

Therefore, from these examples: because they imitate **scorpions** with their roots, the **scorpion-killer** <note>original: "thelyphonon"</note>, **dog-killer** <note>original: "cynoctonon"</note>, and species of **aconite** heal their bites. The **oak**, **snakeweed** <note>original: "bistorta"</note>, and common **viper's grass** <note>original: "scorzonera"</note> imitate **serpents** with their roots and bring aid against their venoms. The flowers of **orchids** <note>original: "cynorchidum"</note> and **legumes** represent **flies and butterflies** and are effective for fertility. Thus, **polypody fern** is for the **polyp** <note>referring to both the sea creature and nasal growths</note>, and **fleawort** <note>original: "psyllion"</note> is for **fleas**. The spotted skins of serpents are shown by **cuckoo-pint** <note>original: "aron"</note>, **dragon arum** <note>original: "dracunculus"</note>, **arisaron**, and **bloody garlic**. The **scales** of the **pine**, the **pitch-pine**, and **sea holly** <note>original: "eringia"</note> excel against the venom of scaled creatures. From the limbs of wild beasts: **viper’s bugloss** <note>original: "echion"</note> demonstrates the head of vipers; **snapdragon** <note>original: "antirhinon"</note> that of a calf; **cynocephalon** that of a dog. **Goat's-horn** <note>original: "tragoceros"</note> shows the horns of goats; **ox-horn** <note>original: "buceros"</note> those of an ox; and **yellow rattle** <note>original: "alectorolophos"</note> the combs of a cock. **Forget-me-not** <note>original: "myosota"</note> represents the ears of mice; **dittany** <note>original: "dictamnos"</note> those of hares. **Hog's-eye** <note>original: "hyophtalmos"</note> represents the eyes of swine, and **dog's-eye** <note>original: "cynopsis"</note> those of dogs. The mouth of wolves is shown by the **iris**, and the mouth of the dragon by the **dragon arum**. The tongue of the ox is shown by **oxtongue** <note>original: "buglossum"</note>...

# PLANTS REVEAL THE DISEASES THEY CURE BY THE SIMILARITY OF THEIR PARTS TO HUMANS
## *Chapter XIV*

<image-desc>Decorative initial R within a square border featuring foliage and a bird.</image-desc>
PLANTS also correspond by the similarities of their parts to human diseases—so much so, in fact, that it can be reasonably conjectured that they are able to assist in that disease. This occurs in two ways: either by simply figuring the disease itself, or by the fact that the plant can assist an afflicted human through the same types of "sicknesses" by which the plants themselves are troubled. To carry this out, the parts of plants must be examined with diligent inspection: the root, the trunk, the leaf, the flower, the fruit, and the seed, to see if they reveal diseases by some parity. Examples follow. Plants that release a wine-like juice when pressed, and are of a faded color, strike the head with drunkenness—such as the mandrake (*onothera*), sowbread (*cyclaminus*), and mandragora. Conversely, those that pour out a cheerful, purple juice turn away drunkenness, such as the rose, iris, myrtle, and violet. Spotted plants abolish spots of the face—such as the cuckoopint (*arum*), buttercup (*ranunculus*), and water-pepper (*persicaria*), which directly resemble spots. Scaly plants cure scales <note>referring to skin conditions like psoriasis or scabs</note>, such as scabious, devil's-bit, and the chameleon thistle. All perforated plants are wound-healers, such as St. John's Wort (*hypericon*) and the species of gentian called "cruciata" <note>crosswort gentian</note>. Sticky plants have extraordinary power for wound ointments, such as greater comfrey (*consolida maior*), mistletoe, and holly. Square and three-sided stems remove quartan and tertian fevers <note>malarial fevers that recur every three or four days</note>. Animals that wander by night are effective for dull eyesight and night-blindness, such as the goat, the dog, and the owl. Those whose eyes regrow after being pierced—such as the swallow, the wood-pigeon, and the lizard—provide, in our opinion, no better remedy for the wounds and scars of the eyes. Seeds of stony hardness, such as the stone-seed (*lithospermon*) and Job's tears, are never praised enough for driving out kidney stones. Figwort (*scrophularia*), which teems with tubercles and nipple-like heads, and the lesser arum, soothe the tonsils and hemorrhoids. Even the defects of trees benefit the diseases of men. Long-lived animals and plants equally bestow life, such as the olive, the palm, the pine, the raven, the crow, and the serpent. Conversely, those born from rot are harmful to life. Fat things are effective for fattening: the olive, the pine, the nut, the sow, the kid, and the lizard. For inducing thinness, all things that are themselves thin are used: the ash tree, gum ammoniac (*cancamum*), the hare, and the wolf-fish. For gangrene, the chickpea is used; for worms, the laurel, lupine, and chickpea. Those things which grow upon branches and foliage against the order of nature—such as the agaric fungus—heal the overgrowing parts of human limbs. Those that sustain cracks in their trunks—the olive, the elm, and resin-bearing trees—are found by the most certain experience to be most useful for scars and wounds. Those that shed their bark—the vine and resin-bearing trees—are for flaying the skin and for defects of scales. Gummy plants exude an excellent medicine for "gums" <note>likely referring to gum-like swellings or sores</note>: the plum and the peach. Exuding and weeping plants are effective for tears and sweats: frankincense, myrrh, and greater things which we promise to complete in the fifth book.

# THAT WE CAN OBTAIN THE POWERS OF PLANTS FROM THE SIMILARITY OF THEIR ACTIONS
## *Chapter XV*

<image-desc>Decorative initial N within a square border featuring a landscape with a tower in the background.</image-desc>
NOT only do they emulate diseases by their appearance, but they also reflect the actions of humans and other animals, from which diligent hunters of hidden things can conjecture much. We call the "actions" of plants their manner of being born, flowering, conceiving, and proliferating (lest I leave this as a matter of controversy for the philosophers), as well as considering the timing and number...

Regarding movement and similar signs, which are more numerous than can be taught or written, we shall explain some, so that by these examples a person of refined intellect might be able to investigate very many more: for if we dared to add everything, the work would grow to an immense size. Prolific plants, which send out a numerous offspring near the shoots of their roots, serve us in the matter of progeny <note>procreation or children</note>, such as the dwarf palm <note>original: "chamaeriphes"</note>, asparagus, knotgrass <note>original: "crataeogonum," literally "strong-birth"</note>, and bulbs. Conversely, roots that are devoid of "grandchildren" <note>offshoots</note>, such as the fir, pine, and cedar, destroy the fetus even in the mother's womb. Herbs deprived of stem, flower, and fruit warn man that they are most dire regarding infertility <note>original: "atocia," a Greek term for the inability to conceive</note>, such as the poplar, the willow, the savin, and the mule-fern <note>original: "hemionitis"</note>. Many-fruiting plants, like the oak, contribute to the fertility of women. Trees that excel in helping other sterile trees to conceive are effective for making the sterile fertile, such as the fig and the palm. Whether very beautiful plants are effective for procreating beautiful children, I do not know so much as I easily believe, such as the palm, the crocus, and the golden-sunflower <note>original: "eliochrysos"</note>. Herbs that bore through and break rocks with their roots possess remarkable power for breaking stones <note>kidney stones or "calculi"</note>, so that you will hardly find another that performs this better: thus, all related plants have a similar virtue. It is important to observe the time when plants show their flower or fruit, for they are suitable for diseases that grow strong at that same time, by a dutiful gift of nature, which demonstrates the remedy and forewarns of the time to be feared; for example, dragonwort <note>original: "dracunculus"</note> and the ash tree <note>original: "fraxinus"</note> are helpful when applied to the bites of serpents. Indeed, serpents flee the ash tree from so far away that they will not touch even its morning or evening shadows; and at the first spring-awakening of serpents, the dragonwort thrusts itself from the earth and is hidden back in the earth along with them, nor does the serpent appear at all when that plant is hidden. The golden thistle <note>original: "scolymus"</note> flowers at the time when women are most greedy for lust and men are most sluggish for intercourse. One must observe the places in which certain diseases flourish, for there the remedies are born together with them. Africa, most fertile in serpents, brings forth spices. In Argos, where there is an abundance of scorpions, the locust is born there to rise up against the scorpions. In the West Indies, where the "French disease" <note>syphilis; original: "gallica lues"</note> occurs, the guaiac wood also grows there. Every animal brings a remedy for its own poison. Skinks <note>original: "stelliones," a type of spotted lizard</note>, when devoured by those they have bitten, heal them. The fat of the crocodile, dripped into an ulcer, heals its own poison. The scorpion, the sea-dragon, and the stingray, when cut open and placed upon the wounds, are helpful. From the beauty or deformity of plants, we conjecture whether they are healthful or noxious: just as the rose, the lily, and the iris provide us with proof that they possess very many virtues, so, on the contrary, hemlock and aconite are the most certain causes of destruction. Scents also betray the virtues of others; the scented geranium, the white rose, and others emulate the scent of the musk animal and assist the heart and brain just as the animal itself does. The little-goat herb <note>original: "hirculus"</note>, the goat-saxifrage, and others recall the odor of a goat and provoke lust, just like the goat. More abundant examples will be given in the sixth book.

## THE CHARACTERISTICS OF PLANTS AND ANIMALS
### How they may be conjectured. Chapter XVI.

<image-desc>A small square woodcut illustration depicting a scholar or physician in period clothing, seated at a desk or table and engaged in study or writing.</image-desc>

Plants represent the behaviors of animals just as they do their actions, but they are masters of virtues as much as they are of behaviors. Yet it is necessary first that the powers of animals be sought out: we seek out these powers from their behaviors, lest we be deceived in our search, since it is more difficult to investigate the behaviors of plants and animals than to recognize them by the similarity of their parts. A method will be handed down by us by which, I hope, the powers of animals can be easily investigated; indeed, we can weigh on a scale whether the things found and handed down by the ancients are true or false, and infinite other things can be discovered. And this is by no other reasoning than by their behaviors; and behaviors are known from apparent things, not from the anatomy of internal and external parts. For the Supreme Craftsman <note>God</note> made the parts of the animals' bodies accommodated to fulfilling their functions, so that they could easily carry out their behaviors. We call "behaviors" things such as being clever or dull, watchful or sleepy, talkative or silent, and similar things. The elephant, the deer, the monkey, and the parrot excel in the ease of learning; they contribute to memory, put forgetfulness to flight, and favor the intellect; conversely, mice, rams, and donkeys lead toward ignorance,

... and they incline toward a lack of teachability. Regarding wakefulness: just as crabs, kingfishers, and nightingales possess a natural vigilance, so too are the hare, the pig, the hedgehog, and the bear—being drowsy creatures—offered for the purpose of inducing sleep. Those things which dream cause us to have dreams <note>original: "insomnia," which in this context refers to dream-filled sleep or the quality of dreams rather than the modern definition of being unable to sleep</note>, such as the hare, the monkey, and rams, and sometimes these dreams are true. Melodious and noisy animals lead to talkativeness, such as the goose, the rooster, and the dog. And those that are vocal at night are effective so that things done in dreams may be recounted, such as the frog, the goose, the nightingale, and the owl. Conversely, the wolf, the bramble-toad, and the voiceless tortoise induce silence. The strongest animals, like the lion, the dragon <note>original: "draco," which in Renaissance natural history often referred to a large serpent or a python-like creature</note>, and the rooster, provide fortitude. Wrathful ones, like the dog and the bear, kindle anger. 

Furthermore, there are dissimilarities and certain mutual hatreds of natures between deaf things, even those lacking sensation, such as stones, herbs, and animals; they burn with such blind discords that they hinder each other's powers and are restrained. On the other hand, there are also equal similarities of substances, so that—as if having entered into a certain treaty—they do not resist one another, but willingly reach out to enjoy a friendly companionship. These the Greeks call "antipathy" and "sympathy," and we call them the "manners" of plants and animals, from which miraculous powers are tracked down. The elephant shudders at the horned viper <note>original: "cerastem"</note>; for this reason, serpents are used to heal elephantiasis <note>a term used then for various skin diseases that made the skin thick and rough like an elephant's</note>. Horses hold wolves in hatred; wolves provide a cure for the "short-winded" <note>original: "anhelosis," a respiratory disease in horses</note> which afflicts horses. The serpent and the hedgehog are mutual enemies; the flesh of the hedgehog provides relief for those bitten by serpents, and the serpent spoils a birth by its mere presence, forcing immediate labor, whereas the hedgehog lingers in the labor of enduring. Francolins <note>original: "attagenae," a type of game bird</note> love the deer, whose brain stirs up lust, a condition to which deer are prone. The fox lives in a friendly manner with the serpent; the flesh of both is healthful for elephantiasis. The vine dreads the cabbage; for this reason, cabbage drives away the drunkenness of wine, even when taken as a drink. There are also other wonders of nature which will be described in the seventh book, so that we do not delay the reader any longer.

### THAT MALE AND FEMALE POWERS ARE CONJECTURED FROM MALE AND FEMALE PLANTS. Cap. XVII.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap "R" inside a square woodcut frame decorated with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

It remains for us to take signs of powers from the similarity of male and female parts. For the most diligent searchers of nature have distinguished both sexes in almost all trees and herbs; they have taught us many things worthy of observation and knowledge, discovered by testing this distinction of sex in plants. For just as in human Physiognomy <term>Physiognomy: the practice of judging character or health from outward physical appearance</term> the greatest knowledge of internal character depended on the distinction of the parts of the sexes, so too in this "Phytognomonics" <note>the study of plant signatures</note>, the sex of plants is marked off—sometimes clearly, sometimes more obscurely—by the great kindness of Nature. 

For the female is by nature weak or less robust; therefore, "female" herbs are less potent and are used in medicines for women. The male is more robust; for this reason, the "male" plant, which has much more vigorous powers, is suitable for men. For the protection of the wombs, female plants provide many benefits, while male plants are harmful to them. Hippocrates <note>the famous Greek "Father of Medicine"</note> praises the "female" Mercury-herb <note>original: "mercurialem foeminam," likely Dog's Mercury</note>, which lacks "testicles" <note>rounded seed pods</note>, with wonderful praise for the use of women. In this manner, no physician knew how to expel the menses or promote fertility better. 

But because the great philosopher and student of Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher known as the father of botany</note>, and their followers, have spoken too carelessly regarding the distinction of sex, we shall distinguish them in this way based on the Physiognomy of animals. The male is endowed with a tall body, robust, bony, sinewy, with strong ribs, articulated arms and hands, with harder and drier flesh that is hairy, rough skin, a darker color, and is strong and upright in action. The female is the opposite: with a small body, fleshy, fat, and smooth, in which neither nerves, bones, nor veins appear, of a white color, fertile, with weaker strength, and is deceitful and fraudulent. 

So in trees, the male grows as a bush with a taller body, dry, with dense, strong, woody, sinewy, and knotty branches that are stubborn against breaking; it is covered with more colorful wood and a rougher bark, with little fruit (or often sterile), of a harsh taste, scented, slow-growing, and finally approaching a more "wild" habit, with strong powers and firm in action. On the contrary, the female tree is content with being shorter, wider, and fatter, with loose, weak, somewhat soft wood, without knots or "nerves" <note>fibers</note>, fragile, pale, with a smooth and "cheerful" bark, and large, pulpy fruit...

For when the texture of the body is looser and moister (as if it were an imperfect kind), it grows and ages easily: for imperfect things are less laborious, complete their work more quickly, and take on growth. In the male, the cause of sterility is density, which does not transmit [nutrients], and by too much strength, with which it draws nourishment, it looks out for itself and lives for itself alone, converting all juice to its own advantage, since nature cannot satisfy both parts—both growth and generation—for generation requires a surplus portion of nourishment. The female, however, does not consume the nourishment for herself, but imparts it to the fruits, because she is weak, according to **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle; he is often called the "Father of Botany" for his systematic study of plants.</note>. The male conceives in another; the woman in herself; the plant conceives and generates in itself, which is the female. In animals, very many conceive without a male; it is reported of the <term>sea bass</term> <note>original: "channe." Ancient naturalists believed the serranus or sea bass was hermaphroditic or could reproduce without a mate.</note>, and that in hares there is both the power of the male and the female, and of others, as we shall say. From these things, a tree that is harder, more rigid, leaner, and hairier as it begins to grow is said to "become male," being born especially in sandy, rocky places, ruins, and sunny spots. Likewise, that which becomes softer, wider, fattier, and smoother is said to "become female," in rich, manured, and moist lands, or shady places, as Greek and Latin writers frequently use regarding turnips, radishes, and others: and we have already read of many females changed into males. But let us see if the elders subscribe to these views. **Theophrastus** says the male <term>linden</term> <note>original: "tilea." The linden or lime tree.</note> differs from the female in every way. For the wood of the male is hard, knotty, redder, and more fragrant, the bark is also thicker and inflexible when stripped, and it bears neither seed nor flower. The female is a thicker tree with white, very compliant wood, from which cradles and chests are made, and it brings forth flower and seed. Regarding the **oak**, differences are certainly understood; however, the common distinction by which the female and male are distinguished is that one is sterile and the other fruitful; where both are fruitful, the female provides the better fruit. It is peculiar to the **beech** and the <term>sea-oak</term> <note>original: "haliphloeos," likely referring to the cork oak or a similar species with thick bark.</note> that in the male kind, the acorns become stony at the back part. The female **oak** has a body that is neither erect nor tall, but its foliage grows in a circle and is twisted into wings, hollow with a frequent curve of branches, and its acorn is the sweetest. The <term>Turkey oak</term> <note>original: "cerrus."</note> is among the kind of strong oaks; the male has a tall body and robust wood, its acorn is very bitter, and it never grows in cultivated places. Among **reeds**, the "armory" reed <note>original: "armamentaria." Reeds used for making shafts or tools.</note> differs from others in the excellence of its nourishment, for it is seen to be fatter, fleshier, and overall more wanton in its female appearance, and it has a larger and whiter leaf with less down; and there are those which are entirely smooth, which they call "eunuchs" <note>original: "spadonias." Barren or seedless varieties.</note>. The Indians report the body of the male to be denser, and the female more spacious. The male **dogwood** has a sinewy and thin bark, a trunk no less thick, but its wood is without a heart and entirely solid, so that it matches horns in its density; the female has a spongy trunk, grows in shoots like a shrub, is weak, gaping, soft, full of pith, tubular, and useless. On Mount Ida, the male is sterile and the female fruitful. **Pliny** confirms that sex is manifest in none more than in **palms**, and that females are not produced without males, and around each male, several females nod toward him with more enticing foliage, while he stands bristling with erect leaves; he "marries" the others by his breath, his very sight, and even his dust <note>This is an early, poetic description of wind-pollination (anemophily), where "dust" refers to pollen.</note>. If this tree is cut down, the females afterward become sterile widows, so that their "intercourse" was devised by man: by scattering the flower and down from the males, and sometimes only the dust, upon the females. While the male is flowering, men cut off the <term>spathe</term> <note>The woody sheath that protects the palm flowers.</note> and shake it over the fruit of the female; by that sprinkling, she does not lose her fruit, whence it happens that the male is able to be of two-fold help to the female: for they call the female "fruitful" because it is, as it were, a marriage. It must be said no differently of the **fig** and the **wild fig**. For the wild fig is the male and wild kind, a fig never ripening, but what it does not have itself, it grants to the females; for when placed around the fruits of the female, it causes her fruits to ripen and not fall: therefore, they are permitted in dry plains according to the direction of the wind, so that the breeze may be carried into the figs, or its fruits, brought from elsewhere and tied together, are cast upon the fig tree. The wild fig has less milk, is more robust, denser, less fruitful in its own fruit, and more long-lasting in appearance, and much stronger than the [domestic] fig, for any fierce bulls [tied] to their branches...

# THAT PLANTS BEAR LIKENESSES TO THE STARS,
### metals, and gems through their motion, color, and other shapes,
### and share in their same powers. Chapter XVIII.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'R' at the start of the paragraph, set within a square frame featuring elaborate floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>

**P**lants also reflect the likenesses of the stars in their form, color, and other qualities; and if they do not fulfill them perfectly, they at least shadow them forth. For if they were made otherwise, they would also demonstrate the faces and powers of those things they imitate in a different way. From these signs, the diligent researcher—by contemplating things that have hitherto lain hidden by uncertain reasoning and the concealed majesty of nature—will confess that he sees no vain spectacle. **Solar herbs** are so called either by form, because their flowers have a "bossed" little ball in the center like a prominent shield-hub <note>original: "umbonem." Porta is describing the disk florets of composite flowers.</note>, with petals arranged in a series surrounding the edge so that they appear radiated, creating the image of eyes or the face of the sun, as in the **chrysanthemum** and **chamomile** <note>original: "anthemidi"</note>. Or by color, because they shimmer with a yellow color like the sun. Or because they follow the course of the sun, and are called **"sun-followers"** <note>original: "solsequiæ"</note>, such as the **castor oil plant** <note>original: "ricinus"</note>, the **heliotrope**, the **sun-spurge** <note>original: "helio-scopius"</note>, and **ferides**. Or those which contract at sunset and are hidden in the waters, and emerge in the morning as if heralds of the sun's course, opening their mouths at the sunrise, like the **Egyptian lotus**. Or those that grow under the sun's path where it is most vigorous and hot, as in Africa; such as the **aromatic spices**. Because the sun is the prince of the stars, all these plants serve the heart (the prince of the internal organs) with great benefit, and are of a hot and dry temperament. **Lunar herbs** are those that are either white-flowered, like **garlic**, **marjoram**, **dropwort** <note>original: "œnanthes"</note>, and **dittany**; or those which have round leaves representing the full orb of the moist Moon; or those with leaves shaped like a crescent or horns, like the **lesser moonwort** <note>original: "lunaria minor"</note>. Or those in which black grime or white spots appear on the flower, leaf, and stalk, so that they seem to imitate the marks that mar the face of the Moon, such as the **cyclamen**. Or those that indicate the Moon's changes by growing and shrinking—even in reverse, like the **onion**, which withers as the Moon waxes and grows as it wanes; for this reason, the Egyptian inhabitants of **Pelusium** decreed that the onion must not be eaten. Or because they bring forth flowers every day as the moon grows, but drop them as it wanes, and return to the same cycles. Or because their pods shine with a silvery color and appear flaming at night by the reflection of the lunar light, so that they reflect the Moon's light, as in the...

But let us move away from the study of plants. Metals and stones follow the same lot: indeed **gold**, which imitates the light of the sun, greatly aids the heart; likewise **silver** aids the brain. They are also effective for the other things we have mentioned, all of which will be described more fully in the book I am privately preparing on the virtues of metals. The **hyacinth** <note>The gemstone, not the flower</note> aids the heart because of its color, which reflects the sun; thus **sapphire** helps with melancholy, and **amethyst** wards off drunkenness because it rivals the color of wine. The **ophites stone** <note>original: "ophites lapis"; Serpentine, named for its snake-like patterns</note> is effective against the bite of serpents, because:

> It is colored with more markings on its variegated belly
> Than the small spots that stain the Theban ophites.
<note>A quote from the Roman poet Lucan's Pharsalia, describing a type of marble or stone with snake-like patterns.</note>

A small fragment of the **Dionysius stone**, broken off and dissolved in water, smells like wine, and for that reason is effective against drunkenness. The **aetites stone** <note>original: "Aetites lapis"; the "Eagle Stone," which contains a loose inner stone that rattles</note>—as if it were pregnant—when shaken, with another [stone] sounding in its womb, preserves the fetus in pregnant women when the womb is not tenacious enough, if it is bound to the left arm. But for those about to give birth, let it be removed from the arm and bound to the thighs, so that she may give birth without pain. Other things will be described in the final book; for I could have piled up six hundred examples here if it were permitted.

### THAT THE MIXED APPEARANCES OF PLANTS CLAIM MIXED AND
### CONTRARY POWERS FOR THEMSELVES. Chapter XXIIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting a seated figure in classical robes, likely a scholar or philosopher, in an outdoor setting with a tree and distant landscape.</image-desc>
We have spoken of simple forms; now we speak of **mixed plant forms**. For just as we remembered long ago that the twofold characters of men can be recognized from human signs—those of a reprobate nature, whom we called wicked and traitors, so that you might never know what they want or do not want, nor are they consistent with themselves; rather, they are of contrary characters: pious and cruel, greedy and prodigal, timid and murderous. We shall not deny that these same characters exist in plants; and not only similar mixed qualities, but contrary faculties, such as to cool and warm, to moisten and dry, to kill and heal, to destroy and to help—which doctors call **mixed and adversarial faculties**.

To understand this, know that something can be called "mixed" or composed of two natures, like **amphibious animals**, or "double" ones like the **beaver** <note>original: "castor"</note>, which is both a quadruped and a fish, living on land and in water, retaining the qualities of both. In plants, you have an example in the **scorodoprasum** <note>The "garlic-leek"</note>, or **alliporrum**, a plant mixed from garlic and leek, whose nature is promiscuous, with the properties of both parents tempered within it. Or we call something "mixed" that is uniform and pure in itself, but is forged from various colors, scents (not to mention flavors), and forms.

In identifying these plants, we are aided by those same clues and conjectures that helped in recognizing men of a dual nature—namely, stones <note>Refers here to the "iris" or spots</note> in the eyes of various colors, and especially those that are uncommon, such as saffron mixed with fiery tones, or green ones mixed with grey, or multiple circles of blue and blood-red surrounding the pupil, or unequal circles of the pupils, or dirty circles with fiery and turbid spots. The **Phytognomon** <note>Porta's term for the practitioner who reads the "signatures" or signs of nature</note> will recognize almost the same signs in the flowers of plants, which represent their **eyes**. For where he notices a mixture of colors in them, interspersed with little dots and streaks—which they call "mournful letters" <note>original: "lugubres literas"; a reference to the markings on flowers like the Hyacinth, which legend says spell "AI AI" (alas!)</note>—or multicolored leaves, roots, and stalks, or those described with reddish, dark, saffron, or blackish notes, or where they perceive varied scents, or something unusual that is not seen in others, as if it were beyond the norm of nature, he can...

# PHYTOGNOMONICA

...it immediately shows that it possesses within itself not only mixed but even opposing powers. We will provide an example. The **Lily** <note>original: "Lilium"</note> of immaculate whiteness has saffron-colored filaments within; the flower is of the sweetest scent, but the leaves exhale something foul and poisonous, demonstrating mixed qualities. In **Great Centaury** <note>original: "Magno centaurio"; *Centauria centaurium*, a plant traditionally used for healing</note>, the flower is purple leaning toward blue, and the juice of the root is yellow-reddish. This presents contrary qualities and effects: by its yellow color and heat, it provokes menstruation and expels the fetus from the womb; yet, by its ability to glue wounds together, it shows it shares in **terrestrial coldness** <note>In Galenic medicine, "cold" and "dry" (earthy) qualities were thought to contract tissues and stop bleeding</note>, which comes from the reddish sap and the bluish flower.

### ON THE METHOD OF JUDGING, AND WHICH SIGNS ARE TO BE PREFERRED. Chapter XX.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting a crane or stork standing in a marshy landscape with hills and a small building in the background.</image-desc>

Having now discussed many signs with a very accurate review, from which no small benefits of plants might come to light, it is now worthwhile to indicate which signs should claim the primary role in judging, and which should be considered secondary. We said in our previous work, *Physiognomony* <note>The author, Giambattista della Porta, previously wrote a famous work on reading human character from facial features</note>, that those marks assume dominance over others which proceed from a specific property. These "proper" signs were those that appropriately related to the parts of animals through comparison; for instance, having large extremities indicated great strength because they were characteristic of the **lion**. Similarly, among us, we recognized that the **cock’s comb** <note>original: "alectorolophon"; likely *Rhinanthus*, named for its resemblance to a rooster's crest</note>, by putting forth leaves similar to a rooster’s crest, was effective for **sexual allurements** <note>original: "venerea illicia"</note>.

Second in line follow those signs which mimic human body parts. Examples include **maidenhair fern** <note>original: "adiantum"</note> and **spleenwort** <note>original: "trichomanes"</note>, which, with their somewhat stiff curls and slender fibers, expressed the appearance of hair and made hair thick, curly, and more beautiful. Furthermore, there are those that signified diseases by their own images—such as plants with stone-like seeds that were effective for breaking up **kidney stones** <note>original: "calculos"</note>. These were called "proper indices" because they followed the **substantial form** <note>The inner essence of a thing that determines its outward appearance</note>. 

There are also other marks which are rather secondary and indicate manifest qualities: form, color, odor, taste, smoothness, hairiness, and the like. These often changed due to a change in location, and frequently shifted into far different, and perhaps contrary, states. 

But someone might rightly ask, as was asked in human Physiognomy: which signs are firmer—those taken from the face, the chest, the back, or the feet? We said there that the primary signs are from the face, and especially from the eyes; next from the chest, then the back, and lastly the feet. Observing the same in this, our **Phytognomonica** <note>The study of plant signatures</note>: because the most worthy part is the **seed**, toward which nature especially aims—**Theophrastus** <note>Ancient Greek philosopher, the "Father of Botany"</note> calls the seed the most perfect gift of nature, and **Aristotle** said that plants were born for the sake of the seed, because they live only until the seed is produced and then wither after "giving birth"—therefore, firmer signs are to be sought from the seed. Because **Viper’s Bugloss** <note>original: "Echium"</note> reflects the head of a viper with such sharp marks that it differs not at all from it, it is effective in no common experiment; not only for those bitten by a serpent, but it prevents those who have drunk its decoction beforehand from being struck. Indeed, if placed upon a viper, it induces a stupor and kills it. 

Other signs are to be taken from the flowers. The flower corresponds to the **eye**. **Alexander of Aphrodisias** <note>original: "Aphrodiscus"; a Greek commentator on Aristotle</note> remarked that the eye is the most beautiful part in man, and the flower was most liberally given by nature to adorn and make the genus of plants beautiful. Eyes are composed of the thinner and more transparent parts of the body so that they may be clear; likewise, flowers are made from the thinner and purer juices, which is why they are mostly transparent. Almost every root is white, the foliage is green, and the trunk is covered in bark; only in the flowers is there a mixture and variety of colors. In them alone are the mixtures of internal juices and colors to be seen, and from these, hidden powers are inferred. 

And if in human Physiognomy we said the soul lives in the eyes (because from there the internal and deeper characters and thoughts of men are known), so in the flowers the nature of the plant sits and smiles. From there, as if with hidden words, it reports its powers and the treasures of hidden things to sick mortals. And if nature is admirable in the entire fabric of our body, she is surely more admirable in the eyes, for in a small space she composed humors, tunics, colors, and mixtures—as we have said: blue-gray, green,

# BOOK ONE

...green, goat-colored, tawny, and varied; so too in the formation of flowers a wonder can be seen: in a small space, Nature has constructed and composed leaves, tips, stamens, and such varied colors. For in these there is the thinner fire of the **carbuncle** <note>original: "carbunculi"; a deep red gemstone like a garnet or ruby</note>, the shining purple of the **amethyst**, the green sea of the **emerald**, the burning flame of **sulfur**, and all these things shining together in an incredible mixture. But who can speak of the marvelous property of Nature in flowers? Do they not especially revel in such great joy during the most happy time of spring's cheerfulness? 

Thus, the signs that are taken from the roots are the same as those taken from the heart. **Aristotle** calls these the causes of life, since they nourish the plant and make it live. **Democritus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher</note> said that twisted trees live longer for this reason: because they are supported by a more vigorous root. Those signs that relate to life, we said, were markings taken from the stomach, while the smallest signs are those from the leaves, much like those taken from the hair. 

We can also investigate with another method of inquiry. The ancient **Physiognomists** <term>Physiognomists: Scholars who practiced the art of judging a person's character or health from their physical features</term>, in searching out human character, said that traces were to be taken from those members in which a particular passion was exercised. For instance, because the heart is subject to anger, they took the signs of anger from the heart, and these were prior to those taken from the brain, the head, and other parts. Likewise, signs of strength were to be taken from the arms, shoulders, and feet, because they used those limbs in wrestling; it is no different in our **Phytognomonics** <note>The study of plant signatures</note>. 

If we must purge humors, the humors of plants are to be inspected, and those should be taken which are similar to our own. If we must choose any medicines for the eyes from plants, we shall collect them from the flowers rather than from other parts; those for the stomach from the roots; and finally, those for the "seed" <note>reproductive health</note> from their own seeds. 

Furthermore, let us not forget what was to be remembered in human Physiognomy: a single sign is not to be trusted, especially a common one, but many congruent signs around one thing must be observed, so that a judgment may be brought forth from many things agreeing as one. There is a similar difficulty in this method: if smoothness occurs in the leaves, one must not immediately conclude the plant is of a moist quality; rather, the birthplace, the site, and the sky must be inspected, and a judgment made after considering all these things. 

Finally, we thought it necessary to advise those who devote strenuous effort to this science that they must be most practiced in the discernment of plants. The external face must be known before the internal, hidden faculties; for that knowledge must come first. No one could ever guess the powers of those **simples** <term>Simples: Medicines made from a single constituent, usually a single herb</term> which they have never looked upon. But when one has taken the plant in hand, let them first consider it as a whole, then its parts as diligently as possible—namely the root, the trunk, the leaves, the fruit, and the seed. Then consider the birthplace, the site, the air, and where it is usually born; and the time when it buds from the earth, grows up, and bears fruit. Let them weigh most attentively the manner of budding, growing, and fruiting. Finally, when they have gathered many agreeing points into one to support the conjecture, then let them bring forth their judgment.

### EXAMPLES OF CONJECTURING THE VIRTUES
#### *of plants.*
#### *Chapter XXI.*

But let us practice in this investigation of virtues. Let us contemplate the **rose**, and hunt for its hidden gifts from an inspection of its external face; first let us track its manifest qualities, then its hidden properties. Because the outer edges of the flower's petals are red, the "claws" <note>the white base of the petal where it attaches to the stem</note> are white, and in the middle saffron-colored stamens are seen, we shall predict a quality that is not simple, but mixed. 

The redness warns us of a fiery subtlety, heat, and **stypticity** <note>original: "stipticitatis"; the quality of being astringent or able to stop bleeding</note>. The proof is that if the redness is extracted by some artifice, the scent, the stypticity, and the thinness of its action depart with it. The whiteness in the "claws" and in other species of rose argues for coldness and watery humidity. The saffron color indicates heat, while its dry, parched, rough, and sun-drenched birthplaces suggest dryness and astringency. 

But let us descend to the internal things. By its beauty and grace, it seems to breathe a certain celestial majesty; for this reason **Didymus** <note>Likely Didymus of Alexandria, an ancient scholar</note> said it was powerful in divine virtues. The primary colors in it are red in the leaves and saffron in the filaments; from this [signature of] dissolving, it draws out yellow bile and purges the blood of it, or conversely...

<meta>This page continues the specific application of the "doctrine of signatures" to the rose, demonstrating how its various colors and physical structures—such as its petal bases and thorns—indicate its medicinal uses. It then transitions into Chapter 23, which formally defines "Phytognomonics" as a scientific method.</meta>

According to **Simeon Sethi** <note>An 11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician</note>, the rose excels at treating fevers arising from bile. The saffron-yellow color of the stamens indicates that it is very well suited for treating jaundice <note>original: "icteritiae"</note> and for promoting the flow of urine, as is held by **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a Persian Christian physician</note>. Its blazing flame-red color helps with "sacred fire" <note>Erysipelas, a skin infection characterized by large red patches</note> and inflammations, especially of the stomach. The color is so blood-like that the Poets imagined white roses turned red from the wounded foot of **Venus**, or from the blood of **Cupid**; because of this, it suppresses blood, stops the spitting of blood, and is usually mixed into wound-healing antidotes, according to **Dioscorides**. Petals mixed with white and red colors inhibit female flows, both red and especially white, according to **Pliny**. Because it also emulates the lovely color of wine, a garland of roses removes the harmful vapors of wine <note>original: "temeti"</note> from the head. 

Among human limbs, it represents the eye, and the Poets call the rose flower the "eye of the earth." For this reason, **Zoroaster** says in the *Geoponica* <note>A 10th-century collection of agricultural lore</note> that whoever first sees the buds enclosed on the plant and rubs their eyes with three of them—while leaving the roses themselves on the plant—will not suffer eye pain for a whole year. Dew sitting on roses, collected with a clean feather and smeared around the eyelids, heals bleary eyes. The white parts at the base of the petals are called "nails" <note>original: "ungues"</note> because of their resemblance to human fingernails; for this reason, they excel against "nails" of the eyes. According to **Celsus**, these "nails" in the eyes are certain nervous, attached membrane excrescences growing from the larger corner of the eye, usually proceeding toward the iris so that they sometimes cover the pupil; the Greeks call them <term>πτερύγια</term> <note>original: "pterygia"; meaning "little wings," now known as a surfer's eye growth</note>. 

The "nails" of the rose are healthy for watery eyes, for the rose cleanses ulcers of the eyes, except at the beginning of the discharge, when it should be applied dry with bread, according to Pliny. However, the petals without these "nails" are useful for ophthalmia, specifically during the stage of inflammation, according to **Avicenna**. It is no less effective for "wings" of the fingers <note>hangnails</note>; Dioscorides says it is usually mixed into compositions called *antherae*, which were used by Celsus, **Galen**, and **Paul of Aegina** for hangnails. Being thorny and infested with very sharp points, the rose—when crushed—extracts thorns and splinters that are stuck in the flesh. The little pill-like bud <note>original: "alabastri pilula"</note> resembles warts, which it removes according to Avicenna. The saffron hairs in the center <note>the stamens</note> resemble a head of hair; for this reason, the wild variety wonderfully restores hair loss. It is useful for many other things. Powders are made from it to restrain sweat, so that after baths the bodies dry off and are then washed with cold water, according to Pliny. Against the stench of sweat, it should hang from the neck in place of a garland, by Avicenna’s advice. Because of its beauty, it is dedicated to Venus. Distilled water from the bud brings luster and redness to a woman's face, and its petals are used to beautify the eyelids and other things which would be long to recount.

->WHAT PHYTOGNOMONICS IS. Cap. XXIII.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial E featuring a landscape scene with buildings and foliage.</image-desc>

Phytognomonics is a method of investigating the powers of plants from their parts and their life, which are found in fixed and mobile signs. But let us give the reasoning for this definition. We called it a "firm method of investigation" because the method of investigating plant powers is firmer and truer than determining men's characters from their physical signs. For as we said, humans have the choice of vice and virtue through the reason of the intellect, which plants lack. **Zopyrus** <note>A famous physiognomist of ancient Greece</note> saw signs of luxury and stupidity in **Socrates**, but those vices were not in his soul because he had removed them through the study of philosophy. 

We said "of powers" so that we might embrace both vices and virtues. We said "from the parts and life" because the plant demonstrates human parts and diseases not only by the resemblance of its physical parts, but from its very way of living—the similarities in how it buds, bears fruit, and the like, as mentioned above. We said "by mobile and fixed signs," for signs can be both. Fixed signs are those taken from seeds, roots, and flowers, which are always the same in every place and climate, such as in the seed of viper’s bugloss <note>original: "echij"</note> and orchids. But mobile signs are odor, taste, color, form, hairiness, and smoothness, which change with the change of soil, climate, and cultivation, as we shall see in the case of urban and wild plants. 

Regarding the declaration of the name: <term>φυτόν</term> <note>phyton</note> is a plant, and <term>γνώμων</term> <note>gnomon</note> is knowledge. For <term>γνώμονες</term> <note>gnomones</note> are the teeth of beasts of burden from which their age is discerned. There are also magistrates in Athens called by this name, being men of accurate prudence; thus, it is the science of knowing plants. And just as in <term>φυσιογνωμονία</term> <note>physiognomonia; Physiognomy</note> human character is judged from the appearance of the body, so in <term>φυτογνωμονία</term> <note>phytognomonia; Phytognomonics</note> the genuine powers of plants can be divined from their appearance.

->PREFACE.<-

<image-desc>A historiated initial letter 'I' in a square frame, depicting a figure standing in a landscape with trees and distant buildings.</image-desc>

**Having** now laid the foundations of the things to be discussed, it is at present pleasing and proper to proceed to the particular account of each plant. We shall begin our historical series from their kinships and places of birth, both because this knowledge is simpler and requires less labor—serving as the basic rudiments of our subject—and because if these were ignored at the start, the clearer teaching of the remaining matters would easily be lost to us. We have previously stated that some powers of plants are manifest <note>obvious or observable</note> and others are hidden; we shall begin with the manifest ones. We will show that these arise from the nutrients they consume and the climate in which they are born. From those mixtures in which they grow, they are nourished, they consist, and they operate; and this can be clearly known by anyone from a close inspection of each plant itself. For from the nature of the soil, the condition of the sky, the spirit of the place, and the charms of cultivation, it happens that just as the physical form <term>effigiatura: the outward shape or "signature" of a plant</term> varies, so too do its gifts <note>original: "dotes," referring to its medicinal virtues or natural properties</note>. For some plants desire to be born in wet, stagnant, flowing, or salty waters; others in parched, white-soiled places <note>original: "alfiosis locis"</note>, others on the highest ridges of mountains, or on steep cliffs, or in sunken valleys; others live in hot, cold, or temperate regions of the sky; others, renouncing all cultivation, stretch themselves out of their own accord in the woods; while others seek to be cherished by the charms of cultivation in green gardens.
