## THAT EVERY PART OF THE WORLD PRODUCES PLANTS ACCORDING TO THE QUALITIES OF ITS OWN SKY
### *and from its earthly mixture.*
### Chapter 1.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring a figure, possibly a child or cherub, seated amidst ornate scrolling foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

If we demonstrate through authority, reason, and experience that all plants are born from a mixture of earth and water, and that they feed on the same mixtures by which they are produced according to the various qualities of their locations, it will be an argument clearer than the sun that plants obtain their temperaments from their native places. We shall begin first from the opinions of the ancient masters of nature. Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, writing to Lechinon, said that the earth is the mother of plants, and the sun is the father. Theophrastus says that Anaxagoras reports that the air contains the seeds of all things, and he asserted that when these are brought down together with the rain, all things are born. Diogenes believed that plants are born from putrefying water that takes on a certain mixture with the earth; but Cleodemus thought that not only plants, but animals are born from that mixture, and that the more they come from turbid and cold mixtures, the more they are deprived of the nature of animals. But he said these things were somewhat removed from the senses; however, what is observed is that rains cause certain putrefactions and changes in the ground, and when moisture descends deeply, plants born by that reasoning can be nourished and increased by the Sun heating and drying them—just as the greater part of authors confirms that the generation of animals is also accomplished. 

And the earth, when stirred, always produces things familiar to that place. In the Island of Crete, in whatever place someone moves the earth, unless something else is sown, the cypress <note>original: "cupressum"</note> is born and immediately springs up; and in half-damp cornfields, if they are moved, the caltrop <note>original: "tribulum", a thorny weed</note> rises up. So too laser <term>laser: likely Silphium, a legendary and now-extinct medicinal plant highly prized in antiquity</term> arose in Libya after a certain pitchy and thick rain; but those things which are of an annual and herbaceous nature come out more easily. Pliny said that the waters falling from the sky are the causes of all things born from the earth, a truly wonderful nature. 

Thus far concerning the opinions of the ancients. I myself have always judged it consistent with the truth that both plants and certain animals are born from the earth, because there is moisture in the earth, spirit in the moisture, and throughout it a "vital heat," so that all places are full of life. For this reason, even without pre-existing seed and without any labor of men, just as different tracts of land are diverse in their juice, sun, situation, and other constitutions, so too they have produced diverse plants marked with diverse qualities. For the habit of a body is usually according to the humors by which we are nourished, and such juices are produced as are the foods on which we feed. 

An experiment brought this to my mind: when I had collected earth dug out from the deepest foundations of houses (so that any suspicion of scattered seeds might be removed) and had exposed it to the open air in very high places, so that the wind might not have carried seeds from elsewhere, not many days later, various kinds of herbs arose from the various qualities of the earth in those pots—but they were plants familiar to the Neapolitan soil and sky. For clay produced some, Puteolan dust <note>original: "pulvis puteolanus", a volcanic ash from Pozzuoli used in Roman cement</note> produced others, and crushed pebbles or tufa <term>tufa: a porous rock formed from volcanic ash</term> produced others. Thus, each earth according to its quality produced stems of that same quality: for the tufa-like earth produced bitumen-clover <note>original: "asphaltite trifolium"</note>, which is why the tufa mountain looming over Naples was called "Trifolinus" by Galen, from the abundance of this clover. It also produced nettles, brambles, mercury, and similar things. So too we see everywhere in mounds of earth dug out from wells and exposed to the sharp air, that spontaneously growing herbs clothe the surface and decorate it with a pleasant greenness. 

But why wander further, if these things are clear by the testimony of the Sacred Scriptures? Moses says that when God created the earth and divided it from the waters, He commanded: *Let the earth bring forth green grass, which bears seed according to its kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth.* Thus the earth brought forth green grass, making seed according to its kind, and the tree making fruit, each having its seed according to its species—as if he were saying that when God had created the earth and marked all its places with various qualities, by the magnificent abundance of His omnipotence, every part of the world produced herbs according to its own qualities. Then the snowy ridges of the Northern mountains raised up the yew, the thuja, and the celastrus; and under the path of the Sun, the glowing...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of plants specific to certain regions from Chapter 1 and transitions into Chapter 2, which argues that animals are also produced spontaneously from the specific "mixture" of the earth in different locations.</meta>

<page-num>35</page-num>
<header>BOOK TWO</header>

Fragrant Libya sent its aromatic spices. Judea, a part of Syria, alone sent its balsam; Cyrene its silphium <note>original: "laserpitium", a medicinal plant highly prized in antiquity, possibly extinct</note>; the Sabaeans their frankincense; Arabia its myrrh, cassia, and cinnamon; Egypt the sycamore; Media the citron, the *Persea*, and the gingerbread tree <note>original: "cuciopheram"</note>; the island of Phanos the lotus; Rhodes the thorny aspalathus; Babylonia the palm; Mount Lebanon the cedar; Corycus the saffron; Troy the beech; the Bactrians the terebinth; Mount Haemus the tamarisk; Crete the cypress and the herb dittany; the Cyclades the cyperus; Pontus the wormwood; in Europe, Illyria produced the iris, Macedonia the parsley, Athens the olive, Olympia the wild olive, and Mount Cyllene the moly <note>a mythical herb from Homeric legend, here categorized as a real plant</note>; the hills of happy Campania produced the vines, famous through all lands for the juice of noble intoxication; the East of the Indians gave ebony and silken fleeces <note>likely referring to cotton or "tree-wool"</note>; the West and the island of Tylos gave wool-bearing trees and guaiacum <note>lignum vitae, used to treat syphilis in Porta's time</note>. Nor did the rivers, lakes, and marshes rest from their duties. The Nile produced the papyrus, the Euphrates the lotus, the Strymon the water-caltrop, Lake Orchomenus the reed, and near Lebanon grew the rush and the fragrant calamus; Colchis and Galatia produced the sweet flag, and the Egyptian marshes the colocasia. And finally, every individual part of the world raised individual plant stocks as its own quality dictated, belonging to that same property; but when their seeds were moved elsewhere and sown with allurements <note>human cultivation/care</note>, they corrupted their own qualities.

## THAT EVERY PART OF THE WORLD ALSO PRODUCED ANIMALS FROM THE EARTHLY MIXTURE. Cap. II.

Even if it seems doubtful to some that plant stocks are generated from a watery mixture, let them consider that very many animals—even "perfect" ones <note>meaning complex organisms with organs</note>—are generated from the foulest rot. The birth of these is judged more difficult than all others, yet there are various confirming opinions of the Philosophers regarding their origin. Porphyry asserts that among the decrees of the Phoenicians and Egyptians, it was held that kinds of animals crawled forth from the bowels of the earth through the acting power of the Sun. Archelaus the Athenian says that animals are born from the heat of the earth, which strained out a slime very similar to milk to serve as food. Anaxagoras of Clazomenae said all things emanated from earth, moisture, and heat; and this is read in Diodorus as not displeasing to Anaxilaus and his disciple Euripides. Indeed, in *Melanippe*, Euripides writes that when heaven and earth had withdrawn to their own places, the earth produced trees, birds, wild beasts, and the race of mortals. For the earth, being entirely rotten and soft, produced swellings on its surface condensed by the sun, each containing its own decay. While the night surrounded them, the air provided dew, and the sun consolidated them; finally, it brought those decays to their peak, namely when the time of birth was ripe. The membranes <note>original: "utriculis", little skins or bags</note> being broken, it excluded all kinds of living things. Those which obtained a greater portion of heat became high-flyers; those with more earth became serpents; and those whose elements were carried into watery kinds turned out to be fish. Avicenna says that a thing generated through the power of reproduction is not prohibited from being generated in another way <note>referring to spontaneous generation</note>. For it can be that generation exists to produce a species, but the "making" <note>original: "factio"</note> concerns the individual, and that individual can afterwards reproduce. A certain friend of his procreated scorpions, and those scorpions generated other scorpions; and it is possible for a human to be "made," and that human to generate and preserve the species; thus, "making" and "generation" help one another in turn in saving the species. Witness the insects, which the Greeks call *ostracoderma* <note>shell-covered creatures/shellfish</note>; they are generated from rotting foamy slime on ships or on pottery thrown into the sea. Purple-fish are born from rotting matter and slime; the same is the origin of trumpetshells. Oysters are born in muddy places, mussels in sandy ones, as well as "claws" and scallops; barnacles and sea-cucumbers in the little hollows of rocks; limpets and nerites on the surface; and sea-pens in muddy and sandy places. Finally, all shell-covered creatures are made from slime, according to the difference of the slime. But perhaps someone will say this happens in these cases because a congress of bodies or a mixing cannot occur, but they are born in the manner of plants. We shall show the same in more "perfect" animals. Eels are generated from dreggy ponds after all water has been drained and the mud removed, if a great deal of water flows back in. Small fry <note>original: "aphiæ", referring to whitebait or minnows</note> are also born in the foam floating on the sea after many rains. The origin of the mullet and the carp is the same. Indeed, one may see a place hedged in on all sides by valleys, which no spring irrigates, and no lake washes...

PHYTOGNOMONICA BOOK I.

...finally, it admits nothing but celestial rain, and when the rains fill it, it is immediately filled with various kinds of fish. All of these things are made clear by the testimonies of Aristotle, Aelian, and Athenaeus <note>Aelian and Athenaeus were Roman-era authors who wrote extensively on natural history and curiosities.</note>. Even frogs, which have their birth in the waters, are generated from marshy slime; nor are they born from slime alone, but even by themselves, when only the dusty sands of the shores and paths are sprinkled with rain. These are called "temporary" frogs; the same is true for serpents. Macrobius wrote that in Egypt, mice are born from the earth and rain. I pass over those ducks, or birds of their kind in Scotland, in the Orkneys, and by the River Thames, which are born from shells <note>original: "conchis nascuntur". This refers to the medieval myth of the "Barnacle Goose," where it was believed that geese hatched from barnacles attached to driftwood or ship hulls.</note>; these are plucked from the moss of ships and the half-rotten hulls of slime. Those falling on dry land die, but those which the sea tide washes are hatched from the shells.

### THAT SOME PLANTS HAVE ENDURED MIGRATIONS, OTHERS
### NOT AT ALL, AND OTHERS ARE OF A MIDDLE NATURE. Cap. III.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' containing an architectural structure with a doorway and floral patterns.</image-desc>

Of the PLANTS we mentioned above, some are of such a mild and urban character <note>original: "vrbanoq; ingenio". Porta uses "urban" here to mean sophisticated, adaptable, or civilized, as opposed to "wild".</note> that, having migrated to us from their own regions and found a soil suited to their nature, a stretch of sky, and a nourishment very similar to that by which they were fed in their own places, they have forgotten their native sky and become so tamed that they seem like locals. For many were carried to Rome by that majesty of the Roman people, the prince of lands. The **peach** <note>original: "Persicum", literally "the Persian fruit"</note> from Persia, and the **cherry** from Cerasus, a town of Pontus, were brought into Italy by Lucullus <note>Lucius Licinius Lucullus, a Roman general famous for his luxury and for introducing the cherry to Italy after the war against Mithridates.</note> after Mithridates was defeated; and they are so fertile among us and spring up so joyfully that the Persians and people of Cerasus seem rather to have sought them from us than to have sent them to us. **Jujubes** and **tubers** <note>original: "Ziziphia & tuberes". Tuberes here likely refers to a specific grafted fruit mentioned by Pliny, rather than truffles.</note> are equally foreign, and writers say that Sextus Papinius brought them from Syria and Africa. Vitellius first brought **pistachios** into Italy from Syria; likewise **almonds** from Thasos, a city of Thrace, and **chestnuts** from Castana, a town of Magnesia, as Nicander says. That **walnuts** are foreign and were transferred by Kings such as Alexander the Great and others is indicated by their Greek names, for they are called "royal nuts" <note>original: "nux basilica"</note>. They say Hercules brought the **citron** from Media, or the gardens of the Hesperides, into Greece; **quinces** from Cydonia, a town of Crete; **pomegranates** from Carthage, and for that reason they claimed for themselves the name "Punic apples" <note>original: "mali punici". The botanical name Punica granatum still reflects this Roman history.</note>; and the **sebesten plum** and **Damascene plums** were brought from Damascus in Syria. Others, however, either because the sky is envious or the soil is resistant, are plants of such a crude, stubborn, and wild character, and so untaught to be born anywhere else than where they began, that they do not travel into foreign lands; so much so that even with many kindnesses and the allurements of sowing, they could not become accustomed to this region of ours. But having spurned the mercy of the sky, the pleasantness of the gardens, and the company of the other plants, they finally retreated to their own places from which they drew their origin. **Balsam** loathes being born elsewhere; the **cinnamon** shrub does not have the strength to reach the neighborhood of Syria; the delicacies of **amomum** and **nard** do not endure traveling by ship even from India to Arabia; King Seleucus also tried this. And if we have often persuaded the trees themselves to live and migrate, and have obtained somewhat from the soil to nourish foreign and stranger plants, the sky can in no way be bent. Virgil says:

> ->*Different trees have different homelands: India alone*<-
> ->*Produces black ebony; the frankincense branch belongs only to the Sabaeans.*<-
> ->*Why should I tell you of the balsams sweating from the fragrant wood,*<-
> ->*And the berries of the ever-blooming acanthus?*<-

There are other plants which, even if they live in foreign places, having been forced to live by the greatest diligence of cultivation on account of the different constitutions of sky, earth, and nourishment, have been able neither to grow nor to bear fruit. Babylonia is famous for **palms**; they are in Europe, but sterile; they bear fruit in the coastal regions of Spain, but it is harsh; sweet in Africa, but vanishing <note>original: "euanescentem", meaning the sweetness or the fruit itself does not last or reach full maturity</note>, and in no other part of the lands except in a hot one, but nowhere fruitful except in a scorching one: for even if...

<summary>This page discusses the spontaneous generation of animals from elements like rain and mud, followed by a historical account of how various fruit trees (like cherries and peaches) were successfully acclimatized to Italy, while other "stubborn" plants like balsam and cinnamon refuse to grow outside their native climates.</summary>

BOOK TWO.

...sent them forth, and she shows that she loathes to nourish those things which she brought forth as if against her will. But if someone carries our own palm tree to the Babylonians, it becomes fruitful and similar to the native plants of that place. The pepper tree lives in Italy, and even the cassia <note>original: "casiæ". This likely refers to a fragrant bark similar to cinnamon, highly prized in antiquity.</note> in the northern regions; the frankincense tree once lived in Lydia. But from where can they draw the sun that absorbs all their sap and "cooks" it into tears <note>original: "lachryma". In botanical texts, this refers to the resin or gum that exudes from a tree, such as frankincense or myrrh.</note>? The *Persea* <note>The Persea was an Egyptian fruit tree, often identified as *Mimusops schimperi*, not the modern avocado.</note> bears fruit in Egypt and nearby places, but in Rhodes it only reaches the stage of flowering. Theophrastus reported the same regarding the Egyptian mulberry. Cold is an enemy to the laurel; around the Cimmerian Bosporus, in the city of Panticapaeum <note>Modern-day Kerch in the Crimea.</note>, King Mithridates <note>Mithridates VI of Pontus, a famous king known for his botanical knowledge and use of poisons.</note> labored in every way to have laurel and myrtle for the sake of sacred rites, but he did not succeed. Theophrastus stated that ivy does not grow in the upper Syrian part of Asia, nor in India, except on Mount Meros. Indeed, even Harpalus <note>A childhood friend of Alexander the Great and his treasurer, known for attempting to plant Greek gardens in Babylon.</note> labored in every way to plant it among the Medes, but it was without fruit. Likewise, centaury is fertile in the fields of Elis, but infertile in mountainous areas; in the plains it enjoys only a small flower, and in hollows it does not flower at all, except poorly. The cassia, if it grows in our world, is not fruitful. For this reason, Plato most excellently said that various places on earth are seen to have various generations of things. And Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher.</note> noted that a place is a principle of generation no differently than a homeland; for this reason, any plant or animal is not born everywhere in all places.

## CERTAIN ANIMALS ARE NOT FOUND IN SOME PLACES,
### while some suffer from relocation, and others are of a middle nature.
### Chapter III.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring scrolling leaf and vine patterns.</image-desc>
One may observe the same thing in animals. There are rough and alpine men who scorn the delights of cities, and can live nowhere else but in their own huts <note>original: "mapalibus". This term originally referred to the portable huts of Numidian nomads.</note>. In some places, certain creatures cannot be born; in others, they are born smaller, with shorter lives, and do not prosper. It is certain that most of this difference arises from the region itself. Regarding these, Pliny says: Nature has not only given different animals to different lands, but has even denied certain creatures to specific spots within the same region. In the Moesian forest of Italy, dormice <note>original: "glires". These were a Roman delicacy.</note> are found in only one part. In Lycia, the gazelles do not cross the mountains neighboring Syria; nor do the wild asses cross the mountain that divides Cappadocia from Lycia. In the Hellespont, deer do not travel into foreign territories; and around Arginusa they do not go beyond Mount Elatus—even though they have split ears on that mountain. On the island of Pordoselene, weasels do not cross the boundary. In Lebadia in Boeotia, moles flee the soil itself, while nearby in Orchomenus they undermine the fields with their digging. Hares die if brought into Ithaca; on Ibiza <note>original: "Ebuso".</note> there are no rabbits, yet they teem in Spain and the Balearic Islands. In Cyrene, the frogs were mute, but when vocal ones were brought from the mainland, their kind persisted. They are also mute now on the island of Seriphos, but the same frogs sing if moved elsewhere. In Italy, the bite of the shrew-mouse <note>original: "muribus araneis". Ancient naturalists often considered the shrew's bite to be venomous like a spider's.</note> is poisonous, but the region beyond the Apennines does not have them. On Mount Olympus in Macedonia there are no wolves, nor on the island of Crete, where indeed there are no foxes or bears, or any harmful animal at all, except for the *phalangium* <note>A type of venomous spider.</note>. More wonderfully, on that same island there are no deer, except in the region of the Cydonians; likewise no wild boars, francolins <note>original: "attagenas". A type of game bird.</note>, or hedgehogs. In Africa, there are neither bears, nor wild boars, nor deer, nor roe deer. In the nearby places of the Milesian field, cicadas are born in alternating years; in the other years they are not. In the Black Sea <note>original: "Ponto".</note> there are neither soft-bodied creatures nor those with shells. In Illyria, Thrace, and Epirus, donkeys are considered small. In the lands of Scythia and the Celts, there are none, because of the immoderate cold. Lions are found rather in Europe, panthers in Asia, but none in Europe. The Ibis is peculiar to Egypt. And finally, there are many things which, if transferred to other places against their will, grow sick and die.

While the previous page established that certain plants simply cannot grow in unsuitable climates (like the laurel in the frozen north), this page explores the "mutation" of qualities—how a plant’s flavor, scent, or even toxicity changes when it is moved to a different environment.</meta>

PHYTOGN. <note>Short for *Phytognomonica*, the title of Giambattista della Porta’s work on the "physiognomy" or visible signs of plants.</note>

# THE QUALITIES OF PLANTS ARE CHANGED BY A CHANGE OF PLACE
## and those of animals as well. Chapter 1.

[Ornamental woodcut initial 'S' showing a figure seated in a landscape next to a tree.]

But who does not know that foreign plants living in other places, if they find the same soil and the same sky—so that they seem to have been moved to a familiar home—will possess the same powers? Yet if the spirit <note>original: "genio"</note> of the place does not agree, because of the internal qualities of the soil and sky, it seems natural that they would take on different temperaments. Part of their former virtue <note>In a botanical context, "virtue" refers to a plant's medicinal potency or inherent power.</note> is abolished, while part remains. However, when places are separated by great distances, so that they encounter an entirely contrary soil and nourishment, they will depart from their own nature. Scarcely any traces of their former selves will remain, and they will take on almost a different nature, as we shall see shortly, when they decline into a defect or turn into other species. 

Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer whose work often touched on the natural properties of materials and environments.</note> proves more explicitly that the qualities of plants are imparted by the properties of the soil. He says: "These things are perfected with different flavors due to the property of the earth, as is also seen in fruits. For if the roots of trees, or vines, or other seeds did not produce fruit by taking in sap from the properties of the earth, they would be of one kind in all places, and the flavor of all would be the same in every region. But we notice that the island of Lesbos produces *protropos* wine <note>original: "vinum protropum". This refers to wine made from the must that flows from the grapes under their own weight before they are pressed.</note>, Maeonia produces *catakekaumeniten* <note>original: "cataceaumeniten". A Greek term meaning "burnt," referring to a volcanic region in Lydia famous for its wine.</note>, likewise Lydia produces *meliton* <note>original: "meliton". A honeyed wine.</note>, Sicily produces Mamertine, Campania produces Falernian, and in Terracina and Fundi, Caecuban is made. In many other places, an innumerable multitude of types and virtues of wine are produced. This cannot happen otherwise than when the moisture of the earth, infused with its own properties of flavors into the roots, nourishes the material. As this moisture rises to the top, it pours out a flavor of fruit peculiar to its place and its kind. 

If the earth were not different and diverse in its types of moisture, then scents would not exist in the reeds, rushes, and all the herbs in Syria and Arabia; nor would trees produce frankincense, nor would they give berries of pepper, nor droplets of myrrh; nor would *laser* <note>original: "laser". The resinous sap of the Silphium plant, highly prized in the ancient world for medicine and cooking.</note> grow in the stalks of the giant fennel at Cyrene. Instead, all things would be produced of the same kind in all regions and places of the earth. These variations in regions and places are caused by the inclination of the world and the specific force of the sun making its course nearer or further away, which creates such moistures in the earth. These qualities are discerned not only in these things, but even in flocks and herds." 

Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany," a student of Aristotle.</note> says that fruits happen to change due to the qualities of the place and the earth, for these are what supply them with nourishment. Not only seeds and plants, but even animals are changed. Fruits change in scent, color, juice, and size: black seeds are changed into white, and white into black. The myrtle in Egypt surpasses others in the sweetness of its scent. Acidic pomegranates turn out more excellent in Egypt and Cilicia; for some become sweet and wine-like, while others become "without wood" <note>original: "sine ligno". Likely referring to pomegranates with soft, edible seeds.</note> and beautiful to look at. This change does not happen immediately, but in the third year. Ultimately, the quality of the nourishment does everything. 

It is said that the *Persea* <note>As noted on the previous page, this refers to an Egyptian fruit tree, not the modern avocado.</note> in Persia is such a swift poison that it kills those who eat it; but when translated and "naturalized" in Egypt, the sky having mitigated its nature, it turned into a fruit pleasant to eat. Hemlock <note>original: "Cicuta".</note> among us has exhausted powers; because of this, Thrasias of Mantinea and his disciple Alexia judged that hemlock should be taken not from just anywhere, but from Susa, or other places known to be extremely cold and shaded. Black hellebore is dull and weak in many places, but on Mount Oeta it is most excellent, and better than that of Parnassus, due to the variety of air and nourishment. For this reason, Hippocrates, wishing to cure Democritus, took care that it be collected from the mountains. 

Iris <note>The Orris root, used in perfumery and medicine.</note> will be better in Illyria than in Macedonia. In Thrace and other colder places that resist the "cooking" process <note>Ancient science viewed the ripening and scent-production of plants as a "cooking" process (*pepsis*) performed by the sun’s heat.</note>, it lacks scent entirely. They believe that *Dictamnus* <note>Dittany of Crete.</note> and *pseudodictamnus* have the same nature, but that which comes out in more lush places degenerates and is falsely named. And finally, he affirms that there is no place that is unable to change a plant. The *Arum* <note>A genus of plants often called "Cuckoo-pint" or "Lords-and-Ladies."</note> in Cyrene provides the least acrimony, so much so that it is preferred as food over turnips; but in certain colder places it is so burning and biting that it burns the mouth and throat of those eating it. Cabbage <note>original: "Brassica".</note> is not eaten in Egypt because of its bitterness, but in Italy, and especially in Naples, it is a most sweet vegetable. The caper in Libya is wonderfully sharp, but in Apulia it is a daily and long-lasting food. The flowering stalks <note>Perhaps broccoli or cauliflower.</note> which are carried from Cyprus to Venice, flourish among us...

<meta>catchword: claui- (likely referring to *clauiculi*, little nails or tendrils, or a related botanical term starting the next page)</meta>

<summary>This page explores the environmental theory of "mutation," explaining how the chemical and medicinal properties of plants (like flavor, scent, and toxicity) are dictated by the specific soil and climate of their location. Drawing on classical authorities like Vitruvius and Theophrastus, the author argues that a plant's "virtue" can be entirely transformed—turning a poison into a food or a sweet herb into a bitter one—based on the "genius" of the land.</summary>

<keywords>acclimatization, soil properties, Vitruvius, Theophrastus, wine varieties, Persea, hemlock, hellebore, medicinal potency, environmental influence</keywords>

--- Page 43 ---
<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the discussion from Chapter 1 regarding how plants adapt to their environment. Having established that soil and sky can alter a plant's "spirit," the author now moves to specific examples of how flavor, physical hardness, and even the colors of animals are dictated by the local "juice" or nourishment of the land.</meta>

PHYTOGNOMONICA <note>Short for *Phytognomonica*, Giambattista della Porta’s work on identifying the inner powers of plants through their outer appearance.</note>

...they produce small stalks <note>original: "cauliculos"</note> in the first sowing, as in Cyprus, but by the second or at least the third sowing, they transition into local varieties. Both Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet who wrote on farming and morality.</note> and the asphodel and onions demonstrate the same thing everywhere: their sharper or milder flavor follows the condition of the field. Theophrastus <note>The "father of botany," a student of Aristotle.</note> records that "cookable" seeds can become "uncookable," and vice versa, based on the nourishment they receive. For thin, sun-drenched locations provide easy and submissive nourishment—as seen in Lemnos and Egypt due to the climate—whereas colder, dense places (like potter’s clay) or damp and marshy ones provide "uncookable" fruits that are dry, woody, and stubborn. Because of this, crops that remain in the open air on the threshing floor become more stubborn and resistant than those taken away immediately. Stony pears grow in rocky places; grain and other crops weigh more depending on the richness of their nourishment. 

In the practice of grafting, the flavor, scent, size, color, and form of the fruit are changed by the quality of the host trunk, as I have discussed more extensively in my books *On Agriculture*. Finally, the sap <note>original: "succus"</note> traveling through the pores of the plant to all its parts can transform them so that they turn to stone—or even to iron, so to speak—if they grow over iron mines, while keeping the same skin but taking on the weight and hardness of iron. As Georgius Valla <note>An Italian humanist who wrote on medicine and natural philosophy.</note> reports, in certain places abundant with petrifying sap, this liquid is drawn up through the roots and trunk pores, converting the roots, trunk, branches, leaves, and flowers into stone. 

These same things happen in animals: for nourishment, such as water, changes their color and quality. Aristotle says that the colors of all animals are altered by the waters they drink. There are the Cephisos and Melas rivers in Boeotia, and the Crathis in Lucania, and springs in the fields of the Clazomenians, Erythraeans, and Laodiceans, from whose drink—though the animals be white—they become greyish-white <note>original: "leucophea"</note>; in others, they become dark, and in others, the color of a raven. In the plains of Troy, the Scamander river makes herds reddish-brown; for this reason, the people of Ilium call this river the Xanthus <note>Xanthus means "yellow" or "golden-red" in Greek.</note>. In Scotland, sheep have yellowish wool, which writers say comes from what they drink or graze upon. Theophrastus says that in Macedonia, those who want white cattle born to them lead them to the Haliacmon, and those who want black or dark ones, to the Axius.

### PROVEN BY THE EXPERIMENT OF ART AND NATURE
->*that plants draw their powers from the qualities of the earth.*<-
->Chapter VI.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative historiated initial 'A' featuring vine and leaf motifs.</image-desc>To elucidate this truth—that plants draw their qualities from the various juices of their locations—if anyone judges the authorities and examples I brought forward above to be insufficient, we shall bring forward numerous experiments of both art and nature. We shall see that if we can achieve this effect by chance or by skill, it is much more credible that nature can achieve it. This occurs not only in plants but in animals as well. First, naturally salty earth spoils the flavors of wine and fruit, as Virgil teaches:

> But salty earth, and what is called bitter,
> Unhappy for crops—it does not soften by plowing,
> Nor does it preserve the lineage of Bacchus <note>Bacchus is the Roman god of wine; here used to mean the quality of the grape.</note> or the names of fruits.

Theophrastus recounts a variety of wild chicory <note>original: "eleaticus"</note> growing among vines that renders the wine so diuretic that all who drink it become extremely thin in the belly. Pliny says hellebore-wine is made similarly from black hellebore. Cato teaches that "scammony-wine" is made the same way. The nature of vines to draw in foreign flavors is wondrous; the harvests of the Paduans in marshy areas smell of salts. Likewise, hellebore, wild cucumber, or scammony is planted in Thasos to make what they call "abortion-wine" <note>original: "vinum ectromatium"</note>, because it causes miscarriages. Columella <note>A prominent Roman writer on agriculture.</note> forbids the application of manure to vines because it spoils the flavor of the wine. If mandrake grows near vines, it produces a sleep-inducing wine. If the mercury plant <note>original: "mercurialis"</note> grows abundantly in vineyards, it infects the wine with its own flavor,

PHYTOGNOMONICA <note>Short for *Phytognomonica*, Giambattista della Porta’s work on identifying the inner powers of plants through their outer appearance.</note> 118

...it infects the crop, and it is rendered unpleasant to those drinking it. Lupines planted in vineyards produce a wine of bitter flavor. Wild garlic <note>original: "Syluestre allium"</note> is seen as a nuisance by the farmers of France and Brabant <note>A historical region in the Low Countries (modern Belgium and Netherlands).</note> in their fields because, growing among the wheat, it communicates a foul odor and taste, which imbues the flour and the bread. Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist, author of *De Materia Medica*.</note> asserts that those who eat the Rue that grows in Macedonia near the Haliacmon river die, as that place is mountainous and swarms with vipers. Nor can one observe a less clear experiment in plants that grow upon other plants. Dodder <note><term>Cassitha</term>: Now usually called *Cuscuta*, a parasitic vine that lives on other plants.</note> attaches itself to neighboring plants with its little tendrils; once it has obtained more abundant nourishment, its own little roots wither away, and it defrauds the host by sucking out an alien spirit <note>original: "alienum genium"</note>. The ancient Greeks did not record its powers because it possesses no powers of its own, but rather emulates the powers of the plant upon which it grows. Physicians of the Arabic school say that if it clings to a "hot" plant, it will acquire a hot faculty; if it lies upon a "cold" one, it will claim a cold power for itself. Those who have assigned specific faculties to it promise that its powers flourish much more if the nature of the "parent" host supports it. The little fern <note>original: "Filicula"</note> that grows on the trunks of trees is nourished by a purer and more refined sap; for this reason, it is preferred by Mesue <note>A famous Persian or Arab physician (Yuhanna ibn Masawayh), often cited in medieval herbals.</note> over that which grows on the ground or on mossy stones, for the latter is gassy and upsets the stomach due to its raw moisture; the same is true of others, such as mistletoe, *hipeari*, and *stelo*. 

Great care must be taken by those who eat mushrooms, for edible ones can become deadly for many reasons. For if a boot-nail, or steel, or some rust, or a decaying cloth is present, or if they grow near a serpent's den, they immediately boil down all that juice into poison; or if they grow on harmful trees, such as the Yew <note>original: "taxo"</note>, *thapsia*, and the like, they suck up the venom through a natural kinship for such poisons. There are some herbs growing above mineral deposits that drink in a certain metallic virtue, whose juice can freeze mercury <note>original: "hydrargyron"</note>, which at times has caused no small admiration. In Nearer Germany, within the Danube region, they write that vines emerge which bear tendrils and often leaves made of gold. We read that the same happened in Pannonia <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans.</note>, the cause of which they attribute to gold mines hidden beneath the vine. Wild saffron, which grows in the sulfurous Phlegraean mountains, drinks in the poison of the sulfur and tints tin with a beautiful golden color. 

The same can also happen by human art: for by changing the nourishment, says Theophrastus, we see all kinds of trees transformed; indeed, wild ones are made milder. When nourishment is applied to the roots, all of it is transmitted and distributed by them; beginning at the roots, it immediately alters the stalk and finally changes the fruit; for it is necessary that what proceeds from the beginning follows the nature of that beginning. Watering makes pomegranates sweet and soft, as they grow with either no wood or softer wood inside, and become better. For pig manure applied to their roots turns acidic juice into sweet. Cucumber seeds soaked in milk and honey-water produce sweeter juices. Cato <note>Cato the Elder, Roman statesman and author of *De Agricultura*.</note> places bundles of black hellebore <note>original: "atri veratri"</note> around vines that have had the soil loosened to move the bowels; when a small measure of wine from these vines is added to another drink, it moves the bowels without danger. Purgative plums are produced by pouring water into the roots in which colocynth <note>The "bitter apple," a powerful laxative.</note> has first been boiled; in this way, the roots of a vine or fig are infected with poisonous juices so that they produce medicinal fruits. Therefore, if art can cause the faculty of a buried thing to pass into the fruit, who would think otherwise than that when the property of the earth is of this nature, the plants will be shaped by the first influence on their roots?

### IT IS PROVEN BY THE EXPERIMENT OF NATURE AND ART THAT animals draw their strength from their nourishment. Chapter VII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring a landscape scene with a figure and foliage within a square border.</image-desc>

We experience the same thing in animals. The water of the Pyrean field, says Theophrastus, makes not only the plants but also the men who wash in it lepers. Boys drink in their character <note>original: "ingenium"</note> from their nurses along with the milk. Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a Greek grammarian and sophist.</note> says that giving wild animal blood with milk to dogs makes them more fit for hunting. For the "milk" of plants is the sap drawn from the earth through the roots, and the character of the plant is shaped by its quality. The Arcadians, not with medicines...

# BOOK SECOND

...to humans, as Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note> and Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> relate, but they are treated with milk around the springtime, since at that time the juices of the herbs swell most greatly, and the udders are medicated by the pastures. Moreover, they drink cow’s milk, because cattle are "all-eaters" of herbs. In whatever places the livestock feed upon scammony <note>original: "scammonium"; a species of bindweed used as a drastic purgative.</note>, hellebore <note>original: "veratrum"; a toxic plant used in antiquity to treat madness and as a purge.</note>, or mercury-herb, all their milk upsets the belly and the stomach, as Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and author of the most influential herbal of the pre-modern world.</note> recorded occurs in the Justinian mountains. Indeed, goats that have fed upon white hellebore vomit at the first sprouting of the leaves, and their milk, when drunk, creates nausea and pours out the stomach into vomiting. But goat's milk generally troubles the belly less, because this animal feeds for the most part on astringent fodder, such as oak, mastic <note>original: "lentisco"; the resinous tree *Pistacia lentiscus*.</note>, olive leaves, and the turpentine tree: whence it is usually rendered most suitable for the stomach. Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,300 years.</note> relates that livestock grazing on scammony and hellebore move the bowels entirely. The milk of livestock eating garlic smells of garlic. Serpents that feed on balsam are not lethal, since balsam cures poisons, by the testimony of Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric who wrote about the nature of animals.</note>. Theophrastus writes that livestock are purged by silphium <note>An unidentified plant, highly prized in antiquity and now extinct, used as medicine and spice.</note>, and that they grow exceedingly fat, and their meat is wonderfully sweet. Bees produce the best honey, and sometimes poisonous honey, from the flowers of the herbs on which they feed. The bees of Heraclea, gathering honey from the flower of the "goat-bane" <note>original: "aegolethri"; likely a species of rhododendron or azalea.</note> in Pontus, produce poisonous honey. Another kind of honey in that same region of Pontus they call *manicon* <note>original: "manicon"; from the Greek word for "madness."</note> or *maenomenon* because of the insanity it causes; it is thought to be contracted from the flower of the rhododendron, with which the woods teem. That produced in Sardinia contains a venom; the Sardinian or Colchian honey is reported as infamous for its bitterness. Honey from boxwood loosens the belly. Those who eat small birds that have devoured the yew berries of Italy are seized by a flow of the bowels. The people of Cyrrha do not catch partridges for food because they devour garlic and have unpleasant flesh. The seed of hellebore is a most pleasing food for quails, for which reason the tables of the wealthy have condemned them. One must beware of crows caught in summer, because at that time they feed on serpents. The rennet of a hare is best for curdling milk, because they feed on milky herbs, such as wild lettuce. If the roots of a vine are touched with *elaterium* <note>original: "elaterio"; the potent juice of the squirting cucumber.</note>, birds will not touch the grapes. From these observations comes the best invention of physicians: so as not to cause nausea in those who admit medicines with difficulty, they nourish animals with those things they wish the sick to take, and then they give the product to the sick person to drink. An example would be: if someone wishes to treat a stone <note>meaning a kidney or bladder stone.</note>, he sates a male goat with laurel for a week; the goat's blood, given to those suffering from the stone with a cup of wine, will be beneficial, for laurel also heals those with stones. For those with dropsy <note>original: "hydropicos"; an old term for edema or swelling.</note>, the blood of a goat that feeds on mastic is effective. For the spleen, the blood of a wild goat that feeds on ivy. Young chickens fattened on milk and breadcrumbs exhibit a most excellent flavor and find wonderful favor with the palate. And a goose nourished on dried figs <note>original: "caricis"; specifically dried figs from Caria.</note> is best both for medicine and for the taste of the glutton, and especially its liver. The meat of any quadruped is worse when it is born in marshy places than in higher ground. Nor shall I omit that girl sent as a gift to Alexander the Great <note>The king of Macedonia and conqueror of the Persian Empire.</note> by the Queen of the Indians, who from infancy had been fed on the poison of serpents, whose nature had passed into that of a serpent, so that she was nourished by them just as others are by customary foods; she would have killed a man with a single bite, or if anyone had had intercourse with her. But Alexander, at the warning of Aristotle <note>The famous philosopher and tutor to Alexander.</note>, abstained from her. I would add other experiments too, lest I be thought too long-winded.

### THAT THE POWERS WHICH ANIMALS POSSESS
### proceed mostly from their food. Chapter VIII.

IT will not be irrelevant to mention in passing that the powers animals possess for the most part arise from their foods: for the variety of fodder is the cause why not only different animals, but even animals of the same kind, differ in flesh, juice, flavor, and form; and locations are different by reason of the fodder. For some feed on bark, leaves, thorns, and twigs, and are astringent; others are seed-eaters, others carnivores, and the like. We shall set forth some examples, so that we may demonstrate the things we have written to be truer, and provide an occasion for the learned to conjecture the powers of foreign animals. Averroes <note>A 12th-century Almohad polymath and physician from Al-Andalus.</note> says in his *Colliget* <note>His medical encyclopedia, the *Kitab al-Kullyat fi al-Tibb*.</note> that animals which...

...[those that] eat the products of the earth are of a balanced temperament <note>original: "complexionis"; referring to the humoral balance of the body</note>, such as cattle and oxen; and winged creatures, such as chickens and partridges: their mouths have small openings; they are solid-hoofed <note>original: "solipeda"</note> or have split hooves, since they graze without conflict. The donkey feeds on thorns (while they are still tender), leaves, willow branches, or a provided bundle of brushwood, chaff, barley, and barley bran. To stop blood flowing from any part, donkey dung is applied; its ash heals those suffering from dysentery and stomach ailments <note>original: "cœliacis"; refers generally to intestinal or digestive distress</note>, according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist and author.</note>. The horse shares the same fodder; according to Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and pharmacologist.</note>, horse rennet is suitable for stomach ailments and dysentery; dried dung, when sprinkled, stops bleeding, and even the scent of fresh dung does so, according to Pliny. The ox feeds comfortably where there are grassy woods, thickets, shrubs, reed beds, and crops, according to Columella <note>A Roman writer on agriculture.</note>; it plucks only the tops of the herbs with its teeth. If blood is being coughed up, they say ox blood taken in moderation with vinegar is effective, as well as for remedies for those with stomach and intestinal ailments. For the camel, its food consists of thorny and woody things, hay, and barley; its fried blood is beneficial for dysentery and for a long-lasting flow from the bowels, according to Hali <note>Likely Haly Abbas, a Persian physician.</note>. Its dung stops the flow of blood from the bowels and the nose, according to Pliny. The goat herd desires thickets rather than open plains; it grazes best in rough and wooded places, for it is neither repelled by brambles nor hurt by briars; it takes the greatest joy in small trees and shrubs, such as the Mediterranean buckthorn <note>original: "alaterno"</note> and wild fodder-shrub <note>original: "cytifo agrefti"</note>, and no less in the shrubs of the holm-oak and common oak, according to Columella. Virgil <note>The Roman poet, writing here in the *Georgics*.</note> writes:

> *Departing then, I order that the leafy*
> *Strawberry-trees be supplied to the goats:* and elsewhere:
> *Indeed they graze in the woods: and on the heights of Lycaeus,*
> *Among the bristling brambles and the bushes that love steep places.*

Their burnt hair stops all flows of blood and dysentery, as do the blood, fat, and marrow, according to Dioscorides and Galen <note>An influential Greek physician whose medical system dominated for centuries.</note>. Wild goats graze on the highest mountains, on herbs springing forth from the stones and on "stone-breakers" <note>original: "saxifragis"; plants that grow in rock crevices, often thought to help break up kidney stones.</note>. Martial <note>A Roman poet known for his epigrams.</note> writes:

> *You will see the wild goat hanging from the highest cliff*
> *You might expect her to fall, but she deceives the hounds.*

For this reason, the urine of wild goats is given for bladder stones, according to Aetius, Alexander of Tralles, Philagrius, Pliny, and others. The same food serves the sheep, whose fat stops bleeding and whose milk helps those with dysentery. Deer graze on shrubs and herbs. Their blood stops the bowels according to Pliny, and benefits those with dysentery and stomach ailments according to Dioscorides. Elephants find tree trunks to be a most pleasing food; they knock down taller palms with their foreheads and take the fruit from those lying on the ground, according to Pliny and Solinus <note>A Roman grammarian and compiler.</note>. When fodder fails, they dig up roots to feed on; besides other foods, they eat barley; tame ones eat barley, chaff, and leaves, according to Aelian <note>A Roman author and teacher of rhetoric.</note>. Ivory has an astringent <note>A substance that causes the contraction of body tissues, typically to stop bleeding.</note> power, according to Dioscorides. Hedgehogs live in thorny hedges and vineyards; they feed on fruit gathered during the summer while they hide in trees during the winter; their kidneys cure dysentery. The musk deer feeds on fragrant herbs, spikes of nard, and myrrh; for this reason, its blood, collected in the navel, becomes musk; it strengthens the heart, refreshes failing senses, strengthens the brain, and performs other actions common to fragrant substances. The "fragrant nail," called <term>ὄνυξ</term> <note>original: "onyx"; here referring to the operculum (lid) of a certain species of sea snail found in the Indian Ocean.</note> by the Greeks, is the lid of a shell found in the marshes of India where the nard-bearing region is; it feeds on the leaves of nard, and for this reason it is fragrant; when used as a fumigant <note>A substance burned to produce smoke for medicinal or aromatic purposes.</note>, it revives suffocated women and those falling from a "strangulation of the womb" <note>A historical term for hysteria or respiratory distress believed to be caused by uterine displacement.</note>, according to Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note>, and other such things that are fragrant. The pig, greatly desiring roots, eats acorns with pleasure; its roasted liver stops the bowels, and the ash of its dung is given for dysentery, according to Pliny. There are also carnivorous animals. Averroes <note>A medieval Andalusian polymath and philosopher.</note> says: Animals are diversified according to the diversity of their foods, since those eating meat are of a hot and dry temperament. They are beneficial for those whom these qualities help, namely in medicine for hemorrhoids, colic, paralysis, gout, and melancholic diseases, but in food they increase these conditions, according to Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>. Their mouth openings are wide and they are armed with claws, since they live by hunting. The lion feeds on raw meat and devours many solid parts without any tearing; its meat declines...

# BOOK TWO. #

...leads toward dryness, generates black bile <note>original: "bilem atram"; one of the four humors, associated with melancholy and cold, dry conditions</note> in food, and is hotter than others. Blood is beneficial for those with paralysis. According to Rhazes <note>An influential Persian physician (c. 865–925 AD).</note>, the fat cures cancer; the meat cures those suffering from hallucinations <note>original: "phantasticos"</note>; the heart cures quartan fever <note>A fever that returns every four days, often associated with malaria.</note>; and if someone sits upon its skin, their hemorrhoids will recede, according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note>. The **Wolf** is carnivorous; it gulps its food rather than eating it, even swallowing hair and bones. It generates black bile in bodies and causes wicked imaginations. Its flesh heals those with colic and is beneficial for the eyes, just as the meat of all predatory animals is. Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and author of *The Canon of Medicine*.</note> praises it for hemorrhoids; when boiled in oil, it is used for gout <note>original: "podagras"; a painful form of arthritis</note>; its fat is mixed into ointments for the joints. Sextus <note>Likely Sextus Placitus, a 4th-century medical writer.</note> says it heals those who are troubled by demons and by shadows that appear as apparitions. The **Voracious Dog**: the ash of its head, when sprinkled, heals cancerous ulcers (according to Pliny); a dog's tooth tied to the body cures quartan fevers; its rennet and dung take away colic. The **Cat** hunts various kinds of mice and birds; it has a marvelous appetite for fish, yet it ultimately feeds on the same things as dogs. Its meat cures hemorrhoids. The liver of a killed cat, drunk in wine before the onset of a quartan fever during a waxing moon, drives the fever away; Pliny says the same for its excrement, and it also cures those with gout. The **Fox** is an omnivorous animal; it snatches rabbits, hares, and chickens. It draws mice out of their burrows with its breath. Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire.</note> says it is of a dry temperament. Oil in which a fox or a hyena has been boiled is effective against arthritis and gout (according to Galen); its liver, tasted before the onset of quartan fevers, cures them; its dung heals putrid ulcers and leprosy. The **Hyena** devours men and their corpses; Pliny and Solinus <note>A Roman grammarian and compiler.</note> state that it is the only animal that digs up graves in search of bodies. We have said it is effective for those with gout and quartan fevers, as well as against night terrors and the fear of shadows. **Voracious Mice** expel melancholy and benefit those in a frenzy <note>original: "phreneticis"</note>; when dissected and applied, they soothe gout. The fiber of the liver drunk with a harsh wine <note>A dry or tart wine.</note> cures quartan fevers; Serenus <note>Serenus Sammonicus, a Roman physician and poet.</note> uses its fat for hard tumors <note>original: "scirrhis"</note>. The **Panther** catches monkeys, fawns, and gazelles <note>original: "dorcades"</note> by attracting them with its scent; Galen states its meat is the hottest and driest after that of the lion. It is useful for paralytics and those suffering from heart palpitations if its scent is inhaled; its suet <note>original: "seuū"</note> removes wild scabies and skin eruptions according to Rhazes. The **Weasel** feeds on mice, snakes, and birds; its blood heals gout, and its ash heals elephantiasis <note>A term used in antiquity for severe skin diseases, including leprosy</note> (according to Pliny and Aesculapius). The **Bear** is an omnivore; it devours fruit, crops, foliage, and meat. Its fat is effective for joint and gouty diseases; according to Pliny, its gall cures spreading cancers, gangrene, and leprosy; according to Rhazes, it cures hemorrhoids and acts as an astringent. The meat of **Birds of Prey**—those having curved beaks and talons—is effective for the same ailments and for the eyes, according to Avicenna. The **Hawk** is of the predatory kind; it resists melancholy and mental disturbance, and is conducive to treating dimness of the eyes, according to Pliny and Galen. Its eyes, when hung [as an amulet], cure tertian fever <note>A fever recurring every three days.</note>, and the dust in which it rolls itself cures quartan fever, according to the *Cyranides* <note>original: "Kirannide"; an ancient book of magico-medical lore.</note>. Species of **Eagles** are carnivorous; they delight in the meat of lambs, fawns, hares, and geese, which they snatch away. According to Pliny, the clarity of sight is restored by a combination of the eagle’s eyes, gall, and brain; they also help those with colic. If a roasted **Stork** is eaten once in a year, gout, hand-gout <note>original: "chiragra"</note>, arthritis, and whatever passions of the nerves will flee from that person (according to the *Cyranides*); its ash is useful in eye-salves for defects of the eyes. Aetius <note>A 6th-century Byzantine physician.</note> prepares an ointment from it for gout. The **Raven** feeds on the corpses of humans, quadrupeds, and fish; its ash is effective for gout, white leprosy <note>original: "alphos"</note>, leprosy, and the like. The **Vulture** also seeks out corpses; its feet contribute to the cure of gout (according to Alexander of Tralles); its blood for leprosy (according to Pliny) and for mists over the eyes (according to Aesculapius); and finally, it can do everything an eagle can. The **Owl** <note>original: "bubo"; specifically the horned or eagle owl</note> is a carnivorous bird that lives on prey of animals that walk at night. It purges scabies; its excrement is excellent for quartan fevers, according to Pliny. The **Crane** is effective for paralysis, ulcers, and cancers; the **Swallow** for quartan fevers. Rabbi Moses <note>Maimonides, the famous medieval Jewish philosopher and physician.</note> praises the **Little Owl** <note>original: "noctuam"</note> for paralysis, melancholy, and the mentally disturbed; so too the **Bat** for gout and all arthritic pains. The **Seed-eaters** <note>original: "Spermologæ"; birds that gather seeds</note> generally coincide with the first group [of animals described]. **Aquatic Animals**, because they live on aquatic herbs and seeds, such as duckweed and the like, heal St. Anthony’s Fire <note>original: "igni sacro"; a skin infection also known as erysipelas</note>, quartan fevers, inflammations, coughs, and similar diseases. Pliny says frogs boiled in the manner of a fish-broth heal coughs. The **Water Turtle** is praised by Rusius <note>Lorenzo Rusio, a 14th-century veterinarian.</note> for coughs in horses; Pliny commends its fat crushed with the herb houseleek <note>original: "aizoo herba"</note> for quartan fevers. The **Goose** delights in watered herbs and cold, moist foods according to Aelian <note>A Roman author and teacher of rhetoric.</note>; its fat heals inflammation <note>original: "phlegmoni"</note> according to Galen, and St. Anthony’s Fire according to Pliny; its dung in a drink mitigates coughs according to the *Cyranides*.

PHYTOGNOMONICA

# THAT BY CHANGING THE SOIL AND CLIMATE, NOT ONLY ARE THE QUALITIES OF PLANTS
## *and animals changed, but one passes into the other, as will*
## *become clear. Chapter VIIII.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring a zoomorphic creature, possibly a dragon or long-necked bird, entwined with scrolling acanthus leaf foliage.</image-desc>

FINALLY, I do not know by what clearer argument I could demonstrate that plants draw their qualities from the soil, if earth and climate do not only change the qualities of animals and plants, but force one to pass into another: for when the nourishment is changed, the qualities are changed along with the form. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 371–287 BC) and student of Aristotle, often called the "Father of Botany" for his systematic study of plants.</note> demonstrates that some plants change their qualities along with their appearance; for the white poplar turns into the black. And a plant changes either into a nearby, related, and kindred type—as when wheat <note>original: "triticum"</note> turns into darnel <note>original: "lolium"; a weed often found among grain crops</note>—or into a foreign and more distant type rather than a neighboring genus, like flax into darnel. For he says: Time, nourishment, and climate effect alterations in animals and plants alike, and we judge it necessary to establish the quality and quantity of nourishment appropriately for changing the genus entirely. Water is said to bring about some change, but above all and most evidently, the nature of certain places and of the climate are noted to be the cause of the change. Wheat degenerates into darnel, and darnel is changed into wheat; since no grain is seen to be stronger than these, they undergo such a great change: this happens from the frequency of rains in the springtime, and simultaneously when the sun grows hot. Also, wheat and wild barley, when their wildness is softened through an equal amount of time, become tame as cereal crops, and these things seem to happen by the change of place and cultivation.

Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist (23–79 AD).</note> says that oats <note>original: "auena"</note> are a defect of grain, and oats are like grain, especially since the peoples of Germany sow them and live on nothing but oat porridge; this defect happens mostly due to the moisture of the soil and climate, for it is held too long under the earth before it breaks through, or if it has become decayed. Red wheat <note>original: "Robus"</note> among us, sown in a place not its own, turns into fine winter-wheat <note>original: "filiginem" (likely a variant of "siligo")</note>, becoming worse in weight, color, and the redness of its flour; from this it is easy to see that by the diversity of lands, the earth does not always return everything similar, but this happens in marshy and low-lying fields. Wheat is also turned into cat-tail <note>original: "typham"</note> and spelt <note>original: "zeam"</note>, and spelt and cat-tail into wheat, and that happens by a certain preparation if it is sown after being crushed, and that not immediately, but in the third year. Barley is also changed into oats, and spelt also turns into oats, and flax into darnel, even though these are very different from each other. For winter-wheat falls away into spelt, into barley more rarely, and finally, either by reason of the earth or for another cause, oats appear in barley, wild vetch <note>original: "aracus"</note> in lentils, hatchet-vetch <note>original: "securidica"</note> in yellow-vetch <note>original: "aphacis"</note>, and in almost all things there is that which is born and mixed in. But I think they are transmuted into these kinds by the fault of the soil or the year.

Basil <note>original: "Ocimum"</note> exposed to the sun passes into wild thyme <note>original: "serpillum"</note>, because with the approach of greater dryness, the leaf hardens from lack of nourishment, and the sharpness of the scent increases. Martialis Graecus <note>A name likely referring to the writer Gargilius Martialis, who wrote on agriculture and medicine.</note> affirms that its flowers are changed into white, rosy, and purple ones, and it falls away now into wild thyme, now into water-mint <note>original: "sisymbrium"</note>. Old women are so powerful in certain things, according to Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a Roman scholar and writer on agriculture.</note>, that they can change nature; and they say that from old cabbage seed sown, turnips are born, and conversely, cabbage from turnips. Water-mint is emasculated by excessive cultivation and passes into mint through the sharpness of its scent. The Poet <note>Referring to the Roman poet Virgil, citing his *Georgics* (Book 1, 197-198).</note> says:

> I have seen seeds long gathered, and tested with much labor,
> Yet they degenerate still

Mint, wild mint <note>original: "mentastrum"</note>, and water-mint agree so much with each other that, as if by a mutual token of nature, one passes into the other: namely, mint into wild mint, this into water-mint, and that into mint. This change also happens in animals, and in these, the changes are more natural, and more are seen according to the change of places. A water snake wastes away when the marshes are dried up, and from a moth comes a caterpillar, and from a caterpillar a butterfly is born; so too of the soul-butterfly <note>original: "psyche"; in Greek, the word means both "soul" and "butterfly."</note> and the chrysalis. But why do I linger on individual cases, especially in a matter that is not obscure?

BOOK TWO.

# ON AQUATIC PLANTS, AND WHAT THEIR NATURE
## AND VIRTUES ARE. Chapter 10.

I NOW seem to see that I have sufficiently demonstrated that plants suck out their virtues <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the medicinal properties or inherent powers of the plant.</note> from their birthplaces by their site, climate, and cultivation. Now it is right to review what those places were. But so that our speech may be made clearer, we shall begin from the diversity of locations; and we say with Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC) was a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle; he is considered the father of botany.</note> that every difference in plants ought to be understood from their locations, since perhaps they cannot be understood otherwise. These locations seem to allow for a certain general distinction between aquatic and terrestrial plants, just as in the animal kingdom. For there are some plants that cannot live except in water, which are distinguished according to the type of moisture, such as those in lakes, marshes, and rivers, and those that are born in the sea itself. We shall divide them thus: the locations of plants are either in waters or on lands. Waters are fresh—such as the lake, marsh, and river—or salt, as in the sea. The variety of lands is rich, lean, middling, rocky, or sandy. Amphibious plants are those which are born both in lakes and on land, or in the sea and on mountains, or in spray-drenched places and along the shores.

<meta>Continuity Note: This page follows the introduction to Book Two, Chapter 10, where Giambattista della Porta began classifying plants by their habitat. Having established the general distinction between aquatic and terrestrial environments, he now focuses on the specific physical characteristics—the "physiognomy"—of plants that live in lakes and stagnant waters.</meta>

PHYTOGN. 81

We shall begin with the inhabitants of the waters, both because they are more easily distinguished and because they less frequently abandon their places of birth. For it is easier for a mountain plant to live in marshes than for a marsh plant to live on mountains. Furthermore, their true nature is less deceptive. Soon we shall come to the marine, terrestrial, and "ambiguous" <note>Referring to amphibious plants that grow in both water and on land.</note> plants, starting first with those that cannot live except in water. Now we shall sketch the face, the idea, or the archetype of the lake-dwellers. We do this not because every single plant living in water retains all the marks we have collected, but to highlight the more common and less deceptive ones. By comparing these, we may judge the shared powers of other related plant parts. Thus, the more a plant retains of this description, the closer it approaches the nature of a true aquatic plant.

A plant that is a companion and nursling of the waters emerges from lakes or stagnant pools with a **LARGER FORM** than terrestrial plants of its own kind, appearing succulent, fatty, tender, and soft. It puts forth a stem that is round, smooth, without nodes <note>original: "enodem"; nodes are the "joints" or bumps on a stem where leaves often grow.</note>, soft, and stuffed with a flaccid pith. It is crowded with a very dense and numerous multitude of leaves. The leaf is very large, of a circular roundness or a blunter circumference, smooth, thick, fleshy, and without visible veins. It rests upon a longer stalk and is of a pale green color, though it becomes darker and blacker as it dries. The flower is of a whitish-pale hue. The fruit is colorless, odorless, tasteless, and for the most part sterile. The root is large, tuberous, and spongy, supported by numerous fibers that are quite slender and long. Its medicinal powers are weak <note>original: "virium effoetarum"; literally "exhausted of strength." Aquatic plants were often considered less potent than their mountain counterparts.</note>. It sprouts prematurely. It is short-lived. Its wood, when burned, is smoky.

But let us provide the natural reasons for this **Physiognomy** <note>The practice of determining a plant's inner nature or medicinal "virtue" from its outward appearance.</note>, so that our instruction may be made more certain; for these are the foundations of what must be said. Regarding the fact that those plants born in water are always larger than those that arise in both places (namely in water and on land), we shall provide the reasons from Aristotle when we speak of animals born in the water. Furthermore, Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC), the successor to Aristotle, often called the "Father of Botany."</note>, in his book *On the Causes of Plants*, said that those things grow more easily which are moister, rarer, and looser; and at its height, humidity provides the sprouting and the increase in size. For this reason, females grow more easily than males. Virgil said of herbs growing in moist places:

> *Moist land nourishes larger herbs: and is itself*
> *Broader than is just: ah, let it not be too fertile for me,*
> *Nor show itself too powerful with its first ears of corn.*
> <note>Quoted from Virgil's *Georgics*, Book 2, lines 251-253. Virgil warns that soil can be too rich, causing crops to grow too much foliage at the expense of grain.</note>

They are mostly without nodes, not because they entirely lack joints—for there is almost no tree of such a kind—but because they seem to have none, such as the rush, the cattail, and the sword-lily. However, by the order of nature, they may have a few nodes, as do the elder and the fig. Finally, marsh plants and those growing in shaded places, where they can receive density neither from the sun nor from cold or winds, are less knotty because they are moister and looser, according to Theophrastus. The flowering rush <note>original: "butomus"</note> is allotted a peculiar stem without a node. They have a spongy pith, as they are produced prematurely by nature and consist of a watery nature, as can be seen in rushes, flowering rushes, galingale, papyrus, elders, and willows. Terrestrial plants, however, such as the oak, the holm-oak, and mountain plants, are filled with a harder, horn-like nature. Theophrastus noted that the "armory reed" <note>original: "armamentariam harundinem"</note>, having obtained a moister condition, is seen to be fuller, fleshier, and altogether more wanton in appearance; its leaf is larger, whiter, and shorter. They have a round leaf by reason of their humidity; and if they are angular, they are at least depressed and blunt at the center. For things that are moister flow easily and are poorly defined by their own boundaries, because terrestrial dryness and tenacity are absent. "Urban" <note>In this context, "urban" (urbana) likely refers to cultivated or garden plants, which are better watered.</note> plants, because they are moister, have rounder leaves; wild ones, because they are drier, are angular. Furthermore, when plants first sprout, they bear rounder leaves because they are moister; as they mature, they dry out and curve into angles. Moreover, the circular figure is simpler; and when nature produces something more hastily, it uses a circular figure: in angular shapes, there is need for greater preparation. Children at birth have smoother, more rounded limbs; in adults, they are more contracted. The leaf of the castor bean <note>original: "ricinus"</note> is first orbicular, but soon the edges spread out from a single-angled leaf into many angles. Theophrastus says that in every generation, the mass is first confused, and then the work proceeds to articulation, for that which is simple is easier. One experiences this in moist herbs— <meta>catchword: mentum (experi-mentum / experience/experiment)</meta>

<summary>Della Porta describes the "archetype" of aquatic plants, noting their large size, soft stems, and round leaves as results of their high moisture content. He cites ancient authorities like Aristotle, Theophrastus, and Virgil to explain why water-dwelling plants are physically looser and less "knotted" than terrestrial ones.</summary>
