->### BOOK TWO###<-

...you will take as evidence. Another kind of water-mint <note>original: "sisymbrij"; likely *Sisymbrium*, a genus including watercress relatives</note> growing in streams produces leaves that are round at first, but as they mature, they become deeply divided. The leaves of Garlic Mustard <note>original: "Alleariæ"</note> are round when they first burst forth, but when they have grown, they become jagged along the edges. Saw-wort <note>original: "Serratula"</note> initially bears leaves similar to betony, but as it thrives, it is cut into deeper lobes. Legumes are more humid than grain-bearing plants; therefore, they have rounder leaves. Mushrooms <note>term: "fungi" - in early botany, fungi were often classified alongside plants</note> are extremely humid and consist of a round form. Navelworts are round and humid. Duckweed <note>original: "Lens palustris"</note> is round, similar to a small lentil, and is of a cooling nature. Watery pears abound in humidity and are distinguished by a round leaf, and so it is with others. They also have very large leaves because of the watery moisture in which they abound. The white poplar is more humid than the black, and therefore has larger foliage, especially in its youth; but in old age, due to a lack of sap, it produces narrower leaves, as Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> says. Spinach abounds in watery moisture and has thick leaves; it cooks in its own juice. Bugloss and lettuce, which abound in watery moisture, have broad leaves. Water plantain bears larger foliage than its kin. Horse-parsley <note>original: "Hipposelinum"</note>, which grows in the water, flourishes with broader leaves than its relatives, and the same must be said of the Great Water Dock <note>original: "hippolapatho"</note>. Aquatic fleabane <note>original: "Coniza"</note> is larger than the mountain variety. The taro <note>original: "colocasia"</note>, which has its origins in the water, has a vast leaf. Finally, the leaves of garden vegetables are larger than those of trees because they are aided by the waterings we provide for food, as we have already taught in the section on Agriculture; this can be seen in orach <note>original: "atriplice"</note> and blite, which are humid and consist of larger foliage. Lake plants also abound in leaves, as Theophrastus said.

As for why aquatic plants are colored with a paler green and soon turn black as they dry, Aristotle gives the reason in his *Book on Colors*. Foliage buds in early spring with a bright green because they are then more humid, but with the progress of summer, they become leek-green <note>original: "porraceæ"</note> and darker. However, when they are pulled from the water and dry out, the moisture is scorched by the sun, and they are colored with a blacker green. For old moisture, as it dries, turns black, as can be seen in the plaster of cisterns. This also happens to stones hidden under water and then exposed to the sun. Water in the clouds is a cause of blackness, and so it is in the earth and other things. And Theophrastus wrote that the underside of a leaf always turns black because of the moisture rising from the earth, which is why the upper side differs from the other. 

Flowers are mostly white or growing pale. In a flower, excessive moisture perishes; therefore, lake flowers are pale. Among metals, lead—the most humid—becomes bluish-grey <note>original: "liuescit"</note>. In all things, a white color usually signifies weakness, by the testimony of Aristotle and Theophrastus; aquatic plants are weak, and for that reason, they ought to have white flowers. There are also pale and colorless fruits, such as peaches, yellow-apricots <note>original: "chrysomela"</note>, plums, grapes, mulberries, and others that grow in marshy and hollow places. For color comes from "concoction" <note>term: "concoction" - the process of ripening or "cooking" by internal heat</note>. Things that are humid can be concocted less and require more time for ripening; therefore, when fruits first emerge, they are pale because they are then most humid. 

Theophrastus assigns the cause of insipid-tasting fruit: things that come forth from marshy ground taste of water, which is tasteless. Those that are diluted and tasteless are almost all sensed as odorless, as are those nourished by a more abundant and forceful food, like marsh plants. Flavor can exist neither in dryness nor in excessive moisture. Legumes that grow in watery places are difficult to cook <note>original: "incoctilia"</note> because of their excessive humidity and coldness. But from tastelessness, they turn somewhat toward sweetness, a fact he did not keep silent regarding the bean, papyrus, and *manasio* <note>possibly a reference to a specific marsh reed or tuber</note>. They are also odorless, because scent follows the logic of taste. There is a great kinship between scent and taste, for both are born from dryness and a more complete concoction. Plants that seek to bear a scented fruit desire less muddy or fatty earth; indeed, heat besieged by moisture and stickiness is less able to perform its duty. Those that live in diluted and shaded regions are found to be unscented. In Thrace and other places where moisture is plentiful and violent, and where winter fights against the "cooking" process, plants lack scent entirely. Water, by its own nature cold, can attract nothing because it is thin, simple, and meager; it cannot protect a scent it has received without it slipping away, pouring out, and vanishing, as if there were no sediment in it by which the scent might be fixed and held together. And they are mostly sterile. Theophrastus said that plants greedy for water are mostly sterile, such as the willow, poplar, and tamarisk. Averroes <note>A medieval Andalusian polymath and physician</note> in the *Colliget* calls them "plants of a single element," such as the aquatic ones, and for that reason, they are sterile.

Della Porta cites classical authorities like Aristotle and Theophrastus to explain how water prevents the "concoction" or ripening necessary for vivid colors and strong flavors.</summary>

PHYTOGN.

He called them sterile, such as duckweed <note>original: "lens palustris"</note>; and humans, like other animals, become sterile from excessive humidity. From this excessive humidity, their vital powers are exhausted. Everywhere among the best writers—Aristotle, Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Galen, and others—it is noted that plants born in the mountains and dry places are more robust, active, and possessed of the greatest strength. Conversely, those born in humid places are weak and feeble, as can be seen in the aloe, wild celery <note>original: "eleoselino"</note>, horse-dock <note>original: "hippolapatho"</note>, fleabane <note>original: "coniza"</note>, angelica, and the rest. And in Mount Telethrius, since the location is shady and slick, everything grows for the worse; better things are produced at Aegae, since that place was very dry. Regarding large and spongy roots, Aristotle seems to have provided the reasoning in his *Problems*: for trees that occupy places exposed to the wind and sun become small and dense because the wind and the sun, by drying them out, hinder their growth and make their mass smaller. But those that remain in hollows and well-watered places become large and spongy; for the presence of water prevents their nourishment <note>original: "pabulum"; the "food" or sap of the plant</note> from drying up and vanishing. By this same reasoning, Galen always considered a woman who has cold and humid legs and fat, loose, and swollen thighs—and those who swell with a dull magnitude—to be worse than those who have a well-protected and firm substance. Theophrastus says that those things in marshes germinate more quickly than those on the plains. He also said that the life of aquatic plants is shorter than that of terrestrial ones, as is clearly seen in the animal kingdom; Aristotle adds the reason for this in his *Problems*. For those things living in hollows and marshes age more quickly than those in high places, for old age is a kind of rot, and that which is stagnant rots. In marshes, the air is always impure and decaying; on the other hand, in high places, the air is moved by the blowing spirit <note>original: "spiritu"; here meaning a breeze or moving air</note> from all sides and becomes purer. And finally, Theophrastus did not hide the fact that their wood is smoky. Generally, those that are humid are smoky, such as marsh plants like the plane tree, the poplar, and the willow.

# THE VIRTUES OF AQUATIC PLANTS.
## Chapter XI.

<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap 'S' featuring a figure seated in a landscape with a building or ruin in the distance.</image-desc>
But let us investigate the qualities of aquatic plants and discuss what the Philosophers first thought about them. Mnestor, following the opinion of Empedocles which he held concerning animals, judges that aquatic things are hotter; he argues this by the example of the fragrant rush, the reed, and the sword-lily <note>original: "gladioli"</note>, and for that reason, they withstand the cold so they do not freeze. To this, he added a reason regarding tinder-wood <note>original: "ignarijs"; materials used to catch and hold fire</note>; for he said tinder is made from aquatic plants, which quickly catch fire and burn, as a thing that contains more heat. To this Theophrastus responds that a contrary thing is fit neither to nourish nor to preserve, but humid things resist other humid things not by contrariety, but rather by an affinity of nature; the internal moisture becomes one with the external moisture, like the wood of the alder, which is incorruptible under water. As for what he notes about tinder, someone might say it is perhaps not a sign of heat, but rather of a more violent friction, so that very thin moisture, thinned by rubbing, becomes like air and catches fire. Lucretius and Vitruvius among the Latin authors followed these opinions, as we have said elsewhere. But the truth of the matter is that bodies are preserved by contraries in contrary places and times, but are harmed by similar things. Against their natural bodily habits, they enjoy and are preserved by similar things, but are harmed by contraries. We add that water, surrounding the plant on all sides, soaking and permeating it with its moisture, and being drawn in by the necessity of nourishment, introduces a constitution <term>complexion</term> similar to its own temperature; and from the variety of waters, their qualities vary. Averroes, in the *Colliget* <note>A famous medical encyclopedia by the Moorish philosopher Averroes</note>, calls plants "imperfect" in which one element predominates, and says their "complexion" <note>the balance of the four humors</note> is cold and humid, and from the vast size of the body, the humidity is increased. Theophrastus said aquatic things are cold. From this, the powers they possess can be inferred: namely, being cold and humid, they may heal such things as the "holy fire" <note>original: "igni sacro"; likely Erysipelas, a painful skin infection</note>, consumption <note>phthisis</note>, and headaches arising from a "hot" cause and similar ailments; likewise, they induce a love of water <note>hydrophilia</note> and especially make sexual desire <note>venerem</note> languish. But let us give examples of lake-dwelling herbs.

It maintains the central argument that the environment (humidity and stillness) dictates the physical and medicinal qualities of the organisms found there.</meta>

->49<-
->BOOK TWO.<-

**Duckweed** <note>original: "Palustris lens"</note> floats upon still waters and those that do not flow. It is a moss similar to a lentil, though recent researchers have observed that it puts forth roots and eventually becomes a full plant. **Dioscorides** <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> stated it has a cooling nature. It is applied as a poultice for **erysipelas** <note>original: "igni sacro," literally "holy fire," a skin infection</note> and gout. It has recently been discovered to heal inflammations, pestilential fevers, red eyes, inflammation of the eyelids, and headaches. In the same way, a herb they call **frogbit** <note>original: "ranæ morsum"</note> stands upon sluggish waves; it is similar to duckweed, with a round leaf, interspersed with small milky flowers, and many root filaments reaching deep down to the bottom, where frogs prefer to live—hence its name. Nothing grows more familiarly in slow-moving streams and stagnant waves than the **water-caltrop** <note>original: "tribulo"</note>; from these waters, it thrusts out a head adorned with round, broad, thick leaves resting on a long stalk—partly floating on the water, partly creeping and submerged at the bottom. It has a thick, succulent stem, which **Dioscorides** said was of a cooling nature, and therefore useful for inflammations, the gums, and tonsils. In both lakes and waters moving in a gentle stream, there floats a mucous or **fennel-leaved plant** <note>likely water-milfoil or similar</note> with innumerable slender leaf filaments, coming out from the stem in a wing-like pattern at equal intervals. It is soft, tender, and brownish-green in color, with a pale root that is easy to pull up and a tasteless flavor; we collected this from **Lake Agnano** near Naples, and it possesses the same medicinal powers. The **Egyptian lotus** <note>original: "Lotus ægyptia"</note> grows in flooded fields; with its white, lily-like flower, it retreats entirely into the lake in the evening, then emerges out of the water at sunrise. Its cooked root is eaten as bread. **Serapio** <note>An influential medieval Arabic medical authority.</note> said it heals joint pain. **Pliny** <note>The Roman author of Natural History.</note> says: any herb collected from brooks or rivers before sunrise and tied to the left arm—so that the patient does not know what it is—is said to ward off tertian fevers. **Mushrooms** grow in damp places or from excessive humidity; once plucked, they rot very quickly. With a round cap <note>original: "vmbone"</note> and a tender stem, it is a cold and humid plant. They are applied with water for dog bites.

# ON THE FORMS OF ANIMALS LIVING IN WATER,
## and their powers. Chap. XII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' depicting a landscape with trees and a building in the background, framed within a square border of scrolling foliage.</image-desc>

ANIMALS follow the same logic. Even if the locations of animals are harder to know, since those endowed with feet wander far from the places where they live; nonetheless, wherever they more frequently stable, gather, and dwell, we shall call those their "places." This shall be their form.

**AQUATIC** animals consist of a larger form than land animals of their own kind, with round limbs, smooth and soft skin, flabby flesh, pale color, and are odorless, tasteless, and short-lived. We shall provide the natural reasons for this. As to why they are of a larger form than land animals of their kind, **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher whose biological works were foundational to this text.</note> gives the reason in his book of *Problems*. In land animals, the body is consumed by the power of the sun, and the supply of nourishment is drawn away; hence, those that live hidden are more vigorous. Since the aquatic kind is immune to these disadvantages, it grows to a larger body. And **Pliny** says: the cause for aquatic animals being larger than terrestrial ones is the evident luxury of moisture. As for why they are round in form: we have seen in human **physiognomy** <note>the study of physical features to determine character</note> that women, or humid men, or newly born children—who are truly more humid—have rounded, smooth, and somewhat soft limbs. They also consist of loose flesh because they are humid and feed on moist food, water, mud, and slime; it is otherwise in those that feed on roots, herbs, or other harder things, for they consist of harder and more vigorous flesh. **Aristotle** gives the causes of the pale color in his *Problems*, stating that moisture produces paleness when it rots, and it also happens because of immobility; for this reason, those who dwell in marshes are pale. Why they are tasteless and odorless, we have already given the cause in aquatic plants. But let us track the powers of aquatic animals and examine the opinions of the ancient philosophers. **Aristotle**, in his book on the parts of animals and respiration, reports that **Empedocles** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who theorized on the four elements.</note> did not judge well when he said that those animals are the hottest and have the most fire which are

PHYTOGNOMONICA

aquatic creatures: for fleeing an excess of natural heat, when they are deprived of cold and moisture, they adopt these contraries from the place itself, for moisture is less hot than air. And the coldness of the place is balanced by the heat of their own nature. Theophrastus reports the same. Empedocles <note>A Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed the theory of the four elements.</note> thinks the constitution of fish is very hot, and for that reason, they were banished to the coldest element. He believed that contraries could endure in contrary places: hot things in cold places, and cold things in hot. For they claim that nature generated things this way in the beginning, and that a thing perishes from its own likeness through excess, but can best be preserved by contraries, as if by some leaping middle temperament. To which he <note>Likely referring to Aristotle or Theophrastus critiquing Empedocles.</note> responds thus: That a contrary thing is fit neither to nourish nor to preserve, but rather a similar thing; and that Empedocles asserted foolishly that nature transferred to a place of moisture those things which it generates in the dry. For in what way could the living inhabitants of the waters have persisted for even the shortest time in the dry, if indeed they are similar to those of our own times? Likewise, what we perceive to happen in generation in our times clearly declares the matter: for we see that the entire genus of animals and plants can both be generated and remain only in its own proper place. Therefore, they cannot be affected by their own place, but are open to affections from the contrary and the adverse, especially since great distraction and change occur in that way. But as we said of plants, the excesses of bodily effects are preserved in contrary places and times, and are destroyed by similar ones; whereas they rejoice in and are preserved by things similar to the natural habits of the body. 

But the powers that we can gather from animals that live in fresh water will be these: since they are moist and cold, they help those who have need of cooling, as we have already said, both for drunkenness and for <term>canine diseases</term> <note>referring to rabies or "canine madness"</note>. For dry animals induce madness and <term>hydrophobia</term> <note>literally "fear of water," a historical term for rabies</note> by their own diseases—such as the cat, the wolf, the fox, the weasel, and others—and aquatic animals cure them. Galen, following Pelops, thought that only the crab could do this. But let us come to examples. The ash of a **river crab** is greatly beneficial for the diseases of a rabid dog, for the reason we stated; this power belongs to many animals, though the ancient physicians attributed it to this one alone. It also benefits those with wasting diseases and soothes **carcinomas** <note>cancerous growths</note>. The **seahorse** <note>original: "Hippocampus"</note>, an aquatic animal, induces a love of water in anyone who swallows it, so that perennial rivers, flowing springs, lakes, and shores become pleasing to them; it has salutary powers against the bites of a rabid dog, from which the fear of water arises, according to Aelian. **Frogs**, even if they sometimes live out of water, are numbered among the aquatic creatures; having flabby and smooth flesh, they are applied to those with hectic fevers and <term>phthisis</term> <note>tuberculosis or similar wasting of the lungs</note>; they soothe headaches and cure "holy fire" <note>erysipelas, a skin infection</note>, tonsils, and similar diseases. The **water turtle** consists of a cold juice; it is given to those with hectic fever and phthisis for cooling; it is also effective for burns, just like frogs, as well as for holy fire, headache, and drunkenness. **Eels** live in waters and mud and are usually prescribed for almost the same remedies. Drowned in wine and drunk by a drunkard, they take away intoxication. Most **fish** benefit those with hectic fevers, as is held in the books of the Physicians. A **mullet** drowned in wine is effective against drunkenness. The **goose**, an aquatic animal, is the only animal that does not go mad, according to Aristotle; for this reason, it is used against hydrophobia. The **diver** <note>original: "Mergus," likely a cormorant or similar water bird</note> lives in waters and the sea; by a wonderful experiment, it is effective against the bites of a rabid dog, so that those with hydrophobia immediately demand water, according to Aetius. The **kite** <note>original: "Miluus"</note>, which frequents the waters, fends off drunkenness.

Hence, they reflect a mixture of the forms and powers of both earth and water. Their nature will be as follows.

### BOOK TWO.

...mixed. With a large, bitter root, and a scented one with more vigorous powers, and finally, it is almost similar to the one already mentioned, except that it is somewhat hairy on its earthy parts.

But let us assign the reasons for these physical forms. Excessive dryness makes stems angular: we have said that moist things are rounded, therefore dry things are restricted into angles. Wild plants, because they are drier, as we shall describe, are more angular and furrowed. Moist plants rise with a hollow and pithy stem, according to Theophrastus: for he says of vines that "loose" vines are those which have more pith than wood, and these have many wide channels and require a large supply of nourishment; for this reason, they should be planted in rainy and moist soil. Therefore, those which abound in large amounts of pith are moist, while those with little, solid pith are dry, such as the oak, olive, cornel, ebony, and boxwood. He also says that things which are flexible have an easy bend and a stubborn break; humidity tempered by dryness provides this suppleness and compliance. The flower is partly white and partly saffron-yellow, which happens when dryness is mixed with humidity, as we shall say regarding the colors of flowers. The foliage is partly angular: for dryness makes leaves narrow and sharp, and adds veins and hairiness, as we will discuss. The root is small <note>The Latin 'vesca' can mean small, thin, or edible; in this botanical context, it usually refers to the meager size of roots in certain dry conditions.</note> and somewhat scented, which results from dryness. Theophrastus, in the sixth book of *On the Causes of Plants*, said that flavor can reside neither in excessive dryness nor in excessive humidity. Stems that are outside of water are unpleasant due to excessive dryness, for they cannot receive sweetness; but in roots, dryness is tempered by humidity: and the principle of scent follows flavor, so that it may be somewhat sweet and scented. They possess more vigorous powers because strength comes from moderate nourishment, provided that dryness supplies that moderate nourishment. Wild plants are stronger than cultivated ones in the robustness of their powers because they are drier. The powers they possess are cold and dry due to their watery and earthy essence, yet they are not entirely dry: because they have more water, they are only "dryish." Because they dry things gently and without irritation, they are helpful for burns, spreading ulcers, dysentery, intestinal disorders, hair loss, female discharges, St. Anthony's fire <note>original: "igni sacro"; a historical term for various skin infections, most commonly erysipelas.</note>, inflammations, heat-burns, scrofula <note>Swelling of the lymph nodes, often associated with tuberculosis.</note>, and the binding of wounds. Examples include:

Near the streams in the Nile marshes, the papyrus grows as a shrub with a rush-like, three-sided stem, filled with a downy pith; it rises bright above the depth of the waters, and has leaves nowhere except at the very bottom, with infertile seeds. It is useful for making ropes because it is compliant. They eat the root both raw and cooked: after the juice is swallowed, they spit out the chewed remains. The Arabs contend that it is cold and dry; Galen said it binds wounds together. Similar in its origins is the *sari* <note>An Egyptian sedge or similar marsh plant described by ancient authors.</note>, which rises from shallows where a receding river has left flat lands; it has a triangular stem and a flower decorated with a beautiful head of hair, like the papyrus, and an edible root which they spit out after chewing; so also says Mnasius, quoting Theophrastus. The Egyptian bean <note>The sacred lotus, *Nelumbo nucifera*.</note> grows in marshes and ponds, with a soft reed-like stalk and a leaf remarkable for its width and hollowness, so that it can hold water inside; the root is eaten raw, roasted, or boiled, and the bean turns black when dried. Dioscorides said it possesses an astringent power and is useful for the stomach and dysentery victims. From the muddy bottom of lakes and stagnant waters, the water lily (*nymphea*) draws its waters, and for this reason, it claimed that name for itself; many very large leaves float on the surface of the waters, and many also stretch out at the bottom, rounded like a circle, with a white flower having saffron-yellow parts in the middle, a smooth stem, and a root like a club. Galen said it cools without irritation and provides refrigeration: according to Dioscorides, it heals intestinal disorders, dysentery, hair loss, and "venereal dreams" <note>referring to nocturnal emissions or excessive sexual desire.</note>. The name *Potamogeton* <note>Pondweed.</note> comes from the fact that it is a "neighbor of rivers," but also of slower gliding or sluggish waters. It has a hairy leaf like a beet, a spiked flower of a faded purple color, and a taste that is astringent and drying. To stagnant and marshy places, nothing is more familiar or more vivid than rushes; they rise with a smooth stem, without nodes, filled with a spongy pith, of a compliant suppleness—for this reason, the rush is called *iuncus* from *iungendo* <note>Latin for "joining" or "binding."</note>, and from ropes and thongs it is called *schoenos* <note>A Greek-derived term for a reed or measuring rod.</note>; it is very suitable for weaving mats; it stops the bowels and the frequent discharges of women. According to Galen, it is cold and dry. A native of watery places is the water plantain. It rises with a tall stem, a smooth, thick leaf, and a small white flower. It cures prolapses, soothes reddened gout and headaches arising from a hot cause, and heals bloody phlegm and urine. The horsetail is called <term>hippouris</term> <note>Greek: "horse-tail."</note> because it delights in marshy and damp places; it puts forth stalks that are slightly rough, hollow like a rush in appearance; the leaves mimic the hair of a horse's tail, with white flowers. It is used for blood from the nose and for wounds...

### Chapter XIV.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut drop cap 'N' containing a scene with a person standing in a landscape or room.</image-desc>

NOW let us follow the plants that inhabit flowing waters. But let no one say that because they live in moist channels and gliding waters, they obtain a moist or cold temperament; rather, they are extremely hot and dry in excess, since they live in those places by necessity, so that they may be washed by ever-new cold and passing waves, as if they were in need of refreshment and colder nourishment. For gliding waters are colder, and these plants cannot live anywhere but in these places; their form usually deceives those who study their physical signs <note>The "Physiognomones" mentioned here are those who interpret internal qualities from external shapes</note>, since they have some marks of moist plants because they live in water, but others of hot plants because they consist of a hot and dry nature.

THEREFORE, the inhabitants of flowing waters rise with a smooth but slender stem, a smooth leaf that is somewhat fatty but divided by many notches, a white flower (though usually yellow), and a tender but small root, with a pungent taste that blisters the tongue.

The causes are as follows. They live with a smooth stem because they are born in water, but a slender one from heat; a smooth and somewhat fatty leaf from the moisture in which they are born, while the notches are from dryness and heat; a tender root from moisture, but small, scented, and sharp-tasting from heat; a small white flower from moisture, but yellow usually from heat; and finally, they retain the appearance of both hot and aquatic plants. They have such hot powers that they blister the tongue and the skin: for this reason, they cure leprosy, psoriasis, mange, brand marks <note>original: "stigmata," likely referring to scars or skin spots</note>, rough nails, hair loss <note>original: "alopeciam"</note>, and the stone. They named the *Ranunculi* <note>Buttercups</note> after frogs <note>original: "ranis"</note> because they delight in the same rivers and lakeside places, and their flowers are "frog-colored" <note>original: "ranatis"</note>, that is, yellow mixed with green, as they are companions to frogs and drinkers of the waters. The leaves are round at first, then notched; the flowers shine with a golden brilliance. It has a slender stem and a small, white root with a burning taste and a not unpleasant smell. They remove rough nails and erase brand marks, creeping warts, and hair loss. Galen said they are hot and dry. But there are many species of *Ranunculi*; among these is the "flaming" one <note>original: "flammeus"</note>; its leaves are narrow...

### ON THE PHYSIOGNOMY AND POWERS OF PLANTS GROWING IN SEAWATERS. Chapter XV.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' featuring scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

HAVING BEEN LED OUT FROM fresh waters, we now come to salty ones. We shall speak of marine plants, but before we descend to their forms and powers, let us see whether plants can be born and nourished in salty environments, so that we may gather from this what they excel in. With clear arguments, Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany," a student of Aristotle</note> proves that in the genus of plants no saltiness is felt, nor can anything be produced in salty conditions, in this manner: Salt neither nourishes nor is fit for generation. The argument is that nothing grows in salty tracts of land. Furthermore, even if we see something born in salty environments—such as plants, fish, and other animals—which are "sweet" <note>meaning fresh-tasting or non-salty</note>, it must not be thought for that reason that they are born or nourished from the sea itself. For that which is to become the matter of something must necessarily be transmutable <note>capable of being changed into another substance</note>, for generation is transmutation; furthermore, salt is not transmutable. Therefore, nothing perfect, nor anything at all, can be generated from it in any way. For the internal heat of the plant and the sun draw up moisture to serve as the plant's nourishment; this moisture is purer and lighter, but all salt is earthy and heavy and cannot be drawn up because it sinks. A second reason is that salt dries out and erodes all faculties, so that the power of generation is withered. Whence that which prohibits generation in others seems to be the cause of trouble even to itself—that is, what is useless to others for reproduction will also be useless to itself. Moreover, things which undergo no change or decay must necessarily have a quality utterly opposed to plants; salt is such a thing, for it saves all things from rotting. There is another argument: That which is not much emptied out does not need much nourishment; a plant is not "emptied" because it lacks excrement, therefore it does not need much nourishment, and thus they are not forced to suck up anything that is useless for feeding. Plants do not have excrement, because if it were in them, it would be excreted; nor would it reside on the surface, having been raised to that point by the power of the sun. He then adds other reasons to investigate why saltiness exists in plants, for the flavor of saltiness that inheres in plants is either internal or external. If it is internal, it would be nourishment and suit their nature; if it happens externally, from where does it enter, and from what? Either from the surrounding air, which enters into the plant's channels, or from the vapors of fluids drawn up from the root, carried upward, then forced out from the pith and breaking out to the skin like dregs? Indeed, saltiness often seems superficial, but for the **chickpea** <note>original: *ciceri*</note> it is native and necessary; if it is washed away by rains, the plant perishes. Whence it is established that salt is natural to it, so that it might be able to protect and preserve itself. There is also saltiness in the leaves and branches of certain plants which, when placed in water and washed, is clearly detected by taste—not only in those parts, but in the fruits too, if one does not [consume] the fruit...

# PHYTOGNOMONICA

...the tongue warns against it <note>original: "mandat, sed lingua consulat," likely referring to the chickpea, which has a salty residue on its surface</note>, for the saltiness is stored not in the flesh, but in the coverings. This is done as if by nature’s design, so that the enclosed seed may be protected from the stain of corruption and preserved by the brine. While the plant is green, the salt is in the stem and the pod; but once it matures and dries, the salt resides in the husk as if arriving from within. It is widely evident, therefore, that saltiness is a natural and innate thing; for wherever such a plant is carried, or if it springs up elsewhere without being sown, it will be salty even if the field itself was not. Indeed, those things that grow in salty places do not acquire their saltiness by chance, such as **Sea Purslane** <term>halimus, a coastal shrub</term>, **Saltwort** <term>kali, from which soda ash is derived</term>, and many others.

Elsewhere, regarding salty waters, the author <note>Theophrastus</note> has this to say: in the category of waters that taste of **soda** <term>nitrum, or natron</term>, or **alum**, or anything else of that kind, he stated that plants can neither be nourished nor born. However, he noted there are certain plants of a private nature to which unique nourishment is owed. He attributed such generative powers to the sea that it recognizes its own peculiar plants there which cannot grow on land—just like its own living creatures, the fish. Furthermore, there are other trees that live in estuaries; these do not take their nourishment from the sea, but from subterranean veins. For the "virus" of saltiness is filtered out as the marine waters pass through, and the plants draw sweet water from the inner bosom of the earth to live on, while the surrounding sea does no harm because it flows in and out with the tides. 

After the estuary plants, he adds another species of coastal plants, acting as a middle ground between those mentioned. These enjoy a salty subterranean moisture both for nourishment and for strength, so that they not only live from it but thrive. Examples include the **palm**, **cabbage**, **beet**, **rue**, and **rocket**. So far is salt from being harmful to these that it even brings benefit. If **cabbage** is cultivated in salty soil, it acquires a glassy brittleness, so that if it is struck against the ground, it shatters into pieces. Both its sharpness and bitterness are also removed. 

But if salty moisture is able to nourish plants, it does so poorly; for it prevents growth by drying them out—growth being something that comes from moisture. **Galen** stated that salty water has a dry and drying nature, since such a power resides in bitter things; for this reason, it must be considered entirely unsuitable for nourishing the body. In the **bituminous lake of Syrian Palestine** <note>The Dead Sea</note>, no animal or plant is seen. When the river **Jordan**, which flows near **Jericho** and teems with a multitude of fish, enters this lake, no fish at all pass beyond the mouth of the river; if any are caught and thrown into the lake, they quickly die. 

Yet we see such vast kinds of fish born in the sea, nourished, and living most comfortably, so that we cannot believe otherwise than that what is familiar to their nature is sweet and pleasant. If it were otherwise, it would certainly be easy for them to enter the mouths of rivers and flee; but it is established that out of such a wondrous multitude, only a few enter the rivers. 

If it seems strange to anyone that fresh water is contained in the sea, let him consult **Aristotle**, who said that if a wax vessel is immersed in the sea, fresh water is drawn out through filtration. Coastal inhabitants, who lack fresh water, also separate fresh water from salty by digging wells in the sand only three cubits deep. 

There are those who say trees are not nourished by sea water, just as land animals are not, because trees are chiefly offended by dryness; sea water dries things out, or perhaps the "oil" it contains consumes the stalks when smeared on them. Or perhaps sea water participates in much fatness and therefore burns, or because it is bitter due to the residues of "burnt earth" <note>Aristotle's theory on the origin of salt in the sea</note>, and thus the plant rejects the drink. Indeed, **lye** <note>original: "lixivium"</note> is made from fresh water passed through ashes. They say that in the **Red Sea**, there are woody materials and stalks that grow like shrubs; they produce no fruit and grow large because rivers bring much mud into the sea, and thus they are not far from land. 

**Plutarch**, in his book *On Causes*, denies that plants can be nourished by salty things. **Averroes** claimed the water of the "Greater Sea" is saltier and more bitter than others, and for that reason no animal can live in it, because bitterness is at the ultimate extreme of opposition to the nourishment of animals, which is sweetness. But it is not of great interest to us to investigate this too subtly. We have recited these things so that we might examine the powers of marine plants from them. Those things that are born in the sea, therefore, present this appearance:

They generally rise without a stem, or with one that is hollow, empty, and spongy. They have hair-like leaves, or no leaves at all; they are devoid of fruit and lack a root, because they adhere to rocks in the manner of **limpets** <term>lepadum, a type of clinging shellfish</term>. The whole plant is soft and without wood, so that they cannot be battered and broken by the surging of the sea. They are red in color.

The causes of this form are as follows: As to why they lack stems, leaves, and seeds, we have stated the cause from...

# SECOND BOOK

Averroes states that if all plants consisting of a single element are imperfect, then marine plants are the most imperfect of all, because they live in salt, which is an enemy to the process of generation <note>The author follows the Aristotelian idea that salt inhibits the "life-giving" heat necessary for reproduction and growth</note>. Furthermore, plants born in dry places and among rocks lack flowers, fruit, and stems. They are reddish in color. We shall explain the causes of this reddish color when discussing the animals of those same regions. We declare their medicinal powers to be cold and dry: cold because of the water, and dry because of the salt, which is undoubtedly known by everyone to have a drying effect. For this reason, they are excellent for those diseases helped by cold and dry qualities, such as **hot gout** <term>podagra, a painful inflammation of the joints</term>, **dropsy** <term>hydrops, or swelling caused by excess fluid</term>, inflammations, and flowing blood. There are several kinds of **seaweed** <term>phuci, from the Greek 'phykos'</term>: one is broad, another is longer and red, and a third is white, which blooms in Crete. They are effective against gout, inflammations, and poisons, but they should be used while moist. Galen said they both cool and dry. **Sea moss** grows on rocks and shells not far from the sea; it is slender, hair-like, and lacks a stem. Its primary power is to thicken; it restrains swellings and is beneficial for gout where cooling is required. Galen says it is composed of a watery and earthy essence, both of which are cold; it is certainly astringent and visibly cools hot conditions. **Sea-bryon** is a marine herb which, according to Pliny, is not hair-like but has leaves similar to lettuce, wrinkled as if shriveled, without a stem, with leaves emerging from the bottom of the root. It grows mostly on rocks and shells covered with earth. Its primary power is drying and thickening, restraining all swellings and inflammations—especially gout—and anything that needs cooling. **Androsace** <note>original: "Androfaces"</note> grows in coastal waters; it is a very small plant, shaped like a navel, with smooth, slender, frequent, and upright tendrils, each supporting a "navel" in its center. It promotes urine in those with dropsy and is applied as a poultice for those with gout. According to Galen, it is moist and sharp; when dried, it has a drying effect—so say Aegyneta and Pliny. But for some it acts as a diuretic, and I suspect a mistake in Galen's text. **Marine coral** is a shrub which, when pulled from the deep, immediately hardens; it is moderately astringent and cooling, restrains growths, clears scars from the eyes, and helps with the coughing up of blood and difficulty in urination. **Antipathes** <note>A type of black coral</note> is a species of coral and has the same powers mentioned above.

## THE APPEARANCES AND POWERS OF SALT WATER
### animals. Chapter XVI.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'A' featuring an architectural column flanked by floral scrolling within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

Animals that live in salty waters reflect a different quality and appearance; indeed, they vary in their powers and nutrition, differing from land animals not only by the variety of their locations but also by the food they eat. For different parts of the sea produce fish of different qualities. Pliny prefers the **Aquitainian salmon** above all other marine fish; the **Byzantine bonito** <note>original: "amia bizantia"</note>, the **Rhodian thresher shark** <note>original: "vulpecula rhodia"</note>, the **Boeotian eel**, the **Pontic mouse-fish**, the **Megarian tunny**, the **moray eel** from the straits and Tartessus, the **mullet** from Sciathos, the **kid-fish** from Melos, and the **Pelorian shellfish** are all highly commended. Their form is as follows:

**IN MAGNITUDE** they fall slightly behind the inhabitants of fresh waters; they have a harder and scalier skin, firmer flesh, and are more fragrant and savory; they have reddish fibers <note>original: "capillo rufo," literally 'red hair,' referring to the internal muscle fibers or veins</note>, are easier to cook, possess more potent virtues, and have a longer life.

The reason for this description is as follows: We have said that the moisture in which they live is the cause of the size for both, but salt always diminishes size by drying. This same dryness is the reason why they have harder flesh and more scales. Indeed, many scales, spines, bones, spurs, and claws in fish are praised, because in these they show there is much of an "earthy" quality—something contrary to their own temperament—because they are drier and are born in stony places. Such "rock-fish" are of a finer substance and have fewer waste products than others, as Averroes notes in the *Colliget* <note>The 'Colliget' is the Latin title of Averroes' 'Kitab al-Kulyat', a foundational medical encyclopedia</note>. They also have more savory flesh. Galen noted this difference most diligently; he distinguishes the species of **sea mullet** from that which occurs in rivers, ponds, lakes, or the small streams that purge city sewers. For the flesh of the latter is very full of waste and slimy, while the best is from those that live in the pure sea; in other places, they are not only unpleasant but...

And in the writings of Columella, there is a quite witty saying on this matter. When Philip had come to a host in Numidia and had tasted a handsome sea-bass served to him from a nearby river, he spat it out and said: "May I perish if I did not think it was a fish!" He believed it differed so much from a Tiber or marine sea-bass that he judged it unworthy of the name "fish." As for why they are reddish in color, Aristotle provides the reason in his *Problems*: for all who live in the sea have reddish hair <note>Aristotle uses "hair" or "bristles" analogously for various animal coverings</note>, because since the sea is hot and dry, it can produce such colors, just as **lye** <term>lixivium, a caustic alkaline solution</term> and **orpiment** <term>auri pigmentum, a deep orange-yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</term> do.

These are their powers: water changes the nature and substance of fish, pervading them from all sides. Drawn in by the necessity of nourishment and cooling, the water brings with it a constitution similar to its own temperament. For salt water is dry because of the salt, and it makes its inhabitants dry; water itself is cold, which is why they help with those diseases for which cold and dry remedies are beneficial. **Sea crabs** are dry by nature because of the mixture of salt, whereas freshwater ones are different, as Galen reports from Pelops. **Marine gobies** differ greatly from river ones, for Galen orders the marine ones to be given to the sick, commending the goodness of their juice; however, the river gobies are far inferior in this quality, for their flesh is soft and tasteless, having small scales, as they feed on water and mud. There are both marine and river **eels**; those born in the Sicilian Strait between Reggio and Messina are praised above the rest. Diphilus said that marine eels are sweeter than those from marshes.

### ON THE APPEARANCE AND POWER OF TERRESTRIAL PLANTS,
### *and first, those that grow in rich soil.*
### Chapter XVII.

Now, having left the aquatic herbs behind us, we shall teach about those that draw their powers from the earth. But first, it would be proper to investigate the varieties of earth. Since these are innumerable, lest our discourse be drawn out too long and we weary the minds of students, we shall mention only the primary ones. For they vary in color—some are dark, some ashen, and some yellow—and they also differ in taste, such as rich, sweet, bitter, salty, or astringent. So too they vary in other qualities: dry, dense, loose, sandy, and stony. Our books on agriculture are full of these details, so we refer the readers to them. We shall only report the qualities of rich, lean, average, and sandy soil. From these, the industrious **Observer of Plants** <term>Phytopta, a scholar who studies the nature and "signatures" of plants</term> will be able to investigate the rest. We shall begin first with rich soil. Rich earth is that which, when moved to the tongue, displays a certain oiliness and becomes sticky like glue. Let us now describe a plant that inhabits rich ground.

*This table presents four terrestrial plants to the eyes: on the right side, it shows the **mallow** (*malua*), an inhabitant of rich ground, for the current chapter. Next, it features the **urban lotus** (*lotus vrbana*), a dweller of average soil, for the nineteenth chapter. Third is **gromwell** (*lithospermon*), which grows in dry lands, for the next chapter following. In the last place is the **wild fennel** (*agreste foeniculum*), flourishing in sands, for the twentieth chapter. These are expressed so distinctly from life that you may easily recognize others by their likeness to these.*

# BOOK TWO

<image-desc>A detailed botanical woodcut illustration showing four distinct plant forms arranged side-by-side, sharing a common ground line. On the far left is a plant with rounded, five-lobed leaves and five-petaled flowers. In the center are two taller, upright stalks with compound pinnate leaves and elongated racemes of small flowers. A lush plant rises, a dweller of rich soil, very large in its appearance and with many branches packed together. It has a rich and cheerful appearance, and flourishes nowhere better. The trunk is rounded, moist, and swollen. The bark is smooth, shining, and juicy. There is an excessive abundance of leaves, dark green and thick from early budding. The fruit has a rich, juicy, and crumbly pulp, soft, or with a small woody part inside, with a sweet taste and not much scent. The flowers and fruits show certain growths upon them. The roots are large, creeping here and there.

These are the causes for its depiction. According to **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle; he is often called the "Father of Botany" for his works on plants.</note>, the inhabitant of rich places grows like a shrub with a very large body, huge branches, and numerous, large, fleshy leaves. This is because the plant's root descends deep into the soil, and reaching the bottom of the juicy earth, it draws much nourishment. This it cannot do in dry and meager soil, since its root would cling to the surface and draw very little nourishment. For trees in rich soil draw such a large abundance of nourishment that they can bud excellently and achieve great size, but they cannot bear fruit, because they do not **concoct** <term>concoquunt: a classical botanical term for the "digestion" or ripening of nutrients into fruit</term> as much as is produced in abundance. Rich soil is warm; through this warmth, the roots become more vigorous and draw up more food, which is more abundantly turned into foliage and branches. **African grain** and the **dragon-plant** <note>original: "dracontias", likely referring to *Dracunculus vulgaris* or a similar arum</note> bear a thick stalk because they only grow in a fertile field where they can drink in juice more abundantly. **Columella** <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella (4 – c. 70 AD), an important Roman writer on agriculture.</note>, speaking of rich soil, says:

> *A rich field is one which bears crumbling clods and loosened surfaces,*
> *and when dug, it resembles fine sand,*
> <note>original: "Pinguis ager putres glebas resolutaq; terga / Quigerit, & fossus graciles imitatur arenas," from Columella's *De Re Rustica*.</note>

*And the nature of the soil is fit, where with broad grass*

<note>original: "Atq; habilis natura soli..." This verse passage describes the natural fertility of certain lands where wild fruits and trees thrive without human intervention.</note>

<margin>a</margin> Those skilled in the art of agriculture have said that trees which possess a light, moist, smooth, and swollen bark provide evidence of a rich soil. Conversely, those covered in a scabby, crusty, and scrawny skin are an argument for a parched and stony soil. Plants sown in a rich field have exceedingly numerous leaves and flowers; for gardeners, by applying rich manure, increase the leaves of vegetables which <margin>b</margin> are used for food. Even the traders <note>original: "mangones" – a term often used for deceptive dealers who "beautified" their wares; here it refers to florists who manipulate plants for aesthetic appeal.</note> of flowers, through the enticements of richness and cultivation, cause flowers to depart from their original form, rendering the family of stems and flowers multiple and leafy, and inducing an extraordinary beauty in the blooms, as can be seen everywhere in lilies, narcissus, daisies, <margin>c</margin> carnations, and others. From the richness of the fields, we have seen the red rose rendered "hundred-leaved," from the middle of which clusters of petals burst forth in heaps; and in jasmine, we have seen one flower sitting upon another, both fragrant; and on the leaves of the oak, a small round pill <note>The author is likely describing "oak galls," which are abnormal growths caused by insects, but here attributes them to the soil's richness.</note> growing, as also happens in the elm and other trees, which occur either by the mercy of the sky or the year, or by the richness of the place. <margin>d</margin> Nature, when suggested with frequent and abundant material, luxuriates by varying and multiplying the brilliant breeding of leaves, flowers, and fruits; so, on the other hand, when nourishment fails her, something is found wanting in the plants. <margin>e</margin> In Thessaly, so that the crops do not become too luxuriant in their foliage (as the fields there are very fruitful), farmers are accustomed to let livestock graze upon them or to shear them back. But the cereal grains, which bloom with a single stalk, are content with a meager and slender soil, whereas those that are multiple require a rich one. *Typha* <note>Cattail or bulrush.</note> and its seed are examples of this. When rich fodder is offered to the stems, the flesh of the pulp is increased and the bone—or the covering—is diminished, as <margin>f</margin> we shall teach more broadly in the causes of cultivated plants. Every cultivated plant bears fruit with a smaller stone or seed than the wild variety, because they become more moist and draw more abundant nourishment to increase the pulp, and they also ripen juices that are agreeable for our use. For rich soil <margin>g</margin> differs little from the cultivated. The reason they germinate quickly is that they prevail in strength and abound in nourishment; for example, almonds and pomegranates are more wild than cultivated because they are hardier, whereas moisture and softness contribute most to sprouting. For that which is dreggy and thick is neither easy to pass through nor has an abundance of material. Rich soil acts in place of manure, and manure, by its own heat, opens the pores of the plant and renders the roots vigorous, <margin>h</margin> so that it fruits quickly. As for why they have little scent: scent, as we have said, arises from dryness; but not from every kind of dryness. Truly, because rich earth is slow and sticky, and a cause of moisture and sluggishness, the heat cannot equally perform its office; for this reason, it cannot produce very fragrant fruits. <margin>i</margin> And as we have said of the branches, so it must be understood of the roots: they are large and running forward. The plant has hot and moist powers, because rich earth is hot and moist, and the plant inhabiting such a place retains those same faculties. <margin>k</margin> For wheat, a rich and rested soil is suitable according to the opinion of **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus of Eresus, the primary source for botanical theory in antiquity.</note>; and among others, **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon, the influential Roman physician whose theories on "humors" and "temperaments" were applied to plants.</note> said in his second order of heating things that it can neither cool nor dry—therefore, it must moisten. <margin>l</margin> Sesame demands a crumbly soil according to **Columella** <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a Roman writer on agriculture.</note>, or richer sands. Galen said it heats moderately. <margin>m</margin> **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, author of 'De Re Rustica'.</note> writes that flax requires a rich soil; it is hot, but balanced in moisture and dryness. <margin>n</margin> *Zea* <note>Likely emmer or spelt wheat.</note> desires a rich fallow land, though Theophrastus said nothing burns the earth more; it is medium in temperament between barley and wheat. So also are *colyra* and *siligo* <note>Ancient varieties of winter wheat.</note>. <margin>o</margin> Mallow is delighted by a rich place and rejoices in the moist dung of gardens, being hot and moist. <margin>p</margin> Kidney beans are born in a rich and rested place according to Columella; they heat and moisten in the first order according to Galen. <margin>q</margin> The apple and the pear, in the opinion of **Palladius** <note>Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius, a 4th-century writer on farming.</note>, desire a light and rich soil. The same is to be said of the service-berry, the temperaments of which are hot and moist.

### SECOND BOOK.
### ON THE FORM AND POWER OF THOSE BORN IN LEAN SOIL. Chapter XVIII.

We have spoken of those things which are born in rich and fertile soil; now we speak of those in dry, thirsty, and rough soil, whose appearance and power are the opposite. We have said in **human Physiognomy** <note>Physiognomy is the ancient practice of judging character or nature from physical appearance.</note> that the indicators of a hot and dry body are lean and hairy flesh, hard and dry, black hair, and visible nerves and veins: so

> ->We have demonstrated the plant that dwells in **LEAN soil** in the third place of the table in the chapter just recently described; for this reason, we refer those anxious to know it back to that place, lest we cause boredom rather than utility for our readers by a repeated placement of the same figure.<-

This squalid and lean stalk, as it is mostly found in the open ground, testifies to its unhappy birth by its meager and thin appearance. For it has a withered stem, stiff, bristly, juiceless, slender, and forked. Its foliage is narrow, or sharp, or cut into deeper fringes. The flower is yellowish, sometimes somewhat reddish, most often in umbels <note>An "umbel" is a flower cluster where stalks spring from a common center, like the ribs of an umbrella.</note>. The fruit is small, bony inside, and less juicy, breathing out a pleasant scent, with a bitter or harsh taste. It bears fruit slowly. It has a slender root, supported by few fibers. It grows slowly, but is of a longer life.

But let us give the reasons for this description. That they are of a small body, we have said previously following **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany," student of Aristotle.</note>: just as those born in fertile ground were of a very large and tall body, so those in slender, less deep earth—since the roots cling to the surface and drink in less nourishment than is suitable—grow with a short body. The foliage is cut with deeper fringes. We have said what the order of Nature required: that if plants growing in watered areas have more rounded or blunt angles, by contrast, those born in dry places are cut with deeper slits and fringes, or pointed angles. Dryness renders the leaves narrow. The **White Poplar** (*Populus alba*) has broader leaves in its youth, but the same tree in old age, due to a lack of nourishment, produces narrow leaves and scabby bark. **Basil** (*Ocymum*) born in moist and shady places has a broader and rounder leaf, but when exposed to the sun, it contracts its leaves so much that it seems to turn into wild thyme, because it is vehemently dried out, as we said. The same must be said of the urban and wild **rocket** (*eruca*). 

Wild **lettuce** is round-leaved and broad-leaved, which they call **hawkweed** (*hieraciam*), because hawks—by scratching it and anointing their eyes with its juice when they feel dimness—dispel the darkness; if sown in dry places, it will be born with shorter leaves and cut with deeper divisions; it also turns out this way when its age changes as it grows old. We shall speak more often of the "bone" <note>original: "osse" – referring to the pit or stone of a fruit.</note> and the "pulp" of fruit. Plants that come from cultivated and rich soil, we said, have more pulp and less bone; so those from juiceless and stony soil have more bone and less pulp for the opposite reason. It bears fruit and buds slowly because, from little and dry nourishment, they are woody, solid, and thick; but things that are dry, solid, and thick are not easily permeated, and since they do not have an abundance of material, they bud slowly, as we said. They have less strength, since they enjoy the minimal nourishment. 

The fruits are **fragrant**, because things that are dry have little moisture; what little there is can be easily "cooked" <note>original: "excoqui" – the ancient idea that the sun "digests" or ripens the fluids in a plant to create scent or flavor.</note>. The sweetness of the scent consists of this "concoction"; those things which suit the sense of smell have neither sweetness nor any grace of flavor. In arid places, everything is cooked to the full, as in **Cyrene** <note>An ancient Greek and Roman city in North Africa, famous for its medicinal herbs.</note>, whose land is thin and dry. As to why they have a harsh taste, **Aristotle** gives the reason in his *Problems*. **Thyme** in the Attic land is of the sharpest taste because that land is thin and dry, wherefore the things born in it do not obtain much moisture. Thyme is dry by nature and not at all sweet; for due to poverty, it retains only as much moisture as fits its kind, which is by no means sweet; but the sun draws out what is sweetest, so that the sharpest part is left behind. Things are sharp when, having little moisture, the sun vehemently cooking them and taking away the sweet and the lightest parts, there re-

PHYTOGN.

...is very sharp. Dittany, which grows in rough soil, heats up and is sharp; "false dittany" <note>original: *pseudodictamnum*</note>, which grows in more fertile places, Theophrastus called "sluggish." The reason why it grows slowly we shall bring from the same author, and when we bring his reasons, we think nothing greater can be brought, since he is held as most eminent in the philosophy of plants. From moisture comes a rarity <note>In this context, "rarity" refers to a porous or loose physical structure.</note> of the body, and through the pores, percolation happens easily and without any impediment; thus, things that are of a dense nature can grow with difficulty. For in that which is dense, dry, and bitter, the nature of fire resides, and hence its growth is slow. On the contrary, that which is rare, loose, and humid grows quickly. 

To produce umbels <note>An "umbel" is a flat-topped flower cluster, like those seen on carrots or parsley.</note> instead of a single flower is characteristic especially of dry and hot plants, since almost all umbelliferous plants are of a dry quality. Evidence of this is found in masterwort, celery, moonwort, lovage, anise, caraway, dill, cumin, bishop's weed, wild parsnip, carrot, hog's fennel, cow parsnip, angelica, sweet cicely, imperial masterwort, deadly carrot, fennel, alexanders, pellitory, giant fennel, yarrow, sweet maudlin, parsnip, skirret, samphire, toothpick-weed, bur-parsley, Greek mint, berry-bearing parsley, dropwort, mooncarrot, and others. 

Those made of dry flesh have a longer life, and trees that have a thin and dry bark on the inside are indeed long-lived; nor do they rot easily. So it is in animals with tortoises and whatever is of that kind, according to Hippocrates in his book *On Humors*. These plants are of a hot and dry temperament and of a thin essence; they move urine and the menses, are effective for epilepsy <note>original: *comitialibus*, the "comitial disease."</note> and snake bites, and aid in childbirth. Because they are sharp in taste, they are "incisive" <note>In Galenic medicine, "incisive" substances break up thick, sticky fluids in the body.</note>; therefore, they purge the chest and lungs and kill worms. 

Sea and mountain Eryngo seek out low, rough, and uncultivated places; and the rougher the land, the more grace and aromatic quality the plants have to the taste. They are surrounded by many thorns, with deeply notched fringes and prickly heads, colored a greenish-white or bluish-gray from the heat of the place. It moves urine and menses and heals snake bites, "backward-stretching" spasms <note>original: *opisthonicis*, or opisthotonos, a severe muscle spasm where the body bows backward.</note>, and epilepsy. Galen said it is of a thin essence. 

There is an ashy paleness to the pale sage, such as that born on sunny, scorched, and rough hills, named *elelisphakos* <note>original Greek: $\epsilon\lambda\epsilon\lambda\iota\sigma\phi\alpha\kappa\omicron\varsigma$</note>, as if it were parched by the sun and "star-struck" <note>The term "syderata" implies the plant was affected by the heat or influence of the stars/sun.</note>. It bushes out with multiple woody forks, a rough leaf, wrinkled and scaly, but of a pleasant scent. It moves urine, menses, and childbirth; it aids against the stings of the stingray <note>original: *pastinacæ ictibus*. The stingray was often called *pastinaca* in Latin due to its shape.</note> and purges foul ulcers. It is used for "cold" afflictions of the head, joint pains, epilepsy, lethargy, numbness, and defects of the chest. It heats, dries, and cleanses. 

Thyme bushes with tiny and woody forks, with small, narrow, and hard leaves and a purple flower; it comes from stony and meager soil. It benefits those with orthopnea <note>Difficulty breathing except when upright.</note> and those panting for breath; it drives out intestinal worms, moves menses, birth, and urine, and assists with sciatica. Galen clearly stated that it heats. 

Savory <note>original: *Saturea*</note> grows in rough and rugged places; it is a small herb with slender, twiggy, and woody branches, with crowded, narrow, and somewhat rigid leaves, sharp and fragrant to the taste. It is whitened by a faded purple color throughout and has a woody root. It has the same power as thyme, but with less sharpness. 

Anthemis <note>Chamomile</note> flourishes with numerous little forks divided into "wings," to which adhere many small, finely cut leaves from a tiny root, with the very narrow division of dill. Its flowers are white and abundant. It grows in rough places, heats, and thins. It drives out menses, moves urine and birth, and heals defects of the liver. 

Gromwell <note>original: *Lithospermum*</note> is found in lean places or where cultivation has ceased, with slender, hairy, reaching, and hard branches. Its leaves are narrow and rough to the touch; small white flowers grow in the "axils" <note>The angle between a leaf and the stem.</note>, and at the top, along the leaves, are translucent, round "pearls" of stony hardness and fracture. It possesses dryness, cleansing power, and a bit of sharpness. It moves urine. 

Dittany is similar to pennyroyal; its leaves grow with down and woolly hair. It grows in rough places; if it grows in fertile soil, it is called "false dittany." It heats vehemently. Theophrastus said it is powerful for women's labor; it diminishes the spleen and aids against snake bites and poisonous stings. 

Lonchitis grows in thirsty and rough places. It moves urine. 

Horehound <note>original: *Marrhubium*</note> is a shrub branched from the root, somewhat hairy, with four-angled branches and rough flowers. It grows near buildings, ruins, and rubble. It ejects thick phlegm from the chest, extracts the menses and the afterbirth, and is effective against poisons and snake bites. Galen called it hot and dry.

BOOK THE SECOND.

### ON THE FORM AND BENEFITS OF PLANTS GROWING IN MODERATE 
### soils. Chapter XIX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting a scholar or gardener in a tunic standing in a landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc>
We have spoken of the extremes; here the middle way introduces itself—that is, a plant growing in moderate soil, neither rich nor parched, neither rocky nor sandy, but in soil that is loose and light. Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BCE) was a Greek philosopher and the primary authority on botany in the ancient world.</note>, when describing the best quality of soil, says it is that which maintains a "middle mixture" of the extremes: a blend of the loose and the dense, the light and the heavy, the dry and the moist. Where the upper layers correspond moderately to the lower ones, it is best for trees and crops; for indeed, it seems to harmonize with the state of the air, containing nourishment within itself while offering an easy path for the roots. But let us move to their form.

->*In the seventeenth chapter, in the second place of the table, you will find the plant*<-
->*that dwells in moderate soil; contemplate it there.*<-

The form of those living in and familiar with moderate land is more common than needs to be depicted with artistic drawings, for it imitates both extremes in a blended way; whoever knows both extremes will surely know the middle. Its size is a little below that which settles in rich soil; so too in its height and the luxury of its leaves, which excel in those plants that are well-watered. It grows neither with a single stem nor is it propagated with many shoots. The leaf is gently notched <note>original: *crenato*</note>, and its color is neither too sharp nor too dull. It is not smooth, nor is it shaggy, but covered in a soft, somewhat stiff down. It breathes out an odor that is neither foul nor aromatic, yet not unpleasant. All other things are similar in their moderate habit.

The forms and benefits are similar: for they are not hot, nor cold, nor dry and moist, but <term>temperate<gloss>In the medical tradition of Galen, "temperate" substances possessed a perfect balance of qualities, making them safe for daily consumption as food rather than just as potent medicine.</gloss></term>, and familiar to our own nature, so that they serve as food rather than as medicine. For examples: Theophrastus assigns thin soil to barley <note>original: *hordeo*</note>, since it requires light and little nourishment. The same is true of "three-month" wheat <note>Spring wheat.</note>, as they are of a temperate or slightly cool temperament. Wheat <note>original: *triticum*</note> warms just a little: it cannot manifestly dry out or cool, and it grows in every soil. Spelt <note>original: *zea*</note> holds a middle faculty between wheat and barley—that is, between hot and cold. The "urban lotus" <note>likely *Melilotus*</note> is placed by Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 CE) was the most influential physician of the Roman Empire.</note> in the middle of coldness and heat, as it is somewhat temperate. Asparagus is neither hot nor cold; Didymus <note>A reference to Didymus of Alexandria, an ancient writer on agriculture.</note> said it delights in plain soil. The daylily <note>original: *hemerocallis*</note> has a power that is gently "digesting" <note>In a medicinal sense, this means it helps resolve or disperse fluids or humors.</note>.

### ON THE POWER AND FORM OF PLANTS GROWING IN SANDS. 
### Chapter XX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a man walking through a hilly landscape.</image-desc>
From the rough and thirsty places, we have come to the sands, which are endowed with a greater dryness, because they feed upon a drier and thinner nourishment.

->*In the last place of the table described in the seventeenth chapter, you*<-
->*will find the plant growing in sandy soil, whose form you*<-
->*may look upon there at greater length.*<-

It has a face similar to its place of birth, as the matter of the sands—parched, thirsty, and dry—testifies by its own appearance. It is mostly defective, lacking a stem, flower, or seed. The stem is woody, thin, rough, knotted, and hairy. The leaf is tiny, hard, and veined. The flower is quince-yellow <note>original: *melino*</note> or purplish. The root is hard but vigorous. Giving the reasons for this description, Theophrastus says that in sandy places, the lowest part (the root) is best established, but the upper part is faulty <note>original: *vitiofa*</note>. This usually happens when the soil is sandy, or porous, or scorched underneath; for the strength of the root exceeds the norm, but they transmit much nourishment to the upper parts...

# PHYTOGNOMONICA

Since these plants have been introduced previously <note>referring to the tables in the preceding chapters</note>, it did not seem necessary to repeat them here; instead, let us prepare ourselves to discuss their powers. These plants are of a hot and dry temperament, and because they consist of "thin parts" <note>original: "tenuium partium"; a term in Galenic medicine referring to substances with subtle, volatile, or penetrating qualities</note>, they promote the flow of urine. According to Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BCE), the "Father of Botany."</note>, the **Caper** delights in thin, sandy places and grows near ruins. It has a slightly hairy leaf and stem, with a woody root. According to Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, author of the highly influential 1st-century herbal "De Materia Medica."</note>, it promotes menstruation and urine, and "consumes" the spleen <note>meaning it reduces swelling or congestion of the spleen</note>. Galen said it is made of thin parts, heats, and dries. **Cabbage** loves sandy or rugged soil according to Theophrastus. It promotes urine, the bowels, and menstruation; it acts as a remedy for the bites of vipers and for those with spleen ailments. **Horseradish**, by the observation of farmers, is seen to thrive in sandy places. It is hot and dry, and promotes urine. **Wild Fennel** dries strongly and grows successfully in sands. It is hot and dry, promoting both menstruation and urine. **Sea Orach** <note>Halimus</note> grows in coastal sands. It is hot and dry according to Galen, but because it is near the sea, it is somewhat moist; for this reason, it possesses a mixed faculty. **Pennyroyal** grows in sands; we have seen this ourselves, and it is confirmed by the experience of others. It heats and promotes menstruation, urine, and the afterbirth; it helps against the bites of serpents and aids those with spleen issues. The **Wild Cucumber** grows in sands, gravel pits, and ruins; Galen said it promotes menstruation, draws out urine, and is hot. **Thrasi** <note>likely an edible sedge or Tiger Nut</note> grows in the sands of Libya and Lilybaeum in Sicily; it is hot. **Alkanet** <note>Anchusa Alcibiadion</note> has great and medicinal power: for it is sharper and hotter than the others, while other kinds of this plant are cooling. It flourishes most in gravelly places.

### ON AMPHIBIOUS PLANTS, AND FIRST ON LAKE PLANTS,
#### and the Physiognomy of the terrestrial stock. Cap. XXI.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' featuring floral flourishes and architectural elements.</image-desc>Hitherto we have spoken of the simple birthplaces of plants; now we speak of those that mimic both habits—namely, the terrestrial and the aquatic. The Greeks call them <term>amphibias</term> <note>original: "amphibias"; meaning "living a double life," like an animal that lives on both land and water</note>, and we call them of "doubtful life," because they live in both places, on land and in water. Among these also, says Theophrastus, if anyone wishes to inquire more closely, he will find some living a common and, as it were, doubtful life, such as the **Myrtle**, the **Willow**, and the **Alder**. And elsewhere he says: In both places—that is, land and water—the willow, the reed (except for the kind used for flutes), the **gladiolus**, the **cattail**, the **reed-mace**, and the **flowering rush** come forth. Because they retain a composite form and the medicinal powers of plants born in both places, having already spoken of the former types, we shall now speak of these.

BECAUSE they are inhabitants of both places, they present a mixed appearance from both. From the water, they have smooth, numerous, and fleshy leaves, large and winding roots, and multiple stems. From the earth, they have somewhat rigid stems and leaves, and are somewhat flavorful and aromatic. Thus, they also have a temperament mixed from both, and mostly from opposites, possessing "double powers," so that you can adapt them to the remedies of either temperament. From fresh waters, they have the powers which we have already said come from cold and moist environments; but from foul or stagnant waters, they take those which come from hot or dry ones. **Water Germander** <note>Scordium</note> grows in mountains and marshes, with a square stem, a red flower, and the smell of garlic. Galen says it is of multiform flavors and qualities; with its bitter taste, it cleanses and heats. It is effective against the bites of venomous serpents, promotes urine and menstruation, helps dysentery, draws pus from the chest, and "glues" wounds together. Dioscorides wrote that **Sharp Dock** <note>Oxylapathum</note> grows in marshes, though I have always seen it in dry and thin places. Galen said it is of a mixed faculty: it digests, repels, and constricts; it heals dysentery, diarrhea, and discharges. **Rough Bindweed** <note>Smilax aspera</note> grows in marshes and rugged places, with a thick and hard root; it is an antidote for poisonous substances. Galen said that because it is pungent, it heats.

BOOK TWO.
