# THE FORM AND POWERS OF DOUBLE-NATURED ANIMALS.

->Chapter XXIII.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a figure seated at a desk or pulpit, likely representing a scholar or authority.</image-desc>There are also very many animals that live in both the waters and the lands, leading a <term>double life</term><note>original: "ancipitem vitam"; referring to a life divided between two elements</note>. We call them **amphibians**, as they live now in the waters, now on the lands, so that you might not know whether to call them terrestrial or aquatic. Because they are of a double nature and power, they likewise possess a double form—that is, a form composed of both, as we have said regarding herbs. For this reason, they are covered with hair like terrestrial animals, but also have hard, rough flesh, coverings, and scales like aquatic ones, or perhaps smooth and soft flesh. Finally, just as they reflect the form of both elements, so they retain the powers of both elements—that is, a mixture of opposites, such as hot, cold, moist, and dry. Because of this, they are effective for many remedies, especially for those who enjoy these opposite or similar qualities.

The **Beaver** <note>original: "Fiber"</note> has front feet like those of an ape, which it uses on land, and hind feet like those of a goose for the water; with the former it digs a burrow for itself, and with the latter it swims. It has a scaly tail like a fish, and therefore it is always in the water, yet its body is like a land animal. Thus it obtains the powers of both, and because these are so manifold and varied, we shall look to brevity and say that **Archigenes** <note>A prominent Roman physician of the 1st century CE.</note> wrote a book on its powers, in which all the powers derived from both water and land are contained. According to **Aristotle**, the **Goose** dwells around lakes and rivers; it has wide, webbed feet for swimming, but is covered in feathers for flying over the land. According to **Galen**, its meat is "excrementitious" <note>A Galenic medical term referring to food that produces excess waste fluids or "superfluities" in the body.</note>, as it has meat that is moister and hotter than all other domestic animals, according to **Simeon Seth** <note>An 11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician.</note>; however, according to **Albertus Magnus**, it is cold and dry, and thus used for various remedies. The **Duck** is of the same kind of form and power, whose meat is the hottest of all domestic birds according to **Avicenna** and **Serapion**, but according to **Psellus** <note>Michael Psellos, a 11th-century Byzantine polymath.</note> it is moist and excrementitious, and according to Albertus, cold and melancholic. **Swans** live around lakes and marshes; **Oppian** <note>A Greco-Roman poet who wrote on natural history.</note> records that others live in ponds, having the same power and temperament as the goose and the duck according to the doctrine of the Physicians. The **Pigeon**, although a land animal, delights in being rinsed and moistened by water; its meat is hot and excrementitious. The **Pig** delights in water and frequents marshes; it has meat that is excrementitious, moist, and hot, and the fatter it is, the moister it becomes. Some **Elephants** are marsh-dwellers, others mountain-dwellers, and others field-dwellers, and they differ among themselves in both habits and character; but their proper nature is "dewy," loving marshy places, and even if they are not truly "river-dwellers," we shall call them "riverside-dwellers" according to Aristotle and **Aelian**. Their meat is cold according to **Rhazes** <note>The Latinized name of the influential Persian physician Al-Razi.</note>; likewise the amphibious **Turtle**, and the **Toad** <note>original: "rubeta"; likely the common toad, often associated with damp thickets.</note> in moist places.

# ON THE APPEARANCE AND POWER OF AMPHIBIOUS PLANTS BORN IN SPRAY-DRENCHED PLACES.

->Chapter XXIIII.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting a figure in an interior or landscape setting.</image-desc>NOW we have been carried from the waters and lands toward the spray-drenched rocks. Our discourse shall now concern those amphibians which live simultaneously on rocks and in waters, or on wet stones and in the caves of springs. We shall find no more suitable place for them in this entire history of ours, for they possess a face mixed from both of their birthplaces.

It rises, therefore, with a woody, dark, and slender stem; the leaf is small, oblong, veined, nervous <note>meaning fibrous or having prominent veins</note>, and smooth, growing slowly. The scent is unmanifest. It is mostly sterile.

The reasons for this description are: Because just as water gives flexibility and compliance to osiers <note>willow branches</note>, so the earth gives fragility. The juice which it draws from the earth procures a cold tenderness, so that they have a fragile stem. They are mostly sterile because, as Aristotle and after him **Theophrastus** recorded, hot and moist animals are fertile, while cold and dry ones are sterile for the opposite reasons. We have assigned the remaining reasons above. They are of a cold and dry temperament, for they derive coldness from the waters in which they live, and dryness from the rocks to which they cling. This is what Galen felt when speaking of **Lichen**: it cools by reason of the water, and dries by reason of the earth...

PHYSIOGNOMONY BOOK II.

64

[...the plant] is born from the moisture in rocks. In human Physiognomony <note>The study of determining character or temperament from physical appearance.</note>, such were the signs of a cold and dry temperament: a body that is hard, slender, and hairless, with fat dispersed throughout the body, growing slowly, breathing heavily, and sterile. Because of this, since it is astringent <note>A substance that shrinks or constricts body tissues.</note>, it is used for hair loss, dysentery, and snake bites; it binds the bowels and strengthens the body. **Hart’s-tongue fern** <note>original: "Phyllitis"</note> grows in ruins and on damp rocks; it lacks a flower stalk and seed; the root is blackish, fibrous with many small hairs, and has a bitter, drying, and astringent taste. It has many uses for the spleen. **Lichen** clings to spray-drenched stones. Pliny describes it as having a somewhat fatty, gristly leaf, divided by a fringe, with thin heads, long leaves, and a single small stalk. It checks flows of blood, inflammations, skin eruptions, and discharges of the mouth and tongue. **Maidenhair fern** <note>original: "Adiantum"</note> is a tiny plant, clinging to the edges of rocks, stony watering places, cliffs, springs, and small wells; it rests on small, hairy stalks, has tiny leaves, and lacks a stem, flower, and fruit. It stops the bowels, aids in difficulty of urination and snake bites, checks stomach fluxes, blood, and falling hair. **Maidenhair Spleenwort** <note>original: "Trichomanes"</note> has the same origins and powers but is similar to a fern: with thin and slender leaves on thin branches that shine with a rosy color. **Small Stonecrop** <note>original: "Sedum minus"</note> follows the spray of walls, the caves of springs, and dripping rocks. With slender stalks and thin leaves, its power is to cool and bind. It is used for St. Anthony’s Fire <note>original: "Igni sacro"; a historical term for the skin infection erysipelas</note>, fire burns, eye inflammations, headaches, gout, spider bites, dysentery, and flows of the bowels. Galen said it cools and dries. **Cinquefoil** <note>original: "Quinquefolium"</note> grows in water channels and irrigation ditches; it bears branches like straw. It cures flows of the bowels, dysentery, St. Anthony’s Fire, wounds, and hernias <note>original: "enterocelis"</note>. Galen said it dries powerfully but has very little heat.

### ON THE STRENGTH AND POWER OF AMPHIBIOUS 
### PLANTS of the sea and land. Chapter XXIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a large bird, possibly a stork or heron, standing next to a coiled serpent or dragon in a grassy landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc> There are also plants that grow near the sea, so that they are amphibious <note>original: "amphibiæ"; living in two worlds</note> of sea and land, so that they may be called coastal and marine. They live in estuaries, such that you would call them neither marine nor terrestrial; nor are they found elsewhere except in those places, as if by the breath of the sea coast, so that they enjoy and draw for nourishment the salty subterranean moisture, from which the whole plant becomes salty in taste. We will speak first of the form, then of the nature.

**COASTAL** plants rise up in a shrubby appearance, with stalks that are not very tall, almost downy, rounded, fleshy, and whitish, with round, fatty, tender leaves. They have a purplish-whitish flower of a faded color, and a reddish seed that is salty in taste and fragrant. They germinate very prematurely.

We will assign the reasons for this. We have said they are rendered in a shrubby appearance according to **Theophrastus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher known as the father of botany.</note>, who said that those things which look toward the South drink in less nourishment and digest better what they have drunk. The result is that they do not grow in length but turn out shrubby, since they take on thickness and are split in many ways because they take many beginnings—namely, with the heat thoroughly cooking and directing them in every direction. And the maritime shore, because it is deprived of all shelter, the winds coming out of the sea render the plants twisted and shrubby in appearance. No "urban" <note>cultivated or inland</note> tree seeks a windy and restless place; for small, distorted, and meager ones come forth from the strike of the winds. They have stalks with fleshy, whitish leaves, which happens from the breath of the sea; for when the air is rendered salty, not only the foliage and stalks but the stones and walls grow white, either because of the air brought there or because salt sits on their surface, making them appear as if blooming. They are also tender because salt renders all things tender: for we have seen hardness removed by the benefit of salt, for example in the **cabbage** <note>original: "brassica"</note>, which, if it has been watered with nitrous waters, is rendered more brittle. Theophrastus said that salt eats away the moisture and, by drying, abolishes the moisture of the cabbage, by which the adhering parts are held together. But someone will say: why do small roots, or other things growing old with their juice lost, become overcome? It must be said that by heat and age very many [things...]

# SECOND BOOK

->65<-

# HEADER: SECOND BOOK.

The dissolved air passes into vapor; therefore, that stickiness of the terrestrial parts remains with a little moisture. But in fresh **cabbage** <note>original: "brassica"</note>, watered with nitrous waters <note>Water containing naturally occurring sodium carbonate or saltpeter.</note>, there is a moisture made glassy by the hardening of the salt; in the same way, frost makes everything more tender. For frozen stalks are more tender. Most say they have a salty taste because of the nourishment they suck up from salty waters, as we have seen in **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 371–287 BC) often called the "Father of Botany."</note>. But in my view, it is unlikely that anything can be nourished by salt; rather, they are salty because of the air that comes from the salt water. Having become more refined, everything around the sea becomes salty-tasting as the air enters through the plant’s pores and resides on its surface. This is also seen to "bloom" on rocks, stones, and tree trunks. An argument for this is also found in the **saltpeter makers** <note>original: "salnitrari"</note>, who produce saltpeter from the manure of cattle; if they stable the animals in the maritime breeze, they produce useless saltpeter because of the excessive salt with which it overflows. The same **Theophrastus** said that near Tarentum, olives are "burned": for a silent wind <note>A wind that is not loud or gusty but has a physical effect.</note> is perceptible to the senses, as many things are burned by it; such a wind occurs coming from the sea, so that the flowers are corroded and perish by the incoming salt spray. It comes to mind from **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher (129–c. 216 AD) whose work dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> that when he asked a Marsian <note>The Marsi were an Italic people known in antiquity as healers and snake-charmers.</note> how a **viper** differs from a **dipsas** <note>A legendary snake whose bite was said to cause unquenchable thirst.</note>, the Marsian replied that dipsades are vipers living on the shores; because they feed on salty things, they are salty themselves, and for that reason, they induce thirst. Maritime places, because they are warmer, produce [fruit] more quickly. **Theophrastus** relates that around the place called Acta in the Peloponnese, and in Phalecus in the Megarian territory, maritime places are faster to ripen both grain and other fruits. Among us, the **Puteolan fields** <note>The area around Puteoli (modern Pozzuoli, Italy), famous for its fertile, volcanic soil.</note> bring forth all things early, and **Vitruvius** <note>A Roman architect and engineer (1st century BC).</note> said that southern places and those near the sea are the warmest. Since coastal plants are salty, it is necessary that their powers savor the nature of salt in some way. **Aristotle** said the sea is hot and dry because of the salt; **Aphrodisias** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a commentator on Aristotle.</note> said the sea is dry in its power, even if it presents a moist appearance. **Theophrastus** said salt is most suitable for drawing out and consuming moisture. Doctors say that salty juice moves the bowels. But let us look at the powers of salt. There is an old saying that "nothing is more useful than salt and sun." According to **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and author of "De Materia Medica," a foundational text on herbal medicine.</note>, salt binds, purges, dissipates, represses, thins, and induces scabs; it protects against rot, and removes **itchy skin** <note>original: "psoras"</note>, growths, and **pterygia** <note>A wing-shaped growth on the white of the eye.</note> in the eyes. It is infused in enemas and is effective for those with dropsy, itching, lichens <note>A type of skin eruption.</note>, leprosy, quinsy <note>Inflammation of the throat.</note>, tonsils, the uvula, ulcers in the mouth, gums, and **phagedenas** <note>Sloughing, spreading ulcers.</note>. It is effective against the stings of scorpions, serpents, horned vipers, centipedes, and crocodiles; it heals head pustules, "warts" <note>original: "thymis"</note>, swellings, boils, and tumors of the testicles. It works against opium and fungi, and is good for gouty people, earaches, **St. Anthony’s Fire** <note>original: "igni sacro"; a skin infection like erysipelas.</note>, and creeping ulcers. But let us see if other things born from the sea share these same powers. **Alcyonians** <note>A sponge-like or coral-like sea growth named after the Halcyon bird.</note> are effective for women’s **cleansing soaps** <note>original: "fmegmata"</note>, for freckles, lichens, leprosy, skin spots, blackness, and stains on the face and body. They aid urination, sand in the bladder, afflicted kidneys, the dropsical, the spleen, hair loss, whitening teeth, and as **depilatories** <note>original: "psilothra"; hair removers.</note>. **Adarce** <note>A salt crust that forms on reeds in salty marshes.</note> also, because it is like a hardened salty-film, is effective for leprosy, freckles, lichens, and skin defects; in short, the power of the air draws out the moisture that has hardened in the deep, and it benefits those with sciatica. **Rock Samphire** <note>original: "Crithamon"</note> grows on maritime rocks; it is a shrubby herb with thick, numerous, whitish leaves, a white flower, fragrant seed, a salty taste, and a heavy-smelling root. It helps with difficulty of urination, menstruation, and **jaundice** <note>original: "regio morbo"; literally the "royal disease."</note>. **Galen** said it dries and cleanses. **Sea Orache** <note>original: "Halimus"</note> is a shrub with leaves like an olive but wider; it grows in maritime places. The root mitigates convulsions, ruptures, and griping pains, and creates an abundance of milk. **Galen** says it has a salty taste, an astringent and mixed faculty: the greater part of its substance is warm with unconcocted moisture, and slightly flatulent. **Kali** <note>Glasswort or Saltwort.</note> was unknown to the ancient Greeks, named only by the more recent Arabs. It shrubs in maritime areas with a fleshy, reddish stalk, leaves like stonecrop—round and long—with a salty taste. From this is made *Kali*, or what is called **soda**, which they use for smelting glass. It burns no differently than a caustic; it possesses a cleansing power, and because of this, it removes skin-cleansers <note>Referring here to the spots that require cleansing.</note> and stains from the face. There is also a lesser **Kali**, and another kind called **Glasswort** <note>original: "salicornia"</note>, very common on maritime shores. Many little stalks, two cubits high, shrub from a more fibrous root; they look like tender shoots of branches, thick, fatty, round, jointed, inserted like little boxes through frequent joints, like little alabaster jars, with a taste that is not unsalty, nor in temperament or use different from the others. To these should be added that species of samphire thought by many...

# PHYTOGN. <note>Short for "Phytognomonica," the title of the work.</note>

...growing in maritime places, with thick, pale leaves and a salty taste. **Anthyllis** <note>likely *Anthyllis hermanniae* or a similar coastal legume</note> has soft leaves and a thin root; it grows in salty lands and has a taste that is not unpleasant. It seems the name "Anthyllis" comes from its grayish downy pubescence <note>original: "à cana lanugine pubeſcentibus"</note>, or perhaps from the smallness of its florets. Indeed, there are many types of Anthyllis, some saltier than others, with small flowers turning from white to purple, and a salty, slightly acidic taste. They are used to treat the urine, the kidneys, and wounds. **Sea Orach** <note>original: "Marina atriplex"</note> is similar to common orach and spinach, with whitish leaves and a salty, nitrous taste; it grows near shores and salt pans. It cleanses and stimulates the bowels. **Empetron** <note>Sea Fennel or Rock-samphire</note> grows in maritime areas and has a salty taste, but the closer it grows to the dry land, the more bitter it becomes. **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose views dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> said it is effective for those conditions where a salty substance is needed. Among the salty plants, the **chickpea** <note>original: "cicer"</note> is listed by **Theophrastus**. **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*.</note> states that it promotes urine, expels the menses and birth-remnants, and is effective against "ant-like" warts <note>original: "verrucoſas formicationes"</note>, the itch, head ulcers, skin eruptions, cancers, malignant or "bad-natured" <note>original: "cacoethes"</note> ulcers, dropsy, and jaundice. **Sea Cress** <note>original: "Naſturtium marinum"</note> has the form of the cultivated variety, except its foliage is rounder, whiter, more tender, and salty in flavor. Cultivated cress is warming and helps the spleen, childbirth, and kidneys; it is applied to leprosies and skin eruptions, and used for snake venom, hair loss, hip pain, tumors, and abscesses. But the sea variety has more vigorous powers, especially for expelling kidney stones <note>original: "calculos pellendos"</note>, as we have experienced to our great admiration. **Cabbage** <note>original: "Braſſica"</note> has a nitrous quality. It promotes urine and is useful for viper bites, foul ulcers, and gout; it brings on the menses and helps with "sacred fire" <note>original: "igni ſacro," likely referring to Erysipelas or shingles</note>, carbuncles, thinning hair, and the spleen; it cleanses the skin and freckles and moves the bowels. **Sea Cabbage** is saltier in taste with a fleshy, thick leaf. It moves the bowels most violently.

### ON THE AMPHIBIOUS PLANTS OF THE SEA AND MOUNTAINS, AND 
#### animals, and their powers. Chap. XXV.

There are also amphibious plants of the marine waters and the mountains. **Theophrastus** includes among these some that are undoubtedly terrestrial but sometimes live in the sea, such as the palm, the squill, and the asphodel <note>original: "albucum"</note>. These for the most part have similar forms, shaped by both the sea and the land.
**IT RISES UP** <note>original: "ASSVRGIT"</note> therefore with a smooth, whitish leaf, a white fragrant flower, and a thin, fragrant root. It also possesses powers combined from both locations—namely, hot and dry. It is hot from the earth and dry from the salt mixed into the sea waters. The **Myrtle** grows in both the mountains and on the shores, according to **Virgil**.
<margin>Shores are most pleasing to myrtles. Virgil, Georgics Book 2.</margin>
And they call it "Venereal" <note>belonging to Venus</note> because it grows in the sea, where Venus was born. It is endowed with contrary qualities: the cold-earthy nature prevails in it, but it also possesses the heat of the earth and dries powerfully. It is effective for the discharge of blood, erosion of the bladder, urine, bites from venomous spiders <note>original: "phalangiorum"</note> and scorpions, eye inflammations, fistulas of the eye <note>original: "ægilopis"</note>, and other ailments. **Tripolium** <note>Sea-starwort</note> grows in maritime places where the wave strikes and leaves again as it recedes, so that it is neither in the sea nor on dry land. It has a leaf like woad <note>original: "glaſti"</note> but thicker, with a white, fragrant root and a hot taste. It works against poisons and disperses water <note>edema</note> and urine. Truly amphibious animals of the land and sea include the **kingfishers** <note>original: "alcyonij"</note> and **seals** <note>original: "vituli marini," literally "sea calves"</note>, whose powers are likewise mixed.

# BOOK TWO

<warning>Significant bleed-through from the reverse side of the page makes text from the following page visible in the background.</warning>

Just as plants correspond to the climate <note>original: "cœlum regionis," literally the "sky of the region"</note> of their territory in their appearance and quality, I believe it is possible for us to investigate the forms and powers of plants from those same heavenly quarters. We have already seen this in the descriptions of the human form: those who inhabit the scorched regions of the sky <note>the tropical or "Torrid Zone"</note> have short bodies, thin legs, curly hair, little blood, and a hot, dry temperament. Similarly, plants—which share no small amount of correspondence <note>original: "symboli," referring to the Hermetic idea of "signatures" or sympathies between different parts of nature</note> with human bodies—follow this pattern. In THIS illustration, we have depicted three small plants corresponding to three segments of the sky:

The inhabitant of burning places has a parched and lean appearance; it grows into slender, dense, sapless, twisted, and rigid twigs, covered in a scaly bark. Its leaves are tiny, narrow, curled, and jagged, and not very green in color. The flowers are sometimes saffron-colored and very fragrant; the fruit is small and fragrant, with a sharp taste. The seed is black, and the root is small and woody. These plants are of longer duration <note>they have longer lifespans compared to lush, watery plants</note>.

But let us approach the reasoning behind these physical lines. Those plants that live in the South, in scorched and parched places, draw in less nourishment, but they "cook" <note>original: "coquunt," referring to the metabolic process of "concoction" where internal heat matures the plant's nutrients</note> what they have drawn in more thoroughly. ### PHYTOGNOMONICS BOOK III.
#### I
<meta>catchword: proue-</meta>

Plants do not turn out tall, but rather shrubby and somewhat thick; they are also more branched because the sap is spread outward more than it rises upward, as is held by Theophrastus <note>original: "Theophrasto," the Greek "Father of Botany"</note> in his book *On the Causes of Plants*. They rise up with sturdy stalks because the cause is dryness; for just as a humid plant is soft, weak, and ineffective due to water, so a plant from dry earth is stronger and more stable in its function. Likewise, the Ethiopians, being drier and living under the Torrid Zone, are curly-haired, lean, muscular, and robust, according to Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>original: "Aphrodiseo," a celebrated commentator on Aristotle</note>. 

Regarding why plants might be born with curly leaves, Aristotle, in his *Problems*, gives the reason when explaining why cucumbers buried in the earth grow larger: he says the sun and the spirit <note>original: "spiritus," likely referring to moving air or "pneuma"</note> impede growth by drying out what is exposed to them, making the mass both smaller and curlier, just like trees that are exposed to the wind and their leaves. And Avicenna <note>the famous Persian physician and philosopher</note>, giving the reason why hair curls, says that just as leather curls when scorched by fire, so the hair of the head can be curled by its own heat or by the fervor of the sky. This can be applied to foliage without being out of place. Hair can also turn out curly if the skin is dense and the pores are narrow; hair, iron, or anything else of that kind that is forced through a narrow space becomes curved. Thus, the density of the bark caused by the heat of the sun and narrow pores can make the foliage curly. 

Wild herbs have curlier leaves than cultivated ones, which have smooth and extended leaves, because the wild ones are drier. Curly-leaved cabbage <note>original: "Brassica crispifolia"</note> is superior to the smooth kind according to Theophrastus because it is drier and, for that reason, more flavorful; for we have said that flavor consists of a state of incomplete dryness. The same should be said of lettuces, among which the curly one is more flavorful because it is drier than the humid ones. In the aging sow-thistle <note>original: "soncho"</note>, the leaves curl because it becomes drier. Ground ivy <note>original: "Hedera terrestris"</note> has curly leaves and is hot and dry. It has a tiny flower, saffron-colored or reddish, which is proof of immoderate dryness and heat. The leaves are less green in the South, for the greenness is diluted by heat as the moisture is resolved.

But let us speak of scent. Aristotle said that in all parts of the earth that face the East, plants are born more fragrant than those in the North, and those in the East more than those in the South, because the regions of Syria and Arabia are more fertile and "earthy," whereas Africa is sandy and thirsty. For it is necessary that moisture neither be excessive (for excessive moisture cannot be <term>concocted</term> <note>the process of ripening or "digestion" by natural heat</note>) nor entirely absent, for in that case no vapor can be drawn out. Likewise, in plants that are hot and dry by nature, their moisture is not dreggy but can be concocted more quickly. This is also evident in the regions of the earth which, as they are more burning, are thus more fragrant—such as Syria and Arabia—and it can be proven in the towns of those regions which we know to be dry and hot. 

Theophrastus likewise says that fragrant plants are born in regions verging toward the East and South, such as in Arabia, Syria, and India—such as frankincense, myrrh, cassia, <term>laser</term> <note>a resin from a now-extinct or unidentified plant, likely silphium</note>, cinnamon, and others. Burning places are fertile in scents, and plants which elsewhere lack scent are fragrant in these places, such as the reed and the rush. This is especially true in Syria and in those places that are arid, like those which grow in Cyrene <note>a Greek colony in modern-day Libya</note>; for they are more fragrant for no reason other than their dryness. For a thin, dry field, not excessively burning, with pure and serene air surrounding it—all these are most fit for creating scent. And those plants placed in sunny spots are more fragrant than those in shady ones, especially those facing South, because they draw in less nourishment and better "cook" <note>concoct</note> what they have drawn. Dryness is more suitable for scent, and all fragrant things tend toward it. The proof of this is that in sweltering tracts, more and better kinds of fragrant things come forth.

Theophrastus gives the reason in the place cited above as to why they have a pungent and powerful taste: since pungency and scent follow one another closely. For scent comes from a thinner, drier moisture that is easily diffused, whereas pungency comes from dryness. For this reason, scent exists where there is pungency or oiliness, as in wild thyme, water-mint, rue, parsley, and mint. Furthermore, things that experience scorching are bitter; under the Torrid Zone all things are scorched, and therefore they are almost all bitter. The experiment of lye is proof: it is made from ash produced from burnt wood and is notably bitter. African iris is more bitter than the Illyrian or Macedonian varieties. So also <term>arum</term> <note>Cuckoo-pint or Jack-in-the-pulpit</note> in the region of Cyrenaica possesses the least pungency, but in Pergamum (the fatherland of Galen <note>the influential Roman physician</note>), it is more pungent. Likewise, the caper in Libya from the Red Sea is wonderfully and immoderately pungent, so much so that it raises blisters in the mouth, while in Apulia it is edible. And so with the rest. Their seed is black or saffron-colored inside; for while some aromatic seed is being ground, the flour is black or dark.

...this happens, as can be seen in pepper, cinnamon, cubebs <note>original: "cubebe," a pungent spice related to black pepper</note>, and others; whereas those plants that grow in our own region mostly yield a white flour. But before we speak of the medicinal powers of plants living under the Torrid Zone <note>the tropical region near the equator</note>, we must clear up the opinions of the ancient philosophers. Empedocles—as we have already said—held this view, and Mnestor followed it according to the reports of Theophrastus <note>the "Father of Botany"</note>: he claimed that plants able to endure in freezing places are allotted more internal heat, such as the fir, pine, cedar, and juniper; for such trees could not survive in these places except by reason of their heat. Aristotle seems to follow this opinion in his *Problems*, for he says that nature behaves contrary to the environment; because if a field were similar to its inhabitant, it would quickly fail—thus those who live in hot places are cooled internally, and those in cold places are warmed. Theophrastus thinks this was foolishly said, since each thing is best able to endure in a similar environment where it cannot be harmed; on the contrary, things are vulnerable to influences from their opposites. Averroes <note>the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher</note> says in the fifth book of his *Colliget* <note>his medical encyclopedia</note>: "Plants that grow in hot places are for the most part hot in nature, like those brought from India; and those that grow in cold places are mostly cold. And it can sometimes happen by accident that hot plants grow in cold lands, like the pine which grows in Illyria <note>the western Balkans</note>, and cold plants in hot lands, like tamarinds which grow in the land of the Arabs. This happens for two reasons: either because their bark is dense on the outside, or because they are submerged under water—conditions that can provide both cold and heat in any region; because much heat existing within them is contracted inside on account of the external coldness." I say it happens by reason of placement: hot plants can live in the North if they are planted in a spot facing the South, and cold plants can live in the South if facing the North, as we shall discuss more extensively. Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>a commentator on Aristotle</note> says that places facing the South possess miraculous virtues. Theophrastus said, on the authority of Homer, that many poisonous things grow in Egypt, and he says that Helen received her poisons there.

Southern plants serve as remedies for poison: for the bites of snakes differ by location, and the types of serpents born in sweltering places are more pestilential; colder regions produce less terrifying snakes. Because of this, by a wonderful kindness of nature, where the evil abounds, there also is the remedy. Almost all herbs growing under the equator are effective against the bites of venomous creatures. Aromatics—which the Greeks did not record, but the Arabs did—are also excellent for conditions of the heart. And because they are as if scorched by the excessive heat of the Sun, they become bitter; for this reason, they can kill or expel the fetus in the womb, and likewise the humors. They are also somewhat sharp, therefore they have an incisive quality <note>term: "inciding" (incidunt) refers to the medicinal ability to break down thick fluids or obstructions in the body</note>, which is why they are suitable for those with kidney stones, and they promote urine and menstruation; they also heal the spleen, since they are of a thin essence. **Myrrh** grows in Troglodyte Arabia <note>referring to the "Cave-dwellers" of the Red Sea coast</note>. It is a thorny tree with a hard, twisted trunk, rough bark, and a leaf more crinkled than an olive. It grows in clay and sandy soil. It warms, dries, and binds. It promotes menstruation, expels the birth quickly, and kills worms and moths. **Frankincense** <note>original: "Thus"</note> is a native of Arabia, so much so that the region is called "incense-bearing." A small tree with leaves like the lentisk <note>the mastic tree</note>; it warms and binds. Galen <note>the influential Roman physician</note> said it dries. **Styrax** <note>a fragrant resin</note> grows in Pisidia, Sidon, Cyprus, and Cilicia. It warms, digests, softens, promotes menstruation, and resists poisons. **Bdellium** is the "tear" or resin of a Saracen tree: it grows in Arabia, Media, India, and Babylon. It is a black tree, the size of an olive, with a leaf like an oak. It warms and softens, crushes stones, moves urine, and helps those bitten by serpents. **Cardamom** comes from Commagene <note>an ancient kingdom in modern Turkey</note>, Armenia, Arabia, and India. It has a sharp and somewhat bitter taste. It warms. It is used for epilepsy <note>original: "comitiales," the "falling sickness"</note>, sciatica, menstruation, ruptures, griping pains, tapeworms, kidney issues, difficulty of urine, and other ailments. **Amomum** <note>a spice similar to cardamom</note> grows as a small shrub in Armenia and Media, with a small flower, leaves like bryony, and reddish inner bark; the Median variety has a veined shrub with the scent of oregano. It warms, dries, and binds. It heals the bites of the scorpion. **Cassia fistula** <note>the purging cassia</note> warms; Galen said it dries. It promotes urine and menstruation, and is effective for snake bites and vices of the kidneys. **Cinnamon** has very tender branches, surrounded by frequent knots; it is sharp. ...biting, it warms and cooks <note>the digestive "cooking" of humors</note>. It promotes urine and menstruation, aids in childbirth, and expels broadworms. **Pseudo-costus** <note>original: "Pseudo-costus," a plant often confused with the aromatic ginger-relative Costus</note> has leaves like a parsnip, but rougher; the flower is the color of honey. **Fragrant rush** <note>original: "Iuncus odoratus," likely Camel Grass</note> comes from Africa, Arabia, Nabataea, or Babylonia; it possesses a fiery heat on the tongue, is astringent, and is composed of fine parts. It promotes urine and menstruation and is mixed into antidotes. **Balsam** is produced in Judea and Egypt, having a thin and hair-like foliage. It warms. It moves the menses, urine, and childbirth, and is effective against poisons and sciatica. **Spikenard** <note>original: "Nardus"</note> grows in Syria: it heats and dries. It promotes urine and is effective for kidney defects, poisons, and eye remedies. **Laserwort** <note>original: "Laserpitium," the source of the famed ancient spice Silphium</note> grows in Syria, Armenia, and Libya. It is sharp and warms; Galen stated it consists of fine parts and possesses an airy and fiery essence. It is excellent for those suffering from sciatica, poisons, eye-sight issues, and epilepsy <note>original: "comitialibus," the 'falling sickness'</note>. **Sweet flag** <note>original: "Acorum"</note> is found in Colchis, Galatia, and Crete: it warms, and Galen said it has a very fine essence and is drying. It promotes urine and treats epilepsy, ruptures, snake bites, and dimness of vision. India and Arabia export **Agarwood** <note>original: "Agalochum"</note>. It is hot and dry. Likewise, **Cyperus** from Cilicia, Syria, and the Cyclades islands is hot. It promotes urine and helps with bladder stones, snake venom, and inducing menstruation.

## THE FORMS and qualities of ANIMALS LIVING UNDER THE
## HOT ZONE. Chapter XXVIII.

We shall say the same things regarding animals living under the Hot Zone <note>the tropical regions near the equator</note>, whose form shall be as follows.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' with floral patterns.</image-desc>
ANIMALS inhabiting burning places are of SAVAGE appearance and character, with curly hair <note>original: "capillo vibrato," literally vibrating or flickering hair</note>, splayed feet, and black bodies; and they are of longer life.

These are the causes according to physiognomy <note>the study of physical features to determine character</note>. *Aristotle* in his *Problems* reported that animals born under excessive heat or cold have savage appearances: and the cause is the excess of cold or heat, which displaces and perverts the temperament of the body, from which the form arises. He declares in the same place that they have splayed feet: for just as wood is warped by heat, so their bodies are usually distorted by heat, which is also shown by the hair, which they bear more curly than others; for curliness is, as it were, a "splaying" of the hair. The reason for curly hair is heat, as we have said, for dried hair bends and curves. They are usually of black color and have black eyes, for all things are scorched by heat, and those things which are scorched are black; and the color of the eyes is assimilated to the rest of the body's color, so because they themselves are black, the eyes are black as well. They are also of longer life because they consist of a drier nature: for that which is dry is firmer and more lasting. Or perhaps because [internal heat] is accustomed to cool cold places, but in hot places it is more devastated and consumed by the surrounding heat.

But let us come to their specific powers. *Aphrodisiensis* <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, an influential commentator on Aristotle</note> said that the animals inhabiting the Hot Zone are hot. *Empedocles*, as we have mentioned, felt the opposite. These are the powers of those which are hot and dry. *Oppian* said **Lions** are born in Libya; they are numerous in Africa and Syria; in Europe they are found only between the rivers Achelous and Nessus, where they are far more powerful according to *Aristotle*; today they are not born in Europe because they require a greater abundance of heat. **Lion** meat surpasses all others in heat, according to *Isaac* <note>Isaac Judaeus, a prominent 10th-century physician</note>. The East grazes **Camels** among its herds, of which there are two kinds: the **Bactrian** and the **Arabian**. *Rhazes* <note>the Persian physician al-Razi</note> said they are of a hot and dry temperament. **Gazelles** <note>original: "dorcades"</note> are in Libya according to *Aelian*; *Philostratus* says they are found beyond the waterfalls of the Nile; *Pliny* testifies that **gazelles** and **hyenas** do not cross the mountains of Syria. *Simeon Sethi* wrote that its meat is drying. The **musk-bearing deer** <note>original: "Moschica preolus"</note> is found in the regions of Africa, Egypt, and Syria. Musk is held to be hot and dry according to the same author and *Avicenna*. According to *Aristotle*, there are no **Panthers** in Asia or Europe; *Rhazes* reported their meat to be hot and parched. The **Skink** <note>a lizard used in traditional medicine, often as an aphrodisiac</note> is brought to us from the East and Egypt; *Dioscorides* says it comes from *Lydia in Mauritania*; it is hot according to *Avicenna* and dry according to *Paul* <note>Paul of Aegina</note>.

### ON THE FORM AND POWER OF PLANTS AND ANIMALS Dwelling in the North. Chapter 38.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'S' containing an illustration of a plant with long, thin leaves and a distinct root system, representing the Aconite plant mentioned in the adjacent text.</image-desc>

<insert>
NEAR THE FRONT of the twenty-sixth chapter, there is a table where, in the last place, we have depicted the **aconite** plant <note>original: "aconiti plantam"; commonly known as monkshood or wolfsbane</note>, a nursling of the dewy heavens; behold it there.
</insert>

Opposite [the southern plants], there follow those that live in the freezing northern regions; for they are allotted contrary forms and powers. We have stated in human Physiognomy that those living under the North <note>original: "Septentrione," referring to the constellation of the Great Bear used to denote the North</note> are of immense and tall stature, with whitish skin and eyes, thickening legs, and soft, long hair.

WITH AN EXTREMELY LARGE and more robust body, upright, tall, and without knots, the plant of cold places rises, fierce in appearance and soft. The flower is white, with a faint or foul odor. It germinates and bears fruit late. It is difficult to fruit, or of poor and often poisonous nourishment.

The reasons for the assigned appearance are these. That it rises with a tall, knotless, simple, and straight stalk, Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher, often called the "father of botany"</note> explains, saying: "Wherever the part of the whole forest facing the North produces denser and more beautiful wood, and generally better and altogether more robust ones grow, increase, and flourish in the North winds <note>original: "Aquilonijs," from Aquilo, the north wind</note>: they are thick in length rather than width, and therefore knotless, straight, and tall; and the best oars are made from these." Fruits ripen late in cold places: the reason according to the same author is that it is heat which "cooks" <note>original: "concoquit," the vital process of metabolic maturation or ripening in ancient science</note>; excessive cold dries out and makes things bitter, while a moderate temperature nourishes most conveniently. In food, things grown in cold, rainy places are raw and difficult to digest because they draw a more abundant and stronger nourishment. Boeotian grain <note>from Boeotia, a region in Greece</note> is heavy, as are the other fruits of that field, because the soil is very rich and the air is cold. The North wind produces many poisons. **Aconites** are so named because they grow on steep cliffs <note>original: "præruptis cautibus"</note> and in the coldest places; so too **hemlock** <note>original: "cicuta"</note> near Susa in the cold mountains. Columella <note>Roman writer on agriculture</note>, describing the best quality of garden soil, adds that it should not produce poisons—that is, it should not have a cold climate.

> *But it denies hellebore, and those harmful with galbanum juice,*
> *Nor does it suffer yew trees, nor does it pour out vigorous toxins.*
> <note>A poetic fragment, likely referencing Virgil or Columella, asserting that good soil rejects poisonous plants.</note>

We must attribute this to nothing less than the supreme kindness of Nature, who sent poisons away to such remote places so that men might not eat them inadvertently; she willed that salutary and harmless herbs should be with us. Hence it is reasonable to believe that in cold air, open sun, and even with modest nourishment, poisons are at their most potent. For this reason, more seem to grow in the mountains, especially those that are highest and most vast, according to Theophrastus. But medicines that grow in northern, cold, and dry places are superior to those in damp ones; thus, those produced by Euboea were better, while those from Telethrium were worse, for in the former they grew drier, and in the latter more humid. They are foul-smelling because a certain rawness of "excrement" <note>waste products within the plant</note> is the cause of a bad odor; for this reason, some sweats, and sometimes flatulence and the belches of those with indigestion, smell more foully. Thus, the hotter regions of the earth are more fragrant, while the colder ones, because they can "cook" <note>ripen/digest</note> less, are ill-smelling, as Aristotle says in the *Problems*. But only the **Iris** grows among the Illyrians and breathes more toward the North. Their powers, like their form, correspond to the character of the region: hence no one need fear that northern plants are cold and dry. **Aconites** are so named because they come forth on the peaks of mountains; in Pontus, and on the Justinian mountains of Italy, with a yellow flower, and a slightly hairy stalk and leaf. No one doubts that all are poisons and bring certain death. **Hemlock** <note>original: "Cicuta"</note> with narrow leaves, a whitish flower, and a foul odor, kills by cold. Avicenna <note>Persian polymath and physician</note> said it is cold and dry at the end of the third degree; but in the coldest places it is poisonous, and therefore should be sought from Susa. The **Yew** <note>original: "Taxus"</note>, similar to the fir, is described by Theophrastus as having poisonous properties and growing in very cold places. It is of such immediate poison...

it is said that those sleeping under its shade may die. Ivy hates heat and loves the cold, which is why it can barely grow in burning climates; for this reason, it did not survive in Babylonia, being unable to endure the contrary conditions of that region. It is reported that the sky there is so heavy and sweltering that it dries out and exhausts the water-filled skins <note>original: "utres," leather bags used for carrying liquids</note> upon which merchants sleep. Indeed, when Alexander ordered Harpalus <note>Harpalus was Alexander the Great's treasurer and governor in Babylon</note> to plant ivy in the Babylonian gardens—so that in those places burning with heat, the leafy foliage of the ivy might ward off the discomforts of the sun with its shade—tradition says it failed to take root, despite Harpalus's great efforts to plant it in that region; instead, it wasted away and completely dried up. Tryphon <note>A Greek grammarian and physician</note> claims it causes delirium, much like henbane, and moves the mind toward madness, along with other destructive qualities. 

But the form of animals living in the North <note>original: "Septentrione," referring to the northern constellation of the Great Bear</note> is as follows: They have large bodies, a fierce look, long and soft hair, a whitish color, grey-blue eyes, thick legs, and a tasteless flavor to their meat. As for why they have a fierce look, we provided the reason in the previous chapter; regarding their yellow and whitish color, and the nature of their eyes and hair, we discussed these in our work on human Physiognomy under the same qualities. Cold regions produce **bears**; according to Pliny, there seem to be no bears, deer, or bees in Africa. Herodotus says there are bears in Media <note>An ancient region in modern-day Iran</note>: an animal that is cold, moist, and full of phlegm. Pliny says the **swine** genus is not born in Arabia. If the Scenite Arabs <note>Nomadic "tent-dwelling" Arabs</note> introduce them there, they die. According to Solinus, India has neither wild nor tame swine, as Ctesias <note>A Greek physician and historian</note> writes. Aristotle notes that Germany abounds in swine, and those of Belgium are fierce. Their meat is cold and moist. **Wolves** in Egypt are smaller than those in Greece; Aristotle said they are much larger than foxes. Africa and Egypt produce **dogs** in their cold regions <note>The author likely means the cooler mountainous areas or is misattributing the climate</note>. Their meat is cold and dry according to Rhazes <note>An influential Persian physician and polymath</note>. **Toads** <note>original: "Rubetæ," specifically bramble-toads</note> are found in cold and moist places and in shady groves; they are more venomous in cold regions than in hot ones. They are an extremely cold and moist animal. Many **badgers** <note>original: "Meles"</note> are found in the Alpine regions.

### ON THE APPEARANCE AND POWER [OF LIFE] IN THE TEMPERATE ZONE
->*of the plants and animals growing there. Chapter XXVIIII.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring elaborate foliate scrollwork within a square frame.</image-desc>
There follows, between the two extreme locations, the middle one: namely the temperate zone where we live. Sloping toward the South, it is warmer; toward the North, it is colder; therefore, in the middle, the temperament of the air is more indulgent. In the extremes there are poisons, but in the middle there is nourishment and things beneficial to man; and if any things from the North or the South are brought to our regions, their wildness is tamed by the indulgence of the sky and they become milder, more suited to human nature. The form shall be this:

> *IN the table described in the middle of the twenty-sixth chapter, we have depicted a **rose**, which grows in a temperate climate; look for it there.*

The plant does not present itself to the eye with the scrawny and parched habit of Africa, nor the swollen and elongated habit of the North; instead, the temperate tracts—which nourish these plants like the gardens of the entire world—produce a form midway between the two, with a more cheerful appearance. The indulgent sky provides it with just enough sap and substance <note>original: "faginæ," literally "beech-mast" but used here to mean food or bulk</note> that it may appear more robust than the southern plants and less starved than the northern ones. Leaves clothe the branches to the very tips in a dense sprout; they are not wider or more flourishing than the northern ones, nor narrower than those of Libya. Flowers of various colors and scents crowd the stalks. They have a manifold and dense fruitfulness of apples <note>original: "pomorum," a general term for fruit</note>, from which no foul spirit or odorless air comes (like the children of the cold sky), nor do they smell of heavy spice (like those of the south), but a fragrant scent fills the nostrils. The flavor is not burning, sharp, or tasteless, but very pleasant, so that it serves as food and profit for human life, not a detriment. The root is swollen and not without strength; and finally, in appearance and power, it is not unlike a plant that loves moderate earth, but emulates it so closely that you will often take one for the other.

We have frequently brought forth reasons for such a description from its opposites. Lest we rather...

We have decided to omit these details, lest we cause more weariness than benefit to modern readers. Their strengths also maintain a balance between the two extremes, lightly touching upon the hot, cold, moist, and dry, or rather leaning toward heat and moisture, so that they are able to digest, soften, or provide nourishment. The grapevine, impatient with too cold a sky, produces very little fruit under such conditions; however, in a temperate sky, it pours out life with a wild luxuriance, acting as a "wine-fountain" <note>original: "vinifunda"</note>, easily granting a fruit that is the chief of all in sweetness and health, from which man—the prince of animals—draws his drink. It flows with a liquid of heat and moisture, which is very familiar to human nature. Wheat, called *sitos* <note>original: σιτος</note> by the Greeks because it serves as food for all of mankind and sustains life, or "frumentum" <note>the general Latin term for grain</note>, is what we enjoy. Under a favorable sky, it comes forth with the most fertile ears of seed; and although it is grown in all regions out of necessity, the fruit of Italy surpasses the others. This was the opinion held during the reign of Alexander the Great, when Greece was the most powerful nation in the whole world. As the poet Sophocles said:

->*And fortunate Italy, shining white with pale grain.*<-

When applied, it warms and moistens; it is most familiar to our nature. There is also little difference between wheat, winter wheat, and spelt: for when the former grain is lacking, we eat these, which receive the same praise and recommendation. Indeed, they are very similar to wheat, very abundant, and pleasant to all living creatures. It possesses a middle temperament between barley and wheat. The same is true of rice-wheat, oats, rye, sorghum, and similar grains. The same must be said of legumes, as they do not differ much from these strengths and characters. Licorice is also familiar to our nature. Similarly, the rose rejoices on warm hills and in a temperate sky, and its power departs little from the middle; so also the lily, the white violet, and trees like figs, pomegranates, apples, pears, and olives. So too are the qualities and forms of animals in middle regions. In peaceful regions, peaceful animals live, and they also obtain a middle form among them. For instance, they have a medium size, and their hair is neither long nor curly, but straight and soft; their colors are moderate, the causes of which depend on what was said before. All our regions abound in oxen; Galen said that beef <note>original: "bubulas carnes"</note> provides us with a significant and suitable nourishment. Goat meat is similar to our own temperament and provides much nourishment; for this reason, Clitarchus of Carthage, a follower of the New Academy, wrote that a certain Theban athlete lived on this meat and surpassed the other youths of his age in strength. However, kids are preferred over goats. Lambs provide us with hot and moist nourishment, and those one year old are in better condition than those older, according to Oribasius; their milk provides the most nourishment of all. Among the birds, hens surpass all others and are easily digested; similarly, partridges, francolins <note>original: "attagenæ," a type of game bird</note>, and doves hold the highest praise for their meat among birds; producing neither thin nor thick humors, they are sought after by everyone for their excellent nourishment, according to Simeon Seth. Phoenicides, in the writings of Athenaeus, says he has tasted various delicacies, but none of them could be compared with the francolin. The francolin is an Asian bird, especially those born in Ionia, and is numbered among the choice foods, according to Gellius and Martial. Thrushes are also praised among foods, producing neither thin nor thick humors, like animals of a temperate climate, as are nearly infinite other animals.

### ON THE LOCATION, AND ON THE APPEARANCE
### and powers of mountain plants. Chapter XXXI.

We have spoken about the influences from the heavens; now we shall speak of location <note>The author uses "situs" to mean the specific environmental setting or microclimate of a plant.</note>, for it performs the same role as the atmosphere. Mountains, hills, plains, and valleys change the climate; by reason of its location, a site can maintain cold conditions or create warmth. Conversely, it can dry out damp places or moisten dry ones. Indeed, in hotter regions, the parts of mountains facing North <note>original: "Septentrioni"</note> are cold, while in Northern regions, the parts facing South <note>original: "Meridiei"</note> are warm. Finally, within the small circuit of a single estate, we can have a miniature of the entire world: the heat of the South, the chills of the North, and the mildness of the middle region. This is to "marry the sky with the earth," which is what our ancestors so greatly desired.

*We have placed at the head of this chapter some herbs showing the varieties of location, expressed in this table, believing their figures will be sufficient for demonstration. From the right <note>The author likely refers to the order in the accompanying woodcut.</note>, the first inhabitant of the mountains, hyssop, appears; the second, a native of the plains, is <term>samphire</term> <note>original: "crithmus," a coastal plant often found in rocky, flat areas near the sea.</note>; the third, from the valleys, is the mandrake; and the last, from the hills, is the grapevine. These will be described in their own specific chapters—twenty-five, twenty-six, and twenty-seven—so that we are not forced to repeat each one here.*

### BOOK TWO

K 2

By such a method, we make plants brought from cold, northern climates or from parched Africa into inhabitants of our own regions, by positioning the former to face the South and the latter to face away from it. To favor recent discoveries and not break the order of our discourse, now that we have spoken of the segments of the heavens, we shall speak of location, beginning first with the mountains, and we shall describe the powers and forms of mountain plants. But first, let us look at the forms of the animals living on the high peaks of the mountains. For the inhabitants of the Alps or the mountains are rough in appearance, lean, and parched; they have swollen throats <note>original: "guttura habentes strumosa," a reference to goiters, which were historically prevalent in alpine regions due to iodine deficiency</note>, yet they possess a healthy complexion and live quite long. The animals there are rougher and wilder, with more robust strength than those dwelling in the plains.

**ROUGH**, scrawny, lean, and with a rather somber appearance, mountain plants testify to their unhappy birth; the entire form of their body rises up short and delicate. They have a thorny stem—or, if you prefer, a rough, knotted, hairy, twisted, parched, solid, and rigid one. The leaf is small, curled, and hairy, with nerves or little ridges standing out, projected like rays from the stem to the edges. The flower is colorless and less fragrant. The fruit is flavorful, sometimes sharp when cooked, small, and no less scented. It sprouts, flowers, and ripens its fruit late. The root is small, resting on tiny fibers, but it is a gift highly recommended for medicinal uses. These plants are perennial <note>original: "vitæ perennis," meaning they live through many seasons</note>.

But let us explain the causes of such a physical appearance. The fact that the plant is short and delicate is caused by the nature of the place, which is arid, drained of moisture, and thirsty. Aristotle, giving the reason in his *Problems* <note>A reference to the Aristotelian work *Problemata*</note> as to why animals of small bodies are produced, said it was by reason of nourishment: if it is meager and there is a great lack of food, large bodies cannot be produced. Because of this, they seem to consist of childlike limbs; thus, though they are quite small, they have all the parts of their bodies in proportion, like <term>Maltese puppies</term> <note>original: "melitenses catelli," a breed famous in antiquity for its diminutive size</note>. They are indeed curled, knotted, and solid, and this also proceeds from the condition of the place: for trees exposed to the wind and the sun turn out this way. Aristotle brings forward the reasons in the same place: for the sun and the drying winds hinder growth, making the bulk both smaller and more curled; thus they grow small and solid, with no surrounding obstacle to provide more abundant nourishment or to prevent the food from drying up or vanishing.

Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> also wrote that in places exposed to blasts of wind and in sunny spots, or in thin and loose soil, plants come forth short and knotted: for the winds roughen them and create knots for the sake of "twisting and consistency" <note>original: "retorsionis & consistentiæ causa," referring to the plant's structural reinforcement against the wind</note>. And elsewhere he relates that in dry and rocky places, rough things are born; for this reason, the mountain-dweller is rough, and mountain ashes are pleasingly colored, curled, and solid, and men use them for more elegant craftsmanship. Finally, mountain plants, because of the cold, are rougher, thornier, more knotted, and smaller in size than those born in the plains. We experience this in ourselves: whenever we shiver from cold or wind, an unevenness immediately arises on the skin as the heat and moisture are driven inward. Thus the flesh sinks, the hairs protect the place with their stiffness, and the skin becomes roughened <note>A description of "goosebumps" used as a biological analogy</note>. 

He also said elsewhere that mountain plants are more knotted than those of the fields, and in sunny spots they are knotted and twisted. Apples and pears produced in the mountains are short, knotted, and thorny, while in the plains they are larger, more beautiful, and better to look at, both in their wood and their fruit; yet mountain plants are more useful in practice. Those that grow in the mountains are also thorny because they are dry; for thorniness and bristling come from dryness. Nowhere is there a more suitable place for producing thorns than a mountain. But as we are about to speak of thorns, let us look at the cause of thorns in plants, and first what Aristotle said in his book *On Plants*. He says that in such plants there is a certain "rarity" <note>In this context, a porousness or lack of density</note> through which cold moisture ascends, which then hardens by the power of the sun. 

This seems false to me: for almost all thorny plants are denser than others of their kind, and there is less passage for moisture through the spaces of their body. An example is the pear tree, which, when moved from wild places and given cultivation, lays aside that wild habit along with the thorns it would have borne when mature; at the same time, that density seen in its wild relatives is relaxed, whence it was transposed to a better nature. Nor should we agree that they arise from cold moisture: for many stalks, as long as they are somewhat cool, bear no thorns; when they have grown warm through a more advanced age or the heat of the year, they finally become prickly. Let the lettuce be taken as an example: when it begins to grow prickly, it is more bitter and hotter; so too are the artichoke, eryngium, aloe, and nettle. These examples will lead this opinion captive under the triumph of the senses <note>The author argues that direct observation/sensory evidence proves Aristotle wrong</note>.

ducent.

<summary>This page discusses the morphological characteristics of mountain plants and animals, attributing their small, gnarled, and thorny nature to harsh winds, sun, and lack of moisture. The author challenges Aristotle's theory on the origin of thorns, arguing instead that they result from plant density and heat rather than cold moisture.</summary>

# PHYTOGNOMY

...they lead. <term>Albertus</term> <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on natural philosophy and botany.</note> says that in thorny plants there is a scarcity of transverse pores coming from the head of the plant to the skin, and this is the path through which a thorn grows. The material of the thorn is a "terrestrial juice," which is extremely hot; because of the intensity of this material, its "cooking" <note>original: "decoctio," referring to the metabolic process of ripening or hardening in pre-modern science</note> is hastened right from the beginning of the plant's formation. This boiling, dry, and sharp material is drawn out through the scarcity of those transverse pores, and as it emerges on the outside, it is dried by the sun and hardens very strongly. That thorns arise from dryness is proven by the wild olive, the wild pine, the apple, and the wild pomegranate; while they live neglected in the woods, they are clothed in thorns, yet these same plants, once tamed by cultivation in gardens, develop smooth bark and their thorns vanish. In the same way, city plants neglected in the woods cast off their milder habit and turn into thorns, as we have said. And therefore <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BCE), often called the "Father of Botany."</note> says: "The wild plant has this peculiar trait above others, that it turns out harder and thornier in every part." Lettuce, as we have said, sends out thorns when it dries up; the same can be seen in the sow-thistle. For as we said regarding knots, plants that live in wintry, sunny, meager, and arid places become thornier, since a thorn is nothing but a sharper knot. Those that are born in moist, flat, and shady places are knotless and less thorny—or if they do have thorns, they are fewer, softer, and less sharp at the point. From this, it is judged that thorns happen because of dryness. Nor are the things <term>Theophrastus</term> said about city and wild plants far from our purpose: for land plants, because of their "earthy" nourishment, produce more woody fruits; on the other hand, city plants, because of their moist nourishment, produce less woody and more fleshy fruits, as can be seen in the almond.

It occurs to me now that <term>Aristotle</term> said in his book of *Problems* that roses with a rough "umbilicus" <note>The central part or receptacle of the flower.</note> smell sweeter than those with a smooth one, saying: "They smell sweeter because they have followed the limit of their nature, as a rose should be thorny." And <term>Theophrastus</term> said those roses are fragrant which have a rough lower part. And I would say that thorns argue for dryness, and those things which are dry are more fragrant, for the power of scent consists in dryness. Thus, thorns in plants are like the hard hair, horns, scales, and spines in animals; they show that their temperament <note>original: "complexionem"</note> is drier than others. <term>Athenæus</term> says: "Gudgeons, scorpions, flounders, and similar fish are called 'rock-dwellers'; they provide a dry nourishment to the body and are easy to digest, producing neither much excrement nor gas." And wild boars, because they live on drier food, have hard hair and stiffer, more prominent teeth, and they provide a drier nourishment, just like other wild animals. <term>Averroes</term> <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician.</note> felt the same in his *Colliget*, noting that a multitude of bones in animals, along with claws, nails, scales, and the like, signify that there is much "earthy" matter in them. In fish, scales and spines are praised because they signify a quality contrary to their temperaments <note>That is, the "earthy" hardness counteracts the natural "cold and wet" quality of the fish.</note>. And that the juice of these is of better and more excellent nourishment is shown by God in the Sacred Page, who forbids them to eat soft fish, which the Greeks call <term>malakosarkos</term> <note>original: μαλακόσαρκος; "soft-fleshed."</note>, such as thrushes, blackbirds, and the like.

But since thorns are pyramidal in shape—that is, proceeding from a thick base to a point—let us see what <term>Aristotle</term> says in his book *On Plants*. He says the "peculiar air" of the plant, poured out upward, increases its parts through the intensity of the material, which is what happens to the plants themselves, for they have a thinner top. <term>Albertus</term> brings another reason: the air enclosed in that material, which makes it "spirituous," increases the more it is elongated from the plant in which it breathes, and it vanishes into thin breezes; therefore, it must necessarily become sharper. But it does not seem to me that Aristotle has clearly hit upon the cause. Rather, the cause of the shape in a thorn is that the base is closer to the nourishment and therefore wider; this is also the case with the appearance of clusters, pine cones, and almost everything else. 

But we have dwelled enough on thorns; now let us move on. Mountain plants are more solid. <term>Theophrastus</term> wrote that in sunny places, they grow and stretch out in thickness and depth; for this reason, they rise up more crooked, more knotted, and altogether more solid and dense. Being made stronger and denser by the nature of the place, they are drier and more steadfast, since mountain places are more "airy" <note>original: "spiratiora," likely referring to better ventilation or "spirit" in the air.</note>. They are also more colorful. <term>Theophrastus</term>, speaking of the maple, says that in the mountains it is born yellow and pleasingly colored, but in the plains, it is white. Likewise, the ash tree in the mountains is colorful, but in the plains, it is colorless; in short, more colorful things are born in the mountains. <term>Aristotle</term> also says in the *Problems* that places with good ventilation provide a brightness of color, both to those who live on ships and those in the moun-

<summary>This page explains that thorns and hard structures in plants and animals are caused by environmental dryness and "earthy" material. It also notes that mountain plants are typically hardier, more fragrant, and more vibrantly colored than those in the plains.</summary>

# BOOK TWO

...are seen in the mountains with a more cheerful color than those in the plains. Those in sunny places are more fragrant than those in the shade, and especially those facing South, because they draw in less nourishment and better "cook" <note>original: "coquunt," referring to the internal metabolic process of ripening and refining nutrients through heat</note> what they have drawn in; the location ensures they do not grow tall but instead become shrub-like, as they gain thickness and split into many branches. This is because they take on many "beginnings" <note>buds or growth points</note> due to the heat thoroughly cooking and directing the growth in every direction. Mountain wines are fragrant. However, speaking of roses, violets, and other flowers, <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle, often called the father of botany.</note> said: In the mountains, they grow far less fragrant. Scents are produced not in a state of excessive and absolute concoction, but in the first stage; in the mountains, which are dry and sunny, they are cooked more than is proper. The plant produces smaller and lesser fruit because of the scarcity of the nourishment on which they feed. <term>Alexander of Aphrodisias</term> <note>A celebrated Peripatetic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 CE).</note> gives the reason: high and rocky places of the earth produce little fruit because they lack moisture, while low-lying places are wetter and thus found to be more fertile. Similarly, from a lack of moisture, the upper part of the head goes bald because it is thinner, while the lowest part is more hairy because it is more humble <note>lower and wetter</note>.

<term>Aristotle</term> gives the reason for sharper sap in his *Problems*. It occurs from thin and dry soil because the things growing in it do not possess much moisture. Therefore, things that are naturally sweet, due to the moderate amount of moisture they contain, are easily cooked once the Sun has consumed the greatest part. Indeed, to cook a great deal is a major task, but a moderate amount can be finished more quickly; hence, fruits created sweet by the law of their nature turn out even sweeter. Those that are dry and not sweet by nature retain only as much moisture as fits their kind due to the scarcity. The Sun, however, removes the sweetest and lightest parts, and so the sharpest parts are left behind; they lack the superfluous moisture that other fruits possess. 

There are also lighter foods, such as legumes, which, when grown in dry soil exposed to the Sun, are born "easy-to-cook" <note>original: "coctiua," meaning they soften quickly when boiled</note> because the power of the Sun pre-cooks them more. They sprout and bear fruit later, and this is by reason of the cold which constricts the trees. <term>Marcus Varro</term> <note>A Roman scholar and writer (116–27 BCE) known for his works on agriculture.</note> said that mountain places are milder, healthier, and produce later than the plains. Theophrastus said that in the mountains, they sprout last of all. For the same reason, roots are smaller than those in the plains.

The inhabitants of the mountains, both plants and animals, each in their own kind, live longer than those of the plains. Aristotle says in his *Problems*: those who dwell in high and open places age more slowly, while those in the plains age more quickly. For old age is a kind of rot, and that which is still rots, while that which moves is less affected—like flowing water. In high places, the air is stirred by the wind blowing from every side; in hollows, it remains motionless. Furthermore, in open places, the air is kept pure and varied because of its movement; in marshy places, it withers away. They grow slowly. The same author, giving the reason why some among the animal kinds give birth in a short time and others after a long time, said: "Thirsty air does not quickly nourish its offspring."

But let us observe what powers they provide to Physicians. The air in the mountains is thinner and more agile because it moves—proven by the fact that they freeze less. From the meager soil, plants of a dry temperament are born; from the sunniness of the location, they are hot. For those facing South are immediately exposed to the ever-increasing Sun. Because of their thin and meager nourishment, which is perfectly "digested," they consist of thin parts <note>original: "tenuium partium," referring to a subtle, volatile, and penetrating physical composition</note> of the same species. Physicians have tested that the medicines the mountains bear are more powerful than those of the plains. Because they are sharp and bitter, they kill internal parasites; because they are usually drier and hotter, they are caustic; they are effective against leprosy, skin eruptions, and scabies, and for destroying a fetus in the womb. By their sharp scent, they struggle against the bites of venomous creatures and put them to flight with their pungent odor. Because they are sharp and hot, they digest, thin out, and cut through thick humors, and they serve as remedies for those with elephantiasis. 

Because they consist of thin parts, they extinguish gas. <term>Galen</term> <note>The most influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire (c. 129–216 CE).</note> says that for the bites of venomous animals, any medicines that are hot, sharp, and made of thin parts should be taken like cauteries, as they easily attract the surrounding quality to themselves from deep within. Examples follow. **Rue** <note>original: "Ruta"</note> is common in gardens, but in the mountains, it has more vigorous powers and a more vehement scent according to <term>Dioscorides</term> <note>A Greek physician and botanist, author of "De Materia Medica."</note>; if eaten too copiously, it may kill. It has narrow leaves and rigid little stalks. It heats and dries; it provokes urine and menstruation, kills the fetus, is effective against serpents and poisons, drives away moths, and removes skin spots, crawling rashes, warts, and eruptions. It profits those with the "comitial disease" <note>original: "comitialibus," a historical term for epilepsy</note> and sciatica. More on the types of spurges...
