PHYTOGN.

There are several types: <term>characias</term> <note>shrub spurge</note> grows in mountains and rugged places; <term>myrsinites</term> <note>myrtle spurge</note> also grows in rugged places; <term>dendroides</term> <note>tree spurge</note> grows among rocks. Of all these, the *characias* is the most powerful, then the *myrsinites*, and after that the *dendroides*. Finally, there is the <term>paralios</term> <note>sea spurge</note>, which grows in maritime regions, and the <term>helioscopius</term> <note>sun-spurge</note>, which grows around towns; both of these have weaker powers, according to the judgment of <term>Dioscorides</term> and <term>Galen</term> <note>Two of the most influential medical authorities of antiquity.</note>. They remove <term>impetigo</term> <note>a skin infection</note>, stinging warts, hanging warts, <term>pterygia</term> <note>wing-like growths of tissue, often on the eye or around nails</note>, and similar conditions. <term>Oreoselinon</term> <note>mountain parsley</note> and <term>hipposelinon</term> <note>horse parsley</note> are more potent than others because they grow among rocks, according to Galen. <term>Hellebore</term>, on the authority of <term>Theophrastus</term>, grown on Mount Oeta, is far better than the Parnassian kind; indeed, in many places, both black hellebore and other roots are seen to be weaker. Dioscorides says it induces menstruation, kills the fetus <note>original: "partus necare," referring to its use as an abortifacient</note>, and heals scabies, <term>vitiligo</term> <note>skin depigmentation</note>, leprosy, and impetigo. Galen stated that it heats and dries in the third degree. There are two kinds of <term>polium</term> <note>germander</note>: the mountain kind is called *teucrium*; the other is more shrub-like, not quite as strong in scent, and weaker in its powers. <term>Pliny</term> calls the shrub-like one "field" and "greater" germander, and the wild one "lesser," which is called *teucrium*. It is used for snake bites and spleen disorders, to move the bowels and induce menstruation, and its smoke drives away serpents. Galen declared it hot and dry in the third degree. There is both mountain and garden <term>Hyssop</term>, but the mountain kind performs everything more effectively, according to <term>Mesue</term> <note>A famous Persian physician and pharmacologist.</note>. It has the power of thinning and heating; it kills worms and cures those with spleen disorders and <term>dropsy</term> <note>edema or swelling caused by fluid</note>. Galen said it consists of fine parts, dries and heats in the third degree, induces menstruation and urine, and sharpens the eyesight. <term>Calamint</term> is triple: mountain, field, and aquatic—but the latter is ineffective in its powers. They expel menstruation and urine, resist poisons, kill internal parasites, help those with <term>elephantiasis</term> <note>a disease characterized by thickening of the skin and underlying tissues</note>, assist in childbirth, and when burned, put serpents to flight; they help with sciatica. But for all these uses, the mountain kind is more effective; when tasted, it burns intensely and is sharp. There are two kinds of <term>Nard</term>: Syrian and Gangetic. It is called Syrian not because it grows in Syria, but because the part of the mountain where it originates faces the Syrians; Gangetic comes from the Ganges River flowing past the mountain. The latter is weaker in power, while the mountain kind is more fragrant, with a short and stunted spike. It moves the urine and clears the bowels. The variety of <term>Wormwood</term> that grows on Mount Taurus is superior. The powers of <term>Alkanets</term> are not the same: the *onoclea* variety has thinner leaves but more powerful virtue. The same must be said of *Polemonia*, *ptarmica* <note>sneezewort</note>, *thymelaea* <note>spurge flax</note>, *vincetoxicum*, peony, Alexandrian laurel, *daphnoide*, angelica, the second *tragium*, and juniper; all these grow in the mountains and acquire more vigorous virtues than their lowland counterparts.

-> ### THE FORM AND VIRTUES OF ANIMALS DWELLING IN THE MOUNTAINS. ### <-
-> ### Chapter XXXII. ### <-

We shall say the same regarding animals, and first concerning those of the mountains, whose form is lean, thin, and hard; their hair is stiff and colored, their eyes saffron-yellow, their hooves hard, and their flesh tasty and more potent in action. We described the reasons for these traits in the previous chapter. There are many herds of wild asses in Phrygia and Lycaonia, according to <term>Varro</term>. Asia and Africa produce herds of wild beasts, according to Pliny; they love high places and rocks. Pliny, after reviewing the remedies derived from domestic asses, adds that all the same remedies are more effective when taken from wild asses. <term>Gazelles</term> and wild goats prefer to graze in mountain places rather than the plains, according to Varro. Wild goats inhabit the highest crags and rocks; for this reason, physicians say that remedies should be sought from wild goats. Some elephants are from the marshes, others from the mountains, and others from the plains; those who dwell in the mountains differ from the others by their greater virtue and intelligence. There are mountain, field, and marsh hares, but mountain hares differ from field hares in their blackness, size, ferocity, thicker fur, and virtue. The <term>unicorn</term> <note>original: "monoceros"</note> frequents high mountains and solitudes; they say it is effective against poisons, the plague, and the <term>comitial disease</term> <note>epilepsy, so called because a seizure was considered a bad omen that would stop a Roman 'comitia' or assembly</note>. The panther is found chiefly in the mountains; its meat is dry. <term>Herodotus</term> wrote that monkeys live in the mountains. The Caucasus abounds with them, according to <term>Philostratus</term>; in the mountains of India, there is such a great multitude that they frequently terrified the troops of <term>Alexander the Great</term>. There are wild sheep and cattle in the mountains, according to <term>Aelian</term>; all of these are shown to have a more solid and potent virtue than their counterparts in the plains.

BOOK TWO.

# ON THE PHYSIOGNOMY OF PLAINS PLANTS
## and their powers. Chapter 34.

The situation of plains and hollow places is the opposite of mountains; and just as the location is opposite, so opposite powers and forms arise from opposite causes. Let us look at the forms of lowland animals: they are softer than mountain animals, shorter-lived, and lazier in their strength; they are thicker and weaker, yet more cheerful in grace and form. And if in the mountains everything was tiny due to a lack of nourishment, in the plain, where nourishment is abundant, everything will be fuller.

->You will find the illustration of the lowland <term>Samphire</term> <note>original: "Crithmi"</note> plant at the beginning of the twenty-second chapter.<-

Lowland plants rise with a vast and remarkable magnitude, appearing thick, moist, and lush. They have a shining stalk of notable smoothness, round, and crowded with many leaves that end in a round or broad point, colored a dark green. The flower is quite pretty, fragrant, and vigorous. They pour forth an insane, playful abundance of fruit—well-formed and beautiful—but they are more diluted in taste and smell, spoil more quickly than mountain fruits, and provide less nourishment. The root is large, spreading out with multiple "legs," stretched out in length, and ultimately does not differ much from a root that grows in rich, oily soil.

**The Causes.** Because the plant shines more cheerfully, <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the 'father of botany.'</note> says that among plants growing in both mountains and plains, the lowland ones always turn out larger in size, straighter, more beautiful to look at, and less knotty. Thus they are also looser in body, smoother, paler, and more colorless; the fruits are also sweeter, fleshier, and very large. We saw above from <term>Aristotle</term> in his *Problems* that animals and plants attain greater size from more nourishment; now, the plains and low-lying places produce abundantly because they are more humid, as <term>Alexander of Aphrodisias</term> <note>A famous commentator on Aristotle.</note> relates. <term>Marcus Varro</term> <note>A prolific Roman scholar.</note> said that everything in the plains fruits and sprouts faster than in the mountains; we have the reason for this from Aristotle's *Problems* by the opposite rule: plants fruit later in a thirsty field, therefore they fruit sooner in a humid and rich one. A sweet taste arises from a thickening juice and a full <term>concoction</term> <note>The process of "cooking" or ripening nutrients within a plant via natural heat.</note>; however, smell is different, as it consists of an initial and incomplete concoction. Therefore, plants that live in the plains, since they abound in nourishment, moisture, and heat, are able to achieve a perfect concoction, and for that reason bring forth fruit of a sweet taste; but they have a weak odor, since the mixing moisture dulls it.

But let us see what their birthplace contributes to the attainment of medicinal powers. Marcus Varro says there are three elevations of fields: mountain, hill, and plain; the mountain is cold, the hill is temperate, and the plain is hot. Therefore, where there are wide plains, there is more heat, and thus in <term>Apulia</term> <note>A region in Southern Italy known for its hot, flat landscape.</note> the places are hotter and there is much fodder; consequently, the powers [of plants there] are moderately hot and dry. Therefore, they are effective for those things which moderately hot things benefit: such as snake bites, and promoting the flow of urine and menstruation, fertility, and similar things. <term>Amomum</term> <note>An aromatic spice, possibly a type of cardamom.</note>, which grows in Media, heats, dries, and is effective against scorpion bites. <term>Eryngium</term> <note>Field Eryngo or Sea Holly.</note> grows in flatlands; it expels menses and urine, removes cramps and gas, and, being hot and dry, cures snake bites, ingested poisons, and the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>. <term>Verbascum</term> <note>Mullein.</note> grows in the plains and is used against scorpion stings. <term>Galen</term> <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire.</note> said it heats, dries, and constricts from the outside. The lowland <term>Calamintha</term> <note>Calamint.</note>, which is far inferior to the mountain variety, helps against poisons, intestinal parasites, and promotes menstruation and urine; it is hot and dry. <term>Leontopetalos</term> <note>Lion's leaf.</note> grows in plowed fields and grain crops; it is effective for snake bites and sciatica. According to Galen, it is hot and dry. <term>Fuchsius</term> <note>Leonhart Fuchs, a 16th-century German physician and botanist.</note> said that <term>Mercurialis</term> <note>The plant Mercury.</note> grows in the plains and has the power of dispersing [humors].

PHYTOGNOMONICA, BOOK II.

### THE POWER AND FORM OF PLANTS GROWING IN HOLLOW PLACES.
## Chapter 34.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' depicting a landscape with a multi-storied tower or castle on a hill and a radiant sun with a human face in the sky.</image-desc>
The shady depth of valleys stands in contrast to mountains that face the South; in the same way, the form of plants dwelling in hollow, damp places is the opposite of those found on mountains. For shady hollows contain continuous, thick vapors that cannot easily be scattered or changed. Let us describe the universal form of the plant that those born in the shade maintain, or ought to maintain.

->*You will find the MANDRAKE <note>original: "Mandragoram"</note> growing in shady places in the third position of the table at the beginning of the thirty-second chapter.*<-

A plant born in depressed hollows and shady places rises with a pale and somewhat sickly appearance, yet with a swollen and lustrous form, visible with a high "brow" <note>The author uses "high eyebrow" metaphorically to describe a prominent or haughty structural appearance</note>. Its stem is tender, smooth, without knots, and tall—so much so that because of its inherent weakness it can scarcely support its own weight—with a rich production of leaves drooping toward the ground. The leaf is large, fleshy, smooth, soft, and blunt at the edges, colored a dark green or a reddish-purple <note>original: "punicante"</note>. The flower is mostly sterile. The fruit is large, tasteless, scentless, and colorless. It bears fruit late. The root is large and spongy, and short-lived; in the end, its powers and lines are almost identical to those of a plant that seeks watery birthplaces or grows in wet and dripping spots, so that if anyone knows one of these, they will recognize both, and anyone would take one for the other.

But let us bring forward the reasons for these physical features. <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>A 4th-century BCE Greek philosopher known as the "Father of Botany" for his systematic descriptions of plants</note> affirms that trees which live in dark places, turned away from the winds and the sun, grow tall, smooth, and very high. Indeed, trees which by their nature are not suited to grow straight or tall will take on that very habit when hosted in such places, becoming straight and lofty. For example, they say that on Mount Haemus <note>The Balkan Mountains in modern-day Bulgaria</note>, oaks become so smooth and straight that they almost equal the heights of fir trees. This is because the plant matter is looser, more humid, and weaker in these locations, as they cannot receive the tempering diversity of the sun, the cold, or the winds. Ash trees especially become smooth and tall in hollow, wet places. Likewise, the fir tree is most beautiful in the shade, such as in Arcadia around the place called Crana, in a certain hollow spot shielded from the winds where they say the sun never reaches; there they surpass all others in both height and thickness, but their wood is not of fine quality. For this reason, these are used less for finer works and other grand objects, but are most excellent for ships, houses, yards, and masts due to their outstanding length, though they are not as strong as those exposed to the Sun. Thus the Yew, the Bird Cherry <note>original: "Padus"</note>, and the <term>Thraupalus</term> <note>An ancient name for a tree, possibly a type of buckthorn or spindle tree</note> delight in the shadiest places.

The reason is that those occupying shady places direct their natural force into only one direction, since the branches do not grow in thickness but rather in length, and they are also suitable for walking sticks, as is evident elsewhere and around the Rock-rose <note>original: "Cisthum"</note>. But very humid plants situated in these places are consequently twisted, because due to the abundance of nourishment they cannot sustain their excessive height. Just as <term>Aphrodisieus</term> <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a prominent commentator on Aristotle</note> mentions that the feet of a eunuch <note>original: "spadonis"</note> tend to be deformed because of too much moisture; the limbs are so soaked and softened that they carry a resulting weakness, for it happens that when the weight of the body is placed upon them, the legs—not strong enough to support it—become distorted. The leaves are either of a reddish-purple color or tending toward it; for as it is held from <term>Aristotle</term> <note>Referring to the work "On Colors," historically attributed to Aristotle</note> in the book *On Colors*, in humid and shady places, the color changes from grassy green into reddish-purple <note>original: "puniceum"</note>, as can be seen on damp pavements in shady spots. This happens through humidity: when it is dried out by the air or the Sun, it contracts into a reddish hue. We said earlier, following Theophrastus in his book *On Causes*, that those things which are humid are scentless, and that odor resides most of all in dryness. Those plants living in diluted and dark regions are scentless because they are humid; for the moisture, mixing itself in more largely, blunts and dulls the scent. Furthermore, humid things are soft, and scent and softness cannot dwell in the same seat. Flowers and garlands in a humid and thick atmosphere can smell less; for indeed

<header>BOOK SECOND.</header>

In Egypt, flowers and plants used for garlands are almost always born of the poorest quality, because the sky is held to be misty and dewy; in such places, almost no scent can be gathered because the capacity for "cooking" <note>The author uses the term "cooking" or "decoction" (coquendi) to describe the natural process where solar heat matures a plant's essential oils and scents.</note> is absent, whereas in arid places, they are far better refined by heat. And if we frequently see cold places and fragrant regions producing flowers and fruits—as can be seen in the Illyrian iris <note>original: "iride illyrica"</note>—we must attribute this to the force of heat locked within the earth, for the force of the cold compresses the heat inside. However, the soil ought to be neither silty, nor fat and sticky; indeed, when plants are beset by moisture and sluggishness, heat can never properly perform its office. Rather, in hollow and shady places, the moist, cold, and sluggish earth—combined with a misty air resulting from that coldness—can only produce plants that are less fragrant. They are mostly of a sterile bloom, for while moisture-loving plants are frequently flower-bearing, they are often not fruit-bearing: they produce a flower not for the sake of fruit, but to receive and preserve the celestial dew and rain. We can see this in those plants that have flowers shaped like little vessels or alabaster jars, which can store the water they have received for a long time for their own benefit.

Aristotle asks in his *Problems* <note>Referring to the "Problemata," a collection of questions on natural phenomena attributed to Aristotle.</note> why some plants lack fruit even though they have flowers, such as the cucumber, the gourd, and the pomegranate? Is it that fruit is not lacking in these, but rather the parts upon which the flower sits are considered the fruits themselves? For the fruit is that which bears the flower, and it is clear that the flower clings to the cucumber. Indeed, melons, gourds, and cucumbers are full of moisture. Aristotle also gives the reason in his *Problems* as to why roots and plants become spongy and large in hollow places, and the opposite elsewhere: for if those exposed to the wind and sun become smaller and denser, those in hollows and well-watered places are made the opposite, and turn out contrary. They are short-lived, as we reported regarding aquatic plants. We shall say, therefore, that their powers are cold and moist due to the marshiness of the soil and the absence of the sun; they heal those conditions for which cold and moist remedies are beneficial, such as "holy fire" <note>original: "igni sacro." This refers to Erysipelas or "St. Anthony’s Fire," a painful skin infection that feels like it is burning.</note> and others, as we have said. The "morion" mandrake <note>original: "Mandragoras morion." Likely a reference to a specific variety of Mandrake described by ancient botanists as narcotic.</note> is born in shady places and near caves, with a heavy odor and sleep-inducing power, useful for all inflammations, holy fire, and similar ailments. Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> said it was cold and moist, and somewhat warm. Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist, author of "De Materia Medica."</note> said that violets are born in shady and rough places. Mesue <note>Likely Mesue the Younger, a medieval author of influential pharmaceutical texts.</note> states they moisten and cool; they help a burning stomach, aid sleep, and soothe inflammations of the eyes.

### ON THE PHYSIOGNOMY AND POWERS OF PLANTS GROWING ON HILLS. ## Chapter 35.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'N' featuring a figure in a landscape with trees.</image-desc>
Now we shall speak of small hills, seeing as they hold a certain middle ground between mountains, valleys, and plains; thus they reflect a "middle" appearance, habit, and power, and possess a temperament that adheres more closely to the human one. Averroes <note>A 12th-century philosopher and physician from Al-Andalus.</note> says in his *Colliget* <note>original: "Colliget," from the Arabic "Al-Kullyat," meaning "General Rules of Medicine."</note>: Of the things born of the earth, those that grow on little hills are perfected, because it appears from the eminence of the mountains that they ought to generate more growth than other places, provided they are temperate with good evaporation and a good mixture of heat and moisture. This ought to be the case in them because they rise into the air and are closer to the influence of the celestial bodies, and those plants born of the earth have a full complement of leaves, flowers, and fruits. But let us come to the "physiognomy" of the plant. For the body color of the men who inhabit the hills was white mixed with redness. The hair was decently thick, and the constitution decently fleshy. The hair was neither soft nor hard, neither shaggy nor smooth.

->FINALLY, in the place of the table, the vine <note>original: "vitis"</note> is seen as born on hills, attached to the thirty-second chapter; let the observer contemplate its nature there.<-

Thus, the "mistress" of the most pleasant hills, where a more indulgent temperance of the sky entices, is more elegant and cheerful than all those known so far from their birthplaces. Her beauty commends her immediately to the one looking at her and makes her better known. The form is more robust than that of mountain plants, and drier than those of the fields: not as rich in flowers, leaves, and fruits as the latter, nor as destitute as the former.

<header>PHYTOGNOMONICA</header>

...neither hairy, nor smooth, neither hard, nor soft, but uniform and moderate, an inhabitant of both the ground and the sky, so that he who has not seen this plant but desires to know it may contemplate it; however, its taste, smell, and color are more conspicuous.

The following reasons underlie this description of form. Aristotle says in his *Problems*: "Those who inhabit sunny and elevated places age more slowly, unlike those in hollows and marshes." For in elevated places, the air is stirred on all sides by the blowing wind; in hollows, it remains motionless. Furthermore, in open places, the air is considered pure due to constant agitation, while in marshes it is impure and always decaying. And elsewhere, well-ventilated places can provide a brightness of color, whereas moisture makes one pale when it putrefies. Theophrastus says that plants growing in gently ventilated and slender <note>referring to thin or well-drained soil</note> places are the easiest to grow, because the plant draws less nourishment, whereas it is otherwise in flat and cold places. Their powers are temperate because the temperature of the location is moderate. What grows here is used for food rather than medicine. Vines grow on hills, as Virgil says:

->*Bacchus loves the hills, etc.*<- <note>original: "Bacchus amat colles"</note>

As we have frequently said, wine possesses a hot and moist temperament and is exceedingly familiar to our own nature. Red Satyrion <note>original: "Satirium erithronium," likely a type of orchid traditionally associated with aphrodisiac qualities</note> grows in mountainous, sunny places; it has a sweet taste, not unpleasant to the mouth. It excites Venus <note>A poetic way of saying it acts as an aphrodisiac.</note>. Galen says it is moderately hot and moist. Common bugloss and borage grow in fields and hills; Galen states they are of a moist and hot temperament, and when cast into wine, they bring joy and cheerfulness. The same should be said of the spider-herb <note>original: "phalangio," referring to Phalangium, used against spider bites</note> and wild cumin.

## ON THE CULTIVATION AND NEGLECT OF PLANTS, AND FIRST CONCERNING
### *The Physiognomony and capacity of wild plants.*
### Chapter XXXVI.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'T' featuring floral patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

THUS we have reviewed the appearance of plants and their medicinal powers, which are born in various lands, according to the regions of the heavens and their aspects. This next place is claimed by the competition between art and nature—namely, cultivation and neglect. For Art, through the allurements and charms of cultivation, makes plants forget their origins and makes them inhabitants of our gardens; it changes both their nature and their appearance in any soil, atmosphere, or stretch of region. For this reason, we have deliberately saved this discussion for last. It was necessary to remember the previous points first, so that we might look to a clearer order and teaching. As we are about to speak on the Physiognomony <note>The study of internal character through external appearance.</note> of wild and cultivated plants, we shall begin with the wild. For wild things are prior by nature to tame ones, and we shall first arrive at those things which we said in our books on human Physiognomony. For we saw there how much the renowned physiognomists Polemon and Adamantius valued the cultivated habit; for after they had held a discourse on all the parts of the body, they taught regarding the wild and tame form and character, because these things most greatly change the character. But let us approach the nature of wild things.

->In this place we offer you two images of "spirits," <note>original: "vaporum," here referring to the essential character or outward "breathing" of the plant's nature</note> one of the urban and<-
->cultivated, the other of the neglected and wild; the cultivated one<-
->is for this chapter.<-

# BOOK TWO

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting two botanical specimens. On the left is a plant with a large, bulbous taproot resembling a radish or turnip, from which several large, broad, oval leaves with prominent veining emerge. On the right is a more slender plant with a thin root system and elongated, deeply lobed or jagged-edged leaves, with several thin stalks rising to small flowers at the top.</image-desc>

Wild plants possess a certain character entirely lacking in embellishment; their nature displays something rough, hairy, harsh, rustic, and as if of a degenerate sort, owing to the remote and icy places where they dwell. Their appearance is meager and thin, yet they present a vigorous aspect to the observer. They raise a woody, knotty, angular stem, furrowed with ridges, rigid, and covered with a rough and bristly skin. They bear a numerous offspring of leaves, but these are short, deeply divided, angular, hard, and standing upright; they are notched at the edges, or cut with small teeth, or jagged, with many nerves and veins extending lengthwise and keeled <note>shaped like the hull of a ship</note>, fading into a pale green, and shaggy with spines, hairs, or a bristle-like down. 

The flower is tiny, of a diluted, faded, or faint color. It germinates and fruits quickly, showing more fruit than it matures. These fruits are of a sharp and bitter taste—unpalatable—lacking in pulp but rich in woody kernels. Their scent is not unpleasant, yet it smells of something somewhat poisonous <note>original: "virosi," which can mean smelling of venom, or simply a strong, rank, or intoxicating odor</note> or powerful. The root is deep, bearded with thin tendrils and tiny filaments, woody, and very widely accepted for medicinal uses. 

In short, the form, powers, and features of a wild plant differ in no way from those of a mountain plant, so that he who has seen one will know both—except that the highest peaks of mountains are scorched, perpetually covered in snow, and swept by winds, which gives them a twisted, shriveled, and rough appearance. Therefore, if you add to one or take away from the other, they will be entirely alike.

But let us provide the reasons for the delineation of this form. Why the wild kinds rise more robustly and joyfully than their cultivated <note>original: "mitibus," literally "mellowed" or "tame" plants</note> counterparts is explained beautifully by Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A celebrated Greek commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD) known as "The Commentator."</note> in his *Problems*: he says that the earth is the mother of wild plants, but the stepmother of cultivated ones. This is because the skill...

# PHYTOGNOMONICA

<note>original: "morem"</note> ...the character of nature, not the creation of human ingenuity: for it lacks that excessive abundance of moisture which over-saturates stalks, making them loose and effeminate. Instead, wild plants are those born and raised in their own place, not as strangers, but as citizens of their own soil, for whom it is necessary that the sky itself and the mixture of the earth have conspired; thus the native soil possesses so many privileges. As Virgil says:

> ->*For they rise up joyful and strong,*<-
> ->*Since nature itself lies hidden in the soil.*<-

Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BCE) was a Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note> assigns a reason for the shortness and smallness of the leaves and stalks, adding a distinction between the <term>cultivated</term> <note>original: "urbanum," meaning plants of the city or garden</note> and the <term>wild</term> <note>original: "sylvestre," meaning plants of the forest</note>. He says that the wild plant is similar to the cultivated one, but with shorter leaves, branches, roots, and overall form. Indeed, they tend to become rougher, denser, harder, and more twisted—just as their entire nature is—as well as drier, thinner, and even more thorny, except for the spurge-olive <note>original: "cneum," likely *Daphne oleoides*</note>, which is softer and lighter than the cultivated variety.

Furthermore, Aristotle in his *Problems* <note>A work of questions and answers attributed to Aristotle, often discussing natural phenomena.</note> gives the reason why black myrtles have more frequent foliage than white ones, noting that the black ones are of a wilder kind. The evidence for this is that they grow in rustic places and are least improved by cultivation. All moist things are covered with thicker foliage because, being less able to "cook" <note>Ancient science believed that the sun's heat "cooked" or concocted raw sap into fruit; if a plant was too cold or moist, it couldn't finish the process and grew leaves instead.</note> their fruits, the nourishment turns instead toward the leaves; Theophrastus follows him in this. The Egyptian variety of myrtle is drier than the others, which is proven by the narrowness of its leaves, the smallness of its fruit, and its color. All these traits arise from dryness, and it is certain that dry things have little moisture.

The leaves are hard: for as we have said in human <term>Physiognomy</term> <note>The study of physical features to determine temperament or character.</note>, those with hard hair are of a hot and dry nature and are "earthy," because among the elements, earth provides hardness. Among hot and strong animals, the lion, the boar, the eagle, and the rooster have hard feathers or hair; likewise, wild animals have hard hair because their nourishment is dry. The oak has the hardest leaves and is more "earthy" than others; for this reason, Theophrastus says the charcoal of the oak is the worst. So it is with old trees: the drier they are, the worse they become. Those with hard leaves are drier, and for that reason, they are <term>astringent</term> <note>Having a tightening or drying effect on tissues, often associated with tannins.</note> because they are earthy. The oak has hard leaves and is astringent; so too are the chestnut, the carob, the rock-rose <note>original: "cithus," likely *Cistus*</note>, the labdanum-bearing shrub, the service tree, and the medlar.

Wild plants are simply more knotted than cultivated ones of the same genus, such as the wild olive to the olive, the caprifig to the fig, and the wild pear to the pear. These are indeed more knotted, and all dense plants are more knotted, largely because they have "rare" <note>meaning porous or thin-textured</note> bodies. For "males" and wild plants are denser, except for those which, due to excessive density, are entirely without knots or have very few, such as the boxwood or the hackberry.

Wild plants are by nature drier and denser. They flower, but the production of leaves lasts only a short time, with the exception of the hyacinth, which flowers longer. Uncultivated and wild plants precede the mild, cultivated ones—such as the vine, olive, fig, and apple—in their germination. First, this is because they are not pruned or broken like cultivated ones, and thus do not suffer or shrink back from wounds. Second, because they are not dug around or hoed, which would cause the natural heat to be released and escape, thereby cooling the plant. Furthermore, in wild plants, the tiny branches that ought to be removed by the art of agriculture remain unharmed; in these, because of their smallness, the "reproductive principles" are easily stirred by the surrounding air. Finally, because they are drier, where there is less moisture, there is less work to be done. 

And since wild plants are stronger and drier, they "show" more fruit beforehand, but they actually ripen less of it. This happens because of excessive fruiting; the perfection of the work is hindered by this over-expenditure, and the ripening of the fruits is not completed. For this reason, it is cautioned by the law of agriculture that excessive abundance should be removed from the tree. Another cause is that wild plants are lower quality and drier, and they claim the nourishment for themselves rather than administering it to the fruits. That which is to bear fruit must be loose, relaxed, moist, and permeable, not dense—as is also apparent in animals. All wild plants are thornier, heavier, harder, and altogether more robust than cultivated ones, and "males" more so than "females," since they are less fertile than the more fruitful ones, and those bearing poorer fruit are firmer in almost every part. Nor should the cause found in "coldness" be dismissed as to why wild plants fruit less. Furthermore, every wild or uncultivated plant produces fruit whose seed or pit is fatter, but the pulp is leaner; for while the moisture—

# BOOK TWO

...imparts its character to the fruit, taking away and snatching from the pulp so that it may provide more abundantly for the seed. Because of this, the plant becomes somewhat <term>masculine</term> <note>In ancient and Renaissance botany, "masculine" qualities referred to being drier, harder, and more concentrated, whereas "feminine" meant more moist and lush.</note> in nature, remaining crispier and drier. These plants also produce their seeds protected by a very large shell, just as the bones of animals are protected; for these defenses are made from woody and earthy nourishment, while the nucleus is made of the purest material. In taste, they are altogether sharper and more powerful—as with savory, oregano, cabbage, rue, and wild dock—making them more pleasing to the palate, though they are sharper when dry. No one will deny that wild fruits consist of a more bitter taste, for a harsh flavor arises from a dry and earthy nature. Because of this, Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BCE) was the primary authority on botany in the classical world.</note> suggests irrigating the trees of pomegranates so that the seeds within may become sweeter and the wood softer; for the hardness and bitterness, which comes from earthy dryness, is diluted and softened by moisture. Almond shells are bitter because the force of nature separates all the impurities and calluses of the earth into them. Wild and uncultivated fruits are more fragrant than those of their own kind in the city <note>original: "urbanis," meaning garden or cultivated varieties</note>, such as apples, pears, service berries, and medlars. Of the apples themselves, both wild and cultivated, those that are the most bitter smell the sweetest; and since scent is concentrated by a kind of <term>cooking</term> <note>original: "coctura," a term used to describe the internal biological process of ripening or "digesting" nutrients.</note>, those that have been "cooked" more by nature must be thought to smell better. Truly, the measure of scent depends less on absolute ripening than on timing, as evidenced by the fact that service berries and pears give off more scent if they are not fully ripened. For the wild kind, content with its initial ripening, conceives a more powerful odor. Furthermore, it is of no small importance for scents if the dryness proceeds with a scarcity of nourishment and favorable ventilation, since those plants that break out from dry places, content with less nutriment and fanned by a gentle breeze, are undoubtedly born more fragrant. Moreover, the wild kind is seen to be drier, endowed with a leaner habit, and not silent against the wind, but more and more open to the breeze. Here, a more fervent nature breathes through, and the thinner, dry habit easily gives way, since it does not carry juice mixed into the flesh in the manner of garden plants; when these factors come together, the scent within flourishes significantly. Two things establish scent: earth and air. If both are dry—not with any dryness, but a moderate one—then those plants that arise during dry nights, in which a gentle heat smiles upon them, excel in scent. For this reason, wild plants are fragrant, but not fully so, as they consist of a sharper scent. There are also wild plants that are thorny and rough, which happens to them from excessive dryness, as we said regarding thorny plants; indeed, roughness comes from dryness. The leaves are of a diluted green, and the flowers of a weaker color in wild plants, which can easily be inferred from the lack of moisture, as they are born in dry air and soil. Leaves of a leek-green color come from much humidity, but yellow or faded colors come from dryness, as the author of the *Book on Colors* <note>A work attributed to Aristotle or Theophrastus in the period.</note> proves happens in vegetables and grains. Flowers that shine with a bright color arise from rich and moist food, as is seen daily in hanging gardens. Stock, and "little flames"—which they call <term>clove pinks</term> <note>original: "garyophyllos" (carnations), named for their clove-like scent.</note> from the scent of cloves—and roses shine with a saturated purple because they occur in well-manured and watered places; on the contrary, those in wild and neglected places are of a faint color due to their poverty. One sees flowers opening at early dawn being more colorful due to the night’s moisture, but in the evening, because of the excessive heat of the Sun, they are pale and faded. The same can be seen in recently born flowers, which are more colorful due to their native moisture, but in advanced age are paler, discolored, and deformed, for they become drier with age. Because of this, Theophrastus, writing about stock and roses, says: "Violets, as they grow old, continually bear whiter flowers, and roses become worse." Wild roses bear a flower that is less fragrant and not of the same size. It also happens that the outermost edges of leaves and flowers are discolored, because the extremities dry out more quickly, being more exposed to the air and Sun than the inner parts, which cling to their origin. And in Apulia <note>A region in Southern Italy known for its hot, dry climate.</note> we have seen clove pink flowers of a blood-red color degenerate into white or a marbled pattern, and the blue flowers of bugloss turn reddish, due to the excessive heat of the region. Aristotle writes in his *Problems* that thin rootlets are sharper than larger ones; for the latter, having been more fully "cooked" over a longer space of time, become mild. Country people think wild plants are long-lived and claim none are short-lived. But as far as can be said simply, the life of wild plants is longer than that of garden ones: and generally for those which can be distinguished as opposites, such as the wild olive vs. the olive, the wild pear vs. the pear, and the wild fig...

...than the fig tree: indeed, they are more robust, denser, and less productive in fruit. As an example of those that bear fruit enclosed in woody cases and coverings and are astringent in taste, there are the pine, cedar, cypress, and all conifers; the oak, which bears acorns, galls, and other woody fruits; the chestnut, carob, almond, Indian nut <note>Likely referring to the coconut, which was known to Renaissance botanists as *nux indica*.</note>, walnut, hazelnut, pistachio, and similar trees. Some deny that wild plants have deep roots because they grow from seeds on the surface, but they are incorrect; for it can happen that as they live longer, they send their roots quite far. Theophrastus <note>The primary Greek authority on botany.</note> attributes woody roots for the most part to wild plants, such as wild rocket, basil, and the like. Finally, the wild plant does not differ from the mountain plant, for Theophrastus says, <note>original: "montana syluestria sunt, & frigoris cupida"</note> "mountain things are wild and desire the cold." But let us see what qualities the experts in medicine give to wild plants. Theophrastus says: an uncultivated and neglected field, such as a wild one, is colder, both because a thicker air surrounds it and because it is less "breathable" <note>Meaning the air does not circulate as freely.</note>; the cause arises from the dense bushes, by which the movement of the air is hindered, and because it does not admit the Sun to dry it out. The sap of figs curdles milk, but that of the wild fig <note>original: "caprificus"</note> does so the least; for this reason, wild figs are colder. Averroes <note>A 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician.</note> said in his *Colliget*: "Those things which are in the woods have more coldness." But wild things consist of the greatest dryness, whether they are hot or cold, as it is accepted by all that wild things are drier and more astringent than the milder ones of their own kind. Because they generally have a sharper scent than others, they are effective against the bites of wild beasts; and Theophrastus, speaking of fleabane <note>original: "coniza"</note>, says the female has a sharper scent and is therefore more convenient against the bites of beasts. And it was surely fitting for the majesty of Nature that after she had made the woods abundant with venomous animals, she should make herbs of a sharper scent in the same place, so that their sickness could be healed on the spot. Wild cabbage is hairier, whiter, and more bitter than the cultivated variety. Galen <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire.</note> said it is in a way hotter and drier than the cultivated kind, just as all other wild things are stronger than the domestic versions of their own kind in both qualities. Wild leek <note>original: "ampeloprason"</note> heats more than the garden leek. Galen says it is sharper and drier than the domestic one, just as all other wild things are compared to domestic ones. Wild woad <note>original: "isatis"</note> dries more powerfully than the cultivated, and it also resists moist putrefaction more powerfully. The wild lupine is more bitter and, according to Galen, stronger for all uses than the domestic. The cultivated mallow is as much weaker in power as it has more watery moisture than the wild. For that is the distinction between the two: namely, that wild things are drier, and mild ones are moister, according to Galen. The wild carrot <note>original: "daucus"</note> is less suitable for eating than the domestic; however, it is more fervent in all things, and the domestic is indeed edible but weaker. Wild rocket <note>original: "eruca"</note> is much sharper than the cultivated and drives out urine more vehemently, according to Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*.</note>. The wild parsnip is more effective than the mild, but less fit for food, which Galen confirms. Bitter almond oil is considered more effective in all things than the sweet. Wild oregano is stronger than both cultivated kinds; Galen calls it "Heraclean panacea," with thin branches and a thin, superfluous root. Alexanders <note>original: "smyrnium"</note>, being like a wild celery, is stronger than the cultivated, and so it goes for the rest.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial E featuring a landscape with a building and a figure in the background.</image-desc>The same must be said of wild animals, and first of the beasts of prey, since they are prior by nature. Their appearance is lean, foul, and emaciated, bristling with hard, dense, and rigid hair. Their flesh is fibrous and rough. The bones, claws, and spines are large and hard. The hair is yellow in color, the eyes saffron, and the dung is less stinking. They bear fewer young, and they abound more in bones, horns, claws, and hair than domestic animals. Their strengths are more vigorous in action.

But let us provide the reasons for this description. Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A Greek commentator on Aristotle.</note> said that the dung of wild animals is less stinking than that of domestic ones; for the excrement of some smells slightly of spice because they eat drier and simpler food and work more vehemently. But the dung of domestic animals stinks more because they use varied and moist food, and they indulge in food more than is necessary, exercise less, and abound less in heat; hence when...

...food is less digested, and cannot be sufficiently dispersed due to its abundance; it putrefies somewhat, and therefore smells more foul. Bony animals have more of this, because of the earthy nourishment they use, as we said regarding plants. They have saffron-yellow eyes because of a bilious temperament. But wild animals are especially armed with horns, claws, and protruding teeth, and even "lichens" <note>This refers to the callosities or "chestnuts" found on the legs of horses and related animals, which ancient naturalists thought resembled the mossy growth on trees.</note> on their legs, from which they are endowed with the greatest power of constriction; for these things arise from the earthy mixture of which they are composed. The more they are endowed with these features, the greater dryness they demonstrate, and an earthy mixture, as we said of plants: and the more they are covered with longer thorns, woody fruits, and barks. Dense and very hard hair can show the same. Averroes <note>A famous 12th-century philosopher and physician from Al-Andalus.</note> says in his *Colliget*: "Claws, nails, and thorns simply signify that there is much earth in them." Many scales are praised in fish, and those that are more scaly and covered with harder flesh are more "wild."

The strengths of wild animals, as we have said, are always more powerful in action than those of their domestic counterparts. "Greater power belongs to the wild beasts of the same genus of animals," said Pliny. But this will become clearer with these examples. The **onager** <note>The wild ass.</note> is a wild donkey with harder feet, a lean body, and is very swift according to Oppian, strong in the head and untameable in body. Pliny, when he had recounted a remedy against certain poisons from donkey's milk and bones, added that all the same things are more effective from onagers. **Buffaloes** are of the genus of wild oxen; they are more robust, with very hard skin, lean limbs, black hair, a rough and curly forehead, twisted black horns, hard flesh, and a solid, earthy hoof. In **roe deer** or **gazelles**, the body is reddish, the feet long, the head adorned with horns, and the ears tall and hairy. Pliny said that the dung of goats expels stones, and more effectively so from the wild ones, whose flesh is cold and dry.

The **wild cat** has denser and longer hair, of a dark, specifically yellowish-brown color; its fat, like all its other members, is more effective than that of domestic cats, according to Rhazes <note>An influential Persian physician and polymath.</note>. **Boars** are wild swine, of a chestnut-blackish color, with very hard hair. It is a brutish and terrible animal; when angry, it scorches the hair of dogs with its teeth. Its callous flesh dries and strengthens, according to the authors Hippocrates and Celsus: the effects of the remedies from both <note>Domestic and wild swine.</note> are similar, differing only in that the parts of wild animals are less humid and less cold than those of tame animals. None of the animals is more horned than the **Stag**; in the beauty and size of its branching horns, it excels all wild beasts, according to Oppian. The **Bear** is effective against dysentery. **Rams** are horned; they are effective at stopping menstrual flows. The **bull** is also horned, and it restrains blood according to Galen. The **Elephant** has protruding teeth <note>Tusks.</note>, the use of which is for spitting blood, according to Dioscorides. The **Sow** is stiff with protruding teeth and hard bristles; its ash is effective for inhibiting flowing blood according to Sextus, and for a prolapsed seat <note>A rectal prolapse.</note> according to Aetius. The **Badger** is armed with teeth and excels at stopping blood in the stool. The **Turtle** is greatly crested <note>Referring to the ridges on the shell.</note>; its burnt shell heals fistulas and thinning hair. The **Hawk** is armed with claws and a beak; its ground claws are effective for dysentery. The **Rooster** is empowered by its claws, beak, and spurs; it is effective for the flow of blood and wounds. The **Goose** has a very wide beak; its blood stops blood, according to Pliny. The **Duck** serves the same purpose. The **Swan** is substituted in its place. The **Porcupine** bristles with quills, which it has in place of hair; it strengthens the stomach and mitigates dropsy by its dryness. The same should be suspected of others.

# PHYTOGNOMONICA

It seemed most fitting that the "urban" and "sylvan" are not separate in the family of plants, but rather that "wild" plants are those born in wild and neglected places, while "domesticated" <note>original: *cicures*</note> are those nourished by gardeners in gardens. We have treated these matters more extensively in our books on *Agriculture*.

->☞ ON THE RIGHT, in the thirty-seventh table attached to this chapter, you will see the image of a cultivated turnip,<-
->for if we had painted them for every single chapter, the task<-
->would have been made too laborious.<-

The joyful appearance of the cultivated plant presents itself to onlookers with a more pleasing sight and delightful elegance, appearing almost wanton in its feminine softness. For it rises with a taller, rounder stem, notable for its smoothness and thickness, and is crowded with many leaves at the top. It puts forth softish leaves, bent backward and sloping downward, as if failing under their own weight; they are wider, thicker, and round—or, if you prefer, spreading wider with a blunt tip. There is a beautiful crown around the edges of the leaves, a deep green, and many flowers. The flowers are cheerful and beautiful, shining with great grace in milky white, sweet red, or blood-purple, though they exhale a weaker scent. It matures the fruits it shows, often bearing twice a year—in spring and autumn—with no woodiness inside, or very little, being sweet and savory: the whole plant is sweet and edible. Its roots are extensive, creeping far and wide, but are less effective for those skilled in medicine. Finally, the form of the cultivated plant is so similar to those that dwell in the plains that unless you look closely, you would think them the same. It is only that the cultivated one, through many flatteries in the gardens and the artifice <note>original: *mangonio*, referring to the "furbishing" or "grooming" of goods for sale, here meaning the artificial improvement through gardening</note> of skill, displays something more delicate and substantial.

But let us provide the reasons for the appearance of cultivated plants. We said above, following Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A 2nd-century philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note>, that because they are tenderer or softer, the earth is like a "stepmother" to cultivated plants; through the flatteries of cultivation and more humid food, the plants are relaxed and "effeminated." For opposite reasons, Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany," a student of Aristotle.</note> attributes larger leaves, branches, bark, and an overall larger form to cultivated plants; indeed, they are more loose, soft, and straight on a smoother stem. They are many-flowered, and he said they bloom longer due to the art of cultivation. This also happens in well-tended hanging gardens, which are heaped with many leaves and flowers. They have soft leaves, as Aristotle indicates in his book of *Problems* when speaking of sheep's wool. For anything that is "concocted" <term>concoction: the ancient process where vital heat matures or "digests" nutrients within a living thing</term> is softer than the unconcocted, and an abundance of waste produces softness in the hair; cultivated plants are more concocted due to the manure, and more abundant nourishment is provided through irrigation. Garden nightshade has a softer leaf than the wild variety; the same is true for "helxine" <note>likely Pellitory-of-the-wall or a type of bindweed</note> and basil. The plane tree is moist and noted for its wide leaf, as is the fig. Cultivated plants are preceded by wild ones in budding and fruiting because, as we said, through manuring and "digging around" <note>original: *ablaqueatione*, the practice of exposing the roots of trees to air and water</note>, the "genital heat" <note>the vital warmth believed to drive reproduction and growth</note> leaves the trees, dissipates, and they grow cold. For it is heat that moves trees to bud; then, through pruning, they are constricted by their wounds and, being weak, they suffer. The small branches from which buds first break are cut away by art; finally, since cultivated plants are more humid, the sap must stay longer to be perfected. But as much as the cultivated tree yields to the wild one in the speed of budding and fruiting, it surpasses the wild one in the appearance, quality, and abundance of the fruit. For the wild ones hurry, as they do not have the same supply of material in their storehouse; in cultivated plants, however, hesitation supports the fruiting. For when that force gathers itself, it performs its work and fruiting with readiness and promptness. The sap does in them what happens in water: when blocked by some obstacle, it finally breaks out with great force. Furthermore, maturity is hindered in robust plants by an uneven "unwinding" of the task; but in mild plants, because there is less bulk, the work is finished more precisely. Moreover, the art of agriculture removes all superfluous things; thus trees become more "breathing" and thinner, and air is more easily admitted. By applying dung, they become looser and more humid; because of this, they do not absorb their juices into a compact density like wild plants, but once the "interceptor" branches are removed, they bestow them toward perfect fruiting. These are the views of Theophrastus, but I would add that in the "birth" of wild plants, the weather is still somewhat harsh, while the "gentle" cultivated plants have the air as a supporter and co-administrator in a milder season. In wild trees, the seed and wood were perfected for the propagation of the species; in the gentle ones...

# BOOK TWO
->M<-

Indeed, through the works of agriculture—namely digging, manuring, and watering—the pulp of the fruit becomes more edible for human consumption. Sap is reclaimed from the tree for its own nourishment, as well as from the pulp and the seed within; but it is first drawn out by the tree, and for this reason, where a tree is very succulent, the fruits are fewer. As much is withdrawn and stolen from the fruits as is added to the tree. The two remaining parts, namely the seed and the fruit <note>meaning the fleshy pulp</note>, are in opposition to one another: if the stone or kernel luxuriates, the pulp becomes leaner; if the pulp is fertile, the seed becomes more shriveled, and the size of the protruding bone <note>the pit or stone of the fruit</note> is restrained. There is a mutual response of loss and gain. There is another principle: that trees are "feminized" by cultivation, and that these "females" are more fecund. For they become looser through cultivation, and through their channels, sap is drawn up more abundantly. This sap is modified by the heat of the plant itself, which is increased by human art so that it does not run wild. The duty of cultivation, as Aristotle says in his book of *Problems*, is to concoct <note>original: *concoquat*; the process of "ripening" or "digesting" nutrients through heat</note> the nourishment and make it effective, which is what produces a mild and "urban" kind of fruit.

Therefore, those things created by this kind of softening and shaping we designate by the term "urban," because they turn out better as if they had been educated and learned through human ingenuity. These urban plants consist of a sap that is less sharp and vehement. Fruits become softer, sweeter, and more savory through cultivation, and they change in flavor, scent, color, and size, all because of their nourishment; through cultivation, they move from being "sylvan" to "urban." The woodiness of pomegranate seeds is removed with pig dung, and watering them makes them sweeter. Similarly, the use of urine, leather scrapings, and filth heaped around a myrtle causes it to produce fruit without an internal stone when the buds burst forth. The bitterness of the almond is also removed by the sharpness of dung. The harshness of a plant is summoned and drawn out by salt. And by the sprinkling of boiling water, the spring apple and the myrtle are improved. Cucumber seeds soaked in milk or honey-water <term>melicratum: a mixture of honey and water</term> gain a sweetness of sap. Vegetables improve, become sweeter, and grow more tender when superfluous parts are pruned away, because the roots are invigorated by a stronger draught of nourishment, and their bitterness is removed. If basil is watered with warm water, it springs up more joyfully. Also, when salt water is provided to cabbages and palms, the innate bitterness of the cabbage and the harshness of the palm are removed, and sweetness takes the place of both.

Through digging, the size, flavor, and pleasantness of the fruit are secured; for in the walnut and the almond, the shells, husks, and fibers—which are the outermost defenses—become smaller and easier to open, while the kernels grow larger. Indeed, due to the abundance of nourishment, the trees become moist, the fruits increase their pulp, and the tree acquires strength and goodness in its fruit. However, these fruits exhale their scent more weakly; sweet things have no odor, and the sweeter they are perceived to be, the less scent they have. Sweet apples release the least scent because sweet sap is thicker and more "earthy" when it is admitted into the fruits, whereas scent is composed of a thinner, drier moisture that breathes out easily. Thus, sweetness is considered too stubborn to be able to breathe a thin vapor into the nostrils. The sweetness of flavor comes from the thickening of the sap; for as the fruit ages and the Sun provides heat, it is made sweeter. Fruits thicken when the watery part is removed, and the "cooking" of the flavor is not completed unless it is fully ripened. But scent, as we have said, is only produced by the first stage of "cooking," so that it does not exist in the fully cooked fruit. For this reason, sap that is already fully "cooked" can belch out less breath and vapor; less scent will be ejected then, and since it emerges thicker from the cooking, it will take on a sweetness pleasing to the sense. The "urban" plant, which attains a more perfect concoction and is saturated with nourishment, turns its saps toward sweetness but gathers a laziness and dullness of scent. Indeed, moisture that admits itself too largely blunts the scent and dulls its sharpness, since it carries dryness mixed with the flesh. Furthermore, things that offer a large scent represent no softness to the taste; since all urban things are soft, they cannot smell as strongly.

But let us look at their powers. A cultivated field is rendered drier and thinner because, the trees having been cleared, it receives the heat of the Sun and is blown through by winds from every side. Also, "mild" <note>cultivated</note> plants are warmer than "wild" ones; milk is curdled by the sap of a domestic fig, but the sap of a wild fig <term>caprificus: the wild or "goat" fig</term> does it not at all, or poorly; therefore, the mild ones have greater power. Averroes <note>The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician</note> also says in his *Colliget* <note>original: *Kitab al-Kullyat*, his medical encyclopedia</note>: those things that grow in gardens have more humidity, such as figs growing in gardens. Thus, just as wild plants were colder and drier than the mild ones of their kind, so the mild ones will be warmer and more humid than the wild ones of their kind. They are of a duller virtue because they are larger; a wife used to call her husband a "beet-like man" <note>original: *bliteum virum*</note> when he had a large body but was weak. We have said in—

PHYTOGNOMONICA <note>Original header: PHYTOGN.</note>

The physiognomic principle is that large men are less robust, and we discussed the opposite cause in the preceding section. Cato writes that the **Turnip** <term>Rapum; Brassica rapa</term> desires a fertile and rich field; Columella says it should be crumbly, loose, worked by many plowings, and well-watered. Galen notes that if it is not grown in such soil, it transforms into a cabbage, being of a hot and moist nature. The **Navew** <term>Napus; a type of rapeseed or rutabaga</term> grows in fat, loose, and soft soil; in any other place, it degenerates into a turnip, which is why Columella says it requires soil worked by many plowings and satiated with plenty of manure. Galen said it is powerful due to its heat and much "excrementitious" <note>in the sense of surplus bodily fluids or waste products</note> moisture. **Bugloss** grows in fat, loose, moist, and well-worked soil; according to Galen, it is hot and moist. Cato and Palladius wrote that **Asparagus** demands a well-worked, thick, and moist location; Avicenna <note>a Persian polymath and physician</note> says it is hot and moist. The **Mallow** rejoices in rich soil and moist manure according to Palladius; Pliny notes that it makes the soil in which it is sown rich itself; they write that it is hot and watery. The **Onion** seeks rich land, heavily worked, irrigated, and manured according to Columella; Avicenna said it is hot with a superficial moisture. The **Thistle** requires the same land according to Palladius; it is hot, leaning toward moisture according to Avicenna.

Next follow the domestic animals, whose form and powers we judge by the same opposites, just as we did with plants. The appearance of **urban animals** is nobler and more cheerful, with soft, extended, silky hair, almost like down. Their flesh is fatty, soft, and delicate, where neither nerves nor veins are apparent. Their claws and bones are small, their color a cheerful red, and their eyes are amber-colored <note>original: charopi; a bluish-gray or amber glint often associated with lions or sharp-eyed animals</note>. They are very prolific. Their meat is sweet and flavorful. Their strength for labor is exhausted. Compared to others of their kind, they are hotter and moister. The **Pig** is a domestic animal and has the best meat of all; those that are not too fat are superior, being the easiest to digest and the sweetest. They are hot, moist, and full of surplus fluids. **Goat** meat is solid, sweet, and temperate in the summer time according to Hippocrates. Of the rest, the same principles apply, which are very well known.

## THAT PLANTS WHICH RETAIN THE LIKENESSES OF THE LEAVES OF OTHER PLANTS POSSESS SIMILAR VIRTUES.

### Chapter XXXVIIII.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'E' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or monk, in a landscape or garden setting with foliage visible.</image-desc>
We have taught that virtues are obtained from the appearance of the parts of plants; it follows, therefore, from these things that whatever plant is similar in its image to another will also be equal in its powers, so that one may stand in the place of the other—what physicians call "vicarial" or "substitute" herbs. From these examples, the truth of what we have said shines forth more clearly. Nor will shared virtues be recognized solely from the similarity of parts, but also from the scent, color, the manner of fruiting, flowering, and growing. We omit flavors, as they have been treated more than enough by others. We said in *Human Physiognomy* that he who is similar to another in appearance is also similar in character; we pronounce the same regarding herbs. This is easily seen in herbs of the same genus, which possess the same virtue; the more they resemble each other, the more their virtues are alike, and the less they resemble each other, the further their powers will differ.

We shall begin with the leaves. **Madder** <term>Rubia</term> has rough stems with a circular arrangement of leaves at intervals, clinging to clothes with its roughness; it is entirely similar to **Cleavers** <term>Aperine</term>. The juice of the leaves helps against the bites of serpents. **St. John’s Wort** <term>Hypericum</term>, **Ascyrum**, **Tutsan** <term>Androsaemum</term>, and **Coris** are so similar to one another that there is little or no difference between them, so that if one is known, the others cannot remain hidden; when rubbed with the fingers, they pour out a blood-red juice. They are effective for nearly the same things: for sciatica, burns, wounds, and for expelling bilious waste. The appearance of **Spignel** <term>Meum</term> and **Dill** <term>Anethum</term> is by no means different, so that from the habit of looking at them frequently, you can scarcely distinguish them. They cure difficulty of urine and griping pains, and they dispel gas. **Dill** so emulates **Fennel** <term>Foeniculum</term> that it frequently deceives those gathering them, unless they consult the taste and smell. They fill the breasts with milk, settle the menses, and provoke urine. **Sweet Flag** <term>Acorus</term> and the **Iris** have the same appearance: both are warming, and they cure griping, convulsions, and spleen ailments; they are applied interchangeably for serpent bites and female complaints. The **Fragrant Rush** is very similar to the odorless one. Both retain the power of provoking urine, they expel the menses, weigh down the head, are mixed into antidotes, and help those coughing up blood. **Dittany** <term>Dictamnus</term> has such a great likeness to **Pennyroyal** <term>Pulegium</term> that by some it is called "wild pennyroyal." It is effective for all the same things as cultivated pennyroyal. **Savory** <term>Satureia</term> is similar to **Thyme**; in its utility,

...lity and capability: if they are consumed in a similar manner. If you closely examine the leaves, flowers, and appearance of **Wall Germander** <term>Teucrium chamaedrys; original: teucrium trissaginis</term>, even those less familiar with them would colloquially call them all by the single name "Chamaedrys": they are effective for those with spleen ailments and against poisons. **Watercress** <term>Nasturtium</term> is related in appearance and power to **Mustard** and **Rocket**; they treat mange <note>original: alopecjis; refers to patchy hair loss or skin conditions</note>, the spleen, leprosy, itchy skin eruptions, and other conditions. Among the **Fern**, the **Small Fern**, and the **Oak-fern**, there is a manifold and harmonious similarity, as if they belong to the same family: their leaves expel wide tapeworms, and the fresh leaves are eaten cooked in potherbs to soften the belly. Mule-doctors give Oak-fern to horses to swallow against intestinal worms, and the power of the Small Fern is particularly noted for loosening the bowels. The appearance of **Female Southernwood** seems entirely to match **Sea Wormwood** <term>Seriphium</term>, based on a mutual comparison by Dioscorides <note>a famous Greek physician and botanist</note>: they possess almost the same powers. Sea Wormwood kills internal creatures and tapeworms, and Galen <note>an influential Roman-era physician</note> writes that Southernwood can provide the same benefits, since its bitterness destroys roundworms.

The **Sycamore-fig** is of a dual nature and form, a tree mixed from the **Fig** and the **Mulberry**, retaining the capabilities of both trees. The fruits of the Sycamore-fig are harmful to the stomach, but the juice is applied against serpent bites and disperses swellings that resist maturation. The **Mulberry** is useless for the stomach but is effective against the bites of venomous spiders and disperses tumors. The juice of the Sycamore-fig knits wounds together and softens them. **Figs** harm the stomach, but their milky sap, when applied, disperses hard swellings and softens ear-tumors and boils; for the strikes of venomous creatures, it knits wounds, fills them with flesh, and joins the edges together, no differently than the plasters applied to bloody wounds. The same must be said of **Garlic-leek** <term>scorodoprasum</term>, **Wild Wheat** <term>zeopyrum</term>, and others. 

And from the blended natures of the **Oak** and the **Holm-oak**, Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher known as the "Father of Botany"</note> named the **Cork-oak** <term>original: phellodrun</term>. Between the **Pine**, **Wild Pine**, **Pitch Pine**, **Larch**, and **Fir**, there is no difference in appearance or nature, neither in the trees themselves nor in their resins. Between **Mastic trees** and **Turpentine trees**, there is such a close similarity that they are not unlike in appearance, and thus they possess similar powers according to Dioscorides; likewise, their resins are prepared in the same way and act similarly when taken. **Savin** has been allotted a great similarity to the **Cypress**: it treats carbuncles and urinary issues. **Juniper** and **Cedar** are not dissimilar in form, especially in their berries: they aid in removing the harm of venomous animals and help with coughs, leprosy, ruptures, and convulsions. The **Ash** and **White Dittany** bear similar leaves: they are powerful against serpent strikes and lethal poisons. The **Oak**, the **Greek Beech**, the **Italian Oak**, and the **Holm-oak** not only look alike but produce related fruits <note>acorns</note> and perform similar functions. **Rockrose** <term>Ledum</term> and **Cistus** are similar and possess the same effects. The **Carob** <term>Siliqua</term> and **Cassia** are related: both loosen the bowels and provoke urine. **Rough Bindweed** <term>Smilax aspera</term> greatly imitates **Sarsaparilla** in its appearance and its long thongs running deep underground, so that many consider them the same, and their powers are in no way different. The **Arum** <term>Aronis</term> does not differ at all from the leaves of the **Dragon-arum**; its root, seed, and leaves are found to have the same benefits. **Privet** <term>Phyllirea</term> has leaves like the **Olive**: it is useful for the same things as the **Wild Olive**, so that one may succeed as a substitute for the other when cauterization is needed. The same should be said of others, lest this discourse be drawn out too long.

### PLANTS WITH SIMILAR ODORS POSSESS THE SAME POWERS. Chapter 40.

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap letter 'S' featuring a landscape scene with a building or ruin in the background and a figure or animal in the foreground.</image-desc>

**SO** it is that if they recall the same odor, they will also retain the same powers. Thus, if there are any who deny that powers can be perceived from odors, they are clearly lying. We shall bring forward some examples so that the **Plant-observer** <term>original: Phytoptae</term>, having been taught by these, may infer others for himself. **Zedoary** <term>a root related to ginger</term> recalls the odor of a **Citron**; it possesses the same capabilities as that fruit, aiding the heart and acting against poisons according to Avicenna <note>a Persian polymath and physician</note>. **Melissa**, called **Lemon Balm** <term>citrago</term> because of its citron-like odor, resists the poisons of serpents and scorpions, heals pestilential fevers and bile, and benefits the heart. **Lemon Basil** <term>Ocymum citratum</term> is so named because it smells like the rind of a citron fruit; it differs from it in no way, having an exceptional fragrance and being most pleasant to the heart, which is why it is usefully given to be swallowed to recall fainting spirits in those whose minds have slipped away. **Clove-pinks** <term>Garyophylli; likely Carnations or Gillyflowers</term> are the most beautiful of all, so called because they have an olfactory kinship with exotic **Cloves**, and their little cups have some similarity to the "flower-cloves" <term>antophyllis</term>; they mix these into antidotes against pestilential afflictions, and they are also wonderfully recommended for those with the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>
