# PHYTOGNOMONICA

...and others, for which **clove buds** <term>antophylli</term> are effective. There is a type of **Basil** <term>Ocymum</term> that exhales the fragrance of cloves, which he calls **Clove-scented Basil**. There is also another among us whose leaves and whole plant possess a scent of cloves mixed with the pleasantness of citron: smelling it strengthens the heart and head, assists with heart ailments, and turns the mind’s sorrow into joy. There is an herb whose root possesses an extraordinary scent of cloves, known to everyone: indeed, it exhales the sweetness of cloves and is commonly called **Avens** <term>garyophyllata; likely Wood Avens, Geum urbanum</term>. There is no doubt it has attained the same medicinal powers, as have its other varieties. **Camel Grass** <term>Schoenanthos</term>, when rubbed in the hands, is known to everyone for its rose-like quality and fragrance: it is useful for those coughing up blood. **Cassia** also, which is called **Zizi**, recalls the scent of a rose: it serves the same purposes as the rush <note>referring back to Camel Grass</note>; for this reason, combs are made from it to clean the head—which are quite healthy due to the grace of the scent—as are perfume jars, boxes, and other items of that kind. **White Sandalwood** <term>Santalum album</term> is fragrant with the scent of roses: it is effective for headaches, joy of the heart, and palpitations. **Baccharis** <term>Baccharis; likely Ploughman's-spikenard</term> has the extraordinary fragrance of **Cinnamon** root: it promotes urine, drives out the menses, is given most usefully against snake bites, draws out the fetus, is included in precious ointments, and is excellent for eye defects. **Galingale** <term>Cyperus</term> rivals **Spikenard** <term>Nardum</term> in scent: it promotes urine and treats stones, is mixed into antidotes, and is effective for ailments of the womb and dropsy <note>original: aquæ intercuti; literally "water under the skin"</note>. **Asarabacca** <term>Asarum</term> has the scent of spikenard, which others call **Wild Spikenard**: it helps with urination and those suffering from dropsy. According to **Mesue** <note>a famous medieval medical authority</note>, it is administered for blockages of the liver, for fluids under the skin, and for jaundiced overflows <note>original: felleis suffusionibus</note>. Some have called **Valerian** <term>Phu</term> "Wild Spikenard" because it breathes with a certain heaviness of spikenard's sweetness: it is mixed into antidotes and moves urine. In our aromatic **Lavender** <term>Lauendula</term> there is a good deal of grace and the fragrance of **Spike** <note>referring to Spike Lavender</note>: it does not depart far from the powers of spikenard, it strengthens the stomach, and frees the liver from blockages. **Sweet Cicely** <term>Myrrhis</term> is named for its scent, which tastes of **Myrrh**; it moves the menses and childbirth. From **Hemp-agrimony** <term>Eupatrio</term> flows a resin similar to myrrh; **Theophrastus** <note>an ancient Greek botanist</note> thought it was entirely myrrh; **Dioscorides** calls it **Smyrnion** <term>Alexanders</term>, with a medicinal scent that is pleasant with a certain sweetness, sharp, and with the taste of myrrh, so that one may take the place of the other: it treats coughs and difficulty breathing <note>original: orthopnoicis</note>, draws out the fetus, glues wounds together, expels the menses and the afterbirth, and is effective against fevers. The root of **Evening Primrose** <term>Onothera</term>, when dried, smells like wine: given in a drink, it calms wild beasts and makes them tame; also, as an ointment, it soothes foul ulcers. **Ambrosia** <term>Ambrosia</term> produces small clusters with a wine-like, sweet scent: applied as an ointment, it restrains humors that have settled in any part, and it is astringent like wine. **Oak of Jerusalem** <term>Botris</term> breathes a sweet scent; the Cappadocians call it "Ambrosia," also because of the scent of wine: it soothes difficulty breathing. **Amomum** <term>Amomum</term> has the scent of **Oregano**: it is suitable for bites from poisonous animals. **Dittany** <term>Dictamnum</term> smells like **Pennyroyal**, which is why it is called "Wild Pennyroyal" by some, as it is similar to pennyroyal: it performs everything that cultivated pennyroyal does, but much more effectively. There is another Dittany with leaves like **Water-mint** <term>sisymbrij</term>; the scent of the leaves is most pleasant, between water-mint and **Sage**: it expels a dead fetus and assists with the bites of venomous creatures, just like sage. **Water Germander** <term>Scordion</term> sprouts leaves that some perceive as having a foul odor: it promotes urine and is effective against viper bites, for an old cough, and for the menses. **Garlic Mustard** <term>Alliaria</term> recalls **Garlic** with its tedious scent and taste, from which it obtained its name: its powers are like garlic, but not as strong. **Watercress** <term>Nastrutium</term> is similar to **Mustard** and **Rocket**: it treats mange <note>original: alopecijs</note>, the spleen, leprosy, itchy skin eruptions, and other things. The leaves and roots of **Candy-tuft** <term>Iberis</term> are similar to watercress and share its scent: they are most usefully applied to the hips. **Cocklebur** <term>Xanthium</term> imitates the scent of watercress: it is most aptly placed on tumors, for watercress dissolves tumors and collections of fluid. **Ground Pine** <term>Chamæpithys</term> imitates the pine in its scent: it assists with difficulty urinating, defects of the liver and kidneys, the stomach, and crawling ulcers. **St. John's Wort** <term>Hypericum</term> imitates the scent of resin in its seed; because of this, some have called it "Ground Pine": it moves urine and heals burns. **Great St. John's Wort** <term>Ascyrum</term> has a resinous fruit, not unlike St. John's Wort: it treats sciatica and burns. The flower heads of **Tutsan** <term>Androsæmum</term>, when crushed, give off a resinous scent: they are also useful for burns and sciatica. **Bitumen Trefoil** <term>Trifolium asphalition</term> has fresh leaves whose scent is like **Rue**; when mature, they smell of bitumen: it brings help to those with epilepsy, pleurisy, womb defects, and the diseases of serpents, and it promotes cleansings: like rue, it moves urine, is an antidote for lethal drugs, and for side pains, strangulation of the womb, epilepsy, it moves the menses, and renders the venom of serpents ineffective. **Burnet** <term>Pimpinella</term> is commended for its scent of **Melon** and **Cucumber**; it restores the sense of smell,

## *HOW THE TRUE BIRTHPLACES OF PLANTS ARE TO BE INVESTIGATED,*
## *and thoroughly learned. Chapter 41.*

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'I' featuring floral motifs and scrolling leaf patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

I believe we have now sufficiently demonstrated how plants draw their manifest qualities from their native places and their ancestry, and how they may likewise be thoroughly known from their outward appearance. We said the same in human **Physiognomy** <note>the study of physical features to determine character</note>: that men take their characters from their regions. But the same difficulty that arose regarding man seems to apply to plants as well. For if a man always remained where he was born, his character and qualities would be easily and immediately known; but because he now wanders here and there through various regions and mingles with other nations, the various qualities of men become altered and corrupted through mixed and adulterated lineage. The same must be said of plants: for if plants always remained where they arose from the mixture of heaven and earth, and were never moved from their places, their manifest properties would be easily discerned. But because both plants and seeds are carried to different places, a confusion and corruption of their forms and qualities arises from this. **Theophrastus** <note>a Greek philosopher and the "Father of Botany"</note> declares this most clearly. Trees claim the places suited to them—not only those which nature created with a laborious and peculiar character, but even those held to be common and ordinary. Indeed, some love dry regions, others crave damp ones; some desire wintry places, others those exposed to the Sun; some rejoice in shade protected from the wind, others in open places; some delight in marshes, others in mountains, as authors have been accustomed to categorize them. But perhaps they do not always seek the same places, nor for a single reason, but for various reasons—though they are also led to their proper place by a natural kinship, just like those things which grow of their own accord.

Spontaneous growth shows the nature of a plant more expressly: for it is necessary that their generation, nutrition, and the distinction of individual parts are driven by the same forces: namely, heat, cold, dryness, and moisture. For all things seek what would be convenient for them according to their own **temperament** <note>the specific balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>. I add that similar things require a similar place, and dissimilar things a dissimilar one, especially when some natural diversity is present. The **Plant-Observer** <term>Phytoptam; from the Greek for one who looks at plants</term> ought to be best advised in these matters: we command him to be well-versed in the true birthplaces of plants. For he must not immediately judge a plant to be a "child of the water" or a marsh plant simply because he sees it growing near water or streams, and conclude from this that it is moist in nature. Nor should he call whatever he sees on mountain peaks "dry," for a mountain plant can easily conceive, live, and bear fruit if situated near water by chance or by artifice, and likewise marsh plants can grow in the mountains. We can even force a plant brought from a hot zone to live among us through pampering and other allurements. Many foreign things were sown and brought to Rome, but they always gradually failed and returned to their own nature <note>original: "ad sua loca reuersa sunt", meaning they reverted to the traits of their original climate or died out</note>. But through frequent inspection, one ought to attend to and observe in what kind of soil, sky, site, and cultivation it is accustomed to be born and live; and when he has observed this for a long time, then without doubt he will be able to pronounce what sort of place it is an inhabitant of. The histories of **Theophrastus**, the prince of plant description, can contribute much to this; then **Dioscorides** <note>a Greek physician and author of 'De Materia Medica'</note>, who transcribed almost everything from him—both what he knew and what he was ignorant of—and then other writers of agriculture and plants. This should be observed more in wild herbs and those growing spontaneously than in domestic ones, for the wild ones are less deceptive and more simple. Urban plants often falsify their habit and form; when all these things have been considered, then he will be able to offer a judgment.

# OF GIAMBATTISTA DELLA PORTA
## OF NAPLES
### PHYTOGNOMONICS
### *BOOK THREE*
### PREFACE.

*We have already explained both the forms of plants and their manifest qualities, which they drew from their birthplaces. Now there present themselves the similarities which Nature, the parent of all things, adds, so that they may serve as evidence and benefit for us in penetrating into her innermost recesses and discerning her more secret powers. This method, not yet fully known, corresponds to that by which, in human **Physiognomy** <term>Physiognomonia: the art of judging character from physical features</term>, we examined internal character from the traits apparent on the face. We shall bring forward many examples, as we previously promised, in our specific mentions of them; through these, the **Phytopta** <note>original: "Phytopta"; literally "plant-observer"—a term Porta uses for a student of his system who observes the "signatures" of plants</note>, being warned and instructed, will be able to conjecture many wonderful things for himself. But to begin our task, it will be worthwhile to divide what we are about to write into a summary order, and once divided into order, to embrace it for the sake of clearer teaching. In this book, we shall more carefully set forth the similarities of plants—those which mimic the parts of our body in appearance and shape—since **Nature** <note>Porta personifies Nature as a deliberate designer who leaves clues for humans to find</note> has acted so that they can heal those limbs, or bring aid to those diseases which occur in those same limbs*

*...tend to happen to the limbs. But because all parts of the body are either similar or dissimilar: we call the humors, nerves, flesh, bones, and the like "similar"; "dissimilar" parts are the mouth, eyes, nose, hands, and such, and we subdivide these into external and internal. The external are those visible to the eye, such as the testicles, teeth, and hands; the internal are the liver, heart, spleen, and lungs. With these established as the highest points of our discussion, we shall begin with the humors.*

# PLANTS CONSIST OF HUMORS JUST LIKE HUMANS, AND CAN INCREASE AND PURGE THE HUMORS OF OUR BODIES.

## Chapter I.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>

We have said in the threshold of this work that just as in the bodies of humans and other animals, so in the bodies of trees there are bones, marrow, veins, and blood. For the humor that lies within their body ought to be understood as their blood; it overflows with black or yellow bile, or phlegm, and we shall name a plant based on whichever of these humors predominates within it. For we are accustomed to call plants bilious, choleric <note>associated with yellow bile</note>, pituitous <note>associated with phlegm</note>, and sanguine <note>associated with blood</note>. And just as in human **Physiognomy** <term>Physiognomonia: the study of physical features to determine internal health and character</term> we examined various temperaments from the colors of the humors—namely, whether they were sanguine, bilious, choleric, or pituitous—so may we be permitted to recognize from the colors of plant humors which humor predominates in them, and which diseases they can cure. For a yellow humor abounds in some plants, black in others, and in others sanguine, white, milky, watery, or green; in some these are seen in the roots, in others the fruits or leaves, but in all they are observed especially in the flowers. 

But since there are very few plants that claim a single color for themselves—one color might be in the roots, while another is in the fruit, leaf, and flower—the judgment of predominance will be weighed as either simple or mixed. We use plants and animals for food, medicine, or both. If certain plants are in continuous use and eaten by us, their substance is converted into our own nature, and they imprint upon our bodies those qualities which they possess. For example, if they are excessively bilious, they make our bodies bilious; if they are choleric, they make us choleric and induce in us diseases that are the offspring of black bile: such as psoriasis, scabs, skin eruptions, leprosy <note>original: "elephantiafes" (elephantiasis); in early modern medicine, this term often referred to various severe skin diseases</note>, and through their dark color, obscurities of the vision. **Mithridates** <note>Mithridates VI of Pontus, a king famous for supposedly making himself immune to poison by taking small daily doses</note>, by drinking poisons daily, found them harmless through habit, so that when he was captured by Pompey, he could not kill himself in prison with poison. Likewise, we spoke of the girl sent to **Alexander the Great** <note>A reference to the "Poison Maiden" legend, where a girl was raised on poison until her very touch or breath was lethal</note> whose body had been converted into poison. 

On the other hand, if we use these same plants rarely or as medicine, they cure our diseases. Those which are bilious, when administered in the manner prescribed by medical experts, will purge those same humors and cure the diseases that depend on them. For the humors taken into the body, by an alluring sympathy, draw those similar humors to themselves and lead them out. This settles the question debated by physicians: by what reasoning do simple medicines purge the humors of our body? We see this happens only through similarity and kinship. Nor could the noble diligence of obedient Nature—sparing no effort in creating similarities—demonstrate the gifts of plants to mortals in any simpler way than through the colors of their flowers and other parts. In these, there is such variety that Nature sports in painting them in the great joy of her fertility, so much so that not even human strength is sufficient to conceive of so many diverse things. But because colors are rarely simple, as we have said, a simple humor is rarely cured; rather, two or three are often treated together. For this reason, yellow bile is often expelled with phlegm, and frequently with... 
<meta>phlegm</meta>

<summary>Porta argues that plants possess humors (blood, bile, phlegm) just like humans, and their medicinal effects are revealed through their colors. He establishes the principle that "like cures like" based on the physical signatures of plants.</summary>
<keywords>humors, doctrine of signatures, pharmacology, Mithridates, Alexander the Great, medical botany, physiognomy, yellow bile, black bile, phlegm</keywords>

--- Page 100 ---
<meta>This page concludes the introductory discussion on the humors of plants and begins Chapter II, which focuses on the homeopathic principle that nature often provides the cure within or near the source of the ailment.</meta>

<page-num>96</page-num>
<header>PHYTOGNOMONICA BOOK III</header>

...blood with phlegm. We shall speak first of the simple ones, then of the mixed; the simple humors are so easy to recognize that not even unlearned women, nor the more ignorant, can err in distinguishing them. But this work, as it is great and most useful, is likewise full of difficulty, both because the colors in flowers are not stable—for there are some which have various colors through the stages of their lives: at the beginning, due to weakness, they show one color, but as they grow more mature and claim their full strength, they show another—and because the colors of plants are varied by the differences of the air, the site, the cultivation, and the soil. For a plant made wilder is rendered bilious <note>associated with yellow bile</note> due to dryness; yet when made gentler by cultivation, it becomes more humid, just as we see in animals; and we have spoken abundantly of these things in our **Physiognomonics** <term>Physiognomonia: Porta’s earlier work on judging character/health from physical appearance</term>. Furthermore, the ancients who wrote about plants, in describing their colors, spoke so variously and perplexingly that not only is there disagreement between them, but the same author is not even consistent with himself. For one is accustomed to call a color red, russet, blood-red, crimson, or scarlet; and another blue, purple, red, yellow, and black; or perhaps saffron, yellow, red, and hyacinth-colored. It therefore behooves the Plant-Observer <note>original Latin: *Phytoptæ*</note> to weigh the colors themselves with diligent examination and firsthand observation <note>original Greek: *autopsia* (αὐτοψίᾳ)</note>, especially those of his native place. He should take it as a confessed truth that Nature demonstrates the colors of herbs in no more fitting way under any sky, earth, or site than we might wish, so that we may bring aid to the diseases of that specific region. For tracts of the world that are separated by a long distance produce different diseases and different colors of plants. Pliny, forecasting this **Phytognomonics** of ours, said: "Nature herself had painted remedies in the flowers, and by their very sight had invited our minds, mixing help even with delights." From this, she devised some plants that are shaggy in appearance and fierce to the touch, so that we almost seem to hear the voice of Nature herself as she shapes them and gives her reason: lest the greedy four-legged beast graze upon them, lest bold hands snatch them, lest they be trampled by neglectful footsteps, or lest a perching bird harm them; by protecting them with these prickles and arming them with weapons, she keeps the remedies safe and sound. Thus, even this quality which we hate in them was devised for the sake of mankind.

---

## THAT THE SAME HERBS AND ANIMALS WHICH CAUSE HARM ALSO PROVIDE REMEDIES.
### Chapter II.

But because I see many people tormented by anxiety, unable to accept that the same things which are foods can also be medicines, and that the same things which cause harm can also offer remedies, even if we have argued this at greater length elsewhere, I wish now to prove by several examples that in all the works of the greatest God, where there is evil, there is also the remedy. Wine, when ingested too liberally, intoxicates and disturbs the citadel of the mind; Democritus relates that the craving for wine is abolished by the sap <note>original: *sanie*, literally 'ichor' or 'discharge'</note> that flows from pruned vines, if it is offered to the drunkard in a drink without his knowledge; and thus the vine may atone with its own sap for the harm it brought through its vices. Beritius promises to bring the drunk back to health if they drink an abundance of vinegar. The laurel offends the vine with its scent and causes the wine to spoil, yet branches of laurel protect wine from the stain of corruption when the sky is shaken by thunder. Beet and cabbage grow together: if the flavor of wine in a vat is spoiled by cabbage, it is repaired by the scent of beet or by submerging its leaves, according to Pliny. If by chance wine has been turned into vinegar by a beet root, it will return to its former state if a cabbage root is put in. There is a marvelous difference: white beets loosen the bowels, while black ones bind them. Cabbage, when not thoroughly cooked, softens the bowels; the same cabbage, cooked twice, restrains them. Lentils bind the bowels; yet the same in food, if undercooked, moves them. Plums make the bowels fluid; yet the bark from the root, boiled in harsh wine, checks the flow. Cherries move the bowels; yet the same, when dried, stop them, according to Pliny. Fresh figs are eaten for the sake of moving the bowels, which they do easily. The root of dock with wine restrains the bowels; the leaves, with salt added, move the bowels; the herb itself also moves them, but the seed causes constipation. The juice of grapes relaxes the bowels, but that of sour grapes constricts them. The ripe mulberry moves the bowels; the unripe one stops them. The juices of the ripe fruit stain the hands; those of the sour fruit wash them clean. Pliny said that the stains on the garments of a menstruating woman cannot be washed away except by the urine of the same woman. The raisin tries the stomach and the intestines, but the seeds <note>original: *nuclei*</note> found within the grapes themselves provide the remedy.

The use of mint and green rue excites sexual desire <note>original Latin: *Venerem concitat*</note>; yet, according to Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD), author of *De Materia Medica*</note>, when the dried leaves are applied to the womb before intercourse, they prevent conception. The frequent use of apples <note>original: *melorum*</note> diminishes the seminal fluid and takes away the impulse toward sex, but the dried seeds produce the opposite effect, according to Simeon. Orchids <term>Testiculi: literally "little testicles," referring to plants with paired tubers like the Orchis genus</term> have a double arrangement, an upper and a lower; drinking one or the other produces different results, for the upper root serves to stimulate intercourse, while the lower serves to inhibit it. The gladiolus <note>original: *Xiphium*</note> grows with twin roots, one sitting upon the other; the upper, drunk in wine, is a stimulator of desire, while the lower resists it. Asparagus makes one more prone to sex according to Pliny, but according to Dioscorides, given to males it consumes the seed, and bound to a woman it causes miscarriage. Hellebore <note>original: *Veratrum*</note> terribly provokes vomiting, yet its pith, given during excessive purging, restrains vomiting, according to Pliny. Dried figs stimulate thirst, while fresh ones quench it. Salt eaten in food provokes thirst, but held and rolled under the tongue, it drives away both hunger and thirst, so that one does not feel hunger for two days.

The power of monkshood <note>original: *Napellus*</note> is so wild and immense that almost no remedies can counter its lethal effect on humans; however, there grows with it, or nearby, the "counter-poison" <note>original: *antitora*, referring to *Aconitum anthora* or Wholesome Wolfsbane</note>, an antidote against its deadly poison, according to Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note>. Another variety called "mouse-monkshood," the worst of the former type, carries flies in its flowers or has them constantly sitting upon it; these are the antidote to its poison. The oleander carries the same, which resist its poison, according to recent findings. Blister beetles <term>Cantharides: poisonous beetles historically used in medicine and as an aphrodisiac</term> are born from wheat and crops; a cream of grain, groats, or rice is effective against them if they are swallowed, according to Dioscorides. Legumes are very often born "uncookable"; near them grows broomrape <note>original: *orobanche*</note>, which, when added to them, hastens the cooking, according to Dioscorides. The sawdust of juniper and ash is lethal when drunk, yet the plants themselves are powerful against poisons. A blow from a giant fennel stalk <note>original: *Ferula*</note> induces a bruise, according to Aristotle in his book of *Problems*, but its juice removes the marks. The "deadly carrot" <note>original: *thapsia*</note> performs the same, according to Pliny. 

A staff made of holly <note>original: *aquifolium*</note> thrown at any animal—even if it falls short because of a failure by the thrower—will of its own nature glide closer to the animal as it lies on the ground, according to Pythagoras <note>The Greek philosopher/mathematician; Porta often cites him for mystical plant properties</note>; by its own nature, it also mends broken bones. Thorny plants, because they frequently wound the unwary and the thorns remain in the wound, also draw thorns out of the body and heal the wounds they have made: the Hawthorn <note>original: *Oxyacantha*, "sharp thorn"</note> strikes the hand with stiff prickles when touched, but its root applied as a salve extracts prickles and thorns. Christ's Thorn <note>original: *Paliurus*</note>, a type of thorn, pierces the hand cruelly, but its root decocted and applied draws out things fixed in the body, according to Pliny. The same is to be said of sea-holly <note>original: *eryngium*</note>. Arrows are made from reeds; the arrowhead plant <note>original: *sagittaria*, called *naston*</note>, as if "stuffed," extracts a shaft from the body when its root is crushed and applied, according to Dioscorides. *Holcus* grass grows in rocky and dry places and has thin bristles <note>original: *aristas*</note> at the top; this, bound around the head or arm, removes bristles from the body, which is why some call it *aristida*, according to Pliny. 

A cut onion provokes tears, yet by its very smell it cures tearing and dimness of sight, according to Pliny. Watercress <note>original: *Nasturtium*</note> has fiery effects, and for that reason it affects the head according to the commentator on Nicander, but taken with vinegar, it calms a disturbed mind. The mandrake called *morion*, if swallowed, intercepts the use of reason and renders the senses helpless; physicians use it when there is a necessity for cutting or incising; its root drunk with "manic" nightshade <note>original: *manico solano*</note> is an antidote, according to Dioscorides. Cashew nuts <note>original: *Anacardia*</note> are noxious and deadly, yet they do not lack a remedy: the oil expressed from their kernels is the cure, according to Serapio. The juice from the squirting cucumber <note>original: *e cucumere syluestri*</note>, unless it is cut early, leaps out with danger to the eyes, yet it heals the defects and obscurities of the eyes, according to Pliny. The pimpernel <note>original: *Anagallis*</note> that produces a crimson flower draws out the bowels, while the one that produces a blue flower restrains a prolapse, according to Dioscorides. Fig milk curdles milk like rennet, yet by that same action it later dissolves it, according to Dioscorides. The nettle <note>original: *vrtica*</note> on its outermost surface itches, burns, and heats; its internal juice soothes the feverish heat of the heart; although by a light touch it immediately produces itching and pustules like a burn, the remedy is in its own oil. The virtue of roses and violets is purgative in their upper parts, but their astringent and strengthening power lies hidden in their inner parts. Raw lupins do not digest well; when soaked, they stir up an appetite for food and remove nausea from the stomach. Mnesitheus of Athens records that Euboean nuts <note>chestnuts</note> are difficult to cook; but when roasted, they cause no trouble to the stomach. Apples are so strangely heavy for pack animals to carry, even just a few, that some animals succumb even if they are not unequal to the work in strength; the remedy is if some are given to them to be eaten first, or certainly...

# PHYTOGN.

...are given, from Plutarch and from Lucian in *The Golden Ass* <note>Two ancient authors who wrote versions of the story of a man transformed into a donkey</note>. The same things happen in animals that we have said happen in plants. There is no poisonous animal that does not contain its own <term>antipharmacum: a counter-remedy or substance that acts against a poison</term> within itself. A dog's bite induces madness and <term>hydrophobia: a terrifying symptom of rabies where the victim is unable to swallow and fears water</term>; to ward off these fears of water, they use the tooth of a dog called the "canine." According to Dioscorides, this tooth is taken from the dog that did the biting, placed in a small pouch, and tied to the arm as an amulet. According to Galen, hair placed upon the inflicted bite will heal it. According to Avicenna, worms from a dog's carcass bound to the body, or its blood, work against these fears. According to Pliny, saliva given in food, or the ash of a dog’s head, or the worm found under the tongue of a rabid dog is used; or, according to Galen and Paul of Aegina, a roasted liver.

It is agreed among all that if water and drink are dreaded because of a dog's bite, the fear is immediately dispelled if a scrap of cloth <note>This refers to a cloth dipped in menstrual blood, a common folk-remedy in antiquity</note> is placed under the drinking cup. Clearly, that <term>sympathia: a natural connection or "feeling together" between things</term> immediately prevails, especially since we have said (following Pliny) that the tasting of menstrual blood is what causes madness in dogs in the first place.

The meat of a goat induces a foul smell in sweat, which was a charge brought against a certain Theban athlete. However, according to Marcellus, if the armpits are rubbed with the shaved horn of a mature buck, or with its gall, the heavy stench is abolished. Eating the meat and liver of goats induces <term>epilepsiam: the "falling sickness" or epilepsy</term> if eaten continuously; yet, according to Pliny, the meat of a goat roasted on a man’s funeral pyre benefits those suffering from the "comitial disease" <note>Another term for epilepsy, so named because a seizure was seen as a bad omen that would halt Roman political assemblies (comitia)</note>. Anyone who eats the meat of an elk will be seized by the same disease, but the hoof of its right hind foot is an amulet; when placed into the left ear, the person is healed.

The tips of deers' tails contain a venom which, if drunk, leads to <term>syncopem: a sudden loss of consciousness or fainting</term> and death, according to Avicenna; the <term>antidotum: an antidote or remedy</term> for this is the deer's own eye, according to Ponzetto. The *chalcis* <note>A type of lizard or perhaps a stinging insect</note> brings either death or intense pain with its bite; yet, according to Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen, it heals its own bites if drunk in wine. The sting of a sea-scorpion is cured by applying the same scorpion's liver. The sea-dragon <note>The weaver fish</note> stings with a venomous spine; the fish itself, cut open and applied to the wound, heals it. The land scorpion that delivered the sting, if crushed and applied to the spot, is the remedy for its own strike. Even the shrew-mouse that inflicted a bite pays for its deed if it is cut open and applied to the wound, according to Straton in the writings of Aetius. According to Dioscorides, the head of a viper, or the whole snake crushed and applied to the wound, heals it—and this is true of all serpents.

Spanish flies <note>original: *Cantharides*</note> are an <term>antidotum: antidote</term> to their own poison if their feet and wings are preserved with honey, according to Galen on the authority of Asclepiades. The toad <note>original: *Rubetæ*</note> has a double liver: one is deadly, the other is an <term>antipharmacum: a counter-poison</term>. Its spleen helps against the poisons made from the toads themselves, according to Nicander. The venomous stings of bees are no different in their remedy; those who have been stung should drink the bees. It is a marvel, however, that while they carry poison in their mouths and sting with it, the bees themselves do not die from it. Or, <term>propolis: a resinous "bee glue" used to seal the hive</term> extracts all stingers that are stuck in the body.

Among all venomous things, the wickedness of the salamander is the greatest; others strike individuals and do not kill many at once, but the salamander alone can kill entire populations of the unwary. It is appropriate to apply their meat over the wound. A worm, dried and reduced to powder and given to one suffering from worms, kills them all and ejects them from the body. A small stone ejected by a sufferer of bladder stones, if bound over the pubic area, is said to relieve others of the same ailment. The stench of burnt animals puts to flight animals of their own kind. On the authority of Diophanes, the stench of a burning scorpion immediately puts all other scorpions to flight. By the scent of a single burnt ant, the rest are turned to flight. If you catch locusts and burn some of them, the rest, offended by the smell, are struck blind as if by a covering mist. Farmers burn some caterpillars to drive the rest from their gardens, and so it is for others.

Bythus of Dyrrachium relates that mirrors dulled by the gaze of a menstruating woman regain their shine if she looks at them again from the opposite side. A gecko <note>original: *Stellio*</note> held in the left hand excites sexual desire, but if moved to the right hand, it inhibits it. From a toad, the bones from the left side make one more prone to desire, while those from the right side inhibit it. Scales scraped from the top part of a turtle shell and given in a drink restrain intercourse; this is all the more marvelous since the flour of the entire shell is said to kindle <term>libidinem: sexual desire or lust</term>.

Hence, even animals that bear horns, tusks, wild teeth, and protruding fangs, and are accustomed to inflicting great wounds, bring with them the healing for those wounds. The bull, a most robust animal, is powerful in the strength of its head and neck; it has a strong forehead suitable for battle, and Nature gave it hostile horns with which it inflicts the greatest wounds. The most excellent glue is made from the shoulders and geni- <note>original: *& geni-*</note>

...and from the genitals of bulls, it is recorded by Pliny that when liquefied, it heals fresh wounds, and is removed on the third day. Male goats attack with their horns and knock men down; the ash of a burnt goat's horn binds wounds together and stops the flow of blood, according to Pliny. The wild boar has large and protruding teeth; when it is stirred up by hunters during the chase, its tooth becomes so heated by its inflamed breath that if it touches the pursuing dogs with that tooth, scorched marks are immediately impressed upon their skin, according to Oppian, Xenophon, and Pollux. The dung of the wild boar is drunk with vinegar for ruptures and convulsions, according to Dioscorides. A dog inflicts sharp wounds with its teeth; a dog’s brain heals fractured bones when a linen cloth is placed over them, which heals them steadily within about fifteen days, according to Pliny. A horse strikes with its teeth and hooves; its blood is mixed with other medicines and smeared on fractures and dislocations, according to Theomnestus. We could have added other examples, were we not afraid of being tedious, believing that these descriptions by the ancients will be entirely sufficient for those who object; we omit greater things found by us and more recent authors, as they would lack credibility among meddlers <note>original: *ardeliones*; refers to busybodies or pretentious skeptics</note>, as if they were made up by us.

### THAT WE MAY NATURALLY TRACK SOMETHING OF THE INTERNAL NATURE FROM COLORS. Cap. III.

But let us demonstrate from natural causes whether we can track something of the internal nature, or of manifest qualities, from colors, and what our ancestors thought of them. Galen, and after him Averroes in his *Colliget* <note>The *Kitab al-Kullyat*, a comprehensive medical encyclopedia by the Andalusian philosopher Averroes</note>, said that the signs of colors are futile, because colors reside only on the surface of the colored thing, and it very often happens that the quality of the part in which the color resides is quite different from the quality of the whole colored object; therefore, the same color is seen in both hot and cold things. Whiteness, they say, is seen in snow, lime, camphor, and salt; it happens differently in tastes, which reveal the qualities of internal things. 

But these men do not seem at all to be strict seekers of the truth, because they do not weigh the matter in a just scale, or bring it to the test. For what does snow have in common with lime? Or salt with camphor? Since we are not speaking of every "white" thing generally, but of a single genus or species of flowers; and in animals, a white or black color proceeds from a diversity of substance, just as we believe it should be judged regarding the colors of plants. Nor do we speak of color spread merely on the surface, but that which is in the whole; for the internal and external colors of leaves or flowers should be mixed together by the pressure or rubbing of the fingers, and the predominant color discerned from the mixture, just as happens in tastes; for while we grind things with our teeth, the tastes of the surface and the depths are felt mixed together. 

There is an unspotted whiteness in the skin of the lily flower, but if you press it with your fingers, the mixture becomes saffron-colored; the same happens in musk roses. The flowers of *Hypericum* <note>St. John's Wort</note> are golden; the leaves are green and saffron-colored, but if you rub them in your hands, the hands are stained with the color of black gore <note>original: *atri cruoris*; this refers to the red pigment hypericin, which leaks from the plant when crushed</note>. No one denies that the same can happen in tastes. And so that all suspicion of ambiguity may vanish, tastes are changed just as colors are, by a change of nourishment, sky, location, and cultivation, as was discussed in the previous books; and the quality changes with the taste and color. 

The *Chamaeleon* herb varies according to the change of its leaf, according to Dioscorides, so that it arises green in one place, and saffron, black, or blue in another. Through the course of ages, colors change along with quality in some herbs. The *Leucoion* <note>Likely the Wallflower or Stock</note>, feeling its old age, degenerates; and if it was purple in the beginning, it produces hoary flowers in its old age. Carnations <note>original: *garyophylli*</note> and roses, while they are young, burn with a glowing color; when they grow old, they turn white and cast off their former grace; so too with the snapdragon <note>original: *os leonis*, "lion's mouth"</note>, lesser centaury, Canterbury bells <note>original: *violæ marianæ*</note>, and others. The same may be experienced in animals. The color of vipers varies according to a change in their native place. When the water of the River Clitumnus <note>A river in Umbria, Italy, famous in antiquity for its white cattle</note> is drunk, white oxen are sired. Virgil says:

> ...and the Clitumnus in the wide fields. <note>From Virgil's *Georgics*, 2.146, referring to the white herds used in Roman triumphs</note>

### BILIOUS PLANTS TAKEN AS FOOD
->increase bile. Chapter III.<-

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'N' decorated with foliate scrolls and a figure reclining in the background.</image-desc>
NOW let us come to the humors. The mass of humors, which is called blood, either overabounds or putrefies. The humors in the blood that overabound and putrefy are phlegm <note>original: *pituita*</note>, yellow bile, or black bile; or they overabound and do not putrefy, such as milk, semen, and the menses. If they do not overabound but are instead secreted, they are superfluous and pass away into excrement: from blood comes ichor <note>the watery part of blood</note>, or serum, urine, and sweat; from phlegm comes mucus, spit, and tears. Now we must consider what humors the various colors of plants generate and secrete. Among the leaders of philosophy, there are those who claim the color of water is white and its taste is sweet (I would prefer to say tasteless); that the color of earth is dark <note>original: *fuscum*</note> and its taste is bitter (I interpret "dark" as blue, green, and black, but the taste as not bitter, but styptic <note>astringent or mouth-puckering</note>, for if the taste of the earth were bitter, I would hope for nothing to sprout from it); that the color of fire is red (and I say it has no color, and is styptic and bitter); and that the color of air is saffron-yellow. But in its proper place, I shall say what I think about the colors of plants.

I shall demonstrate with many examples that plants of a yellow color, when taken as food, increase yellow bile, and when used as medicine, they expel it. Indeed, by continuous eating and use, these plants increase yellow bile, induce the disease of jaundice <note>original: *icterum morbum*; also known as the "royal disease"</note>, discolor the limbs, and make them unsightly; therefore, those who care for their beauty ought to avoid all these. The types of orach <note>original: *atriplicum*; a leafy vegetable similar to spinach</note> turn black from a yellowish-lead color, or shimmer with a dark red <note>original: *xerampelino*; the color of dried vine leaves</note>, or turn purple from saffron. It was accused by Pythagoras of causing jaundice and pallor, and he complained that nothing grows near it in gardens except what is sickly. Dionysius and Diocles added that many diseases are birthed from them—specifically bilious ones, according to Pliny. Nor, by the sluggishness of its nature, is the spinach plant obscure; it is equal in nature to the orach, which, though neglected, degenerated into this vegetable, not forgetting its former nature.

Cumin is a pale, dull yellow color; it produces pallor in those who drink it. Thus, they certainly say that the followers of Porcius Latro (famous among masters of oratory) imitated the likeness of the color he had contracted from his studies <note>the students drank cumin to look pale and "studiously exhausted" like their teacher</note>. And a little before, it was said that Julius Vindex, that champion of liberty against Nero, was enticed in the same way by the pursuit of a legacy. The appearance and pallor of bishop's weed <note>original: *ammi*</note> is the same; it also changes the color of those who drink it into pallor, according to the same Pliny. Saffron has the flaming color of the crocus, and is more than golden; by the immoderate use of its flowers, both pallor and disgust are contracted. Musk is somewhat yellowish in color; it discolors the limbs of those who use it with pallor, according to Aetius. Because the grain of Ceres <note>bread/wheat</note> is not excessively yellow, bread generates a minimum of yellow bile. The roots of turnips and radishes are wet with saffron-colored juice; for that reason, they increase bile. The leaves and flowers of the beet fade from green into a yellowish hue; Galen said that eating it generates bile. Melons <note>original: *melopepones*</note> are yellow; according to Galen, they generate "cholera" and yellow bile; for that food very easily degenerates into yellow bile, which is why it offends the bilious, and those who drink wine after eating them are more susceptible to harm. The Indian nut <note>likely the coconut</note> turns yellow from red, as does its juice, the eating of which is forbidden to bilious people. Ripe figs are dry and yellow, as Nicophon says. If anyone takes a midday nap after eating figs, a fever immediately rushes in, which draws out a vomit of yellow bile. Spring apples become saffron-colored as they ripen; they produce bile, according to Dioscorides. Pears are of the same condition. Nut trees have leaves that turn from green to saffron, and the kernels inside the fruit are saffron-colored; they are bilious. Honey is of a yellow color, and its use increases bile. Of the same kind is sugar, which has been found to turn into bile. Yellow wine is bilious, especially the sweet kind; for red wine is mostly harsh <note>original: *austerum*</note>, as we shall say. Frogs of a saffron or leaden color—those who frequently eat them, [take on the same] color...

<summary>Della Porta discusses the "Doctrine of Signatures" regarding yellow-colored plants and substances, arguing that their color indicates they generate yellow bile in the human body, leading to conditions like jaundice and pallor.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how the colors of natural substances—specifically yellow and saffron hues—indicate their medicinal relationship with yellow bile. It moves from discussing foods that increase bile to plants that purge it, following the doctrine of signatures.</meta>

# THIRD BOOK

[Lead-colored substances] are stained with a leaden color, which is why Physicians order that they should be taken not as food, but as medicine, since they make the body prone to putrefaction. Because roosters <note>original: *Galli*</note> are mostly yellow, Galen forbids them to those suffering from jaundice <note>original: *ictericis*</note> in his pamphlet on the cure of jaundice. Pheasants, being of the same color and quality, are also forbidden. It is not only the eating of things, but even the sight of them that changes the humors. The saffron-colored toad <note>original: *Rubeta crocea*</note> is ugly and discolored, as Philes <note>Manuel Philes, a Byzantine poet who wrote on the characteristics of animals</note> says. If anyone looks at it for too long, even if they have the best complexion, they will become pale and freckled, just like someone with jaundice. The spotted lizard <note>original: *Stellio*; likely a gecko</note>, which is yellowish and freckled—if one dies in wine and someone drinks it, it will cover their face with saffron-colored freckles. The Arnabo, or zedoary <note>a root similar to ginger or turmeric</note>, is a tree growing in the East whose leaves fade from green to yellow; through frequent use, it creates yellow bile in hot bodies.

---

->THE SAFFRON COLORS OF PLANTS PURGE BILE.<-
->CHAPTER V.<-

Likewise, the yellow juices of plants, roots, and flowers, when taken as medicine, purge yellow bile. For they attract the yellow humors of our body and, once attracted, drive them out through the lower parts <note>the bowels</note>. These are the examples. Aloe, with its saffron-colored juice and flower: Mesue <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a celebrated physician of the Islamic Golden Age</note> said it purges bile. He also said nothing is more praiseworthy or proven for purging bile than senna <note>original: *sena*</note>, whose flowers are pale yellow. Wormwood <note>original: *Absinthium*</note> draws away bile that has stuck to the stomach or belly, being crowned with a golden flower. Another species of lesser centaury, which produces a leaf and a yellow flower, does the same. The saffron-colored flowers of all the spurges <note>original: *Tithymalorum*</note> provoke vomiting and bowel movements, and they draw out bile. *Ascyron* and *androsaemon* <note>species of St. John's Wort</note> with their yellow flowers cast down bile. Colocynth <note>the bitter apple</note>, wild cucumber, and honey-melons <note>original: *melopepones*</note> are all yellow in flower and fruit; when they begin to ripen, they draw out bile. Thapsia <note>the "deadly carrot"</note> bears umbels and yellow flowers upon them; its use in medicine is for purging bile from both ends <note>as an emetic and a laxative</note>. The castor oil plant <note>original: *Ricinus*</note> has a yellowish flower; through its seed, bile is cast out through the bowels. When the leaves of the ground-pine <note>original: *Chamaelee*</note> are drunk, bile is expelled through the bowels; it has a saffron flower. Another type of *Thlaspi* <note>pennycress</note> with a saffron flower draws bile from both ends. Dodder <note>original: *Cassutha*</note>, with its tendrils and filaments equal in thickness to the strings of a lyre, and being yellowish, winds itself around neighboring trees: it relieves the belly and the veins of bilious humors. Certain fruits of the Myrobalan <note>a plum-like fruit used in traditional medicine</note> are yellow, or yellowish with a grass-green color, and these cast out inflamed bile from the body; likewise, those that are black are most effective for driving out black bile. The white kind, called *empelicum* <note>the Emblic myrobalan</note>, draws out phlegm <note>original: *pituita*</note>; but the small onions that are reddish-brown purge the blood of melancholy. These kinds, differing in color, seem to have been given to man by the highest providence of God, and indicated by their colors for purging all the humors of the body, as we learn from Mesue. The *Empetron* of the Greeks, or the *Calcifraga* <note>literally "stone-breaker"</note> of the Latins, delights in a small yellowish flower: when drunk, it draws out bile. Cassia *syringodes* <note>the purging cassia or "pudding-pipe tree"</note> has very long tubes, red or blackish-yellow in color; it expels burning bile from the belly, especially that which has turned into black bile, according to Actuarius <note>Joannes Zacharias Actuarius, a Byzantine physician</note>, because yellow juice is seen to degenerate into black. Citrons and oranges have yellow rinds and juice, and they quench yellow bile. We have said honey is golden; *apomeli* <note>a mixture of honey and water</note> excretes bilious humor. Dewy honey, or the manna of the Arabs, which gathers into honey-like lumps on herbs, trees, and stones, is the color of honey: it expels yellow bile by simple reason. The juniper has a yellow berry, wood, and a liquid which sweats from its trunk like a tear, and by the action of heat hardens into a yellow-colored gum, which in the common tongue is called *varnish* <note>original: *vernix*; likely sandarac resin</note>; it heals the stomach when it has poured out bilious vomit. Rhaponticum <note>a relative of rhubarb</note> is red and yellow in color, and when chewed it is saffron; according to Mesue, it purges bile. *Fragula* <note>likely Alder Buckthorn, *Rhamnus frangula*</note> has wood so yellowish that when chewed it stains with a saffron color, like rhubarb: its bark is black, sprinkled with grey spots: in the same way, it moves the bowels and purges bile. The root of birthwort <note>original: *Aristolochia*</note> is pale grey-yellow <note>original: *glauca*</note> and performs the same work. So too the roots of dock <note>original: *lapathi*</note>, fern, and Mercury <note>the plant *Mercurialis*</note>. Yellow-colored animals provide the same benefits.

### LIKEWISE THE COLORS OF PLANTS ARE EFFECTIVE AGAINST JAUNDICE.
#### Chapter VI.

The disease of jaundice <note>original: *Icteritiae morbus*</note> discolors the entire body with a hostile paleness of bile. Nature, who can never be praised enough, teaches mortals through a very clear proof that this discomfort can be countered by saffron-colored plants, animals, stones, and all things born from the earth. These substances do not only purge that causing humor when swallowed; but when hung up or even looked at, they drive out and shake off such a disease, liberating the besieged body.

We teach that by the sight of yellow things, the yellow bile—which is the parent of the "royal disease" <note>original: *regij morbi*; a common historical name for jaundice</note>—is stirred up and drawn to the surface of the skin. Once called outward, it is easily dispersed. Therefore, we instruct those suffused with yellow bile to gaze upon yellow things; likewise red for the blood, and black for melancholy. But let us bring forth examples of all these by induction, lest someone mock me as having dreamed this or speaking without authority. 

Orach <note>original: *Atriplex*</note> has numerous yellowish little flowers; when its leaves wither, they turn from yellow or pale to gold. For this reason, both Dioscorides and more ancient writers called it *chrysolachanon* <note>Greek: "golden vegetable"</note>. According to Pliny, this herb, when tied to those having the royal disease so that they can see it, heals the evil. The smaller Madder <note>original: *Erythrodano*</note> has flowers that are pale yellow, and a root that fades from reddish to yellow. Drunk in honey-water, it heals the royal disease. Dioscorides also records that it heals if the shrub is merely tied on and looked at; for this reason, it was called the "golden cup" <note>original: *aureum poculum*</note> by the ancients. 

The kinds of wormwood <note>original: *Absinthij*</note>—Pontic, Santonic, and Periphian—are all gifted with a golden flower. In the royal disease, its infusion or decoction is healthily drunk at three measures <note>original: *cyathis*</note> per day. According to Pliny, cattle in the region of Pontus grow fat on them and are consequently found without gallbladders. The Greater Celandine <note>original: *Chelidonio maiori*</note> has a yellow flower; even when wounded, it releases a saffron juice. The root drunk with white wine heals the royal disease. 

Ox-eye <note>original: *Buphthalmon*</note> produces golden flowers, such that the poet Alcman shows a golden necklace consists of its flowers. They claim that for those with the "bow-disease" <note>original: *Arquatis*; another term for jaundice, referring to the rainbow-like color changes in the skin or eyes</note>, who drink it regularly, a good color is restored for a time. It is called *Chrysanthemon* <note>Greek: "golden flower"</note> because it is seen to shine with a certain golden splendor. It restores a cheerfulness of color to those with jaundice, especially if drunk after a long stay when exiting the baths. 

From the wild cucumber, *elaterium* <note>a potent purgative</note> is made, which is beneficial for this disease. Chamomile <note>original: *Anthemis*</note> brings forth golden flowers on the inside and honey-colored ones on the outside; it removes suffused bile, as do Celtic and Syrian nard. Among the types of *Osyris* <note>Toadflax</note> is one that produces yellow flowers; the decoction drunk helps those with jaundice. Also *Conyza* <note>Fleabane</note>, Horse-fennel <note>original: *hippomarathum*</note>, and Groundsel <note>original: *senecio*</note> according to Pliny. Also lettuce, Cinquefoil <note>original: *pentaphylon*</note>, asparagus, aloe, rosemary, *cachrys*, Ground-pine <note>original: *chamaepitis*</note>, Butcher's Broom <note>original: *ruscus*</note>, Hedge-mustard <note>original: *erysimum*</note>, Wild Succory <note>original: *ambubeia*</note>, the leaves of Coltsfoot <note>original: *tussilaginis*</note> according to Pliny, cabbage, Mercury <note>original: *mercurialis*</note> with its yellowish leaves and flowers, and Verbena according to Pliny, strawberry, Stonecrop <note>original: *illecebra*</note> with its yellow stalks, among the types of Columbine <note>original: *aquilinae*</note> with golden flowers, Marigold <note>original: *caltha*</note>, the herb commonly called *turcha*, senna, cumin, and *asarina* <note>Wild Ginger</note> by the experiment of certain moderns; wild rocket, hops, and *laserpitium*. 

So also the leaves of some, like Lichen, are yellow-green; there are also little star-shaped yellow flowers, Spleenwort <note>original: *asplenium*</note> with a yellowish leaf, the leaves and branches of Tamarisk, and also Savin. There are also yellowish roots: the yellow root of Dock <note>original: *lapathi*</note> is effective for jaundice, as is Rhubarb. The root of the Greater Centaury fades from red to yellow and heals the royal disease according to Mesue. Yellow parsnip is also given to those with jaundice, as are Asphodels according to Galen. Turmeric <note>original: *curcuma*</note>, when chewed by druggists <note>original: *seplasiarijs*</note>, yields a saffron juice and is effective for the same. 

So the fruits and seeds of certain trees, such as Citron according to Avicenna, help those with jaundice; also Winter Cherry <note>original: *solani heliacacabi*</note>; Tamarinds, which are tawny, excel at the same. So too certain legumes like the pea, chickpea, bitter vetch, and chewed lupins, when used frequently, improve a person's color according to Pliny. The purging Cassia tree is the color of boxwood as far as the bark, and according to Mesue, it benefits those with jaundice. Dodder <note>original: *Cuscuta*</note> has yellowish tendrils and brings the same help. 

One may also see this in animals, and even more in sentient things, since they are alive and more easily stir and attract bile—the proof being that they themselves die immediately. The *Galgulus* <note>the Golden Oriole</note>, or Jaundice-bird, reflects a pale and sallow color according to Pliny. Speaking of the "Jaundice-gem" <note>original: *icteria gemma*</note>, he says: "The Jaundice-gem is similar to the sallow bird, and is therefore thought to be healthy against royal diseases." Grammarians say that sallow [means]...

## Those Afflicted with Jaundice <note>original: *Arquati*; literally "the arched ones," a term for jaundice victims possibly referring to the rainbow-like colors of the eyes or the curved shape of the gallbladder</note>

A bird called the *icterus* <note>the golden oriole</note> is named after its color; it is said that if a person looks at it, the illness is healed, but the bird itself dies. I believe this bird is called the *galgulum* in Latin, according to Pliny. The *icterus* is a certain bird named for its color; if anyone held by this disease looks at it, they will soon be entirely freed from the sickness, according to Oppian. Gerard of Cremona, following the *Cyranides* <note>an ancient book of magic and medicine</note>, calls the *charadrius* bird <note>likely a stone-curlew or plover</note> the "royal bird," precisely because it is sought after by kings for the cure of the "royal disease" <note>jaundice</note>. Aristotle mentions it, and it certainly seems that the "arched disease" <note>jaundice</note> corresponds to it, since its legs, beak, and the iris of its eyes shine with a yellow or saffron color; only the underside of its body pales with a reddish hue. Aelian meanwhile mentions this bird in connection to sulfur (perhaps because sulfur also repels the royal disease). The *charadrius* bird cures the royal disease if it is merely looked at by the patient; for this reason, those who sell the bird hide it, lest the sick person see it before they have bought it and thus be cured for free, according to Euphronius. 

But Andreas says it cures not by sight, but by being eaten. The *charadrius* neither looks at nor tolerates one suffering from the royal disease; instead, it closes its eyes and presses its eyelids together, turning away—not out of malice (as some believe) toward human health, but as if receiving a blow. It feels itself being wounded and affected by a contagion, transferring the ailment into itself through the gaze of the other, like a sort of flowing stream, as Heliodorus mentions in the third book of his *Ethiopian History*, and also Aelian. But Philes adds: if anyone looks at a toad <note>original: *Rubetam*</note>, no matter how healthy their color, they will be affected by paleness as if jaundiced; and conversely, by looking at the *charadrius*, they will be freed. Suidas reports the same from Hipponax. 

There is a type of woodpecker that hangs its nest from branches, says Pliny, in the shape of a cup so that no other bird can approach; some call it the *chlorion* <note>the golden oriole</note> because of its yellow or golden color, which it radiates except for its wings, which are more greenish. I hear it is called a *horiolo* by our people because of its golden color. More recent writers say it cures jaundice, unless they are confusing it with the birds mentioned above. There is a bird called the *paro* <note>the titmouse</note> whose breast is saffron-colored and reddish below; there are those who attribute the same power to it as the golden oriole. This bird seems to have obtained such a nature that it attracts the defect to itself and seizes it, drawing the sickness out from the eyes like an overflow. 

The parrot <note>original: *Psitaco*</note> has a yellowness throughout its body, except for its neck which is marked by a vermilion ring; they record that its meat helps those with jaundice. The partridge is tile-colored <note>reddish-brown</note>, and on its back and tail it appears adorned with black, red, and yellow; its brain, drunk with three small measures of wine, resists the royal disease according to Pliny. The eagle is entirely yellow, and its eyes are not grey-blue but amber-colored <note>original: *charopi*</note>, like a lion’s; it has the same power as the partridge's brain. 

Lizards are entirely green with a certain paleness, which is why the Greeks call them *chlorosaura* <note>literally "green-lizard"</note>. Hippocrates says the royal disease is pale with a green tint, like the paleness of these green lizards, in the third book of *On Epidemics*. If a live lizard is caught, placed in a small bag, and tied over the jaundiced person until the lizard dies, it draws the color of the jaundice to itself—a fact we have confirmed by most certain experiment. 

There are chickens of various colors, especially those entirely saffron or yellowish, but there are many kinds that have saffron feet, like jaundiced people, of which Pliny writes: a hen resists the royal disease if it has yellow feet, first purifying it with water, then washing it with wine, which should then be drunk. The same is said of the lion, the bear, and other saffron-colored animals, lest we wander too far. These same things heal jaundice of the eyes and cataracts <note>original: *glaucomata*</note>. Pliny says: they burn the green lizard with a long neck found in sand-pits to remove cataracts. A hawk has the same power as an eagle, though weaker; hawk dung with Attic honey is effective for the same things, and they also have saffron feet according to Pliny. The *charadrius* also removes dimness and mist from the eyes and brings back clarity. According to Pliny, partridge eggs boiled with honey in a bronze vessel remove cataracts; likewise, its gall helps gray-clouded eyes <note>original: *glaucedinem*</note> according to Galen. The eyes of a kite are pale or saffron, just like the eyes of those with jaundice, according to Suidas; it is of the hawk family, differing only in size, and has the same power as the hawk to help those with the "arched disease." There are also other saffron-colored things, such as the resins of the pine and larch, sulfur, and egg yolk according to Dioscorides, and urine and honey according to Varro and Pliny. Nor [is there any] better...

PHYTOGNOMONICA

...we hold from Diocles and Theophrastus that the royal disease <note>original: *regio morbo*; a historical term for jaundice</note> can be better treated [with these plants] than with amber, whether it is drunk in wine or worn on the person. ### THAT HUMORS CAN BE PURGED EVEN BY THE SIGHT OF THE EYES. Chapter VII.

<image-desc>Decorative initial P featuring floral patterns and scrolled borders, framed in a square.</image-desc>

Since we have fallen into a discussion of colors, we shall open up other matters in passing, which may perhaps be not unpleasant to those who investigate the miracles of nature more scrupulously, nor useless to medical practice. Indeed, many diseases are cured even by colors; and if the use of this has faded among more recent physicians, it has taken root with me. We have tested many things, conjectured many things, and the outcome of events has very often favored and supported our conjectures and hopes. For by the remaining colors, the remaining humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health and temperament</note> have been cured and purged by sight alone. Just as by the presentation of red things, such as the blood-red dye of brambles and mulberries, we have often purified, drawn out, or stayed the blood. In the same way, we assist melancholy and phlegm by calling upon flowers, gems, and stones for that purpose. For while we gaze longer at those colors, they prick and provoke our vision; our senses are affected by the colors they encounter, and the spirits <note>Internal vapors believed to carry sensory information and vital force through the body</note> excited and disturbed by the color are either dispersed or belched out through the empty openings of the pores. This we shall fulfill more clearly through examples drawn from animals, both those already mentioned and those to be brought forward.

It is well known that the color red drives oxen, bulls, and buffaloes into a rage, so that those dressed in red clothing do not approach them; for they attack with their horns and tear them apart. Whence many, to their great misfortune, have suffered various losses because of their colored clothing. The cause is their blood, which is more full of fibers than that of other animals, and for that reason it thickens and hardens very quickly, as is held by Aristotle; thus they are provoked by the sight of a blood-like color. It has been observed in the blood of certain animals that certain small bodies appear, like the image of hairs, which are oblong. This indicates a force of terrestrial excess; hence the blood, becoming heated, remains so for a long time, and thus the affected animal turns out to be wrathful, very persistent in its indignation, and most daring. For fibers of that kind burn like glowing coals, which is also recognized in the pig.

Likewise, hawks abound in blood, an argument for which is that they are spirited; armed more by spirit than by strength, they fly high and do not hesitate to attack prey far and wide through the air. They testify to this not so much by a greed for food as for glory; for the bird is extremely wrathful because of its blood, and for that reason it flies alone. The kite is of the hawk kind, and it especially dreads the color red; for it does not perch on a pomegranate tree <note>original: *punico malo*</note>, nor can it endure the sight of it. From this comes an opening for a story from Oppian: A man, having lost his wife from whom he had a daughter named Side (for *Side* means pomegranate), burned with lust for his daughter. Side, lest she be contaminated by her parent, killed herself over her mother’s tomb. The gods, pitying this misfortune, produced a pomegranate from her blood, and transformed the father into a kite, who flees from the monuments of his own calamity.

The pig, an animal extremely phlegmatic <note>original: *pituitosum*; dominated by the humor of phlegm</note> and moist—nearly the moistest of all land animals that serve as food for men—is driven wild at the sight of the color white. They say that sows in heat are driven so wild that they tear a man apart, especially one dressed in a bright white garment, according to Pliny; this madness is mitigated by sprinkling vinegar, according to nature. Bears are extremely phlegmatic and moist; a white cloth excites them most of all, and they are provoked by it, according to Seneca. A scarlet, black, or variegated color agitates deer, who are melancholic <note>dominated by black bile</note>. Ausonius said they are terrified by the sight of a red feather, in these verses:

> Or when with your brother, through pathless thickets, you surround
> The wandering deer with spots, and the feather in the many-meshed snare <note>A reference to the "formido," a hunting net decorated with red feathers to scare deer into the trap</note>

Virgil mentions the same thing in the *Georgics* where he treats of deer.

BOOK THREE.

> Scarlet feathers drive the fearful with dread. <note>original: *Puniceae agitant pauidos formidine pennae*; a reference to the 'formido,' a hunting cord decorated with red feathers used by ancient hunters to steer deer into nets.</note>

Xenophon says in the *Geoponica* <note>A collection of ancient agricultural lore</note> that deer especially fear a rope from which feathers are suspended, undoubtedly imagining the very movement of the feathers is a threat. The lion is the hottest of animals and the most "fiery," and for this reason, it dreads fire. Homer writes:

> And blazing torches, which, however much he rages, he dreads.

Aristotle and Aelian report that this happens because of the lion's excessive internal heat; it is well known that the lion suffers from a continuous burning fever, and if its bones are struck together, fire is sparked out. Because its nature is so fiery, it is considered sacred to Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire and metalworking</note> by the Egyptians. Due to the abundance of its internal fire, it looks upon external fire with great distress. Aelian, and Philes following him, state that the lion naturally fears fire as a fervent animal; lions are terrified by the turning of wheels and the crests of roosters—and even more by their crowing—but most of all by fires. They are even driven into nets by hunters using fire during the chase. Nor can they endure walking in the harsher sunlight, since they have sharp vision; for the same reason, they flee from fire during the day, according to Alexander of Aphrodisias. Wolves are also "hot" creatures, endowed with eyes of fire that shine like flames at night; they are terrified by fires, especially those sparked from flints. Similarly, elephants are affected by bright colors, and the same must be said of other animals, which we shall remember to mention in their proper places.

## WHAT THE SAFFRON COLOR NATURALLY SIGNIFIES.
### Cap. VIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring a central figure seated among foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

WE HAVE SAID in human Physiognomy <note>The study of physical features as indicators of character or health</note> that a citrine <note>lemon-yellow</note> color in the hair signified a temperament balanced between heat and cold, though Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher</note> said it meant a diminished coldness, in which there was more heat than cold. But if this citrine hue inclines toward a reddish color, it signifies an "intention of heat" <note>an intensification of the fiery quality</note>; as Aristotle said, those endowed with such a body would be maniacs due to the excessive heat. Yet in the short book *On Colors*, he says the saffron color <term>croceus color</term> arises from deficient nourishment: for falling fruits turn yellow, even if their final color is not yellow. Leaves that fall in autumn turn yellow because all nourishment fails during the process of "concoction" <note>the metabolic 'cooking' or ripening of nutrients</note>. Furthermore, the yellow color somewhat represents the Sun or a flame. We shall cite several herbs with yellow-colored flowers or juice that are "hot" in nature; indeed, there are few or none that are cold without some very powerful reason. Anagyris <note>stinking bean-trefoil</note> has a saffron flower and, according to Galen, is hot and dry; so too are yellow stoechas, St. John's wort, tutsan, honeywort, coris, bugle, thapsia, all species of spurge, wild cucumber, elecampane, cultivated and wild fennel, cachrys, mugwort, wormwood, southernwood, buttercups, bitter apple, Celtic nard, asarabacca, costus, balsam, saffron-colored aspalathus, saffron itself, all yellow resins, juniper, germander, fenugreek, lupin, and—according to Avicenna—chickpeas, hercules-allheal, seseli, alexanders, dill, samphire, cumin, wild rocket, bishop's weed, yellow asphodel, pellitory, greater and lesser celandine, giant fennel, restharrow, sulfur-root, broom, Greek mint, chamomile, rue, fleabane, mullein, goldilocks, helichrysum, ageratum, and honey (according to Avicenna). There are others we omit which you may seek out yourself, as no others come to mind at present.

## THAT GRASS-GREEN FLOWERS PURGE LEEK-GREEN BILE,
## and pale flowers purge pale bile, and what a color of this kind naturally
## signifies.
### Cap. VIIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'B' decorated with ornate floral patterns and a central vertical motif.</image-desc>

THE TYPES OF BILE are leek-green <term>prassina</term>, rusty-green, pale, and citrine. We shall speak of the leek-green bile, which is expelled by plants of a green or grass-like color; and because this species of bile is usually evacuated through vomiting and is clearly seen as a liquid, plants of this kind usually purge it through vomiting. The flower of the Narcissus is described by Pliny as "herbaceous" <note>grass-green</note>; Dioscorides says it is an emetic <note>induces vomiting</note> so that it may evacuate this species of bile. Blite has a grass-green flower, and if according to Dioscorides...
