# PHYTOGN.

...is described as being of no use in medicine; indeed, Pliny stated it disturbs the mind so much that it causes "cholera" <note>original: *choleram*; in ancient medicine, this referred to a violent upset of the humors or an overflow of bile, rather than the modern bacterial disease</note> in some people. There is a species of this plant which produces flowers and foliage that represent every variety of bile: yellow, leek-green, copper-green, red, and vitelline <note>original: *vitulinam*; resembling the yellow of a calf or an egg yolk</note>. It induces vomiting and clears out all types of bile. Orach <note>original: *Atriplex*</note> has a grass-like flower, and its seed provokes vomiting. Galen says a species of *thlaspi* <note>a type of cress</note> brought from Crete is a color between saffron and yellow; Dioscorides said the variety from Cappadocia draws out bile through vomiting and through the lower parts, even to the point of drawing blood. But truly, through vomiting, it draws out red and vitelline bile. There is also a thorny species of broom with green leaves like rue; some use its saffron-colored flowers against "green jaundice" <note>original: *viridem icterum*</note> with great success. 

However, according to Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and theologian</note>, a true green color is not naturally found in flowers. He believed this color arises from a thick, watery, undigested, floating, and dreg-filled humor, which cannot be the material for flowers, since a flower arises from the thinner and simpler parts of the plant. Even if that color is not truly found in flowers, they often appear marked with herbaceous or green lines, from which we can predict they consist of moisture and coldness. Among gems, the emerald is green in color and cold in quality, as authors testify it is effective at calming venereal urges and cooling passions. Jasper also consists of a bluish-green and is considered to be of such great coldness that it is said if thrown into boiling pots, it can cool them immediately and refresh the burning rages of the heart. Similarly, orach and blite <note>original: *blitum*; a leafy vegetable</note> are of a cold and moist quality according to Galen.

There is also another type of bile that is pale, which pale flowers draw out, as we have said based on similarity <note>referring to the "Doctrine of Signatures," where like cures like</note>. The flowers of bryony are pale, and Dioscorides said they draw out phlegm. The female mandrake is marked by pale fruit and draws out bile and phlegm through vomiting; this phlegm is always pale due to a mixture of black bile. The flower of the daylily <note>original: *hemerocallis*</note>, when it begins to open, is of an exceedingly pale color; when drunk, it draws water from the blood. 

But let us see what heat or cold this might signify. To investigate this cause, many men say many things. Aristotle, in his book *Problems*, says that easy breathing creates a pleasant color, while strangulation and constipation must necessarily do the opposite. For this reason, runners who run with naked bodies have a more cheerful color than those who run clothed and anointed with oil under their clothes, who appear pale. Indeed, the air cools the excremental residues that remain, and thus the body dissipates and evaporates them more easily. But for those anointed with oil—because the oil is thin and moist when spread underneath—it warms the passages of the body and neither allows the humor and spirit to flow out from the body, nor allows the external spirit to be admitted. Therefore, the idle matter in the body, rotting in its moisture, can induce paleness. Elsewhere, he says that those who stand on mountains have better coloring than those in marshes, because breezy places provide a more pleasant color. Moisture, when it rots, causes paleness; this usually happens because of weakness, and for that reason, those who live in marshes are pale. 

And in his booklet *On Colors*, Aristotle says that those flowers obtain a proper color which acquire proper heat and "concoction" <note>the "cooking" or ripening of humors by internal heat</note>. Flowers that appear in summer are more colorful than those in winter, because the heat opens the passages and the humor evaporates; but those that appear in winter, because they are constricted and condensed by the cold, become paler. But Averroes <note>a medieval Andalusian philosopher</note> said this is caused by a mixture of watery parts with earthy parts; when it occurs in moist things, it signifies a cold and moist temperament. This is different from that "beautiful whiteness," which results from a mixture of earthy parts with airy parts, signifying heat or a balanced temperament. 

We, however, proved in our *Human Physiognomy* <note>Della Porta's famous work on reading character from physical appearance</note> that such a [pale] color is to be rejected, signifying nothing good; we stated that pale men are traitors and reprobates. For this reason, we believe those plants which bear pale flowers, fruits, roots, and seeds are least to be trusted. Examples include: Monkshood <note>original: *Napellus*</note> is of a somewhat pale color, and Galen said it has a putrefying and lethal power. Thorn apple <note>original: *Stramonium*</note> is of a pale herbaceous color, and with a pale white flower near the calyx, it induces lethargy and death. Hemlock <note>original: *Cicuta*</note> has a whitish flower and a cooling and very deadly power, as Dioscorides said; it is effective for a thousand such evil deeds, as we have experienced. The pale mandrake produces evil fruits; whoever drinks its juice is weighed down by a lethargic...

Its species is commonly called *molengiana* <note>original: *molengiana*; likely the eggplant, then known as *melongena*</note>, with a whitish or pale flower; its frequent use introduces obstructions of the spleen and bladder, elephantiasis, headaches, sadness, long-lasting fevers, and bad physical conditions. Henbane <note>original: *Hyoscyamus*</note> has a pale flower, from which insanity and sleep are brought on by cooling. Mushrooms are of a pale color, and the paler ones are the worst and cause wasting; the white ones are more harmless.

### DARK COLORS OF PLANTS, AND BLACK ANIMALS
->they generate black bile, announcing the worst diseases and death.<-

### Chapter V.

Now we will speak of the black colors of plants, which specifically increase black bile <note>original: *atram bilem*; in the theory of the four humors, black bile was associated with the earth element, autumn, and melancholic temperaments</note>, from which they announce the worst diseases, blindness, rages, delusions, and dire portents. Theophrastus denies that black colors are found in flowers; however, there are faded purple and rust-colored ones, interspersed with black spots and dots, which indicate the same thing. The ancient natural Magi said that this color warns of death, because it was worthy of being signified by obscure marks. According to Pythagoras's opinion, the color black is ill-famed; he was accustomed to say that things of a dark color pertain to death. Macrobius, citing the testimony of Veranius in his book on the words of the priests, said that black trees are "unhappy" <note>original: *infelices*; in Roman tradition, this meant barren or associated with ill omens</note>, while those bearing white fruit are "happy." Tarquinius Priscus, in his book on tree omens, says that trees which are under the protection of the gods of the underworld and those to be turned away are called "unhappy trees"—such as the bloody-red tree, the black fig, and those which bear a black berry and black fruits. From this, fruit of a black color or flowers indicate black bile, portending darkness of vision, loss of the eyes, or dire death. Nature itself, by showing dark dreams, announces death to the microcosm <note>the "small world" of the human body</note>, as Hippocrates holds in his book on dreams. Examples are at hand. The bean <note>original: *faba*; specifically the broad bean or fava bean</note> has a multi-colored flower, partly purple and partly marked with certain black spots, which Marcus Varro calls "mourning letters" <note>original: *lucubres literas*</note>. Festus Pompeius testifies that the souls of the dead dwell in them. It is thought to dull the senses of those who eat them and cause terrifying dreams. Because of this, Amphiaraus was the first to command abstinence from beans, because he believed they hindered prophecies gathered in sleep in no small way, since their flatulence interrupted peaceful rest and disturbed the mind during sleep. Orpheus forbade the eating of beans.

->*O wretched ones, wretched ones, withdraw your hands from the bean,*<-
->*For eating this bean is equal to eating the head of one's parent.*<-

Since, as the Magi passed down, the souls of the dead were in them, the poet Callimachus was of the same opinion, as he left written:

->*He moved his hand, saddening those eating the bean.*<-
->*This, as Pythagoras had ordered, I myself shall speak.*<-

Cicero is of the opinion that the Pythagoreans were forbidden from eating beans because they take away error from the soul and the peaceful tranquility sought by the mind—since it was well-known that this food, having the greatest amount of flatulence, was contrary to these goals. Furthermore, blossoming beans, even if they exhale a sweet odor, when inhaled through the nostrils even from a distance, so disturb the brain—especially if the person is melancholic—that it turns them away from a sound mind and makes them almost insane. They breathe out such a foul spirit that it has passed into a proverb regarding those who do not possess a sound mind: "He walked among the blossoming beans." The Egyptians and the Priests of Jupiter <note>original: *Flamines Diales*</note> among the Romans, as the grammarian Theon relates, [avoided] beans...

they held them among the funeral items; they neither ate them nor looked upon them. These were used by the 
heathen in ancestral rites, and they were cast before the ghosts; for this reason, the ancients thought it was 
not safe to be among them, to rest, or to sleep, and that doing so by night was more dangerous than by day. 
Of this kind is the **Egyptian bean**: it bears wasp-like nests on its stalk, in which black beans, bitter in 
smell and taste, swell out from their coverings. Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a thousand years.</note> says it is not far different in nature 
from the first. It produces black bile <note>original: *atram bilem*; one of the four humors thought to cause melancholy and various illnesses if in excess</note> and the diseases which it is accustomed to excite; 
with continuous use, it discolors the body with paleness. Of the same faculty are many kinds of legumes which 
produce a dark purple flower, such as the **lentil**, whose food—if eaten without moderation—stirs up 
cancers and creates elephantiasis <note>A term often used historically for various severe skin diseases, including leprosy</note>, because it easily degenerates into the black bile that is the parent of 
these vices; it dulls the sharpness of vision, produces thick and slow-flowing blood, generates obstructions 
of the liver, excites inflations of the spleen, and brings about tumultuous dreams, headaches, and harm to 
all the nerves. The **garden bean** <note>original: *Hortensis smilax* or *hortensis phaselus*; likely refers to the kidney bean or similar species</note>, creates a flower of variegated purple, and a very black and red fruit; it has a flatulent nature, is 
digested with difficulty, and produces beast-like dreams. The **vetch** produces a dark purple flower: a 
legume stubborn in digestion, troublesome to the stomach, harmful, and creating a thick juice, quite suitable 
for generating black bile. There are several kinds of **celery** <note>original: *Apij*</note>, with black leaves and 
even blacker seeds. The ancestors admitted none of these into their meals, considering them ill-omened because 
they were dedicated to the funeral feasts of the deceased, as Pliny reports from Chrysippus. Graves were 
crowned with celery: from which the proverb was born, *He needs celery* <note>original: *Indiget apio*</note>, 
concerning those who were in failing health, according to Plutarch. They say that little worms are born in 
their stalks, and that those of both sexes who eat them become sterile: and that those infants who have 
drunk from the breasts of those who ate it will perpetually suffer from the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy</note>. 
The white variety is more innocent, and for that reason, it is not condemned among the ill-omened shrubs. 
**Henbane** is called *hyoscyamos* <note>original: *υοσκυαμος*; literally "hog-bean"</note> by the Greeks, as if it were a 
"swine bean," because, as Aelian said, wild boars are seized with convulsions from drinking this bean. There 
is one black kind with a black flower, dark purple seed, and a grim appearance. Xenophon recorded that 
stupor and insanity are produced by it, as well as dizziness of the head. Scribonius says it is named 
*altercum* <note>The "dispute" plant</note>, because those who eat it are alienated in mind, with a certain 
argumentativeness of words; they also affirm that a delirium occurs if it is washed into the intestinal 
tract when an ulcer is felt there. A kind of **poppy** with a black seed is called *phthisis* <note>Wasting disease</note>; 
it causes lethargy and kills. Diagoras, as Erasistratus recorded, condemned its use, forbidding it to be 
poured into the eyes for bleariness, because it would harm the sight, dulling the eyes’ sharpness and 
creating a stupor. Andreas adds that those smeared with it are utterly blinded, if it is not diluted. 
Mnesidemus allowed its use only as far as smelling it, to seek sleep from the scent; otherwise, he 
forbade it to us as harmful. It is deadly during sleep; many, when unendurable health had made them hate 
life, have brought death upon themselves with this juice. Thus Pliny writes that the father of Licinius 
Caecina, a man of praetorian rank, was killed. Many very useful things are recounted about **white 
sow-thistle**, but it is otherwise for the **black** kind, which Cleomporus prohibits eating as it causes 
disease, though he agrees regarding the white. There are two kinds of **thyme**, one white, the other 
with a blacker leaf and flower; while many excellent things are offered in medicine regarding the white, 
Aetius condemned the black for us, because once received inside, it easily rots and creates bilious humors. 
Castor records two kinds of **horehound** <note>original: *marrubij*</note>, black and white, and he 
approves more of the white. **Thistles** produce a dark purple flower, and their black juice stains the 
hands and teeth. Galen said it creates black bile, so that from its hard part black bile is born, and 
from its juice a bilious humor. **Blite** <note>original: *Blitum*; a leafy green like amaranth or spinach</note> 
has a black leaf and disturbs the belly so much that it causes cholera <note>In this context, severe gastrointestinal distress</note>. 
The white kind with a black seed dulls the eyes; likewise, the **leek** is bad for the stomach and is 
processed by the belly with difficulty, due to some fibrous quality in it; the juice of raw leeks taken 
in large quantities is counted among the poisons: for the story goes that Mela, of the equestrian order, 
summoned by the Emperor Tiberius to stand trial for his administration, in total desperation drank leek 
juice to the weight of three silver denarii and immediately expired without torture, according to Pliny. 
Hippocrates commended the **onion** more for its appearance than for eating, saying it was good to see 
but bad to eat: it must be especially avoided by those devoted to working by lamplight and the study of 
letters, for it ruins the eyes, darkens the vision, and sharpens the bile,

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "doctrine of signatures," specifically how the color black in plants, animals, and substances indicates a "melancholic" nature. It lists various species that, according to ancient and medieval authorities, produce black bile and lead to physical or mental ailments.</meta>

### BOOK THREE.

From Pliny: Diocles said that all bulbs dull the eyesight. The lethal **yew tree** <note>original: *Taxus*; known for its toxic alkaloids</note> makes the veins black with its berries. **Cabbage** <note>original: *Brassica*</note> with black or bluish seeds, stalks, and leaves is accused by Erasistratus, Galen, and others of causing a "heaviness of the soul," harming the teeth and gums, blunting the sharpness of vision, and generating a melancholic juice. **Truffles** <note>original: *Tubera*</note> are black on the outside; according to Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note>, they produce thick humors, and Simeon Sethi <note>An 11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician</note> claims that frequent use gives rise to epilepsy and apoplexy. **Eggplants** <note>original: *Molengianę*; likely the *Melanzana*</note>, commonly so called, have fruit ranging from purple-blue to dusky violet; the common people, having experienced them to be deadly and harmful, called them "insane apples" <note>original: *mala insana*</note>. According to Avicenna, they generate bilious humors and blockages of the liver and spleen, from which long-lasting fevers arise. We shall demonstrate that black-colored animals also cast darkness over the eyes. Therefore, it has been observed in stones and other things that eating them in large quantities induces melancholy, quartan fevers <note>A form of malaria where the fever recurs every fourth day, historically associated with black bile</note>, cancers, and other ulcers and diseases of the same family. Almansor <note>Likely referring to the Persian physician Rhazes, who dedicated a book to the ruler Al-Mansur</note>, speaking of the flesh of animals, says that red or black meat produces melancholy. The **buffalo** has black skin and hair; its meat is rejected by doctors as being excessively melancholic. Of **cats** of many colors, and especially the blackest ones: eating the brain causes madness <note>Medieval medicine occasionally suggested animal parts as cures or warned of their effects if consumed</note>, obstructing the passages of the brain so that it hinders the animal spirits <note>The subtle fluids thought to travel through the nerves to control movement and sensation</note>. According to Ponzetto, its hair is poisonous and its breath can induce a "hectic" or wasting fever. Peter of Abano <note>original: *Petrus Apponensis*; a 13th-century philosopher and physician</note> says they make men stupid and as if subject to magical illusions. There are some whom they harm with a fixed stare, and others by their mere presence alone. **Donkeys** are prone to black bile, as are **camels** and **horses**, all of a dusky color; their meat provides the worst nourishment, is most difficult to digest, generates melancholy, and harms the stomach—and according to Galen, those who eat donkey and camel meat become like the animals themselves. Doctors write that the meat of **wild game**, because it is darker and drier, produces "wild" blood and melancholy. **Venison** <note>original: *Ceruina caro*</note> is dark, similar to buffalo meat, and increases black bile; Avicenna said that quartan fevers are induced by the immoderate eating of this meat. The meat of **lions**, **wolves**, and other predators easily generates black bile in bodies, according to Rhazes. **Hare** meat produces melancholic blood according to the same author. Aetius records that **fox** meat is of the worst nourishment; a certain Boeotian in Aristophanes' *The Acharnians* seems to mock the Boeotians as being very crude men because they held foxes in no less esteem as delicacies than hares. The **swallow** has black meat and very black feathers; it is called "dark-blue" <note>original: *cyana*</note> by Simonides in Athenaeus, and "variegated" by Aristophanes because its back and wings are black, its belly white, and its throat red. Doctors say it is a harmful and "fervent" food. Its warm dung blinds the eyes, according to Albertus <note>Albert the Great, a medieval scholar</note>, as happened to the weary **Tobit** <note>A biblical figure from the Book of Tobit</note> returning home from a burial; while he was sleeping next to a wall, warm swallow dung fell into his eyes from a nest, whereby he was blinded. The **bat** has black leathery wings and a black body, as befits a nocturnal animal. Arnaldus de Villanova <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> said its dung causes blindness, and sometimes its heart and tongue induce rabies <note>original: *hydrophobiam*</note>. Among the ancients, it was an omen of bad luck because of its blackness; for this reason, they were hung on houses to ward off evil. Columella wrote:

->*Hence Amythaonian Chiron taught many things,*<-
->*He hung the nocturnal birds on crosses, and on white*<-
->*Rooftops he forbade them to wail their deathly songs.*<-

The **hoopoe** <note>original: *Vpupa*</note> is variegated, distinguished by white and black feathers, its wings mottled with alternating spots. The ancients fabled that Tereus was transformed into a hoopoe so that he might look upon his calamity in his own black and foul face; it always lingers in tombs and human dung; it seeks the deserts of the forests and pathless regions—a mournful and nocturnal bird. Its blood, when smeared, so stirs the melancholic humor that it produces demonic phantoms. **Peacocks** are black <note>Likely referring to a specific dark variety or the appearance of their meat</note>; Simeon Sethi said they are of poor juice, generate black bile, and harm those with liver and spleen ailments. Land **tortoises** vary on their backs with black and yellow colored spaces, like the skin of a salamander. Tortoise powder used in eye-salves induces blindness. Indeed, if it is thrown into a bath-cauldron, everyone who bathes there will be blinded, according to Rhazes.

<meta>This page continues the transition from describing the harmful effects of black substances to their curative powers. While the previous page focused on how black foods and plants can generate "black bile" (melancholy), this page explores the medicinal principle of "like cures like"—how black-hued plants and animals are used to purge that same melancholy and treat associated ailments.</meta>

# PHYTOGNOMONICA

## THAT BLACK PLANTS AND ANIMALS CURE BLACK BILE AND
### its related diseases. Chapter XI.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring floral and leafy ornaments within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

THE SAME colors—namely black, deep blue, purple, and dusky brown—when applied as medicine, exert a contrary power <note>The author suggests that while these colors might signify the humor in a raw state, when prepared as medicine, they act against the disease of that same color.</note>, curing melancholy itself and the diseases it fosters. We have already noted that the color black is rarely found in flowers; instead, its place is taken by deep blue, purple, or sea-purple <note>original: *halurgum*</note>. We should also point out that colors of this kind that are shining, cheerful, and pleasant retain a medicinal power to gladden the soul, while those that are pale and faded bring about the opposite. Here are some examples. The flower of the **Violet** <note>original: *Viola*</note> shines with a deep saturation of purple: Mesue <note>A famous Persian physician</note> says it purges bile, but I have seen it expel black bile. The flowers of **Bugloss** <note>original: *Buglossum*</note>, or the common **Borage** <note>original: *Borago*</note>, all shine with an extraordinary purple or blue; they are used for conditions of the heart and for melancholic diseases, as well as for tertian and quartan fevers <note>Forms of malaria that recur every third or fourth day</note>. It increases the soul’s delights, which is why the Greeks call it *Euphrosyne* <note>meaning "Merriment"</note> and also *Alypon* <note>original: *ἄλυπον*; meaning "without sorrow" or "grief-dispelling"</note>, as it scatters sadness. There is a common little verse:

->Borage says, I always bring joys.<-

Another species is evergreen, excellent for heart and melancholic conditions. **Senna** <note>original: *Sena*</note> has a blue flower; it dispels parched and black bile and clears cloudiness in the eyes when taken in a chicken broth. **Chickpea** <note>original: *Cicer*</note> and **vetch** <note>original: *cicercula*</note> have purple flowers: they improve skin eruptions, "ant-crawling" rashes <note>original: *formicas*; a type of inflammatory skin lesion</note>, and itchy scales. They are applied to gangrene and those sores called "malignant habits" <note>original: *cacoethes*; referring to stubborn or cancerous ulcers</note>, and they diminish the chills of quartan fever. **Oregano** <note>original: *Origanum*</note> excretes dark humors through the bowels, as do *heraclion* and *onitis* <note>Varieties of wild marjoram</note>, which have purplish flowers. **Pennyroyal** <note>original: *Pulegium*</note> drives out black bile through the bowels. The other **Dittany** <note>original: *Dictamnum*</note> mentioned by Dioscorides <note>The famous Greek physician and botanist</note> bears a darker flower and is effective for the same things. **Thyme** <note>original: *Thymum*</note> bears purplish heads: Dioscorides wrote that it evacuates humors and should be given to those suffering from melancholy. **Dodder of Thyme** <note>original: *Epithymum*</note> excretes black bile from the lower parts. The plants called **Palma Christi** <note>The Castor Oil plant</note> have purplish flowers: Avicenna ordered them to be given to melancholics. Those who illustrate **Alypum** <note>The "purgative" herb</note> attest to its purple flower; according to Dioscorides, its seed brings down black bile. **Mint** <note>original: *Mentha*</note> suppresses bilious attacks when drunk in vinegar. **Calamint** <note>original: *Calamintha*</note>, a related genus, is eaten to treat elephantiasis <note>A term often used historically for severe leprosy or skin thickening</note>. **Galeopsis** <note>Hemp-nettle</note> is effective against carcinomas. Mesue said **Fumitory** <note>original: *Capnos*</note> purges the blood of "burnt" humors and is beneficial for carcinomas and elephantiasis. **Basil** <note>original: *Ocymum*</note>, as Martial affirms, bears flowers that are sometimes rosy and sometimes purple; it is effective against quartan fevers. **Betony** <note>original: *Betonica*</note> is for quartan and tertian fevers. **Cuckoopint** <note>original: *Aron*</note> consists of a dark purple flower; its juice miraculously heals ulcers of all kinds, whether they be "eating" sores <note>original: *phagædenas*</note>, carcinomas, spreading sores, or polyps in the nostrils. **Savory** <note>original: *Satureia*</note> has small flowers that are white-ish with purple; it performs the same functions as thyme and sharpens dim eyes. **Sage** <note>original: *Salvia*</note> has a bluish-gray and purple flower: it cleanses foul ulcers. **Wild Thyme** <note>original: *Serpyllum*</note> has a somewhat purple flower; it is given to those who are delirious <note>original: *phreneticis*</note>. **Black Hellebore** <note>original: *Veratrum nigrum*</note> has black leaves and roots: Dioscorides said it benefits the melancholic and the insane, but Actuarius <note>A 13th-century Byzantine physician</note> said it expels black bile. **Hog’s Fennel** <note>original: *Peucedanum*</note> has a root that is black on the outside: it helps the delirious. **Cabbage** <note>original: *Brassica*</note> with a bluish, blackish leaf is effective for gangrene and "eating" ulcers that accompany black bile. The female **Mandrake** <note>original: *Mandragora*</note> has a black root; it purges black bile through vomiting. **Wild Nettle** <note>original: *Urtica sylvestris*</note> has black leaves and seeds: it is effective for gangrene and carcinomas. Common **Viper’s Grass** <note>original: *Scorzonera*</note> has a root that is black on the outside: it is given to those with heart trouble and those prone to heart palpitations and tremors; it dispels sadness and brings about cheerfulness. They praise **Lemon Balm** <note>original: *Melissophyllon*</note> with wondrous words for its effects on the heart; its specific property is to gladden a person, to put to flight the soul’s anxieties, and to remove the troubled imaginations arising from black bile: it has a black leaf. Black **Myrobalans** <note>A plum-like fruit used in traditional medicine</note> draw out black bile and take away grief. Even black animals, used as remedies, purge melancholy, and consequently benefit the "companion disease" <note>original: *comitiali morbo*; epilepsy</note>; for those who labor under melancholy are more often seized by the companion disease, and epileptics often become melancholic. The **Raven** <note>original: *Corvus*</note> is of the blackest color: Al-Kindi <note>An Arab polymath and philosopher</note> said it is effective for leprosy and white skin spots. The **Swallow** <note>original: *Hirundo*</note> is black: it comforts the heart and expels quartan fevers, according to Pliny. The **Magpie** <note>original: *Pica*</note> is of a black color: it is effective against melancholy. The **Peacock** <note>original: *Pavo*</note> tends toward blackness: its burnt bones improve leprosy. The **Hawk**...

The **Lion** <note>original: *Leo*</note> is of a sooty color: its blood is effective against phantoms <note>Hallucinations or terrifying dreams.</note>, according to Aesculapius, Sextus, and Serenus; its heart for quartan fevers, according to Pliny. The dark **Deer** <note>original: *Ceruus*</note>: against fevers and cancers, according to Hermes and Pliny. **Elephants** <note>original: *Elephantes*</note> are mouse-colored: for elephantiasis <note>The author draws a connection between the name of the animal and the skin disease.</note>. It assists universally in all diseases which black bile excites—insanity, bewitchment, epilepsy, and countless others—and it purges copiously through the bowels, the mouth, and even through the pores by insensible perspiration, as shown by multiple experiments performed by us. But the method of purifying and administering it, and the results of our experience, have already been made manifest to you, the Illustrious **Marina Bobali** <note>A noblewoman to whom the author likely dedicated this portion or shared his findings.</note>, even to the point of wonder; so that we have not hidden these things, nor others which we keep silent, discovered clearly by this method. **Jet** <note>original: *Gagates*</note> is a black stone; it is administered for heart conditions, according to Aëtius, who testifies to its wonderful power. The **Sapphire** <note>original: *Sapphirus*</note> is of a blue color: it purges black bile, and for this reason, those who wear it are terrified by no fear; crushed with milk, it heals foul ulcers, chases away carbuncles <note>original: *anthraces*; severe skin abscesses.</note> by touch alone, and bestows a pleasant complexion. Another species of **Hyacinth** <note>Here referring to a gemstone, likely a blue zircon or sapphire-like stone.</note> is blue, so named for its resemblance to the flowers of that name. Martial says in his second book:

### *You give famous scarlet garments, and violet ones to an adulteress.*
<note>original: *Coccina famosa donas, & hyanthina mœcha.*</note>

That is, purple and violet garments: it puts to flight sadness and vain suspicions if you hang it from the neck or wear it on your fingers, and it provides security. Avicenna said it especially drives away all weaknesses of the heart arising from melancholy. These same flowers also sharpen the eyesight; for by purging melancholy through the bowels, they remove the darkness of vision, as Hippocrates said of the leek. **Garlic** <note>original: *Allium*</note> has a black seed; eating it continuously dims the eyes, but as a medicine, garlic is beneficial to the eyes, for since it moves the bowels abundantly, it frees the vision from darkness. **Cabbage** <note>original: *Brassica*</note> with a black leaf: according to Pliny, its raw juice applied even just to the corners of the eyes contributes to clarity of vision. **Lettuce** <note>original: *Lactuca*</note> with a blue flower: its milk is most useful for the clarity of the eyes when rubbed on the head, according to Dioscorides. **Pimpernel** <note>original: *Anagallis*</note> with a purple flower: its juice dispels the darkness of the eyes. **Forget-me-not** <note>original: *Myosotis*</note> likewise with a blue flower: the Egyptians report that if anyone is anointed with the juice of this herb in the morning before speaking during the month of August, they will not suffer from bleary eyes that year; the root heals eye-sores <note>original: *ægylopas*; a lachrymal fistula or ulcer in the corner of the eye.</note>, and the juice is pressed out to restrain the shivering of quartan fever.

## THAT BLACK-COLORED FLOWERS BRING ABOUT A CHEERFUL
### SKIN COLOR. Chapter XII.

COLORS of blue and purple flowers render the human complexion cheerful, pleasant, and beautiful, both for those who are discolored by long illness and for those whose faces are marred <note>original: *mangonizantur*; literally "furbished up" or altered artificially, here likely meaning damaged or made to look unhealthy.</note>. The same can be inferred regarding animals: for these plants, by stimulating the bowels and casting out melancholic humors, change the body into a better color and hide skin defects, or adorn the outermost skin of the body with a pleasant color. Wine is of a cheerful and, above all, a graceful color: blood and human color are nourished by wine, so there is less redness in those bodies, and more paleness, less strength, and less endurance for labor in those who drink water, according to Pliny. The **Chickpea** <note>original: *Cicer*</note> has a blue flower...

The **Cherry** <note>original: *Cerasus*</note> drips with dark blood; it purges the blood of black bile and restores a more pleasing brightness to the skin.

### FLOWERS TENDING TOWARD A DARK COLOR, OR
### SIMPLES ALSO EFFECTIVE AGAINST DEMONIACS.

->Chapter XIII.<-

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial 'N' depicting a figure seated in a landscape with classical foliage.</image-desc>Now we shall speak of melancholics, whom they call demoniacs, who are easily healed by blue, sea-purple <note>original: *halurgi*</note>, or blackish flowers, stones, or animals. First, we will say that there are two kinds of demoniacs: one which can truly be called "possessed by demons," when demons are introduced into human bodies to punish their impious works, by God’s permission; these are cast out by the exorcisms, prayers, and fasts of the Holy Roman Church, and of these we shall not speak. The other kind is caused by **black bile** <note>original: *atra bilis*</note>, which produces wonders in human bodies. Melancholy is a strenuous and fierce humor which, when violently agitated in the body, moves the mind to such an extent that wondrous effects are seen from it. For just as sparks are struck out from the collision of flint and steel, so from the collision of sharp humors—as is seen in the most burning fevers—it is struck out so that they speak in various tongues and dispute about things they have never heard. The human intellect is capable of the greatest disciplines, or, as Plato prefers, before it is joined to the body, it is full of all knowledge; though oppressed by the body it lies hidden, like fire sleeping under ash, but when excited and moved by the humors already mentioned, it shines forth and shows the wealth that had been hidden in its treasures. There are many things which do not show their virtue unless excited and moved. **Amber** <note>original: *Succinum*</note> does not attract chaff unless rubbed, nor does **Pyrite** <note>original: *pyrites*</note> draw out fire unless struck, and many herbs do not cast out their scent unless crushed by the hands. He who is closer to death, his soul already separated from the body, speaks of lofty things, prophesies, and, as if a participant in divinity, speaks of wondrous heavenly matters. But to speak of such species; there is a type of melancholy which, because of the effect with which it affects men, they call **lycanthropy** <note>original: *lycantrophia*; the delusion of being a wolf</note> and **cynanthropy** <note>original: *cynanthropia*; the delusion of being a dog</note>, according to Aetius and Paulus. In the month of February, they go out at night, imitating wolves or dogs in everything, and wander especially around tombs until dawn. They recognize those affected by these signs: they are pale, they have a dull gaze, their eyes appear hollow and dry, their tongue is rough, they neither spit nor weep, and they are always thirsty. The Greeks call this evil "lycaona" after the King of Arcadia, **Lycaon**, whom they say was changed into a wolf by Jove because of his crimes, hiding the alienation of the human mind under this veil of a fable, imagining in him all the things that happen from this vice of black bile. There is also another kind of disease from the same species of black bile, which they call the **leonine demon**, named after the lion, because those possessed by this disease rage against other men like lions. **Avicenna** also named it **Lycanthropy** <note>A mental disorder where a person believes they have turned into a wolf; from the Greek "lykos" (wolf) and "anthropos" (man).</note> when speaking of *cutabub* <note>original: "cutabuto," a Latinization of an Arabic term for this melancholic delusion</note>: the Greeks call this the "divine passion," and those held by it seem to be possessed by certain greater powers, and for that reason they are called "enthusiasts," as if filled with a God. These diseases are cured by those herbs, those animals, gems, and stones that are black, blue, and purple in color, which gladden the black bile, make it clear, and purge it. More recent authors prefer **Herb Paris** <note>original: "Herbam paridem"; a woodland plant also known as True Lover's Knot</note> for this and extol it with wonderful praise. It consists of a black leaf and a stem like a blood-red rod, with a flower of yellowish-green, in the center of which stands a purple and wine-colored globule, like a grape berry, and a pale root: if its seed is taken in the weight of a drachm <term>drachm: an ancient unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</term> in powder form for up to twenty days, one is restored to former health; this most excellent remedy is taken from the *Pandectarius* <note>Referring to the *Pandectae Medicinae*, a famous 14th-century medical encyclopedia by Matthaeus Silvaticus</note>.

**Betony** <note>original: "Betonica"</note> has a black leaf, with purple seed and flower. It has such renown that a house in which it is planted is considered safe from all sins <note>or "piacular crimes," meaning things requiring ritual purification</note>: the seed of betony drives out all evil medicines <note>referring to poisons or sorcerous charms</note> through the bowels, [taken] in honey-wine, or raisin wine, or meal in four cups of old wine, but the patient must be forced to vomit or to drink again: for those who taste it daily, they believe no evil medicines will be harmful.

**Verbena** <note>Vervain</note> has flowers of pale purple. No herb has more Roman nobility than *hierobotane* <note>Greek for "holy herb"</note>, so called because it was a sacred and lustral herb used for sweeping Jupiter’s altars; it was recommended for the purifications and ritual cleansings of houses, and for the driving out of demons. Indeed, if a dining room is sprinkled with water in which it has been soaked, the banquets become more cheerful; this was achieved only by purging that black melancholy.

A species of **Orchid**, called **Palma Christi** <note>literally "Hand of Christ," named for its hand-shaped roots</note>, with a beautiful purple flower, is given to maniacs with great benefit, and its root, when worn, is an amulet. And **Pliny** says the female *satyrios*, nicknamed *orchis*, is distinguished by its joints and a more branchy shrub, with a root useful against fascinations <note>the "evil eye" or malevolent spells</note>.

**Alyssum** <note>Madwort</note> with a purple flower: hung in a house, it is considered healthy, and is believed to be an amulet against the witchcraft of those who bewitch men and the four-legged kind. **Rue** <note>original: "Ruta"</note>, because it scours out the yellow humors arising from melancholy, is effective against fascinations with its bluish-gray and dark green leaves; and **Aristotle** handed down in his *Problems* that it is good against melancholic suspicions.

The same is provided by animals that are dark, dry, and melancholic. They say the dried **snout of a wolf** resists sorceries, and for that reason, they nail them to the gates of farmsteads: the skin from the solid neck is thought to provide the same. **Massurius** <note>Massurius Sabinus, a Roman jurist</note> records that the ancients gave the prize to **wolf fat**: therefore, new brides used to anoint the doorposts with it, lest any evil medicine be brought in. He who eats boiled wolf meat will not be disturbed by demons, shadows, and phantasms, according to **Sextus** <note>Sextus Placitus, author of a late antique book on animal remedies</note>. Boiled wolf meat taken as food cures those suffering from phantasies, according to **Aesculapius**.

The same things should be said of the **dog** as of the wolf, since they are of the same kind and quality. A dog's genitals buried under the threshold of the door, they say, is an amulet for the whole house against evil medicines. The **blood of a black dog** sprinkled on all the walls of a house in which there is witchcraft removes it: the **gall of a black male dog** used as a fumigant is an amulet for the whole house, and purifies it against evil medicines; and perhaps alluding to this expiation of the house, the ancients gave the *Lares* <note>Roman household gods</note>, whom they called the presiding spirits of the house, a dog's head, or garments made of dog skins.

Let us pass to stones. **Jet** <note>original: "Gagates"</note> is a very black stone: **Marbodeus** <note>Marbod of Rennes, author of a famous 11th-century lapidary</note> said it is effective against demons, and by "demons" he understands melancholic phantasms, which are called demons by **Evax** <note>A legendary King of Arabia credited with a book on gemstones</note>. **Mesue** <note>an influential Arab physician</note> also records that oil of jet is effective against the demoniacs, and **Proclus** <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> said that demons are put to flight by a fumigation of water and asphalt. It is not, therefore, alien to reason that in counting sacred prayers <note>referring to rosary beads</note> they use beads of jet. A black stone like a bean is also found in the Nile, at the sight of which dogs do not bark, and it likewise drives away demons, according to **Thrasyllus** in his *Egyptian Matters*, as **Stobaeus** cites. **Antiphanes** <note>likely referring to *Antipathes*, or black coral</note> is coral, differing from that black color; and Marbodeus said it is effective against demonic shadows. **Armenian stone** <note>Azurtie</note> is effective for diseases of black bile due to its blue color,

...blue, so **lapis lazuli** <note>original: "lapis azuli"</note> casts out black bile and is effective for the same conditions, according to **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*.</note>. There are many species of **Jasper**; in India, it resembles an emerald; in Phrygia, it is purple; and in Cappadocia, it is a bluish-purple. Because of this, **Marbodeus** <note>Marbod of Rennes (c. 1035–1123), author of a famous lapidary (a book on the properties of stones).</note> said it was effective against melancholic illusions and harmful phantasms. A black species of **chalcedony** hung around the neck is effective against illusions and phantasms born from melancholy. **Pomponazzi** <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), a renowned Italian philosopher.</note>, a most learned man, records that ancient exorcists, before they would attempt the exorcisms of the Church, would purge the bodies of the possessed of black bile; for they were frequently besieged by twin diseases of both the mind and the body. But how those truly possessed by demons are liberated, we do not discuss here, since they are freed by sacred exorcisms. 

There are, however, certain natural things that put them to flight, infest them, and torment them, which were celebrated even in antiquity. **Squill** <note>A bulbous plant in the lily family.</note> hung on the threshold of a doorway removes the harm of an evil potion, which they say **Pythagoras** accepted. I suspect the reason is that it alone among plants flowers three times, showing forth the most holy mystery of the **Trinity**. The first species of **Buckthorn** <note>original: "ramni"</note>, which they call *spina cervalem* <note>original: "spina cerualem"; literally "deer thorn," likely *Rhamnus cathartica*.</note>, bristles with straight thorns around the branches—most rigid, sharp, and robust—raging with a terrible point. It is rumored among the ancients that branches of this, placed upon doors or windows, drive away sorcery; I suspect that the crown prepared for Jesus Christ our Lord in his most cruel passion was fashioned from this, and for that reason it is commonly called the **holy thorn** <note>original: "spina santa"</note>. **Rue**, as we have said, is effective against those who are bewitched, perhaps because of the sign of the cross impressed upon its seed. **St. John's Wort** <note>original: "hypericon"</note> most violently casts out demons, for which reason it is commonly named the **"flight of demons"** <note>original: "fuga dæmonum"</note>; those possessed can neither bear to smell it nor carry it upon themselves. I suspect this is because of the scent of frankincense which it gives off when rubbed in the hands, since frankincense was given to God alone. By using these in baths, or as fumigants, or by carrying them, we have seen those possessed by demons very often liberated.

-> BLACK-COLORED FLOWERS AND ANIMALS ARE EFFECTIVE AGAINST <-
-> impotence in Venus. Chapter XIV. <-

<image-desc>A decorative square initial 'I' depicting a human figure, possibly a scholar or physician, standing in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>This same disease of melancholy hinders sexual intercourse through a vehement imagination; hence, melancholics very often think themselves bewitched and say they are "bound." For intercourse consists of movement and imagination; thus, he who imagines himself bewitched immediately loses the power of intercourse, especially since melancholics suffer from this imagination, and since their complexion is cold and dry, it is hostile to **Venus** <note>The goddess of love, here representing sexual function.</note>. Therefore, those same things we mentioned—black, green, dark, or purple animals, stones, and herbs—have the same power to ward off this kind of infirmity. The **Woodpecker** <note>original: "Picus Martius"</note>, or a bird of that kind, called by us in the vulgar tongue *turzolopico*, which **Ovid** depicts in the fourteenth book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> „With his hard beak he strikes the wild oak
> And in his anger wounds the long branches,
> His feathers took on the purple color of his cloak:
> What had been a golden buckle biting his garment,
> Becomes plumage, and his neck is encircled by tawny gold.

It prevails with the greatest power against the "binding" <note>A type of folk magic (ligatures) intended to cause impotence.</note> of intercourse and closures. For when a wedge has been driven in [to a tree] by shepherds, and a certain herb is applied by these birds, it slips out. This is according to **Pliny**, citing **Trebius**. For the herb is contrary to the stone <note>Or hard object/wedge.</note>, and he places it against the stone; the stone, as if offended and unable to bear the power of the herb, leaps out and again opens the hole. This is according to **Aelian** and **Oppian**. This bird, eaten roasted or boiled, quickly restores health to the sick and releases those bound by incantation, according to **Kyranides** <note>An ancient compendium of magico-medical lore.</note>. The common **Magpie** <note>original: "Pica vulgaris"</note> with its black head and neck is also effective for the same, according to **Gilbert** in the works of **Arnold** <note>Likely referring to Gilbertus Anglicus and Arnold of Villanova.</note>. The **Raven** is black and is effective against melancholy. Bile mixed with oil and smeared on the body releases a man so that he cannot perform intercourse, according to **Rhazes** citing **Cleopatra**. The **Peony** bears seeds that are reddish-black, with others black in the middle and purple; for as the pods open, the seeds are seen in an alternating weave of color by a wonderful decree of nature... <meta>catchword: magna</meta>

...there is a great sympathy with this woodpecker <note>The "picus martius" or Black Woodpecker was associated with Mars and believed to guard certain plants.</note>: for they command that the fruit or root of the **peony** be gathered at night, because the Mars woodpecker is said to attack the eyes [of the gatherer] during the day; otherwise, the "seat" of those digging the peony root falls out [prolapses], if we believe **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany" (c. 371–287 BC).</note>. If a branch of **Southernwood** <note>original: "Abrotoni"</note> is placed under a pillow, **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, author of *Natural History*.</note> said it stimulates Venus [sexual desire], and it was held to be most effective against all sorceries by which intercourse is inhibited.

### ->WHAT THE COLOR BLUE OR BLACK CAN NATURALLY<-
### ->*signify. Chapter XV.*<-

**Averroes** <note>A 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician.</note>, in his *Colliget*, states that blackness and greenness necessarily arise from dry and earthy parts; sometimes they arise from great heat, such as the blackness in **Ethiopians**; at other times through coldness, such as black wine; and this difference is indicated by the process that produced it. **Albertus** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a medieval polymath.</note> claims that a blue, black, or purple color is caused by earthy, smoky, burnt, and dark vapor. **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician.</note> says that dark brown signifies the dominance of **black bile** <note>original: "choleræ nigræ"</note> in the body, and that blackish vapor rises from burnt humors. **Aristotle**, in his book *On Colors*, said: Heat acting upon moisture causes a black color; and in his *Problems*: Everything that is burnt is accustomed to become black. I would say that a black color indicates things that are burnt, and things burnt are deprived of heat and moisture: for heat consumes moisture, and what remains is therefore dry. An example is the **hyacinth** of purple color, which according to **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire (c. 129–216 AD).</note> is cold and dry. The **cornflower** <note>original: "Cyanus flos"</note> cools and constricts; as do the **purple violet** and similar plants.

---

### ->WHITE-FLOWERED PLANTS AND ANIMALS INCREASE<-
### ->*phlegm. Chapter XVI.*<-

Plants and animals of a white color, which are of such mild sharpness and flavor that they are used for food, increase **phlegm** <note>original: "pituitam"; one of the four bodily humors, associated with cold and moisture.</note> itself. **Basil** <note>original: "Ocymum"</note> has a white flower; **Galen** and **Paulus** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note> rejected it from meals because its "excremental humor" <note>Waste fluid produced by digestion.</note> is harmful to the internal parts, and for this reason he forbade us from immoderate eating of it: for if anyone were to use it as abundantly as other pot-herbs, it would harm the intestines with the waste-filled humor with which it is imbued. Being poorly digested by the natural heat of the plant, and as if superfluous, it quickly fosters rot. The flowers of the **gourd** <note>original: "Cucurbitæ"</note> are white, and its internal flesh cools and nourishes the body's humor with its tasteless eating; Galen prohibits it from food as "insane" [unhealthy] and stubborn to digest, as it weighs down the stomach with nausea and a troublesome weight. The **red onion** is sharper than the **white**. **Mushrooms** are white, born from the earth or from the phlegm of tree roots; Galen said that for those who eat them, they produce a cold phlegm, unconquered by harmful juice—the proof being those who vomit them up only emit them congealed and cold when they are expelled after being eaten. **Lettuce** is white, and physicians warn that it must be avoided by those prone to phlegm. 

And passing to animals: of all land animals, the **pig** has the whitest and most humid flesh, and especially the newborn, which generates a great deal of phlegm and superfluities. Next in whiteness is the flesh of the **lamb**, which has more moisture, stickiness, and mucus, and is exceedingly phlegmatic. **Geese** and **ostriches** are white with white meat; of all birds, their flesh is the most "excremental" and humid, and for that reason, according to Galen’s book *On the Faculties of Foods*, putrid fevers are born from it. There are also **frogs**, somewhat livid and ashy, with white flesh when skinned; its substance is so loose and humid that it is ready for quick rot; hence those who use frogs frequently are made a leaden color, and the body is rendered prone to putrefaction.

->WHITE-FLOWERED PLANTS ARE EFFECTIVE AGAINST PHLEGM<-
->Chapter XVII.<-

Plants that are white in their fruit, flower, or root, when taken as medicine, purge pituita <note>Also known as phlegm, one of the four bodily humors in ancient medicine, associated with coldness, moisture, and sluggishness.</note> or phlegm. Here are the examples: In **Spurge Laurel** <note>original: "Daphnoidi"</note> the flower is white; it drives out phlegm through the bowels whether the leaf is used fresh or dry. **Chamaelaea** and **Thymelaea** <note>Species of the spurge family, such as Mezereon.</note> are of a related nature and form, for even the flowers of the other species of Chamaelaea are pale, like little silver flasks; they retain the power to cast down phlegm. **Horehound** <note>original: "Marrubium"</note>, with its gray-white flowers and leaves, ejects thick phlegm from the chest. **Sea Buckthorn** <note>original: "Hippophaës"</note>, with its white leaves and flowers and a root dripping with milk, draws phlegm through the lower parts. In **Bur-parsley** <note>original: "Caucalidi"</note>, the white umbrella-like cluster at the top thins the phlegm of the kidneys, according to **Pliny**. **White Hellebore** <note>original: "Veratrum album"</note> drives out all humors with the greatest force, and especially phlegm. The **Great Heliotrope** <note>original: "Heliotropion maius"</note>, with white flowers at its head, casts down phlegm through the bowels. In **Elder** <note>original: "Sambuco"</note> and **Danewort** <note>original: "ebulo"</note>, tiny white flowers are gathered in elegant umbrella-shaped clusters; their very soft leaves are eaten to draw away phlegm. The tip of **Pellitory-of-Spain** <note>original: "Pyrethri"</note> provides shade like the flower-head of Dill; the Romans call it "salivary" <note>original: "saliuarem"</note> because it is held and chewed in the mouth to dry out saliva and the phlegm of the mouth. **Hogweed** <note>original: "Sphondylion"</note>, with its pale white flower, casts down phlegm through the bowels. A white flower bursts forth from the **Caper** <note>original: "cappari"</note>; it draws out phlegm from the head and that which has gathered in the belly. There is one type of **Anemone** in which white flowers emerge at the top, sometimes sprinkled with a faint purple; the root of all of them, when chewed, draws out phlegm. The white flowers of **Angelica** clinging together in an umbrella-like cluster digest phlegm-like and sluggish humors on their own; among these, the white-flowered variety draws away thick phlegm when taken in a drink and digests the stickiness of the humors. **White Bryony** <note>original: "Vitis alba"</note>, commonly known as *vitrabula*, which they consider a fertile species of *clematis*, is drunk to drive out phlegm through the bowels. The **Castor Oil plant** <note>original: "Ricinus"</note> bears yellowish-white flowers; its seeds cast down phlegm through the bowels. **Privet** <note>original: "Ligustrum"</note> [cures] the phlegm <note>Likely referring to "the pip," a respiratory disease in birds marked by mucus.</note> of poultry. The white flower of the **Laurel** cooks down and extracts phlegm. **Beet** <note>original: "Beta"</note> is also white, named "Sicilian" by **Theophrastus**; it cleanses the head when inserted into the nostrils. A species of **Cabbage** <note>original: "Brassice"</note> also has a white flower; its juice, placed in the nostrils, draws out phlegm and relieves other humors. **Mustard** <note>original: "Sinapi"</note> with a white flower is held in the mouth against phlegm until it melts and is chewed. The **Leek** <note>original: "Porrú"</note> thins thick humors and digests sluggish ones; for this reason **Aetius of Amida** <note>A 6th-century Byzantine physician.</note> did not forbid them to those who have gathered sticky and thick phlegm. The same must be said of the **Wild Leek** <note>original: "ampelopraso"</note>. There is also a type of **White Lettuce** with very crinkled leaves which digests the stickiness of phlegm. There are plants that have little flesh but consist of much "corrupt matter" <note>original: "sanie"; in this context, the milky or viscous juice of the plant.</note> in which the seeds seem to float, such as the berries of **Winter Cherry** <note>original: "solani vesicarię"</note>, **Bryony**, and the fertile **Cyclamen**; for if they are pressed when ripe, a copious phlegm flows out, which feels sticky and tenacious, as in the other Cyclamen, though thinner in the rest. The root of **Cyclamen** with honey corrects phlegm. **Bryony** has pale white flowers, effective for the same purpose. **Jasmine** <note>original: "Iasminon"</note> with its white flower digests the stickiness of phlegm in cold, elderly people. **Watercress** <note>original: "Nasturtium"</note> checks white phlegm and clears the defects of the head. **Isos** <note>A plant mentioned by ancient authors, possibly a type of ivy or houseleek.</note> is white according to Theophrastus—Aetius calls it *ilion* (if it is the same)—and it draws out phlegm when eaten. **Dead-nettle** <note>original: "Lamium"</note> with a white flower heals scrofulous swellings <note>original: "strumis"</note> generated from phlegm. **Wood Sorrel** <note>original: "Oxys"</note> with a white flower, and **Hops** <note>original: "Lupulus"</note> with an ashy-white color, expel the stickiness of phlegm through the bowels. An **Onion** <note>original: "Cæpa"</note> with a very white body likewise digests the stickiness of phlegm. **Mastic** <note>original: "Mastiche"</note> is white and helps those in whom sticky phlegm collects, and it expels the phlegm-like humor.

White eyes signify weakness and humidity. The same author <note>Aristotle</note> says: All living creatures that are sustained by a small amount of food, whether due to weakness or a premature defect of nature, turn out white; thus the white hare is found, as are the deer and the bear; and among birds, the quail, the swallow, and the partridge, especially when they have inherited weakness from the very beginnings of their life. **Theophrastus** in his *Book of Causes* says that all white things are weaker and more fragile than black things, both in animals and in plants. **Aristotle** also said in his booklet *On Colors* that whiteness arises from humidity, using the argument that rose leaves and fruits are white at the beginning, but finally, through the <term>concoction</term> <note>original: "concoctione"; a process in ancient medicine where bodily heat "ripens" or "digests" humors and nutrients</note> of the juice, they change into a scarlet and sea-purple color. The "nails" <note>The base of a leaf or petal</note> of foliage always turn white where they are attached to their source, because there, humidity from the supply of nourishment is abundant, and the sun <term>concocts</term> it less; but the tips of the leaves are more colored because there is less moisture and more "concoction" there, as they are more exposed to the sun and the surrounding air. Weak heat renders urine white and undigested. **Averroes** in the *Colliget* says that whiteness occurs from the mixing of watery parts with earthy ones; when it is in moist things, it signifies a moist and cold <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of the four humors within an individual or substance</note>. However, a beautiful whiteness in humans arises from the mixing of earthy parts with air, and it signifies a balance of color, as we have said. **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus</note> adds that when transparency is present with whiteness in a watery moisture, there is little earth, except as much as suffices for the boundary of the transparent moisture; but where there is diversity, there is more earth. Let us bring forward some examples in plants. The **Gourd** <note>original: "Cucurbita"</note> has a white flower and is cold and moist according to **Galen**. The essence of **Chickweed** <note>original: "Alsines"</note> is watery, cooling, and moistening. **Mushrooms** <note>original: "Fungi"</note> are entirely white: they possess a harmful power due to their extreme coldness and humidity. We have said that in **Knotgrass** <note>original: "Poligono"</note> there is a watery coldness, and the **Water-lily** <note>original: "nympheam"</note> moistens and cools. **Cherries** with white flowers are cold and moist, as are **Pears** and **Apples**. **White Roses** are less hot than red ones, which is why we use them for inflammations of the eyes. He said **Basil** <note>original: "Ocymum"</note> and **Coriander** <note>original: "coriannum"</note> are cold. **Dioscorides** and **Simeon Seth** say **Grass** <note>original: "Gramen"</note> is moistening and cooling, and so with similar things. We have said that white animals are moist, cold, and full of waste products: as with the goose, the swan, the ostrich, and similar creatures.

->THOSE THINGS WHICH ARE RED IN COLOR, BY CONSTANT CONSUMPTION,<-
->INCREASE THE BLOOD. Chapter XIX.<-

Red things follow, and what we have said of others, we shall say of these: by constant eating, they increase the blood. For example: the common **Lettuce** <note>original: "lactuca"</note> reddens somewhat on the outside while it grows; but the Cyprian kind is reddish from white. We have seen one that was entirely soaked with blood-red juice, the "Caecilian" variety, of a dark, almost purple color, according to **Columella**. The schools of Physicians proclaim that by constant use or eating, this vegetable generates a copious amount of blood, so that Nature has compared it to no other vegetable. And there are those who consider its use a vice and condemn it on that name, against whom **Galen** inveighs, because they clearly fall away from the truth; for while some vegetables produce very little blood, and that of a faulty kind, lettuce alone produces much blood, and it is not bad, but praiseworthy in every respect. **Wine** is of a blood-red color; when pure and unmixed, and drunk in moderation, it generates blood, nourishes strength, fills the veins, and is easily distributed into the limbs. Other examples are not available.

Even if the blood itself is not purged (since it is the blood itself that is purged of other humors by various means), we shall nevertheless prove by many experiments that those things endowed with blood-red juice are effective for certain purgings, and also for other medicines of the blood. This color is found in flowers, roots, juice, or other parts. ## RED PARTS OF PLANTS, AND THE <unclear>BLOOD-LIKE COLOR</unclear>, also vulneraries. Chapter XXI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure in a classical landscape with hills and trees.</image-desc>

THE SAME red things, or those of a blood-like color, are effective for restraining blood, and for this reason, they are called <term>vulneraries</term> <note>From the Latin 'vulnerarius', meaning 'pertaining to wounds'; plants used to heal cuts and stop bleeding</note> by surgeons, because they are applied to wounds. These shall be the examples of them. The fruit of the Mulberry is blood-colored; it stains the lips and hands of those eating it, polluting them as if with a bloody decay. When immature, it turns red, and then it especially binds the blood; when mature, it turns black, and then it loosens the bowels. It restrains blood most effectively when it bears the greatest resemblance to it. They tell marvelous things about it: if the future fruits (which the Greeks call *ricinos*) are ordered to be plucked with the left hand before the leaves come out—provided they have not touched the ground—they stop blood when tied to the body, whether it flows from a wound, the mouth, the nose, or hemorrhoids; for this purpose, they are kept in storage. A branch is also said to perform the same if broken off during a full moon when it is beginning to have fruit. If it has not touched the ground, **Pliny** says it is tied specifically to a woman's upper arm against an abundance of menses. The Bramble imitates the fruit of the mulberry; it restrains the flows of women. **Galen** said it glues wounds together and heals dysentery, flows of the belly, and the spitting of blood. So also does the Raspberry. The Pomegranate is of a Phoenician <note>A deep scarlet or crimson</note> color; its fruit and flower come to the aid of those spitting blood and those suffering from female fluxes of the womb. The *Cytini* <note>The blossoms of the pomegranate</note> "glue together" bloody things, according to **Dioscorides**. The flowers that are brought from Crete and Cyprus, or those which burn with a more reddish color, are superior to others for the same tasks. The *Cistus* with its rose-like flower, the color of a pomegranate, and likewise the reddish *Hypocistus*, is beneficial for those spitting blood and for the flows of women, whether applied as a salve or drunk. *Polygonos* <note>Knotgrass</note>, also known as *sanguinaria* <note>Bloodwort</note>, is effective for bloody ulcerations and the menses of women, according to **Dioscorides**. **Galen** says it is a "gluer" of bloody wounds and stops flowing blood; the "male" kind, which has a Phoenician flower, is more powerful than the "female," which is distinguished by a flower of another color. The second kind of *Lysimachia* <note>Loosestrife</note> shines with a red-colored flower; it is a vulnerary and is effective for bloody fluxes and excretions. *Bistorta* <note>Bistort or Snakeweed</note> has a red or somewhat purple flower, a reddish root, and likewise a reddish underside of the leaf. If women sit in its decoction, or if it is smeared on the pubic area, it restrains menstrual rejections and glues together what is injected. The distilled water of the smaller kind, when drunk, is powerful against a hepatic bloody sweating. The *Amaranthus* has a purple spike rather than a flower, but nothing more pleasing or delightful to the sight can be seen, for it surpasses Tyrian purples with its flaming brilliance; by its use, it is established by the experience of the "neoterics" <note>Modern or recent physicians of Porta's era</note> that it restrains the abundance of menses and bloody spitting. The third kind of *Sideritis* <note>Ironwort</note> has a purple flower; applied to a fresh wound, it suppresses the blood. *Rhus* <note>Sumac</note>, which is called *erythros* <note>The Greek word for 'red'</note>: the scarlet color of its little berries gave it this name; for female...

### BOOK THREE

...stops the abundance of fluids, according to **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the 1st-century Natural History</note>. **Strawberries** (*Fraga*) swell with scarlet juice; they heal wounds and restrain dysentery. **Cornelian cherry** berries (*Corni*) turn red when ripe and are effective against dysentery and excessive menstrual flow; notably, the white berries of this plant are used for white discharges <note>The author highlights how the color of the fruit corresponds exactly to the color of the bodily fluid it treats</note>. **Cherries** (*Cerasa*), which we call *amarendulae* <note>sour or amarelle cherries</note>, being endowed with a diluted blood-red color, heal flowing blood. **Hawthorn** (*Oxyacantha*) bears red berries; they are used for menstrual issues. Of the same species is the **Azarole** (*aronia*), also called *akzarolus* <gloss>azarole</gloss>, which is also effective against dysentery. The fruit and bark of the **Myrtle** (*Myrtus*) are red: they help with bloody excretions and menstruation, especially that species of scarlet color rather than the black one. The small berries of the **Mastic tree** (*Lentiscus*) turn red: they are used against the spitting of blood and dysentery. The fruit of the **Turpentine tree** (*Terebinthus*) is of the same color and medicinal faculty. The **dyer's grain** <note>Kermes, a red dye derived from insects living on the Kermes Oak</note>, which grows from the berry-bearing holm oak, glows with a cinnabar-red blood: **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> recommended it for wounds. **Tragium** <note>likely *Pimpinella saxifraga*</note> has a reddish seed: it heals women's discharges. **Common Balsam** (*Balsamina*) has fruit that is purple-scarlet inside; it is especially gifted for gluing wounds together, for stopping hemorrhoids, and bleeding of the seat <note>the rectum</note>. Red seeds of the **Peony** (*Paeonia*), when drunk with a harsh wine, stop menstruation. **Stinking Iris** (*Xyris*) has a red seed and root, used for wounds and fractures of the head. **Lesser Centaury** (*Centaurium minus*) has a reddish-brown root: it is used for eruptions of blood and menstruation; its power in wounds is so great that it is said even flesh grows back together if they are cooked together. **Chiron** <note>The wise Centaur of Greek myth, teacher of Achilles and Asclepius</note> is said to have been cured by this, according to **Pliny**, when an arrow fell on his foot while he was handling the weapons of **Hercules**, who was being received as his guest. **Stone Comfrey** (*Symphitum petreum*) has a reddish root, used for dysentery, red discharges in women, and for gluing recent wounds together. The roots of **Alkanet** (*Anchusa*) stain the hands with a blood-like color: **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note> says it heals discharges. **Bugloss** (*Lycopsis*) is of the same species and root: it is a wound-healer, according to **Dioscorides**. **Cinquefoil** (*Potentilla*) relies on a root that is purplish on the outside: whether drunk or applied, it helps with dysentery and discharges of the womb. The plant called **Wintergreen** (*Pirola*) has a small, reddish root: it excels in wound-healing potions and for "soldering" wounds. **Goldenrod** (*Virga aurea*) has a root that is reddish at the top and a stem that also reddens slightly; it is praised for stopping blood and binding wounds. **Tormentil** (*Tormentilla*) has a red-colored root and reddish stems: it compresses menstruation and blood flowing from wounds; it removes dysentery and glues wounds when taken as a drink. **Pliny** describes *Symphona*, which others call *cromphena*, as having alternating green and rosy leaves along the stem; he says it heals those spitting blood when taken in vinegar-water. **Indian Millet** <note>Sorghum</note> has a flower wrapped in red panicles and also a red root: it stops women's discharges. The leaves of **Blite** <note>an amaranth</note> redden so much that they seem stained with scarlet: **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine"</note> stated that menstruation is stopped by eating it, according to **Pliny**. **Water-pepper** (*Hydropiper*), or *persicaria*, has black spots on blood-red leaves: it is of miraculous virtue for healing wounds. **Meadow Clover** (*Trifolium pratense*) has varied droplets or spots on the leaves—red in one variety and white in the other—by whose help we have found by experience that the former works for red and the latter for white discharges of women. **St. John's Wort** (*Hypericum*), *ascyrum*, **Tutsan** (*androsæmum*), and *coris* have leaves and flowers which, when pressed by the fingers, stain the hands with dark blood: they are effective for wound balms. There is also a **Beet** (*beta*) that is entirely red in its leaves and root: it has an astringent faculty; from which, by no vain conjecture, I judge it to be effective for wounds. A species of **Burnet** (*Pimpinella*) called *sanguisorba* <note>meaning "blood-drinker"</note> grows with a reddening stem: it is most effectively beneficial for women's discharges, dysentery, and head wounds. The small stems and leaves of **Sorrel** (*Oxalis*) turn red; they stop menstruation. **Saracen's Consound** (*solidago saracenica*) rises with a reddish stem, having received the name *solidago* <note>from the Latin *solidare*, to make solid</note> because it can close and make solid the lips of wounds, and is mixed into wound medicines. The small stems of **Horsetail** (*Equisetum*) are reddish: its juice binds blood breaking out from the nostrils; it benefits dysentery and for gluing wounds together. **Aspalathus**, or red sandalwood: restrains fluxes of blood according to **Avicenna** <note>The 11th-century Persian "Prince of Physicians"</note>. **Agarwood** (*Agallochum*), or aloe wood, is reddish and astringent. **Oak** (*Quercus*) wood is distinguished by red veins throughout; for this reason the name *robur* <note>meaning both "oak" and "strength"</note> was given due to its redness, according to **Festus**, because it has red veins everywhere: it is effective for flows from wounds, blood in the excrement, and dysentery. Its leaves "glue" so well that **Galen** applied them to a wound when he had no other medicine at hand, by grinding the leaves with a smooth stone and applying them to the injury. **Camphor** (*Camphura*) exuding from the bark of the tree, has reddish spots at the beginning, but later is "cooked out" by the force of heat, or whitened by the force of fire: it checks breaking blood and binds it. Then...

This follows the Doctrine of Signatures, where a plant's physical appearance reveals its medicinal purpose.</summary>
