# PHYTOGNOMONICA

...sweet-smelling with a reddish stalk; its fragments tend toward purple: its flower suppresses the spitting of blood. **Hematite** <note>A reddish-black mineral (iron oxide) whose name literally means "blood-like"</note>, being of a blood-red color, restrains women's fluxes and the spitting of blood. **Dioscorides** <note>1st-century Greek physician</note> attributes the same power to **Cinnabar** <note>Mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral</note> as to the hematite stone. **Sinopian Earth** <note>original: "Rubrica sinopica"; a high-quality red ochre from Sinop</note> tends toward the appearance of the liver: it is commonly mixed into plasters for wounds and is given to those suffering from liver defects. **Red Chalk** <note>original: "Rubrica fabrilis"; ruddle used by craftsmen for marking</note> is inferior in both color and potency. **Coral** is greatly effective against the spitting of blood. The **Coroneolus stone** <note>likely carnelian</note> stops blood flowing from any limb, and especially female fluxes. To the **Heliotrope** <note>the bloodstone gemstone, known for its green color with red spots</note> this name was given because, when placed under water in the sun, it reflects a blood-red sun: it binds the flow of blood. **Sard** <note>a reddish-brown chalcedony</note> is of a red color: it is effective for stopping blood. We know that if **Antimony** <note>original: "Stibium"</note> and **Copperas** <note>original: "chalcanthum"; iron or copper sulfate</note> are burned, they turn a blood-red color; they wonderfully restrain blood bursting from a vein in the brain or from the chest; and so it is with others, lest we be too long.

### WHAT THE RED COLOR NATURALLY SIGNIFIES.
->Chapter XXII.<-

Now we must investigate what the color red can naturally demonstrate from its manifest qualities. **Averroes** <note>12th-century Andalusian philosopher</note> said that the red color demonstrates heat because of the fire seen within it. **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus, 13th-century scientist and theologian</note>, no unsuccessful philosopher, says that red color is caused by clear water and subtle earth being burned, with a smoky substance floating on top which converts the water and earth into red. To me, however, it seems that red color arises from an excess of earth, for white is the clearest of colors, and red is very dark due to its earthy parts; for this reason, all red colors are styptic <note>astringent or blood-contracting</note>, as can be seen in red wine. Fruits that are destined to be black turn red as they ripen and are bitter; but having reached their final maturity and being most "cooked" <note>the process of *concoctio*, or ripening by the sun's heat</note>, they turn black, as can be seen in cherries, mulberries, pomegranates, olives, grapes, myrtles, and others. **Roses**, **wallflowers** <note>original: "leucoia"</note>, and **carnations** <note>original: "garyophylli"</note>, if neglected or planted in arid places, turn red from excessive dryness; but in cultivated ground, becoming moist through irrigation and dunging, they turn black. The red rose is moist and warm according to **Galen** <note>The influential 2nd-century Greek physician</note>. **Campion** <note>original: "Lychnis"</note> is warm and dry, as is **Oleander** <note>original: "nerium"</note> according to **Avicenna** <note>11th-century Persian physician</note>. **Aspalathus** <note>a scented wood</note>, or **Sandalwood**, is warm and dry, and even the flowers of the **wild poppy** are warm, even if all other doctors say they are cold: I have deferred the reasons for this to their own specific sections.

---

### THAT MIXED COLORS OF PLANTS RESTRAIN MIXED HUMORS.
->Chapter XXIII.<-

We have spoken of the pure colors of plants, which drew out the simple humors <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> of our body; now let us examine the boldness <note>original: "petulantiam"; here meaning variety or striking diversity</note> of many colors. **Theophrastus** <note>The "Father of Botany" and student of Aristotle</note> says that some flowers are of one color, others of two, and others are multicolored. **Aristotle**, in his book *On Colors*, says that one part of a flower is red, another scarlet, another white, or they shine with purple, from which it is clear that flowers are noted as being variegated in appearance. The reason for this is that one part is more "cooked" <note>ripened</note> and the other less, or that a specific or varied humor exists in different parts. But why there is a greater boldness of colors in flowers than in leaves or fruits, the same author teaches in his book of *Problems*, speaking of the colors of the tongue: that as many colors are seen in it as in the skin because it is covered by a very thin cuticle, so that even the slightest variety can be detected; likewise, the most subtle and transparent parts of plants are seen in the flowers. But colors that are stained by other colors in flowers or leaves show various virtues and defects, following the reasoning of those previously mentioned. A bicolor flower possesses both virtues, and thus multicolored ones possess many: whence it happens that the same plant has various and conflicting qualities, which from various and...

# BOOK THREE

...consists of opposing humors. **Mastic** <note>original: "Mastiche"; a resin from the mastic tree used for digestive health</note> wipes away, digests, and strengthens, while **vinegar** cools and heats; they possess contrary powers because their individual particles come together through juxtaposition <note>placing side-by-side</note> rather than through a total blending—much like how sand, if glued together by a slow-moving liquid, is compacted into a single body, not by the merging of its tiny particles into what appears to be a single substance, but by their joining and contact. Therefore, if this is the case, it is not absurd to think that contrary qualities are instilled in the different particles of mastic or vinegar, and that they refuse to be blended into one another, as **Alexander** <note>likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle</note> notes. In human **Physiognomony** <note>the practice of judging character from physical appearance</note>, we used to say that men who have eyes marked by various colors possess varied characters, and are often deceitful and untrustworthy, whose company we said should be avoided. Likewise, plants marked by a mixture of various colors possess varied and often mutually opposing qualities, and they are not to be trusted; rather, they must be considered with the greatest scrutiny.

The same must be said of animals, gems, and stones, which share the same cause and nature: for this reason, they do not purge simple humors <note>the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, since multi-colored plants do not contain simple colors, but rather the distinctions of various colors joined together indiscriminately. And just as the humors of our body pass into others through digestion—as bile into "cholera" <note>here referring to the yellow bile humor, not the modern disease</note>—so yellow flowers turn into saffron, red, or purple through age or cultivation. Here are some examples: if the flowers are white and yellow, they purge both phlegm and bile simultaneously. **Chamomile** <note>original: "Anthemidi"</note> has flowers that are white around the edges like rays, surrounding a yellow tuft; according to **Galen** <note>a famous Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note>, they heal phlegmatic and bilious fevers. **Feverfew** <note>original: "Parthenium"</note>, with a flower white around the perimeter and honey-colored inside, draws out bile and phlegm. **Elder** <note>original: "Sambucus"</note> and **Danewort** <note>original: "ebulus"</note> bear umbels <note>umbrella-like flower clusters</note> that produce a white flower, yellowing at their center; both evacuate phlegm and bile because of the kinship between their flowers. The tree commonly called **Buckthorn** <note>original: "frangula"</note> produces white flowers, but the inner wood is yellow-saffron in color, and it purges phlegm. There are also white and black roots (since black is rarely found in flowers) which purge phlegm and melancholy <note>black bile</note>, such as the **female Mandrake**, which relies on a root that is black on the outside and white on the inside: it extracts phlegm and black bile through vomiting. **Apios** <note>likely the knobbed spurge, *Euphorbia apios*</note> has a root whose body is white inside and black outside the bark; it extracts bile and phlegm through vomiting. There are those that purge bile and blood, such as **Rhubarb** <note>original: "rhabarbarum"</note>: the root is black on the outside, and when cut open, it is yellowish and grayish with some whiteness. **Mesue** <note>a Persian Christian physician and apothecary</note> says it casts down bile but clarifies phlegm and blood. **Cassia** is saffron and red: it purges bile, drawing the bile out with it. The **Iris** consists of a beautiful mixture of multiple colors; what is seen in various other plants comes together to be viewed in this one flower: for it consists of a lovely yellow, purple, and white. Primarily extracting phlegm and bile, it is effective for hemorrhoids and six hundred other remedies. **Dioscorides** <note>a famous 1st-century Greek herbalist</note> said it is of great use for all things. So also the **rose**, **lily**, **star-wort** <note>original: "aster atticus"</note>, and the flowers of the **caper** are made of many components and consist of diverse qualities, even those fighting amongst themselves.

It remains to say something wonderful about colors that change from time to time, which indulgent Nature, concerned for the health of men, most mercifully demonstrates. For if harmful **mushrooms** are picked, they change colors in a short moment: for at first they are white, then they turn green with a diluted venomous hue, having a rancid appearance, a livid color inside, a cracked streak, and a pale lip around the edge, so that they truly strike horror; these colors are all seen in the faces of those who have been strangled by the poison of mushrooms or by a noose. This variety of colors is not seen in harmless ones. Nature, never praised enough, shows the same in the **sea starwort** <note>original: "tripolio"</note>; indeed, it changes colors three times a day: it shows white in the morning, purple at noon, and crimson in the evening, and it is especially effective against poisons; for those killed by poison are seen to turn from pale to purple or crimson. The same can be seen in animals, such as in the multi-colored **water turtle**, in **hens**, and others. In animals and stones, there are as many virtues and types of harm as there are colors. A **snake** marked with many and varied spots has as many ways of doing harm as it has distinct colors, according to **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a medieval physician</note>. And the bite of a **Salamander** requires as many doctors as it has spots. The **opal** gem has as many virtues as it has colors.

Q

It provides numerous botanical examples, such as Iris and Rhubarb, and notes that sudden color changes in nature, like in poisonous mushrooms, serve as warnings of danger.</summary>

PHYTOGNOMONICA
<meta>catchword: MILKY</meta>

## MILKY PLANTS AND ANIMALS are effective for producing MILK. Chapter XXIV.

<image-desc>Decorative initial A featuring floral motifs and scrolled leaves within a square frame.</image-desc>
But if blood is overabundant and does not putrefy, as discussed in the previous sections, it generates milk, seed <note>original: "sperma"</note>, and the menses, one of which serves for generation and the other for the nourishment of those generated. We shall speak first of milk. For milky plants, or those that bear a resemblance to milk, generate milk in the body, as the transition into a similar substance is easier than into a dissimilar one. The very name of **Lettuce** <note>original: "Lactuca"</note> is derived from milk <note>original: "lac"</note>, because it contains more milky sap than many other plants: when eaten by women, it increases their milk. The **Sow-thistle** <note>original: "Sonchus"</note> sheds a little milk-like sap when its skin is wounded; it is similar to lettuce, except that it is thorny. Its boiled stalk provides an abundance of milk to nursing mothers; according to **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a 1st-century Roman naturalist</note>, it is most useful for those who feel their milk beginning to curdle or thicken. **Iasone** is a wild vegetable with much milk: Pliny says that if eaten raw with vinegar, it provides an abundance of milk for women. Pliny also states that when water is added to the root of the **Marshmallow** <note>original: "Althea"</note>, it begins to whiten and turn milky, and it is effective against ailments of the breasts. Equally well-known is the **Woolly-plant** <note>original: "lanaria"</note>, commonly called "lactoris" <note>the milker</note>, which is full of milk; if given to fasting sheep, it creates an abundance of milk, according to Pliny. The root of **Bryony** produces milk: its stalks, boiled with wheat and then drunk, create an abundance of milk. **Tragium** <note>likely Goat’s-thorn</note> has something milky about it, similar to a gum: in the absence of milk, it refills the breasts and is uniquely medicinal for them. There are also herbs that have spots upon their leaves, a sign granted by Nature to demonstrate their effectiveness for milk. **Milk Thistle** <note>original: "Carduus lacteus"</note>, with its very large leaves, has milky veins in the leaf and, as it were, milky spots; the common folk among women provoke a bounty of milk by eating it. There are also **Honeywort** <note>original: "cerinthe"</note>, **Bugloss** <note>original: "lycopsis"</note>, **Borage**, and similar plants which have milky droplets, but their virtues are as yet untested. There are others which, when crushed or chewed, reveal a milky juice, such as **Tree-medick** <note>original: "cytisus"</note>, which provides milk for all living creatures; even if this is not recorded by medical writers, it is well known to devoted farmers and shepherds, as held by **Columella** <note>a Roman writer on agriculture</note> and others. **Milk-vetch** <note>original: "Glaux"</note> is of the same species: it is used to restore the abundance of exhausted milk; for this reason, the Greeks call it *eugalacton* <note>original: "εὔγαλακτον"; meaning "good milk" or "rich in milk"</note>, according to Pliny. Of the same species is **Milkwort** <note>original: "poligala"</note>, whose name is derived from milk. The chewed seed of **Black Cumin** <note>original: "Nigella"</note> presents a milky appearance: women use it to make their faces white and milky; if taken every day, it increases milk in women. In the same way, the **Chickpea** <note>original: "cicer"</note> increases milk in the breasts. Thus grain and barley become milky, just as milk is abundantly supplied from starch and barley-water <note>original: "ptisana"</note>. **Almonds**, **hazelnuts**, and legumes such as **beans**, according to **Avicenna** <note>a 10th-century Persian physician</note>, generate milk, as they turn milky when chewed. So too, animals that abound with much milk—namely those that are "multipara" <note>giving birth to many young at once</note> and have many teats—are effective for provoking and multiplying milk. **Aristotle** asks in his book of *Problems* why goats and sheep have the most milk in proportion to their bodies? He suggests it is because in larger animals, the abundance of nourishment is consumed by the body itself, while in others it turns into "excrement" <note>original: "excrementum"; in ancient biology, this refers to any surplus residue, including milk or seed</note>; in sheep and goats, however, whatever grows into residue all passes into milk, or perhaps because they produce more offspring than those of large body size; therefore they attract more residue, which overflows due to the weakness of the body—for it is certain that milk consists of residue. Avicenna says: some have said that eating the udders specifically of sheep and goats, along with the milk contained in them, is very useful for this purpose, either because of the similarity or because of a specific property within them. Furthermore, cheese from goats or sheep greatly increases milk. The **Sow** is multiparous, and she brings forth and nourishes her offspring perfectly: the number of her fertility reaches twenty, and Nature has produced nothing more fertile. A sow of Aericia had birthed thirty piglets. If sow's milk is drunk with honey-wine <note>original: "mulsum"</note>, it assists women in childbirth; if drunk for its own sake, it refills the failing breasts of new mothers, according to Pliny. The **Cow** abounds in milk: cow's cheese given to nurses increases their milk, as does butter, according to Avicenna. There are also **milky stones**, or those marked with milky drops, which increase milk in nurses, such as **Galactite**, according to **Dioscorides** <note>a 1st-century Greek physician</note>, and others.

<summary>This chapter explains the "Doctrine of Signatures" regarding lactation, arguing that plants with milky sap (like lettuce and sow-thistle) or animals with high fertility and milk production (like sows and cows) can be used medicinally to increase human breast milk.</summary>
<keywords>lactation, milk production, lettuce, sow-thistle, Pliny, Avicenna, Aristotle, sow fertility, milk thistle, galactite stone, signatures of nature</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of the "Doctrine of Signatures," specifically focusing on how plants with milky saps or watery fluids (serum) correspond to similar fluids in the human body, such as reproductive "seed" and the watery humors. It transitions from the general discussion of milk to the more specific medical applications of these fluids.</meta>

BOOK THE THIRD.

### MILKY PLANTS AND SPERMATIC ANIMALS produce seed. Chapter XXV.

We have also said that seed <note>original: "sperma"; referring to the reproductive fluid of both plants and animals</note> is a useful byproduct of the blood; because the milk in plants also bears a resemblance to seed, it likewise generates seed. We shall provide examples. The common name for **Spurge** <note>original: "tithymalis"</note> was created from the milky juice with which they swell, and **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a 1st-century Roman naturalist</note> said that Spurge makes men more prone to Venus <note>In this context, "Venus" refers to sexual desire and reproductive potency</note>. The **Poppy** is milky and increases seed, according to **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher of the Islamic Golden Age</note>. **Dandelion** <note>original: "Dens leonis"</note> benefits those from whom "Venus flows out" <note>likely referring to the involuntary loss of reproductive fluid</note>. According to Pliny, **Iasone** <note>likely a species of hawkweed or wild lettuce</note> stimulates failing sexual intercourse; so too does the milky root of **Dragon Arum** <note>original: "dracunculi"</note>. Fruits which, when chewed, show milk, are effective for generating milky seed. **Almonds** are excellent for recovering strength and bolstering Venus, according to **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire</note>. **Pine nuts** are milky and are highly recommended for increasing seed. **Pistachios**, when chewed, serve the same purpose. The small radish of **Thrasius** is an incentive for Venus. **Legumes** provide the same use. The **Chickpea** <note>original: "Cicer"</note> generates abundant seed; its grains are given to stallions, as is **Gorse** <note>original: "cytisus"</note>. The **Fig** is milky and is effective for Venus. From **Rice**, a milky cream is drawn out that generates seed. **Kidney beans** and all milk when drunk are effective for the same.

### THE SEROUS HUMORS OF PLANTS PURGE SERUM. Chapter XXVI.

But if the blood does not overabound in the veins but is secreted from them to become a waste product, then **ichor** <note>a watery discharge</note>, or **serum** <note>whey or the watery part of blood</note>, urine, and sweat are born. **Dioscorides** <note>An ancient Greek physician and the father of pharmacology</note> says that milk contains serum which, once it has been separated from the milk, is rendered much more powerful for purging. Milky plants are also "serous" <note>watery</note>; after the milk has been extracted, if it sits for a short while, the serum will separate. Because of this, it powerfully excretes the serous humors of the body. Avicenna says: Serum, or wateriness, is dissolving, cleansing, and thinning. All the **Spurges** are milky, as we have said; **Mesue** <note>an influential 9th-century Christian physician in Baghdad</note> said they most powerfully draw out the water trapped between the skin <note>referring to edema or dropsy</note>. The **Caper Spurge** <note>original: "Lathyris"</note> shrub swells with an abundance of milk; its grains, drunk in water, heal those with dropsy and draw water from the belly with great force. Of the same species are both the **Round-leaved Spurge** <note>original: "peplus"</note> and the **Petty Spurge** <note>original: "peplis"</note>. The milk of the **Fig** loosens the bowels; it benefits those with dropsy when applied as an ointment. The bark of the **Mulberry** <note>original: "Morus"</note> root is milky, loosens, and purges the bowels. The **Sycamore** <note>original: "Sycomorus"</note>, sharing in the nature and form of both <note>the fig and the mulberry</note>, has the powers of both: it is scratched with iron nails, for otherwise it does not ripen, and it abounds with much milk throughout every summer; its power is midway between the fig and the mulberry. The juice of the **Gourd** <note>original: "Cucurbitæ"</note> is milky; the Greeks believe the belly is smoothed by eating them. When wounded, the **Sea Cabbage** <note>original: "Marina brassica"</note> lets out a white liquor; when cooked in food, it most vehemently moves the bowels. The name for **Lettuce** <note>original: "Lactuca"</note> comes from the milk <note>original: "lac"</note> that it flows with; if its milk is given as a drink, it extracts watery chyme <note>partially digested food/fluids</note> from the belly, according to Avicenna; both the cultivated and wild varieties are recommended for dropsy by **Crateuas** <note>A Greek pharmacologist and physician to Mithridates VI</note>. **Hawkweed** <note>original: "Hieracio"</note> has a white or milky juice; it is gathered during the harvest by cutting the stalk. The juice, drunk in vinegar-water, purges the belly; Crateuas prescribes it to those with dropsy. **Hippophæs** has a root overflowing with milky juice that casts out water. **Chamelæa** <note>Dwarf Olive</note> flows with milk and draws waters down through the belly.

### PLANTS THAT CURDLE MILK also coagulate human seed, and those that dissolve milk destroy conception and act against poisons. Chapter XXVII.

Now that we have happened upon the mention of milk, it would not be out of place to enumerate those plants and animals that have the power of curdling milk—not because we are concerned with curdling milk itself, but because those things which do so are also able to coagulate human seed (which bears a resemblance to milk), so that they might be useful to us for generation. Likewise, those things which thin out milk prevent it from curdling; thus they are to be avoided by us, as they dissolve the seed and render the generation void.

->PHYTOGNOMONICA<-

In many ways, divine wisdom <note>original: "phronea"; referring to the purposeful design of nature</note> has revealed the paths for propagating generation by showing similarities. These examples will follow. The **Spiny Thistle** <note>original: "Carduus spinosus"</note> is thorny and has a root which, as it hardens, emits a milky juice that curdles milk just like rennet <note>original: "coagulum"</note>. This same plant increases prolific seed. Of the same species is **Safflower** <note>original: "cnicus"</note>, whose seed also curdles milk. Rural folk and shepherds use the flowers of the **White Thorn** <note>original: "Spinae albae"; likely Hawthorn</note> to curdle milk and to thicken it into cheese. The **Fig**, and much more powerfully the **Wild Fig** <note>original: "caprificus"</note>, curdles milk into cheese with its own sap; we have already said it is effective for women’s issues and for conception. **Lady’s Bedstraw** <note>original: "Galion"</note> found its name from the fact that its flowers, by their power of thickening, curdle milk; it is also effective for provoking sexual desire <note>original: "Venerem"</note> and for conception. The **Balsam** tree has the power of curdling milk, which is why the test for its purity is whether it curdles milk; adulterated balsam will not do this, and indeed, when thrown into water, it turns milky. For this reason, it is said that when placed in the womb or applied as a vapor to women who have ceased to conceive, it brings back fertile fecundity. Among animals with cloven feet, only the **Hare** possesses rennet, according to **Pollux** <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century Greek grammarian and sophist</note>; rennet is formed within it because it feeds on herbs with milky juice, and all milk is curdled by its rennet. According to **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, the rennet of a hare, applied to the womb with butter like a pessary <note><term>pessary</term>: a medicinal plug or suppository used in the vagina</note> after menstrual purgings, ensures that women conceive. **Sextus** <note>Sextus Placitus, a 5th-century medical writer</note> states that if four drachms of hare's rennet are given in a drink of wine—the female hare's for a woman and the male's for a man—and they engage in intercourse and then abstain, she conceives immediately.

On the other hand, substances that dissolve and return what is thickened to a fluid state make the seed <note>original: "sperma"</note> useless and destroy the generation. For in the uterus, where the seed must thicken into a sort of curd by natural heat or formative power, if this is entirely prohibited by some external force, or happens faster or differently than it should, the formation of the conceptus and fetus is hindered. If the nature of the woman is disturbed by a medicinal force from a pessary or from the man's member being coated in such a drug, the seed cannot curdle as is proper, but is rendered fluid, or too dense, or ill-disposed. **Mint** leaves submerged in milk prevent it from coming together and thickening, as witnessed by Dioscorides; and **Aetius** <note>A 6th-century Byzantine physician</note> notes that when applied to breasts in which milk has thickened into lumps, it dissolves it. Therefore, when applied to the female genitals like a pessary before intercourse, it takes away the power of conceiving, as per Dioscorides, many examples of which you can see among authors. But we thought it necessary to warn that the same things that condense milk also dissolve it once it has been curdled. For this reason, the timing of the dose must be observed: for after the seed has been released and curdled, if you admit it to the womb, it dissolves; but before, it curdles.

The rennet of a **Fawn** <note>original: "Hinnuli"</note> is most highly praised by **Aristotle** for curdling milk, yet it is also used for dissolving what is curdled. According to Dioscorides, if it is applied privately to the uterus for three days after purgings, it intercepts the hope of offspring, and thus scatters the curdled seed. **Hemp** <note>original: "Canabino"</note> seed has such a power of curdling that it curdles water poured upon it, but if taken too largely by a man, it extinguishes his generative seed; yet if taken in moderation, as we said, it can bring aid to conception. **Salt**, eaten in moderate amounts, aids conception, but in large amounts, it prevents the seed from curdling, just as it does with milk. Salt sprinkled for sheep—but only in moderation—increases their milk, provokes desire, and aids fertility; but too much renders them sterile, because it dissolves what is curdled. Furthermore, whatever makes milk in the stomach or curdled bull’s blood fluid is likewise effective against conception. Such things include **Calamint** leaves, **Laser** <note><term>Laser</term>: resin from the silphium plant, used as a spice and medicine</note>, salt, vinegar, lye, **Cabbage** seed, unripe figs swollen with milky juice, pepper, and the rest. For this reason, a cabbage flower placed in the womb as a pessary after conception ruins the conceptus, and one should imagine the same for the others; let it be enough to have touched on these.

It would not be irrelevant to add some things that now come to mind: that venomous animals which eject venom in the form of milk, or sweat out milk, can be healed by those same milky herbs, either by dissolving or curdling the virulent milk. When a **Salamander** is struck, it flows with milky gore, and when irritated, it vomits milk, according to **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola, a 16th-century scientist</note>. The remedies are **Pine nuts**, according to Dioscorides and **Aegineta** <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Greek physician</note>, as well as fresh milk (especially from a cow) and **Scammony**, whose juice is not without milk, for it turns milky when touched by the tongue. The **Toad** <note>original: "Rubeta"</note> exudes milk from the compressed bumps that roughen its back; the rennet of a hare, human milk, balsam, laser, poppy, and those things which we said curdle milk, are effective against its poison. From the wounds of **Water Lizards**, a milky, venomous gore flows, as in the salamander, and in the same way its poison...

### BLOOD-RED PLANTS ALSO STIMULATE THE MENSES.
->Chapter XXVIII.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a figure in a garden or field setting.</image-desc>

THERE IS also the menstrual blood, which comes from an overflowing of humor, yet is useful for generation, as it is that by which the infant is nourished in the mother’s womb. Now, in another way, blood-red plants stimulate and draw out the blood of the menses. **Madder** <note>original: "Rubia"</note>, with its red root and seed, is cultivated by dyers because wool and hides are stained by it; its root and seed draw out the menses. There is also the **Red Chickpea**, more powerful than the white, which draws out the menses. **Butcher’s Broom** <note>original: "Ruscus"</note> bears red or blood-colored berries; it is effective for the purging of women. **Cassia**, which rivals coral, and reddish **Cinnamon**, draw out the menses. The fruit of the **Laurel** is blood-red, and the "Ethiopian tear" <note>original: "oleae lachryma aethiopicae"; a resin from an Ethiopian olive variety</note> of the olive tree excites the menses. The red berry-clusters <note>original: "corybi," likely "corymbi"</note> of the **Ivy**, when crushed and applied as a pessary, move the menses. **Cyclamen**, with its purple or dark-red <note>original: "colossinis"</note> flowers, excites the menses whether through a drink or an application. The **Anemone**, with its scarlet flower, moves the menses. The root of the **Great Centaury** turns red; it extracts the menses. **Mock Privet** <note>original: "Phillyrea"</note>, with its red fruit, excites the menses. The root of the **Parsnip** <note>original: "Pastinacae"</note> is so red that it is soaked in blood-colored juice; it moves the menses. One type of **Stock** <note>original: "Leucoium"</note> with a purple flower expels the menses. The red grains of the **Peony** excite the menses. The flower of **St. John’s Wort** <note>original: "Hyperici"</note>, when crushed between the fingers, gives off a blood-red juice—for which reason it is called **Man’s Blood** <note>original: "androsemum"</note>—and when applied, it drives out the menses. All these details are from **Dioscorides**. The red berries of the **Juniper**, the oil of which excites the menses. Two drachms of the **Red Arum seed** <note>original: "Semen aricoccincum," likely Aris coccineum</note>, which is red in the manner of coral, are effective for women to bring on the menses, along with infinite other things. 

Now let us look at the animals which abound in menses and are effective for summoning them, and those which lack them and stop the flow. **Cows** are purged by menses, indeed in greater measure than **sheep** and **goats**; in warm regions, they appear every fifth month, according to **Aristotle**. For this reason, the **gall of a bull** helps the purging of women when applied with greasy wool <note>original: "lana succida"; unwashed wool containing lanolin</note>. **Olympias of Thebes** <note>a famous female midwife and author of the ancient world</note> adds **wool-grease** <note>original: "oesypum"</note> and **natron** <note>original: "nitrum"</note>, according to **Pliny**. The menses of the **ewe** and the **goat** are indicated at the time of mating; the same happens after mating for a time, then it soon ceases until they give birth, at which point they are indicated again, and a purging follows abundantly after the birth, according to **Aristotle**. Wool-grease summons the menses, according to **Dioscorides**. **Does** <note>female deer</note> are purged after birth by a certain phlegmatic humor; a pessary made of **deer marrow** is recommended for summoning the menses by **Agricola**. The **mare** does not have menses; indeed, she is accustomed to emit the least among quadrupeds. She is free of such purgations in the manner of birth and emits very little blood, clearly in proportion to her body size, according to **Aristotle**. By the ash of **horse hair**, blood is stopped, when applied to every flow, according to **Pliny**.

### THE TEARS AND SWEATS OF TREES ARE EFFECTIVE FOR
### our own tears and sweats. Chapter XXX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a landscape with classical structures and foliage.</image-desc>

THERE ARE also tears and sweats in plants, and it has been discovered that these are effective for the flowing of our own tears and sweats. **Frankincense** <note>original: "Thus"</note> is the tear of a tree which drips from the "pregnant" bark of its body during the most burning heat; its soot halts the fluxes of the eyes. By this example, from **myrrh**, **resin**, and **storax**, every kind of "tear" is finally gathered for these same uses. Even the tear that drips from the **Ethiopian olive tree**, which is shaped like small breasts in minute droplets, clears dimmed eyes when applied as an ointment, and wears away scars and white spots in them; our local olives pour out the same drop, and it is also to be sought in the **wild olive**. The water that emanates from an egg while it is cooked over a fire is effective for tears of the eyes. There is also the tear of **tragacanth**, which hardens as it flows when the root is wounded; the use of this has become frequent for eye medicines, for muffled voices, and other <term>distillations<gloss>catarrhs or bodily discharges</gloss></term>. The same must be said of sweat. Gums emerge from the breathing-holes of the bark just as sweats do from the pores; thus they may rightly be called the "sweats" of trees. The **giant fennel** <note>original: "Ferula"</note>, when wounded at the base of the stalk, emits **sagapenum** <note>a medicinal resin</note>, and this induces sweating. **Myrrh** is the tear of a tree growing in Arabia: it is applied with liquid alum against underarm sweat and foul odors; it soothes long-lasting discharges and fills eye ulcers. **Amber** flows like sweat and stimulates sweating. **Smyrnium** <note>Alexanders</note> earned its name because it exudes a juice with the flavor and smell of myrrh, so that one may take the place of the other; just as myrrh stimulates sweat. The "old" **fig** <note>original: "Anus ficus"</note> drips a tear in the manner of a gum and then dries. **Figs** stimulate sweat: for this reason, they are considered unhealthy in autumn, because bodies become chilled by the sweating caused by this food; the **wild fig** also elicits sweat, and old oil, by warming the body, disperses sweat. **Panax**, a type of giant fennel, has its root cut in autumn and its stalks during harvest; in Macedonia, the juice breaks out spontaneously and is called **opoponax**. It is gathered when the tear—or sweat—has recently broken out, and it induces sweating. Giant fennel also induces sweat in those anointed with its oil.

The leaves of the **Ledo** <note>a species of Cistus or Rockrose</note> are fatty at the tip, similar to a tongue, abounding in a large amount of juice and always green; held in the mouth under the tongue, they cool and [produce] saliva...

# THAT FLESHY PLANTS MAKE MEN FLESHY,
## and heal those wasting away. Chapter XXXII.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap letter D depicting a man in a landscape with hills and trees.</image-desc>
We have spoken of the humors and excrements; now let us approach the body parts, first the "similar" parts <note>A term from Galenic medicine referring to tissues that are uniform throughout, like flesh or bone, rather than complex organs.</note>, and among those, starting with the flesh. Flesh, nerve, and vein are parts common to almost all, and are regarded as the basic elements of plants. Flesh lies between the vein and the nerve, and sometimes constitutes the bark, and sometimes the leaves. **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher often called the "Father of Botany."</note> stated that certain roots are "fleshy" because they consist of flesh, such as **radishes**, **turnips**, **arum**, **saffron**, **beets**, **king’s spear** <note>original: "hastulae regiae"; likely yellow asphodel</note>, **bulbs**, **squills**, **onions**, and **chives** <note>original: "gethyj"</note>. The flesh is stretched out in width in the leaves of beets and cabbages; and finally, the garden vegetables <note>original: "oleracea"</note> that are brought into and cultivated in gardens have, for the most part, fleshy leaves. They are "fattened" by skill and cultivation so that they are very suitable for nourishing man. According to **Pliny**, flesh is generated from water, and bones from milk. 

Because these fleshy plants provide great nourishment and are more easily transformed into human flesh, they are effective for making men fleshy. Physicians prescribe them to those with **consumption** <note>original: "phthisicis"; a historical term for tuberculosis or any wasting disease</note> and to those **wasting away** <note>original: "tabidis"</note> whose flesh has melted and decayed, just as they prescribe fatty things for the lean, as we shall discuss. **Cabbage** with its fleshy leaf and a stem swelling like a turnip, when thoroughly cooked, is a remedy for those wasting away. Among the bulbous plants, the **leek**—either its juice or the vegetable itself in food—is beneficial for consumption, according to Pliny. Fleshy **melons** <note>original: "melopepones"</note> are also used: a milky cream made from them and **barley gruel** <note>original: "ptisana"</note> is given to those wasting away. The **fig** fruit consists of a fleshy pulp; it fills the internal organs with flesh. **Plantain** has fleshy leaves which, if drunk, heal consumption. 

The **asphodel** <note>original: "albucus"</note> consists of a root similar to medium-sized turnips; no other is more numerous, often having eighty bulbs heaped together. This was once eaten toasted in ashes with salt and oil added; the crushed root was also a particular delicacy when mixed with figs. **Aristarchus** also reports that its root is edible and pleasing with a grateful smell. Regarding emaciated bodies and those wasting away, it is well established that asphodel bulbs boiled with barley gruel provide a most obvious cure, and bread made from them mixed with flour is very healthy. All **bulbs** are fleshy, provide much nourishment, and create flesh. The **bean** has a very fleshy leaf and produces flesh. According to **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian polymath and physician.</note>, the **mushroom** <note>original: "fungus"</note> is nothing but flesh and provides much nourishment. The **Italian oak** <note>original: "esculus"</note> and the **common oak** have fleshy fruit and leaves; their acorns nourish greatly and create solid flesh in pigs. Men of the first age used to feed on their fruits, and the *esculus* oak took its name from *esca* <note>the Latin word for food</note>; for before the grain of Ceres <note>cereal crops</note>, sustenance was provided to mortals from acorns. Among animals, the **tortoise** and the **crab**, once their shells are removed, are fleshy and moist because they live in water, and they heal those with consumption. Seek out other examples from these.

# THAT BONY PLANTS HEAL THE BONES.
## Chapter XXXIII.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap letter N with scrolling floral and leaf motifs.</image-desc>
Now we shall speak of "bony" plants, namely the woody ones, for the woody part of a plant corresponds to bones. Indeed, wood is in a plant as a bone is in flesh, and it performs that same function, as we mentioned when we spoke of the similarity between a plant and a man. Hence, we call those plants "bony" which abound in a great deal of wood; we said the opposite above, for those which abounded in flesh lacked wood. Theophrastus said that many roots are woody and dry in the plants used for garlands, and far more so in **southernwood**, **rocket**, and for the most part in wild plants...

<keywords>fleshy plants, wasting disease, consumption, asphodel, Doctrine of Signatures, woody plants, anatomy, Pliny, Theophrastus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the "Doctrine of Signatures," specifically moving from the comparison of fleshy plant parts and human flesh to the correspondence between woody plant structures and human bones, then beginning a new chapter on "nervous" (fibrous) plants and their relationship to human nerves and tendons.</meta>

in part. The roots of orache <note>original: "atriplicis"</note>, amaranth <note>original: "bliti"</note>, dill, sorrel, coriander, and most woody of all, basil, are woody; in short, this is true of all plants with many stalks. Bones require dryness during their diseases, and we have said that wild plants are drier than cultivated ones, which is clearly recognized in their appearance, as they are parched. Physicians say that those things which dry out and have some cleansing power are best for covering bones with flesh: for to reclothe bare bones with flesh, they use substances that cleanse and dry at the same time, without being overly heating. **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle, famous for his botanical works.</note> says the **myrrh** tree rises up twisted, hard, and rough: it heals bare bones. The **elm** is a woody tree: its crushed bark is effective for broken bones, according to **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>. The **myrtle** is a woody tree covered in a thin bark; it also heals broken bones. In the same way, the **mastic tree** <note>original: "lentiscus"</note>, a decoction of whose leaves is effective for cementing together broken bones, as Avicenna testified. **Balsam** is a shrubby tree, very similar to broom and the turpentine tree, according to **Strabo**; **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and pharmacologist whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical manual for 1,500 years.</note> said it removes scales from bones. **Holly** is a wild tree, shrubby with woody branches, by whose help broken bones are cemented together. **Mullein** <note>original: "verbascum"</note> has woody branches: it helps broken and dislocated bones. Southernwood, lavender, *libanotis* <note>Rosemary or a similar aromatic herb.</note>, and similar plants that are wild, dry things out, but these have remained unexplored for a long time.

---

### ON NERVOUS AND CARTILAGINOUS PLANTS, AND THAT THESE ANIMALS BENEFIT THE NERVES AND CARTILAGES. Chapter XXXIIII.

We call a **nerve** <note>original: "nervum"; in the Renaissance, this term referred interchangeably to nerves, tendons, and plant fibers.</note> in plants that which is seen to be continuous, easily split, and very long, but solitary and incapable of producing a bud. Theophrastus called giant fennel <note>original: "ferula"</note>, *ferulago*, and fennel "nerve-stalked" and "nervous" plants. There are also nervous plants whose stalks we use for ropes or cords—namely those that are flexible, willow-like, and yielding, such as **flax**, **hemp**, and **nettle**. There are also the fronds of plants which have nerves on the underside, like a hand: for nourishment is carried to those parts through the veins and nerves. Whence some fronds consist of nerve, bark, and flesh, like the fig and the vine; others consist almost entirely of nerve, such as the reed and grain. The hardest trees are those in which the nerves are hardest. Nerves seem to be tempered from wood and flesh; they are thinner or drier than flesh, but softer than wood; the entire plant is bound together and strengthened by them. 

But let us bring forward some examples. The Ionians call **Burnet** <note>original: "poterion"</note> *neurada* because it is a nervous plant: it sends down nervous and firm roots of two or three cubits in length: when crushed, with the nerves removed, they are applied to glue wounds together; a decoction of them also benefits afflictions of the nerves, according to Dioscorides. The root of **mallow** is very nervous, so much so that it cannot be broken or pulled up: **Pliny** <note>A Roman author and natural philosopher.</note> said that, when boiled, it benefits the nerves. A species of this is **marshmallow** <note>original: "althea"</note> with a nervous, very hard root: Dioscorides proclaimed it excellent for stiffness of the nerves. **Hog's fennel** <note>original: "peucedanum"</note> sends up a fennel-like stalk: applied as an ointment, it benefits all defects of the nerves in general, as well as convulsions. **Silphium** <note>original: "laserpitium"</note> grows in Syria with a fennel-like stalk; it helps in cases of nerve convulsions. **Sagapenum** <note>A yellow-brown resin from an Umbellifer plant.</note> is the juice of a fennel-like herb: it is given against paralysis of the nerves and for convulsions. **Euphorbia** is a fennel-like plant in Libya: **Mesue** <note>A common name for several influential Arabic medical writers.</note> wrote that it purges obstructions of the nerves and benefits those with convulsions. **Wheat** has a reed-like leaf; its flour is effective for discharges of the nerves. Pliny wrote that milk produces bones, grain produces nerves, and water produces flesh. The **fig** has fronds conspicuous for their nerves; their ash is applied with oil for nerve defects and convulsions. The **vine** has nerves standing out upon its leaves: wine both benefits and harms the nerves: for they are injured by old wine, but they are soothed when it is applied externally, and the ash from the cuttings is effective for thickening of the nerves. **Iris** has a reed-like and nervous leaf: it is effective for those with convulsions. **Sweet flag** <note>original: "acorum"</note> is of the same species and virtue. **Lavender** consists of a small stalk girded by four nerves along its length: it benefits those with convulsions: and in the same way, **sweet sedge**, **galbanum**, **stinking iris** <note>original: "xyris"</note>, and *libanotis* benefit those with convulsions. **Hemp** is nervous: it softens contracted joints, according to Pliny. **Dill** for nerve pains, according to Avicenna. **Horsetail** <note>original: "equiferum"</note> consolidates wounds even in the nerves, according to Avicenna.

<summary>This page discusses the medicinal use of woody plants for bone healing and introduces the "nervous" (fibrous) nature of certain plants, linking their physical structures to the treatment of human nerves, tendons, and convulsions.</summary>

**Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian physician (c. 980–1037) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> says that both **turpeth** <note>original: "turbit," a root used as a purgative</note> and **asphodel** <note>original: "albucus," specifically the King's Spear</note> are effective for the nerves. According to **Pliny** <note>A Roman author and naturalist (23–79 AD) who wrote the "Natural History."</note>, asphodel is fibrous and impossible to uproot. The same logic should be applied to animals. Snakes and worms are so sinewy that they seem to consist entirely of nerves <note>In historical medicine, the term "nervus" often referred interchangeably to nerves, tendons, and sinews.</note>. **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary source for herbalism.</note> stated that snakes are helpful for ailments of the nerves. Crushed earthworms can be applied to nerves; even if the nerves are severed, they can weld them back together. The bull is a sinewy animal, and its tendons are used for making glue; it is effective against spasms. Pliny also notes that the sloughed skin of snakes <note>original: "serpentum senectus," literally "the old age of snakes," referring to the shed skin</note>, when tied inside a bull's hide and worn, prevents spasms, and their marrow loosens contractions of the nerves. Nor would it be out of place to mention those things which are fibrous and also "stiffen the nerves" <note>A euphemism for the penis and sexual potency</note> during sexual encounters, such as flax, nettle, giant fennel, certain onions <note>original: "cephiliones"</note>, thistles, sword-lily, and galangal. In the same way, cartilaginous plants heal cartilage. Cartilage is a flexible softness provided by Nature’s providence so that parts of the body might not be broken; once ruptured, it does not solidify back together. Pliny calls the "cartilaginous" type of herbs those consisting of fleshy layers, such as cucumber, gourd, radish, turnip, rape, and parsnip. Similar to the parsnip is the **marshmallow** <note>original: "hibiscas"</note>, which some call "wild mallow" and others "pistolochia"; according to Pliny, it heals cartilaginous ulcers and broken bones.

### THAT PLANTS AND ANIMALS resembling tufts or hair heal baldness. Chapter XXXV.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'S' decorated with a curling serpent-like creature and botanical flourishes.</image-desc>
**THE LAST** of the "similars" <note>parts of the body that look like parts of plants</note> will be the hair. For there is in plants a "tress" <note>original: "coma," referring to foliage or flower clusters</note> which has borrowed its name from its resemblance to human hair. We call "tresses" whatever adorns the tops of branches or stalks with a cheerful beauty in the manner of hair. Often flowers, or the stamens of flowers, clusters, and umbels, when the top is leafy, "wear their hair" with their own charm. We claim that these can heal defects of the hair. These will be the examples:

**Maidenhair fern** <note>original: "polytrichon" or "adianton"</note> produces small stalks that are shiny black, thin, and just like hairs. It obtained the name *polytrichon* from its effect, because it produces a "multitude of hairs." It is also called *callitrichon* because it makes the hair "beautiful and black." It is commonly called "Venus's hair" <note>the "Capillus Veneris" fern</note> because it makes the hair lovely and attractive; it also works against the falling out of tresses. To **Apuleius** <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Apuleius, the author of a 4th-century herbal</note>, *polytrichon* is a small herb that brings forth thin, slender hairs instead of stalks, the loss of which the roots restore. **Trichomanes** <note>Spleenwort</note> also has thin, hair-like branches; it is effective for the same things as maidenhair. **Thapsia** <note>The "deadly carrot"</note> has a fennel-like or hair-like leaf; its juice, when rubbed on, fills in bald spots <note>original: "alopecias," referring to alopecia or mange</note>. Avicenna testifies that it has no equal in covering the head with hair. **Southernwood** <note>original: "abrotano"</note> has leaves cut into tiny segments; **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) in the Roman Empire</note> says its burnt ashes are suited for baldness. The oak tree bears a certain growth that they call a "hair"; this is a small ball bearing a soft, woolly tress. It also bears another hair-bearing ball which, in the springtime, stains the hands with a honey-like juice, according to **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle, often called the "father of botany."</note>; but Pliny said that these balls, mixed with bear fat, refill bald spots with hair. There are also downy flowers which are composed of hairy fluff at the tips of their heads, and as the flowers bloom, they turn into "pappus" <note>The fuzzy down on seeds like thistles or dandelions</note>. The **thistle** <note>original: "carduus"</note> produces a fruit that quickly turns gray and blows away with the breeze; before it flowers, if crushed and the juice is expressed and smeared on, it cures baldness. When the top of a **reed** <note>original: "harundini"</note> grows old, a thick down grows out, as is seen in marshes during autumn; many call it a plume. The ash of reed bark, rubbed on with vinegar, is applied to baldness. There are also flowers that spring from the highest rays of umbels, representing a head of hair in a certain round shape, like fennel-like plants. **Laserwort** <note>original: "laserpitium"</note> is a type of giant fennel; smeared on with vinegar, pepper, and wine, it fills in bald spots, according to Dioscorides. **Euphorbia** is likewise a fennel-like plant and bears a rounded, circular umbel; it also refills baldness with hair, according to Avicenna’s treatise on baldness.

### PHYTOGNOMONICA

<image-desc>A botanical engraving at the top of the page. The upper portion shows several flowering plants with thin, branching stems and small leaves. Below them is a detailed illustration of the back of a human head with thick, wavy, and curly hair. Positioned to the right of the head is a plant whose roots or stems form dense, tangled, hair-like fibers, creating a visual parallel between the plant's anatomy and human hair, typical of the "doctrine of signatures."</image-desc>

**Wild Alexanders** <note>original: "Smyrnium sylvestre vmbelliferum"</note> of the umbellifer family <note>Plants with umbrella-like flower clusters, like carrots or parsley.</note>: from this same plant, a preparation is applied to fill back the hair lost to **alopecia** <note>A medical term for hair loss, often occurring in patches.</note>. Likewise, the resins **ammoniacum**, **fagapenum**, and **opoponax**, which come from the giant fennel family, are administered for the same purpose in the medicinal compound known as **Hiera Logodion** <note>A famous ancient "sacred" bitter remedy used for various ailments.</note>. Onion juice is rubbed onto alopecia because it quickly draws out the hairs; garlic works the same way. Flowers with prominent stamens demonstrate the same property—specifically those which have hair-like filaments inside them. Just as **myrtle** flowers contain stamens within, they also increase the growth of hair. The **olive** tree bears myrtle-like flowers and is excellent for the same treatments. The **Martagon lily** <note>The Turk's cap lily, known for its recurved petals.</note> restores falling hair, as do the common **lily** (according to Pliny), the **water lily** with its lily-like flower, the **laurel**, and **St. John's Wort** <note>original: "hypericon"</note>. There are flame-colored stamens in the **saffron** flower, shaped with the thinness of a hair; when these are removed from the center of the flower, they benefit the hair. 

In hard **thyme**, there are also tendrils and curls, like locks of hair, called **epithymum** <note>A parasitic plant, also known as "dodder of thyme," which grows in tangled, hair-like masses over the host plant.</note>; in the manner of a vine's tendril, they wrap around the foliage of the thyme and decorate it with a kind of "head of hair." According to **Avicenna**, these "maned" plants cover a smooth, bald head with abundant locks. 

The most **shaggy animals**, those with curly, dense, or prickly fur—or those that bear spines in place of hair—demonstrate that they provide the greatest help for generating hair. These very hairy animals inhabit the coldest places so that they may be protected from the frost by their fleece. The **hare** is the hairiest of animals; according to **Aristotle** and **Pliny**, it alone has hair inside its cheeks and under its feet. From the leg of a hare, or from its plucked wool, a medication for alopecia is made, according to **Dioscorides**. The **bear's** hide is extremely shaggy, and those from Numidia <note>A region in North Africa.</note> have even longer hair, according to **Solinus**; its fat helps against alopecia, as noted by Dioscorides and Avicenna. The hair of **pigs** <note>Bristles</note> is thicker than that of cattle or elephants, and they do not usually lose it in winter like other four-legged animals; its lard <note>original: "axungia"</note> provides aid for thinning hair, according to Pliny and **Paul of Aegina** <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note>. The **fox** has a hairy pelt, even hairier in Germany; its head, if burnt and applied as an ointment, will cure alopecia. The **hedgehog** and **porcupine** have spines,

**sea urchins** <note>original: "echini"</note> have spines in place of hair, for indeed hairs can degenerate into spines. According to Galen, the ash of a burnt sea urchin is effective against the falling out of hair. **Goats** have a small tuft <note>original: "spirillum"</note> hanging from the chin; these are thick and shaggy hairs, the ash of which, according to Dioscorides and Pliny, wonderfully restrains thinning hair. The crest of a **seahorse** <note>original: "hippocampo"</note> bristles with hard hairs and is used to correct **alopecia** <note>patchy hair loss</note>. The same effect may be expected from similar creatures.

### YELLOW AND BLACK PARTS OF PLANTS AND ANI-
### mals excel at turning hair yellow or black. Chapter XXXVI.

Since we have fallen into a discussion regarding hair, we shall also teach, based on their apparent nature, how women may please their husbands and men their wives—specifically, how we may make the hair blonde. By observing the yellow parts of plants—whether roots, trunks, flowers, or fruits—if we see them most excellently colored with a yellow hue, we recognize through Nature’s demonstration that they are effective for the decoration of the hair. **Loosestrife** <note>original: "Lysimachia"</note> has a golden flower; both Dioscorides and Pliny report it is called *lytron* by another name, which is thought to be a corruption of *luteum* <note>the Latin word for yellow</note>. Vitruvius says that those who cannot afford **malachite** <note>original: "chrysocolla," here referring to a green pigment</note> may use the herb called yellow-weed; they soak it with blue pigment to create a most vibrant green. Such is the use of loosestrife among our dyers; for by applying it over the blue color with which **woad** <note>original: "glastum," a plant used for blue dye</note> tints, they produce a green color. If it is used by itself, however, it yields a yellow color. Because it makes the hair yellow, painters have surmised that by grinding yellow and blue together, they can produce green. The seed of the **cocklebur** <note>original: "Xanthium"</note>, which is found in the prickly burr of the plane tree, turns reddish before it withers; when collected and crushed in an earthenware vessel, it turns the hair yellow. When needed, about half a pint <note>original: "heminæ vnius"</note> is smeared on the head in warm water, provided the head has first been prepared with **natron** <note>original: "nitro," a naturally occurring soda used as a cleanser</note>. It is thought the River Xanthos was named from this use. **Henna** <note>original: "Ligustrum, siue cyprum," Porta distinguishes the true henna from common privet</note>, which is brought to us from Turkey and commonly called *alkanna*, has crushed leaves that are saffron or red; they turn the hair red, as Dioscorides says. This is not, however, the common privet of **Mattioli** <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>; the true henna has a saffron leaf when the leaves are soaked in the juice of the root. **Madder** <note>original: "Erythrodanum"</note> is called *rubea* by the Latins because its seed and root are red; these are used to dye wool and skins, and for this reason, it is diligently cultivated by dyers. Its leaves also tint the hair. **Golden-herb** <note>original: "Chrysolachanon," likely Orache</note> found its name from its color, which fades into a yellow that rivals gold; it could not have been called by a more fitting name. Pliny seems to confirm its gold-rivalling color when he mentions that hair is dyed particularly with the wild variety of orache. **Hawk’s foot** <note>original: "Accipitrinus pes"</note> is of a yellowish color, by which hair is tinted a reddish hue. The wood of the **boxthorn** <note>original: "Lycij lignum"</note> turns reddish when crushed, as does the root; when crushed and steeped, it returns a saffron juice that makes the hair yellow. The **lotus** <note>likely the European nettle tree or jujube</note> has a saffron-colored root and fruit; Pliny said the root dyes wool, skins, and barks, but Dioscorides says it reddens the hair. Whether it be the common lotus or the African variety which we call the **jujube**, our women also boil its saffron or crimson fruit to "gild" their hair. We read in the poet Theocritus of a type of herb called **Thapsos**, useful for dyeing wool, which also reddens the hair; I judge this to be no different from *thapsia*, since *thapsia* bears umbrellas at its tip similar to dill, and yellow flowers above them. **Honey** is of a golden color; above all else, it makes hair yellow, red, and golden. For a "water" and an "oil" are extracted from it by chemical vessels <note>alchemical distillation</note>, as we shall teach; the oil tints hair red and the water tints it a wonderful gold, with a color that lasts for many days. **Rhubarb** <note>original: "Rhabarbarum"</note> has a yellow juice, excellent for dyeing hair, and it does not harm the head. A decoction is prepared from golden **litharge** <note>original: "lithargyro," a lead oxide mineral</note>, which is wonderfully useful for dyeing hair a golden color, according to Pliny. There is a tree called **euonymos** <note>the Spindle Tree</note>; our people call it *fusanum* <note>from "fusus" for spindle</note> because it is famously used by women for spinning; it has a yellow flower, four-angled pods, and a seed enclosed in a saffron-colored membrane, with wood like boxwood inside. Our women prepare an ointment from it, with which

are used for making the hair beautiful and flaxen <note>original: "flauos," meaning golden or blonde</note>. And not to wander too far afield, almost all yellow things produce yellow hair. We have used a decoction of this sort very often: Take a piece of **rhubarb** <note>original: "rhabarbari"</note> the size of a bean, a handful of **fenugreek**, and equal amounts of **wild saffron**, **licorice**, the plant called **tobacco** <note>Porta is writing in 1588, shortly after tobacco was introduced to Europe as a medicinal curiosity</note>, **orange peels**, and **wheat straw**. Add **oak ash** to these and boil them until the water level has dropped by "three fingers" <note>an ancient measurement of depth</note>, and then let the hair be washed with it. By the same method, the black parts of plants—whether seeds, roots, or leaves—and black-colored animals, produce black hair. 

Let us turn to examples. **Ivy**, according to Dioscorides, has clusters that are first herbaceous and then turn black; it blackens the hair. The **myrtle** has black berries; the same author advised that it should be used for the blackness of hair. The **blackberry bush** <note>original: "rubus"</note> grows with black mulberries, staining the hands like dark blood; by this, the hair is dyed a black color. The **mulberry tree** has fruit that is red when growing and black when ripe, just as the fruit of the **black vine** stains the hands with a blood-like, dark color. A mixture of **grapevine** and **black fig leaves** boiled together in rainwater <note>original: "aqua coelesti," literally "heavenly water"</note> dyes the hair. The fruit of the **sumac** <note>original: "rhois"</note> turns red, then blackens when ripe; a decoction of it then blackens the hair. **Maidenhair fern** <note>original: "adianto"</note> has little stalks like rushes or hair, blackening with a dark or silken color, and it dyes the hair; for this purpose, according to Pliny, it is boiled in wine with **celery seed**; some call it *callitrichon* and others *polytrichon* <note>Greek terms meaning "beautiful hair" or "much hair"</note>, both named for its effect. **Bitter vetch** <note>original: "eruo"</note> has a black seed; its green pods, before they harden, if crushed with their stem and leaves, stain the hair black, according to Pliny. The black leaves of the **cypress** blacken the hair when mixed with vinegar. The juice of the mature seeds of **acacia** is black, though it turns reddish when bitter; according to Demetrius, the black variety with a dark flower is preferred; the hair is stained black by it. Pliny said that **polemonia**, which has black seeds in its clusters, gives blackness to the hair when boiled in oil. **St. John's Wort** <note>original: "hypericum"</note> has black seeds and blood-red juice; it blackens the hair, according to Pliny. The **holm oak** <note>original: "ilex"</note> has black wood, leaves, and roots; the bark of the holm oak root, if boiled until it softens into a honey-like consistency and is applied all night, is said to blacken the hair, provided it is first cleaned with **Cimolian earth** <note>a type of clay used as a detergent</note>. Burnt **oak galls** boiled in vinegar return black hair. **Litharge** <note>lead monoxide</note> of silver, boiled in a lye made of oak ash and lime until it perfectly dyes a piece of white wool thrown into it, wonderfully dyes the beard and hair a very deep black; the dye lasts a long time and is not easily discovered. **Labdanum** <note>a resin from rockrose</note> has black leaves; it preserves the blackness of the hair and keeps grayness away. 

We are accustomed to using this mixture for the beard and hair: Take as much common lye as you wish, boil in it **sage** and **laurel leaves** with the **husks of green walnuts**; then wash, or rinse with a soaked sponge, and you will be delighted by the effect. Indeed, the walnut is very powerful for blackening hair; this is first discovered by those who handle them, as their hands become stained. Ovid says:

> *Our injury marks the fingers with a dark juice,*
> *The staining rind having touched the hands.*

The same rule applies to animals. **Leeches** <note>original: "sanguifugae," literally "blood-fleers"</note>, which are very black, blacken the hair if they have rotted in black wine for sixty days. Others order a pint of leeches to rot for the same number of days in two pints of vinegar in a leaden vessel, and then to be applied in the sun. Sornatius relates that they have such great power that unless those who apply the dye hold oil in their mouths, he says even their teeth will blacken, according to Pliny. A **crow's egg** <note>original: "cornicis ouum"</note> mixed in a copper vessel and stirred for a long time, if applied to a shaved head until the egg is consumed, produces black hair; but until it dries, oil must be held in the mouth lest the teeth turn black, according to Pliny. The **eggs of swallows**, which are very black, achieve the same thing.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of hair treatments from the previous page, specifically focusing on depilatories (hair removers) and how the shape of plants determines whether they can curl the hair. # BOOK THREE

to break out. This remedy is accompanied by the myth of the boy **Hyacinth** <note>original: "Hyacinthi"</note>, whom **Apollo** loved; because it makes men appear youthfully hairless, they rub the lower bellies of boys with the stalk and root so that the hair of puberty might break out more slowly. **Galingale** <note>original: "Cypero"</note> has a smooth and hairless stalk; it is attributed with the power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <note>a Greek-derived term for a depilatory or hair-remover</note>, because it immediately removes hair. **Oak-fern** <note>original: "Dryopteris"</note> has smooth little stalks, similar to a fern; its crushed root acts as a depilatory. Animals with smooth skin are also effective as depilatories. The **Tuna** <note>original: "Thumnus," likely referring to the Thunnus or tuna fish</note> is entirely bare of all scales, with a plainly smooth skin, according to **Aristotle**. The **Sea-lung** <note>original: "Pulmo marinus," a type of jellyfish</note>, if it is the same thing, is transparent like crystal and smooth, made of a phlegmatic substance that dissolves in water. The **Sea-hare** <note>original: "Lepus marinus," a sea slug</note> is also smooth, similar to a squid. **Pliny** says a depilatory is made from the blood, gall, or liver of the tuna, whether fresh or preserved; even the liver, ground and mixed with cedar oil and kept in a lead box. This is how the midwife **Salpe** <term>beautified boys</term> <note>original: "mangonizauit," referring to the practice of slave-dealers (mangones) using depilatories to keep boys looking prepubescent</note>. The sea-lung has the same power. So too do the blood and gall of the sea-hare, the ash of the marine centipede <note>original: "scolopendræ marini," perhaps a sea worm</note> mixed with oil, or the brain of a **torpedo fish** <note>an electric ray</note> mixed with alum and applied during the sixteenth moon. The discharge of small **frogs** is a most effective depilatory if applied fresh, or the frogs themselves can be dried, crushed, and then boiled down from three half-pints to one third. **Leeches** roasted in a clay vessel and applied with vinegar have the same effect against hair. **Salamanders** liquefied in oil pull out hair, according to the same authors. Likewise, the **toad** <note>original: "rubeta"</note> makes one hairless, according to **Cato**, through bathing and washing. A **green lizard** boiled in oil makes hair cease to grow once it has been plucked, according to **Galen**. The **chameleon** is effective for removing hair from the eyelids, according to **Galen** and **Archigenes**, though **Pliny** uses its gall. 

Great beauty is added to the head by curly hair, which is highly sought after by women. We are taught how this can be achieved by **Nature** herself, through the similarity of leaves or other parts of plants. **Maidenhair fern** <note>original: "Adianto"</note> has a leaf that is, as it were, curly; a decoction of it with celery seed and a generous amount of oil makes the hair curly and thick, according to **Pliny**. **Celery** <note>original: "Apium"</note> is distinguished by leaves that are lightly curled, divided, and delicately fringed at the edges; it works for the same purpose, which is why it was joined with maidenhair fern by **Pliny**. The fronds of **cow parsnip** <note>original: "Sphondilij"</note>, insofar as they are curly at the tips, make the strands of hair curly when the head is anointed with them, according to **Dioscorides**. Similarly, the "urchins" <note>husks</note> of **chestnuts** seem to imitate the curly hair of the head with their prickles; they also make the hair curly. The hair of a **camel** is naturally curly; **Pliny** said that hair could be made curly using the ash of its dung mixed with oil, or even with the blood of an **owl chick**.

## ON THE PARTS OF PLANTS WHICH REPRESENT HUMAN
## parts, and first those which resemble the head, also animals with large heads.

### Chapter XXXVIII.

<image-desc>Ornamental initial letter D depicting a landscape with a classical building, foliage, and a cloudy sky.</image-desc>

WE HAVE SPOKEN of the <term>similar parts</term> <note>simple tissues like fibers or skin</note>; now we turn to the <term>instrumental</term> and <term>dissimilar parts</term> <note>complex organs like heads or limbs</note>, and we shall divide these into two categories: external and internal. First, we begin with the external parts, starting with the head. We give the name "head" to certain parts in plants due to their similarity to the human form, because they are gathered into a sphere; hence, parts that grow into a globular tuber immediately claim the name of "head" for themselves. There are some roots that swell out to the size of a head, such as **sea squills** <note>original: "scillis"</note>, and likewise fruits, such as **gourds** and **pomegranates**. Sea squills grow so large that they approach the size of a human head; their use is for <term>the falling sickness</term> <note>epilepsy</note> and other ailments of the brain, especially those arising from coldness. The **sea daffodil** <note>original: "Pancratij"</note> is of the same genus, form, and virtue. Among the types of celery, there is a "headed" variety which we have seen pulled from the ground in Campania that looks just like a human head; by a certain property, it affects the head because it bears black leaves and seeds, yet it wards off drunkenness, according to **Simeon Sethi**. The **Indian nut** <note>the coconut</note> produces a very large fruit of a rounded shape like a melon; an oil is extracted from it for pain and other defects of the head. **Quinces** <note>original: "Cotonea ftruthea"</note>, which rival the head in their size, are beneficial to the head and brain. **Gourds** and **melons**, being vaster than other fruits, are used against head pains (an ailment the Syrians call <term>syriasis</term> <note>an inflammation of the brain or sunstroke in children</note>) by applying their shavings. The cultivated **poppy** <note>original: "Papauer"</note> is "headed"; it is given to those who need to summon sleep. Finally, we shall not omit that point from **Pliny** taken from similarity: a herb that has grown on the head of a statue, if collected in some part of one's gar-
