PHYTOGNOMONICA

...they say that [a remedy] wrapped in a cloth and tied with red linen immediately soothes a headache. Animals with large heads are robust and show a perfection of the brain; by the indulgence of Nature, these are shown to be effective against the defects of our own heads. The donkey has a large head, and the bull’s is somewhat large in proportion to its body: for this reason, **Pliny** says that a small amount of water from the same source where an ox or a donkey has drunk, when taken or sipped, effectively removes a headache, and the brain of a donkey is healthy for those with the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: "comitialibus," referring to epilepsy</note>. The elephant has a very large head, according to the description of **Oppian**: **Aetius** believed that memory is greatly helped by elephant tooth sawdust <note>ivory</note> drunk in <term>honey-water</term> <note>original: "mulsa," a mixture of water and honey</note>, and **Pliny** notes that a headache is relieved by the touch of its trunk, which also heals those with the falling sickness. The pig has a large head: there are two small perforated bones in its head on the right and left which, when hung by a thread, remove a headache, according to **Marcellus**. The beaver <note>original: "Castoreo"</note> has a rather large head: this itself is smeared on for headaches, according to **Pliny**: **Galen** said its scent or inhaled smoke is useful for the head; **Pliny** notes it is given with <term>oxymel</term> <note>original: "aceto mulso," a mixture of vinegar and honey</note> to those with the falling sickness; when rubbed on, it heals vertigo, and when poured over them, it awakens those suffering from lethargy or "the drowsiness," <note>original: "veterno," a historical term for a state of heavy, pathological sleep</note> according to **Dioscorides**, **Pliny**, and **Avicenna**. The owl <note>original: "Noctuae"</note> has a very large head relative to its body size; it emerges from the egg tail-first because of the weight of its head, and its brain, when eaten in food, is a remedy for headache, according to **Pliny**. The hoopoe <note>original: "Upupa"</note> has a large head: its feathers placed upon a person's head soothe a "foul" headache, and its tongue, when hung [around the neck], prevents forgetfulness, according to **Rhazes**. Of the same kind is the screech-owl <note>original: "ulula"</note>, whose bones tied to the head heal a headache, according to **Pliny**, **Galen**, and **Sextus**: its brain taken in food cures the falling sickness, according to **Aetius**. Eagles have a head slightly larger than normal; its head bone, when tied on, is a remedy for <term>cephalalgia</term> <note>a general medical term for a persistent headache</note>. The ostrich <note>original: "Struthiocamelo"</note> has a very small head, and therefore no remedies for head defects are derived from it.

## FLOWERS THAT REPRESENT THE APPEARANCE OF EYES,
## and animals [that do the same], heal their defects.

->Chap. XXXVIIII.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'F' featuring stylized foliage and floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc>Flowers that show a resemblance to eyes have a central "navel" <note>the botanical disk or center</note> representing the pupil, and surrounding leaves <note>petals</note> that encircle that rounded tuft, appearing to show rays. We say that all of these heal the eyes. And we shall show the method. **Anthemis**, or chamomile, has a golden navel in the center with small petals radiating around the perimeter, circular in shape and white or purple: when applied, it heals <term>aegilops</term> <note>original: "aegilopi," an ulcer or fistula in the inner corner of the eye</note>. **Aster atticus** produces a flower at its tip, divided around the perimeter like chamomile, with petals radiating like a star: it heals inflammations of the eyes. The larger **houseleek**, or *aizoon*, is called "Jove's Eye" <note>original: "Iouis oculū"</note> by the Romans, and others call it <term>buphthalmon</term> <note>ox-eye</note> or <term>zoophthalmon</term> <note>animal-eye</note>, and "the eye," according to **Pliny**, because the leaves in the perimeter reflect the image of eyes. **Dioscorides** said it heals eye inflammations. A species of **Celtic nard** is seen with a white radiant flower, a rival to the ox-eye: it is stored away for eye medicines just as Celtic nard is. The **marigold** <note>original: "Caltha"</note> reflects a flower rounded into a circle, with a conspicuous boss emerging in the center in the appearance of an eye or a light. It seems to be called *buphthalmum* by **Columella**.

> "...and the yellowing lights of the marigold." <note>original: "et flauentia lumina calthæ"</note>

For the use of this plant, the sharpness of the eyes is improved daily: and a distilled water from its flower keeps away redness and inflammation of the eyes, if it is dropped into the eyes or if linens soaked in it are placed underneath. **Hawkweed** <note>original: "Hieracium"</note> has flowers rounded at the perimeter: **Pliny** says that hawks <note>original: "accipitres"</note>, by scratching it and smearing their eyes with the juice, dispel darkness when they feel it [coming on]: it is effective for all eye defects, for clouds, mists, and <term>epiphoras</term> <note>excessive watering of the eyes</note>. The plant commonly called **scorzonera** <note>viper's grass</note> puts forth a flower rounded in a circle crowned by many small petals, so that it imitates the rays of the eye. The milky juice from the root sharpens the eyesight.

### ANIMALS WITH LARGE EARS ARE EFFECTIVE FOR THE HEAVINESS
### *OF HEARING. Chapter 40.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop-cap letter 'P' featuring a seated figure holding a book, surrounded by architectural and foliate patterns.</image-desc>

We shall speak later of plants whose parts imitate the ears of animals, when we demonstrate the parts of plants similar to the parts of animals; now we speak of the ears of animals. Ears are the instruments of hearing prepared for perceiving sounds, given to animals for defense, so that, terrified by sound, they may flee dangers; for this reason, those with larger and more winding ears have better hearing. It is hardly certain in what part fish hear, for which reason their sense of hearing is more blunt, as it is less necessary for them; but let us come to examples. The **hare** is endowed with large ears because it is a timid and defenseless animal: to consult for its safety in dangers, it was fitting for it to be well-eared, so that it might perceive dangers and traps from further away and provide for itself in time. Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note> calls someone "auritus" <note>eared</note> from large ears, or from the faculty of hearing. Plutarch, in his *Table Talk* <note>original: "Symposiacis"</note>, said the hare excels in sharpness of sense and is endowed with the keenest hearing: therefore, the Egyptians, when intending to designate "hearing" in their sacred letters <note>hieroglyphs</note>, depict a hare. Among the Greeks, the name *lagos* <note>original: "λαγωὸς"</note> comes from the faculty of hearing: *ous* <note>original: "ὦς"</note> is "ear," and *la* <note>original: "λα"</note> increases the meaning <note>suggesting the hare is "all ear"</note>: it is effective for hearing if there is a heaviness of hearing; they praise hare's rennet <term>coagulum</term> with a third part of a denarius weight and a half-part of sagapenum <note>a medicinal gum resin</note> in Aminaean wine <note>a high-quality ancient white wine</note>, according to Pliny: goat's gall, warmed after being cooked and poured into the ear, restores hearing to one who hears nothing, according to Galen. The **donkey** has long and wide ears; no animal is said to hear more sharply than the donkey, except for the mouse, according to Suidas in his entry on *Midas*: fresh donkey dung with rose oil is instilled warm for heaviness of hearing, according to Pliny. A **cow** hears the lowing of the bull—a signal of love, like a token of Venus giving—from thirty stades <note>roughly 3.5 miles</note> away: for this reason, the Egyptians worship the cow and depict Isis with cow horns, according to Aelian. If there is heaviness of the ears, Pliny applies ox gall with goat urine, and so does the rest of the family of Physicians, or it is cured merely by old urine heated and rising <note>as steam or vapor</note> through the neck of a flask <term>langena</term>. They think **goats** have the keenest sense of hearing, as do animals endowed with cloven hooves, according to Aelian; and Egyptians, representing a man of sharp hearing, depict a goat, which hears with its ears and a certain part of its throat. Goat fat instilled in the ears heals the deaf, according to Aesculapius: or ox gall with goat urine buried in a goat's horn for twenty days, according to Pliny. The **fox** is an animal of clever hearing; when about to go to or return from feeding, it does not cross rivers and frozen lakes unless it has applied its ear to the ice to guess the thickness of the frost, according to Plutarch and Aelian: fox fat is effective for remedies of the ears. The **boar** hears excellently. The common verse says:

> The boar excels us in hearing, the lynx in sight, the monkey in taste,
> The vulture in smell, the spider in touch.

For ears that hear poorly, they instill urine <note>from a boar</note> kept in wine and warmed into the ears, according to Pliny. The **dog**, especially the keen-scented one, has large ears: it is said in a proverb that nothing is keener than a dog: dog fat with wormwood and old oil soothes the heaviness of ears, according to Pliny. The **goose** is a bird sharp at noises. Virgil...

# THIRD BOOK.

,, *...or the goose, more watchful than dogs.* <note>original: "canibusue sagacior anser"</note>

When the Gauls had conquered the Romans, they rushed into the city and took Rome, except for the Capitoline Citadel, which was difficult to climb. They attacked in the dead of night, for it was not being guarded, and the citadel would have been captured had the geese not intervened. Since it is in their nature not to be restrained from making noise, at their loud cackling, the surrounding guards were awakened; this is according to Aelian, and Lucretius adds to it:

->*The white goose, savior of the citadel of Romulus’s descendants.*<- <note>original: "Romulidis arcis seruator candidus anser"</note>

Goose fat dripped into the ears is effective for heaviness of hearing, according to Apollonius in the works of Galen. The crane is also effective due to the sharpness of its senses; according to Oppian, it signals whatever it perceives with its voice. When that fat is cooked over a fire, the part that overflows, if dripped into the ears, removes heaviness of hearing, according to Simeon Sethi. <note>Simeon Sethi was an 11th-century Byzantine physician.</note>

### PLANTS AND TOOTHED ANIMALS PROVIDE AID FOR TEETH AND
->teething. Chapter 41.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring intricate floral and vine patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

There are fruits and roots of trees that so skillfully resemble human teeth that we may know for certain Nature has shown these similarities for no other reason than to remind man that they are effective for toothaches and teething. Let us bring forward some examples to demonstrate this. Pomegranate seeds truly represent teeth: authors testify that a decoction of them is effective for diseases of the gums and for the firmness of teeth. Pine kernels mimic the incisor teeth perfectly: pine leaves boiled with vinegar soothe the pains of teeth. I hear that the herb **Toothwort** <term>Dentaria</term>—whose root, by a marvelous artifice of Nature, consists of a series of compact scales so that it truly resembles teeth—is beneficial for the teeth. This is easily possible, as it is endowed with great bitterness.

We shall next speak of which parts of animals represent teeth. There are those among animals that are armed with very strong and large teeth, remarkable in their position, number, and size: these are also effective for us in strengthening teeth and for the teething of children. In robust dogs, the teeth are serrated and meet like the teeth of a comb <term>pectinatim</term>, lest they be blunted by striking against each other, and they are strong so that they may very easily break bones. The ash of a dog’s tooth mixed with honey helps those who are slow to teethe; and according to Pliny, one who suffers pain is helped by scarifying the area around the tooth with the largest left canine tooth of a dog.

Wolves have serrated and robust teeth, which is why their bite is extremely harmful. The canine tooth of a wolf is held in high regard for great works: for it rubs the gums of infants so that the teeth may come forth more easily, according to Pliny. The lion has serrated teeth, and among those that have such teeth, the lion does not lose its canines, according to Aristotle. If a lion’s canine tooth is hung from a boy's neck before the [baby] teeth fall out, and during the emergence of the second teeth, it will render him safe from the pain of the same, according to Rhazes. <note>Rhazes was a celebrated Persian physician of the Islamic Golden Age.</note>

Mice on the island of Paros are said to eat and consume iron. Amyntas writes in his *Babylonica* that those in Teredon used the same food, according to Aelian. Gyaros is one of the Sporades islands where mice gnaw through iron, according to Suidas and Stephanus. Aristotle writes in his *Wonderful Things* that the same happens in Cyprus, as does Heraclides regarding the Chalcidians. Plutarch, in the *Life of Marcellus*, wrote that they gnawed gold in the chamber of Jupiter. Pliny orders that mice be eaten twice a month to prevent toothaches. 

The hyena, a species of wolf, has serrated teeth: various ranks of writers record that its teeth are beneficial for toothaches, either by touch or when tied on as an amulet. The **Lamia fish** <note>Likely a Great White Shark or similar large shark</note> has very sharp, dense teeth of a triangular shape, serrated on both sides, of which there are six rows: those of the first row project out of the mouth and incline forward; the second are straight, and the rest are curved back into the mouth. Women hang these from the necks of children to aid teething. Dolphins have teeth that meet like a comb: the ash of dolphin teeth with honey also contributes much to the gums and teething of infants, as does touching the gums with the tooth itself.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration from Giambattista della Porta's Phytognomonica, comparing human anatomy to botanical structures. Centrally, a human mandible (lower jaw) is shown with its teeth. Above the mandible, a pomegranate (malum punicum) is cut open to reveal its seeds (acini), which are presented as analogous to teeth. To the right is an intact pine cone, and to the left is a branch showing a pine cone with its scales removed, exposing the internal seed-bearing structure. Below the jawbone, individual seeds and extracted teeth are displayed side-by-side to emphasize their visual similarity.</image-desc>

The tope shark <note>original: *Canis galeus*</note> has sharp teeth that are curved at the sides, as does the *glaucus* fish. The ashes of the teeth of both fishes are very beneficial for the gums and teething of infants. It is also helpful to touch the gums with their teeth, or to wear them suspended from the neck. The pig, elephant, and hippopotamus have protruding teeth <note>tusks</note>, which were given to them for defense and strength; according to Aristotle, these teeth do not fall out. Brain <note>Likely hare's brain, a common folk remedy of the time for teething</note> smeared on the gums of children is effective for easy teething. There are also the robust beaks of animals, which were given by Nature in place of strong teeth for grinding food and for defense. Woodpeckers strike any trees, even oaks, with their beaks, so that they are called "oak-beaters" <note>original: *dricolaphi*, from the Greek *dryokolaptes*</note> by the Greeks, as Aelian notes. They feed on worms and hollow out trees so vigorously that they might even fell them; according to Aristotle, they can even pierce very hard almonds with a third strike and eat away the kernel. Their beak, suspended from the neck, removes all toothache. According to Aristotle, birds of the crow family are given a very hard beak; Pliny records that toothache immediately departs once it is tied on. Fighting cocks also have a strong beak, enough to even break small stones. Pliny notes that if one scarifies the gums with a small bone from a hen and then throws the bone away, the pain departs immediately, and so it is for the others.

BOOK THREE.

### PLANT AXILS ARE EFFECTIVE AGAINST HUMAN ARMPIT AILMENTS. Chapter 42.

Between the stem and the branches, certain bends are usually born from which new offspring emerges; these are commonly called "wings" <note>original Latin: *alae*, which translates to both wings and armpits</note>, a name transferred from human armpits, acting like a fold or an angle where two parts join together. Thus, the hollows of the "wings" and these folds are the same thing. Whenever we observe these structures to be more conspicuous than usual in herbs and trees, Nature warns us by that sign that they are powerful against the foul odors <note>original: *virosos odores*</note> of human armpits; for men who have deep hollows there are usually prone to this defect. It will be enough to demonstrate this with a few examples. The golden thistle <note>original: *scolymus*</note> rises with broad axillary hollows between the stems, branches, and foliage. It corrects the heaviness of the armpits if one ounce of the pith of the root is boiled in three <term>hemins</term> <note>A Roman measure, roughly half a pint</note> of Falernian wine until reduced by a third, and drunk in single <term>cyathi</term> <note>A small cup measure, about 0.04 liters</note> after bathing while fasting, and likewise after a meal. Dioscorides wrote that it draws out a copious and foul-smelling urine. The teasel <note>original: *dipsacus*</note> has joints with two leaves embracing them, forming a keeled axillary fold in which rainwater remains as if in a small jar or basin, from which the plant seems to have taken its name. Some smear the juice on their armpits for the same purpose, as it is drying and cleansing. The Alexanders <note>original: *smyrnium*</note> has a stem passing through the middle of the leaf so that the round leaves surround the perforated stem, appearing like the hollows of armpits; writers describing this call it "axil-like" <note>original: *alofum*</note>. Theophrastus said its nature was similar to myrrh, and that it differs in no way from myrrh, as if it were born from myrrh seeds. If the armpits are smeared with myrrh and liquid alum, they extinguish that tedious stench. But *smyrnium* corrects the burden of heavy breath for those whose breath is foul; for this reason, common women eat celery <note>original: *apium*</note> so that the power of the scent may drive away the heavy odor and their mouths may exhale a more pleasant breeze. The same should be said of woodbine and perfoliate, but their powers are as yet untried. The *albucus* <note>possibly white asphodel</note> is an "axil-like" plant; for this reason, Dioscorides and Pliny said it was effective for armpit ailments. Goats have very deep "wings" <note>armpits</note> and smell most wretchedly; hence the "goat-smell" <note>original: *hircinus odor*</note> of the armpits is named after them, and the remedy comes from them. The horn of a mature goat, scraped or boiled down, is mixed with goat gall, and an equal weight of myrrh is added; the armpits, having had the hair removed, should be rubbed diligently with this, according to Marcellus <note>Marcellus Empiricus, a 5th-century medical writer</note>.

### FINGERED AND JOINTED PLANTS ARE EFFECTIVE FOR FINGERS AND GOUT. Chapter 43.

We shall speak of the hands and the joints of the hands or feet; thus, plants that mimic such members are effective for the joints, gout <note>original: *podagras*</note>, and their ailments. For there are knotty herbs, either "kneed" <note>original: *geniculate*</note> or jointed, which swell into certain knots. That which falls between the joints and the "knees" we call the "internode" <note>original: *internodium*</note>; the thicker parts gathered into knots, where the ends of the internodes meet, are called "vertebrae." The roots of the <term>hermodactyl</term> <note>Literally "Hermes' Fingers," likely *Colchicum*</note> resemble the shape of a finger, in which even the image of the nails can be seen at the tip, and which branch out into four or five roots. By the advice of Serapion and Paul <note>Serapion the Younger and Paul of Aegina</note>, they have a primary power against the flux of the joints. There are also yellow "fingers" of the orchid family named by Avicenna, which show a resemblance to the human hand; for this reason, the common people call it "the Palm of Christ" <note>original: *Christi palmam*</note>. Its root is divided at its lowest part into four or five unequal parts, like fingers; it helps those oppressed by the obstruction of the nerves and pituitous refuse <note>An excess of phlegm or waste in the body's humors</note>.

> *The plants called "Palma Christi," "Hermodactyls," and the common "ischemi" or "Pliny's fingers" belong most particularly here, noting the fingered hands, as they appear unequal in the upper part, but in the lowest part, the hand with its fingers is seen.*

### FINGERED AND KNOTTED PLANTS.

There is a grass growing on walls called *fingered grass* <note>original Latin: *gramen digitatum*</note>, so named because its top is divided into five little forks that display the likeness of an open hand. Some call it *ischaemon* <note>Greek for "blood-stancher"</note>, others call it Pliny’s "prickly grass." Pliny says: There are three kinds of prickly grass, for there are prickles at the top, usually five in number; they call these *dactylon* <note>from the Greek *daktylos*, meaning finger</note>. They insert these, twisted together, into the nostrils and pull them out for the sake of inducing a nosebleed <note>Ancient medicine sometimes induced bleeding to purge "corrupt" humors from the head</note>. There is another kind, similar to houseleek <note>original: *aizoo*</note>, used for whitlows <note>original: *paronychia*, an infection of the fingertip</note> and skin growths around the nails <note>original: *pterigia*</note>; when the flesh has grown over the nails, they use this plant with lard, calling it *dactylon* specifically because it heals the fingers <note>original: *digitis medeatur*</note>. The castor oil plant <note>original: *Ricinus*</note> has leaves divided into five parts; for this reason, some call it the *Hand of Christ* <note>original: *Christi manus*</note>. Mesue <note>A prominent Persian physician</note> said it purges the waste matter that flows down into the junctions of the joints; it is also beneficial for joint pains, namely for those suffering from gout <note>original: *podagricis*</note>. The fig tree also has such a leaf; it is applied as a poultice for the joints. The knotted shoots of the vine are also relevant: wine is effective for warming and soothing the joints, and so it goes for others, even if it is commonly joked:

->*Medicine knows not how to loosen knotted gout.*<-
<note>A famous line from the Roman poet Ovid, suggesting that even the best medicine cannot easily cure the "knots" of advanced gout.</note>

Nevertheless, we shall demonstrate that it can be countered with certain herbs, specifically the "knotted" ones. But let us seek from the master which herbs are considered knotted. Theophrastus <note>The "father of botany" and successor to Aristotle</note> said some trees are knotted and others are knotless, such as those that grow in marshes. Knotted trees are the wild olive, the wild pine, and those that grow in sunny, dry, or cold places, such as mountain trees. Wild plants are more knotted than cultivated ones, and "knees" <note>original: *genicula*, the botanical term for nodes or joints on a stem</note> appear in reeds and grasses. If we wish to reduce this to natural causes: knotted plants are wild and dry; but because joints are often stuffed with phlegmatic wastes, they are dissolved by these dry plants. The reed is interrupted by frequent "knees"; Avicenna <note>The influential Islamic polymath and physician</note> wrote that it is good for the instru-

...said to be effective for the ligaments of the joints. **Knotted sarsaparilla**, which is interrupted by frequent joints, is quite effective for pains of the nerves. **China root** <note>A medicinal root from the *Smilax* family, imported from the East</note> is reed-like and works against gout. The **roots of the iris**, like the reed, are jointed and used for gout and the hardening of the joints. **Sagapenum** <note>A resinous gum from a plant in the fennel family</note> comes from a jointed, fennel-like stem; according to **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a famous Persian physician</note>, when applied in whatever amount to the connections of the joints, it is effective and soothes pain, as it completely destroys the sluggish humors that stir up torment in these areas. **Ammoniacum**, **thapsia**, **meum**, **elder**, and **dwarf elder** benefit those afflicted by gout in the same way. **Barley** is effective for gouty inflammations. The **gourd**, with its jointed shoots, cools them, as do the **cucumber** and **bitter apple** <note>original: *colocynthis*</note>, according to Mesue. **Birthwort** <note>original: *Aristolochia*</note>, creeping with knotted shoots, offers help to gout sufferers according to **Galen**. **Cabbage leaves**, where they attach to the stalk, show a very large knot, and the bottom of the stalk swells like a turnip; it is smeared on gout and joint diseases.

# PLANTS DEMONSTRATING THE INSTRUMENTS OF
## generation, and animals effective for generation.
### Chapter 44.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' containing a landscape scene with a tree, foliage, and distant hills.</image-desc>

Nature, busy with procreation and generation, demonstrates many and various similarities in herbs and animals by which humans might provide for their offspring. We call the instruments of generation the scrotum, the testes, and the vulva <note>In this context, "vulva" often refers to the womb or the female reproductive system generally</note>; hence, we should not fear that plants which demonstrate these through their roots, fruits, protrusions, or other means are effective for Venus <note>A common euphemism for sexual function or libido</note>. **Beans** <note>original: *fabæ*</note> show a true similarity to a large penis, and we commonly call it a bean. Furthermore, **Theophrastus** <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note>, demonstrating the germination of the bean, says: "The bean sends out its root and stem from the same part where the connection of the pods also sits, and in it there is a certain principle of germinating that is by no means obscure." In some, one can truly see it shaped in the form of a penis <note>original Latin: *mentulæ formam*</note>, as also in the **chickpea**, and especially in the **lupin**. We have known the bean to be effective for strengthening sexual powers, as it is full of wind <note>flatulence</note> and nourishment. For this reason, it was condemned by **Pythagoras**, because he detested the discharge of venereal matters <note>Pythagoras famously forbade his followers from eating beans, though his exact reasons remain a historical mystery</note>. Thus, as chickpeas, lupins, and other legumes grow, an abundance of seed <note>semen</note> is added, so that they immediately rush into sexual activity and indulge more eagerly in lust. **Acorns** <note>original: *glandes*</note>, furthermore, show the top part of the penis, which the foreskin covers; for the foreskin is the skin by which the acorn <note>original: *glans* - in anatomy, the "glans penis" is named after the acorn</note> is covered, and the organ itself is the penis. There is therefore a great similarity between the acorn and the head of the penis. As the cup [the acorn cap] splits, the top of the acorn is opened, so that with the foreskin removed, the top part of the penis appears. Not without reason, then, could someone take many remedies for the penis from the acorn. The acorn in foods produces much wind, according to **Dioscorides**, and much nourishment. **Simeon Sethi** <note>An 11th-century Byzantine physician</note> said it provides that which is flatulent and nourishing, and it can easily strengthen the shameful parts; for this reason, I also think Pythagoras commanded abstinence from acorns. Now, from the bulbous kind, roots present themselves, and more than those mentioned by the ancients, all of which, from their appearance, they call *orchis* <note>original: *ὄρχις*, Greek for "testicle"</note>, and from their effect *satyrium*, because they are incentives for Venus. But to **Pliny** and **Apuleius**, only a single bulb is *satyrium*. There are several kinds of orchids: those consisting of twin bulbs, in the likeness of human testicles; around the stem at their origin, many small fibers and hair-like threads are present around the circumference, from which they can take nourishment, just as hair grows soft on the pubes. Inside, they are full of liquid juice, viscous like the white of an egg, as if it were genital seed. In wooded, shaded, and damp places, they are so multiple and varied that they cannot be enumerated. They all bloom when the Sun enters Gemini. In Thessaly, women drank it in goat's milk to stimulate intercourse, as Dioscorides said, who took all this from Theophrastus, saying:

---

We have depicted three species of **ORCHIDS**: two of the *didymus* <note>twin</note> type, the third a *triorchis* <note>three-testicle</note>; since most are of a single bulb, we have omitted them. Compare them with the human ones; they will differ in nothing.

PHYTOGN.

<image-desc>A detailed botanical woodcut featuring three different orchid or "Satyrion" plants. Each plant is depicted with its flowering stalk, leaves, and characteristic paired testiculate tubers. Below the main plant illustrations are three additional detailed drawings of the root systems, emphasizing the resemblance of the tubers to mammalian testicles, illustrating the "Doctrine of Signatures" described in the text.</image-desc>

Beyond those things that concern health, diseases, and death, they affirm that other plants can bring different powers to human bodies through their own strengths—for example, the power of procreation in women. Such is the plant called the **testicle-plant** <note>original: *testiculus*; likely referring to a species of orchid</note>, which is said to be quite effective for sexual intercourse when taken with goat’s milk. 

It also yields the **satyrion** <note>A genus of orchids named after the lustful satyrs of Greek myth</note> root, the size of an apple, tawny on the outside and white like an egg within. It should be used when the desire for cohabitation arises, since it makes one more prone to the acts of Venus <note>The Roman goddess of love; a common Renaissance euphemism for sexual activity or libido</note>. 

There is another **red satyrion** <note>original: *erythronium*</note>, with a slender, reddish bark on the root and white inside. It excites lust just as the **skink** <note>A type of lizard used in traditional medicine as an aphrodisiac</note> does, even if held in the hand, and even more so if drunk in wine. 

Following these is the **Serapias** orchid, which has its own peculiar and wonderful power; it was named by the Egyptians after the august name of the venerable goddess Serapis <note>Though Porta refers to Serapis as a goddess here, Serapis was typically a male Graeco-Egyptian deity; the name was applied to certain orchid species in antiquity</note>. According to **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and author of the influential herbal *De Materia Medica*</note>, all bulbs stimulate Venus due to their resemblance to testicles. On this subject, **Martial** <note>A Roman poet famous for his witty and often biting epigrams</note> wrote:

> *When your wife is an old woman, and your limbs are dead,*
> *You can do nothing with bulbs except be full.*
<note>original: *Cum sit anus coniux, cum sint tibi mortua membra, / Nil aliud bulbis, quàm satur esse potes.* Martial is satirically suggesting that if a man is too old for sex, eating "aphrodisiac" bulbs will only fill his stomach, not his libido.</note>

The **greater dragon-plant** <note>original: *Dracunculus maior*; likely *Dracunculus vulgaris* or Dragon Arum</note> is endowed with a singular, round, bulbous root like a testicle; when drunk in wine, it provokes Venus. The same should be said of the **lesser dragon-plant**. 

The **gladiolus** <note>The "sword lily"</note> consists of twin roots, sitting one on top of the other in the manner of bulbs; the lower one is slender, while the upper is more fertile. Dioscorides handed down that the upper root, when drunk in wine, stimulates Venus. 

The **king’s spear** <note>original: *Hastula regia*; usually identified as asphodel</note> is bulbous and consists of many roots imitating testicles; we have often said that Venus is excited by these, whether they are smeared on with wine or honey, or drunk, according to **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*</note>. The same is to be said of **saffron**, **garlic**, **onion**, **wild leek**, and the others. Likewise, those which are oblong—

## BOOK THREE

...show the image of the form of the scrotum. The **leek** <note>original: *porrum*</note> excites Venus <note>a common Renaissance euphemism for sexual desire or "libido," named after the goddess of love</note>, and it is so similar to the scrotum that it has become a proverb. The **onion** <note>original: *caepa*</note> has the same form when it is young. **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, a Roman naturalist and author of *Natural History*</note> says that a greedy desire for sexual intercourse is thought to be produced in men by **arugula** <note>original: *eruca*</note>, and in livestock by the onion. **Apuleius** said that the **wild carrot** <note>original: *staphylinum*</note> was an aphrodisiac, perhaps because it was believed that Venus is stimulated by this food, and therefore they even claimed it helps with conception, according to Pliny. Pliny also thought that Venus is stimulated by the **radish** <note>original: *raphanus*</note>. The **skirret** <note>original: *siser*</note> is of the same shape, and as **Opion** and **Diocles** recorded, it has the same effect; the same must be said of the **turnip** <note>original: *napus*</note>, **rape** <note>original: *rapus*</note>, **parsnip** <note>original: *pastinaca*</note>, and others. 

There are also certain plants and animals that resemble pubic hair <note>original: *pubem*</note>, which I would judge to have the same power; for certain roots have a downiness <note>original: *lanuginem*</note> at their tops, expressing the down of the pubes. **Sea Holly** <note>original: *eryngium*</note> has downy leaves around the roots; their roots, preserved in sugar or honey, are effective so that those who eat them become more lustful. **Lion’s Foot** <note>original: *leontopodion*</note> grows white with a woolly tuft around the roots; **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and father of pharmacognosy</note> records that it is effective for amorous matters. There is a shellfish called the **scallop** <note>original: *pecten*</note> because it resembles the female pubes; it is effective for sexual matters, like **oysters**, of which it is a species. 

Animals also demonstrate the same virtue through some notable sign in their "instruments of luxury" <note>referring to reproductive organs</note>. The **buzzard** <note>original: *buteo*</note>, a type of hawk, has three testicles; the Greeks call them **triorchēn** <note>original: *τριορχην*; literally "three-testicled"</note>. To those who are weaker in Venus, they give the fresh testicles of a buzzard boiled with honey, and they will couple together immediately. **Archelaus** says the **hare** is androgynous <note>hermaphroditic</note>, at one and same time impregnating others and giving birth themselves, which only happens from a superfluous abundance and fecundity in females, signified by its hairiness, according to **Aristotle** in his book *On the Generation of Animals* and his *Problems*. Some physicians think the wombs and testicles of hares are powerful for exciting intercourse in men and conception in women. In **Brileto** and **Tharne**, **deer** have four kidneys, according to Pliny, which **Aelian** also reports from **Apion**. But its genitalia are very sinewy, according to Aristotle; if some part of dried **stag testicles** is drunk, it will excite sexual intercourse with pleasure, according to **Hesychius** and **Varinus**. 

In **roosters** <note>original: *gallis*</note>, the testicles become larger during mating, according to Aristotle; this is also verified in **partridges** and **doves**; and all are effective for sexual intercourse. A bony genital <note>the baculum or penis bone</note> is shown in some, and they provide for the same purpose, as can be seen in the **wolf**, **fox**, **dog**, and **weasel**. So too, animals that complete the act of mating quickly with a great abundance in females—especially those that do not have testicles on the outside, but inside in the loins—must complete intercourse more quickly due to the inconvenience of the embrace. Because of this, they always have an abundance prepared for the females, and the tract from the loins to the testicles is short, as can be seen in **egg-laying animals** <note>original: *oviparis*</note>. For this reason, egg-layers are more lustful, and the substance in eggs is at its highest for "luxury" <note>sexual desire</note>. **Heraclides** in **Athenaeus**, as well as the poet **Alexis**, numbers eggs among the foods that incite Venus, as does **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath and influential medical writer</note>. 

The **partridge** <note>original: *perdix*</note> is of prodigious lust: if the females stand against the males, as Aristotle wrote in the *History of Animals*, they become pregnant by the breeze blowing from him. Panting with their tongues sticking out, they are in heat during that time, and conceive by the breath of those flying over, often just by hearing the male's voice, according to Pliny, which Avicenna and Athenaeus (citing **Alexander of Myndus**) also repeat. The males fight among themselves for the desire of females; the loser in the fight is made to endure the winner's lust. It is recorded by the myth-makers that **Perdix** was a hunter seized by an unspeakable love for his mother; while immodest lust raged on both sides, he was consumed and brought to the ultimate ruin. The meat of the partridge promotes Venus, according to Avicenna; eggs taken as food are called an "amatory potion" by **Kirannides**, because they incite Venus. Roosters have their testicles near their kidneys. Alexander of Myndus in Athenaeus says they are exciters of Venus. 

The same things apply to the **quail** <note>original: *coturnix*</note> that we said about the partridge. **Gessner**, the physician, rubs the fat of the quail with a little hellebore on the private parts to excite the power of Venus; it has its testicles under the liver, as we read in the same author. The meat of the **heathcock** <note>original: *attagena*</note> is effective for the same, according to Avicenna. The right parts of a **vulture's lung**, tied to a person in the skin of a crane, incite Venus according to Pliny. The small kidneys and dried testicles of the **eagle** given in food or drink excite lust in either a man or a woman. These are followed by the egg-laying quadrupeds, which have testicles in their kidneys. In the **crocodile**, the testicles are attached inside to the loins, according to Aristotle; the teeth from the right jaw of a crocodile, tied to the right arm, stimulate sexual intercourse according to Pliny. **Sextius**, via Pliny, records that Venus is ignited by the food of the **salamander**, if it is boiled in honey with its entrails and feet removed. It is also wonderful concerning the [star-lizard]...

...with the ash of the skin, wrapped in a linen cloth and held in the left hand, it stimulates Venus <note>a common Renaissance term for sexual desire or libido</note>; if it is transferred to the right hand, it inhibits it. **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, Roman naturalist</note> says this. To incite Venus, **Oribasius** (as cited by **Aetius**) suggests: grind a live gecko <note>original: *stellionem*</note> as finely as possible, then pour on oil; with this, anoint the big toe of the right foot and engage in coitus. When you wish to stop, wash the toe. The same is found in the works of **Nicolaus Myrepsus**, **Paul of Aegina**, and **Marcellus**. The **Skink** <note>a type of lizard; original: *scincus*</note> increases seed and stimulates lust, according to **Avicenna**. Parts of the skink near the kidneys are drunk as an effective means for "raising the natural parts," according to **Alexander of Tralles**; Pliny says the sides are used, as do other physicians. Among the shelled animals, only the **Turtle** has kidneys: the flour from its shell ignites coitus. The **Beaver** <note>original: *castor*</note> has its testicles near its loins: there is a mythical belief, long ago debunked, that they bite off their own genital parts when in danger because they know they are being hunted for them, as **Solinus** wrote, along with **Andromachus** in his work on venoms; the Egyptians, when describing a man who harms himself, paint a beaver. **Cicero** said the beaver redeems itself with that part of the body for which it is most sought. **Aelian** and **Juvenal** say the same.

**Dioscorides**, Pliny (citing **Sextius**), and others hold the opposite opinion <note>that beavers do not actually castrate themselves</note>. It increases Venus and pleasure during the act if the male organs are anointed with it.

# ON WHAT SHOULD BE OBSERVED IN *plants and animals* REGARDING THE GENERATION OF MALES OR FEMALES.
### Cap. XXXXV.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' with floral scrollwork background.</image-desc>

Before we descend to the more noble internal organs, we shall explain the genital parts, or the *orchides* <note>the Greek word for testicles, here referring to both anatomy and the orchid plant family</note>; for both plants and animals show the male and female form, providing a certain omen for the conception of males or females. In males, the testicles hang from the region of the flanks in an oblong and round shape, such that the Arabs sometimes call them "eggs." In females, they lie inside against the sides of the womb, one near each horn, much smaller in size than in men; in shape they are wide, compressed, and glandular—that is, their outer surface is uneven, as if many glands of the same shape were tied together, soft and hollow as if filled with small swellings. Nature suggests through fruits, roots, or other parts that they provide some help in generating males and females. The **Dog’s Orchid** <note>original: *cynosorchis*</note> consists of a bulbous, oblong root, twin like an olive; the upper one is harder and more callous than the lower, which is softer and more wrinkled. From these roots, we see that if men eat the larger one, males are generated; if the smaller, females. For we see in these twin bulbs that the larger root swells into the shape of human testicles and produces males; the other, being small, shriveled, and not circular but compressed and hollow, produces females, according to **Theophrastus**, **Dioscorides**, and others. Indeed, it was fitting for more perfect roots to produce the more perfect sex. **Navelwort** <note>original: *cotyledon*, or Venus’s navel</note> has a root that is round and oblong like an olive; there is another kind whose root is somewhat large and shapeless, swelling with certain tubercles. **Hippocrates** recorded that by the use of the latter, the female sex is conceived, just as the former produces the masculine. **Theophrastus** records certain herbs for procreating a male or a female, wherefore he calls one "male-making" <note>original: *marificam*</note> and the other "female-making" <note>original: *foeminificam*</note>: both are similar to each other, bearing the appearance of **basil** <note>original: *ocymi*</note>. The fruit of the female-making kind is like olive-colored moss, but paler; that of the male-making kind is like an olive when it first emerges from the moss, twin like a man's testicles. **Dioscorides** offers the same regarding the *arrhenogonon* <note>male-begetting</note> and *thelygonon* <note>female-begetting</note> leaf, not from Theophrastus, but from **Crateuas**; soon forgetting himself, or being ignorant of this, he says in a specific place that it is the **Mercury plant** <note>original: *mercurialis*</note>. The Mercury plant has seeds like basil; in the female they are abundant, hanging down like clusters of grapes; in the male they are small and round near the leaves, always twin...

# BOOK THREE.

...male, connected in the manner of testicles. It is a marvel what is passed down concerning both kinds: that this one causes males to be fathered, and that one females. This occurs if the juice is drunk in raisin wine <note>original: *passo*; a sweet wine made from dried grapes</note> immediately after conception, and if the leaves are eaten, either boiled in oil and salt, or raw in vinegar. Some boil it in a new earthenware pot with heliotrope and two or three spikes of grain until it is cooked down. They command that the decoction be given, and the herb itself be eaten in food, to women for three days on the second day of their purgation <note>menstruation</note>; on the fourth day, after a bath, they should engage in coitus. **Hippocrates** <note>the famous Greek "Father of Medicine"</note> praised these herbs with wonderful honors for use by women, though as yet no physician knows the exact method. He applied them to the womb with honey, or rose oil, or iris oil, or lily oil; likewise for inducing the menses and the afterbirth. He said this same thing is achieved by drinking it or by a warm fomentation. The Greeks call the herb *hermupoan* <note>original: *hermupoam*; likely *Hermu poa* or "Herb of Hermes"</note>, and we call it **mercurial** <note>original: *mercurialem*; likely Dog’s Mercury (*Mercurialis perennis*)</note>, perhaps after **Mercury**, or because of the offspring, on account of the two parts coming together like testicles in the male, and the female presenting a certain appearance of clusters. Thus it is divided into male and female, and was discovered for the purpose of generating births of either sex; for this reason, the leaves are applied to the genital areas. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> records these things, but failing in both, he errs twice. Yet it is no trouble to add this as a finishing touch: that there are male and female plants, and to conceive males, one uses the male plants, and the female for the same sex, whether one uses them by continuous eating, or as a decoction after baths, or in another way, as we have said at greater length in its proper place. Of **Thistles** <note>original: *carduorum*</note> there are two kinds: the male brings forth a compact and closed cone, the female an open one. It is handed down that they benefit the womb so that males are fathered; for so **Cherias** of Athens and **Glaucias** have written. Certain things are to be observed in animals which bear a certain idea of the male, namely that if only males are born, they are effective for producing males; and those where only females are born, for females—not because they truly are so, but because the common people thought it to be so. The **Hare** at one and the same time both impregnates others and gives birth herself <note>a reference to superfetation, where a second conception occurs during an existing pregnancy</note>. **Aelian** writes that a "half-dead" hare was captured and found to be pregnant, such that when the womb was dissected they found three leverets, and yet the parent was a male. Pliny writes that the rennet <note>original: *coagulum*</note> of a hare taken in food causes a male to be conceived. When a **Bull** has mounted a heifer, if he leaps off to the right, it is certain he has sown a male; if to the left, a female. If women eat the meat of a calf roasted with **birthwort** <note>original: *aristolochia*; an herb used in childbirth</note> around the time of conception, Pliny promises they will give birth to males. The **Goat** displays the image of the male, for on the seventh day from which it is born, it mates; if you wish to father a male, devour two roasted testicles of a goat and engage in coitus on the same day, and you will conceive a male, according to **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, medieval scholar</note>. The **Rooster** is exceedingly lewd and pugnacious, and strongly maintains the idea of a man; he is effective for shaping males. Pliny says if women eat the testicles of a rooster immediately after conception, males are formed in the womb.

## PLANTS WHICH BEAR THE LIKENESS OF THE HEART,
->help the heart, and animals with large hearts are effective against fevers.<-
->Chapter 46.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring a figure amidst scrolling vines and floral patterns.</image-desc>
Now let us pass to the internal organs, and let us begin from the prince of organs, the **heart**. Some have called the root the "heart" in plants, others the pith, which have either no similarity or very little with our heart. But there are roots, leaves, and fruits which bear the likeness of the heart, and can be effective for the heart's defects or for fevers. We will bring forward some examples, by which the instructed reader may seek out others for himself in plants.

*FOUR parts of plants occur in this picture: first, in the outer parts, two **Antorae** <note>Yellow Monkshood or *Aconitum anthora*</note> and the roots of **Mountain Nard** <note>likely *Valeriana montana*</note> appear, having in the middle a **Citron** fruit. In the highest position of all we have placed the **Persea** fruit <note>an Egyptian fruit tree, sometimes identified as a species of Mimusops or even an early reference to the avocado family</note>, all expressing the image of the heart as closely as it was possible to achieve in pictures. And next to them, we have painted a heart torn out from a lung, as best as could be done, so that the mutual similarity might be more deeply contemplated.*

### PHYTOGNOMONICA

The **Citron** <note>original: *Citrium*; *Citrus medica*</note> represents the heart by the shape of its fruit: **Avicenna** <note>a famous Persian physician, 980–1037 AD</note>, in his book *On the Strengths of the Heart*, stated that it is especially effective for the heart; more recent physicians use it against pestilential fevers. The fruits of the **Anacardium** <note>the Cashew or Marking Nut tree</note> are similar to the heart in both shape and color—or at least they are not unlike the hearts of small birds, and for that reason they were so named <note>The name *Anacardium* comes from the Greek *ana* (upward) and *kardia* (heart)</note>: they restore failing senses. The roots of the **Anthora** <note>Yellow Monkshood, *Aconitum anthora*</note> show two little heart-like shapes; they aid in all afflictions of the heart, and they say they are no less effective against pestilential fevers. **Mountain Nard** <note>original: *Montana nardus*; likely a species of Valerian</note> similarly produces small roots like a little heart: it is powerful, just like the Indian variety, which heals heart ailments and is effective against fainting spells, not only when drunk but even when applied to the nostrils.

The **Persea tree** <note>likely *Mimusops schimperi*, though often confused with the avocado in later texts</note> is celebrated in Egypt; **Plutarch**, a most weighty author, records that this tree was the most pleasing of all to **Isis**, and was celebrated in Egypt because it bears a fruit similar to a heart and a leaf similar to a tongue. In Persia, its poison is so immediate that it kills those who eat it, because it attacks the heart instantly; yet when translated to Egypt, it bears fruit suitable for food. A type of **Vesicaria** <note>likely the Balloon Vine or Heart-seed, *Cardiospermum halicacabum*</note>, which among us is used in garden-work to shade windows, produces small bladders, and inside are black seeds in which a white image of a human heart can be seen: many have reported that it is effective for the heart. Sicilian women, with Nature as their guide, commonly call it "concord" <note>original: *concordiam*</note> because it reconciles husbands who are quarreling with their wives.

Common **Triphyllon** <note>Three-leaved plant</note>, called **alleluya** <note>Wood Sorrel, *Oxalis acetosella*</note>, produces leaves at the top of its little stems in the shape of a heart: it strengthens the heart, and its distilled water brings aid to those suffering from fever. **Pine** fruits <note>pine cones</note> resemble the heart: the crushed needles of the green pine, given in wine to drink, abolish heart pain. **Lemon Balm** <note>original: *Melissophyllon*; *Melissa officinalis*</note> bears a leaf in the likeness of a heart: the Moors extol it with wonderful praises for its effects on the heart and for bringing cheerfulness to the mind. **Motherwort** <note>original: *Cardiaca*; *Leonurus cardiaca*</note>, or *moluca*, produces leaves like Lemon Balm: it is of excellent quality for the heart. Another species of the same leaf is effective for the same purpose. The **Ben nut** <note>original: *Nux ben*; *Moringa oleifera*</note> is likened to the heart: Avicenna, from [its] pro-

...said to benefit the heart by a hidden property. **Myrobalans** <note>the astringent fruit of several species of tropical trees, used in various medicinal preparations</note> resemble the same and benefit the same, according to the same author. **Quinces** and **pears** express the same shape and are wonderfully helpful to it. Now we shall discuss animals with large hearts, which are beneficial for the heart and for fevers. For those animals endowed with a large heart are colder, and they protect themselves better from the heat of fevers, because their heart is colder than those that have a small heart; for those with a small heart, like the lion, suffer from a continuous fever due to excessive heat. Therefore, those with a larger heart are effective against fevers and for the strength of the heart. The **donkey** has the largest heart, according to **Aristotle**: there is a type of fever which they call *amphimerinon* <note>original: "amphimerinon"; a Greek term for a daily recurring fever</note>; they say one is freed from this if they drink three drops of blood from the donkey's ear vein in two measures <note>original: "heminis"; a Roman unit of liquid measure, about half a pint</note> of water, according to **Pliny**. The **deer** has a very large heart, as do all timid animals, according to **Aristotle**: its meat is effective against fevers. **Pliny** knew certain noblewomen who were accustomed to eating deer meat every day and remained free of fevers for a long life. The bone found in its heart <note>original: "os in corde"; actually a cartilaginous structure in older deer, often used as a medicinal charm</note>, by the similarity of its whole substance, is beneficial to the heart. The **elephant** is endowed with a double heart according to **Aelian**: **Solinus** said that ivory, by its whole substance, strengthens the heart. The **hyena** has a very large heart, as do all timid animals and those who are malicious because of fear, according to **Aristotle** and **Pliny**: for those whose heart palpitates, some part of the [hyena's] heart should be chewed, provided that the ash of the remaining part is smeared on with the hyena's brain. The liver, tasted before the onset of symptoms, eliminates **quartan fevers** <note>a fever where paroxysms occur every fourth day, often associated with malaria</note>. The **hare** has a very large heart, as it is the most timid of all animals: against quartan fevers, they smear the toes with children's urine sprinkled with the ash of a wild ox, and they bind the heart of a hare to the hands: they provide the rennet <note>original: "coagulum"</note> to drink before the onset [of fever], according to **Pliny**. The **panther** has a very large heart, according to **Aristotle**: if the scent of its fat is inhaled while roasting, it is useful for those suffering from heart palpitations, according to **Rhazes** <note>a Persian polymath and physician, 865–925 AD</note>. The **weasel** has a very large heart according to **Aristotle**: it cures fever according to **Ursinus**. **Mice** have very large hearts: against quartan fevers, the **Magi** <note>ancient Persian priests/astrologers often associated with folk medicine and magic</note> order the snout of a mouse and the tips of the ears to be tied on with a rose-colored cloth, and the mouse itself released, according to **Pliny**: but **Serenus** orders a fiber of the mouse's liver to be drunk with harsh wine.

### PLANTS WHICH RESEMBLE THE LUNG, AND ANIMA-
### ls endowed with a large lung, are effective for the lungs.

->Cap. XXXXVII.<-

<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap 'P' showing a central flowering plant with symmetrical leaves and curved vines.</image-desc>

After the heart, we shall speak of the lung, since it contains the heart; we shall also discuss herbs which do not resemble the lung itself (as they are still unknown to me), but those which resemble the whitish spots of the lung. These shall be the examples. There grows on the trunks of oaks or other forest trees, and especially in shaded woods, a certain herb, green in its upper part and pale below, filled with certain spots so that it resembles a lung; for this reason, it is called **Lungwort** <note>original: *pulmonaria*; specifically *Lobaria pulmonaria*, a lichen</note> by most. They use it for consumption <note>original: *tabem*; a wasting of the body</note>, ulcers of the lungs, bloody phlegm, the short-winded, the gasping, and the asthmatic. There is also another herb called Lungwort with a rough, hairy leaf like **Bugloss** <note>likely *Pulmonaria officinalis*</note>, sprinkled around with white spots, bearing purple flowers as in the common **Hounds-tongue** <note>original: *cynoglossum*</note>, with no small power for healing and cleansing lung ulcers. There is also another species to be numbered among the **Chicory** <note>original: *intubaceo generi*</note> genus, which is also varied with white spots and is endowed with the power to benefit the lungs.

But we shall assist our lungs with the lungs of animals; and if all members of animals benefit human ones, that will especially help which is either very large, or which lacks the organ entirely, as if Nature warns us by this sign of magnitude or absence that hidden powers lie within them. The **chameleon's** lung is proportionally the largest, so much so that it has almost nothing else inside, and **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, Roman naturalist and author</note> writes that the whole body consists of almost nothing but lung. Its tongue, along with the root of the **chameleon-herb** <note>original: "herba chamæleonis"; likely *Atractylis gummifera*</note> and **hound’s tongue** <note>original: "cynoglossæ"; *Cynoglossum officinale*</note>, causes one to become mute, according to the **Cyranides** <note>original: "Kirannide"; an ancient collection of magico-medical lore</note>. The **turtle** indeed has a lung under its entire shell, according to **Pliny**: it is effective for <term>consumption</term> <note>original: "phthisi"; a wasting disease of the lungs</note> and hectic fevers. Few aquatic creatures have a lung—for instance, frogs lack them <note>While frogs have lungs, ancient sources often distinguished their respiratory systems from those of land mammals</note>. **Frogs** are praised as food for consumption. The **green frog-plant** <note>original: "Ranunculus viridis"; *Ranunculus* means "little frog," and the plant was named for its shared habitat with the animal</note> is effective for a cough, according to **Pliny**, as are **squills** <note>original: "squillæ"; may refer to sea-onions or certain crustaceans</note> for the lungs and hectic fevers; **crabs** are effective for the same.

Whence the liver of a goose fattened with figs was a principal food at banquets; it is established, therefore, that the fig "seeks" the liver.

# BOOK THREE.

...**fumitory** <note>original: "fumariam"; *Fumaria officinalis*</note>; Leonhart Fuchs <note>a German physician and botanist</note> wrongly thinks it is **birthwort** <note>original: "pistolochiam"</note>. Valerius Cordus <note>a German physician and botanist</note> considers it to be "reed-smoke" <note>original: "capnos phragmitis"</note>, others "reed-celandine," or more accurately, the *capnium* of Aetius <note>a 6th-century Greek medical writer</note>. Its root is a great miracle of Nature; it is round, like a semi-cylinder, but as it matures, it becomes hollowed out. For a long time, the thought of what indulgent Nature wished to demonstrate by this paradox troubled and tormented my mind. Finally, a passage from Aetius came to mind: where he spoke of the liver hardened into a <term>scirrhus</term> <note>a hard, fibrous tumor or swelling of an organ</note>, he mentioned the *capnium* herb. Therefore, considering the hollow root, divided at its edge as if into fibers or lobes, it occurred to me that it is effective for the cavities or hard swellings of the liver in summer. I immediately took care to test this, and the outcome of the matter favored my wish. He also uses dried figs for inflammations of the same organ. **Agaric** <note>a wood-decaying fungus</note> also seems to represent the shape of the liver; Dioscorides <note>ancient Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> prescribes it to those suffering from liver defects.

But let us pass to animals. In some animals the liver is simple, in others it is double—not that we should think they are endowed with two livers, but it is divided into two lobes, appearing as if doubled. In some, it is so fatty that it turns into oil; this was given to us by Nature so we might know those substances are effective for softening the liver. Gigil the Philosopher said that the liver of animals is effective for liver pains, and Rhases <note>the Persian physician al-Razi</note> followed him, saying the same occurs for all members. But this is partly true and partly false. We say, therefore, that the liver in animals which is larger than others, or has some notable quality, was made by Nature so it could benefit the livers of men. We may recognize from their behaviors which animals will have these more notable internal organs. The more peaceful animals have less gall; the more timid have more heart; the more lustful have more liver; the more cheerful have more spleen; the more vocal have more lung. Whence the common rhyme:

> The heart burns, the lung speaks, the gall stirs up anger,
> The spleen makes one laugh, the liver compels one to love.
> <note>original: "Cor ardet, pulmo loquitur, fel commouet iras, / Splen ridere facit, cogit amare iecur."</note>

According to Aristotle, the liver of an **elephant** is four times larger than that of an ox. According to Rhases, the extremity of an elephant's liver eaten with sumac water and citron leaves cures a painful liver. The **horse** has a liver divided into three lobes, according to Herocles. Galen, in his book *On Easy Remedies*, writes that a horse's liver kept in a cedar box and then administered with Chian wine diluted with water prevents an ulcerated liver from being eaten away further. Pliny records that the **wolf’s** liver is considered difficult by some, but it is shaped like a horse's hoof. Galen writes that he has found by abundant experience that the whole substance of a wolf's liver helps those with liver disease. According to Pliny, the dried liver of a wolf taken with honey-wine restores liver pains. The **frog** has a double liver according to Pliny; its decoction is effective against <term>scabies</term> <note>a contagious skin disease causing itching and bumps</note>, according to Avicenna <note>the Persian philosopher and physician Ibn Sina</note>. The **goose** has a large liver; the liver of a goose is effective for the liver. The **vulture** is afflicted by liver pain; when affected, it hunts large birds and devours their livers, according to Rhases. Serenus <note>Quintus Serenus Sammonicus, a Roman physician</note> grants the vulture's liver for liver pains. The liver of the **stingray** <note>original: "pastinacæ"</note> fish is divided into two lobes; boiled in oil, it most effectively soothes itching and scabies, not only in humans but also in four-legged animals. So too the **monkfish** <note>original: "squatina"</note>. From its liver an oil is made which is effective for hardness of the liver when "Caltic" spike <note>an aromatic plant, possibly a type of valerian</note>, or styrax <note>a fragrant resin</note>, or wormwood is added. Galen says the **anglerfish** <note>original: "anthias"</note> has a double liver which turns into oil and is effective for liver hardness. Likewise, the liver of the **centrine** <note>a type of shark</note>, which is effective for softening the liver, also strengthens the heart due to its similarity in substance. The same occurs with the **blue shark** <note>original: "galeo glauco"</note>.

### ANIMALS ENDOWED WITH A LARGE SPLEEN, ARE EFFECTIVE FOR THE SPLEEN AND KIDNEYS.

It is the size of a hand, hollow in shape, convex, and as if crescent-shaped. Therefore, we conjecture that plants which show its shape in their leaves or other parts are effective for its defects. The leaf of **spleenwort** <note>original: "asplenum"</note> has a convex lower part in the shape of a spleen; others call it *hemionion*. It is called *asplenon* because it consumes the spleen in animals, which was discovered in this way...

# PHYTOGNOMONICA

...according to Vitruvius. Near the Potereus river, which is in Crete between the two cities of Knossos and Gortyna: on the right and left banks of this river, flocks were pastured, but those that grazed closest to Knossos had a **spleen** <note>original: "splenem"</note>, while those on the other side did not. The schools of Physicians, investigating this, discovered that a certain herb grew everywhere in those places which, when eaten by the cattle, would diminish their spleens. **Ivy** <note>original: "Hedera"</note> with crescent-shaped or rounded leaves, whether cooked in vinegar or eaten raw, heals the spleen. Damegeron <note>an ancient author on the magical properties of stones and plants</note> is the authority for the claim that if three small slices of **black ivy** are tied in a clean linen cloth and hung as an amulet with a thread around the neck of those suffering from spleen disease, it will free the wearers from this defect within three days. **Lonchitis** <note>likely the Holly Fern, *Polystichum lonchitis*</note> produces flowers like little hoods that thrust out a small tongue; indeed, in these tiny gaping parts, a certain whiteness protruding from the inner lip represents the appearance of a tongue, almost showing the likeness of a spleen. The boiled root of the lonchitis, before it sends out its seed, heals the spleen; the same is applied as a poultice in water. The **Lupine** <note>*Lupinus*</note> demonstrates the spleen by its own image; its decoction is beneficial for those with spleen issues. **Birthwort** <note>original: "aristolochia"</note> imitates a swollen spleen, and for that reason, it is effective for swollen spleens when drunk with water. **Sowbread** <note>original: "Cyclaminus"</note> acts in the same way. 

Let us pass to animals. Not all animals have a distinct spleen; in some it is large and oblong, in others very small and of various colors; in some it is placed next to the liver, in others under the stomach. In oxen, the spleen is larger in proportion to their size; in all other cloven-hoofed horned animals it is round, according to Aristotle. They eat **ox spleen** in honey and apply it topically for spleen pain. To heal the spleen, Pliny says one should buy a **calf's spleen** as if it were a prescribed remedy, without hesitating over the price (since this also pertains to the religious ritual). It should be split lengthwise and attached to the patient's tunic on both sides; the wearer then lets it fall down to their feet, after which it is collected and dried in the shade. It is said that as this happens, the spleen of the sick person's ailment subsides, and they are freed from the disease. 

The Egyptian priests expressed a man afflicted with a spleen disorder through the **hieroglyph of a dog**, for the dog has a very slender spleen; but if death or rabies should seize it, it comes from the spleen, so that whoever dissects a dog suffering from that disease experiences its force by contagion. If a **dog's spleen** is removed while it is alive and taken in food, it relieves spleen pains; some tie a fresh one over the area, according to Pliny. Thus, animals that seem to lack a spleen provide for man, so that his own spleen may be restored. There is a region of Asia called Scepsis, in which Pliny reports the cattle have very small spleens, and from there come remedies for the spleen. A fresh spleen of a farm animal is stretched over the spleen of the sufferer while the healer says they are making a remedy for the spleen, and the patient will be freed. In the **turbot** <note>original: "Rhombo aculeato"</note>, the spleen lies hidden among the coils of the intestines; applied to the spleen and then returned to the sea, it heals, according to Pliny. The **electric ray** <note>original: "Torpedini"</note> has a small spleen; applied, it heals the spleen. The **water turtle** has a small spleen; taken in food, it removes spleen ailments. The **magpie** <note>original: "Pica"</note> lacks a spleen; it is effective for spleen issues. 

We shall not omit the **cowpea** or **bean** <note>original: "dolichi, siue lobi, & lobia, siue phasioli"</note>—not the common ones, but the reddish ones from the garden climbing-ivy, which grow so high in gardens that their branches suffice for topiary work. Their pods contain seeds similar to **small kidneys**. Paul <note>likely Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note>, in a certain composition titled "of the cicadas" <note>original: "diatettigon"</note>, requires these beans for defects of the kidneys.

### hollow passages of the body. Chapter L.

# BOOK THREE

...noted reed <note>original: "commentariam harundinem"</note> differs from others for the sake of proper nutrition: it is fuller and fleshier, which he said arises from an abundance of water. And elsewhere: he said that wheat grows with a stuffed stalk due to calloused nourishment; we have seen this in Apulia, and in the Laborini fields of our Campania, where stalks grow thick because of the dense soil. In our own bodies, the weaker parts receive and then expel fluids that have been pushed out from the stronger parts; for this reason, they are like small channels <note>original: "cuniculi"</note>. We furthermore conjecture that the hollow and empty stalks in plants were made by Nature to expel gases <note>original: "flatus"</note> conceived within the body of the plant, just as they are in our own bodies. 

But let us turn to examples, and speak first of the windpipe <note>original: "trachea"</note>. **Cassia** <note>specifically *Cassia fistula*, the purging cassia</note> is loosening and purgative; it bears a long pod, which is divided inside into transverse, membrane-like cells, just like the "rough artery" <note>original: "aspera arteria," a historical term for the trachea</note> of our body—which others call the throat or the breathing pipe. It is composed of cartilaginous rings, made in the very image of the Cassia pod. By the experience of the Arabs, it is known to be effective for the chest and throat. **Wheat** <note>original: "Triticum"</note> has a reed-like stalk with membrane-like circles, just like a reed; according to Dioscorides, it is given for a roughened windpipe, and its flour is used for bloody excretions. **Barley** <note>original: "Hordeum"</note> is for the roughness and ulceration of the throat. **Mallow** <note>original: "Malua"</note> grows with a hollow stem: a decoction of its roots and leaves used as a gargle soothes a roughened throat, and when warmed and eaten as food, it removes hoarseness. The **Leek** <note>original: "Porrum"</note> produces a hollow stem: according to Pliny, it brings brilliance to the voice. The Emperor **Nero** gave authority to the cut leek for the sake of his voice, eating them with oil on fixed days of every month, eating nothing else, not even bread. **Garlic** <note>original: "Allium"</note> clarifies the voice in the same way, according to Dioscorides and Pliny. **Bugloss** <note>original: "Lingua bouis," literally "ox-tongue"</note> also has a hollow stem: Avicenna said it is effective for a roughened throat. These same plants also cure coughs and shortness of breath. **Sweet flag** <note>original: "Calamus odoratus"</note> does not differ in form from others of its kind: it cures a cough when the juice is sipped through a reed. The fourth type of **Cinnamon** is hollow <note>original: "fistulosum"</note> and is effective against coughs. **Alexanders** <note>original: "Smyrnium"</note> mitigates orthopnea <note>a condition where one can only breathe comfortably while standing or sitting up</note>. **Hawkweed** <note>original: "Hieracium"</note> mixed with hyssop is effective for a cough, according to Pliny. **Horsetail** <note>original: "Equisetum"</note> is for orthopnea and cough. **Borage** <note>original: "Borago"</note> for the same, according to Avicenna; **Mallow** according to Pliny. **Onion** <note>original: "Cæpa"</note> for those coughing, gasping, or asthmatic; **White thorn** <note>original: "spina alba"</note> for those who cough up blood; **Garlic**, **Oats**, and **Valerian** <note>original: "phu"</note> for those coughing and gasping. So too do **Beans**, **Cucumbers**, **Melons**, and **Sow thistle** <note>original: "sonchus"</note>. **Barley**, **Wheat**, **Beans**, **Onions**, **Garlic**, **Wild leek** <note>original: "scorodropasum"</note>, and **Oats** stir up gases. For provoking urine, the following are effective: **White thorn**, **Barley**, **Onion**, **Leek**, **Garlic**, **Wild leek**, **Valerian**, **Hawkweed**, **Alexanders**, **Horsetail**, **Gentian**, **Pumpkin** <note>original: "pepo"</note>, **Cassia**, **Cinnamon**, **Sweet flag**, **Cucumber**, **Lupine**, **Millet**, and **Reeds**.

There are also the fruits or roots of plants that resemble a woman's womb <note>original: "vterum"</note>, which are effective for childbirth. **Birthwort** <note>original: "Aristolochia"</note> truly imitates the form of the female womb, and it best assists women in labor; they gave it this name because it is *ariste locheusas* <note>Greek: αριστη λοχευουσας</note>, that is, "exceptionally health-giving for women in childbirth," as it expels delayed menses, the adhering placenta <note>original: "fecundas"</note>, and all the remnants of birth. **Cyclamen** <note>original: "Cyclaminus"</note> also expresses the likeness of the womb: if a pregnant woman steps over its root, a miscarriage occurs; if worn as an amulet, it accelerates birth. We have spoken of plant roots resembling the womb; next, it will be appropriate to suggest some things concerning the tunics and coverings that envelop the fetus—which emerge together during birth and follow it—which the Latins call the *fecundas* or *secundinas* <note>the placenta or afterbirth</note>. There are many membranes that surround and envelop the fetus on the outside. In no different a way, one can observe in the fruits of plants certain membranes that envelop the fruit in many coverings: first with a calloused or membrane-like rind, and then with a thin and compact skin. In the membranes embracing the human fetus, certain soft bits of flesh are attached and surround it, so that, like a cushion, they may softly cherish and receive it in the womb, and through the umbilical cord...

### PHYTOGNOMONICA

...as they provide nourishment to the growing offspring <note>original: "foetui"</note>. In fruits, besides this protective framework, multiple small veins and unerring ducts extend the juice so that they can grow through the navel <note>original: "umbilicum"; in plants, the hilum or the point where the seed attaches to the fruit</note>, which, in fruits like apples, hangs in the middle and adheres to the tree. They lie upon their own cushioned beds <note>original: "pulvinatis toris"</note>; so diligently has Nature striven to nestle seeds softly. And just as when the time of birth approaches, the membranes surrounding the fetus are broken and the child comes forth into the light, in no different way, when the time of ripening arrives, the seeds withdraw and fall from the tree—as if from a mother’s womb—once the surrounding husks and chambers have burst open. 

There is also something similar in flowers, as if in budding offspring, when they do not yet gape open with their bundles of petals folded together, but certain little heads, slightly tapered to a point, first spring forth from the stalk. As these gradually swell, the pregnant envelopes of the flowers crack open, as they unfold in roses. From this we easily conclude that those envelopes and chambers—which resemble the form of capsules or money-pouches and have claimed the name "wombs" <note>original: "vulgae," a variant of *vulvae*</note> for themselves—serve to facilitate the mother's labor and the bringing forth of the afterbirth <note>original: "secundinas"</note>, since they themselves cherish the seeds in the lap of the embracing mother in such a manner.
