### BOOK THREE

The **Walnut** <note>original: "Iuglans"</note> provides the greatest example of this thing: it is first hidden in a thick, grassy husk, then in a joined box of shells, and soon after in a thin skin. The kernels inside are arranged into four parts, with a woody membrane coming between them; for this reason, **Pliny** says the nut is protected by a double covering—first by a cushioned cup, then by a woody shell. This mirrors the many ways a fetus is protected in its parent—that is, in the small sac and the womb. This is likely the reason why walnuts were sacred at weddings, because the birth is protected in so many ways; it is more than just the fact that they make a dancing sound or a noise when they fall or are stepped on by shouting young girls. They excel in many various ways for the ailments of the womb and for childbirth.

The **Indian nut** <note>the Coconut</note> is also covered by a massive bulk of layers: the outer husk is fleshy, while the inner part is composed of a hairy material; a thin skin clothes the exterior, which, when rubbed, breaks apart into fine threads. Beneath this is a spacious, hard, and woody orb; inside is a sweet, white, and fleshy kernel. The **Pine** produces woody cones composed of many scales, in which they cover the kernels—each in its own little chamber—clothed in a rusty-colored skin. Fertile pine cones, when used in <term>fumigation</term> <note>medical treatment using smoke or medicinal vapors</note>, help expel the fetus.

In the **Arum** <note>Cuckoo-pint</note>, by the skillful craftsmanship of wise Nature, the offspring is shown protected by a multiple membrane. It first brings forth an envelope about a palm’s length, which a small sheath, tapered into a cone, embraces like a pestle and cherishes in its own fold. So diligent is Nature in preserving the seeds of things. But when, pregnant with fruit, it cracks open into a gap, the solid face of the pestle emerges, glowing with a dilute purple, and with the winding passage fully open, the saffron-colored seeds are seen. These are woven in the manner of a crown and encircle its lowest part. This plant extracts the offspring of all animals when smeared around the "door of nature" <note>the birth canal</note>; two drams of the seeds or the root in two cups of wine are sufficient to draw out the **afterbirth** <note>original: "secundas"</note> if the mother is not cleansed after delivery.

Regarding the **Dragon Arum** <note>original: "Dracunculus"</note>, a certain sheath—green on the outside—springs forth from the top of the leaf-stalk. It is nearly a cubit in length, gradually tapering to a point, like an envelope for a birth about to erupt. When it gapes open, it reveals a purple horn pointed at the tip. Distended by the growth of the seeds, it bursts into a crack; finally, as it withers, it turns yellow, dries up, and perishes, leaving behind the horn whose lower part is encircled by the clustered fruit. It is said to have such power that its smell causes pregnant women to miscarry and draws out the birth; physicians say that the same things that induce miscarriage also draw out the afterbirth.

**Garlic** is veiled by very many membranes; inside, it is joined by several kernels <note>cloves</note> which, as if joined by a certain treaty, cling together in a crowd. They are surrounded by very thin membranes, with a larger sac surrounding them all at once. When the root has grown into kernels, the separation of the "ears" soon occurs, and breaking through the skins, each one swells again into its own little bulb. Its boiled "hair" <note>the stems or roots</note> calls forth the monthly flow and the afterbirth when applied to women's ailments; it is also useful when used as a <term>fumigation</term>.

The seeds of **Birthwort** <note>original: "aristolochia"</note> also lie hidden in their own bulging flasks as if in little boxes, not unlike infants in the mother’s womb. When applied as a <term>pessary</term> <note>a medicinal plug inserted into the vagina</note>, they draw out a fetus that has already tried to break forth in vain. It restores the torn membranes of the fetus and the mother—who is nearly exhausted by the dire tortures of labor—to full health, which is how it earned its name <note>derived from the Greek *aristos* (best) and *locheia* (childbirth)</note>.

But let us see whether Nature shows us anything outside the ordinary in animals specifically. **Deer**, immediately after birth, eat the afterbirth; it is impossible to catch it, for they seize it before it can even fall to the ground. Medicinal power is believed to reside in it; according to **Aristotle**, if a stag’s horn is carried by the patient, it is a help, according to **Simeon Sethi**. When a **mare** has given birth, she immediately devours the afterbirth; her fat, when used in a fumigation, expels a dead fetus and the afterbirth, according to **Sextus**, though **Pliny** says it is the hoof. We have seen **dogs** and **cats** devour the afterbirth after delivery; Pliny says a membrane from the afterbirth of dogs calls forth the birth, provided it has not touched the ground. The smoke of feline dung and the gall of a cat extract a dead fetus from the womb, according to **Rhazes**. Similarly, the membrane of **goats** in which the offspring was produced, if aged and given in wine to drink, drives out the afterbirth, according to Pliny.

There is also the stone called the **Eagle-stone** <note>original: "ætites"</note>, which carries another rattling stone inside its belly—which has been shown to us only by the greatest kindness of God. For just as it has another small stone in its "womb," it causes women to retain the fetus in the womb. For this reason, it is tied to a woman’s left arm until the hour of birth arrives; when that time comes, it must be untied from the arm and placed on the left hip, so that she may give birth immediately and without labor or danger, once she has

# BLADDER-LIKE PLANTS, AND ANIMALS ENDOWED WITH LARGE BLADDERS, ARE BENEFICIAL TO THE BLADDER.

We shall show that **PLANTS** which produce little bladders <note>original: "vesiculas"</note> benefit the human bladder, provided by the bountiful luxury of God. ### BOOK THE THIRD.

V 2 IO. BAPTI

The **Winter Cherry** <note>original: *Solanus haliacacabus*; likely *Physalis alkekengi*</note>, that is, the "bladder-bearer," has vesicles similar to human ones, which contain a berry enclosed within. The use of this plant is most celebrated for provoking urine and treating stones <note>original: *calculos*</note>; it also heals the burning inflammations of the bladder. **Bladder Senna** <note>original: *Colutea*</note> is described by Theophrastus <note>an ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> as being peculiar to the island of Lipara. It is a tree of distinguished size, bearing fruit in a pod the size of a lentil, which fattens sheep in a marvelous way. It grows from seed, and especially in sheep dung. The time for sowing is when the star Arcturus sets; it is committed to the soil after being pre-soaked, once it has already begun to germinate in water. It puts forth a leaf not unlike **fenugreek** <note>original: *foenugraeco*</note>. The tree first shoots up with a single stem, and by its third year, it is suitable for being cut into staffs and walking sticks. If someone trims it back too much, it soon dies, since it does not sprout from the sides at all; it then spreads into branches, and by its fourth year, it becomes a full tree. In our regions, a shrub grows with slender branches and the leaf of fenugreek, raising itself into a tree in four years. It has a membrane-like bladder, translucent and very swollen, turgid as if distended by some spirit; children playfully make it burst with a loud crack by squeezing it with their fingers. Inside is a dark, hard seed, the size of a lentil and tasting like a pea. It grows from seed, and especially from sheep dung. The Mauritanians <note>North Africans/Arabs</note> call it **Senna** <note>original: *fene*</note> in their native tongue, and they distinguish two kinds: the wild and the garden variety. Shepherds gather the pods knocked down by the force of the winds, as they are very useful for fattening sheep. **Actuarius** <note>Joannes Actuarius, a 13th-century Byzantine physician</note> said that a drachm <note>a small unit of weight</note> of the powder clears obstructions of the intestines, so that it easily clears the bladder. There are also other bladder-like plants, such as the **Creeping Bladder-weed** <note>original: *repens*</note> and the **Bladder-nut** <note>original: *staphylodendros*</note>. If we were to reveal their powers for driving out stones and other ailments of the bladder, "little scholars" <note>original: *scioli*; a dismissive term for those with superficial knowledge</note> would think they were fabricated and imagined by us rather than true, since they are unknown to the experiments of the older Physicians.

# GIAMBATTISTA DELLA PORTA OF NAPLES
## PHYTOGNOMONICS
### BOOK FOUR.

->P R E F A C E.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial P featuring floral scrollwork.</image-desc>
We have already explained at length the similarities of plant parts that resembled human limbs. It follows now that we should recognize the similarities of those same parts and their behaviors <note>original: *actionū*; referring to the "actions" or functions of the plant, such as how it grows or reacts</note> that imitate the parts and behaviors of animals. By doing so, we may investigate their shared powers; for by comparing one to the other, they mutually reveal their hidden properties. Once these are understood beforehand, the introduction to this present treatise will be easier to grasp. Though these matters are more difficult to master, they are also more useful and certain for the interpreters of Nature to examine closely. We must remember what we stated regarding human Physiognomy <note>The practice of judging a person's character or health from their physical appearance, especially by comparing them to animals; Della Porta was a famous authority on this subject.</note>: that the most excellent signs for judging a subject are those gathered from the parts and actions of animals. We advise that one must insist upon these and devote vigorous effort to them. For the parts or actions of plants that emulate those of animals suggest to us that the plants retain the same powers for which those animals are notable. From an infinite number of possibilities, we shall propose a few examples (for who would dare to promise them all?) to satisfy the eager expectations of recent students. However, lest anyone, through carping criticism, find fault with us by claiming these plant similarities were invented by us or forced to fit the subject matter, we have prioritized only those plant similarities which—since proper names <note>original: *appellationes*</note> were lacking—

<summary>In this preface to Book Four, Della Porta introduces the "doctrine of signatures" as it applies to the animal kingdom, arguing that plants resembling animals possess the same medicinal or physical properties as those animals. He positions this study as a more difficult but highly reliable branch of natural philosophy, building upon his previous work on human physiognomy.</summary>

...names, by the common consensus and opinions of various peoples and nations, have borrowed their names from their resemblance to animals. Because of this, any skilled judge will admit, upon an impartial reflection, that nothing has been fabricated by me, nor sought out by force; for this truth knows no disguises, and learning depends solely on the kindness of God. But we shall speak first of the parts of plants that indicate the parts of animals, then their actions; and among the parts of animals, we will first discuss those that suggest the whole animal, and then those that suggest specific parts.

### PLANT PARTS REPRESENTING A WHOLE SCORPION,
### and their effectiveness against its bite. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'A' depicting a landscape with buildings and trees.</image-desc>

We shall begin, therefore, with plants whose flowers, fruits, roots, or other parts represent a whole animal. First, we will begin with scorpions and serpents—animals familiar to us, which live almost alongside us or are encountered everywhere, and are especially deadly and destructive. In these plants, Nature took delight in depicting their image, not in a haphazard way, but with such an exquisite likeness that only a blind man could be deceived by them. By the greatest kindness of God, it was provided that by skillfully mimicking the shape, He might advise men that these plants possess the same powers <note>This refers to the "Doctrine of Signatures," the historical belief that plants that look like a body part or a venomous animal can cure ailments associated with them.</note>, and that they possess not weak, but vigorous and medicinal strengths against the strikes of those animals. Otherwise, people could not have known this through the usual dogma of Physicians <note>original: *dogmate Medicorum*; likely referring to the traditional Galenic system of balancing humors, which Della Porta felt was less intuitive than observing nature's "signs."</note> or any other human method. If anyone were to believe that these things could be devised by man, he would be showing ingratitude for the gifts of the Gods, as Pliny says. 

But let us bring forward some examples. First, let us hear from the great Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany" (c. 371–287 BC).</note>. He says: "There are some plants which are observed to have a peculiar form, such as the root called the 'scorpion,' which represents the appearance of a scorpion and is effective against its sting." Here it is seen that he does not take issue with our method—namely, hunting for medicinal powers based on similarity. Some have called it *thelyphonon* <note>Greek for "female-slayer," a name for a type of aconite.</note>, and others the "scorpion," due to the similarity of the root, which is like a scorpion. By its touch, scorpions become numb, stunned, and turn pale, confessing themselves defeated; white hellebore aids them, as its touch releases them from this state. It is also said that if scorpions are touched by the genitals of female animals, they die on the same day; the drink of this plant likewise opposes the stings of scorpions. 

There is another species described by Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD), author of *De Materia Medica*.</note> that differs from the first; its roots turn black like the curls of a sea squill <note>A bulbous plant (*Drimia maritima*) found in coastal areas.</note>. They call this *cynoctonon* <note>Greek for "dog-killer."</note> and *lycoctonon* <note>Greek for "wolf-killer"; both names refer to Monkshood or Wolfsbane (*Aconitum*).</note>, and hunters use it to kill wolves, as a "wolf-slayer." Pliny says it is similar to a sea crayfish <note>original: *cammaro*; can refer to a lobster, crayfish, or shrimp.</note>. But I say it is similar to both the squill and the sea seahorse <note>original: *hippocampo*.</note>, the form of which will appear very similar to anyone looking at it. For just as the squill and the sea crayfish have tails composed of little plates, so this root seems to be divided by the separations of its joints, gradually tapering from the top. And certainly, its powers are related to the squill and the seahorse.

> *We have rendered three images of aconite from living plants: the first is Pliny’s panther-strangler, which he says is similar to a sea crayfish; the second is from Dioscorides; the third is from Theophrastus, which reflects a whole scorpion. Below, we have placed the images of the crayfish and the scorpion, so that the close resemblance which they mutually share may be contemplated.*

PHYTOGNOMONICA

The primary feature is their thick, segmented, and curved roots that visually resemble the body and tail of a scorpion or a shrimp. Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author who wrote "On the Nature of Animals."</note> alone wrote of the power of the seahorse <note>original: *hippocampus*</note>, whose belly, when boiled in wine and given as a drink, first affects the person with the sharpest hiccups, coughing, and a violent urge to vomit. If Nature overcomes this, the person falls into forgetfulness and madness; if not, they depart from life. Those who escape with their minds intact are seized by a supreme passion for water; they always crave it, whether it is dripping or flowing, both to wash in and to swim. Physicians have turned this to use, just as they do with wolfsbane <note>original: *aconitum*</note>, for the bite of a rabid dog; for the seahorse induces a love of water <term>hydrophilia: a pathological attraction to water</term>, while the rabid dog induces a fear of water <term>hydrophobia: a symptom of rabies where the victim fears swallowing liquids</term>, as we have said. Wolfsbane <note>original: *lycoctonon*</note> stirs the sexual appetite, as do squills and crayfish <note>original: *cammari*</note>. There is a species among the leopard's banes <note>original: *doronicos*</note>, or wolfsbane, whose root also demonstrates the likeness of a whole scorpion; this plant possesses those same primary faculties. The root is rounded and circular, and it gradually narrows at the bottom; it is jointed with transverse ridges, like little scales, skillfully expressing the small tail—or rather, the tiny corpse—of a scorpion; it represents the body of a scorpion in no small detail. The roots of the galingale <note>original: *cyperus*</note>, similar to oblong olives, black and round, are joined together with fibers or small stalks that look like the arms of a scorpion; these are used against the bites of scorpions.

Next follows the plague of serpents, which slaughters men with no less sharp and poisonous a strike. Nature has simulated their images in the roots of plants, so that everyone may be warned against his own misfortune. These will be the examples: nowhere is the viper <note>original: <unclear>ἔχις</unclear> (echis)</note> serpent,

# BOOK FOUR.

...than it prepares its hiding places among the roots of oaks or beeches. This was noted by Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note>, because it makes its bed in the lowermost turf of the oak. The roots of the oak are white, bent, and twisted, tapering gradually from top to bottom so that they mimic the body of a crawling snake <note>original: *drini*</note>. The oak is both the origin and the remedy; just as the evil proceeds from it, so the remedy emanates from the same place. The fruit of every kind of acorn-bearing tree, as well as the crushed roots applied to the skin, are helpful to a part of the body that has been struck, according to Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek botanist and physician, author of *De Materia Medica*</note>. In the history of herbalists, the plant *britannica*—also commonly called *serpentaria* <note>Snake-weed</note> and *colubrina* <note>Adder-wort</note> by the Germans—shows the shape of a lying and coiled snake because of its contorted, reflected, and intertwined roots. It is a matter of common knowledge and much recommendation among modern scholars for the bites of vipers and serpents. Similarly, "Good King Henry" <note>original: *bonus henricus*</note> is called *colubrina* by some, because its root twists like a coiled snake; its power against snake bites has been proven. There is also the *dracunculus* <note>Dragon Arum</note> mentioned by Pliny <note>Roman naturalist and author of *Natural History*</note>, whose root is shaped in the manner of a coiled dragon, which gives it its name; snakes flee from those who simply carry it.

A small herb, which some call *holostium* or wild buck's-horn plantain <note>original: *coronopum*</note>, consists of thinner roots twisted into the form of a snake; it is wonderfully effective against the bites of serpents, and because of its effect and shape, it is commonly called *serpentina*. There is also an herb commonly called *scorzonera* <note>Viper's Grass</note>, because it is effective against the bite of a certain serpent called the *scorzone* <note>An Italian name for a dark-colored viper</note>, and it is shaped in the form of that same snake. The root is a foot and a half long, thick at the top and gradually tapering to a sharp point, dark in color like the snake itself. No antidote can counter the venom of that snake as well as the juice of this root; hands smeared with it can handle the serpent without harm, and those who have consumed it beforehand are struck by the serpent in vain. Africa is the birthplace of both the serpent and the herb, where it grows spontaneously and perennially, though it lives if sown here. In the West Indies, there is another herb which has a root shaped like a coiled snake; its power against snake venoms is wonderful, as discovered by more recent explorers.

There are also other plants which, by their roots and fibers, seem to resemble worms, from which we judge them to be effective against moths and worms <term>tineas & vermes: usually referring to intestinal parasites like tapeworms</term>. The "Lesser Gentian" <note>original: *Gentiana minor*</note> consists of numerous, whitish, round roots like worms; when crushed and applied to the belly as a plaster, they undoubtedly kill any worms that may be in the intestine. The same is said of common dittany. The fern has wide, far-reaching roots; its juice drives out broad "moths" <note>intestinal worms</note>, as do the roots of costus and chamaleon. There are also certain elongated, panicle-like catkins <note>original: *nucamenta*</note> which hang in scales from the branches, with which pregnant trees swell, eager to bring forth buds; these look like a very long worm, indicating that Nature intended them to be effective against worms, moths, and serpents.

**Examples:** They say the hazel <note>original: *corylum*</note> does not flower, but instead certain peculiar catkins <note>original: *iulos*</note> break out; indeed, when the fruit has already fallen, a callus emerges in the manner of a cluster of grapes, the size of a fat little worm, with a unique stalk which they call a catkin. it opens at the beginning of spring and falls away when the leaves leap forth. Simple country folk have observed that snakes become sluggish if they are struck with a hazel branch or a small fork, and eventually die. The walnut tree <note>original: *nux iuglans*</note> at the beginning of spring, as if with a certain eager conception of leaves, protrudes a very long panicle; it opens up yellow as soon as it begins to produce foliage, and then nodding and falling, it drops away. Nuts consumed beforehand blunt poisons, and he who eats many of them more easily drives out the broad "moths" of the belly. From the chestnut tree (or "Euboic nut"), catkins also hang down; and even if some call them nuts, I believe they are more suited to the acorn family and retain the powers of their tree’s genus. If ground with honey, they help with the poisonous bites of rabid dogs. Some deny that the pine and spruce flower, but say that in place of a flower there are those catkins which the Greeks call *cittaros*. This wood is a very strong defense against moths, and the pitch is used specifically for the bites of the horned viper <note>original: *cerastae*</note>, and for serpents when smeared on with salt, according to Dioscorides.

### FLOWERS THAT DISPLAY FLIES AND BUTTERFLIES,
->are effective for fertility. Chapter III.<-

Very often, in the flowers of certain plants, one encounters the appearance of drones, bees, flies, and butterflies, imitated so closely <note>original: *ementitos*</note> that Nature seems to have played with no small amount of whimsy in painting them. For animals of this kind are as persistent as they are of the most fertile offspring; therefore, where the evidence of their powers and their appearance agree, we judge these plants to be effective for fertility and possessed of extraordinary strength. 

As examples, we shall bring forward the flowers of the dog-orchid <note>original: *cynosorchis*; a type of orchid whose name literally means "dog-testicle" in Greek, further linking it to fertility</note>, in which there hang down certain parts that look like four-legged animals with their legs stretched and spread wide—a feature which, as we have said, is effective for nothing if not fertility. In the flowers of another species, bees are seen with a blackish, white, and purple color, emulating a hornet <note>original: *asilonem*</note> or a drone.

For this reason, they gave **orchids**—which invite men to fertility and lust—the name of **Serapis**, the Alexandrian God, whose temple was once celebrated with songs, dances, and revelry according to Strabo <note>a Greek geographer and historian</note>. ### PLANT PARTS THAT RESEMBLE VARIOUS ANIMALS
### are effective for the same things as the animals themselves. Chapter IV.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'S' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, within an architectural or landscape frame.</image-desc> We also present certain parts of plants that demonstrate the form of whole animals, and so let us come to examples. From Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher often called the "father of botany"</note> we have this: there is no lack of plants seen with a peculiar shape, such as the hairy root of the **polypody fern**, which is full of hollow suckers like the tentacles of a "polyp" <note>original: *polyporum cirri*; here referring to an octopus or squid</note> when someone touches it; they claim the "polyp" <note>a medical growth such as a nasal polyp</note> is born there, and it is suitable for purging the lower parts. With these words, Theophrastus seems to teach <term>Phytognomonics</term> <note>the study of a plant's physical appearance to reveal its medicinal purpose</note>; but as for what those last words mean, I believe there is no one who would dare to claim they know, though I suspect it is an excellent remedy for curing the disease known as "the polyp." For we have many times seen women achieve their desire for children who were beset by the disease called the polyp in the lower seat <note>the rectum or anus</note> by using a decoction of the "polyp" fern, a miraculous remedy. And we have seen in Pliny <note>the famous Roman author of *Natural History*</note> that the dried powder, when put in the nostrils, consumes the polyp disease, speaking of this kind of polypody. Diphilus says in Athenaeus <note>a Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note> that the "polyp" fern also draws out the bowels. If the "polyp" animal is eaten in abundance when boiled, it moistens the belly; and it has often moved my bowels when I ate it.

Whatever is packed with a numerous mass of prickles is called an **echinus** <note>the Greek word for both a hedgehog and a sea urchin</note>, so named because its rounded line of spines mimics the sea hedgehog. The rampart of the **chestnut** is armed with a prickly husk; the head of the **teasel** <note>original: *dipsaci*</note> is said to be prickly; the tops of **thistles** are jagged like a murex shell; and many kinds of herbs threaten with cruel thorns. Chestnuts powerfully stop flows of the belly and stomach, benefit those spitting blood, suppress the menses, and are applied to the bites of rabid dogs. Avicenna <note>a Persian polymath and influential physician</note> says the flesh of the hedgehog animal is useful for flows of the internal organs, and Albertus <note>Albert the Great, a medieval scholar</note> says it is good for dysentery; likewise for hair loss, leprosy, foul ulcers, and similar things. The **porcupine** is armed with the same rampart of prickles; Aristotle considers its quills a kind of hair, and nothing can be seen more horrible or rigid than a porcupine. It is called by some a "mountain hedgehog," and the mountain kind is better than the domestic one and helps more; and Pliny says that whatever is said of hedgehogs will be all the more effective in the porcupine. Dioscorides <note>a Greek physician and author of the most influential herbal of the era</note> believes the land and sea hedgehogs have the same powers. But it would be a long task to recount the prickly heads of plants and the shared powers of the sea and land hedgehogs regarding poisonous bites, leprosy, and such things.

**Fleawort** <note>original: *Psyllium*</note> bears a little head at its top in which there is a black, shiny, and hard seed, truly mimicking a flea; because of this, a fitting name was adapted for it from the flea. There is a report in Dioscorides that if it is brought into the house while green, it does not allow fleas to be born there. The **Castor plant** <note>original: *Ricinus*</note> has its name from the likeness of a tick; for the seed, when stripped of its husks, represents the form of the tick animal so closely that if life were present, it would plainly seem to be a tick. It is a livid and foul animal that clings to dogs, oxen, goats, and other quadrupeds, and does not fall off until it is gorged with blood. The seed of this plant extinguishes "sacred fires" <note>original: *ignes sacros*; typically referring to erysipelas or similar skin infections</note>, which the tick animal also does, according to Pliny. The **nettle** is a biting herb and vexes those who touch it with its itchy stings; indeed, the **sea-nettle** <note>jellyfish</note> when touched also causes a burning sensation in the same way as the land nettle. Those who hunt it, unless they have first oiled their hands, are truly afflicted with pain; it excites an itch in the hands and private parts when touched, and its sharpness plucks at a dormant Venus <note>sexual desire</note>, especially those whose cap-like...

<header>PLANT PHYSIOGNOMY</header>

...it has the form, and as we have said, the terrestrial **nettle** <note>original: *vrtica*</note> also excites a sluggish Venus <note>a common metaphor for libido or sexual desire</note>. The **sea scolopendra** <note>a type of marine worm or centipede</note> is similar to the terrestrial one; according to Aristotle, these are animals that walk with numerous feet. Dioscorides stated that when boiled in oil and applied as an ointment, it pulls out hair. **Ivy** creeps along walls and trees with root-like "feet," numerous like those of a scolopendra; its "tears" <note>resin or sap</note> act as a hair remover <note>original: *pfilothrum*</note>. Among the names for **cyclamen** is *chelonium* <note>from the Greek *chelone*, meaning tortoise</note>, because the root itself resembles the shape of a tortoise. Hippocrates, in his book on the diseases of women, prescribed a medicinal suppository <note>original: *glandem*</note> which, among other things, contains the brain of a sea tortoise to open the womb and extract a dead fetus. Paul of Aegina and Aetius <note>famed medical writers of late antiquity</note> use its dried blood for viper bites. Its right "foot" placed over the right foot of a gout patient, and its left over the left, expels gout <note>original: *podagrā*</note>; Rhazes and Constantine say the same for the hands. Cyclamen, if infants have died in the womb, immediately brings them forth without distress to the mother when tied to her; it also cures the disease of gout, is drunk against all serpents, and has other uses which would be tedious to relate. **Rampion** <note>original: *rapunculus*</note>, or "little turnip," is so called because it displays a small turnip-like shape; it is the thickness and length of a thumb, and like a turnip, it is somewhat swollen in the middle. By Avicenna <note>a Persian polymath and physician</note> it is called the "locust" or "locust's foot," clearly because it matches the form of the locust insect with its appendages. **Locusts** help with difficulty in urination and serpent bites; the "little turnip" likewise helps with serpent strikes, according to Pliny, and with urinary difficulties by my own experiment. There is also a certain plant in the sea, hanging from a single stalk, whose extremities perfectly resemble the expressed flowers of a grape; for this reason, it is commonly called the **sea grape** <note>original: *vua marina*</note>. Its power, according to Pliny, is such that if rotted in wine, it brings a loathing of wine to those who drink it. Likewise, according to Democritus, the water dripping from pruned vines brings a loathing of wine. I hear that among the Tartars <note>Central Asian peoples</note> a plant is found whose fruit resembles a lamb in every way; it is covered with a thin skin, which the inhabitants use for head coverings. The internal pulp resembles the flesh of a crab <note>original: *cammari*</note>, and from a wound in it flows a sweet juice similar to blood. When the root is dug out of the ground, it stands upright as high as the navel; it is further added that as long as it is surrounded by herbs, it lives like a lamb in a lush pasture, but when they are pulled up, it gradually wastes away. To this is added the marvel that it is sought after and devoured by wolves—something I do not fear to say serves the same purpose as a real lamb <note>This refers to the "Vegetable Lamb of Tartary," a famous medieval legend of a plant-animal hybrid</note>.

->### PLANTS THAT DISPLAY THE SPOTTED SKINS OF SERPENTS<-
->### are effective against their bites. Chapter V.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' showing a figure seated in a landscape with trees and plants.</image-desc>
We have spoken of plants that represent whole animals; now we speak of those that represent parts, and first the outermost parts, or skins. For in some plants, they are spotted, hairy, smooth, scaly, and the like. We shall begin with the spotted ones, and those that reflect the image of a serpent visible in every part. By indulging in this conjecture, we see a specimen of Nature intended to teach us that the greatest harm from the foulest of serpents can be met with this great remedy. But let us go to the examples. **Great Serpentaria**, or **Dragon Arum** <note>original: *dracontium*</note>, rises with a straight stalk, smooth and polished, marked on its outer part with dark, dusky, reddish, and pale yellow spots, oblong and transverse like those of a viper. It so expresses the sloughed skin of a serpent that a sudden glance from a distance strikes terror into the viewer. Dioscorides claims that if the leaves are rubbed on the hands, or if the root is carried, one can never be struck by a viper. It also causes miscarriage, which a viper's presence is also said to do. There is also the **Sea Dragon**, which has a back of varying colors, from yellow to white, and has lethal spines in its gills and hurts when handled; its stings are healed by applying their own flesh to the wound.

> *In the present figure, to indicate the spotted skins of serpents, we have depicted Snake Garlic, Arum, Arisarum, and Dragon Arum alone; for it would have been unnecessary to draw all spotted herbs for the sake of these. Below, we have represented the sea dragon and the spotted snake so that they might appear as if alive to the hand.*

<meta>catchword: And Athe-</meta>

<summary>This page explores the "Doctrine of Signatures," arguing that plants resembling animals (like tortoises, locusts, or the mythical Vegetable Lamb) or animal parts (like spotted snake skins) possess medicinal properties related to those creatures. Specifically, spotted plants like the Dragon Arum are identified as powerful remedies for snake bites because their stalks mimic a viper's skin.</summary>

And Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the *Deipnosophistae*</note>, in his book on those whose bite is venomous, says that **moray eels** <note>original: *murænas*</note>, which are born from sea vipers, kill with their bite; they are smaller, round, and varied with spots. There is also another plant called the **little dragon** <note>original: *dracunculus*; likely the Dragon Arum (*Dracunculus vulgaris*)</note> with a smooth stalk the thickness of a staff, variegated with the multi-colored spots of a snake and interspersed with purple lines, so that it clearly seems to imitate the appearance and color of a serpent. This is a marvelous miracle of Nature, warning us that those who smear their hands with its root claim they cannot be struck by a viper; thirty of its seeds, if drunk in <term>posca</term> <note>A common Roman drink of vinegar and water</note>, induce abortion, for even the odor of the limp flowers after they have withered kills the still-tender offspring in the womb.

Furthermore, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of *Natural History*</note> confesses to having known another plant in Portugal <note>original: *Lusitania*</note>, recently discovered there in a host's field, of the same name; it had a stalk the thickness of a thumb, two feet in height, and was distinguished by the multi-colored spots of vipers. They say it emerges at the first <term>vernations</term> <note>original: *vernationes*; the annual shedding of a snake's skin</note> of serpents, remarkable for its gaping dragon's mouth and a hollow from which it sticks out stamens like a serpent’s tongue, with a blood-red head. It possesses the same virtues as the first kind; we have often observed it on the **Hill of Posillipo** <note>original: *Pausilypi*; a coastal hill in Naples</note>.

The **Arum** <note>original: *Aron*</note> also produces a purplish stalk, likewise distinguished by various snake-like spots; it possesses the powers of the *dracunculus*, spoiling a pregnancy by its mere presence. Pliny reports that **Ophiusa** <note>From the Greek *ophis*, meaning snake; a legendary herb mentioned by Pliny</note>, found on the island of Elephantine in Ethiopia, is leaden-colored and grim to look upon; when drunk, it causes terrors and threats of serpents to appear before the eyes, so that people commit suicide out of that fear—for this reason, the sacrilegious are forced to drink it. Among other kinds is the one called **snake-garlic** <note>original: *ophioscorodon*</note>, named for its stalk and leaves which are spotted in the manner of a serpent-plant; it so closely resembles and smells like bear's garlic <note>Wild garlic or *Allium ursinum*</note> that anyone who does not yet know it by sight may recognize it by this. Galen <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire</note> said it is more powerful than the cultivated variety: it drives away serpents with its smell and heals the bites of all beasts whether taken in drink, food, or as an ointment, and specifically for the **haemorrhois** <note>original: *hemorrhoid*; here referring to the *haemorrhois*, a serpent whose bite was believed to cause uncontrollable bleeding from all orifices</note>.

Following the Doctrine of Signatures, these physical traits indicate their power to repel serpents, treat venomous bites, or act as dangerous toxins and abortifacients.</summary>

There are also spots of vipers found in fruits; for in the seed of the **wild lupine** <note>original: *lupini syluestris*</note>, the dark and ash-colored spots, scattered like drops and appearing as if by chance, truly satisfy the visual description of serpents; it is effective as a remedy against the bite of the **asp** <note>A small, venomous snake of North Africa and Europe</note>.

### THAT SPOTTED PARTS OF PLANTS, WHICH REVEAL THE
### *spotted hides of animals, indicate their medicinal powers. Chapter VI.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' containing a landscape scene with a person walking towards a distant building.</image-desc>There are also other plants which, through the spots on their foliage and stalks, display the spotted hides of animals. These simultaneously indicate to us the kinship of their powers, signaling their internal properties through a silent picture, as we shall demonstrate with these examples. There is the leaf of the **spotted lady’s thumb** <note>original: *persicaria*; also known as Redshank</note>, marked with a smudge in the manner of a spot that recalls the image of a horned Moon—a detail that writers should not have omitted. The **panther** has a spotted hide, and **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist and author of *Natural History*</note> records that on its right shoulder is a spot similar to the Moon, waxing into circles and hollowing out its horns in the same fashion. Its fat, according to **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, medieval scholar and naturalist</note>, is effective against **impetigo** <term>impetigines: a contagious skin infection characterized by crusting sores</term>; similarly, **water pepper** <note>original: *hydro piper*</note>, a relative of the spotted lady’s thumb, clears away **bruises** <term>sugillata: dark spots under the skin caused by internal bleeding</term>. There are also some types of **orchids** <note>original: *orchidum*</note> with spotted leaves that resemble the hides of **lynxes**. **Virgil** <note>Roman poet, author of the *Aeneid*</note> writes:

> *Girt with a quiver, and with the spotted hide of a lynx.*

On the island of **Carpathos**, they say that the claws of lynxes, when burned along with their skin, are most effective; Pliny notes that the sprinkling of this ash inhibits the lusts of women. We have already stated elsewhere that another type of orchid suppresses **Venus** <note>original: *Venerem*; meaning sexual desire or libido</note>. **Dioscorides** <note>Ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> calls the **dragon arum** <note>original: *dracunculum*</note> herb "hawkweed" <term>hieracium: from the Greek *hierax*, meaning hawk</term> because of the spots that mark its stalk, representing the **hawk**, which is spotted in such a way upon its breast. The hawk is praised for ointments used for all ailments of the eyes, and the juice of the dragon arum, according to Dioscorides, is summoned for eye medicines. **Cyclamen** <note>original: *cyclaminus*</note> has variegated leaves, with white spots glowing both inside and above them; the **skink** <note>original: *scincus*; a type of lizard</note> has white, dark, and somewhat broad bands, or is decorated with white points, while its neck is dark and its head and tail are white. It is written that the skink is effective for matters of love, which **Theophrastus** <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note> also relates of the cyclamen, and both are effective for skin diseases. Types of **amaranth** <note>original: *bliti*</note> have multi-colored leaves, distinguished by green, yellow, and reddish hues, such that they truly imitate the feathers of a **parrot**. The parrot is as effective as the **goose**, which excels against poisons and especially against the **scorpion**; we have also mentioned it for those suffering from **jaundice** <term>ictericos: a yellowing of the skin and eyes</term>, a condition which amaranth also treats most excellently. The **common toad** <note>original: *rubeta*</note> is also of a pale, green, and saffron color; by a gift of nature, it stops the flow of blood, which amaranth also provides. There are also types of **wrasse** <note>original: *piscium turdorum*; literally "thrush-fish" due to their color</note>, distinguished by a variety of colors—as if Nature seemed to have played within them—with black, red, golden, and yellow spots. These fish are easy on the bowels and cleansing. They also compare them to the shell of a **turtle**, streaked with yellow and black; the turtle is effective for checking the flow of blood, all of which we have said regarding amaranth. For the **black chameleon** <note>original: *chamæleoni nigro*; likely *Atractylis gummifera*</note>, the leaves are distinguished by red; among the varieties of **magpies** <note>original: *picarum*</note>, there are many marked with red spots, which are effective for toothaches. One or another **meadow clover** <note>original: *pratense trifolium*</note>, with drop-like and crescent-shaped spots on the surface of its leaves, seems to imitate the spots of the **spotted lizard** <term>stellionis: a lizard marked with star-like spots, often a gecko</term>; for their backs are painted with circles in the manner of dark stars. **Ovid** writes in his fifth book:

> *The mouth drinks in the spots, etc. and it has a name suited to its color,*
> *its body starred with various drops.*

If the intestines, head, and feet are removed and it is eaten roasted, it is effective for **dysentery** and **hernias** <note>original: *hydrocœlicis*</note>, according to Pliny; we have said that clover is effective for women’s discharges. The **heron** <note>original: *ardea*</note> is called <term>asterias <note>original: ἀστερίας</note></term> or "star-like" because it is elegantly painted and distinguished with points like stars; there is also a **starry frog**, which is effective for eye ailments. **Arum** leaves are distinguished by spots and are effective for **cataracts** <term>albugines: white spots or films on the eye</term> and dimness of vision. **Birch** <note>original: *betulę*</note> bark is streaked with white spots, such that it seems to imitate the **starling** <note>original: *sturnum*</note>; both wipe away skin eruptions and facial spots.

<summary>Della Porta explores the "Doctrine of Signatures" regarding spotted patterns, linking plants like amaranth, orchids, and clovers to animals with similar markings, such as panthers, hawks, and lizards. He argues that these visual similarities reveal the plants' medicinal uses for skin conditions, eye ailments, and blood disorders.</summary>

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

## SCALY PLANTS, WHICH SHOW THE SCALES OF SERPENTS,
## provide remedies against their bites.

->Chapter VII.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' with floral or foliate ornamentation within a square frame.</image-desc>

There are also plants which, through their roots, fruits, stalks, and other scaly parts, display the scaly backs of serpents and are opposed to their poisons; they are also effective against the venomous strikes of scaly fish, for—as we have said—fish also possess power against their own stings. The **Cedar** <note>original: *Cedrus*</note> is a vast tree that produces cones packed together in a scaly fashion: cedar-resin <note>original: *cedria*</note> applied with salt assists with the bites of the **horned viper** <note>original: *cerastæ*</note> and is added to antidotes. The **Pine** <note>original: *Pinus*</note> produces woody cones formed of scales packed into a cone-like shape, and the bark of the young branches is clothed in the same series of scales: it opposes serpents, and specifically, according to **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note>, pitch with barley-meal is effective against the bite of the horned viper. The **Spruce** <note>original: *Picea*</note> is of the same genus, appearance, and virtue, and the same should be thought of the **larch**, **cypress**, and other similar trees. **Catkins** <note>original: *Iuli*</note>, which hang by a compact callus of scales from **hazelnuts**, **walnuts**, **chestnuts**, and similar trees, are effective for the same purposes. **Heather** <note>original: *Erice*</note> has a scaly leaf: the same author <note>Pliny</note> wrote that its leaf opposes serpents. **Tamarisk** <note>original: *Myrice*</note>, having the same leaf, helps with viper bites. Pliny said it works for the strikes of all serpents except for **asps**. **Eryngo** <note>original: *Eryngium*; Sea Holly</note> produces heads that are scaly like a murex shell: eryngo is famous for being born to combat serpents and all venomous things. Both types of **Chameleon plant** <note>original: *chamæleo*; likely the Carline thistle</note> produce a head composed of small scales overlapping each other like roof tiles: when drunk in wine, it resists the poisons of serpents. The numerous species of **Houseleek** <note>original: *Semperviui*</note> bear leaves arranged in a scaly pattern: they oppose the bites of **venomous spiders** <note>original: *phalangiorum*</note> and scorpions. **Scabious** <note>original: *Scabiosa*</note> produces heads covered in a compact order of scales: the herb itself, crushed and applied fresh, is excellent for the bites of venomous serpents. The **Cornflower** <note>original: *Cyanus*</note> produces flowers from a rough, scaly cup: it aids those struck by a scorpion or a venomous spider, and all venomous things. **Pot Marjoram** <note>original: *Origanum onitis*</note> produces a spike in which the seed is scaly: drunk with wine, it is suitable for those bitten by a serpent. In the same way, **Wheat** <note>original: *triticum*</note> produces its own spike: the husks <note>original: *furfures*</note> are powerful against the bites of vipers. The root of **Celtic Nard** <note>original: *Radix celtica nardi*</note> is scaly, or covered in tunic-like scales and arranged like a spike: according to **Dioscorides** <note>Greek physician and botanist</note>, it is effective for venomous strikes; the same is true for **garlic** and **lilies**. Fish that are scaly are effective for the wounds of serpents and venomous creatures, such as the **goby**, **tuna**, **mullet**, **smaris**, **coracinus**, and others.

## HAIRY PLANTS, WHICH SHOW THE HAIRY HIDES OF ANIMALS,
## possess their virtues.

->Chapter VIII.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' with floral or foliate ornamentation within a square frame.</image-desc>

Various kinds of hairs on the leaves of plants show the various coverings of animals, from which we can find an argument for investigating their virtues. An example for us will be the plant commonly called **Mouse-ear hawkweed** <note>original: *pilosella*</note>, which is clothed in a thicker and softer hair and seems to mimic the skin of the **hare**, which is very hairy and is the only animal to have the soles and tops of its feet shaggy: hence the name **shaggy-foot** <note>original: *dasypodis*; Greek for rabbit/hare</note>. According to Dioscorides, hare's blood benefits those with dysentery, abdominal flux, and menstrual discharge; and according to **Galen** <note>Prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note>, its spleen helps with tumors of the spleen. Mouse-ear hawkweed is effective for dysentery, abdominal fluxes, and tumors of the spleen. The leaves of **Mullein** <note>original: *Verbasci*</note> are clothed in a cottony down, a white and thick fuzz; they commonly call it the **bearded badger-plant** <note>original: *taxum barbatum*</note>, because it is likened to the **badger** <note>original: *taxo animali*</note>, whose back is covered with white, black, and hard hairs. Thus, the first two species described by Dioscorides, because they are clothed in rougher leaves that are not soft to the touch, recall the skin of the badger. We see from **Serenus** <note>Quintus Serenus Sammonicus, Roman medical author</note> that the badger is effective against the spitting of blood; its fat is mixed into arthritic compositions according to **Leonello** <note>likely Leonello Vittori, a Renaissance medical writer</note>. Mullein is prescribed for ruptures and fractures according to Dioscorides, and its decoction is used against diseases of the nerves and tremors. Among the names for Mullein is **wolf’s tail**, because of its hairs...

<summary>This page describes the 'Doctrine of Signatures' as applied to scaly and hairy plants. Porta argues that plants resembling serpent scales or animal fur act as remedies for ailments associated with those specific creatures.</summary>

...the soft down of hairs, which it imitates. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> records that the liver of a wolf heals a cough when taken with warm wine. Furthermore, if the belly of one suffering from **colic** <note>severe abdominal pain</note> is bound with its hide, and the sick person sits frequently upon its skin, **Rhases** <note>al-Razi, a Persian physician</note> and **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, a medieval scholar</note> write that it is of great benefit: a decoction of **mullein** <note>original: *verbascum*</note> also heals a cough, and its flowers, ground into powder, are given against **torment of the belly** <note>original: *tormina*; intestinal cramps</note> and **colic** <note>original: *colum*</note>. The leaves of the **campion** <note>original: *Lychnis*</note> are flaccid, thick, and woolly, like those of the **ethiopis** <note>an unidentified woolly plant mentioned by ancients</note>; they seem to express the hairs of mice: it is an undisputed fact for **Dioscorides**, **Galen**, and **Avicenna** that domestic mice, cut into pieces, are most usefully applied to the stings of scorpions; thus the campion assists those struck by a scorpion; indeed, by the mere application of this herb, scorpions become numb and are rendered entirely sluggish. Some call the **maidenhair fern** <note>original: *Adiantum*</note> not "Venus-hair" but "pig's hair" or "pig's tail," undoubtedly because its small stalks bristle like the bristles of a sow, as the ancient commentator on Avicenna notes: we have said that maidenhair fern is effective for thinning hair and **alopecia** <note>patchy hair loss</note>, which **pig fat** <note>original: *suilla axungia*</note> likewise achieves according to Pliny and **Aegineta** <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Greek physician</note>. The Magi call **dill** <note>original: *Anethum*</note> the "offspring of the baboon" <note>original: *cynocephali genituram*</note> or its hair, as is held among the known names of Dioscorides, because it has small leaves spread out like the hairs of a dog. **Aetius** fills the bite of a dog with dried dill, if it is hollow and narrow. A plant is recorded by Pliny called **wool-herb** <note>original: *lanaria*</note>: given to fasting sheep, it causes an abundance of milk, for it has fleeces like a sheep. The **bramble** <note>original: *Rubus*</note> has leaves and a skin that are spiny, and it is effective for defects of the eyes. The **ray** <note>a type of flatfish</note> has a spiny back, tail, snout, eyes, and finally, body: its gall is effective for scars and **suffusions** <note>cataracts or clouded vision</note> of the eyes. There are many plants that rise with curly leaves, like the feathers of the **ostrich** <note>original: *strutiocamelus*</note> and of doves. **Myrrh** has a curly leaf, according to **Theophrastus**: it is effective for eye defects, for it removes **white spots** <note>original: *albugines*</note> and darkness, according to Dioscorides; in the cut-open belly of an ostrich, small stones are found, and these indeed are healthful for the eyes, according to **Aelian**. **Eyebright** <note>original: *Euphragia*</note> likewise has curly leaves and is effective for clarity of vision. **Costus** <note>an aromatic root</note> is likewise applied for the **resolution of nerves** <note>paralysis</note>: the fat of the ostrich, according to Aelian, provides a healthful remedy for the nerves of men. Theophrastus describes a genus of **celery** <note>original: *Apij*</note> with curly leaves, especially the Macedonian variety, the decoction of which expels **calculi** <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>; its seed and root with honey are effective for clarity of the eyes; the inner lining of the ostrich's stomach dissolves stones, according to **Rabbi Moses** <note>Maimonides, the Jewish philosopher and physician</note>.

# PLANTS WITH WOODY FRUIT-COVERINGS indicate the
# woody and stony skins of animals. Chapter IX.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring a landscape scene with a building and leafy plants inside a square frame.</image-desc>

There are also among the fruits of plants those which are enclosed in stony or woody cones, showing the stony or hard skins and hides of animals, which are seen to be effective against the poisons of serpents: for the **crocodile** has a bark-like skin, covered with very hard scales in the manner of oysters, so firm that they strike back against blows driven by any engine with an unconquerable back; its parts are effective against serpents. Thus the **tortoise**, a shelled animal, is surrounded by a hard and rigid bark and is effective against poisons. **Oysters**, or those called **shell-skinned** <note>original: *ὀστρακόδερμα*</note>, all work against the venom of the **sea hare** <note>a toxic marine mollusk</note> and of all venomous things. All types of **nuts** are enclosed in wood. The **pine** covers its fruits with woody cones compacted with frequent nut-scales; thus the **wild pine**, the **spruce**, and the **horned-pine** <note>original: *cerastæ*</note> assist against bites. The **walnut**, protected by a woody fortification, also dulls poisons. In the same way, the **hazelnut** encloses its fruits in a woody shell: it is effective against scorpions and serpents by a well-known experiment. The **almond** protects its nuts with a very hard covering and is covered with a callus. In **pistachios**, under the skin is a bony fruit; Dioscorides said they have the same effects as pine fruits. The fruits of the **cedar-fir** <note>original: *Cedrelates*</note>, or its woody cones, oppose the bites of the **horned viper** <note>original: *cerastæ*</note> and the poison of the sea hare; likewise the woody balls of the **cypress** are beneficial against venomous things, and we can say the same of **chestnuts**, **acorns**, and others. The **pomegranate** <note>original: *Punici malum*</note> is smooth and covered by a membrane, called the **pomegranate-rind** <note>original: *malicorium*</note>; its bark gapes and is opened by the slightest injury even of the air. The **elephant** has no covering of bristles, but a smooth skin, criss-crossed or gaping, attracting flies by its scent and suddenly trapping them, killing them caught in its wrinkles; its fat is effective against the poisons of serpents, and the same fits for it.

Having previously discussed how plants with hairy textures relate to animals with fur or bristles, Giambattista della Porta now transitions to the "head," which he considers the most important part of the body. He argues that plants bearing seeds or flowers shaped like the heads of specific animals are divinely intended to treat the ailments associated with those animals or to share their biological properties.</meta>

# FRUITS AND FLOWERS THAT INDICATE THE HEADS OF ANIMALS. Chapter X.

WE HAVE SPOKEN of skins; now we shall begin with the head, the leader of all the limbs, by enumerating certain flowers and fruits that indicate the faces and heads of various animals. Examples: In the **viper’s bugloss** <note>original: *Echio*</note>, a purple flower blooms among the leaves, and within it is enclosed a seed similar to the small head of a **viper**, mimicking a slender mouth and the faint traces of eyes. **Dioscorides** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> instructs that the leaves be applied to wounds caused by serpents and also be chewed; he claims that those who have taken it beforehand will not suffer if bitten. Indeed, one may observe how the seed gradually narrows from the neck into a small beak, with the upper part being more swollen, so that certain small protrusions appear like the light of eyes. Anyone looking closely with their own eyes cannot help but praise the supreme providence of God for fashioning a herb in the form of a viper because it offers the most excellent aid against its bites. **Nicander** <note>A Greek poet and physician</note> reports that it was named *alcibiaca* because when **Alcibius** fell asleep near a field and was bitten by a viper in the outer groin, he squeezed the juice from this herb, chewed it, and placed the remainder on the wound; by this medicine, he escaped unharmed. **Numenius**, an author of no small authority, left it written that another kind of *echium* is found, called *ocymoides* <note>basil-like</note>, because it has leaves similar to **basil** <note>original: *ocymum*</note>; Nicander had written the same, and Dioscorides and **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> seem to agree, writing that they produce seeds whose small heads are similar to the heads of vipers. When drunk in wine, it has the power to heal the bites of vipers and other serpents. The **wild snapdragon** <note>original: *Syluestre antirrhinon*</note> produces small heads perforated at the top, as if the holes in the upper part of a **human skull** show the locations of the eyes; it seems to be mentioned by Dioscorides in his description of *phyteuma*, where he says: *Phyteuma* has a perforated fruit, and other features which perfectly match the wild snapdragon. Because it represents the figure of a human, he claims it is suitable for **love potions** <note>original: *philtra*</note>. Among the types of chickpeas, there is one called <gloss>krios</gloss> <note>original: κρίος; ram</note> by the Greeks and **arietinum** <note>ram-like</note> by the Latins, because it is similar to a **ram's head**, with a forehead-like shape and an angle somewhat mimicking a horn. It stimulates **Venus** <note>libido or sexual desire</note> and provides an abundance of seed; for this reason, stallion horses, at the time they are called by the females, are fattened with chickpeas so that, strengthened by this food, they are up to the task of Venus. **Rams**, as we have said, are extremely lustful, becoming wild through their libido and favoring the acts of Venus. Another kind of chickpea is called **columbine** <note>pigeon-like</note>, which is white, round, and smooth, resembling a **pigeon’s head**; it is also called "the herb of Venus," perhaps because it assists Venus like the other, and pigeons are most "salty" <note>original: *salatissimae*; a Latin pun implying lustfulness or being "spiced" for love</note>. **Fleawort** <note>original: *Psyllium*</note> is called *cynomia* and *cynocephalon* <note>dog-headed</note> after a **dog** in the lists of Dioscorides; from whom Pliny says: some call *psyllium* *cynoides*, others *cynomia*, with leaves not unlike a dog’s head. But I think there is an error in the text, for it is the flowers, not the leaves, that are similar to a dog's head. **Dog dung** taken as a drink is useful for those with **dropsy** <note>original: *hydropico*; swelling caused by fluid retention</note>, according to **Sextus**, for when smeared on the belly it draws out water; its gall eases **gout** <note>original: *podagras*</note> when smeared on the feet, according to Pliny. Fleawort in wine heals dropsy and cools gout, according to the same author. The **monkshood** plant <note>original: *Napellus*; also known as wolfsbane</note> shows purple flowers on a spike which, before they open, display the **skull of a dead man**. This is by the kindness of Nature, so that by this resemblance to a corpse, she might turn men away from eating or using that plant; for the power of its poison is so deadly and sharp that it can hardly be helped by any antidote. It brings death not only by eating but even by being handled with the hands until it takes hold. It is thought to be called <gloss>arktion</gloss> <note>original: ἄρκτιον; from the Greek word for bear</note> because the seed is round with shaggy, bristly, and prickly hairs, having the likeness of a **bear's head**, and thus it received a plausible name. Dioscorides wrote that **burns** and **chilblains** <note>original: *perniones*; sores caused by cold</note> are healed by it; **bear fat** is also good for burns and chilblains when alum is added, according to Pliny. Since many small plants produce the likeness of a beaked **crane's head**, they obtained the name **geranium** <note>from the Greek *geranos*, meaning crane</note>; for they produce flowers which, as they fall away, leave behind beaked points or needles that end in a straight line from a wider base. We have experienced that **dove's-foot** <note>original: *Pes columbinus*; Geranium molle</note>, a species of this plant, is effective for **griping of the bowels** <note>original: *intestinorum tormina*; intestinal cramps</note>. That which is seen with the leaf of a mallow, according to Pliny, for those recovering...

### HERBS THAT MIMIC THE HORNS OF ANIMALS, AND
->what they are useful for. Chapter XI.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring intricate floral scrollwork and geometric patterns.</image-desc>

After the head, we shall speak of horns and crests, for plants do not lack pods or small sheaths that are sometimes curved into the shape of horns; the same occurs in flowers and fruits. Indeed, horns are given to many aquatic, marine, and serpentine creatures in various ways, but those which are rightly understood as "horns" belong only to the genus of quadrupeds. Nowhere else has the playfulness of Nature sported more with animal horns. She has scattered them into branches, as with **stags**, and also made them simple, as with those called **spikes** <note>original: *subulonibus*, referring to deer with unbranched, awl-like antlers</note> according to the evidence; in others, she fashioned them into palms and sent out fingers from them, which is why they are called **broad-horns** <note>original: *platycerotas*, likely fallow deer</note>. She gave branched horns to **wild goats**, those coiled in a spiral to the **ram** family, and aggressive ones to **bulls**. She gave the **chamois** horns hooked toward the back, and the **fallow deer** horns hooked forward. In the **strepsiceros** <note>an antelope-like animal with twisted horns</note>, the horns are upright, twisted with a circuit of wrinkles, and sharpened to a smooth point. Others have single horns, even in the middle of the head or nose, like the **rhinoceros**. In some they are hooked; in others, they all narrow into a sharp point. To **snails**, she gave fleshy horns to feel the way ahead; to the **horned viper** <note>original: *cerastis*</note>, they are always in pairs, so they may be extended or retracted.

No less is the playfulness of Nature in the various kinds of pods for guarding and producing seeds, which are as stiff as horns, or twisted individually, or curved like sickles into little horns. For in some they are wide, in others twisted, long, and curved, as we shall see. Examples will follow: The **tree medick** <note>original: *Cytiso*</note> has twisted pods like the horn of a **goat**. **Columella** <note>A Roman writer on agriculture</note> writes that it provides the most milk for sheep; and if women are pressed by a lack of milk, it should be given to them to drink in wine, for the abundance of milk is thereby strengthened. Above all, it provides a remedy against diseases for livestock in every use. **Aristotle**, in his book *Problems*, said that goats and sheep abound most in milk in proportion to their bodies, and we have shown above that its cheese provides milk to those who eat it.

Another herb is called **goat-horn** <note>original: <term>tragokeros</term>, likely fenugreek</note> because it resembles them. It is effective both raw and cooked against serpents, and according to **Dioscorides** and others, **goat’s blood** performs the same service. **Lucerne** <note>original: *Medica trifolium*</note> has pods twisted in the manner of little horns; those who raise livestock use it as a fodder, and **Columella** says it is the most excellent thing for cattle for milk, cheese, and breeding. The **turpentine tree** <note>original: *Terebinthus*</note> bears certain hollow structures similar to a nut, like the elm, in which little insects like gnats are born according to **Theophrastus**; but what he calls hollows are actually little horns most similar to those of **goats**. We have said that the turpentine tree excites **Venus** <note>sexual desire</note>, which burns fiercely in the he-goat or she-goat. The **pistachio** tree, which is a domestic version of the turpentine tree, has the same effect. The **mastic tree** <note>original: *Lentiscus*</note> bears the same horns in the same way and has the same power. And **senna** <note>original: *sena*</note> has its moon-shaped pods like the horn of a goat. According to **Mesue** <note>An influential Arabic medical author</note>, senna purges **black bile** <note>one of the four humors, associated with melancholy</note> through the lower parts, cleanses the brain and internal organs, increases strength, delays old age, and brings cheerfulness to the mind. It strengthens the sharpness of the eyes and is effective for all melancholic diseases; it is also beneficial for **epilepsy**. **Goat’s milk** is given to those who are melancholic or suffer from the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note> according to **Pliny**, and it benefits those with poor night vision.

->THE FIGURES of the plants above refer to the horns of the animals below: the first<-
->of the buck's-horn plant to the stag; the second of fenugreek to the ox; the next<-
->of the arum to the unicorn; and the last of the tree medick to the goat. Each<-
->corresponds to the one across from it, so that the diligent observer may<-
->quickly compare and weigh them against one another.<-

**Purging Cassia** <note>original: *Cassia solutiua*, likely *Cassia fistula*</note> produces small black horns, twisted and somewhat wrinkled, so that they match the horns of goats quite well; it is administered to the sick with goat whey because of their similar properties, and it clears the kidneys of stones <note>original: *calculis*</note>. The **Carob** <note>original: *siliqua*</note> is a relative of the former and possesses a very similar power, as it bears black and sickle-shaped pods. **Bean-trefoil** <note>original: *Anagyris*</note> has pods twisted in a similar way: if a dead fetus is stuck, or if the afterbirth <note>original: *secundæ*</note> is delayed, they are tied to those having a difficult labor, so that they may be removed immediately after the birth; according to **Pliny**, this is something that fertile goats also achieve. **Honeysuckle** <note>original: *Hedysaron*</note> bears its seed in pods that are hooked like little horns; it is added to antidotes, and we have said the same regarding the goat. The common people call the herb *sferracauallo* <note>Horseshoe vetch, *Hippocrepis comosa*</note>; it also thrusts out horns in that same likeness and possesses the same powers. However, it expresses the likeness not of a common goat, but of a chamois <note>original: *rupicapræ*</note>, that is, a wild goat. The female **Melilot** <note>original: *Sertula campana*</note> has a hooked pod and is used primarily to heal the eyes; the gall of a wild goat is likewise effective against eye defects. **Wild Cumin** bears hooked little horns: its seed is effective against venomous beasts and those suffering from stones; goat dung is used for stones, and the dung of wild goats for venomous bites. **Broom** <note>original: *Genista*</note>, with its crescent-shaped pods, drives out stones; the gall of the wild goat also drives out stones. **Garden Asparagus** <note>original: *Smilax hortensis*, possibly a variety of cowpea or kidney bean</note> is effective for the urine; goat blood is used for the excretion of urine, such that it benefits those with dropsy <note>original: *hydropicis*, an old term for swelling or edema</note>. **Yellow Vetchling** <note>original: *Aphaca*</note> is effective against venomous bites. **Vetch** <note>original: *Vicia*</note> has the same pod and the same virtue. **Kidney beans** <note>original: *Phasioli*</note> stimulate the passions of Venus <note>original: *Venerem stimulant*, meaning they act as an aphrodisiac</note>; the **broad bean** and **pea** share the same small sheaths and powers. **Fenugreek** <note>original: *Fœnum græcum*</note> produces small pods that are long, round, curved, and pointed like the horns of oxen, in which the seed is enclosed; the Greeks call it "horned herb" <note>original: κερατῶδες - *keratodes*</note> or "ox-horn" <note>original: βούκερος - *boukeros*</note>; the Hebrews also call it "bull’s horn" because of its resemblance to the bovine; according to **Pliny**, the ash from the tips of a bull's horn curbs a cough; of fenugreek

<meta>This page continues the catalog of plants whose physical signatures—specifically their resemblance to animal horns—indicate their medicinal use for conditions associated with those animals, such as ailments of the spleen, eyes, and joints.</meta>

### PHYTOGNOMONICA

Meal <note>likely barley or wheat flour</note> is effective against a long-standing cough; the powder of an ox horn, specifically from the part where it attaches to the head, brings health to those suffering from spleen ailments. **Marcellus** <note>Marcellus Empiricus, a 5th-century medical writer</note> states that fenugreek <note>original: *foenum graecum*</note> boiled in wine and applied as a poultice heals the same condition; it likewise treats gout <note>term: *podagra* (gout or foot-pain)</note>, and in six hundred other ways, these two bring mutual aid to diseases. The **Horned poppy** <note>original: *Papaver κερατίτης* (keratites)</note> has small horns twisted with a slight curve in the manner of fenugreek, from which it takes its name, as it looks like the horn of an ox. According to **Dioscorides** and **Galen**, when applied as an ointment, it clears away *argema* <note>white ulcers on the cornea</note> and "clouds" <note>cataracts or spots</note> from the eyes of beasts of burden. According to **Pliny**, gall, and a certain stony gall-like substance found in bovine gall, is effective for sharpening eyesight. According to **Galen**, the leaves of the poppy cleanse malignant ulcers, and according to **Dioscorides**, bull’s gall is effective for the same. **Stock** <note>original: *Leucoion*</note> bears smooth, twisted pods similar to the horned poppy and fenugreek; according to **Pliny**, bull fat heals gout, and according to **Hippocrates**, the gall draws out the menses. The flowers of the stock stimulate menstruation, and the roots help those with gout, according to **Dioscorides**.

The fruit of **Greater celandine** <note>original: *chelidonij maioris*</note> is long and smooth like the horned poppy; according to **Pliny**, it is effective for vision, the "royal disease" <note>term: *regium morbum* (jaundice)</note>, herpes, the white spots on the eyes of beasts of burden, and toothaches. According to **Galen**, the scrapings from the ankle bone of an ox help the teeth; according to **Hippocrates**, gall helps jaundice, and the rest is as mentioned above. There is also a plant called the **Bull-horn caltrop** <note>original: *tribulus tauroceros*</note> and *bucephalon* <note>Greek: "ox-head"</note>, that is, "bovine head" and "bull horn," by which names it is known among the synonyms of **Dioscorides**. Bovine marrow is used for mouth ulcers, and oak bark boiled in cow's milk is effective for serpent-related diseases, according to **Pliny**; and according to **Galen**, dung is used for inflammations <note>original: *phlegmonas*</note> and for acute vision, for all of which the caltrop is also effective according to **Dioscorides**.

**Buck’s-horn plantain** <note>original: *Coronopus*</note>, or "star herb," is called **stag's horn** <note>original: *cornu ceruinum*</note> by many because it has incisions like those of a deer's horn. Inhaled deer blood stops the flows of "celiacs" <note>those with chronic diarrhea or abdominal distress</note>, and buck’s-horn plantain acts in favor of celiacs according to **Dioscorides**; likewise, according to **Galen**, deer horn and the washings from it are used for vision. Deer horns resemble all fennel-like plants <note>original: *ferulacea*</note> and are effective against poisons, as we said in the first book.

The **Unicorn** <note>original: *Monoceros*</note>, if **Philes** and **Aelian** report the truth, is a wild beast from the middle of whose forehead a horn extends, not curved, but entirely straight; it is a wild and solitary beast, but at the time of mating it becomes tame and joins the herd; lured by the scent of virgins, it leans its head into their lap and is captured. Its horn resists poisons and benefits those with the "comitial" disease <note>term: *comitialibus* (epilepsy)</note>. **Mustard** <note>original: *Sinapi*</note> produces a straight pod: it benefits those with epilepsy, poisonous diseases, and the affairs of Venus <note>libido</note>. According to **Pliny**, **Arugula** <note>original: *Eruca*</note> is also for Venus and poisonous diseases. So too are **Cabbage**, **Navew**, **Wild Radish**, and **Cultivated Radish**.

**Dragon Arum** <note>original: *Dracunculus*</note> thrusts out a sharp-pointed little horn from a reddish flower; **Cuckoo-pint** <note>original: *Arum*</note> also encloses its female part in a sharp, cone-shaped sheath, having the same power as those mentioned before. So too the flower of the Indian grain, or **Maize** <note>original: *maiz*</note>, before it produces seeds. **Wood Sorrel** <note>original: *Alleluya*</note>, with its straight, long, and rigid sheaths, is effective against serpent bites, epilepsy, and poison, according to **Pliny**. We have said elsewhere that the "beaks" of **Geraniums** are also effective against poisons. The **Rhinoceros** has a horn above the tip of its nose, which is reported by the experience of more recent authors to be effective against poisons. We have said that **Dittander** <note>original: *Piperaſtrum*</note> has the strength of pepper, with its oblong, pyramidal, and sharp pod; and pepper helps with the bites of serpents. On the tips of **Oats** <note>original: *Auenæ*</note> there hang tiny things like two-footed locusts; it is useful for poultices, like barley. A porridge made from it stops the bowels and benefits those with a cough; according to **Pliny**, snails are added to plasters and are useful for those with dysentery.

Almost all types of grain bear seeds bristling with awns <note>the "beard" of the grain</note>, and they imitate the horns of crabs; especially those which have "eyes" <note>buds or markings</note>. They are excellent for the bites of mad dogs and vipers, as are the grains themselves. The **Lobster** <note>original: *Astacus*</note> has longer and thinner horns than the locust; the lions <note>referring to a type of crustacean or specific pincers</note> certainly have two very long ones, and the shrimp's are split in the middle so that out of two come four. **Crabs** <note>original: *Cancelli*</note>, like grains, heal poisonous stings; the aforementioned crustaceans are also effective for Venus <note>aphrodisiacs</note>, as are **Ceres** <note>wheat</note>, **Rice**, **Rye**, **Spelt**, **Barley**, and the rest. And if among the shrimp there are lobsters, crabs, and crayfish which have four horns, there are also types of grain which have their awns arranged in two or four rows. Snails are also suitable for gout, for which wheat is also used. **Sextus Pomponius**, father of a man of praetorian rank and a Prince of Hither Spain, when he was presiding over the winnowing of his granaries, was seized by the pain of gout; he plunged himself into the wheat up to his knees and, having been relieved and his feet dried, he used this remedy thereafter, according to **Pliny**.
