BOOK FOUR.

## FLOWERS AND LEAVES WHICH RESEMBLE THE CRESTS OF ANIMALS. Chapter 12.

Crests have been granted to the heads of only a few animals, and none except birds; these are indeed of various kinds: for peacocks, they are like hairy little trees; for the Stymphalian bird <note>a mythical bird from Greek legend, though the author likely refers to a specific real-world species here</note>, a tuft; and for the pheasant, little horns. Furthermore, there is a small bird which was once called *galerita* <note>from the Latin *galerus*, a helmet or cap</note> because of its crest, and later, by a Gaulish word, gave its name even to a Roman legion: the *alauda* <note>The Lark. Julius Caesar’s Legio V Alaudae was named for the lark-like crests on its helmets</note>. Tufts are also found in the genus of coots, the black woodpecker <note>original: *pico martio*</note>, and the Balearic crane. But the most remarkable badge belongs to poultry [roosters]: a fleshy, serrated crest, which we could not rightly call flesh, nor cartilage, nor callus, but rather something unique to itself.

->HERE you will encounter Corydalis, Clary Sage, and Fennel, placed alongside the Lark, the Rooster, and the Peacock, mimicking their crests, so that you may observe their mutual similarities.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration comparing botanical and zoological forms. At the top, three plants are shown: Corydalis (left), with its characteristic spurred flowers; Horminum (center), a sage-like plant with whorled flowers and large basal leaves; and Foeniculum (right), fennel with fine feathery foliage and umbels. Below each plant is the head of a bird with a crest mirroring the plant's structure: beneath Corydalis is a crested lark (Alauda) with its pointed feathers; beneath Horminum is a rooster (Gallus) with a fleshy serrated comb; and beneath Foeniculum is a peacock (Pavo) with its fan-shaped feather crest.</image-desc>

Among the unofficial names used by **Dioscorides** <note>a 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, *corydalion* is listed among the types of fumitory. **Galen** <note>the famous 2nd-century Roman physician</note>, in the eleventh book of his *On Medicaments*, mentions the same *corydalis capnos* <note>original: *corydalis capni*; "capnos" is Greek for smoke, a common name for fumitory</note>, whose flowers are crested and cone-shaped, rivaling the helmet-like crown on the head of the small lark. Therefore, Galen says: "I have added these things to my discourse because I wanted to clearly identify this animal—namely the crested lark—which bears upright feathers on its head, since I have experienced its usefulness against <term>colic</term> <note>severe abdominal pain</note>, and I would like to demonstrate it to those who do not know it, for even the bird itself..."

### PHYTOGNOMONICA BOOK III
<meta>catchword: Latini.</meta>

The herb called **corydalis** <note>original: *corydalis*; likely a species of Fumitory or Birthwort</note> is suitable for those suffering from colic. To explain this more clearly, the Greeks use the name *korydalous* <note>original: κορυδαλοὺς</note> for the bird that the Latins call the **lark** <note>original: *alauda*</note>. Pliny refers to it as the "crested" bird <note>original: *galeritam*</note> because of its peak. The name is derived from the Greek *korys* <note>original: κόρυθος</note>, meaning a helmet, or rather from a skullcap. The name *alauda* was used because soldiers wearing helmets were called "larks." This crest atop the head gave rise to a fable found in the comic playwright Aristophanes: he claimed the lark was born before the Earth itself. When its father died and there was no ground to bury him in, the lark supposedly entombed him within its own head; for this reason, the bird still sports a raised peak upon its crown today.

According to Dioscorides, the crested lark, when roasted and eaten, helps those with colic; however, Galen states that it provides this benefit when boiled in a broth—an opinion shared by Pliny, Aetius, and Aegineta. But Alexander Trallianus <note>a 6th-century Greek physician</note> describes a remedy where, while the lark is still alive, they remove its heart and create an amulet, binding it to the sufferer's left thigh. Some have foolishly thought that **Fumitory** <note>original: *Capnon*</note> was called *corydalion* because of its similarity to coriander; in truth, it is named after the lark because its flowers resemble the bird's crest, and it possesses a marvelous power to aid the colon. There is no doubt it is useful, especially for those suffering from hardened waste in the bowels and the resulting trapped gas; for the juice of the fumitory loosens the bowels, and once they are opened, a path is cleared for the gas to escape.

The reason why the lark is effective for the colon becomes clear through this method. The plant **cock’s comb** <note>original: ἀλεκτορόλοφος (*alektorolophos*)</note>, according to Pliny, has leaves similar to the crest of a rooster; these leaves are rough, hairy, and somewhat bumpy with wrinkles, like the fuzz of a mullein. Some call it **clary sage** <note>original: *sclarea*</note>. It incites the favors of Venus <note>it acts as an aphrodisiac</note>. We have said that the crest is the rooster's most distinguished badge. According to Aristotle, it is neither flesh nor cartilage, and the rooster is the only bird granted such a peculiar crest. Among the temperaments of animals, the rooster is the most lustful of birds, according to Oppian. The crest signifies this lust; for if the crest is removed from a rooster, its sexual drive is also taken away. Similarly, the boar, which is highly inflamed by lust, has bristles on its neck that stand up so stiffly they look like the crests of helmets.

I would also suggest that this signature applies to poisons; for among serpents, only the **basilisk** possesses a crest upon its head, and it is the most venomous of all. **Horminum** <note>a type of Sage</note> is commonly called "cock's spur" by some because its leaf bears a likeness to the rooster's crest. There are two kinds, the cultivated and the wild, and both greatly assist the works of Venus. The Greek word *hormē* <note>original: ὁρμὴ</note> signifies an impulse or instinct to be carried away by great lust. Likewise, the **alectorian stone** <note>a mythical stone supposedly found in a rooster's gizzard</note> is effective for lust. **Vervain** <note>original: *Verbenaca*</note> is called "poultry-crest" by Dioscorides because of the shape of its small branches. Pliny advises that a broth made of rooster is effective against serpent bites, and Aetius and Aegineta recommend it against toxins. Dioscorides and Aesculapius claim its brain performs the function of a *theriac* <note>a universal medical antidote</note>. Furthermore, Rhazes teaches that if a man rubs his member with rooster gall before lying with his wife, she will love no one but him. The alectorian stone reconciles wives to their husbands, according to the lapidary of Sylvaticus.

-> This plant provides incentives for the fires of Venus to flourish, <-
-> Beneficial for a wife who wishes to be pleasing to her husband. <-

Vervain serves the same purposes: Dioscorides reports that its leaves and roots, when drunk or applied, are powerful against serpents. It is called the "sacred herb" and is highly recommended for amulets and purification rituals. In sacred rites and incantations, sorceresses used it and called it the "love-bringer," because they used it to procure love through their crafts. They administer the third joint from the ground along with its surrounding leaves for tertian fevers, and the fourth for quartan fevers. According to Pliny, the Magi <note>ancient Persian priests and healers</note> command that those suffering from fevers be anointed with the burnt and ground spurs and claws of roosters mixed with oil.

**Maidenhair** <note>original: *Adiantum*</note> also seems to imitate the cock's comb; it is recorded by all that if it is given to roosters, they become more pugnacious. Another kind of **Satyrium** <note>a type of orchid</note>, which they call the female, raises spiked, hooded, or "crested" flowers. Indeed, the little flower gapes open like a helmet; the small leaves rising from the sides represent ears, while those rising from the middle represent a crest. We have said that the roots of these plants are effective for sexual intercourse if one lacks the ability, as is true for other species of orchids. The **peacock** carries feathers on its head like a mane adorned with flowers. For this reason, Pliny describes the peacock's peak as a "hairy little tree"; they seem to mimic the **umbels** of flowers. An umbel sits atop the small stalks, acting as a support for the flower, divided into many longer stems which, rising from the same point, radiate outward. Because this resembles a sun-shade <note>original: *umbella*</note>, which women use to protect their faces from the sun, the Greeks called this floral habit a *skiadeion* <note>original: σκιάδειον, literally "little shade"</note>, and were soon imitated by the Greeks...

The Latins called it an **umbrella** <note>original: *umbella*; here referring to the umbrella-like flower clusters of certain plants</note>. The **peacock** is beneficial for the eyesight, as has already been stated. Simeon Seth <note>an 11th-century Byzantine physician</note> claimed that its burnt bones, ground with vinegar and applied as an ointment, are effective against leprosy. The plant **cachrys** <note>a genus of the parsley family</note> bears an umbrella and is also good for the sight and for similar conditions. Furthermore, umbrella-bearing plants can resemble serpents, as some have small flowers and "horns," much like the **horned viper** <note>original: *cerastae*</note> or the **basilisk**, which is protected by a triple-pointed crest on its forehead; for this reason, these plants are effective against venomous strikes. **Celtic nard** is an umbrella-bearer and is good for venomous bites; the same is true of the mountain variety, as well as **costus**, **leek**, **wild leek**, **garlic**, **all-heal** <note>original: *panax*</note>, **cow parsnip**, **lovage**, **parsnip**, **anise**, **caraway**, **wild cumin**, **bishop's weed**, **celery**, **lovage**, **black lovage**, **masterwort**, **deer-fodder**, **cultivated and wild fennel**, **wild carrot**, **rosemary-cachrys**, **giant fennel**, **hog's fennel**, **laserwort**, **sagapenum** <note>a resin from a Ferula species</note>, **spurge**, **galbanum**, **everlasting flower**, **angelica**, **elder**, and others.

## PLANTS WHICH, BY THE LIKENESS OF THEIR FLOWERS AND FOLIAGE, REPRESENT THE EARS OF ANIMALS. Chapter XIII.

<image-desc>Decorative initial A featuring intricate floral and foliate scrollwork inside a rectangular border.</image-desc>

THE EARS OF ANIMALS are larger in some and smaller in others. In **deer**, they are merely split or divided; in **ferrets**, they are hairy; in **seals** and **dolphins**, they are cartilaginous; and **vipers** possess only holes in place of ears. Among winged animals, only the **great horned owl** and the **long-eared owl** have feathers resembling ears, while others have holes for hearing, as do scaly creatures and serpents. We shall review the flowers and foliage in order that exhibit the ears of animals, from which we shall derive the same omens of their medicinal powers.

**Mouse-ear** <note>original: *myosota* (μυοσῶτα)</note> sprouts with narrow leaves that are not without a prominence on the back, being raised and blackish; it found its name in Dioscorides because its leaves, when they creep forth, express the ears of **mice**. He said it heals eye ulcers <note>original: *aegilopas*</note>; according to Pliny, the sight is restored by the ash of mice and their heads applied with honey, and much more so by the wood-mouse or the dormouse. Some call **chickweed** <note>original: *alsine*</note> "mouse-ear" because it imitates the ears of mice: it heals inflammations of the eyes and pains of the ears. According to Pliny, the ash of a mouse dripped in with honey, or boiled in rose oil, soothes ear pain; and according to Galen, the flesh of mice with raw egg yolk most effectively heals eye inflammation.

The very common herb which, because of its shagginess and the hairy surface of its leaves, is called **pilosella** <note>mouse-ear hawkweed</note>, being somewhat concave and representing the shape of a mouse's ear, has been called "mouse-ear" by some. By the experiment of more recent authors, it is effective against **stones** <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>; however, according to Dioscorides, Galen, Pliny, and Avicenna, mouse dung drunk with honey-water and frankincense expels stones, and you will find many other shared virtues among the same authors. 

There is a species among the **vetchlings** <note>original: *cicerculae*</note> which some believe to be the **bean** <note>original: *phaselum*</note> of Dioscorides, whose leaves are veined and thin, similar to the ears of **rabbits**; this name prevails among some. Both are effective for "luxury" <note>likely referring to libido or reproductive health, as rabbits were symbols of fertility</note>. Sylvaticus <note>Matthaeus Sylvaticus, a 14th-century botanist</note> calls **wild dittany** "rabbit's ear," because the common people gave it that name due to its hairiness and shape. Modern physicians are accustomed to applying rabbit fat when something is fixed in the body and they wish it to be removed. According to Pliny, if a splinter is stuck in the sole of the foot, you should place rabbit fat with raw crab on the wounded spot, and on the corresponding part on the opposite side, bind three or four bean flowers, and it will be healed. This property is peculiar to the herb **dittany**, for in Crete, goats pierced by arrows shake them out by grazing on this herb.

Some call the **pimpernel** <note>original: *anagallis*</note> "the bat" <note>original: *nycteridem*</note>, and Aetius mentions it in that ointment which he calls "Helen's," used in the treatment of sciatica; he also says it is effective for the torments of the eyes. Among the names listed by Dioscorides, he calls the pimpernel *nycteris*, as if it were named after the **bat** by the Magi. According to Avicenna, the urine of a bat cures white spots in the eye <note>cataracts or scars</note>, and according to Pliny, its blood is a remedy for snake bites; the pimpernel clears away eye sores and clouds, and the blue variety is drunk in wine against the bites of snakes. 

There are many, such as the Gauls, who call another kind of **comfrey** <note>original: *symphytum*</note> "donkey's ear," because it produces large leaves that curve like the ears of a **donkey**. Donkey's milk, when drunk, benefits those with abdominal issues and dysentery, and its dung stops...

...for blood bursting from the nose, according to Pliny, for which **comfrey** <note>original: *symphyton*</note> is also effective. A type of **sanicle** is commonly called **bear's ear** <note>original: *auricula ursi*; likely the Primula auricula</note>; its leaves are somewhat thick, fleshy, smooth, slightly turned back, and fringed and rounded with a thicker border. It has a specific affinity for arthritic conditions. According to Pliny, **bear fat** <note>original: *adeps ursinus*</note> is effective for diseases of the joints and for those suffering from gout <note>original: *podagricos*</note>.

### PLANTS DISPLAYING THE EYES OF ANIMALS.
### Chapter XIV.

After the ears, we shall speak of the eyes, so that no part of the animal body is omitted from being demonstrated by the parts of herbs. **Ox-eye** <note>original: *Buphtalmon*</note>, as Galen testifies in the seventh book of *Simple Medicines*, was named after its flowers, which seem to possess a certain shape resembling the eyes of oxen; the Romans called it **ox-herb** <note>original: *boariam*</note>, and the peasants commonly call it *ox-eye*. The flowers, when mixed with a wax salve, disperse tumors and hardnesses, and restore a healthy color to those seized by the **royal disease** <term>jaundice</term>. There are some who report that the "royal disease" is driven away by a linen bandage smeared with ox gall, wrapped around the body below the ribs for three days and renewed daily; this is also mentioned by Hippocrates. According to Dioscorides, **bull's blood** disperses and softens tumors when smeared on with pearl barley.

**Weasel-ear** <note>original: *Galeopsis*; likely hemp-nettle</note> takes its name from *gale*, the weasel; it is the "light," as it were, of the weasel or the eye of a cat, named from the shape of the plant, which somewhat resembles the eye of the animal. According to Pliny and Marcellus, a **weasel** taken in food, or its blood, is effective against **strumas** <term>scrofulous swellings of the neck</term>; Archigenes mentions that weasel blood is smeared on **parotids** <term>swellings of the glands behind the ears</term>. The leaves, seeds, and juice of the *galeopsis* herb are effective against these same parotid swellings, according to Dioscorides. *Galeopsis* is also called "spurious pennyroyal" among the false names in Dioscorides; the same is drunk in wine against the bites of serpents and helps by itself against gout. A dried weasel-rod <note>likely referring to a dried weasel penis or a specific bone used in folk medicine</note>, when drunk, heals those bitten by a serpent, according to Hali; and Aetius makes a wonderful **acopon** <term>a soothing ointment for weariness or pain</term> for gout from the weasel.

**Wolf-eye** <note>original: *Lycopsis*; bugloss</note> is named after the eyes of wolves, perhaps because the small, purplish circle of the flower imitates a wolf's eye; it heals **holy fire** <term>erysipelas, a skin infection</term>. **Alkanet** <note>original: *anchusa*</note>, a species of which is *lycopsis*, also helps with holy fire.

The common people call **deer-fodder** <note>original: *Elaphoboscon*; likely wild parsnip</note> the *deer’s eye*, from its resemblance to the eye of a deer; it is effective against serpents, just as the deer is, to whom Nature gave serpents as enemies (for which reason the deer is called *ophioctonos*, or "snake-killer").

**Starwort** <note>original: *Aster atticus*</note> is called *hyophthalmos* <note>pig's eye</note> among the false names of Dioscorides, as if you were to say "swine's eye," because it has a similarity to the eyes of pigs. For the **comitial disease** <term>epilepsy</term>, Pliny says that the preserved testicles of a pig are given in milk; and according to Marcellus, it will be healed by pig's urine smeared on the groin, or by applying greasy wool soaked in it. Dioscorides said the flowers of *aster atticus* help children suffering from epilepsy; and if the dried flower is plucked with the left hand by the person in pain and bound to the groin, they are freed from the pain. But Galen wrote that it heals **buboes** <term>swollen lymph nodes</term> not only when smeared on, but even when hung around the neck, for which reason it is also called *bubonium*.

**Dog-eye** <note>original: *Cynopsis*</note> is mentioned by Theophrastus; Theodorus translates it as "canine eye." This vegetable springs up immediately after the first rains following the equinox, and he places it among the spiked herbs. To me, it seems entirely to be **fleawort** <note>original: *psyllium*</note>, for Dioscorides is accustomed to calling it *cynoma* and *cynocephalos* <note>dog-head</note>. *Psyllium* is spiked, and the flower is like a dog's eye with upturned hairs, while the seed has the appearance of a flea. *Psyllium*, according to Pliny, is also called *cynomium*. Place the vomit of a dog upon the belly of one suffering from **dropsy** <term>edema/fluid swelling</term>, and they will immediately begin to discharge water through the bowels. According to Pliny, dog bile soothes gout, provided it does not touch the ground. *Psyllium* is given in wine to those with dropsy and helps those with gout.

### PLANTS REPRESENTING THE MOUTH AND BEAK OF ANIMALS.
### Chapter XV.

Now we shall report on those plants which, in their flowers and leaves, represent the mouth or beak of animals. Birds have horny and sharp beaks; those living on prey have hooked beaks; those that root through herbs and mud have straight, broad beaks, like the swine kind. Beasts of burden have mouths that serve in place of hands for gathering fodder, while those living on torn flesh have wider mouths.

# BOOK FOUR.

<margin>E</margin> ->**BEHOLD, we offer you three small plants displaying the gaping jaws of animals: the snapdragon <note>original: *antirrhinon*</note> representing a lion's mouth; the dragon-arum <note>original: *dracunculum*</note> simulating a dragon's gape; and the bear's breech <note>original: *acantum*</note> mimicking the gaping mouth of a frog. From these, you shall infer the rest by your own ingenuity.**<-

---

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting three botanical specimens aligned with three animal heads below them to demonstrate morphological similarities. On the left, an Antirrhinum (snapdragon) plant with lipped flowers is paired with the head of a calf or lion. In the center, a Dracunculus plant with large leaves and a long spathe is paired with a dragon or serpent head. On the right, an Acanthus-like plant with a tall flowering spike is paired with a frog's head. All animal mouths are open, mirroring the "rictus" <note>the gaping maw</note> of the blossoms above.</image-desc>

The **snapdragon** <note>original: *Antirrhinum*</note> is distinguished by purple flowers, varying from reddish-violet to rose, which are elongated and drooping at the top. They emulate the cheeks and the open jaws <note>original: *rictum*</note> of a calf or a lion. Sometimes they gape open, and sometimes they are closed as if by little valves, such that the plant should rather have been named "lion-mouth" <note>original: *leonthostomos*</note>. It is handed down—likely because of this lion-like form—that those who rub themselves with these flowers mixed with lily oil become more beautiful (just as the lily is the most beautiful among plants). Furthermore, it is said that one cannot be harmed by any poison <note>original: *medicamento*</note> if they wear the plant as an amulet. Just as the **fat of a lion** <note>original: *leonis adeps*</note> serves as an amulet against those who lay snares, Pliny—citing the Magi <note>ancient Persian priests known for secret knowledge</note>—promises that those rubbed with this fat will find easier favor with kings and common people; he adds that one should specifically be anointed with that fat found between the lion's eyebrows. Democritus calls a certain herb *Helianthes* <note>meaning "sun-flower"; likely a Cistus or similar Mediterranean plant, not the modern American sunflower</note>, found in the region of **Themiscyra** and the coastal mountains of **Cilicia**, with leaves like a myrtle. He claims that when this herb is boiled with lion fat, and saffron and palm wine are added, the Magi and the Kings of the Persians rub themselves with it so that their bodies may appear pleasing; for this reason, it is also named *heliocallides* <note>meaning "beauty of the sun"</note>. Columella mentions this same herb in his poem about his garden:

> „ and it bears a mouth
> „ like the gaping throat of a lion.

PHYTOGNOMONY.

<margin>And elsewhere.</margin>

### The lion also gapes.

Pliny records that this herb is planted among the spring herbs and various types of flowers, such as the white wallflower <note>original: *leucoia*</note>, the flaming-yellow petals of the marigold <note>original: *calthae*</note>, and among the foliage of the narcissus, lily, violet, and rose. It is clear that the name was bestowed because of the shape of the flower, which gapes open like a lion. Others write that it has a purple flower, but they all confess they do not truly know what kind of herb it was. I would say it is the garden snapdragon <term>antirrhinon</term> <note>literally "counter-nose" or "like a nose"</note>, which is more purple and bursts forth in early spring; it is a flower of truly spectacular color that displays a lion’s mouth. Or perhaps I would say it is the Iris: for I remember reading among the false names of the Iris that it was called "the lion," and by others <term>lycostomos</term> <note>Greek for "wolf's mouth"</note>. It has a purple flower and, according to Theophrastus, is among the spring flowers, is grown in gardens, and is planted among roses, lilies, and marigolds, and it shows the mouth of a lion. According to Pliny, a lion's gall helps those with jaundice <note>original: *ictericis*</note>; according to Dioscorides, Iris given in a drink heals the jaundiced. The Iris is also called "the wolf" in the commentaries on Nicander, because the upturned lips of its petals reflect the appearance of a wolf’s mouth. The flower, when applied, is wonderfully effective at hastening and inducing labor; it is also said that eating the flesh of a wolf benefits those in labor, or even having someone nearby who has eaten it. There is also the herb <term>orobanche</term> <note>broomrape</note>, which is called "the lion" among the bastard names in Dioscorides; for at the tops of its stalks it bears flowers showing the lion's maw, according to Sotion the Greek in the *Geoponica* <note>a collection of ancient agricultural lore</note>. It is called the "lion of legumes" <note>original: *osprioleon*</note>. If anyone wishes this herb not to appear at all in their field, they should take five potsherds and paint on them in white pigment Hercules strangling a lion, and place the shards at the four corners and in the center of the field. There is another cure handed down by Democritus of this kind: because the lion as an animal is terrified and shrinks back at the sight of a rooster, if one carries a rooster, held firmly in the hands, around the field, the **lion's herb** <term>λεόντειος πόα</term> will soon be destroyed, as if the plant itself feared the lion. Others, taught by experience, water the seeds to be committed to the earth with rooster blood, as if the future crop will then be safe from the "lion-herb." Nicander handed down that broomrape is an enemy to poison, just as the flesh of a lion is. The flower of the **acanthus** <note>bear's breech</note> resembles the mouth of a gaping frog or a toad; frogs are useful for those with consumption <note>hectic fever</note>, and according to Dioscorides, acanthus is useful for those feeling the wasting of disease. The **dragon arum** <term>dracunculus</term> is zealously planted in gardens as a miracle of playful Nature: it rises with a single stalk, and from the leafy top of the stem a certain small sheath leaps forth into a gradually twisted point. When this opens and spreads itself, it shows the spectacular gaping form of a dragon with a solid horn, just like a tongue, flashing from the hollow curve of the sheath as if from the maw of a serpent. Anyone ignorant of it could not deny that they are looking at a dragon; the name of the serpent, which has become common for it, could not be more aptly used. It is effective against serpent bites, as we have said. In the **friar's cowl** <note>original: *arisaro*</note> plant, an oblong flower emerges from the root, as if from a single rolled leaf; gaping at the top, it displays a serpent's mouth, and from the mouth stamens emerge to imitate a tongue. It is so skillfully formed that if you look at a snake, you would judge it to be thrusting out its mouth in the same way. We have said it is effective against the bites of serpents. In the flowers of **calamint**, an open serpent's mouth is shown with the tongue thrust out; it is effective against its bites. The same image is seen in other flowers with the same effect, which you may investigate in your own manner; let it suffice to have indicated the matter with these examples. Among the types of fungi are the **boletes** <note>original: *fuilli*, likely a typo for *suilli* meaning "piglets"</note>; you will find them from April until the month of May. They are of a pale brown color, with an oblong cap that gathers into a cone, the shape protruding in the middle; they seem to reflect the shape of a pig's snout to some extent, and for that reason, I surmise they were called "piglets" <note>original: *suillos*</note> among the Greeks, Latins, and all nations. These same fungi are smeared on with water for snake bites; Aetius praises pig excrement cooked in vinegar for poisonous bites. The common people call the **sow-thistle** <note>original: *hyosirim*</note> the "pig's thistle" according to Pliny. It is a type of prickly sow-thistle which the Italians call *cicerbita*; the calyxes of the flowers, before they open, reflect a certain figure of a pig’s snout, hence the name **pig's nose** <term>ὕος ρὶς</term>. Ruellius says that the same herb is called "pig's snout" by some, and "lion's tooth" <note>dandelion</note> by others. Pliny says it is similar in its tube, but smaller and rougher to the touch; when crushed, it heals wounds excellently and draws out milk according to Dioscorides—all of which the pig also provides. More recent authors call the **columbine** <term>aquilina</term> the "eagle-herb"; its flowers at the tips of the stalks have four spurs at the bottom part reflected upwards, so that they seem to emulate the beak of an eagle, and from this the name of "eagle" was given. ## WHICH PLANTS IMITATE THE TONGUES OF ANIMALS.
### Chapter XVI.

Tongues are not formed in the same way in all animals. In snakes, it is very thin, three-forked, and black in color, and if you pull it out, it is remarkably long; in lizards, it is two-forked and hairy. In seals <note>original: *vitulis marinis*, literally "sea calves"</note> it is also double, but with the thin filaments mentioned above. In fish, it is almost entirely attached to the mouth; in crocodiles, it is completely attached. In lions, leopards, and cats, the tongue has an overlapping roughness, similar to a file, which wears down human skin by licking. In frogs, the front part is attached while the inner part is free from the throat, which is how they cast their voice; in bees it is very long, and it stands out prominently in cicadas. In those creatures which have a hollow sting in the mouth, there is neither a tongue nor teeth; the tongue is notably wide in the elephant.

->***THESE*** *little plants we present to you, imitating the tongues of animals: "dog-tongue"* <term>cynoglossum</term> *represents the dog's tongue,*<-
->*in the following "ox-tongue"* <term>buglossum</term> *represents the ox's; then "deer-tongue"* <term>elaphoglosson</term> *represents the deer's;*<-
->*and finally "snake-tongue"* <term>ophioglosson</term> *represents the serpent's. Furthermore, the tongues*<-
->*of the named animals appear together on the opposite side: look upon*<-
->*the proposed spectacle, and contemplate it.*<-

# PHYTOGNOMONICA

Now we shall record the plants whose flowers or leaves represent the tongues of animals. **Cynoglossum** <note>original: Κυνόγλωσσον</note>, which you might call "dog-tongue," has leaves like a plantain but narrower, smaller, downy, and quite soft; though they are entirely rough to the touch, they are assimilated to a dog’s tongue by common consensus due to their softness and shape, from which it earned its name. Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> recorded that it is effective against dog bites; as we have said, the skin of a dog’s tongue, like all its flesh, is effective against its own bites. **Buglossum** <note>original: Βούγλωσσον</note> or "ox-tongue" is similar to mullein and has a rough leaf, imitating the tongues of cattle. Dioscorides said it is effective against tertian and quartan fevers <note>Types of malaria-like fevers that recur every three or four days</note> and for the delight of the soul. Apuleius stated it works for heart conditions and against poisons; the common people call it **borage**, as if it were *bouagine*, because it is similar to the tongues of oxen. I attribute this similarity both to its shape and its roughness, and it applies to both our borage and bugloss, both being endowed with the same powers. A liquid mixed from wine and cow’s milk is effective against quartan fevers when taken for several days. **Symphytum** <note>Comfrey</note> has oblong, downy, and rough leaves, following the example of an ox’s tongue. According to Dioscorides, it is effective for "gluing" wounds together; we have already mentioned that glue made from a bull’s neck and hide is effective for binding things together.

**Arnoglossum** <note>original: Αρνόγλωσσον</note>, which you might call "lamb-tongue," is what the common people call plantain, according to Theophrastus <note>The "father of botany," a student of Aristotle</note>. It is a herb of widespread renown, fertility, and utility among all nations, much like lambs and sheep. There is great power in the ash of livestock dung for treating cancers, and according to Aetius, its fresh skin is used for quartan fevers and dysentery. Greasy wool stuffed into a wound is effective after the seventh day for the bite of a mad dog, but lamb’s meat with honey is especially praised for "comitial" disease <note>An old term for epilepsy</note> according to Pliny. According to Rhazes <note>A Persian physician</note>, urine is beneficial for those with dropsy—all of which plantain also provides.

They called the lower ash tree the *ornus*, and from the shape of its fruit, they called it **orneoglossum** <note>original: ορνεόγλωσσον</note>, because it recalls the image of a bird's tongue, according to Pliny. Ruellius <note>Jean Ruel, a French physician and botanist</note> says *orneoglossum* is a tree with the appearance of an elm, leaves like an almond, and very long pods hanging from the tips of the shoots about the size of an olive; inside these is a pith similar to a bird's tongue, hence the name. It stimulates Venus <note>sexual desire</note> and increases fertility, which we have already said regarding birds. **Lingua passerina** <note>Sparrow-tongue</note> has oblong and smooth leaves, and the name was given by the consensus of all men after the tongue of a sparrow, which it imitates; it could be called **strouthioglossum** <note>original: στρουθιόγλωσσον</note>. Dioscorides said it most closely imitates the tongues of sparrows; others call it *polygonum* or *polycarpon* because of the abundance of its seeds, for we have said it is effective for sex and conception. The Quintilii <note>Two brothers who wrote on agriculture</note> say that the *polyspermon* or *polygonos* herb makes animals many times more fertile, which is the same thing we said of the sparrow.

The *Phyllis* of Dioscorides, commonly called <gloss>hart’s tongue</gloss>, fails to match only the length of a deer's tongue, which is why it is also called "deer-tongue" <note>original: lingua cervina</note> in the apothecary shops; it is a hand-and-a-half long, straight, and always green with a smooth surface. Dioscorides said that when drunk in wine, it is a great adversary to serpents, which is the same thing we said of deer flesh. Furthermore, that same flesh is effective against fevers, and we have said that those noble women <note>Referring to historical or legendary figures</note> were always free of fever due to their continuous eating of deer meat. From this, we devised—and confirmed through many trials—that a water extracted from the leaves of the hart's-tongue fern using chemical instruments <note>distillation</note> brings the greatest help against pestilential fevers.

The common sort of herbalists bestow the name **ophioglosson** <note>Adder's-tongue</note> from its form and the shape of snakes' tongues, which it recalls; the nomenclature fits most aptly since the sharp little point of the flower imitates a snake thrusting out its tongue, which is produced from a tender little stalk; it is of no small recommendation for snake bites. **Echio** <note>Viper's Bugloss</note> has oblong, hairy, and whitish leaves; the shops and the countryside call it "goat-tongue" <note>original: lingua hircina</note> from its similarity to the tongue of a goat, and because goats and kids take the greatest delight in feeding on it. Dioscorides said it is effective against serpents and increases milk in women. According to Hippocrates in his book on the diseases of women, goat's meat increases milk, and especially cheese made from its milk. According to Pliny, a remedy against the bite of serpents is made from the ash of a goat’s horn or hair drunk in liquid. There are also many flowers that have certain stamens in the middle, divided at the top, so that they clearly display the forked tongues of snakes; from this, the greediness of these animals is inferred by Aristotle, as if they take a double pleasure from their food. I, on the contrary, would judge that they protect against snake venom, as can be seen in the spiderwort, anchusa, and the so-called yellow flag <note>pseudoacorus</note> and carnations <note>garyophyllis</note>, for they are recommended against poisons and the contagion of the plague.

## PLANTS DISPLAYING THE TEETH OF ANIMALS.

### Chapter XVII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'D' featuring a miniature landscape with hills and vegetation.</image-desc>

There are three kinds of teeth: serrated, continuous, and protruding. Serrated teeth meet like the teeth of a comb <note>original: "pectinatim"</note> so they do not wear each other down by clashing, as seen in snakes, fish, and dogs. Continuous teeth are found in humans and horses. Protruding teeth <note>tusks</note> are found in the boar, the hippopotamus, and the elephant. In many fish, the teeth are serrated and found on the tongue and throughout the mouth so that they may soften food with a multitude of wounds; furthermore, they slant toward the throat so the food does not fall out, as fish have no other way to hold it. These are similar to the teeth of the asp and other snakes, though snakes have two very long teeth on the upper part, right and left, perforated by a thin tube (like the stingers of scorpions) to pour in venom. Some say there is only one, and because it is hooked, it bends back when it has bitten. The scorpion's tooth is in its tail, and most have three. A viper's teeth are hidden in the gums; no birds have teeth except for the bat. In place of teeth, insects have a stinger; the elephant has four internal teeth for chewing, besides those that protrude—the males' tusks are curved upward, while the females' are straight and pointing down. The "sea-mouse" <note>likely the pilot fish, which was anciently believed to lead whales</note> which precedes the whale has no teeth, but instead has a mouth bristling with hairs inside, as are the tongue and palate. Thus far Aristotle <note>A reference to Aristotle’s "History of Animals"</note>.

But let us see why Nature produced thorns. Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle</note> says that Nature armed plants with thorns like little spears to protect them against the bites of animals, a point we have already brought up from Pliny. We, however, say they were given to some plants so they could crawl up nearby stalks, just as all climbing plants are, for they cannot support themselves without a prop; for this reason, they have hooked thorns looking toward the roots. To others, Nature gives <term>awns</term> <note>the needle-like bristles on ears of grain</note> like spikes to protect themselves from birds. On others, thorns are on the trunk so that animals do not shake the fruit from the tree while scratching their backs, preventing it from reaching proper ripeness. Or—what I consider the ultimate reason—to act as a filter for the earthy and dregs-like parts of the sap toward the bark, so they can supply a richer and purer nourishment to the fruits. In human bodies, Nature sends mange, pustules, and similar things to the skin in many diseases to purify the humors <note>The four bodily fluids thought to govern health in ancient medicine</note>.

But let us discuss what can be conjectured from their <term>Physiognomony</term> <note>The practice of determining character or medicinal use from outward appearance</note>. Because there are many animal teeth, stingers, and spines that are greatly hostile to the human race, a provident and wise Nature produced many and innumerable thorny plants. From their appearance, a remedy for the most destructive evil might be found, so that they would be available to us everywhere—not only in gardens, but also in hedges, forests, groves, and other places where such animals more frequently dwell. Nature herself could not demonstrate medicine to man more clearly or manifesty: therefore, we must strive with diligent investigation to imagine the similarity of thorns and see which animal teeth they most resemble. 

There are animals in the sea that inject venom with stingers, such as the stingray <note>original: "pastinaca"</note>, the scorpion-fish, the dragonet, and the sea-hog, which thrust out their stingers. There are also innumerable kinds of snakes, some with hooked and some with serrated teeth, dangerous with their stiff points. There are also the venomous teeth of quadrupeds, such as those of a rabid dog. Because of this, it should not seem strange if Nature produced so many and such varied thorny plants: hooked ones for vipers, straight ones for dogs, and thin, almost downy ones for the stingers of spiders, wasps, and venomous spiders <note>original: "phalangiorum"</note>. 

But for those to whom this method of healing by similarity might be less pleasing, we shall flee to natural causes and the other things for which they are useful. Thorny herbs show dryness, sometimes from a cold cause and sometimes from a hot one, as we have said, and for that reason they are astringent <note>substances that contract body tissues</note>. One can see this in spiny and horned animals—the porcupine, the hedgehog, rays, swordfish, and other animals—which are drier than the rest. For this reason, these plants aid the stomach, break up leprosy and mange, cure dropsy <note>swelling caused by excess fluid</note>, treat swollen gums and teeth, and help with bowel fluxes and excessive menstrual flow. They may do this either through their whole substance, or by strengthening parts of the body so they may expel poison more promptly, or by closing the passages so they are less affected by them. But so that our instruction may proceed more orderly, let us see which plants are thorny. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher often called the "Father of Botany"</note> says some prickly plants are entirely...

...prickles, such as wild asparagus, gorse, and others with prickly parts. Among trees, shrubs, and herbs, the trees that have thorn-bearing branches are the wild pear, the pomegranate, and the Christ’s thorn <note>original: *paliurus*</note>; shrubs include the bramble, the rose, and the caper; and herbs have either prickly leaves—such as the cotton thistle, sea holly, saw-wort <note>original: *enecum*</note>, and sharp-thistle. From this, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist</note> says: "Therefore, some herbs are thorny, and some are without thorns; there are many species of thorny ones." In its entirety, the asparagus and the "scorpion-plant" <note>likely *Genista scorpius*</note> are thorns, for they have no leaves. Some thorny plants are leafy, such as the thistle, sea holly, licorice, and stinging nettle; in all of these, a prickly sharpness <note>original: *mordacitas*, literally "bitingness"</note> resides in the leaves. Some also have a leaf alongside the spine, like the caltrop <note>original: *tribulus*</note> and restharrow. Some have thorns on the leaf and on the stem, like the marsh-grass <note>original: *phleos*</note>. The sea-buckthorn <note>original: *hyppophyes*</note> is jointed with spines, a distinctive property, because it also has thorny fruit. Examples are provided below.

It is peculiar to the puncture vine <note>original: *tribulus terrestris*</note> to have a thorny seed and stiff, very hard spines alongside the leaves; its juice, when drunk or applied, restores those struck by a viper. ...rough and prickly, with a thorny head rivaling a sea urchin <note>original: *echini marini*</note>; not only is it helpful when drunk by those bitten by a snake, but when worn as an amulet, it is believed to drive snakes away. The Christ's thorn <note>original: *paliurus*</note> is a prickly shrub, and citrus trees are armed with stiff thorns: their seed, when drunk, resists venomous beasts, as we learn from Athenaeus. The white chameleon-thistle has leaves rougher and sharper than the sow-thistle, and from there it raises spines like a sea urchin. Groundsel <note>original: *erigeron*</note> is also of the prickly kind. The blessed thistle <note>original: *carduus benedictus*</note> has hairy leaves, which become prickly as the plant matures, with heads stiffening into very sharp thorns. The rough bindweed <note>original: *smilax aspera*</note> has shoots that are prickly in the manner of a bramble or Christ's thorn; it is not only an antidote for venomous creatures, but if wine made from this is given to newborn infants, no poisons will be able to harm them later in life. It is also used in medicines meant to ward off poisons. The box-thorn <note>original: *lycium*</note>, a thorny tree, is effective for wounds from rabid dogs. The currant or gooseberry <note>original: *ribes*</note> is armed with robust thorns around its branches: Pliny praised it with wonderful honors for the bites of a mad dog. The "scorpion-plant" <note>original: *scorpionium*</note> heals with its prickles; these plants are stiff with very small spines, appearing rough so that they seem to have not just thorns, but teeth or stingers, and these same plants heal the stings of wasps and venomous spiders <note>original: *phalangiorum*</note>. It is a peculiar trait of spinach <note>original: *spinaceis*</note> to have prickly seeds: its juice is drunk for the stings of scorpions and spiders. The rough sow-thistle, wild lettuce, and the distaff-thistle <note>original: *atractylis*</note> have thorny leaves and heads stiff with thorns at the top; according to Pliny, the Christ's thorn brings aid to scorpion stings. Two types of prickly "scorpion-herbs" work against animals of their own kind. Asparagus helps those struck by a venomous spider; wild lettuce and nettles, with their burning downy hair, inflict the pain of a sting, much like the stingers of wasps and bees, even if this down appears so thin and soft that it seems unable to penetrate the skin. The hop plant <note>original: *lupus salictarius*, literally "the willow-wolf"</note> has rough, hairy, and somewhat prickly shoots: it can be effective for the same ailments, as it brings help against swallowed poisons.

### ->PLANTS REPRESENTING THE NECK, BREASTS, SPLEENS, AND HEARTS<-
#### ->*of animals. Chapter 18.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' containing a landscape scene with hills and a stone bridge or archway.</image-desc>

**I**T FOLLOWS that we should describe the plants that represent the neck, throat, spleen, breasts, and hearts of animals. Among the various names for rough bindweed <note>original: *smilax aspera*</note> is the name *mergina*; it was called this by the Romans, perhaps a name derived from "neck." Ovid, speaking of Aesacus being turned into a diver bird <note>original: *mergum*</note>, says:

> ,, *The joints of the legs are long*
> ->*The neck remains long; the head is far from the body.*<-

For the diver bird has both a long and curved neck, and the bindweed, by creeping through thickets, is curved and bent in the likeness of the diver's neck. The blood of the diver bird is an "amphictoton" <note>a term for a general antidote</note> and resists venomous wild beasts, especially the rabid dog, according to Aetius. The leaves and berries of the rough bindweed, drunk before or after exposure, are antidotes for venomous things. Among the unofficial names for fumitory <note>original: *fumaria*</note> in Dioscorides is *peristereon*, which means "pigeon-plant" <note>original: *columba*</note>, clearly from the appearance of the leaves, which in some way represent a pigeon's crop or gullet. Aretaeus commands those with elephantiasis <note>original: *elephanticos*</note> to eat partridges and pigeons. Mesue said that because fumitory casts out bile and burnt humors, it heals elephantiasis and "carcinomas" <note>cancers or ulcers</note>. The fruit commonly called *sebesten* <note>the Assyrian plum</note> in the Persian tongue is called "dog’s breast" <note>original: *mamilla canis*</note> by Sylvaticus, even if *sebastos* is a Greek word. This fruit helps with catarrhs <note>respiratory drainage</note>, for which a dog's skin wrapped around any finger is also excellent. They say the roots of the asphodel are similar to the udders of cows: the Greeks pass down the knowledge that all poisons are defeated by them, especially those that cause gnawing and burning sensations, such that if Spanish flies <note>original: *catharides*, a toxic beetle</note> are consumed, everything is expelled by vomiting, according to Dioscorides and Pliny. Furthermore, Nicander recommended it against snakes and scorpions, and placed it under the bedding during sleep to ward off fears. Anacardia <note>cashew or marking nut</note>, the fruit of a certain tree, is not unlike the little hearts of ears, from which it takes its name <note>from the Greek 'ana' (like) and 'cardia' (heart)</note>; it is reddish in color, like a heart. According to the Arabs, they restore failing senses, repair the loss of memory, and bring aid to afflictions of the brain. The flesh of many birds, such as the hawk, strengthens the spirit...

...they work, they resist melancholy and mental disturbance, and they cure the "sacred disease" <note>The "sacred disease" was the ancient name for epilepsy.</note>, according to Maimonides <note>original: *R. Mose*; refers to the 12th-century scholar Moses Maimonides</note> in his aphorisms. The Magi call mallow leaves "goat's spleen" because the leaf bears a resemblance to that organ. Pliny writes that mallow is useful as a liniment for colic; furthermore, he claims it excels against poisons and venomous stings, and is beneficial for women's menstruation, sexual pleasures, conception, epilepsy <note>original: *comitiales*</note>, and bladder stones—just as the goat and other things possess these properties indiscriminately.

# PLANTS REPRESENTING THE TESTICLES OF ANIMALS
## Chapter 19

There are various plant bulbs that imitate the testicles of animals, especially those of lustful creatures. Indeed, they imitate them so skillfully <note>original: *affabrè*</note> that no one who sees them would fail to recognize the resemblance. Nature, being concerned with human generation, indicated through this image of testicles that these plants are effective for sexual potency <note>original: *vires venereas*</note>, for conception, and for producing offspring. The testicles of livestock and cattle hang down toward the legs, while in pigs they are attached; in dolphins they are very long and hidden at the end of the belly, and in elephants they are concealed. In egg-laying creatures, they adhere internally to the loins—the swiftest of these in sexual passion—and in buzzards <note>original: *buteonibus*</note> they are even found in threes.

Species of ORCHIDS <note>The word *orchis* is derived from the Greek word for testicle.</note> come into view once again; the observer will see at first glance "goat-like" testicles <note>original: *hircinos*</note> with their plant, "dog-like" ones <note>original: *caninos*</note>, and finally the "triple-testicled" variety <note>original: *triorchidum*</note>, which is associated with the hawk genus.

<image-desc>Three detailed botanical illustrations of orchid plants. Each plant consists of a rosette of lanceolate leaves at the base and a central vertical spike of small flowers. The root systems are prominently featured to show their anatomical "signatures": the left and center orchids each possess two rounded, ovoid tubers, while the orchid on the right possesses three such tubers (representing the "triorchidum" variety). Below the soil line of the main plants, three additional sets of isolated tubers are depicted in pairs and a trio, emphasizing their visual resemblance to animal testicles.</image-desc>

**Dog’s-stones** <note>original: *Cynosorchis*; a type of orchid whose twin tubers resemble testicles.</note>, which is called "little bulb" by everyone, truly mimics the testicle of a dog. It has leaves softer than those of an olive tree, usually three in number, spread across the ground for half a foot. The root is bulbous and oblong, arranged in a double set: the upper one is fuller, while the lower one is softer and more wrinkled. In **Thessaly** <note>A region in Greece famous in antiquity for witchcraft and herbal potions.</note>, women drink the soft bulb in goat's milk to stimulate sexual desire; the dry one is used to restrain it, as the potency of one is dissolved by the drinking of the other. **Dioscorides** <note>A famous 1st-century Greek physician and botanist.</note> instructs that all bulbs, when smeared on with honey and powdered pepper, are effective against dog bites. He who casts his own urine into the urine of a dog becomes impotent in the matters of **Venus** <note>The goddess of love; here referring to sexual function.</note>. The **Hand of Christ** <note>original: *Palma Christi*; likely referring to the Spotted Orchid (*Dactylorhiza maculata*), which has hand-shaped tubers.</note> resembles dog testicles, if the "fingers" were removed. **Goat’s-stones** <note>original: *Tragorchis*; likely the Lizard Orchid.</note>, or the "hircine testicle," smells of a goat and mimics a hairy beard with its spiral filaments. It inflames one toward sexual desire, which the goat provides most abundantly; it is the most potent of all bulbs, just as the goat is the most lustful of animals. There are also **Fox’s-stones** <note>original: *vulpini testiculi*</note>, which are quite small. To these is added another root gifted with a triple twin-set, and for this reason called **Three-stones** <note>original: *triorchis*</note>; **Paulus Aegineta** <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note> says the Egyptians called it *Serapias*, after the August surname of the Goddess **Serapis**. This plant has powers far superior to all others, and is not sluggish or weak with mold like other orchids. We find that the **hawk** was called *triorchis* because of its number of testicles; the Romans call this bird a **buzzard**, according to **Pliny**. He who is weak in sexual matters should eat the testicles of a **kite** <note>A type of bird of prey.</note>, boiled with honey in perennial spring water, while fasting for three days, and he will immediately be strengthened. The *Triorchis* plant is similar to the kite; to those birds who are most "well-testicled," they attribute the power to provoke sexual capability. There are many who call **Colchicum** <note>original: *Colchicon*; Meadow Saffron.</note> "dog's testicle" because of the similarity of its twin seeds; it is a poisonous herb and kills the unwary who eat it. Likewise, the saliva of a dog is poisonous, for it brings on rabies and death.

## PLANTS SHOWING THE MALE GENITALS OF ANIMALS
->Chapter 20<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial P containing an ornate floral and leaf pattern within a square frame.</image-desc>
**A**FTER the testicles, we shall speak of the penis, by enumerating those parts of plants that can show the male member <note>original: *veretrum*</note> of animals, and are effective for coitus and offspring. 

<margin>With a resemblance to the canine genitals—and not a bad or ungraceful resemblance at that, if one contemplates the plant which, rising from the root with a bare, smooth, and singular stalk, has a cluster of leaves at the top, and emerging among them are flowers gathered together as if in a ball.</margin> **Broomrape** <note>original: *Orobanche*</note> is the herb which antiquity called **dog-knob** <note>original: *cynomorion*; literally "dog's penis."</note>. The Cypriots call it *thersites* because it is almost entirely a stalk <note>original: *thyrsus*</note>, that is, clearly a straight scape; in which form anyone would admit it is like a canine genital standing upright in its top sheath. There are those who call this **Tora**, since it is certain that as soon as cows have tasted this herb, they seek out bulls. **Theophrastus** <note>The "Father of Botany," a successor to Aristotle.</note>, enumerating those things which the oak produces besides acorns, says: "In addition to these, it produces another thing representing the form of a penis; when it is fully formed, it is a hard thing perforated in a mimicking part, and somewhat mimicking a bull's head, which when broken off shows the appearance of an olive pit." We have already said above that this is effective for fertility. From the middle of the **lily** flower, certain stamens are led forth; when these are shaken off, a certain "staff" <note>original: *colus*</note> flashes out, leaving a small head at the peak, showing as if the image of a donkey's scrotum. **Nicander** <note>A 2nd-century BC Greek poet and physician.</note>, describing the lily as an antidote against the poison of *pharicon* <note>A legendary toxic compound.</note>, says: "Take the iris and the flowery head, which Venus hated because it vied with her in color and form; she cast foul reproaches upon its middle leaves, and made the deformed 'club' of a braying donkey grow there." Certainly, by this description of the "donkey's club," he meant the genitals placed in the middle of the lilies—that is, the flower. It softens the womb and provokes the menses, whereby it prepares the womb for conception; they are also effective against serpent bites. The testicles of a donkey are effective for coitus; and by drinking donkey's milk, poisons are extinguished, especially against **henbane** <note>original: *hyoscyamum*</note>, the **sea hare** <note>A marine mollusk once believed to be deadly to touch or eat.</note>, and *pharicon*.

# PLANTS DEPICTING SCORPION TAILS BY THEIR FLOWER, PODS, AND SEED. Chapter XXI.

There are a great many plants which, by their flowers, small pods, seeds, and roots, imitate the tails of animals. They do this either to show that they possess the same powers as those animals, or to show they act as an adversary to their venomous stings. We shall review some of the many examples, starting first with scorpions.

->We have placed at the beginning of this chapter the illustrations of three plants which represent not just specific parts, but the entire image of a scorpion’s tail: first, the **Heliotrope** <note>original: *heliotropij*; specifically referring to the "Turnsole," whose flower spikes curl at the tip.</note> with the curled tips of its flower spikes; second, another type of **wild Cumin** <note>original: *syluestris cumini*</note> with its horn-shaped pods; and third, **Scorpion-grass** <note>original: *scorpioidis*; likely *Scorpiurus muricatus* or "Caterpillar plant."</note> with its small pods that mimic them. At the base, we have included the scorpion itself, so that you may observe the close resemblance.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration featuring three botanical specimens and a scorpion. The plant on the left has large, broad leaves and two tall, hairy flower spikes that curl at the tips. The center plant has finely divided, feathery foliage and several long, thin, segmented stalks that curl tightly like tails. The plant on the right has rounded, paired leaves and curved, segmented seed pods. Below these plants is a detailed depiction of a scorpion with its segmented tail curved upward in a shape that mirrors the botanical structures shown above.</image-desc>

**Scorpion-grass** <term>Scorpioides: a plant named for its likeness to a scorpion</term> is a small herb with the appearance of a scorpion's tail; indeed, it produces certain pod-like "horns," bent in the manner of a scorpion's tail, and thus it obtained the name *Scorpioides* among all people. When smeared on, it provides immediate help against the stings of scorpions, according to **Dioscorides** <note>A famous 1st-century Greek physician and botanist whose work was the standard medical text for 1,500 years.</note>. We see that **Telephium** <note>Commonly known as Orpine or Stonecrop; a succulent plant.</note> has the same kind of root, which rivals the scorpion's tail in shape and is effective against its bites.

# BOOK FOUR.

It is already a settled tradition that these plants are effective. There is also another small herb nurtured in the grain fields, which produces straight, slender stalks, a foot or a foot and a half tall. At the top, it bears little curved horns with sharp points, bent back to imitate the small tails of scorpions with their transverse joints. It also has tiny yellow flowers and small leaves arranged in order on both sides of the veins, like those of the **Caltrop** <note>original: *tribuli*; the *Tribulus terrestris* or Puncture Vine</note>, but more slender. Though its virtues are untested, we can predict the same power from such great resemblances. In the greater **Heliotrope** <note>original: *heliotropij*; the Turnsole plant</note>, there are elegant series of flowers or clustered peaks at the top of the stalks, imitating the bent tails of scorpions; these suggest to us that they are of great use in treating scorpion stings. For this reason, because of its effect, it could be called **Scorpion-slayer** <note>original: *scorpioctonos*</note> or **Scorpion-killer**, as Dioscorides notes. In the Greater Heliotrope, the flower has the form of a scorpion's tail, which is why it is named **Scorpion-tail** <note>original: *scorpioides*</note>; the flower is curved like a scorpion's tail, and it is beneficial when drunk or applied as a poultice against the sting of scorpions. **Wild Basil** <note>original: *Ocimastrum*</note> is also called <term>skorpiouros</term> <note>Greek: *σκορπίουρος*, meaning "scorpion tail"</note> because of its shape—a name found among the "bastard" or unofficial nomenclatures of Dioscorides. This name is more aptly suited to **Viper's Bugloss** <note>original: *echio*</note>, as its series of flowers, arranged and bent on the stalk, more correctly imitates the tail of scorpions; this is also seen in the **Alkanets** <note>original: *anchusis*</note>. Their power is effective against the venom of serpents, and it is not incredible that they are also potent against the virulent stings of scorpions.

According to Theophrastus, **Tragos** <note>A spiny shrub, likely a species of *Ephedra* or *Astragalus*</note> is among the prickly plants; some are entirely composed of thorns, such as the **Scorpio** <note>likely *Genista scorpius* or a similar broom</note>, which bears no leaves at all, only thorns. Dioscorides said that this "scorpion" plant is also called *tragus*. Regarding these, Pliny says: "There are many species of thorny plants; the *tragus* is entirely thorny, and they call this the 'scorpion.' It is endowed with a very great astringent power, and perhaps because of this, we may conjecture that it helps against poisons." And elsewhere: "The herb **Scorpion** <note>original: *scorpius*</note> took its name from the evidence of its shape, for it has a seed resembling a scorpion's tail and few leaves; it is effective against the animal of its same name." There is also another of the same name and effect, but without leaves, having a stalk like an asparagus and a thorn at the tip, from which it gets its name. There is a certain kind of **Wild Cumin** <note>original: *cumini syluestris*</note> which produces horn-shaped seeds that rival the tail of a scorpion, partitioned with segments; when drunk, this is a remedy for the bites of serpents, and I conjecture it works for scorpions as well. For it is established among authors that the nature of these plants opposes the venom of scorpions, centipedes, and all such animals. The **Marigold** <note>original: *Caltha*</note> brings forth seed whose small pods imitate the tails of scorpions; the modern writers say it resists their poison. It bears, moreover, tails or "arms" very similar to those of a crab, for which reason it is called the **Crab-herb** by Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a famous German botanist</note> and others. But I believe it is called the "Crab-herb" because it may cure a **Carcinoma** <note>The word for "crab" in Latin and Greek, *cancer/karkinos*, was also used for malignant tumors</note>. For scorpion tails and crab claws are similar, and Dioscorides taught that the crab cures the "crabs" <note>cancers</note>. Crabs are changed into scorpions due to a certain natural sympathy. Ovid says:

> -> *If you remove the hollow claws from a seashore crab,* <-
> -> *And place the rest beneath the earth; from the buried part,* <-
> -> *A scorpion will emerge, threatening with its hooked tail.* <-

Those who praise the **Cucumber** <note>original: *Cucumim*</note> itself say that it grows in Arabia, then in Cyrene, and others report it in Arcadia; it is similar to the heliotrope, and between its leaves and branches, a seed the size of a walnut grows, appearing like a scorpion with its tail reflected, but white. Some, therefore, call it the **Scorpion-cucumber**; according to Pliny, its seed and its juice <note>original: *elaterio*</note> are most effective against scorpion stings. There are also very many pods of plants whose segments, swollen with seeds, mimic and represent the tail of scorpions, and these are effective against the bites of scorpions and venomous creatures; such as **Radish**, **Navew** <note>a type of rape or kale</note>, **Turnip**, **Bitter Vetch**, **Lupine**, **Rocket**, **Vetch**, **Broom**, and others which are included in antidotes against asps and the poisons of scorpions.

PHYTOGNOMONICA

### PLANTS THAT RESEMBLE THE TAILS OF ANIMALS.
->Chapter XXII.<-

In order not to disrupt the order established from the beginning, we shall mention some plants that display the likeness of animal tails. Tails are found on almost all animals except for humans and apes; they are naked on bristly animals like boars, small on shaggy ones like bears, and very long and hairy on horses. In lizards and snakes, they regrow if cut off. Cattle have a very long tail-bone that is hairy on only one part; the tail of an ass is longer than that of a horse. On a lion, it is hairy only at the lowest part, as it is on cattle and shrews. On foxes and wolves, it is bushy, as it is on sheep (on whom the tail is quite long); pigs twist theirs, while various breeds of dogs curl them back under their bellies.

->*The **Parsnip** <note>original: *Pastinaca*; here referring to the plant, though the author will soon link it to the stingray</note>, **Foxtail grass** <note>original: *alopecuros*</note>, and **Horsetail** <note>original: *equisetum*</note> are most accurately shown in these engravings, claiming for themselves a likeness to the tails of the stingray, the fox, and the horse. I wish for all of these to be most attentively observed by you, so that through these examples, you may investigate and search out other things in Nature that must be thoroughly understood.*<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration featuring three distinct types of plants and two root/tail sections. On the left, 'Pastinaca' is shown with serrated leaves and a root that terminates in a long, whip-like tail. In the center, 'Alopecuros' (foxtail grass) depicts a tuft of grass with long, fuzzy seed heads. On the right, 'Equisetum' (horsetail) shows tall, jointed stems with whorled branches. Below the plants are two separate depictions of a stingray's tail, emphasizing the sharp barb (radius) at the end, used for comparison with the plant structures above.</image-desc>

The fish called <term>Trygon</term> <note>Greek: *Τρυγών*</note> in Greek is the **Stingray** <note>original: *pastinaca piscis*</note> in Latin, according to Pliny's interpretation; but among the Latins, the word *pastinaca* is used because of the tail's color and its roundness, which is similar to the root of a parsnip. On the tail of the stingray, a barb <note>original: *radius*</note> grows; Pliny said that nothing more dreadful is born in the sea than this. Oppian also noted that the poisonous weapons of the Persians yield to its venom and its deadly power, for even when dead, the barb retains its strength,

powers, which it exerts not only upon living creatures but even upon rocks, herbs, and trees; for by its touch they wither and waste away. They say that Circe gave this to Telegonus <note>In mythology, Telegonus was the son of Odysseus and Circe; he killed his father with a spear tipped with a stingray spine</note> so that he might use it against his enemies, though he inadvertently killed his father with it. Aelian stated that this ray is most dangerous and hostile, such that it destroys not only men and animals but also trees; indeed, if you apply the sting to a very large, vigorous, and flourishing green tree, it loses its leaves not long after. Once they have fallen, the entire trunk resembles trees dried out by the burning heat of the sun, which Nicander also confirms. The **parsnip** herb <note>original: *pastinaca*; the author is linking the plant to the stingray of the same name</note> is beneficial for the bites or stings of serpents; it is recorded that those who take it beforehand suffer no injury from snakes. Dioscorides himself says that for one struck by the **marine stingray**, all the remedies we have mentioned for viper bites are similarly appropriate. Celsus also writes that the **wild parsnip** <note>original: *erraticam pastinacam*</note> is useful for such a wound. 

But let us move to other shared powers. Dioscorides said that the parsnip herb, when applied as a pessary, expels the fetus; and the ray of the stingray fish, tied to the navel, makes childbirth easy—provided it was taken from the fish while it was still alive and the fish was then released back into the sea. **Horsetail** <note>original: *Equisetum*</note> produces many thin, reed-like leaves around its small stalks; many black hairs hang from it, and in a circle through the gaps, multiple rows of thin leaves surround it like rays. These are somewhat rough, like bristles, and quite long, effectively mimicking a horse's tail. It stops blood erupting from the nostrils, and its seed, applied with vinegar and wool, is used for every kind of flow; likewise, the ash of hairs from a horse's head, when smeared on, stops bleeding. **Foxtail grass** <note>original: *Alopecuros*</note> does not end in a needle or a beard <note>the "beard" or *arista* refers to the bristly awns on grain</note>. Instead, it bristles with thick down and roughness, forming a spike in the manner of a plantain; however, it does not produce flowers in distinct parts as that plant does, but is scattered throughout the whole spike like grain. A downy little flower emerges from both sides, as Theophrastus depicts it; it takes its name from this, because it stands out as being similar to the tails of foxes. Pliny says of it: Foxtail has a soft spike, thick with down, not unlike the tails of foxes (hence its name), armed with no sharp points or beards. Because it is of the wheat family, it can benefit those with coughs just as wheat does, which is not inconsistent with the powers of the fox, which provides a cure for those suffering from coughs <note>Ancient medicine often used fox lungs or fat to treat respiratory issues</note>. **Hog's Fennel** <note>original: *Peucedanum*</note> is called "pig's tail" by Sylvaticus <note>Matthaeus Silvaticus, a 14th-century botanist</note> because the head of the root is stiff with many bristle-like fibers, which also appears in all types of *seseli* <note>Meadow saxifrage or similar umbellifers</note>. The dried urine of a hog or wild boar, drunk with vinegar, helps with the "falling sickness" <term>epilepsy</term> according to Galen; the knucklebone of a pig relieves headache according to Aetius; for wounded nerves, hog's lard with earthworms is beneficial according to Serenus; against serpents, the fat with honey and resin, or the liver or brain drunk in wine according to Pliny—all of which Hog's Fennel performs according to Dioscorides.

# PLANT PARTS INDICATING ANIMAL FEET. Chapter XXIII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring a figure intertwined with scrolling foliage and vines, set against a dark hatched background within a square frame.</image-desc>THERE ARE also parts of plants that show the hindmost parts of animals, namely the feet. Some animals have solid hooves <note>original: *vngulas*</note>, which are not horned, nor do they have ankle-bones <term>talus</term>; but those that are cloven-footed <term>bisulca</term> do have them. The lynx has something similar, for it has an ankle-bone; the lion's is even more curved, but the ankle-bone is straight in the joint of the foot, protruding at the belly. Among birds, some are fingered, others are web-footed <term>palmiped</term>, and others are in between, with divided toes but added width. But all have four toes: three in the front part, one at the heel. In some heavier birds, spurs <note>original: *radij*</note> are added to the legs.

->IN the foreground we have presented **coltsfoot** <note>original: *tussilaginem*; literally "cough-chaser"</note>, then **ivy**, a little later **sea** or **aquatic holly**, and finally the **fig**; and the animals whose feet they have modeled are in view. For in the first, we have expressed the horse's hoof; in the second, the many feet of the marine centipede <note>original: *scolopendra*</note>; in the third, the feet of aquatic birds or geese; and finally, the feet of the crow.<-

They call it **lion’s foot** <note>original: λϵοντοπόδιον (*leontopodion*)</note>, as if it were a lion's paw, because of the hairy appearance of its leaves (not its flowers), which somewhat resemble a leg attached to a foot. There are also certain small indentations impressed upon the flowers, imitating a lion's track or footprint. Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> said it is effective for love charms and for swellings. Among the Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests often associated with occult knowledge in Roman texts</note>, according to Pliny, it is promised that those anointed with lion's fat will more easily obtain favor with Kings or the people; he also says it is used for hemorrhoids and tonsils. They call another **lion’s petal** <note>original: λϵοντοπϵταλον (*leontopetalon*)</note>, as if it holds some similarity in its leaves to a lion or a lion's paws, even if authors do not explicitly state it: for it has a leaf like cabbage, divided in the shape of a poppy. Dioscorides says that when drunk in wine, it helps against serpent bites, and that no other thing ends the pain more quickly. Just as the power of lion's flesh makes a man safe from all beasts.

Apuleius says that **hare’s foot** <term>Lagopum <note>likely *Trifolium arvense* (Hare's-foot clover) or *Lagurus ovatus*</note></term> is similar to a hare’s foot, and its name was bestowed upon it from this likeness: for it has husks in a hairy spike, and hairy, soft bristles, as it were, which emulate the color and hairiness of a hare's foot. It provides protection for those suffering from "flows" <note>likely chronic diarrhea or excessive bleeding</note>; according to Hippocrates, it promotes the growth of flesh in hollow ulcers and hastens scarring, and is excellent for restraining tumors of the groin and loose hernias. Just as hare’s rennet is effective for flows of the belly, and their dung and blood for those with dysentery or abdominal disease; crushed with honey, it is smeared on **hernias** <term>enterocelis <note>specifically a scrotal hernia</note></term>, and their dung can heal ruptured intestines, according to Pliny. 

The Greeks name a herb **wolf’s foot** <term>Lycopoda <note>likely *Lycopus europaeus*, commonly known as Gypsywort</note></term>, because it is similar to a wolf's paw; for its leaf is formed and divided in the manner of a wolf's foot. It is equal to wild **horehound** <term>marrubio <note>*Marrubium*</note></term>, of a pleasant scent, with an angular, jointed stem, a spongy pith inside, and a root fibrous with frequent hair-like filaments. Its crushed leaves are an immediate remedy for a weak stomach; we now call it **motherwort** <note>original: *cardiacam*</note>, because the ancients used to call the mouth of the stomach the "cardia"—

The wolf possesses a robust stomach; it is voracious and digests everything, and thus [the plant named for it] is beneficial for the stomach. **Coltsfoot** <note>original: *Tussilago*</note>, or **horse’s hoof** <note>original: *ungula caballina*</note> as it is called by more recent writers because it puts forth round leaves from the bottom with six or seven sides and closing at sharp angles, representing the shape of a horse’s hoof—hence the name. Dioscorides says that when the dried plant is used as a fumigant, so that the smoke is taken into the open mouth through a funnel, it heals those who suffer from a dry cough and those with orthopnea <note>Difficulty breathing unless sitting upright</note>, and it expels a dead fetus when drunk. By the fumigation of a horse’s hoof, dead fetuses are also expelled; the saliva of a horse drunk for three days heals a cough, and Pliny <note>Roman naturalist and author of *Natural History*</note> relates that the horse will die [if this is done]; its hoof likewise expels a dead fetus. **Garlic mustard** <note>original: *Allearia*</note> is also called **donkey’s foot** <note>original: *pes asini*</note> in the *Pandects* <note>Likely the *Pandectae Medicinae*, a medical encyclopedia</note>, perhaps because the shape of its leaf is not much different from coltsfoot; it is said to be beneficial to those who cough, which Haly <note>Haly Abbas, a famous Persian physician</note> claims is also achieved if the ground lung of a donkey is drunk.
