Indeed, the physician Heraclides considers it more effective against all toxins and aconite <note>A highly poisonous flowering plant</note> when boiled in goose broth, according to Pliny, who also says that serpents have been seen with goose feet <note>This likely refers to the plant's appearance near them</note>; the goose performs the same actions. There are two types of **fumitory** <note>original: *capnos*</note>, one of the garden and another which they call **cock’s foot** <note>original: *pedem gallinaceum*</note>, growing in ruined walls and hedges, according to Pliny, for it has a resemblance to a cock’s foot. The gall of a cock diluted with water strengthens the sharpness of the eyes and removes white spots <note>cataracts or corneal scars</note>, according to Marcellus. Galen experienced that the broth of old roosters loosens the bowels; the juice of the herb brings clarity to the eyes and loosens the belly, according to Mesue. Among the names for **pennycress** <note>original: *thlaspi*</note>, one also reads **cock’s foot** because of the likeness of the foliage to its feet. If cock’s broth is boiled in summer with unripe grapes, it extinguishes bile on both sides <note>through vomiting and purging</note> according to Nicolaus Massa; and a capon is offered to a feverish youth by Mundella. A measure of pennycress drunk extracts bile from both sides according to Dioscorides. It creeps from the earth like millet, with rough and woolly leaves; it is stuffed into the nostrils. It grows in Italy, and when tied on, it stops blood, according to Pliny. Among us, it is a small grass rising with jointed, upright stalks, each spreading into five or three thin, spiked tails of flowers, arranged like fingers, with an astringent and drying taste; hence, by no empty conjecture, we can consider it Pliny’s *ischœmon*. ...it cures dysentery, though Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, a Roman naturalist</note> notes that the blood of an old rooster is more potent for this. They say that the blood of a rooster is also beneficial for a hemorrhage of the membranes of the brain, according to Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note>; for the spitting up of blood from the mouth and nose, physicians suggest that roasted eggs are effective. **Ivy** <note>original: *Hedera*</note> imitates the **centipede** <note>original: *scolopendra*</note> with its little roots when it climbs a tree; for this reason, it is called the **millipede** <note>original: *millepeda*</note>. The centipede animal is effective as a hair remover <term>psilothrum: a substance used to remove unwanted body hair</term>, according to Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and father of pharmacognosy</note>, and ivy provides the same benefit. **Larkspur** <note>original: *Consolidam regalem*</note>, or another kind of wild cumin, is called **knight’s spur** <note>original Italian: *spron di cauagliero*</note> by more recent writers, but it is better called **rooster’s spur** <note>original: *gallinaceorum calcar*</note>. Because it puts forth little horns looking upward from the other side of the flower, resembling a rooster, it should be called "rooster's spur." Dioscorides said that a drink made from it is a protection against snake bites and helps those suffering from stones <note>original: *calculosis*</note>. A broth made from roosters is a famous cure for snake bites, according to Pliny, as are the small stones usually found in the stomachs of roosters. **Caucalis** <note>original Greek: *καυχὰς*</note> is called **rooster’s foot** <note>original: *pes gallinaceus*</note> or **chick’s foot** by the Romans among the "bastard" <note>spurious or common</note> names of Dioscorides, a name noted by Ruellius <note>Jean Ruel, a French physician and botanist</note>, surely because the tip of the leaf is shaped like a hen’s foot; for the leaves near the bottom of the stalk resemble celery to some extent. Dioscorides says it promotes urine, and Nicander includes it in theriacs <note>universal antidotes</note> against poisons. We have mentioned rooster broth against poisons according to Dioscorides, as it dulls the sharpness of toxins, and against snake bites according to Pliny; furthermore, it offers powerful help in dislodging stones, which **bur-parsley** <note>original: *caucalis*</note> also performs, and they have many other things in common. **Ivy-leaved toadflax** <note>original: *Cimbalaria*</note> has angular, ivy-like leaves, grows on walls, and contains a bit of milky sap; it has a small basket-shaped flower inclining from purple to blue, and a sweet white root, such that it seems related to the wild turnip: it is believed to be useful for the eyes. The appearance of the leaves changes with age, from rounder to longer; but as for which part represents a rooster's foot, I could not easily say, unless perhaps those sharp points into which the calyx <note>the husk or cup of a flower</note> supporting the flower is divided are said to represent it, especially when the flower has fallen or withered, for then they appear stiff and stretched in different directions. We have already said that the rooster is effective for the sharpness of eyesight. **Purslane** <note>original: *Portulaca*</note> is called **chick’s foot** by Macro, and likewise by Sylvaticus. Aretaeus, in his treatment of headaches, praises the flesh of the rooster against snakes, dysentery, as a remedy for the eyes, and for the stomach—all of which purslane provides, according to Dioscorides.

The **lesser sesamoid** <note>original: *Sesamoides minor*</note> is called **crow-plant** <note>original: *coronion*</note> among the spurious names, a name borrowed from crows because the leaves of this plant are equal to **crow’s foot** <note>original: *coronopodi*</note>, that is, the herb "raven’s foot"; indeed, the features are similar, the leaves having the notches and growth of the crow's foot. Pliny says the lesser sesamoid disperses inflammatory swellings <note>original: *panos*</note>, and crow’s dung heals white skin spots <note>original: *alphos*</note>. **Wild Lychnis** <note>original: *Lychnis syluestris*</note> is called **hawk-foot** <note>original: *hieracopodion*</note>, that is, the foot of a hawk, surely from the shape of the leaf among the spurious names of Dioscorides; wild lychnis is called **hawk’s foot** <note>original: *accipitrinus pes*</note> by our people, and it is pronounced effective against scorpions, just as the droppings of a hawk are used against the bites of a spotted lizard. The hawk—or the kite—can also be used, whose liver or heart, when carried, is a preventative <note>original: *prophilaeticon*</note> against snake bites, according to Pliny. Among the names for **Rose Campion** <note>original: *lychnidis coronariae*</note> in Dioscorides, I remember reading **crane-foot** <note>original: *geranopodion*</note>; we have said, following Dioscorides, that it is effective for snake strikes, and the crane itself is effective against venomous animals: for those who fear venomous animals while sleeping at night should keep cranes with them, as Avicenna and Rhazes <note>two influential Persian physicians</note> teach.

## THE RELATIONSHIP OF THE EVERGREEN TREE WITH ANIMALS. Cap. XXIIII.

<image-desc>A decorative initial letter D, showing a lush garden scene with a wooden fence or trellis.</image-desc>

We have spoken of the parts of plants that demonstrated the limbs of animals; now we shall treat their actions which imitate the actions of animals, and we shall divide them into several parts: namely, the manner of living, mating, generating, super-fetation <note>conceiving again while already pregnant</note>, and walking. And first, concerning those that live through winter without food, such as the **evergreens** <note>original: *perpetuifoliae*</note>. We shall investigate the reason for this, and then the Phytognomony <note>the art of knowing a plant's virtues by its appearance</note>. For there are trees, shrubs, firewood-plants, and herbs from which the leaves do not fall; we shall mention some from the Greek and Latin authors, such as the palm, olive, wild olive, myrtle, pine, wild pine, pitch-pine,

# BOOK FOUR.

->**fir, cedar, juniper, carob tree, phillyrea, cork oak, yew, tamarisk, boxwood, holm oak, holly, celastrus, buckthorn, Christ’s thorn, sharp thorn, Greek strawberry tree, strawberry tree, turpentine tree, ivy, rosemary, mastic, and others.**<-

Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle, often called the "father of botany"</note> says that all narrow-leaved plants are oily and fragrant. But let us examine the reason for their "perpetual hair" <note>original: *perennis comae* — a poetic way of referring to evergreen foliage</note>, which we judge to be a difficult task, since the opinions of our ancestors are varied and many. Theophrastus says that trees which flourish with perpetual foliage produce both their buds and their fruit late; this is because of their density and dryness, for the nourishment in them flows slowly, even to the leaves. And if any of the evergreen kind should sprout or fruit early, such as **ivy** or **buckthorn** <note>original: *rhamnus*</note>, it happens either by reason of perpetual heat and moisture, or for all these causes combined. 

In his books of history, he says that plants growing in the fields of Elephantine and Memphis <note>Cities in ancient Egypt</note> never drop their leaves, and in the island of the Delta, very little time passes without the plants being perpetually green. He notes that in the island of Crete there stands a plant that never loses its leaves, and an oak in the territory of Thurii <note>An ancient Greek city in southern Italy</note>; for the region and the moist soil contribute greatly to this endurance. Indeed, plants in dry and thin soils lose their leaves sooner, and older trees lose them before young ones. 

Plutarch <note>A Greek historian and philosopher</note>, giving a reason for the immortality of the ivy’s foliage, says this is not proof of heat or cold, since the **myrtle**, which is classed among the colder plants, remains perpetually green. Empedocles <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed the theory of the four elements</note> suggests it is caused by a certain moderation of the pores and channels <note>original: *spiraculorum, meatuumque*</note>, which draw out nourishment equally and repair the loss of moisture. 

Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, author of the *Natural History*</note>, reporting the opinions of others, says that leaves which do not fall are thick, calloused, and narrow; but this definition is false, as he says leaves do not fall from those whose sap is oilier. For who can understand this in the case of the **holm oak** <note>original: *ilex*</note>? Timaeus the Mathematician <note>Possibly Timaeus of Locri, a Pythagorean philosopher</note> thinks they fall when the Sun passes through Scorpio, by the power of the constellation acting as a kind of poison in the air. Why this cause should not hold true against all plants, we may rightly wonder. 

Aristotle, in his *Problems*, offering a reason why pigs do not wish to lose their hair in winter, says that they are all "hot" <note>Referring to the ancient theory of bodily humors and qualities</note>, and hair clings to the hot part; for it is necessary for fat to be hot. Behold, the reason appears: in hot and oily things, the foliage does not fall. Aphrodiscus <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle</note> offers another reason: why does the front part of the head go bald, but the back less so? Is it because the front of the head is soft and loose? When the hair lacks nourishment—as it does not rest on a solid part in the front—it falls out easily; but the back is drier and denser. For this same reason, foliage does not fall from dense and thick plants.

Aristotle also asks in his *Problems* why some animals change and others do not? Is it because those whose nature cannot conquer or dominate moisture are unchangeable? Elsewhere, Theophrastus, assigning a cause for why in some places the **fig** and the **vine** do not lose their leaves, says it is because they never lack sufficient nourishment, and some plants gain this by their nature, others by their location. But Aristotle and Theophrastus said it could happen from many or all of these reasons, as if they were ignorant of the true cause.

I shall offer my own opinion. I say that the sap is the cause; by its own stickiness <term>lentore: a quality of being viscous or slow-moving</term>, it makes the plant sufficient unto itself. Just as animals that live through winter without food, so it must be understood in these trees that flourish with eternal foliage: they retain their leaves in winter because they have much and sufficient nourishment. By their own heat and stickiness, they preserve the sap in the stems <note>original: *pediculis* — the stalks of the leaves</note> so that it is not destroyed. 

And Nature, as we have often said, brings forth what is beneficial out of necessity. For plants that are born in northern and cold places had to be dense and thick, and not be stripped of their foliage; for those that possess great strength can better resist the cold and allow the force of the frost to enter less, just as wild trees do. Another reason is available: that all these plants do not sprout when the cold arrives, nor do they lose their leaves. 

But let us ask what secret powers we can gain from this study of natural signs <term>Physiognomonia: the practice of discerning character or properties from outward appearance</term>. Plants that are not stripped of their foliage in winter demonstrate the nature of those animals that live without food in caves during winter, living off their own substance—such as **snakes, dormice, hedgehogs, porcupines, turtles, lizards, crocodiles, and swallows**—and they are helpful for baldness, urinary blockages, ear infections, and discharges of the 
eye— <meta>The catchword 'oculo-' indicates the next page begins with a word relating to the eyes.</meta>

## PLANTS THAT IMITATE THE CONCEPTION OF ANIMALS. Chapter XXV.

NOW let us follow with those plants that imitate the conception of animals. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note> said that something notable happens in the **cleavers** <note>original: *aparine*; a plant known for its sticky seeds</note>. For the flower is born within that very rough and bristly part; it does not emerge or show itself clearly, but instead ripens inside and produces seed. This makes it similar to what occurs in **dogfish** <note>original: *galeis*; likely referring to certain sharks that Aristotle identified as having internal eggs</note> and **vipers**. For those animals, once they have produced eggs within themselves, soon give birth to live young; and this plant, containing and maturing the flower within itself, then brings forth fruit. Hippocrates calls it *philistion* and *philetaerion*, because, as Galen <note>A prominent Roman physician and philosopher</note> thinks, the flower matures not openly but in secret, and germinates the seed within itself just like animals that give birth within themselves, like the viper. It is also called *Philanthropos* <note>Greek for "friend of man"</note> because, like a friend, it tends to cling to the clothes of those passing by. 

But these descriptions should be understood to refer to the **greater bur** <note>original: *lappa*; likely burdock</note>, which also clings to clothing with its seed; in that plant, the flower is born not clearly but hidden within, and it conceives inside itself, which is a notable find in that bur. It is not, however, the **cleavers** <note>original: *aparine*</note> of Dioscorides <note>The author of 'De Materia Medica'</note>, in which a white flower shines out, emerging rather than being hidden, and the seed protrudes in the shape of a navel, channeled and visible to all. The tenacity of this plant's foliage clings to clothes, whereas in the other, it is only the tenacity of the burs, not the leaves, that clings. 

Aristotle, in his book on animals, has this to say about the **viper**: "Among serpents, the viper produces a live animal, although it first produced eggs within itself. This egg is covered with a soft skin, like that of fish; the fetus is formed on top and is not contained in a hard shell. It gives birth to small little vipers wrapped in membranes that burst on the third day; it sometimes happens that those still in the womb burst through the membranes by gnawing them." 

Nature shows us first that this plant is effective against the bite of vipers. But Dioscorides said that the juice and leaves of his *aparine*, when drunk, are effective against the bites of vipers and **venomous spiders** <note>original: *phalangiorum*</note>, as well as for ear pain and **scrofula** <note>original: *strumis*; a swelling of the lymph nodes</note>. The **slough of a snake** <note>original: *anguis senecta*; the shed skin</note> itself, boiled in wine and poured in, also heals ear pains. The viper itself treats scrofula and its own venom—an association I believe occurred through the fault of Dioscorides, since he was ignorant of Theophrastus’s *aparine*. There is another kind of flower which Apollodorus reports grows among the Parthians, called **brotherly-love** <note>original: *philadelphum*</note> for the reason that its branches spontaneously join together at intervals, like living creatures, and afterward part ways, conceive, and give birth.

## PLANTS THAT SHOW THE SUPERFETATIONS OF ANIMALS. Chapter XXVI.

THERE is also **superfetation** <note>The occurrence of a second conception during pregnancy, leading to embryos of different ages in the womb</note> in plants, just as in animals. Among animals, the **hare** and the **rabbit** undergo superfetation; among plants, the **citron**, **pine**, **Indian fig**, **carob** <note>original: *siliqua*</note>, and many others. The citron tree bears fruit at all hours; while some are falling, others are budding, and others are ripening, according to Theophrastus, from whom Pliny <note>A Roman naturalist and author of 'Natural History'</note> draws. The citron tree is fruit-bearing at all hours, with some falling, some ripening, and some budding underneath. 

Pliny says that **hares** <note>original: *dasypodes*</note> give birth every month and undergo superfetation; they are impregnated immediately after giving birth, and they conceive even while the young are nursing. And elsewhere: "The hare alone, besides the rabbit, undergoes superfetation, nursing one, while carrying another in the womb covered with fur, and yet another that is just beginning." So say Herodotus, Xenophon, Aelian, and Philes. The ash of a hare’s head, with nard added, sweetens foul breath, according to Pliny. Platina taught that the brain is effective against poisons, and in his *Theriaca*, Nicander extols the hare against the poisons of serpents, scorpions, and spiders...

# BOOK FIVE.

...of parsnips <note>original: *pastinacæ*</note>. Parthian nobles are accustomed to cook citron seeds <note>original: *Citrij grana*</note> in their foods; they recommend them for the sake of the breath, and when drunk, they resist poisons, a history of which is found in Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian who wrote about dining and natural history</note>. According to Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the famous Roman naturalist</note>, the pine tree <note>original: *Pinus*</note> has three stages of fruit at the same time: fresh flowers, already ripe fruit, and others that are decaying. The pine is held in the greatest admiration; it has fruit ripening, fruit that will reach maturity the next year, and then a third set; no tree promises itself more eagerly—in the same month that a nut is picked from it, another ripens, and thus it is distributed so that there is no month in which they do not ripen. Those that have split open on the tree itself are called *zamiae* <note>original: *zamiæ*; these were considered "damaged" or split pine cones that could harm the health of the rest of the crop</note>, and they harm the others unless they are removed. The testicles of a hare <note>original: *leporis testiculi*</note> are effective for promoting intercourse in men and conception in women; the ash of its dung <note>original: *fimi cinis*</note>, drunk in wine in the evening, heals nocturnal coughs, according to Pliny. Pine nuts <note>original: *pinei nuclei*</note> are beneficial for Venus <note>referring to sexual health or libido</note> and conception, as we have said, and they assist with coughs and consumption <note>original: *tabi*</note>, according to Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and the primary authority on herbal medicine in antiquity</note>. The strawberry tree <note>original: *Arbutus*</note> ripens its fruit over an entire year, so that it happens that one set is available while another is about to flower soon, according to Theophrastus <note>The ancient Greek "father of botany"</note>. I have heard that water extracted from the flowers and fruits by distillation is beneficial for the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy; original: *comitialibus*</note>, which the lungs of a hare, preserved in salt and given for thirty days, also provide, according to Pliny. Juniper <note>original: *Iuniperus*</note> and holm oak <note>original: *ilex*</note> are considered year-bearers, and the new fruit hangs on these along with the fruit from the previous year. The holm oak, a species of oak, is effective against serpent bites along with juniper; the rabbit and the hare provide the same, as we have said. The golden thistle <note>original: *Scolymus*</note> flowers late and for a long time, and it is a marvel that without interruption throughout the summer, one part flowers, another conceives, and another gives birth; we have noted it is effective for the same [ailments].

### PLANTS LIVING UPON OTHERS, demonstrating animals living upon others. Chapter XXVII.

SVNT <image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring a figure amidst swirling foliate and floral patterns.</image-desc> & There are also plants living upon others, such as *cadytes* <note>likely a parasitic plant like dodder</note>, mistletoe <note>original: *viscus*</note>, oak-fern <note>original: *dryopteris*</note>, small ferns <note>original: *filicula*</note>, fungi, *hypocisthis* <note>a parasitic plant found on the roots of rockroses</note>, and such things of this kind, which represent animals living upon others, such as snails <note>original: *cochleæ*</note>, lice <note>original: *pediculi*</note>, and others. Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher whose works on biology were foundational</note> says there are animals that arise only in other animals, and nowhere else and in no other way; and Theophrastus follows him. It was given by Nature to many [plants] that they cannot thrive except in others, just as certain animals can only be created within animals—such as those born in shells—and cannot provide food for other suitable animals. There are also crabs that live in the shells of others, according to Aristotle. Some sea lice <note>original: *pediculi marini*</note> cling to dolphins, others to different fish, so that they cannot be driven away, and they do not leave until they have rendered the fish wasted and juiceless; they are found attached to the skins of mullets, sea bass, and rock-dwelling fish. Lice dropped into the ears with vinegar are effective. And elsewhere: stiffness of the neck is softened with the sea creatures called lice, according to Pliny; they are also effective for running ulcers of the head. Mistletoe softens small tumors <note>original: *tubercula*</note> and brings other swellings to maturity; it softens old ulcers and abscesses.

### PLANTS REFLECTING THE ACTIONS OF VARIOUS ANIMALS. Chapter XXVIII.

PLANTAS <image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' containing intricate scrollwork and floral motifs.</image-desc> We will now recount those plants that represent various actions of animals. Clover <note>original: *Trifolium*</note> bristles against storms, just as the skin of a sea calf <note>a seal; original: *vituli marini*</note> does. The fat of a sea calf is mixed for a defect of a "deadened" womb <note>original: *intermortuæ vuluæ vitio*</note>, but its rennet <note>original: *coagulum*</note> is used for those with the falling sickness. Bitumen clover <note>original: *Asphaltites trifolium*</note> is also suitable for the defects of women. A herb is called the chameleon <note>original: *Chamæleon herba*</note> because of the variation of its leaves, for it changes with the color of the earth; here green, there whitish, elsewhere blue are sometimes found, according to Dioscorides. But the chameleon plant does not change colors because of the variation of the earth, but when it clings to something colored; for this reason, the name was not rightly given, nor does it have anything in common with the animal itself; rather, there are vipers that [change] the color of their back...

### PLANTS THAT MIMIC THE ODORS OF ANIMALS.
#### Chapter XXVIII.

M Many are the leaves, flowers, fruits, and roots of herbs that imitate the odors of animals to manifest their powers. First, we shall show those that smell of the goat <note>original: *hircum*</note>, indicating that they are effective for lust, for a goatish odor belongs to those who are lecherous. Indeed, those frequently performing the venereal act, or those of an age sufficient for Venus, smell badly—that is, they reek of the goatish poison. Male stags, when they have satisfied the females, separate themselves because of the heaviness of their lust, and each digs solitary pits and stinks like goats. These things happen to the stag because it is a lecherous animal by its very nature, according to Aristotle. And because the aforementioned animals are also effective against serpents, so too are the same goat-smelling plants effective against serpent bites. Celtic nard <note>original: *Nardus celtica*</note> is often adulterated with an herb called the "little goat" <note>original: *hircula*</note> because of the heaviness of its odor; it is effective against poisonous strikes. There is a genus of nard called *Saphitritico* which reeks of the goatish poison beyond measure and is mixed into antidotes. The *Tragorchis* <note>Goat-orchid</note>, or "goat’s testicle," is so named because it smells of the goat; with its heavy and poisonous odor, it provokes Venus. The most well-known of the pimpernels is the goat-pimpernel <note>original: *Pimpinellarum hircina*</note>, because it breathes the goat; it resists the bites of venomous animals and is excellent for driving out kidney stones <note>original: *calculis*</note>, just as goat's blood is said to do. 

There are many fruits, roots, and herbs that smell of musk <note>original: *moschum*</note>. In the wild goats <note>referring to musk deer</note> that wander and roam the mountains, feeding on fragrant herbs and especially nard, the blood putrefies within the skin and flesh. This collected discharge <note>original: *sanies*</note>, before the abscess breaks, naturally tends toward maturation. When that point is reached, the beast, tormented by the stinging of the irritating humor, rubs itself with great delight against rocks and stones that are glowing from long exposure to the sun. This continues until, an opening having been made in the abscess, the entire foul discharge is poured out from the follicle onto the stones, not unlike how an abscess filled with ripened pus bursts open. The ulcer later forms a scar, and again the rush of blood returns there, filling the "navel" until it swells out into a similar abscess. The local people collect this from the rocks where the poured-out dregs have dried and adhered under the burning sun, according to Simeon and Serapion <note>Medieval medical authorities</note>. It is a theriac <note>a universal antidote</note> for poisons, and specifically for wolfsbane <note>original: *napelli*</note>, according to Avicenna. By its odor, it corroborates the spirits and all the powers of the body, and it does so in a moment because of the thinness of its parts. It is useful for fainting <note>original: *lipothymiæ*</note>, according to Simeon; it corrects vertigo, invites sleep, and stimulates Venus. It strengthens the brain, according to Avicenna and Mesue; it drives away melancholic fear, wipes away the "white spot" <note>original: *albuginem*; likely a cataract or corneal opacity</note> and strengthens the sight, restores the appetite, and destroys "wind" [gas] during the suffocation of the womb <note>original: *matricis suffocationem*; a historical term for hysteria or uterine disorders</note>, according to Platearius. It also improves the breath of the mouth and other things which I am weary to report. Musk-scented octopuses excite Venus, and roses called "musk roses" are beneficial for fainting. A type of geranium called the "musk-needle" <note>original: *acus muscata*</note> gives off a pleasant odor of musk—perhaps the "Latin geranium" mentioned by Pliny. The "bee-grape" <note>original: *vua apiana*</note>, the "musk-pear" <note>original: *pyra myrapia*</note>, and others which breathe the odor of musk are effective for the same purposes. *Bryon*, or *splachnon* <note>Tree moss</note>, is a tree-moss outstanding in odor; it is burned for the delight of its scent to bring about sleep...

# GIAMBATTISTA DELLA PORTA
# OF NAPLES
## PHYTOGNOMONICS
### BOOK FIVE.

->PREFACE.<-

We have completed our account of the similarities of plants that demonstrated the limbs of animals; now those plants come forward whose task is to indicate the diseases and discomforts that afflict the human body. We have already revealed in *Human Physiognomy* <note>Porta refers to his earlier influential work, *De humana physiognomonia* (1586), which claimed a person's character and health could be read from their facial features</note> the method by which we could proceed from the external habits apparent on the face to the routing of internal ailments. Now, the parts of plants—with similarity as their guide—reveal those diseases whose vices and torments they can counter with their own natural gifts. They carry with them the evidence of their own power; indeed, Nature willed that nothing be hidden. Those things which previously relegated us to "blind causes" <note>original: *caeciores causas*; refers to "occult" or hidden properties that were previously thought impossible to explain through logic or the four humors</note> and lulled our senses to sleep in the search for them, Nature now urges and excites us to contemplate, offering her riches unlocked from a more hidden storehouse <note>original: *abstrusiore pænu*; literally a "more concealed pantry" or "inner larder"</note>. But regarding the diseases which plants display—some within themselves, others by mimicking them in their own parts—we shall begin with those they suffer in their own limbs, and then those which, by their parts...

### THE DISEASES OF TREES, AND HOW THEY APPLY TO HUMAN *diseases; and first, how long-lived trees contribute to the longevity of our own lives. Chapter I.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring ornate foliate and vine patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

FOR TREES ARE also infested by diseases: by scorching <note>original: "adustione"; damage from extreme heat or sun</note>, by chilling cold, by "star-striking" <note>original: "sideratione"; a term for sudden blight or canker, historically believed to be caused by the malevolent influence of stars or planets</note>, by worm-infestation, by pain in the limbs, and others; hence, the weakness of their parts shares even the names used for human miseries. In these matters, the greatest subtlety of Nature must be revealed. We might rightly curse her if she had created trees subject to diseases when they enjoy neither movement nor hands with which they might heal or help themselves—unless she did so to call forth the eyes of mortals to this spectacle. She intended for us to contemplate how all things are crafted for our medicine and health, so that we might be reminded that our own diseases can be relieved. She could not have seemed to fulfill her duty unless she had completed her required task in so many and such great ways, even through the display of the diseases of trees. But, lest we refer our readers to our books on Agriculture to distinguish these diseases, we shall touch upon them briefly and point by point. The death of plants is either natural or contrary to Nature. That which is contrary to Nature happens in two ways: it either has external causes or internal ones. External violences are of more than one kind; some are more violent, such as those which are cut down, and others less violent, which proceed from the qualities of the air. There is a three-fold partition of internal causes: either by *dyscrasia* <note>an imbalance of the bodily fluids or "humors"</note>, or by inanition <note>emptiness or exhaustion</note>—which is two-fold, either because nourishment does not reach it, as in cases of drought, or because it is consumed by excessive fertility—and the third way is from an excessive "good condition" <note>over-nutrition or obesity in a plant sense</note>. We shall begin with natural death, for that is what happens in old age. For old age is a natural disease whose boundary is death. Hence, trees were established by Nature so that some enjoy a shorter life and others a longer one, according to the condition and quality of their bodies. From these, we shall take the opportunity to speak of the length and shortness of our own lives—namely, how we might live for a short or long time—leaning upon these principles, which are quite different from those of the Physicians. For instance, rejecting as false what the Astrologers <note>original: "Genethliaci"; those who cast birth charts to predict the date of death</note> say, who fix a goal for life's end, we say instead that those who guard against infirmities and avoid harmful things can lead a longer life. Because life is dear to almost everyone, I judge that our instructions will be all the more precious. We acknowledge, therefore, that those plants, animals, and all things born of the earth which live longer and renew themselves, or which are [less] subject to putrefaction, can—by impressing their qualities upon us—cause us to live longer, be renewed, and be less corrupted. We shall be able to use these for food, baths, ointments, fumigation, and other methods. We shall begin with the plants that are longer-lived; from there we shall come to the rest, and we shall investigate life from their "Physiognomony" <note>here meaning the physical signs or "signatures" of health and age</note> and the histories of authors. Hippocrates, in his book *On Humors*, says that trees which have thin, dry bark and consist internally of dry flesh [wood] are healthy and long-lived, and do not easily rot, just like tortoises and whatever is of that kind. Democritus established the root of trees as the author of life; for he judged that twisted trees have longer and more vigorous roots, and that they both prepare and retain for themselves a great deal of nourishment to enjoy. Because such a tree intercepts nourishment slowly and bit by bit, it transmits it upward to the trunk; certainly, the trunk of such trees is denser and more compact. The passages of straight trees are more extended and without bends, and therefore shorter-lived, because the supply of nourishment is sent up from the root more quickly. Therefore, the roots of these do not consist of as good a condition as those of the former. And since the beginnings of life are established from the roots, in those where the roots are more robust, the future trees will likewise be more robust and of a more prolonged life.

### PHYTOGNOMONICA

of the introduction <note>original: "introductionis"; the page begins with the end of this word</note>. For he asserts that straight roots are weak, as they cannot protect themselves from inconveniences for the sake of preservation. Indeed, trees are shaken by cold and heat, both of which are sent down from the upper parts through straight passages to the roots, thereby corrupting them. And beyond the harms of cold and heat, the trunks are agitated by the force of winds and the reciprocal ebb and flow of fluctuations; by this shaking and tossing, the roots are disturbed and mutilated. 

But Aristotle and Theophrastus feel otherwise: they argue it is not true that the roots of long-lived trees are necessarily long and thick. As an example, they bring forward the fig tree, which relies on a long and thick root yet does not have a perennial life. Nor do trees with straight, upright growth necessarily have a long life—such as the fir, the palm, and the cypress—nor do those that progress with rapid growth. Instead, they identified density, dryness, solidity, and "fatness" <note>original: "pinguedinem"; referring to resinous or oily content</note> as the causes of life, and it is to these that length of life ought to be assigned. 

Elsewhere, Theophrastus said that aquatic plants have a shorter life than terrestrial ones, just as we clearly perceive in the animal kingdom. Regarding terrestrial plants, all country-folk say that the wild ones—indeed, it can be said simply of the wild ones—have a longer life than the "urban" or cultivated ones, and generally those distinguished by their opposite type. For instance, the wild olive lives longer than the olive, and the wild fig longer than the fig, precisely because they are more robust, denser, and less fertile in fruit. 

But we shall investigate the antiquity of trees from the writings of authors. Pliny, citing Theophrastus, notes: the cypress, cedar, ebony, lotus, boxwood, yew, juniper, wild olive, and olive do not feel decay or age. They consider cedar to be the most eternal of all, based on a clear judgment of all materials in the Temple of Diana at Ephesus, especially since it was completed over four hundred years with all of Asia contributing to its construction. It is agreed that its roof is made of cedar beams. Also memorable is the Temple of Apollo at Utica, where beams of Numidian cedar endure exactly as they were placed from its first origin, one thousand one hundred and eighty-eight years ago. 

Because its material was eternal, they were used to making statues of the gods from it. There is a cedar Apollo Sosianus in a shrine in Rome, brought from Seleucia. From the city of Tripoli in Syria, situated at the foot of Mount Lebanon <note>original: "Olybani montis"</note>, on the summit there still endure cedars planted by the hand of Solomon in a *quincunx* <note>term: quincunx — an arrangement of five objects, with four at the corners and one in the middle, like the five on a die</note> pattern. Books that are drenched in its oil are not touched by moths. They record that the books of Numa, found after five hundred and thirty-five years, had been treated with cedar, and for that reason, he believed the moths had not touched the writings of Pythagorean philosophy within them. Because of this eternity of the material, Pythagoras advised that the gods should be honored with cedar, laurel, cypress, oak, and myrtle, as is held from Iamblichus. 

Dioscorides relates the power of "cedria" <note>original: "Cedriæ"; cedar resin or oil</note>, which preserves dead bodies; for this reason, some have called it the "life of the dead." The juniper has the same virtue as the cedar, and its heartwood is more solid than the cedar. In Saguntum, Spain, they say there is a Temple of Diana brought from Zacynthus with its founders two hundred years before the fall of Troy, as the author Bocchus states; and that it is held below the town itself, which Hannibal spared, led by religious awe; its juniper beams endure even now. 

The cypress also does not feel decay or age. It is well known that the folding doors in the Temple of Diana at Ephesus were made of cypress, and even now, after nearly four hundred years, all the material endures looking like new. It should also be noted that the doors were kept in their glued joints for four years before use. Does not the statue of Veiovis <note>note: an ancient Roman god often associated with the young Jupiter or Apollo</note> on the Citadel, made of cypress, still endure, dedicated in the five hundred and fifty-first year from the founding of the city? Thucydides narrates that there were chests made of cypress in which the bones of those who had been killed in war were preserved; they say this was customary because, I believe, it knows nothing of rot. 

Plato judged that public laws and institutes to be placed in sacred places should be written on cypress tablets, because he thought they would be more eternal than bronze ones. Nor do the wild olive and the olive feel old age, as we have said. Olives planted by the hand of the elder Scipio Africanus still endure at Liternum. At Argos, an olive was said to still endure in Pliny's time, to which Argus tied Io after she was changed into a cow. At Olympia, there is the wild olive from which the first Hercules was crowned, and it was then religiously guarded. At Athens, too, an olive is said to endure, produced by Minerva in her contest. The olives are therefore very firm for living, and it is agreed among authors that they last about two hundred years. It grows so slowly that Hesiod denied that any planter of an olive ever perceived fruit from it, so slow a thing it was. But no tree lives longer, nor is the nature of any wood more eternal, than the vine, and especially the wild vine. Theophrastus writes of its life from the planting of the trunk as the beginning of its time...

It cites ancient wonders, such as the Temple of Diana, and philosophers like Plato and Pythagoras to illustrate the "eternal" nature of these woods.</summary>

### BOOK FIVE

...to be completed in at most two hundred years. Pliny observed a statue of Jupiter in the city of Populonia <note>An ancient Etruscan city</note> made from a single vine, which remained uncorrupted for so many ages. Likewise, a libation bowl at Marseille and the temple of Juno at Metapontum stood with columns made of grapevine wood. Even now, the roof of the Ephesian Diana is ascended by stairs made of a single Cypriot vine, since there they grow to an extraordinary size; however, he believes those were made from wild vines. Mutianus, three times a consul, among those who wrote after seeing it recently, stated that the statue of Ephesian Diana was made of grapevine wood and had never been changed, though the temple was restored seven times.

By the providence of nature, two liquids most pleasing to human bodies were granted: oil and wine. **Honeyed wine** <term>mulsum: a traditional Roman beverage made by mixing wine and honey</term> made from old wine and honey is most beneficial. Many have endured a long old age nourished by honeyed wine alone, without any other food—following the famous example of Pollio Romulus, who exceeded his hundredth year. When the Divine Augustus, as his guest, asked by what method he had best preserved that vigor of mind and body, he replied: "Honeyed wine within, oil without."

The power of oil is to warm the body and protect it against chills. Homer testifies that wine contains the seeds of heat when he speaks of "sparkling wine" <note>original Greek: ἄθοπα οἶνον (athopa oinon), often translated as "fiery" or "dark" wine</note>; and they say oil has no less power in heating bodies. They call sorrow the poison of life, and its most excellent antidote is sweet, clear wine, to which Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine</note> is said to have attributed so much that he weighed it in equal balance with the gods. Plato’s opinion supports this: that from the tempered heat of wine, the character and strength receive a wonderful nourishment. The odor of wine excellently nourishes the spirit and quickly feeds the body, while it charms the senses with pleasure; it is considered resistant to poisons and healthful to nature, not only by taste but by smell—just as hemlock is a poison to man, so wine is a poison to hemlock.

The highest authors of the medical art have extolled wine with wonderful praises. Homer proclaims sweet wine for winning over goodwill, but describes as violently stupefying that which Ulysses served to the Cyclops. Niceratus said that wine suits poets and acts in place of a great horse. Democritus thinks that those who abstain from wine are of a harsher nature. Wine, therefore, should be sweet, clear, and fragrant; but watery, cold wine is to be avoided because it putrefies within the veins and quickly turns sour. For watery wine is prone to putrefaction, whereas tempered wine warms a cold habit of the body, cools a hot one, moistens the dry, and dries the over-moist; and as Galen says, it recreates the natural humor and fosters heat. For the elderly, it should not be diluted with water; for old age is cold, says Plato; old age glows with undiluted wine and is made softer, like iron in fire. When Democritus was at the very point of death, breadcrumbs soaked in wine and held to his nose retained his fleeing spirit as long as he pleased, so that he might comply with his friends' wishes.

But wine is made not only from vines, but from other fruits as well. There is a marvelous power in it for drawing out the internal virtues of things, which **Chemists** call the **fifth essence** <term>quintam essentiam: the "quintessence" or most concentrated medicinal extract of a substance</term>, which we ought to use most of all. Oil becomes more potent with age; when pure, it passes into nourishment, adds strength, fattens, restores a good physical condition, and provides a good color. We anoint with oil those things we wish to keep preserved. Plants consist of oil, and animals of fat; for this reason, plants are longer-lived than animals, as oil dissolves less easily than fat. "Fat" trees are of longer life; oily trees are those which pour back an oily moisture, and they shine within from their richness.

Theophrastus relates that the larch and walnut feel old age most slowly; the pitch pine and the pine are most firm against decay and woodworms, and remain durable for many years when buried in the earth. On this account, Pliny says that those forests which are tapped for the sake of pitch and resin are most useful for **consumptives** <term>phthificis: those suffering from phthisis or tuberculosis, a wasting disease of the lungs</term> or those who do not recover their strength after a long sickness. It is well established that the air in such an area is more beneficial than a voyage to Egypt or drinking herbal milk-drinks in the mountain summers. Because of this, ancient physicians judge pine nuts to be most suitable for the elderly, for they have a familiar nourishment—warm, moist, and fatty—so that it soothes all roughness and, while increasing natural moisture, dries out the superfluous and purges the putrid. Hence, those who give one **drachm** <note>A small unit of weight</note> of such kernels daily to the elderly after food bring much help to the liver and stomach. The same is also to be said of pistachios. The palm is immune from destruction and old age, as even the Orphic songs testify.

PHYTOGNOMONICA

# The palm, equal to a long-lived creature in its branches.

The palm of Delos <note>Delos is a Greek island, the mythical birthplace of Apollo</note> has been observed since the age of the god Apollo. The Greeks call the palm a symbol of glory and victory because, among all trees, it is the most "macrobic" <note>long-lived</note>; it is fitting for glory to be perpetual and never grow old. Furthermore, those Greek epithets for the palm—"steadfast-leaved" <note>original Greek: ἐμπεδόφυλλον (empedophyllon)</note> and "ever-leafed" <note>original Greek: ἀείφυλλον (aeiphyllon)</note>—are most appropriate, because it is distinguished by firm and perpetually green foliage. Among other trees, we see none that clearly retain the same leaves; rather, as the old ones are cast down, others grow in their place. Dates are friends to old age and prolong it. According to Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, a Roman naturalist</note>, their chief value lies in their milky, fatty juice, which possesses a certain wine-like flavor within a very sweet honey.

There is a holm-oak <term>ilex: the evergreen or holly oak</term> on the Vatican hill that is older than the city of Rome itself; an inscription on it in bronze Etruscan letters signifies that the tree was already worthy of religious veneration back then. The people of Tibur <note>Modern-day Tivoli</note> also have origins much older than the city of Rome. Among them, three holm-oaks still stand that are older than Tiburtus, the founder of their city, and it is said he was inaugurated near them. Tradition holds that he was the son of Amphiaraus, who died at Thebes one generation before the Trojan War. Near the city of Troy, oaks are said to have been planted on the mound of Ilium at the time the city first began to be called Ilium. In the region of Pontus, near Heraclea, there are altars to "Jupiter the Army-Leader" <note>original: Iouis Stratij (Jupiter Stratios)</note>, and there stand two oaks planted by Hercules. 

In the northern region of the Hercynian Forest <note>A vast ancient forest in Germany</note>, the immense size of the oaks remains untouched by the ages; as old as the world itself, they exceed the miraculous by a nearly immortal fate. It is well known that hills are raised up by the collision of their roots meeting underground; where the earth does not follow, the roots curve into arches right up to the branches. They struggle against one another, bending into the shape of open gates wide enough to let troops of cavalry pass through. 

The fruit of acorn-bearing trees was the first food for man, so much so that the Arcadians were called "acorn-eaters" <note>original Greek: βαλανόφαγοι (balanophagoi)</note>, according to Plutarch. Pliny remarked that acorns were the wealth of many nations who enjoyed peace; they endured long-lived and uncorrupted, as is clear from these authors. Not only are acorn-bearing trees long-lived, but all wild trees are far more perennial than cultivated "urban" ones, as shown by Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher often called the "father of botany"</note>. Just as the life of wild animals is longer than that of domesticated ones, wild trees far surpass cultivated ones in length of life. Indeed, cultivated plants become more prone to decay through manuring and irrigation. For this reason, the prophet Hesiod omitted the use of the dung-pit in his precepts on agriculture; he was looking to health rather than fertility, believing that a field could be made rich by the timely plowing-under of the stalks of lupins and beans.

Authors state that a plant at Delphi was planted by the hand of Agamemnon <note>The legendary king who led the Greeks in the Trojan War</note>, and another in the grove of Caphyae in Arcadia. There is also the region of Aulocrenes, through which one travels from Apamea into Phrygia, where a plane tree is shown from which Marsyas was hung after being defeated by Apollo <note>In mythology, the satyr Marsyas lost a musical contest to Apollo and was flayed alive</note>; even then, that tree was chosen for its great size. 

The orange tree lives for a long time—as many as two hundred years—and its power is to prevent putrefaction in the body. Aloe is endowed with a perpetual and immortal greenness; it lives even when torn from the earth, being almost "un-wilting." It is effective against decay, protecting the bodies of both the living and the dead from rot when mixed with myrrh, according to Mesue <note>A famous medieval Arabic medical authority</note>. The Squill <note>a bulbous flowering plant</note> flourishes with immortal leaves and lives for a long time even when hung out of the earth; when grown in a house, it removes the harm of "evil medicines" <note>likely referring to poisons or spells</note>. It renders the herbs or plants placed near it "immortal" and safe from worms and rot, and it works wonders in humans. 

Now let us pass to the cereal grains. Among these, none rises better than wheat, followed by millet, which can be preserved for a long time—nearly a hundred years if stored perfectly. The Sarmatian tribes are nourished chiefly by a porridge made of this. The Ethiopians know no other fruit of the earth but millet; therefore, the best should be chosen for our food—at least that which has been kept uncorrupted for three years, grown in a field that is not marshy or manured, but from dry hills. 

Grass has an eternal nature, a perennial yield, and a restored fertility; it flourishes at every turning point of the year, in every climate, soil, and constellation, so that it clothes the whole world in a pleasant greenness and adorns it with a graceful beauty as it propagates itself step by step. This is a thing kin to the wheat family and next in nobility. Because of this, the ancients told the story that Glaucus <note>A fisherman who became a sea-god</note>, having been wounded, achieved immortality by eating this herb, as Athenaeus reports from the verses of Aeschion; we shall demonstrate this with a more manifest sign. A species of grass is...

# BOOK FIVE.

...which the Greeks call *coronopon* <note>original: "coronopon," likely buck's-horn plantain</note>, as if it were a "crow’s foot," because a stalk rises from the middle of the leaves and is jointed like a crow’s foot, showing the likeness of a leg. We shall speak of the deer a little later among the long-lived animals. From reeds we extract sugar <note>original: "saccharum"</note>; not only is it incorruptible itself, but it excels others in preventing decay. When applied to wounds, it frees them from putrefaction; we have seen even massive wounds healed by it alone. Therefore, let sugar be a familiar friend to those desiring to prolong their lives, because it permits neither the humors nor food to rot in the stomach. 

Now we shall speak of honey. The shrubs from which bees collect honey have eternal foliage; they are fragrant, rich, and everlasting, as one reads in the works of those devoted to Agriculture. The finest honey is produced by thyme <term>thymus: a fragrant herb known for attracting bees</term>; next in quality to thyme is savory <note>original: "thymbra"</note>, then wild thyme and oregano. Of the third grade, yet still noble, are rosemary <note>original: "marinus ros"</note> and winter savory; however, the lowest grade is "rustic honey," which is taken from wilting vegetables and manured herbs which, as we have said, are closer to putrefaction. Bees delight in no flower more than balm <note>original: "meliphylla," or honey-leaf</note>; so also they gather from heather, the strawberry tree, pine, holm-oak, ivy, acorn-bearing trees, the terebinth <note>a species of sumac</note>, mastic, cedar, Italian starwort, and cinnamon-cassia, according to Columella <note>a Roman writer on agriculture</note>. Nor do we exclude the olive from these, for it is certain that many swarms are produced from the growth of the olive, according to Pliny, even if some people disapprove of it. 

The places where they live are far removed from the odors of sewers, dung-heaps, and baths; they hold hollow rocks and valleys in hatred, but live in the best regions—healthy and purified—such as on the islands of Sicily, Mount Hymettus, and Mount Hybla; and from those places, soon to the island of Calydna and others. There is, therefore, a celestial power in honey and an inexpressible potency of Nature, since it preserves dead bodies and living ones wonderfully from decay, and extends them into eternity. The Greeks, to show the divine nature of honey, say a Nymph named Melissa <note>meaning "Bee" in Greek</note> discovered it, so that the grateful memory of the Nymphs might be celebrated. Pliny writes that a centaur <note>original: "hippocentaurum"</note> was brought from Egypt to Claudius Caesar preserved in honey. Papinius <note>likely referring to the poet Statius</note> recorded that the corpse of Alexander the Great, smeared with honey, remained unyielding to rot. As the Poet says:

> ->*Lead also to the Emathian spirits, where the warlike founder*<-
> ->*of the city, steeped in Hyblaean nectar, endures.*<-
<note>This refers to Alexander the Great (the Emathian) in his tomb in Alexandria, preserved in honey (Hyblaean nectar)</note>

From this method of protecting bodies from decay, it has been found that many have experienced a long old age simply by soaking in mead <note>original: "mulsi," a mixture of wine and honey</note>, as in the famous example we mentioned of Romulus Pollio <note>A Roman official who, when asked by Augustus how he reached 100, replied: "Within by mead, without by oil"</note>. The Pythagoreans <note>followers of the philosopher Pythagoras</note>, in order to keep their bodies whole and unimpaired, ate honey, honeycomb, and bread, as is held from Iamblichus. Democritus, when near death, prolonged his life by the scent of honey and wine until the sacred festival of the *Thesmophoria* <note>a festival in honor of Demeter/Ceres</note> was finished, according to Athenaeus and Laertius. 

Bees have a very long life, and there are those who believe that if they die, they may be revived if they are kept under a roof in winter until they are warmed by the spring Sun and cherished all day in the ash of a fig tree. The scent of honey nourishes greatly and strengthens both the spirits and the brain; hence it is helpful for us to walk and take pleasure in those places where bees live, for they choose the most select spots: clean, fragrant, with pure and harmless air, where the best shrubs and flowers grow. There, honey should be tasted frequently, unless one fears the "fire of bile" <note>an excess of yellow bile, associated with a hot or angry temperament</note>; for it helps greatly toward the safety of life. 

We ought to use these things we have mentioned not only for eating but for smelling, for human Nature is helped by odors, and the spirits are helped; for an odor drawn in through the nostrils is pulled to the heart and the brain. Indeed, there are even regions in hot climates where men live by scents alone, as is held from Pliny. An odor rouses a spirit that is compressed or suffocated, and it retains a spirit that is exhaling <note>fading away</note>. We see the "mouth of the womb" turn itself up and down where a sweet scent breathes; a faint and fleeting spirit is retained by odors, as we have experienced many times. By the scent of the so-called "Elixir of Life," composed of various aromatics, we have retained the exhaling soul of many. Myrrh and frankincense are powerful for preserving bodies so they do not rot, and the trees themselves are incorruptible. We can also use these in baths and ointments by extracting their essence with water or composing salves, and the body is wonderfully refreshed—likewise by extracting oil and using it for rubbing after washing. Furthermore, let people inhabit the healthiest places, where long-lived men, animals, and ancient trees live; for there the air is most healthy and least prone to rot, and the suns are temperate.

...sunlight, winds, and cold. For Plato said that long-lived men are found in high and elevated regions. One should choose animals, herbs, fruits, crops, and vegetables from these places, which are cleared by temperate weather and fostered by the pleasant rays of the sun; where no waters stagnate, and the cultivated lands are not fattened by dung heaps but by their own native moisture. Where such things are born, they are preserved for a long time without corruption. Here, at last, one must dwell; in these regions we ought to walk, among plane trees, olive groves, pine groves, cypress groves, myrtle groves, and citrus groves. Likewise, we should walk among long-lived and sweet-smelling herbs, such as rosemary, savory, wild thyme, sage, and the like: handling them with our hands, rubbing them, and smelling them. Since these are immune to putrefaction, they remove all decay from the heart, brain, blood, humors, and spirits, and they bring about longevity.

## THAT LONG-LIVED ANIMALS ARE EFFECTIVE FOR THE PROLONGATION OF LIFE
### Chapter 11.

<image-desc>A square woodcut decorative initial 'I' featuring a bearded figure, possibly a scholar or holy man, seated at a lectern or desk within an ornate vaulted room or study with architectural details.</image-desc>
We ought to understand the same regarding animals; for those that endure for a long age—their blood, flesh, milk, marrow, and other parts—can contribute to the permanence of life. Hippocrates, as we have said, says that animals of longer life are "dry" and those that have a dry shell <note>original: "corticem," used here to mean a shell or outer covering</note>, such as tortoises. We have said that plants surpass animals in the length of their lives because they are less subject to putrefaction; therefore Porphyry the Pythagorean, relying on the authority of the ancients, detested the eating of animals so that men might live longer. But let us see which animals are long-lived. The deer excels other animals in the length of its life because it lacks a gall bladder, according to Aristotle; as does the dolphin. Hesiod’s poem <note>Hesiod was an early Greek poet; this fragment is often attributed to his "Precepts of Chiron."</note> is well known regarding the life of certain long-lived animals:

-> *The chattering crow lives nine times longer* <-
-> *Than the generation of a man nearing old age,* <-
-> *The deer exceeds four times the age of the crow,* <-
-> *The raven triples the age of the swift-footed deer,* <-
-> *But the Phoenix, the bird of rebirth, multiplies that of the raven ninefold.* <-

The life of deer is undeniably long. To determine their lifespan, Alexander the Great <note>original: "Alexander Magnus"</note> fastened collars onto many deer, which, when captured after a hundred years, showed no sign of old age, according to Solinus. The Arcadians say that a certain Arcesilaus, living in Lycosura, saw a deer sacred to the "Lady" <note>likely referring to the goddess Despoina or Artemis</note>, heavy with age, which had a collar around its neck inscribed with this verse: "I was a fawn captured when Agapenor was at Troy." <note>Agapenor was the leader of the Arcadians during the Trojan War. This implies the deer lived for centuries.</note> By this testimony, it can be confirmed that the deer is a far more long-lived animal even than the elephant, according to Pausania’s *Description of Greece* <note>original: "in Arcadicis"</note>. The deer is renewed by eating snakes; when it feels itself burdened by old age, it draws snakes out of their holes with the breath from its nostrils and, having overcome the destructiveness of the venom, is restored by feeding on them. Pliny knew certain noblewomen who ate deer meat every day and were free from fevers throughout their long lives. Hence, the flesh of the deer, especially a young one, is effective for the length of life. Aristotle considers no animal to be more long-lived than man, with the exception of the elephant. The Afachae (a people of Africa) inhabit the mountains and live by hunting elephants; likewise the nomadic Ethiopians and the Troglodytes who border Ethiopia eat elephants, so that they are called "Elephant-eaters" <note>original: "elephantophagi"</note>, and according to Pliny, they are neighbors to the Macrobii <term>Macrobii: a legendary people of Africa whose name literally means "Long-Livers"</term>. Snakes live for a long time because they are renewed every year. Dioscorides says that those who eat the flesh of vipers experience a long old age. Pliny and Isigonus say that the Cyrni, a race of Indians, live for one hundred and forty years; for the Ethiopians [live as] Macrobii...

# BOOK FIVE

lives, as Seras <note>likely referring to a classical or Arabic authority on medicine</note> believes; and those who inhabit Mount Cason, because they nourish themselves on the flesh of vipers, find that no harmful animals bother their heads or their clothing. Vipers are renewed—indeed, they surpass deer in their ability to be renewed—and they are effective for the renewal of our own bodies and for the delaying of old age. But if we shudder at the thought of eating a viper, we may feed them to hens, and then we shall eat the flesh of those hens; the same should be done with other such animals. The life of the crow is also very long, as Hesiod attributed nine of our human ages to it; hence Juvenal wrote concerning the long life <note>original: "polychronia"</note> of Nestor:

->*His life’s example was second only to the crow.*<-

Hence the <gloss>nine-generation crow</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ἐννεάγενεα κορώνη"</note> mentioned in the works of Aratus, because it lives for the span of nine ages. Pliny believed that the flesh of the crow was useful in the treatment of very long-lasting illnesses. The eagle also lives for a long time, which is proven by the durability of its nest; according to Aristotle, it also casts off its old age and recovers its youth, as we have mentioned elsewhere. They perish not from old age or sickness, but from hunger, because the upper part of the beak grows so long and hooked that it can no longer be opened. The same can be said of the vulture and the hawk, which strengthen the spirit and are effective for the length of life. Geese are long-lived; Albertus Magnus saw a domestic goose that had exceeded sixty years of age. Celsus lists goose among the meats providing the most nourishment. Doctors first nourish geese with spelt and purified water before offering them as food. The meat of peacocks is incorruptible; even when roasted, it can be preserved for a year, and because of its hardness, it hardly feels the effects of rot. According to Celsus, it provides a great deal of nourishment, especially if the bird is raised at home. We have said, following Hippocrates, that tortoises are dry and live for a long time. In the study of ancient agriculture, if one preserves seeds intended for planting in the shell of a tortoise, they remain unfading, according to Anatolius. Doctors say that to restore human blood, one can use the blood of animals, especially those that are long-lived. Screech-owls <note>original: "Stryges," mythological owl-like creatures</note>, because they are said to drink the blood of infants, always grow young again and become long-lived. And if the stomach is too "raw" or weak to digest these things, they can be cooked with honey, sugar, salt, spices, and similar things that do not rot. The same should be said of milk. We can also nourish such animals on incorruptible grains, such as millet, and the fruits of long-lived trees, and then make use of their milk, blood, and flesh. And because eggs contribute much to nutrition, we can nourish birds with such foods and then eat their eggs.

### ON SALT AND GOLD: BECAUSE THEY NEVER ROT, WE CAN USE THEM AGAINST DECAY. Chapter 3.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' containing a figure seated at a desk, surrounded by foliage and architectural patterns.</image-desc>
Nor shall salt be omitted, which, since it knows nothing of decay, most effectively protects all things from rotting. It is healthful for the natural body; for with it, meat is preserved for a year, and it is so conducive to human nature that we do not know how to live without it. When applied to bodies, it consumes whatever moisture is present, and by its binding quality, it contracts the remaining solid substance; thus, it dries preserved bodies and protects them from rot. It can be eaten in combination with everything, as the "seasoning of all seasonings"; indeed, everything that is unpleasant or unusual to the stomach easily becomes pleasant and fit for nutrition once salt is added. Salt can be extracted from all things, especially from the woods already named, from animals, and from herbs, while retaining its specific virtue. "This is the work, this is the labor" <note>original: "Hoc opus, hic labor," a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid regarding a difficult task</note>, which, God willing, we shall reveal in our sections on distillation. Nor should gold be omitted, as it is the most tempered among all metals and is incorruptible; even when held in a fire for a long time, it maintains its immortality, and when buried under the earth for many centuries, it does not gather rust. Because of its tempered nature, we believe it can miraculously assist human heat, balance the humors, and protect them from corruption. By its own power, it penetrates the hidden seats of the heart <note>the text likely contains a typo "coruis" for "cordis"</note> and can greatly cheer it. Hence, if it could be made "potable" <note>liquid gold or "aurum potabile," a legendary alchemical medicine</note>, it would be highly beneficial to human nature. However, it has not yet been discovered, in my opinion; for the ancient doctors wrongly thought that by mixing it with other things or reducing it to thin leaves, it communicated its virtue. We shall demonstrate this in a specific book dedicated to this work, and we shall show the method by which we might achieve this.

PHYTOGNOMONICA

# PLANTS AND ANIMALS OF SHORTER LIFE TEND TOWARD BREVITY 
# of life. Chapter IV.

ALTHOUGH the opposite could be clear from the contrary examples we have discussed, we will nevertheless provide some examples so that men may become more certain and take care for themselves. Plants and animals with shorter lives—those which are finished by old age more prematurely, those born from decay, and those prone to rotting—can similarly induce putrefaction, ruin, and death in us. **Fungi** <note>Mushrooms</note> arise from rain, are born quickly, and rot; their birth and death occur within seven days; indeed, they are born from rotting wood and other decaying things. The faster they rot and are spoiled by decay, the worse and more dangerous they are. If they do harm, they are digested with great difficulty and cause choking, and they stir up the "cholera" <note>In this context, a "choleric" illness refers to an imbalance of the humors causing violent vomiting or purging, not necessarily the modern bacterial disease</note> disease. **Truffles** <note>original: "Tuberibus"</note> share the same logic of rotting as wood; they are all born when the autumn rains have come, and in certain places they are reported to be watery in taste with no remarkable quality; hence, if eaten frequently, they produce thick and "atrabilious" <note>term: "atrabilares" — relating to black bile, one of the four humors thought to cause melancholy or heaviness</note> humors, leading to apoplexy and paralysis. 

Those **fruits** which grow quickly also wither quickly: such as gourds, melons, mulberries, cherries, and the like; those that are born in damp places produce rotting humors in our bodies. Among meats, **fish** have shorter lives; because they are quickly finished by old age, they rot very rapidly. By soaking the limbs in a foreign moisture, even if they provide some necessary moisture to the body, they grant something subject to quick corruption; hence come premature gray hair, pallor, and the wrinkles of old age. **Snails, eels,** and similar creatures are subject to the same vices, as they are born from mud and rotting waters; thus the flesh of damp animals or those living in water is disapproved of, especially those originating from putrefaction, because they are excessively moist. The flesh of **frogs** is subject to rot because it is loose and damp. Therefore, it should be considered safer and far more praiseworthy to forbid these foods, or to take them sparingly, rather than to commit one’s life to such danger—especially for those who are students of a long-lasting life.

---

# FATTY TREES AND ANIMALS TEND TOWARD 
# fattening. Chapter V.

WE HAVE already spoken of "natural disease"—if indeed it is a disease when one wastes away as the natural moisture fails, so that they seem to have perished from old age rather than illness. Now we shall speak of diseases "contrary to nature," and first of that which happens from an excessively "good habit" <note>meaning a state of being over-nourished or overly "fleshy"</note> and from internal causes. Indeed, diseases happen to plants either from an abundance or a lack of nourishment. There is a genus of trees in which an internal state arises spontaneously from excessive fatness, where the roots pass into an abundance of resinous sap <note>original: "taeda" — refers to torch-wood or highly resinous pine</note>, just as certain animals are suffocated by their own fat. **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany," active in the 4th century BCE</note> enumerates the types of pitch-pines and certain other trees which offer no small benefit to us when we contemplate Nature revealing and betraying herself to be effective for our own fattening and beautification. For those things which grow sufficiently fat themselves can also make us fat. 

**Oily trees** are fat, and our bodies increase and grow fat from sweet and fatty foods and drinks; it is already a common dogma among Physicians that the body is diminished by arid, dry things and thirst, and fattened by sweet, moist things and drink. A corruption happens spontaneously to the **pine** genus from an immoderate excess of nutrition; for when it cannot transmit its food through the resinous wood, it perishes; the peasants say they are "strangled" by obesity and fatness, since all things require some breath, or a release, or an openness of the passages. **Avicenna** <note>A Persian physician and philosopher whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard European textbook for centuries</note> teaches that the **pine nut** <note>original: "pini granum"</note> is used for fattening. He reports the same of the **pitch-pine**, since it grows resinous from excessive fatness in the same manner. The **almond tree** swells with fatty juice, according to Theophrastus: it is so strong in the solidity of its powers that it bursts forth into a luxury of sprouts from its excellent nourishment. Peasants, by way of "punishing" the tree, remove the excessive abundance of nourishment by driving pegs <note>catchword: driving</note> into the tree—
