### BOOK FIVE

...by driving them [the plants], or they show their dug-up roots to the rains and the cold. **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath and one of the most influential physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note> says that those who devour sweet **almonds** grow fat. The **pistachio** tree is a known type of nut, for it is essentially a "domesticated turpentine tree." As we have said, it dies from its own fatness, for it is resin-bearing; according to **Pliny** <note>Roman author of the *Natural History*</note>, resin-bearing trees perish from "obesity" <note>original: "obesitate"</note>. Pistachios have the same uses as pine nuts, as they are effective at inducing fatness. There are also **Indian nuts** <note>possibly coconuts or cashews</note> from an oily and fat tree; their substance is so fat that it resembles butter, the primary power of which is to fatten those who are thin. The **hazelnut**, a type of nut rich in oil, grows so fat—unless it is trimmed and pruned—that it consumes all its nourishment into its own bulk and thus becomes sterile. It contributes so much to fatness that it exceeds belief, and it is more than likely that it increases corpulence. 

**Beech** fruits sweat out a fatty oil, as we have said elsewhere, and more copiously than is typical; by eating them, pigs grow wonderfully fat. Indeed, from the "oil-dregs" <note>term: "fracibus" — the pomace or solid remains left after pressing oil</note>, once the oil is extracted, the greatest fatness is induced in animals. It also fattens **dormice** <note>original: "glires" — a delicacy in ancient Rome</note>, and for that reason, when that tree's crop is plentiful, they are caught wonderfully fattened. A great deal of oil is expressed from **flax seeds** <note>linseed oil</note>, the dregs and remnants of which are stored for fattening types of beasts of burden, especially **oxen**. These become notable for their obesity alone, and are sometimes led around city crossroads wearing crowns to show off the mass of their stall-fed fatness. The **walnut** is also oily, and we have found its dregs to be very suitable for fattening livestock.

**Laser** <note>original: "Laser" — likely the resin from the silphium plant or asafetida</note>, a fatty "tear" or sap sweating from plants, is usually eaten by cattle to make them fat. It is no longer brought from the province of Cyrenaica because the tax collectors who rent the pastures, sensing a greater profit this way, let the cattle graze the plants to extinction. **Mistletoe** <note>original: "Hybear, siue viscum"</note>, which grows on the larch and the fir, is oily and fat. It is very useful for fattening livestock, because more nourishment and fatness are produced in the larch and the fir. It first purges the "vices" <note>impurities or bad humors</note> and then fattens those parts that required the purging. **Hedge mustard** <note>original: "Irio"</note>, according to more recent authors, produces a grain similar to the kernel of a beech nut; by eating it, oxen, beasts of burden, and cattle swell with great fatness. 

However, some fats in our bodies are durable, while others are quickly lost. Fatness from slow-growing and slow-maturing trees remains longer, but from those that grow and mature quickly, it departs quickly. **Figs** grow quickly and mature very fast; they fatten, but their fatness leaves at once. **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> proves this from the example of vineyard guards who, while eating figs for two months, become obese and fat, yet the flesh generated from them is not firm; as soon as they stop eating them, it shrinks away. Figs increase the body's bulk, and for this reason, athletes used to use this food in earlier times. **Pythagoras** was the first trainer to transfer them to a diet of meat. **Citrus** fruit is fat and the rind is oily; a great deal of highly fragrant oil is extracted from it, and for this reason, a decoction of it fattens, according to Avicenna. 

Likewise, humans are typically fattened by eating fat animals. We call those animals "fat" which are usually strangled by excessive fatness, or grow fat beyond measure and are swollen. Among animals, the **pig** fattens the most; it reaches such a peak of fatness that it cannot support itself while standing. **Varro** <note>Roman scholar and writer</note> relates that a pig was seen in Arcadia which was so fat that not only could it not rise, but a shrew had even made a nest in its body, eaten into the flesh, and given birth to mice there. Fat grows to a depth of a foot and three fingers, and according to **Aristotle** and Pliny, a pig grows fat in sixty days. **Chrysippus** <note>A Stoic philosopher</note> said that the pig's soul was given to it in place of salt; that is, as **Cicero** interprets it, so that its fatness would not rot, the soul was given as salt to preserve it. We use its fat <note>lard</note> for the seasoning of all things. Galen said its meat is the easiest to digest and the sweetest, especially in middle age; it also generates good blood and nourishes more powerfully than all other foods because of its similarity to human flesh. Those who, out of the necessity of hunger, have tasted human flesh, reported that it was similar [to pork], according to **Simeon Sethi** <note>An 11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician</note>. Castrated animals fatten more quickly. **Albertus** <note>Albert the Great, a 13th-century polymath</note> says: if you want to have an obese bird of prey, feed it pig meat. Others cook butter in a new clay vessel and wash the pork in this decoction, which they feed to the bird twice a day. After pork, the next best is **kid meat** <note>young goat</note>, according to Galen; they are tender, very fat, and of pleasant flavor. Use only kids for those who are lean <note>original: "solis hoedis in macie vtare"</note>, the same author said, for its meat is easily cooked, nourishes well, generates good blood, and especially...

PHYTIOGNOME <note>Short for *Phytognomonica*, a study of the "signatures" of plants and how they relate to the human body and character.</note>

...especially suckling ones are best to eat; indeed, goat meat is so nourishing that Clitomachus of Carthage <note>A Carthaginian philosopher and head of the Academy in Athens</note> writes that a certain Theban athlete, by feeding on this meat, surpassed all other athletes of his age in strength. Goats become so fat that they can become sterile from their own grease, according to **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, author of the *Natural History*</note>. For an excessively thin hawk, feed it small morsels of meat mixed with warts, and you will restore it to health. The meat of calves is better than that of kids and is more easily digested, though **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire</note> said that kids are second best after veal. To fatten birds of prey, **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, a medieval German friar and polymath</note> suggests giving them veal. Among birds, hens fatten the most; to make them even fatter, one should prohibit "the use of Venus" <note>original: "usum Veneris" — meaning sexual intercourse</note>, or cauterize their loins or the inside of their legs with a glowing iron. The meat of the capon <note>a castrated rooster</note> makes the body obese, according to **Platina** <note>Bartolomeo Sacchi, a Renaissance humanist and author of a famous cookbook</note>. If you mix wheat flour with a fat lizard, saltpeter, and cumin, chickens fattened on this food make humans so fat they might nearly burst. Lizards fatten exceptionally well; according to **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard text for centuries</note>, the meat and fat of the lizard vehemently fatten, specifically in women. **Skinks** <note>a type of lizard</note> fatten beyond measure; the flesh of the skink fattens the body, according to **Rhazes** <note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, a Persian polymath and physician</note>. Ducks become obese beyond measure and provide much nourishment; their meat is thicker than that of other domestic animals, according to **Serapion** <note>Likely Serapion the Younger, an 11th or 12th-century medicinal writer</note>. **Avicenna** wrote that they make men obese and contribute greatly to nutrition, though it is not of a very commendable quality. Duck fat fattens the most, which is why **Albertus**, when he seeks to fatten a hawk, feeds it duck meat. Butter made from milk is extremely fatty; when rubbed on the body, it fattens it. Whey <note>original: "aqua casei"</note> fattens, which is why shepherds' dogs are so fat, according to **Avicenna**. Cheese makes the body fat, and it is eaten with honey afterward. Milk performs the same functions. The tortoise swells and makes one fat; hence, those who seek to fatten horses boil a tortoise with soft fodder. This gives the horses a great but "false fatness" <note>original: "falsa pinguedo" — likely meaning it is temporary or unhealthy bloating</note>, according to **Albertus**.

### LEAN PLANTS AND ANIMALS THAT INDUCE LEANNESS
->Chapter VI.<-

If we prescribe the opposites of those things we have mentioned—lean plants, animals, and other such things—they will induce leanness. Here are the examples: The **ash tree** is a dry tree and produces a dry seed, like the wings of flies; its seed relieves an obese body of its burden, gradually reducing it to leanness. The "tears" <note>resin or sap</note> of the **cacamum** tree <note>an unidentified aromatic tree mentioned by ancient botanists</note> achieve the same, as it is entirely devoid of fatness, according to **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*</note>. Animals that are always lean bring about leanness in those who consume them. The **hare** is fleshy but never fat; those who desire to grow thin or lean should use its meat, according to **Blondus** <note>Michelangelo Biondo, a 16th-century Italian physician</note>. The hardness of hare meat means it provides little and slow nourishment, as all hard things do; this same hardness is a sign of evident dryness, according to **Galen**, with whom **Psellus** and **Paulus** <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Greek physician</note> agree. **Simeon Sethi** <note>An 11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician</note>, collecting what was written by the ancients, says: the meat of the hare is very beneficial for those who wish to thin the body. The **partridge** does not grow fat. **Volaterranus** <note>Raffaele Maffei, a humanist scholar</note>, citing **Aelian**, says that a partridge that has tasted garlic grows so lean that it is ignored by the fowler because of its thinness and the foulness of its smell. **Pliny** denies that partridges grow fat; it seems better that they be boiled rather than roasted, as they become drier and more scorched when roasted. **Isaac the Physician** <note>Isaac Israeli ben Solomon, a 9th-century North African physician and philosopher</note> said it is a food of subtle nourishment. The **sea bass** <note>original: "lupus piscis"</note>, since it never grows fat, is noted by **Galen** and **Celsus** <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a Roman encyclopedist known for his medical work</note> as not providing much nourishment and producing a thinner blood. Wild animals, because they are less fat than domestic ones and are drier, therefore cause weight loss, and we prescribe them to be eaten by those who wish to be thinned. Because **salt** is dry and hard and induces thirst, it brings about leanness; therefore, a falconer, to thin a falcon, gives it salted food or salted ham. Salt, or the most potent oil of all made from **vitriol** <note>term: "oleum vitrioli" — sulfuric acid. In historical medicine, extremely diluted acids were sometimes used, but this is highly toxic</note>—we have seen nothing more miraculous for thinning, through frequent experiments, than oil of vitriol if one drop is given daily in wine. **Vinegar** is wine deprived of all fatness; it thins the body most greatly.

<meta>This page continues the fifth book of the treatise, moving from the physical attributes of animals to the diseases of plants. It specifically explores the "Doctrine of Signatures," where the ailments a plant suffers in nature—such as blight or worm infestations—indicate its medicinal use or effect on the human body.</meta>

BOOK FIVE.

### PLANTS THAT SUFFER FROM BLIGHT, ARE 
### effective against gangrene. Chap. VII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring scrolling floral motifs.</image-desc>
Diseases occurring from the outside will be either according to Nature or contrary to nature; for those that occur by reason of time—namely, by heat and cold—are not to be considered contrary to nature. We shall speak later of those coming from the outside contrary to nature. Those occurring from the outside according to nature will be either public (common to all), such as star-blight, plant-gangrene, and worm-infestation; or they will be particular. We shall speak now of plant-gangrene <note>original: "sphacelifmo," a term for necrosis or blight in plants, mirroring "sphacelus" (gangrene) in humans</note>, a name transferred from a similar effect found in animals; it occurs when the heat is extinguished in the roots due to a wound or an ulcer because of putrefaction, like a mortification. In the chickpea, it dies not from a wound, but from washed-up saltiness; star-blight <note>original: "syderatio," a traditional belief that plants were "star-struck" by sudden heat or cold from the heavens</note> results from a wound and depends entirely on the sky, and young trees especially die from it, such as the vine and the fig. According to **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note>, the chickpea, which died of blight, is effective against cancers and ulcers called "malignant" <note>original: "cacoetha," from the Greek for "bad habits," referring to stubborn, non-healing sores</note> when mixed with honey and barley, as stated by **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and author of the influential herbal *De Materia Medica*</note>. The ashen roughness and pale appearance of the leaves of Sage, resembling a dying or wasting parent, as it grows on parched hills, was the occasion for naming it *elelisphakon* <term>ἐλέλισφακον</term> <note>The ancient Greek name for sage, likely derived from words suggesting "wasting" or "shriveling"</note>, as if you were to say "scorched by the sun" or "wasted away." It cures gangrene in dead parts of the body, to which it recalls the native heat and inherent strength by the familiar power with which it thrives. From the ash of burnt fig stalks, a lye is made; a sponge frequently soaked in this and placed over gangrenes is beneficial, as it cleanses and consumes those parts that have dried up. Likewise, raisins, crushed without seeds and applied with rue, heal gangrene and putrid growths <note>original: "chaetas," likely referring to bristly or hair-like fungal growths in sores</note> in the joints. Very often we have seen the roots of pomegranates "star-struck" by excessive heat when they were very tender; the expressed juice of pomegranate seeds is effective for ulcers of the genitals and the seat, for hangnails, and for those things that swell up on the body.

---

### TREES AND FRUITS THAT BREED WORMS,
### generate worms in our bodies, and those not producing worms are effective against them. Chap. VIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring scrolling floral motifs.</image-desc>
There is also another deadly plague of trees: the generation of little worms, lice, and other animals, for they are gnawed and devoured by them. Nature demonstrates that the fruits of these same trees procreate the same animals in our bodies, so that we might avoid them. There is a twofold generation of worms according to **Theophrastus**: one in the wood, and the other in the fruits; just as the generation of little worms is a common death for almost all trees, though it happens more or less to some. It is peculiar to the apple, pear, fig, and vine; indeed, the worms that are born in the fig give birth to other worms, which are shaped like a horned serpent <note>original: "cerastem," referring to the Cerambyx beetle or similar horned larvae</note>. The fruits of trees also suffer from worm-infestation, such as olives, pears, apples, medlars, and pomegranates, but it happens to pomegranates and sweet apples more than others. Little worms also grow in legumes, such as beans, cowpeas, and wild peas, which quickly perish from this disease. Each creates a peculiar animal according to its own moisture, just as wheat and barley create the weevil <term>curculio</term> <note>A type of beetle that infests stored grain</note>, and the bean an animal that some call the *mida*, and in a similar way the lentil, small lentil, pea, and others. **Avicenna** <note>The Persian "Prince of Physicians"</note>, enumerating fruits that create worms within themselves, says they are the moister ones, such as apples, pears, figs, grapes, and their like; and the legumes that create worms in the belly are cowpeas, beans, wheat, and similar ones. The fig does not generate a very good juice, wherefore a troop of lice always accompanies those who continually eat them, as **Galen** says, and after him **Simeon Sethi** <note>An 11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician</note>. Basil, when chewed and exposed to the sun, generates worms, and lice are always generated in it. **Dioscorides** confesses that eating basil creates lice and worms; for this reason, eating it too abundantly should be avoided, and they say this is due to the excremental moisture with which it is imbued, which is poorly digested...

<summary>This page discusses the botanical diseases of blight (sphacelismus) and worm infestation (vermiculatio), arguing through the Doctrine of Signatures that plants suffering these conditions can either treat similar human ailments like gangrene or, conversely, cause parasitic infections in humans who consume them.</summary>
<keywords>blight, gangrene, star-blight, sage, pomegranate, worms, parasites, weevils, Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Avicenna, Phytognomonica</keywords>

--- Page 212 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of plant diseases from Book 5, specifically focusing on how certain plants resist worm infestations (vermiculatio) and how the specific diseases that afflict trees can serve as remedies for similar conditions in humans, following the "Doctrine of Signatures."</meta>

PHYTOGNOMONICA <note>The title of the work, meaning "The Knowledge of Plant Signs."</note>

[...the plant,] driven by its native heat, recognizes a quick putrefaction as if it were superfluous, easily turning into lice and worms. **Diophanes** adds that if basil is covered by a crushed stone, it generates a scorpion; many who were delighted by its wonderful scent have even found a scorpion born within their own brains. There are also trees that do not suffer from worm infestations, and for that reason, they do not allow worms to be born or live in our bodies either; if any are born, these plants quickly expel them. **Theophrastus** <note>The "father of botany," an Ancient Greek philosopher</note> recorded that all trees which are acrid and swelling with milky sap are not infested by worms; those that are bitter and harsh are also least likely to be worm-eaten, not only because they rot less, but because their harshness prevents the birth of these creatures. The **laurel** <note>the bay tree</note> is proof of this: though it rots quickly, it does not quickly breed worms. For the same reason, neither the **wild fig** nor the **cultivated fig** breeds them, as their sap is entirely too harsh. All things planted in the earth alongside **squill** <note>a bulbous flowering plant in the asparagus family</note> suffer less from worm infestation because of its scent and heat. **Lupins** and **chickpeas** are preserved best because they possess a certain bitterness and harshness—qualities that can preserve them without harm. For this reason, even when these rot, they create no pests, nor do any dry and acrid things. **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note> lists laurel berries, the bark of sour pomegranates, and among the legumes, lupins and chickpeas as remedies against worms. Likewise, vegetables that do not breed worms are effective against them, such as cumin, mustard, mint, fennel, celery, cabbage seed, watercress, southernwood, wormwood, and similar plants; also turnips, radishes, arugula, leeks, oregano, savory, and coriander. According to **Theophrastus**, these last seeds are firmer and more stubborn in enduring, and ultimately, those of an acrid flavor are most resistant. Even if gnats or little worms are born in all other vegetables, they are least likely in these. To ensure vegetables do not generate harmful pests, it is said that **mint** planted in several places—especially among wild cabbages—achieves this, as does a small amount of **bitter vetch** <note>original: "ervum"</note> sown specifically where radishes and turnips grow. It is also effective against snake bites, and mint sprinkled into a drink expels creatures from the belly and puts snakes to flight. The **olive** and **wild olive** feel neither worms nor moths; because of their bitterness, these pests do not gnaw the wood, according to **Theophrastus**. **Avicenna** said that olive oil kills worms, especially **omphacine oil** <note>oil made from unripe olives</note> on account of its bitterness. The **cedar** suffers neither decay, rot, nor moths, for it produces a fruit that is untastable due to excessive harshness. It protects bodies from the stain of corruption; it is dripped into worm-infested ears with vinegar; when rubbed on, it destroys nits and lice; and it acts as a protection against worms and moths when poured into the bowels. The **citron** <note>original: "Citrium"</note> feels neither worms nor moths; its juice kills snakes and worms in the belly, and when stored in chests, it prevents the gnawing and damage of little worms in clothing. The wood of the **cypress** feels no decay; the juice of its leaves allows no worms of any kind to touch or gnaw the wood.

## PARTICULAR DISEASES OF TREES 
### heal the same in us. Chap. IX.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' featuring floral or scrollwork design.</image-desc>

We have spoken of the universal diseases of trees; now let us move to the particular ones, in which we are warned by a great spectacle of Nature to look toward the same diseases in humans. The **chickpea** dies when its roots dry up, which happens when rain washes away its saltiness during flowering; this loss of saltiness is like a **gangrene** <note>original: "sphacelismus," referring to tissue death in both plants and humans</note>. According to **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and author of "De Materia Medica"</note>, it is effective against **scabies** <note>a contagious skin infestation</note>, **impetigo** <note>a skin infection characterized by sores</note>, and other diseases of "salty humors." **Theophrastus** notes that **impetigo** and **lichen** <note>In this context, skin eruptions or scales</note> occur largely on the olive tree. The "sweat" flowing from the wood of a young olive tree when it is set on fire, when smeared on, heals lichens, eruptions, and scabies. Although **Cato** <note>Roman statesman and author on agriculture</note> recorded that **red moss** infests the olive, it nonetheless invades many trees, just as lichen does. **Dioscorides** said moss is found on the cedar tree, the white poplar, and the oak; **Galen** <note>An influential Roman physician and philosopher</note> found it on pitch-pines and related plants like the pine, larch, and fir; I have found it most especially on ash and beech trees, and junipers. Therefore, it should be a doubt to no one that trees whose bark is dishonored by diseases of this sort are effective against **leprosy**, **lichens**, and **scabies**. Cedar oil <note>original: "codria," likely referring to cedar resin or oil</note> is beneficial when licked for **elephantiasis** <note>a disease characterized by thickening of the skin and underlying tissues</note> and heals the scabies of four-legged animals, according to **Dioscorides**. The water found in the cavities of decaying oaks...

### BOOK FIVE.

DD

...cures all ulcerous scabies <note>original: *scabiem... ulcerosam*; a contagious, itchy skin condition that produces sores</note>. We have said that the gray, hairy tufts of moss hang from pines and spruce branches; their bark, when applied, heals lichens <note>original: *lichenes*; here referring to scaly skin eruptions</note> and impetigo <note>a common skin infection causing red sores</note>. Larch resin wipes away white skin spots <note>original: *alphos*; a form of leprosy or vitiligo characterized by white patches</note>. The ash of the ash tree and the juniper, when applied with water, removes leprosy. 

We have most carefully observed that on many trees and rocks, moss, impetigo, and lichens very often grow when they are slick with moisture. First, a certain greenness appears on the outside; gradually it gains growth and clothes itself in leaves, as seen on the pear, fig, olive, vine, juniper, and others. By scraping this very "lichen" from the trees, boiling it, and applying it, we have corrected skin eruptions. The milky sap of the fig tree cleanses lichens, vitiligo, and psoriasis <note>original: *psoras*; itchy or scaly skin patches</note>. The "tears" <note>sap</note> of the vine, when applied and rubbed with wine, heal lichens and psoriasis. According to **Dioscorides** <note>a 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, the lichen itself that clings to rocky places cures impetigo. Lungwort <note>original: *Pulmonaria*</note>, which clings to trees like a lichen, is effective for ulcers of the private parts and roughness of the body. 

The fig tree suffers from "balding" <note>original: *glabrationem*</note>: for if there have been excessive rains, the root is peeled, a defect they call *aulam* <note>a disease where the bark of the root sloughs off</note>. This disease happens to the roots a little further up, and it usually occurs from an excess of moisture. The fig, combined with shoemaker's ink <note>original: *atramento sutorio*; often a copper or iron sulfate solution used in tanning</note>, heals almost hopeless discharges of the legs and malignant ulcers. 

A disease peculiar to vines is "joint-sickness" <note>original: *articulatio*</note>, caused either when the buds are carried away by the force of a storm or damaged by unskilled cultivation, the injury of which is felt in the joints of the plant. Raisins placed upon the rots that have arisen in these joints will heal them; they are also rubbed on human gout <note>original: *podagris*; a form of inflammatory arthritis affecting the joints</note>. 

The fig tree suffers from scabies due to too much moisture; this happens when light rains occur during the rising of the Pleiades <note>original: *Virgiliarum exortu*; the Pleiades star cluster, traditionally associated with the rainy season</note>, which stick and seethe where they settle. Its milky sap, mixed with barley meal, cleanses leprosy, lichens, and common psoriasis. 

The vine also experiences "dew-rot" <note>original: *roratio*</note> when the flowers receive dew; they produce a moisture like dew, and if it increases more than is right, it diverts the nourishment. For this reason, the grapes partly fall away and partly remain, so that they do not reach their proper size. Wine drunk in moderation increases digestion in every part of the body and is most effective for strengthening the person. 

The olive tree suffers from the "nail" <note>original: *clauum*; a callus or hard growth</note>—some call it a fungus, others a "pot"—which is a scorching from the Sun. The wild olive restrains carbuncles, hangnails, and spreading sores, and clears away scabs. 

In certain trees, specific growths occur which are effective against growths on our own bodies. Agaric is a growth of the larch tree, much like a fungus; its specific power is to purge waste products that have clung to the spinal medulla, nerves, and muscles. The fungus of tree trunks is a growth of the earth or the wood; **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist</note> said it heals growths in human flesh, for it consumes them immediately. **Theophrastus** <note>an Ancient Greek philosopher often called the "father of botany"</note> said that the oak bears many growths on its small branches. Pellets also grow in the "armpits" of the branches, clinging to the body without a stalk. It also bears a sap that has the power to burn, and many gall-nuts, as we shall discuss. **Dioscorides** said that crushed unripe gall-nuts restrain growths in the flesh. **Pliny** and **Avicenna** <note>an influential Persian physician of the Islamic Golden Age</note> both said that all kinds of galls remove growths from the body. *Eschara* <note>a scab or crust</note>, the excrement of rocks, is effective against growths.

### THAT THE PECULIAR DISEASES OF ANIMALS CURE THE SAME DISEASES IN HUMANS. Chapter 10.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' beginning the chapter, illustrating a landscape scene with figures and classical architectural ruins.</image-desc>
THERE ARE also peculiar diseases of animals that also invade men; we shall show that these can be cured by our own remedies. The goat herd suffers from cloudiness of the eyes <note>cataracts</note>, and the goat knows best how to cure it. When it feels its eye is disturbed and not properly functioning, it moves itself toward the thorn of a bramble and allows it to be pricked. As soon as it has punctured the eye, the phlegm <note>original: *pituita*; the fluid causing the cloudiness</note> is immediately drawn out, and with no damage done to the pupil, it recovers the use of its sight. 

Indeed, **Aelian** <note>a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric</note> believes that men learned this kind of treatment from goats. Physicians call it "paracentesis" <note>original: *παρακέντησιν*; a surgical puncturing or "couching" of a cataract</note> in cases of suffusion <note>cataracts</note>, which is a puncture made with a needle. An eye-salve made from the gall of goats heals the film over the eyes, according to **Rhazes** <note>an influential Persian physician and polymath</note>. These same animals would frequently suffer from bleary eyes <note>original: *lippirent*</note> if they did not eat certain herbs; the same is true for deer. For this reason, **Pliny** orders that one swallow their dung wrapped in new wax during a new moon against this disease. The eyes of goats are "glaucous" <note>blue-gray or pale</note>, so that they seem to suffer from glaucoma continually. **Dioscorides**...

# 2. PHYTOGNOMONICA 811

[He] said that the gall of a wild goat <note>original: *fel syluestris capræ*</note> is effective against glaucoma <note>a condition causing pressure and vision loss in the eye</note>. Others say that a daily illness <note>likely a recurring fever or epilepsy</note> attacks, from which one is not relieved until they have inserted the hoof of the hind foot into the left ear; anyone who carries the hoof, or a part of it, or a ring made from it, wears an amulet against that same disease. The donkey <note>original: *asinus*</note> suffers from one disease in particular, which they call *malida* <note>likely "malleus," a respiratory infection known as glanders</note>. This defect originates in the head and causes a great deal of reddish phlegm <note>original: *pituita*</note> to flow out; if it descends to the lungs, the animal dies. They recommend donkey milk for a cough. If the blood or lung is ground and drunk, it helps with shortness of breath <note>original: *anhelitum*</note> and coughing, according to **Haly Abbas** <note>original: *Hali Arabe*; a 10th-century Persian physician</note>. The donkey <note>likely referring to the wild donkey or onager</note> is a species of elk <note>original: *alces*</note>, and it too suffers from the "comitial disease" <note>original: *comitiali morbo*; an old name for epilepsy, so called because if someone had a seizure during the Roman *comitia* or assembly, the meeting was suspended</note>. From this come many remedies for epilepsy: the donkey's brain in honey-water <note>original: *aqua mulsa*</note>, first infused in leaves and drunk in half-ounce doses for [many] days, according to **Pliny**, is effective for it—but no fewer than thirty days. Likewise the testicles, marrow, or suet, the ash of the hooves, the meat, blood, and milk, and other parts of it are used.

Oxen are afflicted by two diseases: scrofula <note>original: *strumâ*; swelling of the lymph nodes</note> and gout <note>original: *podagra*</note>, according to **Aristotle**. The ash of an ox's hoof applied with water breaks up scrofulous swellings, according to **Pliny**, as does dung applied with vinegar, according to **Dioscorides**. Fresh, warm dung relieves gout, according to **Marcellus** <note>Marcellus Empiricus, a 4th-century medical writer</note>. The blood of bulls is thicker with fibers <note>original: *fibris refertior*</note>, and for this reason it clots and thickens very quickly, according to **Aristotle**; because of this, it is poisonous to drink, according to **Galen**. If blood is being spat up, they report that ox blood is effective when taken in moderation with vinegar—for it is reckless to trust bull blood, says **Pliny**. Burnt bull horns stop bleeding, according to **Galen**.

Dogs suffer from three defects: rabies, quinsy <note>original: *angina*; a severe sore throat or inflammation</note>, and gout, according to **Aristotle**, **Pliny**, and **Pollux**. Puppies are killed immediately in water, according to the sex of the dog that bit, so that their raw liver may be devoured [as a cure]. Some who have been bitten by a rabid dog, to protect themselves from the fear of water <note>hydrophobia</note>, have tied a worm from a canine carcass to themselves. A leather dog-strap wrapped three times around the neck is a remedy for quinsy, according to **Pliny**. Dog fat relieves gout, according to **Aesculapius**. Dogs are also infested with mange <note>original: *scabie*</note>; canine blood cures mange above all else, according to **Pliny**.

**Archelaus** <note>a Greek philosopher</note> is the authority for the claim that goats are never without fever; perhaps for this reason, their spirit is more fiery than that of sheep, and their mating is hotter, according to **Pliny**. Take dried goat dung, ground and sifted, in the measure of a spoonful with four cups of fragrant wine, and give it to a person with a fever while they are fasting and washed, according to **Galen**'s book on *Simple Medicines*. **Pliny** gives one drachma of swallow dung in three cups of goat's milk, sheep's milk, or raisin wine <note>original: *passi*</note> for quartan fevers <note>malaria-like fevers recurring every four days</note> before the fits begin. **Plutarch**, by no means unskilled in the nature of things, reports that the goat is afflicted by the "comitial disease" <note>epilepsy</note> more than other animals; for this reason, the ancient priests strictly abstained from it as being diseased, since by tasting or even just touching it, some of that disease might rub off on them. He provides the cause as the narrowness of the pores; when these are blocked, the breath <note>original: *spiritus*; vital air</note> is very often trapped inside. One may know this best from sheep and especially goats, for these are most frequently seized; if you dissect their heads, you will find the brain moist, filled with sweat, and foul-smelling, as **Hippocrates** has it in his book *On the Sacred Disease* <note>the famous ancient treatise on epilepsy</note>. For those with epilepsy, goat meat toasted on a person's funeral pyre is given, according to **Pliny** and **Sextus** <note>Sextus Placitus</note>. The brain of a goat passed through a gold ring is dripped into infants before milk is given, to protect against the "comitial disease," according to **Pliny**.

He-goats have a stench of the armpits <note>original: *alarum*</note>, which is why it is called a "hircine" odor <note>goat-like smell</note>. The shaved or burnt horn of a mature he-goat is mixed with its gall, and an equal weight of myrrh is added; then the armpits, with the hair first removed, are diligently rubbed with it, according to **Marcellus**.

Deer all contain live worms in their heads, which usually grow under the tongue in the hollow near the vertebra where the head connects to the neck; they are no smaller in size than the largest worms produced by rotting dogs. They are usually born all together and touching, numbering about twenty, according to **Aristotle**, and **Pliny** follows him. Others say they are massed together in the coverings of the intestines and are killed by the eating of serpents, which they draw out of their burrows with the breath of their nostrils. Burnt deer horn, drunk with honey, draws out the long, round worm <note>original: *lubricum rotundum*; intestinal parasites</note>, according to **Galen** in his book *On Theriac* to Piso, and likewise according to **Sextus**, **Marcellus**, and **Rhazes**.

Elephants are afflicted by "flow of the belly" <note>original: *alui fluore*; diarrhea or dysentery</note>, and they do not feel other kinds of diseases, according to **Aristotle**. Powder from elephant bones is given with plantain juice for dysentery <note>original: *dysenteriam*</note>, according to **Platearius** <note>a 12th-century physician</note>.

A horse has three most acute diseases: of the bladder, the "ileos" <note>intestinal blockage or colic</note>, and "cardiacus" <note>heart distress or severe gastric pain</note>; it also becomes asthmatic and rabid. Horse cheese suppresses the belly and removes griping pains <note>original: *torsiones*</note>, according to **Aesculapius**. The saliva of a horse, drunk for three days, heals a cough...

The **Lion** is afflicted by a quartan fever <note>a recurring fever, often associated with malaria, that peaks every fourth day</note>: even when it seems to enjoy health, it is perpetually afflicted; for if this disease did not restrain its strength and ferocity, this wild beast would be far more dangerous to us. **Philes** says: lion fat with rose oil cures daily fevers, according to **Pliny**, though **Serenus** says it is for semi-tertian fevers <note>a fever intermediate between tertian and quotidian</note>; however, the heart taken in food cures quartan fevers, per **Pliny**. Bear gall with twice the amount of water cures all obscurity of the eyes and incipient cataracts <note>original: *suffusioné*</note>, according to **Galen’s** *Euporista*. The **Fox** in summer suffers from a disease named *alopecia* <note>hair loss, named after the Greek word *alopex* for fox</note> after it, which consists of the falling out of hair; hence the skins of captured foxes are usually not only useless but harmful, says **Aetius**. Fox fat heals *alopecia*; in cases where the sores have already scarred over, burn the head of a little fox, and apply ground *alcyonium* <note>a sea-foam or sponge-like substance</note> and leaves of black alkanet <note>original: *anchusae*</note> over the ointment so that the head may be covered with hair, according to **Aegineta**. A disease happens to **Weasels**, or they naturally have arms or parts around the elbow joint or hump that are more swollen and <gloss>swollen-elbowed</gloss> <note>original: *ἀκρωλενιαχοι* (akroleniachoi)</note>; **Hippocrates**, in his book on joints, uses the same word for one who has a small, wasted (*atrophon*) arm and a swollen elbow. **Avicenna** applies the ashes of a weasel for arthritic pains. The **Hawk** suffers from dimness of vision, on account of which it dispels it with the herb *hieracio* <note>hawkweed</note>, per **Pliny**. A hawk boiled in rose oil is thought by **Pliny** to be the most effective remedy of all for eye defects, and by **Galen** for dimness of eyes. The hawk suffers from fever: therefore, its wings suspended from the neck are a healing remedy. **Quails** suffer from the comitial disease <note>epilepsy</note>, and because of this disease they are despised; they are the only animals besides man to feel it, according to **Pliny** and **Solinus**. For epileptics, the brain of a quail ground in myrtle ointment is stored in a tin vessel; smear the face with it, and you will marvel at the effectiveness of the medicine, for the patient will rise immediately, according to **Galen**. The **Harrier** <note>original: *Circius*; a bird of prey</note> limps on one foot: it is effective for gout and joint pains.

There are also other diseases occurring from the outside which grow upon or creep into plants themselves, and bring destruction and ruin by stealing their nourishment; for by their embrace, they take away sustenance and extract the juice: whence they waste and strangle. We must investigate what Nature wished to demonstrate with this portent, full of wonder, as is seen in **mistletoe**, **dodder** <note>original: *cuscuta*</note>, **ivy**, and similar plants, which we conclude are effective for nothing except for wasting away internal organs and extracting pus. **Ivy** sends out little roots from its buds among the leaves, by which it clings to trees, as if displayed by Nature with industry, drawing the juice from the trunk. ### PLANTS AND ANIMALS THAT ENDURE SPLITTING OF THE TRUNK AND WOUNDS ARE EFFECTIVE FOR HEALING WOUNDS.

### Chapter 12.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a figure or landscape within a square frame.</image-desc>

THERE ARE also violent removals coming from the outside that bring death to trees, and these are the removal of parts and wounds. For there are some trees which, if they receive a wound, perish because of their dryness and weakness; just as the palm tree dies if its crown <term>cerebro</term> <note>literally "the brain," referring to the apical bud or heart of the palm</note> is wounded. There are also trees that tolerate not only an inflicted wound, but even the removal of parts of the trunk—specifically those that are moist and sprout very well, like the elm, the plane tree, and those that live near water. There are those that improve when wounded, such as the vine, fig, apple, olive, almond, reed, and pear; they also tolerate the splitting of the trunk. **Theophrastus** teaches the method of producing resin: the pine is wounded, and the resinous wood <term>taeda</term> is removed; a more copious humor flows into the inflicted wound, and so it is in the fir and the pitch-pine. The turpentine tree is wounded in the trunk and the branch. All resin-bearing plants are effective for the gluing together <term>conglutinationes</term> <note>healing by joining the edges of a wound</note> of wounds. For surgeons use turpentine everywhere to consolidate wounds. From the pine and the pitch-pine, a binding agent is made. Turpentine resin is placed in deep ulcers; it generates flesh and heals broken bones, and so with the rest. The wild olive glues wounds together. The elm not only heals wounds, but welds <term>ferruminat</term> broken bones; so does the ash of the plane tree, according to **Avicenna**. The blossom of the vine <term>oenanthe</term> and wine are applied to bloody wounds. From the ash of the fig, a lye is made which glues, cleanses, and fills with flesh, joining the edges no differently than plasters. Pomegranate flowers <term>cythini</term> glue bloody [wounds]. Apple leaves and barks consolidate, or the juice expressed from them, according to **Avicenna**. The same is to be thought of the pear. Myrrh is also cut twice from the trunk to the branches, according to **Pliny**: it glues wounds of the head and heals exposed bones. The balsam shrub is wounded by the blade of a craftsman using glass or bone knives, but only in the bark, from which a drop of extraordinary sweetness remains; it is suitable for wounds of the head, and nothing is more effective than balm of Gilead <term>opobalsamo</term> for gluing wounds without leaving a scar. And so with the rest, for it is tedious to mention others, suspecting those already mentioned will suffice.

Animals also that can be joined and glued together again after being dissected and cut possess the power to be able to glue our viscera and wounds. If someone by chance or on purpose strikes a lizard <term>lacertum</term> <note>likely the green lizard, *Lacerta viridis*</note> on the head and cuts it in the middle with a rod, neither of its parts dies, but each walks separately from the other; and having snatched up its two feet, it lives; then a union of each with the other occurs, and by a certain silent agreement and natural binding they are, as it were, joined and woven together; and from two separate parts, one and the same lizard is made again. And although a scar indicates the trace of the place previously affected, it nevertheless retains its former life and is very similar to one that has never suffered such things. **Aelian**, and from him **Philes**, says: a dissected lizard joins again. Its blood is effective for the rupture of infants when they sit in a decoction of it. In the needlefish <term>acu</term>, wise Nature dilates the crack behind the vent until it has given birth, because after the birth it joins in such a way that it seems to grow together—although it may be possible that it does truly grow together, according to **Aristotle** and **Pliny**. In **England**, fishmongers <term>ichthyopolae</term> dissect pikes <term>lucios</term> with a knife to show those buying that they are fat; those not bought they throw back into the ponds, in which the wound joins and heals. Which the observers of nature ascribe to the tench <term>tincis</term>, because the pikes rub themselves against them so that they may smear the wound with their viscous slime, and thus the edges of the crack are joined so that even to one looking closely they can seem to have grown together: we conclude this is for gluing wounds. We have heard that dissected earthworms <term>lumbricos</term> grow together again, and so also snakes; on that account, they are effective for wounds and cut nerves.

<summary>This page explores the medicinal doctrine of signatures, arguing that plants and animals capable of surviving severe wounds or rejoining their own severed parts (like resinous trees, lizards, and pikes) possess a natural power to heal human wounds and fractures.</summary>

BOOK FIVE. 213

# PLANTS AND ANIMALS THAT EASILY SHED THEIR BARK OR SKIN
# ARE EFFECTIVE FOR CLEANSING HUMAN SKIN.

### Chapter 13.

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial 'C' featuring a landscape with a building and foliage, enclosed in a square decorative frame with floral and scrolling patterns.</image-desc>STRIPPING THE BARK around the circumference <note>This refers to "girdling," a practice that usually kills a tree by cutting off the flow of nutrients.</note> is the common death of trees, or at least most of them, since the bark is the most vital part. The Greek strawberry tree <term>adrachne</term> <note>original: *adrachne*; likely *Arbutus andrachne*</note> is an exception, but this is even truer of the cork oak <term>suber</term>; for while other trees are killed when the bark is removed in a circle, the cork oak is actually helped by it, as the thickening bark otherwise constricts and strangles it. The cherry tree is also accustomed to being stripped of its bark; otherwise, it is more likely to be cut through than to have the bark removed in a single strand. The remaining wood is able to endure and protect the tree, and the tree itself does not die from the loss of bark: for once the outer tunic is removed, a thinner one grows in its place the following year, repairing the loss of the previous one. Between the bark and the wood of the linden tree <term>tilia</term> are thin tunics of multiple membranes, from which linden bonds are made; the thinnest of these are called <term>philyra</term>, famous for the ribbons of crowns. These barks are much sought after for making ropes. In the grapevine, the bark is full of cracks and breaks apart spontaneously; it also falls off the Greek strawberry tree, the common strawberry tree <term>unedo</term>, and the apple tree. Barks from the beech, fir, linden, and pitch-pine are of great use to country folk, who frequently make vessels, baskets, and certain durable containers for conveying harvests and vintages, as well as the coverings for huts. The bark of the oak, a relative of the cork oak, is effective against malignant ulcers and the hard swellings that they call <term>cacoetas</term> <note>from the Greek *kakoethes*, meaning a "bad habit" or a malignant, stubborn growth</note>. The "tear" of the vine <note>the sap or resin</note> which hardens like gum on the trunks, when smeared on—after the area has first been rubbed with soda—heals leprosy and <term>psora</term> <note>a term used for various scaly or itchy skin conditions like scabies or psoriasis</note>. The wild vine possesses these same powers. Resins from the pine, larch, and pitch-pine are effective against leprosy, the itch, and similar skin diseases. If you remove the small tunics from garlic, you do no harm, for it is covered by many layers; the same is true for squills, onions, and similar bulbs—something can always be stripped away from them, according to Theophrastus. These are effective with honey against lichens, leprosy, and <term>furfures</term> <note>literally "bran," referring here to dandruff or scaly skin</note>. Almost all cereal plants consist of little pods, with the grain enclosed by husks and chaff: wheat bran boiled in sharp vinegar and applied while warm drives away leprosy and heals old eruptions <term>impetigines</term>. A poultice of barley put on with sharp vinegar cures leprosy; oats are useful for the same things as barley; and <term>alica</term> <note>a type of spelt or grits</note>, which is spelt <term>zea</term> boiled in vinegar, removes leprosy and clears up the roughness of the nails. Provident Nature also shows that there are very many animals that "strip off their old age" <note>original: *senectam exuunt*; a classical idiom for molting or shedding skin</note>, admonishing man that the quality they possess will be profitable to him—specifically, that it is effective for the "debarking" or renewal of the skin, curing elephantiasis, leprosy, <term>alphos</term> <note>a condition causing white spots on the skin</note>, the itch, eruptions, and scales. Aristotle teaches which animals these are, saying: "Some of them cast off their old age (for 'old age' is the bark or skin that sits on the body like a lid), such as those among the blooded animals that are covered with a soft bark, namely snakes and lizards. Certain insects also cast off their old age: the cockroach <term>silpha</term>, the mosquito, and those whose wings are contained in a sheath, like beetles; indeed, all of them shed it when that which was meant to be born has been formed. Some among the sea-creatures cast off their old age, such as lobsters, prawns, and crabs; snakes cast off their old age in spring and autumn." The flesh of vipers purges the entire body through the skin. Galen says this about them: "In Asia, a certain man was suffering from elephantiasis; his friends, having built him a hut, brought him only as much food as would support life. It happened that a viper fell into a vessel full of wine. When the harvesters noticed this, they feared that if they drank it some evil might happen; out of mercy, they gave it to the man with elephantiasis to drink, thinking it better for him to die than to live in such misery. But when he had drunk it, all that tuberous skin fell off no differently than the shell of an animal, and he was restored to health." The same thing happened in Mysia. A certain man with elephantiasis went to the baths hoping for relief; he had a maidservant who attended him. A viper fell into a jar of wine and died; the maid, thinking it a lucky find, gave that wine to her master to drink, and when he had drunk it, he was healed in the same way we described. Antonius Musa, the physician to Augustus Caesar, gave vipers to be eaten by those who had incurable ulcers, and he healed them with wonderful speed, according to Pliny. The stag, feeling itself weighed down by old age, draws snakes out of their holes with its breath and, trampling them with its feet, devours them after they are killed, and thus it becomes young again. To change their feathers, birds use snakes...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of "signatures" in the animal kingdom, specifically focusing on animals that shed their skin, feathers, or shells. In the logic of the time, because these animals can "renew" their outer surfaces, their bodies were believed to provide medicine for human skin conditions and hair loss.</meta>

PHYTOGNOMONICA BOOK 3. 214
PLANTS

The fowler, having been instructed by Oppian <note>Oppian was a Greco-Roman poet known for his works on hunting and fishing.</note>, relates that a certain serpent, creeping toward a stork’s nest, was devouring the chicks. When the stork lost its brood again the following year, it returned in the third year bringing a new bird, never seen before, which had a large beak as sharp as a sword. While the stork flew further away to find food, the serpent attacked the nest; it ended up stabbed by many blows and lay dead. However, the bird was harmed by the venomous teeth of the snake, and all its feathers fell out. For this reason, when hawks do not shed their feathers quickly, bird-catchers take a native serpent (as it has the least amount of venom) and cook it with wheat. They then feed that wheat to a hen and give the hen the decoction water to drink. Finally, the hawk is fed the flesh of that hen; it then sheds its feathers, is freed from any disease it might suffer, and, decorated with new feathers, remains healthy and cheerful for a long time.

Spotted lizards <term>stelliones</term> <note>original: *stelliones*; referring to the Mediterranean house gecko or a similar spotted lizard</note> shed their old skin in spring and autumn, and they immediately devour the shed skin, thereby snatching away a remedy for the "comitial disease" <term>epilepsy</term>, according to Aristotle, Theophrastus, Aelian, and Pliny. If this skin is given to a hawk in its food, it causes the bird to change its feathers quickly. Lizards are also effective for the same purpose. Green lizards, when burned and sprinkled on meat, accelerate the change of feathers in any hawk that eats them. Demetrius of Constantinople, in his book on the care of hawks, offers the hawk a green lizard cut into tiny pieces in its food. Antipater suggests giving one that has been dried in the sun; they also use this for scabs on the head.

The salamander also sheds its old skin, according to Aelian. On whatever part of the body its saliva falls, or even if it merely sprinkles the bottom of a foot, all the hair on the entire body falls out, according to Pliny. For this reason, certain physicians use it as a <term>psilothrum</term> <note>A depilatory or hair-removal agent.</note>. The commentator on Nicander uses the intestines to pluck out hairs. Dioscorides uses it disemboweled in honey for the same purpose, or melted in oil. Paulus Aegineta uses only the ash of a burned salamander for these purposes. Martial, cursing a woman with baldness, says:

->May a salamander or a cruel razor strip this head bare.<-

Dioscorides says it is added to medicines whose power is to eat away at leprosy. Galen uses its ash for <term>septic</term> <note>Used here in the ancient sense of "corroding" or "breaking down" diseased flesh.</note> or <term>psoric</term> <note>Relating to itchy skin diseases or scabies.</note> medicines. He judges the skink <term>scincus</term> to be of the same species because it also sheds its old skin, and for that reason it is effective for the same infirmities. For example, regarding <term>elephantiasis</term> <note>In antiquity, this term referred to a severe, thickening skin disease, often related to what we now call leprosy.</note>, Aetius records that in the region of the Indians, those affected by elephantiasis were accustomed to being purged through the seat <note>i.e., given an enema.</note> with an infusion of donkey urine, heated to the measure of a <term>hemina</term> <note>About half a pint.</note>. Likewise, they take a land crocodile, cut off its extremities, and throw away the insides; then they wrap it in dough and roast it. Once the dough is removed and the rough skin is scraped off, they provide one <term>drachma</term> <note>A small weight, roughly 3.4 grams.</note> of the flesh daily. Aegineta uses it for <term>alphos</term> <note>A skin condition characterized by white spots or scales.</note>.

The turtle does not shed its skin, but land turtles are born among the Indians which are easily stirred up in deep plowings of the earth. They say that kind of turtle sheds its shell, according to Aelian. So that a hawk may change its feathers, Demetrius offers turtles in their food, and gives them to falcons that are doing poorly. The eagle is long-lived because its youth is renewed by this remedy, according to the verse of the Psalm: "Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's" <note>Psalm 103:5.</note>. The Prophet Micah mentions the casting off of its feathers. It is renewed by putting aside old age—specifically by eating the turtle, as is held from Oppian. The eagle does not die from old age or sickness, but only from hunger, because the upper part of its beak grows so hooked that it cannot be opened.

Thus serpents are said to be renewed when they put aside their <term>leberis</term> <note>original: *leberidem*; the sloughed-off skin of a snake.</note> every year. Eagles seize turtles in their feet, carry them high up, and having spotted a stone, they drop them precisely onto it so the shell might be broken and the meat eaten, as Pliny notes. It is the custom of the eagle to break open turtles by dropping them from on high—a chance event that killed the poet Aeschylus <note>Legend says Aeschylus died when an eagle dropped a tortoise on his bald head, mistaking it for a stone.</note>. Likewise, in the sea, lobsters, crabs, and crayfish shed their annual crust in the spring, just as snakes shed their membrane of "vernalization" <note>The spring shedding of skin.</note> and a new one is born. Because of this, snail shells cleanse leprosy and <term>vitiligo</term>, according to Dioscorides. Mussels, purple snails, and crabs produce an ash that has a caustic power, which is used for leprosy, freckles, and spots.

BOOK FIVE

# PLANTS THAT SWEAT GUMS AND RESINS ARE
### effective for gummy growths and the pus of bodies. Chapter XIV.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter E featuring floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc>
THERE IS a certain disease of trees, as it were—the flowing of gum and resin. There was no more similar way to heal the "gums," pus, and calluses of our own bodies than through the discharge of tree gums and resins, as can be clearly seen in the "French disease" <term>syphilis</term> <note>original: *lue gallica*; syphilis was often called the "French disease" in the 16th century</note> and other illnesses. When we conjectured this ourselves, the outcome favored our hope, which we shall also prove by the testimony of authorities. The gum that sweats from the cherry tree, when dissolved in vinegar, heals the "gum" <term>gummy tumor</term> <note>original: *gummi*; here referring to a soft, gummy tumor or lesion associated with late-stage syphilis</note> that grows in our limbs, and when applied, it dissolves it. We owe this discovery to more recent physicians, as no more excellent medicine has yet been found. Laser <term>silphium resin</term> is a gum obtained from the giant fennel <term>ferula</term> growing in Syria; according to Dioscorides, it is effective for calluses and "nails" <term>corns</term> on the feet if they are first scraped around and then the resin is smeared on. Ammoniacum gum dissolved in vinegar removes calluses from the feet, according to the same author. The same is true of opoponax <note>a medicinal gum resin from the Hercules-all-heal plant</note>, which possesses the same powers. Tacamaca is a gum of the Westerners <note>referring to the Americas or "West Indies"</note> and is effective for the same purpose. Gum is also extracted from Guaiacum wood, aloe, and by other chemical arts; this gum is effective against the "gums" arising from the venereal disease <term>syphilis</term>, as we have learned through many experiments, which we shall teach in the book dedicated to this subject. But just as gum is generated in trees, so are "stones" <term>calculi</term> generated in the kidneys from a viscous, putrid, and undigested matter. This arises from indigestion and is coagulated and thickened by heat. Gum in trees arises from excessive rot or indigestion, condensed by the heat of the Sun; it is effective for dissolving stones. That which sweats from the cherry tree, when drunk in wine, expels stones according to Dioscorides; the same is said of plum, almond, peach, fir, and poplar gums according to Avicenna. One should also note the gum that hardens on the trunks of vines, and bdellium <note>a semi-precious oleo-gum-resin</note>, larch, and other trees, as nothing prevents its use. So too is the "sanies" <term>discharge</term> of trees a resin that exudes through cracks; according to Theophrastus, it truly imitates the pus flowing from ulcers, which is why we argue it heals them. Turpentine resin is beneficial for scars erupting with discharge; amber <note>original: *succinum*</note> helps those spitting up purulent matter from the chest; mastic is used for scabies of the feet and abscesses of the liver; larch resin for gonorrhea, wasting diseases, and deep ulcers; pine and pitch for purulent excretions; frankincense for ulcers dripping from the head; myrrh for purulent ears; and the "cedar-juice" <term>cedria</term> that exudes from the cedar tree for scabies and ulcers of the lungs.

# PLANTS THAT TRANSFIGURE INTO ANOTHER SPECIES ARE
### effective for those diseases that degenerate into others. 
### Chapter XV.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter M featuring floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc>
BY A GREAT portent of Nature, it is signaled to us that those plants which change into other related species, or even into ones far distant—either because the climate is unfavorable or the soil is begrudging—can heal those diseases which degenerate and pass into others. Theophrastus demonstrates that the white poplar turns into the black, and wheat into darnel <note>original: *lolium*; a weed often found in wheat fields that was thought to be a corrupted form of wheat</note>. Wild wheat and barley, once their wildness is tamed, turn into domestic wheat; likewise, wheat can turn into oats, bulrush, or spelt, and conversely, spelt and bulrush can turn into wheat. Barley is changed into oats, spelt into oats, and winter wheat into spelt, and more rarely into barley. Basil, when its leaves change, turns into wild thyme or water mint; mint turns into water mint and calamint; and neglected marjoram turns into oregano. They say that from the seed of cabbage, a turnip is born, and from a turnip, cabbage, according to Varro. There are also many diseases that pass into others. Fevers change into one another, scabies into leprosy, and leprosy into cancer; vertigo into epilepsy, the "French disease" and gout into joint diseases, the celiac disease into lientery <note>a form of diarrhea where food is passed undigested</note> and common diarrhea, and inflammations into hard tumors <term>scirrhos</term>. Wheat ripens and opens boils and furuncles; fresh bread heals old skin eruptions <term>impetigo</term>; wheat flour disperses all inflammation. Pliny writes that it cleanses old ulcers better than other things, as well as gangrene, skin sores <term>lichens</term>, and leprosy when mixed with native sulfur. A cream made from barley flour in water with pitch is used against fluxes of the joints,

it mitigates inflammations, especially gouty ones <term>podagric</term> <note>original: *podagricas*; relating to gout, especially in the feet</note>. Flax <term>Linum</term> does not allow an ulcer to spread; it heals gangrenes when used with water, softens the hardness of joints, and is applied with vinegar for those suffering from abdominal ailments; it cleanses old ulcers, "lichens" <term>skin eruptions</term> <note>original: *lichenes*; a term used historically for various crusty skin diseases</note>, and leprosies. Basil <term>Ocimum</term> is a help for inflammations of the lungs. The leaves of the black poplar are rubbed on for gouty pains, and its seed is useful for those with the "falling sickness" <term>epilepsy</term> <note>original: *comitialibus*</note>. We also notice that the harm of one thing is corrected by another. Basil, if crushed and covered, generates a scorpion; if chewed and exposed to the sun, it produces worms. The Africans say that if someone is struck by a scorpion on the day they have eaten basil, they cannot be saved; indeed, others report that if a handful of basil is crushed with ten sea or river crabs, all the scorpions in the vicinity will gather to it. Chrysippus vehemently censured basil, claiming it is useless for the stomach, harmful to the urine and the clarity of the eyes; furthermore, according to Pliny, it causes madness, lethargy, and defects of the liver. Wild Thyme <term>Serpillum</term>, however, is effective against scorpions when the branches and leaves are boiled in wine; it is drunk with water for headaches, frenzies, and lethargy, against griping pains and difficulty in urination, and for liver complaints. The same should be thought of others.

# SPOTTED PLANTS, AND ANIMALS [THAT]
->*wipe away the spots of our bodies.* Chapter XVI.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'D' depicting two figures, one standing and one seated, in a pastoral landscape setting with trees and hills in the background.</image-desc> WE HAVE SPOKEN of the diseases of trees; now we shall demonstrate those which plants show through their parts universally. First, we shall show how we may abolish the spots of the body that dishonor the outermost surface. It is a very great part of beauty to wipe away spots from the body; hence, spotted flowers, leaves, and stems of plants, and the spotted skins of animals, are effective for wiping away the spots of our own bodies. Rightly indeed, and without any ambiguity, Mother Nature obliterates and abolishes the spots of the bark, the creeping sores of the skin <term>serpigines</term>, and foul freckles through the stems, roots, fruits, or other parts of plants. The spotted stem of the Greater Dragon Arum <term>Dracunculus maior</term>, depicted with spots where the purple ones however predominate, is effectively rubbed on for "vitiligo" <term>skin depigmentation</term>, according to Dioscorides. By crushing its roots with honey and "deer soap" <note>original: *sapone cervino*; likely a preparation made from deer fat or marrow</note>, we most excellently wipe away spots from the hands and the whole body. The Lesser Dragon Arum <term>Dracunculus minor</term>, variegated in the same way, also cleanses vitiligo. Arum has leaves distinguished by various small dots and possesses the same virtues. Snake Garlic <term>Allium anguinum</term> is spotted in the same way; when burnt, it is effective for vitiligo, freckles, and bruises. Cyclamen <term>Cyclaminus</term> has spotted leaves, in which the spots are white both above and below; when smeared on with honey, it corrects the defects of the skin on the face. The leaves of Water Pepper <term>Persicaria</term> are marked underneath with a dark or blood-red color; when applied, it removes bruises and spots, according to the experience of more recent authors. Black Chameleon <term>Chamaeleon niger</term> appears to have black leaves distinguished with red; it wipes away "impetigo" <term>scabby skin eruptions</term>, and corrects vitiligo and defects in the face. A species of Buttercup <term>Ranunculus</term>, which they call wild garlic, has spotted leaves and deletes marks. A species of Orchid <term>Testiculus</term> <note>original: *Testiculi species*; named for the shape of the tubers</note> with spotted leaves cleanses the face, according to Avicenna. The Iris has dots in its flower and corrects freckles and defects of the skin. The Red Lily, or the Hyacinth of the Poets, is as if freckled, interspersed with rust-colored dots or lines. Ovid says:

> *A flower arises, and takes a form like lilies, were it not*
> *That their color is purple, while in lilies it is silver.*
> *The flower itself inscribes its own groans on its leaves, and "ai, ai,"*
> *The flower has inscribed, and the mournful letters are drawn.*

It is a species of lily, and it also corrects freckles. In the flowers of beans <term>faba</term> there are spots and freckles, as we have said. Galen clearly stated that bean meal wipes away the filth of the skin; understanding this, "mangones" <term>cosmetic merchants</term> <note>original: *mangones*; those who furbished up goods or slaves to improve their appearance</note> and women in the baths use these daily; it also wipes away spots contracted from the sun.

The variegated seed of the castor plant <term>Ricinus</term> <note>original: *Ricini*; likely *Ricinus communis*, the castor oil plant</note> clears away skin defects on the face and nose. The seeds of the wild lupine are spotted: the cultivated kind cleanses the face and removes spots, but the wild variety is therefore more potent in its action. Melons <term>Melopepones</term> <note>original: *Melopepones*; a group of fruits described by ancients as having characteristics of both apples and melons</note> have green, spotted rinds; according to Galen, they are excellent for wiping the face clean. Their crushed seeds are used as a cleansing agent. The bark of the birch tree is variegated according to Theophrastus; when its root is perforated with a drill, it ejects water from its body, the power of which is very great for erasing spots and bringing a shine to the skin. We find the same principle in animals: for whatever creatures are marked with variegated spots on their skins, the same power exists. Some possess these by nature, such as the lynx and the panther; others by chance, such as sheep and goats. The salamander is variegated; Dioscorides called it "various." The commentator on Nicander and Aetius say it is similar to the starred lizard <term>stellio</term> <note>original: *stellioni*; a term used for spotted lizards, often geckos or newts</note> or the "starred" heron. Pliny called it "starred" because the skin appeared to be interrupted by markings that look like eyes. Galen stated that it clears away freckles and spots. The starred lizard is so named because it has points or "stars" on its back, or because it is freckled. Ovid wrote:

->,, and it bears a name suited to its color,<-
->starred across its body with various droplets.<-

<header>PHYTOGNOMONICA, BOOK II</header>

Its dung is effective against skin eruptions <term>impetigines</term> <note>itchy, scaly skin patches</note>, freckles <term>ephelidas</term>, and white skin spots <term>alphos</term> <note>a fungal infection or vitiligo-like condition</note>. There are also lizards distinguished by various spots, of which Virgil wrote:
> Let the scaly backs of the painted lizard be absent. <note>original: *Absit & picti squalentia terga lacerti*</note>
For on both sides of their bodies there are several shining points shaped like little stars; in its power, it is similar to the stellion <note>a spotted lizard, often the Mediterranean house gecko</note>, whose dung Avicenna said could heal freckles <term>lentigini</term>. The crocodile is marked underneath with saffron-colored circles and scales; its dung is effective against freckles, according to Soranus and Archigenes in the works of Galen. The skink <term>Scinco</term> is black in color, with many minute white dots on its back and sides; these are also found between the sides and the belly and on other underparts. The rest of the body is also black, and the skin is roughened by these colors and points; it is effective for the same conditions. The blood of the skink, if mixed with borax <term>baurach</term> <note>an Arabic term for various salts like nitre or borax</note> and smeared on the face, very finely erases spots and freckles, according to Galen, Aegineta, and Pliny. The viper, with its varied color and adorned with many round spots, clears the whole body through the skin, according to Odoardus. The hare is marked with blacker spots and points, and for this reason it is called *percnon* <note>from the Greek *perknos*, meaning dark or mottled</note>, similar to the spots on the wings of eagles. One genus is called *percnon* by Aristotle, either because of the intermingled white spots, so that it appears freckled. Its blood, when smeared on, drives away freckles and facial paints, and erases inflammatory swellings <term>panos</term> and marks, according to Serenus and Sextus. The starling <term>Sturnus</term> is variegated, being black distinguished with white or yellow spots, according to Aristotle; its dung is effective for beautifying the face, according to Dioscorides, Galen, and Pliny. You may read more regarding white spots, swellings, skin eruptions, and blotches <term>morpheam</term> in Galen, Aegineta, and Serapion. The lynx is spotted. Virgil says:
> Girt with a quiver and the spotted hide of a lynx. <note>original: *Succinctam pharetra, et maculosa tegmine lyncis*</note>
Its use is for skin marks <term>sphragida</term> and bruises, according to the Arabs. The hawk <term>Accipiter</term> has a spotted breast, adorned with black, white, or red spots; it is effective against "little clouds" <term>nubeculas</term> <note>referring to corneal opacities or films</note>, cataracts, and dimness of the eyes. Male sparrows <term>Passeres</term> are distinguished drop-by-drop with white and black points; their dung purges the face of freckles, according to Hali. Various colors are seen in the peacock; in the tail feathers are "eyes" and gem-like colors. Pliny says there is such a variety of colors, such brightness, and such select kinds of colors that nothing more beautiful can be seen; its bones, burnt and mixed with urine, cure leprosy and skin discolorations <term>vitiligines</term>, according to Sethi. There is a genus of blackbirds <term>Merularum</term> with breasts that are reddish, spotted, and black, or a varied color mixed from black and ash-grey; their dung mixed with vinegar roots out freckles, according to Hali. The hyena is spotted, covered entirely with small circles according to Pliny; its gall is used for white spots on the eye <term>albugines</term>, dimness, and glaucoma. There are also animals that are partly spotted and partly stained by their own color, not by their whole genus, as we have said. The dog is found spotted and variegated; its wool-grease <term>Oesypus</term> <note>lanolin</note> rubbed with honey and applied abolishes spots, according to Pliny. Goats are also variegated; spots are abolished by goat's blood, according to Marcellus. Cats are effective for "mists" over the eyes; ram's dung erases spots.

## SPOTTED PLANTS AND ANIMALS ARE EFFECTIVE FOR
### spots on the eyes. Chapter XVII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a bird perched on a branch within an ornate rectangular frame.</image-desc>SPOTS also occur in the eyes, which both plants and spotted animals erase. These eye spots include the "little cloud" <term>nubecula</term>, the white ulcer <term>argema</term>, the white film <term>albugo</term>, glaucoma, and other diseases; for just as there are flowers of various colors, so too there are eyes that are grey-blue, whitening, amber-colored, yellow, and black. Examples follow. The stalk of the Dragonwort <term>Dracunculi</term> <note>likely *Dracunculus vulgaris*, known for its mottled, snake-like stem</note>, distinguished by various spots, removes clouds from the eyes. The smaller variety does the same, and Arum deletes them as well. In the Cyclamen, white spots appear on the foliage; it is beneficial for cataracts <term>suffusioni</term> and blunted vision when applied with honey. In the Orchis <term>Testiculo</term> <note>original: *Testiculo*; a reference to *Orchis* species, named for the shape of their tubers</note>, there are red and blackish spots; it deletes the same eye conditions. Ebony has black wood, says Pliny. We shall not omit, on account of its miraculous nature, that its sawdust uniquely heals the eyes; when the wood is rubbed on a whetstone with raisin wine, it dispels dimness, and with water it heals white spots <term>albugines</term> of the eyes. Saffron-dross <term>Crocomagma</term> <note>the residue left after preparing saffron oil</note> is approved because it is black; it has the power to delete those things that darken the eyes with dimness. Spots that are of a milky color in plants are effective for white films <term>albugines</term> and ulcers <term>argemata</term>.
