[It] suppresses white ulcers of the eye <term>argema</term> <note>a white ulcer on the edge of the cornea</note>; hawkweed <term>hieracium</term> [heals] all eye defects. Dragon arum <term>dracunculus</term> gives off a milky sap and is effective against white spots <term>albugines</term> <note>white opacities or scars on the cornea</note>. Ground-fig <term>chamaefice</term> <note>*Euphorbia chamaesyce*</note> removes dimness; its milky sap heals white ulcers and spots, according to Avicenna. Those things we said cure jaundice are also effective for cataracts <term>glaucomata</term> <note>In this period, *glaucoma* referred generally to a grayish-blue opacity of the eye, often confused with cataracts</note>; just as the citron is effective for jaundice of the eyes, according to the same author. Next follow the spotted animals. Vipers with spotted skin: their ash removes white spots, and when eaten, they bring clarity to the eyes. Spotted swallows, marked with white and black: they bring clarity to the sharpness of vision. Aquatic turtles, which have their backs dappled with black spots: their gall, when applied, destroys all mistiness <term>caliginem</term> of the eye, according to Pliny. The hawk is used for mistiness, the stellion lizard for dimness, and the lizard for mistiness, according to the same author. Gray or "glaucous" animals help with cataracts. The turtle is for cataracts. The gray lizard living in sand-pits is burned for cataracts. The Otis, or horned owl, a type of owl, has gray eyes: it has power against cataracts, according to Pliny. White animals remove white spots and leucomas <term>leucomata</term> <note>thick white scars on the cornea</note>. Sheep, the cock, and milk are administered for white spots. The blood of black hens is for spots and freckles, according to Rhazes. There are also animals that have blood in their eyes, and these are excellent for removing blood from the eyes. Turtle doves have redness around the eyes; Pliny says their blood is extremely helpful for bloodshot eyes. Pigeons have redness around the eyes; Dioscorides said to use an ointment made from them for bloodshot eyes; wood pigeons are used in the same way. The part above the eyes of the partridge, and the front of the head where the neck begins, are marked with a notable reddish color; it frees bloodshot eyes. A frog has blood only in its eyes; the eye of a frog is removed with a thorn and, tied in a crimson cloth, is placed over the eyes to remove blood. The chameleon has blood nowhere but in its heart and eyes, and even there not in abundance, but a tiny bit; cataracts <term>suffusiones</term> are healed with its gall. The leech has red spots on its breast; it is sought for eyes bloodshot with gore.

### SCALY PLANTS AND ANIMALS REMOVE SCALES FROM THE BODY. Chapter XVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring a figure in a landscape with architectural and foliage elements.</image-desc>

NATURE SHOWS, with a not unpleasing similarity, that scaly branches of plants, barks, flower cups, and seeds—and likewise the skins of animals—are effective against scaly diseases that besiege the skin, namely leprosy <term>lepram</term>, psoriasis <term>psoram</term>, scabies <term>scabiem</term>, and rough nails. Examples follow. Scabious <term>Scabiosa</term> produces flower cups at the tips of its stalks structured in a compact order of scales: it is effective against scabies, from which it claimed its name; it deletes white spots <term>alphos</term>, skin eruptions <term>impetigines</term> <note>scaly or crusty skin patches</note>, moles, and other skin conditions, as is established by the experience of more recent authors. Of the same appearance and power is the plant called "Devil’s Bit" <term>morsus diaboli</term> <note>*Succisa pratensis*</note>, so similar to the other that they are often taken for the same thing; it has flowers in belly-like cups with compact scales. Artichokes <term>Scolymi</term> bear fruit in the shape of a cone, with scales lying over one another like roof tiles <note>the botanical term is "imbricated"</note>. Pliny said they heal leprosy and lichen-like eruptions when used with vinegar. There are also the flowers of the chameleon-plant <note>*Atractylis gummifera*</note>, also with compact scales, which correct skin defects on the face and vitiligo. Stonecrop <term>Sedum</term> comes forth with leaves crowded together like scales; a draught of it removes elephantiasis <note>a term then used for severe, scaly skin conditions resembling a hide</note>. Oregano <term>Origanum</term> produces flowers in a compact series of scales in spikes; the broth of the decoction can help with psoriasis. Plantain <term>Plantago</term> brings forth a spiked flower, namely a spike at the top of the stalk made of flowers lying upon one another, crossing like roof tiles; applied as a salve, it helps with elephantiasis. There are also trees that produce flowers like little worms <note>catkins</note>, with a scaly compact neck, hanging from branches, such as the walnut <term>iuglans</term>; its oil drives away scabies. Pine, wild pine, spruce, larch, and others produce cones compact with scales, from which resin flows, which removes leprosy, skin eruptions, and rough nails. The cypress <term>Cupressus</term> brings forth foliage, cones, and branches armored with little scales; it produces resin which is applied for the same things. Savin <term>Sabina</term> consists of scaly branches and leaves; it can do twice what cinnamon can, according to Pliny: cinnamon, smeared with honey, wipes away freckles and skin defects on the face. The lily <term>Lilium</term> has scaly roots, composed of many bulbs; they correct lichen, leprosy, and scaly dandruff on the face, and clear away vitiligo.

### PHYTOGNOMONICA

**WILD PINE**, scabious, walnut, and lily are represented here, which display cones, small heads, catkins, and scaly roots notable for their roughness. Furthermore, we show scaly animals, serpents, and fish, so that you may contemplate their scales at your will.

Bottom row: a coiled serpent with detailed scales and a fish with prominent, overlapping scales.</image-desc>

Moving on to animals. The crocodile has a rough body, covered with very hard scales in the manner of oysters; its dung is effective against <term>impetigo</term> <note>a skin infection causing red sores and crusty yellowish-brown scabs</note> and similar conditions, according to Soranus and Archigenes, via Galen. In the skink <note>a type of lizard</note>, the entire underside, the chest, and the belly shine with a series of scales; its blood [removes] freckles <term>lentigines</term>. According to Aegineta <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note>, "crocodilea" <note>a substance made from crocodile dung or lizard entrails</note> removes white skin spots <term>alphos</term> <note>a non-contagious skin disease characterized by white patches, often associated with leprosy or vitiligo</note> and cleanses the face. On this subject, Horace [writes]:

> ,, and a complexion
> stained with the dung of the crocodile.
<note>original: "colorque stercore fucatus crocodili", from Horace, *Epodes* 12.11. This refers to the ancient use of crocodile excrement as a cosmetic whitening agent.</note>

Ovid, in his *Art of Love*, when instructing those with dark complexions to maintain a respectable appearance, refers them to the Pharian fish <note>a fish or lizard from the Nile region, likely the skink</note>:

> If you are darker, flee to the aid of the Pharian fish.
<note>original: "Nigrior ad Pharij confuge piscis opem", from Ovid, *Ars Amatoria* 3.270. The "help" refers to a medicinal paste made from the animal's entrails used to whiten skin.</note>

The salamander is scaly, and the skin on its back is rough, especially because of certain dots. Perhaps for this reason it was called *samandra* by Nicander <note>Greek poet and physician, 2nd century BCE</note>, because the skin, being interrupted, appears as if marked by these dots. Galen uses it for white spots <term>alphos</term> and itchy skin diseases <term>psoricis</term> <note>ailments resembling psoriasis or scabies</note>. Vipers and serpents have scaly skin from head to tail; we have often reported from Galen that they are effective against elephantiasis <note>in this period, the term often referred to the most severe form of leprosy</note>. ->**PERFORATED PLANTS AND TUBULAR STRUCTURES**<-
->**are effective for bodily perforations, or wounds and fistulas.**<-

### Chapter XVIII.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring a landscape scene with foliage and buildings in the background.</image-desc>

PLANTS WITH PERFORATED leaves, roots, or fruits demonstrate that they are effective for perforations or wounds of the body. Surgeons can use these in wound-healing potions. There is a species of gentian which herbalists call "gentianella" because of its small size, though its powers correspond almost exactly to the larger gentian; its root is split lengthwise into three or four parts, which is why the common people gave it the name "crosswort" <note>original: "cruciata"</note>, because four holes arranged in the shape of a cross pierce it; it is applied as a wound-healer. The leaves of St. John's Wort <term>Hypericon</term> are perforated, from which it earned the name "perforated" <note>original: "perforata"</note>; when the leaves are turned toward the sun, they appear to be pierced by almost innumerable tiny holes, as if by a needle, allowing both our sight and the light of the sun to pass through—it is also called "thousand-holed" <note>original: "millefora"</note>. It is very well known in medical and surgical use; its leaf and seed are second to none for wound-healing balsams, according to the multiple experiments of the most skilled surgeons. St. Peter's Wort <term>ascyrum</term> is of similar use, as it is also a herb that glues wounds together, having leaves with pierced pores. The Elm, like St. John's Wort, has perforated leaves: Dioscorides said it is effective for gluing wounds if the bark is twisted in place of a bandage, for it can be bent like a leather strap; a decoction of it also makes broken bones solid. 

But the <term>fistulous</term> <note>hollow, tube-like</note> and empty stems of plants are effective not only for wounds but for <term>fistulas</term> <note>narrow, tunnel-like sores that go deep into the body</note>. Nature could not have demonstrated the "aqueducts" and the winding, tunnel-like passages of the human body with a more subtle plan than through the tubular and hollow stems of plants. In very many herbs the stem is hollow and tubular; almost all vegetable, grain, and reed-like plants are topped with a hollow stalk and open with a continuous hole. The stem of the Gentian is hollow; it is applied as a wound-healer and as a cure for those sores that eat away in a tunnel-like fashion <note>original: "cuniculatim depascentium"</note>; its juice is beneficial for the same things with a particular effect. Comfrey <term>Symphitum</term> has a passage through its stem, and like the Sow-thistle it is hollow; it offers aid to wounds. White Hellebore has a hollow stem; if Black Hellebore is sent down into a fistula that has become hardened in the neck, it removes the callus within two or three days. The Lupin has a body that is hollow inside: it heals those flowing ulcers on the head called <term>theriomata</term> <note>malignant, "beast-like" ulcers</note>. 

Finally, nothing demonstrates more clearly or more skillfully that the creeping ulcers of our body can be healed by tubular channels than the "decay" of wood—that crumbling mass or <term>caries</term> <note>dry, powdered rot found in old wood</note> which is seen and found in trunks or old wood. This "flour," I say, when applied or smeared on ulcers, cleanses them and leads them to scarring, or restrains creeping ulcers, according to Dioscorides and others. It provides its effect all the more efficiently if that decay comes from those woods which have a similar power; hence the decay of <term>Guaiacum</term> <note>a medicinal wood from the Americas</note> wood is the most excellent; it heals all ulcers, even those called "evil-natured" <note>original: "cacoeta"</note> and those which arise from the French disease <note>Syphilis</note>. But another great example occurs by which this method of ours is more certainly proven—specifically from Pliny. He says that the worms born in decaying wood heal all ulcers and <term>nomas</term> <note>corrosive, spreading ulcers</note> when smeared on with oil. Galen praises those wood-decays which are taken from the Elm or other astringent woods.

<meta>The previous page discussed how the physical signatures of plants—specifically those with perforations, holes, or hollow stems—indicated their use in treating wounds, punctures, and fistulas. This page continues the theme of plant geometry, moving from holes to angles and sharp points, arguing that angular stems and spiny leaves signify a plant's ability to heal wounds caused by weapons or to penetrate the body with "thin" medicinal actions.</meta>

# ANGULAR STEMS ARE EFFECTIVE FOR WOUNDS.
->CHAPTER XX.<-

It also appears that plants with angular stems, leaves, or seeds show us they can heal inflicted wounds, because wounds are usually inflicted by weapons, spikes, and other angular and pointed tips. This is not a mere coincidence; we can demonstrate it through natural causes. We stated in the second book that angular stems in plants result from dryness—a type of dryness that lacks "biting" <note>An old medical term for irritation or caustic properties</note> or stinging. Galen <note>A Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> claimed that such plants are effective for gluing wounds together. Similarly, spiny plants, which seem to threaten us with wounds from their thorns, show that they are also effective for the same purpose. A few examples will suffice. **Ironwort** <note>original: "Sideritis heraclea"</note> produces a square stem; its leaves, when applied by their own natural power, "solder" wounds without the risk of inflammation. **Lesser Centaury** <note>original: "Centaurium minus"</note> has an angular stem; its application glues wounds, cleanses old sores, and draws skin over scars. **Wall Germander** <note>original: "Chamaedris"</note> has a square stem; Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany" and student of Aristotle</note> said its leaves are effective for ruptures and wounds. **Water Germander** <note>original: "Scordium"</note> has a square stem and joins wounds together. **Betony** <note>original: "Betonica"</note> has a square stem: Antonius Musa, the physician to Emperor Augustus, used it crushed and applied to heal bodily wounds with miraculous speed. Another species of **Comfrey** <note>original: "Symphitum"</note> puts forth an angular stem; applied to fresh wounds, it glues them shut. The **Bean** <note>original: "Faba"</note> has a square stem and soothes the inflammations that wounds provoke. **Clymenum** has a stem like a bean; its crushed leaves applied to wounds lead them to scar over. A certain type of **Plantain** <note>original: "Plantago"</note> with a square stem glues deep, cavernous wounds. **Pygnocomon** has a square stem: applied with barley meal, it extracts embedded spikes and thorns from the body. **Bur-reed** <note>original: "Sparganium"</note> grows with leaves that have a protruding ridge and a sharp edge, which cuts the hand of anyone who grabs it; according to Galen, it possesses a drying faculty that is beneficial for wounds. The **Iris**, among those that have the shape of a little sword <note>original: "gladioli formam"</note>, is flesh-healing <term>sarcotica: a medicine that helps flesh to grow over a wound</term> when used in wound ointments. **Stinking Iris** <note>original: "Xyris"</note> has leaves with pointed tips; it extracts spikes from the body. They call it **Gladiolus** because it bears the likeness of a sword <note>original: "gladii speciem"</note>; it removes spikes from the body. Spiny plants are also prescribed for wounds, such as the **Bramble**, **Caltrop**, **Holly**, **Teasel**, **Burnet**, **Aloe**, **Boxthorn**, **Venus's Comb**, and others, as we shall discuss elsewhere.

---

# SPINY AND SHARP-LEAVED PLANTS ARE SHARP
### *and thin in their action.*
->CHAPTER XXI.<-

Nature demonstrates, not without utility, that sharp-leaved and spiny plants are "sharp and thin" in their medicinal operations. This applies not only to those with a sharp leaf, but to those where the stem, seed, and every part are made very thin by little spines or hair-like leaves. The natural cause may be that plants with spiny, sharp, and thin leaves are of a "dry" quality because they grow in dry places, as we said above; dry and hot things operate with great power. Wild plants act more forcefully because they are drier, just as wild plants with narrower leaves act more strongly than the cultivated versions of their own kind. **Hog’s Fennel** <note>original: "Peucedanum"</note> has a hair-like leaf: Galen said it consists of "thin parts"—as do all the following—which is why they work powerfully and quickly; for this reason, it is effective for those with the "assembly disease" <note>epilepsy, so called because a seizure during a Roman assembly (comitia) was seen as a bad omen</note> and those in a lethargic stupor. **Sagapenum** <note>A gum-resin from a species of Ferula</note> is like a giant fennel: it consists of thin parts, is good for epilepsy, and its smell rouses those suffering from "suffocation of the womb" <note>original: "vuluae strangulatus" — an old term for hysterical disorders thought to be caused by the womb moving upward</note>. **Euphorbium** is a species of thin-leaved fennel; it consists of thin parts and has a burning faculty; it benefits those with sciatica and extracts scales from bones <term>exfoliation</term>, though it is necessary to protect the body with liniments where the bones are being treated. It induces sneezing and, when rubbed on the back of the head, helps those in a deep, death-like sleep. **Pellitory of Spain** <note>original: "Pyrethrum"</note> bears leaves like wild carrot and fennel: it has a burning faculty and a very fiery taste, and is effective for toothache. **Rosemary** <note>original: "Rosmarinum"</note> is fruit-bearing, named "cachryas," and has a leaf like fennel: it has a "cutting" faculty <term>incidentis: the ability to cut through or thin out thick bodily fluids</term>. **Galbanum** is the juice of the Cyrenaic giant fennel; it burns, rouses those with vertigo by its smell, and its fumes put snakes to flight. **Nigella** <note>original: "Melanthium"</note> has thin leaves and consists of thin parts and a subtle essence: it removes leprosy and freckles. **Cotton Thistle** <note>original: "Acanthium"</note> with spiny leaflets and sharp...

<summary>This page explores the "Doctrine of Signatures," arguing that plants with angular stems represent weapons and thus heal wounds, while plants with thin or spiny leaves possess a "sharp" medicinal quality capable of penetrating the body or thinning thick humors.</summary>

### TREES AND ANIMALS THAT SHOW GLUE ARE
### effective for gluing wounds together. Chapter XXII.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring a figure seated within an architectural or floral circular frame.</image-desc>
Nature demonstrates glue in plants—in their roots, leaves, or juices—to the great benefit of mankind, so that divided parts of the body can be glued, soldered, or made solid again; this power is as strong for the internal organs as it is for the gaping wounds that are enemies to nature. Examples of these follow.

**Theophrastus** <note>The student of Aristotle often called the "Father of Botany"</note> writes that the root of the **Marshmallow** <note>original: "hibiscus"</note> can thicken water if you throw it in crushed and leave the moisture out in the open air; it is entirely pregnant with slime and mucilage. He asserts that if you cook it with meats, it brings them together into one mass and binds them strongly. For its use in ruptures and wounds, **Hippocrates** included it in wound medicines, as did **Dioscorides** and **Pliny**.

**Comfrey** <note>original: "consolida maior"</note> has slimy roots; they also force meat to bond if they are cooked together. When crushed and drunk, they benefit ruptures, and when smeared on fresh wounds, they glue them together. Of all the roots we have named, it is the most sticky; it is believed that pieces of meat will be soldered and glued together if cooked with it. It is a wound-healer in both leaf and root.

**Pythagoras** said that the flower of the **Holly** <note>original: "Aquifolium"</note> freezes water, and its bark is suitable for making birdlime <note>original: "glutinum aucupatorium," a sticky substance used to trap birds</note>; it solders broken bones. Men strip the bark from this tree and bury it in waterlogged places in a pit dug in the ground, wrapping it in the leaves of trees and allowing it to rot there, which happens in twelve days. Then they dig up the withered pieces and pound them with a pestle for a long time until they soften into birdlime; finally, they wash it in a running stream so that the remaining bits of bark and filth float away. Nothing is stickier than birdlime; it is especially used for trapping birds by their feathers upon contact.

The green berries <note>likely referring to mistletoe, often confused or categorized with holly in birdlime production</note> are collected at harvest time, dried, and pounded; once dry, they are stored in water and allowed to rot for twelve days, then beaten again with a mallet in a stream. Having lost their bark, they soften into an inner "flesh." Some add **Galbanum** <note>A bitter, aromatic gum resin</note> in equal weight to each part, and in that way, they are used for wounds.

**White Chameleon Thistle** <note>original: "Chamaeleo albus"</note> is called *ixia* by some because a type of birdlime <note>original: "viscum"</note> is found around its roots. **Pliny** said that **Mistletoe** <note>original: "viscum"</note> is born under the "axils" of the leaves during the rising of the Dog Star; it bears a birdlime most useful for wounds. **Sarcocolla** <note>From the Greek for "flesh-glue"</note> is the "tear" <note>a resin drop</note> of a tree growing in Persia, similar to powdered frankincense; its name was given for its ability to glue wounds. From the bark of **Elm** <note>original: "ulmus"</note> roots, we prepare the best glue for wine vessels that leak; it solders broken things.

The **Aloe** has a fatty, thick, and glue-like leaf; it is indeed very useful for joining wounds. **Myrrh** is gluey: sprinkled on head wounds, it acts as a glue and joins broken ears. There are also resinous plants that show glue; for this reason, their primary use is for soldering wounds. **Bloody Pine** <note>original: "Pinus cruenta"</note> glues wounds. **Cedar oil** <note>original: "Cedria"</note> brings the ulcers that sheep suffer from shearing to a scar. The gum they call **Elemi** is used especially in wound medicines. The gum of the **Ethiopian Olive** is effective for ulcers. **Mastic** <note>original: "Lentiscus"</note> is resinous and effective for broken bones.

There are also leaves of herbs that show glue. **Licorice** <note>original: "Glycyrrhiza"</note> bears gluey and gummy leaves; its juice is very useful for wounds. **Labdanum** <note>original: "Laudanum"</note> has a leaf that in springtime sweats out a fatty substance; when goats feed on this, they pluck that visible fat with their beards...

<summary>This page explores the Doctrine of Signatures, arguing that plants with "thin" or "sharp" features treat conditions requiring the thinning of fluids, while plants containing "glue" (mucilage or resin) are divinely intended for healing wounds and mending broken bones.</summary>

...and they remain attached to their hairy legs by their own stickiness: they possess the same medicinal powers as the **Rockrose** <note>original: "cisthus"</note>, according to Dioscorides: the leaves of the **Rockrose** consolidate wounds, according to Galen. **St. John's Wort** <note>original: "Hypericum"</note> has a resinous seed, smell, and stickiness, as do **Great St. John's Wort** <note>original: "ascyrum"</note> and **Tutsan** <note>original: "androsæmum"</note> with their resinous fruit: we have said they are effective for healing wounds. There are animals that have a skin around the neck from which the best glue is made; some call it **bull-glue** <note>original: "taurocollam"</note>, others **wood-glue** <note>original: "xilocollam"</note>, because it is made from the hides of oxen. Pliny says it is made from the ears and genitals of bulls. There is also a mucous stickiness in all hides, less in some, more in others, as in oxen, from which glue is made: it benefits wounds when mixed with honey or resin. <term>Fish-glue</term> <note>original: "ἰχθυόκολλα" (ichthyocolla)</note> is made from the belly of a whale-like fish: it is useful for plasters applied to the head. **Tench** <note>original: "Tincæ"</note> fish are covered in mucus; it is reported that wounded pike rub themselves against them so that their wounds may be glued together by that mucus. The saliva of **purple-snails** <note>original: "Purpurarum"</note> is very sticky, and for that reason, it is used for gluing fresh wounds.

### SWOLLEN PARTS OF PLANTS, AND SWOLLEN ANIMALS
### are beneficial for the swollen parts of our bodies. Cap. XXIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring a landscape scene with a building and foliage inside a square frame.</image-desc>In the depths of the earth and the parts of plants, humors tend to collect and excite certain globular collections and spongy abscesses, just as in our bodies, heat and blood often create scrofulous and glandular **tubercles** <note>Small, rounded swellings or nodes</note>. Nature shows us that these are effective against tubercles; likewise, animals that show only a certain swollen appearance. There are **oak galls** <note>original: "quercuum glandes"</note>, similar to those glands that occur during the plague and at other times of pestilence on various parts of human bodies, such as the neck, armpits, thighs, and similar places, called "glandular flesh" in swine: these can be easily countered by distilled water extracted from young oak leaves, and thus it also helps with poisonous fevers. Dioscorides writes that it is also beneficial for hardnesses which they call <term>cacoetes</term> <note>From the Greek for "bad habit," referring here to malignant or stubborn ulcers</note>. Dioscorides writes that the fruit of the **Wild Cucumber** is similar to glands; and tubercles are broken, and tumors removed by them; Mesues says they destroy hardened abscesses and **scrofula** <note>Swellings of the lymph nodes, often associated with tuberculosis</note>. **Lentils** <note>original: "Lenticulæ"</note> appear on our bodies during pestilential fevers <note>Likely referring to smallpox or typhus spots</note>, which properly mimic the appearance of lentils, and the common people call them "lentils"; nothing counters them more usefully than a decoction of lentils. Aristotle said that the sow conceives "hail," and from this the word <term>to suffer from hail</term> <note>original: "χαλαζᾶν" (chalazan)</note> was made—that is, to suffer from a parasitic infection; round grains are found in the flesh of the sow, similar to hail, or lentils, and of the same appearance: against this disease, they mix some lentils into their feed. **Boa** is the name of a disease of pimples when bodies turn red: they are beaten with a branch of **Elder** <note>original: "sambuci"</note>, according to Pliny, who cites grains of the same likeness. The stem of the **Cabbage** <note>original: "Brassica"</note> swells most around the root; it is especially helpful for tumors. All **Bulbs** are swollen; according to Dioscorides' precept, they are suitable for tumors. **Onion** <note>original: "Cæpa"</note> breaks tubercles. **Testicles** <note>Likely referring to the orchid, whose roots resemble testicles</note> disperse tumors. **Garlic** <note>original: "Allium"</note> heals tumors, according to Pliny. **Spiderwort** <note>original: "Ephemerum"</note> with its bulbous root destroys abscesses, tumors, and tubercles. The root of the **Daylily** <note>original: "Hemerocallis"</note> consists of collected little bulbs; it is effective for collections of fluid in the eyes. **Dragon Arum** <note>original: "Dracunculus"</note> is effective for **chilblains** <note>original: "perniones", painful inflammation of the skin caused by cold</note>. A tubercle also grows in the eyes, which the Latins call **hordeolum** <note>A stye</note>, because it bears a resemblance to a grain of **barley** <note>original: "hordei"</note> in length and width; the common people call it <term>orgiolum</term>: women disperse it by pricking it with a grain of barley. Tubercles occur in the eyes similar to a **pearl** <note>original: "vnioni"</note>, which the common folk also call "pearls" from their resemblance: pearl powder injected into the eyes dilutes them and restores clear vision, which has been revealed to us by frequent experiment. The **Gladiolus** <note>Sword-lily</note> consists of a jointed root, in the manner of small bulbs, one sitting upon another, the lower one slender, the upper more vigorous: it cures scrofula, as proven by innumerable trials. The **Fig** <note>original: "Ficus"</note> swells in the manner of a scrofulous tumor; it is effective for the same, according to Pliny. The plant called ***Scrophularia*** <note>Figwort</note> has a root rough with tubercles and provided with nipple-like heads, with a scrofulous sod extending beneath: it is quite suitable for scrofulous wounds, cavernous ulcers, cancer, or consuming sores; it helps by softening tubercles frozen by cold humor.

# BOOK FIVE

We have presented a species of **Sow-thistle** <note>original: "SONCHI"</note>, **Lesser Celandine** <note>original: "chelidonium minus"</note>, and **Figwort** <note>original: "scrophulariam"</note>, the roots of which are surrounded by almost innumerable small globules at the bottom, to demonstrate their effectiveness against the swellings of <term>scrofula</term> <note>original: "strumorum"; a swelling of the lymph nodes, usually in the neck</note> and hemorrhoids.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration showing three different plants. The plant on the left has slender stems and small flowers at the top, with clusters of small, round tubers at the base of the roots. The central plant has heart-shaped leaves and a composite flower similar to a daisy, with a dense cluster of thick, rounded tubers at its base. The plant on the right has broad, serrated leaves and small clusters of flowers, with several elongated clusters of small, seed-like tubers hanging from its root system.</image-desc>

There is also what is called the *lesser figwort*, a small herb with leaves like ivy, whose roots consist of several small, hanging callouses, gathered together like a heap of wheat grains, three or four of which extend further out. More recent physicians use this with great power and proven results in removing **scrofula**, <term>fig-piles</term> <note>original: "ficubus"; growths or tumors resembling figs</note>, and hemorrhoids. **Sowbread** <note>original: "Cyclaminus"</note> has a round root, packed with scrofulous tubercles; Mesue <note>a famous 8th-9th century Persian physician</note> said it heals scrofula. **Dragon Arum** <note>original: "Dracunculus"</note> has scrofulous roots, and its applied leaves dissolve these swellings. **Mandrake** <note>original: "Mandragora"</note> dissipates scrofula and tubercles in the same way. The root of the **Iris** is, as it were, scrofulous; it deletes scrofula. A species of **Sea Holly** <note>original: "Eryngij"</note> has a scrofulous root: it dissipates tubercles and heals scrofula with a decoction; the **Black Vine** <note>original: "vitis nigra"</note> does the same. There is another species of **Cuckoo-pint** <note>original: "Ari"</note>, from the middle of whose spreading roots numerous thin little bulbs and globules hang like fibers: it is conveniently applied to the tonsils and hemorrhoids. The **Lesser Arum** is also useful for these same conditions. **Lesser Celandine** is used against hemorrhoids. **Dropwort** <note>original: "Oenanthes"</note>, otherwise known as **Filipendula**, is an equal match according to many experiments: for by its suspension alone, it dissipates hemorrhoids. A certain species of **Sow-thistle** has globules; writers say they are effective for collections of fluid. A **Turnip** <note>original: "Rapum"</note> worn as an amulet heals the groin, according to Simeon Seth <note>an 11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician</note>. In the **Elm** <note>original: "vlmo"</note>, certain small pods grow filled with water: they are effective for <term>intestinal hernias</term> <note>original: "enterocœla"</note>. There grow in the anus growths like the fruit of the **Mulberry** <note>original: "mori"</note>, bloody and soft, and also in the scrotum, which after being torn away, burned, and cut off by other doctors, have sprouted again. We, however, have restored health using a powder made from mulberry fruits and scrofulous swellings. A species of **Hedge-mustard** <note>original: "Erini"</note> heals the "fig-piles" growing in the anus—

PHYTOGNOMONICA

...from Dioscorides and Pliny. A fungus growing on the anus is removed by a fungus, according to Pliny. Warts are removed by the seeds of the minor heliotrope, called <term>achrochordonas</term> <note>original: "achrochordonas"; from the Greek for a hanging, wart-like growth</note> in Greek. For the species of warts known as "ant-warts" or hanging warts, it is taught that on the first day of a new Moon, one should touch each wart with a single grain of **chickpea** <note>original: "Cicer"</note>, tie those grains in a linen cloth, and throw them away behind one's back; they believe the warts will fall off in this way, according to Pliny: for the chickpea resembles the shape of a wart. **Thyme** <note>original: "Thymum"</note> removes hanging warts that have the color of thyme. 

Turning to animals: venous growths on the tongue often cause cattle to lose their appetite; veterinarians call these "frogs" <note>original: "ranas"; likely referring to a ranula, a cyst under the tongue</note>. Columella said these kill by the ninth day unless they are treated. The Greeks call a swelling on the tongue, especially with inflammation of the part, <term>batrachion</term> <note>original: "batrachion"; Greek for 'little frog'</note>. It is cured with a wooden spike that has been used to transfix a **common toad** <note>original: "rana rubeta"</note>; it is even better if the toad has dried upon the spike. Water from frogs is effective for all "hot" tumors, according to Rufus. 

Pestilential abscesses often arise from poisonous matter; these correspond to the pestilential tubercle <note>a bubo or swelling of a lymph node</note> that usually grows under the tongue, which Pliny also mentions. Among more recent authors, there are those who place a dried toad upon a pestilential bubo, teaching that the poison is miraculously drawn out. Others place a live frog upon it, and if it dies, they substitute another, repeating this until one remains alive—a successful remedy. 

The body swells in the manner of **crabs** <note>original: "Cancris"</note>; a decoction with honey soothes chilblains <note>painful inflammation of small blood vessels in the skin</note> and <term>carcinomata</term> <note>original: "carcinomata"; cancerous growths, named for their crab-like appearance</note>. The swollen tortoise <note>original: "testudo"</note> resembles the swollen belly of those with **dropsy** <note>original: "hydropicorum"; edema or fluid retention</note>. The tortoise cures dropsy once the feet, head, tail, and intestines are removed and the remaining meat is prepared so it can be eaten without disgust, according to Pliny; it easily fattens horses, though this is a great but false fatness, according to Albertus. 

There are also animals that, by their little caps, crests, and tuberous protrusions, show they can cure tubercles. The **woodpecker** <note>original: "Picus martius"</note> carries tufts on its head: the woodpecker, roasted in salt, is applied to internal and external protrusions of the anus, according to Aetius. The **hen** has a crested head: Pliny uses egg white for the treatment of the "seat" <note>the anus</note>, even for infants if there is a prolapse there. **Pigeons** also have a little cap on their heads. Celsus, writing on the <term>condyloma</term> <note>original: "condilomate"; a knob-like skin growth</note> tubercle, says rightly that the tubercle should be fomented with egg, but the person should first sit in water in which <term>verbena</term> <note>sacred herbs or plants used in medicine</note> has been decocted.

### PLANTS WITH FLAME-COLORED FLOWERS ARE EFFECTIVE
### AGAINST INFLAMMATIONS. Chapter XXIV.

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'S' is set against an etched background of a landscape featuring a tall, tiered tower and several smaller buildings, suggesting a Renaissance-era town or fortress under a light, cloudy sky.</image-desc>

THERE are certain plants that have flame-colored flowers and reflect fire in their color; I would conjecture that these are effective against "sacred fires" <note>original: "sacros ignes"; usually referring to erysipelas, a painful skin infection, or shingles</note> and inflammations. Even if I could attribute this to natural causes based on what I have naturally recorded about colors, I prefer to attribute it to resemblance. The examples that are available are these:

The **Rose** glows with a flame-like color and is effective against inflammations. **Saffron** <note>original: "Crocum"</note> is used for the same, and for those tending toward "sacred fires." The **Apple** <note>original: "Malum"</note> aids against "sacred fires" and burns. The **Corn Poppy** <note>original: "Papauer erraticum"</note>, according to Galen, helps eye inflammations and "sacred fires." The **Anemone** is similar to it in all respects and is effective for eye inflammations. The **Argemone** <note>a type of poppy</note>, with a less saturated color, checks inflammations. The **Pimpernel** <note>original: "Anagallis"</note>, which has a red flower, resembles the scarlet flower of the **Pomegranate**, and is effective for the same, according to Avicenna. The roots of **Alkanet** <note>original: "Anchusae"</note> are for burns and "sacred fires." **Lycopsis** <note>Bugloss</note> has the same root and faculty. **Cistus** <note>Rock Rose</note> with a rose-colored flower also helps burns. Another **Knotgrass** <note>original: "Polygonum"</note> with a scarlet flower brings aid to "sacred fire." 

**Almonds**, **red beet** (for "sacred fire" and burns), and **Ivy** with red berry-clusters heal burns. The **bramble** <note>original: "rubus"</note> is for "sacred fires," **strawberries** for liver inflammations, **mulberry** fruit, and **red grapes** for inflammation of the spleen; so also **rhubarb**. Finally, the red type of carbuncles—which Pliny knew had consumed men of consular rank—is healed by **oak charcoal** <note>original: "querneus carbo"</note> crushed with honey. Thus, even in things deemed cursed or worthless, there are some remedies. 

Woods which, when rubbed together, excite fire, warn us that they are effective for the same heat-related ailments. Theophrastus records the trees from which fire-sticks <note>original: "ignaria"</note> were anciently made: **ivy**, **laurel**, and **linden**; Mnestor adds **mulberry**. The **fig** and **olive** are most fit for receiving fire. Although tinder <note>original: "Fomites"</note> can be made from many things, the best is from the **nut tree**, in Mnestor's opinion. # BOOK FIVE.

...those from the plant called <term>attagena</term> <note>original: "attagena"; likely a species of brushwood or heath used for kindling</note>, from which they make the receiver <note>the stationary "female" piece of a fire-drill</note>, while they make the drill <note>the rotating "male" piece</note> from **laurel** <note>original: "lauro"</note>; for they are not made from the same wood, so that one may act and the other be acted upon; they also use **buckthorn** <note>original: "rhamno"</note> and **holm oak** <note>original: "ilice"</note>. **Ivy** <note>original: "Hedera"</note> and **mulberry** <note>original: "morus"</note>, as we have stated, and **laurel**, and the acorns of the **holm oak** soothe inflammations; **olive** <note>original: "olea"</note> and **buckthorn** soothe the "sacred fire" <note>original: "ignem sacrum"; a term often used for erysipelas or inflammatory skin rashes</note>. According to Pliny, the **fig** <note>original: "Ficus"</note> is effective for inflammations of the tonsils, and the **walnut** <note>original: "iuglans"</note> for inflammations of the breasts. There are also herbs which the ancients used for lamp-wicks <note>original: "ellychnijs"</note>—lest anything be omitted in which some sign of Nature might shine forth—which possess hairy leaves; when smeared with oil, these maintain a lit flame. We can also refer this to natural causes. We said in our work on human *Physiognomy* that hairy men are hot, and hairy plants are hot and dry. There are some, however, who say that the "hair" <note>the fine fuzz or down</note> on leaves arises from moisture: for they believe that nourishment is carried to the underside through the top side, because the underside is always damp and woolly; but Theophrastus says they have not judged correctly, nor does this happen without its own specific nature. Nourishment is carried equally to both parts through the veins and nerves, for there is no reason for it to be carried from one side to the other when there are no passages or depth for it to go under. I would say instead that it is meant to catch celestial rain and dew, so that the dryness or heat of the plant may be moistened, by which it can sustain itself. Theophrastus said that a certain oak bears a small hairy ball, carrying a woolly, soft mane, which was used in the lights of lamps, for it burns well, like a **black gall** <note>original: "galla nigra"</note>; Pliny said it heals burns. The species of **mullein** <note>original: "Verbasci"</note> are woolly; among them are two herbs called *phlomides*, suited for lamp-wicks: they are effective against inflammations of the eyes. **Marshmallow** <note>original: "Althea"</note> is woolly: it is excellent for inflammations of the womb and the seat <note>the rectum</note>; likewise **pennyroyal** <note>original: "pulegium"</note>, **dittany** <note>original: "dictamnum"</note>, and the **stinging nettle** <note>original: "vrtica urida"</note>, being gifted with a woolly down, are effective for the same. **Goldylocks** <note>original: "Chrysocome"</note>, or yellow **stachys**, gray with a soft little fleece, settles inflammations of the lungs.

### WINE-COLORED AND SHINING COLORS SOOTHE DRUNKENNESS, AND ###
### those things which fill the head with intoxication. Chap. XXV. ###

<image-desc>Large decorative initial P containing floral scrollwork and stylized leaves.</image-desc>Before we depart from the subject of colors, let us speak of those plant colors that resemble the inflammations of the face caused by drunkenness, and are effective at soothing the intoxication of wine. Although we have discussed diseases that occupied the whole body, we now address those that affect specific parts, and the face comes first from the head, which the redness of wine occupies. The fruit of the **strawberry tree** <note>original: "Arbuti"</note>, stained with a saffron-red, is commonly called <term>imbriagola</term> <note>original: "imbriagola"; likely derived from the Italian 'ubriaco' meaning drunk</note> because it represents the faces of drunkards; eating it is harmful to the head, according to Galen's testimony. There are also joyful purple colors of plants that demonstrate the color of wine, such as those that specifically resemble the **amethyst** <note>original: "amethystinum"</note> color; just as the amethyst stone settles a hangover and wards off drunkenness, while men are inviting each other to drink more freely, they ought to use certain things called "amethysts" to prevent drunkenness, so that they are not carried away so far that neither foot nor hand can properly perform its duty. The amethyst color is that which approaches the color of wine; before one tastes it, it fades into a violet, and there is a certain purple brightness in it—not entirely fiery, but fading into the color of wine, like a gently rosy brilliance shining forth in purple from a carbuncle. A custom grew among the ancients that, after dinner, garlands <note>original: "corollæ"</note> were passed around to the guests, which were constructed from a multicolored mix of flowers. This was not merely so that the sight and smell might be captured by these charms—since flowers breathe out wonderful scents and represent an unspeakable variety of colors—but the curious skill of the wise, knowing the "antipathy" <note>natural opposition</note> in the nature of things and that nothing exists without a counterpart, placed flowers around the head so that when the vapor of too much wine has besieged the fortress of the senses, the mild breeze of the flowers inhaled through the nostrils might come to the rescue. It protects the head against drunkenness like a defensive wall: for if the flowers are endowed with a hot nature, they loosen the pores through which the wine-vapor may escape; but if the garlands are constructed with cold flowers, such as violets and roses, they cool the skull already over-heated by wine and repel harmful breaths, for they bind by their own strength and correct the heaviness of the head by their scent. There is no one who does not know that garlands were invented for the convenience of drinkers. Ovid:

### PHYTOGNOMONICA BOOK III.

-> *A drunken guest, his hair bound with linden-bark,* <-
-> *Dances, and recklessly employs the wine-god's art.* <-

But let us bring forward examples of flowers which have been given the property of repelling drunkenness. The **Violet** <note>original: "Viola"</note> displays the color of wine with its shining purple; by its own gift, it shakes off hangovers and heaviness of the head, whether by wearing it in garlands or by its scent, according to Pliny. The **Rose** <note>original: "Rosa"</note> also glows with a purple color, representing the rosy hue of wine; its use in garlands was so excessive among the ancients that they were called *rosaria* <note>rose-gardens or rose-festivals</note>.

> *Let my gray hair be drenched and grow rich with excessive balsam,*
> *And let my temples be burdened with fleeting roses.*

**Ivy** <note>original: "Hedera"</note>, with its purple clusters of berries rivaling wine, protects one from a hangover if the berries are taken beforehand. According to Tertullian, it defends the head from the effects of "yesterday's food"—that is, the yawning and half-sleep of a lingering stupor. It is said that Liber <note>another name for Bacchus, the god of wine</note>, the discoverer of wine, when he had found a medicine that was both very sweet and very potent, brought ivy into honor and value because its powers resisted wine; he taught his followers (*Bacchantes*) to be crowned with it so they would feel the harm of wine less, as the cooling force of the ivy extinguished the intoxication. Not without reason does Ammonius, in Plutarch's *Symposiacs*, marvel that this shrub is twisted into garlands, since it is believed to quench unmixed wine with its coldness. Furthermore, a cup made of ivy, called a <term>cyssibium</term> <note>original: "cyssibium"; a rustic drinking bowl carved from ivy wood</note>, was passed around at banquets for two reasons: both because, as we have said, it warded off the intoxication of wine, and because the frauds of innkeepers who mixed wine with water could be detected by such a vessel. The flower of the **Iris** shines with a most pleasant purple color; it not only dispels vinousness but, as Africanus writes, when eaten, the mouth does not smell of wine even if it has been drunk quite copiously. **Cabbage** <note>original: "Brassica"</note>, specifically the kind that grows redder than the others, is most suited for overcoming drunkenness if the juice expressed from its stalks is swallowed. The **Almond** <note>original: "Amygdala"</note> has a purple flower and imitates the color of wine: according to Pliny, if three or four bitter almonds are taken beforehand, the harm of wine is removed. Plutarch of Chaeronea relates that in the circle of Drusus, son of Tiberius Caesar, a certain physician used to feast who would challenge everyone to a drinking contest and yield to no one in the consumption of wine; he was finally discovered to eat five or six bitter almonds before drinking so that he would not be gripped by intoxication. Indeed, those who were forbidden from devouring them could not resist even a small amount of such drink. Athenaeus reported the same in the second volume of the *Deipnosophists* <note>or "The Banquet of the Learned"</note>; the same should be thought of the **cherry**, **peach**, and **cornel**. We have seen the blue **Eryngo** <note>original: "eryngium"</note> of Puglia with a most brilliant purple color; taken beforehand, it wards off a hangover. **Myrtle** berries are purple and wine-like: one species among the rest, if taken beforehand, wards off wine and hangovers; it is slightly heated and the juice expressed from its seed, otherwise it would contract an acidity. **Pomegranate** wine truly imitates wine and, according to Avicenna, is beneficial for drunkenness. Those who drink **Saffron** <note>original: "Crocum"</note> beforehand do not feel a hangover, as it resists drunkenness; garlands made from it also soothe intoxication, according to Pliny. **Red Sandalwood** <note>original: "Santalum rubrum"</note> imitates the color of wine; indeed, those who counterfeit wine (*scamnidici*) make it from its shavings; Avicenna said it is suitable for a hangover. We must not omit the **Sea Grape** <note>original: "marina uva"</note>, which mimics the color and likeness of a grape quite beautifully; its clusters, when rotted in wine, bring a loathing of wine to those who drink it unknowingly, according to Pliny. The leaf of the **Amethyst herb** <note>original: "Amethysti herba"; likely a species of lavender or similar purple plant</note> rivals the color of more potent wine; they say this is powerful against drunkenness. Plutarch, in the third book of the *Symposiacs*, demonstrates that the **Baccharis** <note>original: "baccharem"; an aromatic plant with purple flowers</note> induces sleep and leads drinkers to peaceful rest; it causes a light breeze and a gentle flow of scent, by which the inequalities arising in the bodies of the intoxicated are dissipated, and once tranquility is achieved, the hangover is blunted and boiled away; its flower glows with purple.

# BOOK FIVE.

### CHAPTER XXVI: ANIMALS THAT SEE AT NIGHT ARE EFFECTIVE AGAINST NIGHT-BLINDNESS.

The supreme goodness of God shows us that animals which see at night are effective remedies for those who are dim-sighted and suffer from night-blindness <note>The author uses the terms *lusciosos* (dim-sighted/owl-eyed) and *nyctalopas* (night-blind)</note>. **Celsus**, in the third book of *On Medicine*, while discussing the weakness of the eyes, says that those who see perfectly during the day but nothing at night (a condition that does not occur in women whose menstruation is regular) are called *nyctalopas* by the Greeks and *lusciosos* by the Latins. We proclaim that animals which see almost nothing during the day but see most clearly at night are effective for these dim-sighted people; for by communicating their power and quality to us, they enable us to see at night. 

But let us learn which animals see little by day and enough by night. Know that animals born blind see at night, and those born with blind eyes are those with sharp claws. Among quadrupeds, only the **lioness** <note>original: *leæna*</note> gives birth to cubs that can see, according to **Democritus**, because they are born incomplete due to the way they tear at the mother’s womb with their claws. From this, I declare the philosophers' conjecture to be false: for if an animal gave birth to blind offspring, it would be producing imperfect young, but in Nature, nothing is born unless it is most perfect. Rather, Nature shows us these blind births to indicate that these animals are effective against night-blindness. 

**Pliny** records that **goats** <note>original: *Capras*</note> see no less by night than by day; indeed, their eyes shine in the darkness and cast out light. Therefore, if those called *nyctalopas* eat a goat's liver, their evening vision is restored. **Dioscorides** and **Galen** state that the juices dripping from a roasted goat's liver, when used as an ointment, benefit the dim-sighted; they instruct that while it is cooking, the patients should keep their eyes open and let them be treated by the steam; it is also beneficial when eaten toasted. **Celsus** says: "Those suffering should be anointed with the blood of a liver, especially from a he-goat <note>original: *hircini*</note>, or failing that, a she-goat, collected while it is being roasted; and the liver itself ought to be eaten while fasting." 

**Sheep** <note>original: *oues*</note> are of the same kind and see at night; for this reason, sheep's liver heals night-blindness. They also advise washing the eyes with the liquid it was boiled in, according to **Pliny**—this is even more effective if it comes from a tawny sheep. According to **Marcellus**, the liver of a white sheep, thoroughly boiled, soaked in water, pounded, and applied, also cures night-blindness; for those who have light-colored eyes see better at night, which is why Marcellus specified a white sheep rather than a tawny one as Pliny did. 

The **wolf** <note>original: *Lupus*</note> is born blind; it sees at night and wanders. A wolf’s eyes shine and cast out light, as noted by **Pliny** and **Oppian**. It has a most keen and sharp sight, so that in the dead of night, or even when the Moon itself is silent <note>a poetic way of describing the New Moon</note>, it enjoys the use of light. Hence, the twilight is called *nyktops* <note>original Greek: *νυκτώψ*, meaning 'night-eye'</note>, since it holds the perception of light for these animals alone by the gift of Nature. Rubbing the eyes with wolf fat is beneficial against inflammation, according to **Pliny**. It is also helpful to smear cataracts with wolf excrement, or to be anointed with their ash mixed with Attic honey, according to **Oppian** and **Sextus**. The right eye of a wolf, if a man's right eye suffers (or the left, if the left suffers), thins out cataracts and removes the symptoms, says **Sextus**. 

The **hyena** <note>original: *Hyæna*</note> is of the wolf kind and has much in common with it; it prowls at night and sets its snares at night, because it sees more sharply then, whereas it may wander dazed during the day, according to **Oppian**. **Aphrodisias** provides the reason why the hyena sees at night and almost nothing by day. **Dioscorides** says that cataracts are healed by the juices of a fresh liver being roasted, smeared on with skimmed honey. The gall of a hyena sharpens the eyesight and scatters darkness; it provokes clarity better than an old medicine, and heals white ulcers <note>term: *argemas*, small white ulcers on the cornea</note> and bloody growths in the eyes. 

The **mouse** <note>original: *Mus*</note> gives birth to blind young, steals at night, and hides by day. They say that the ash of mice's heads and tails, smeared on with honey, restores clarity to the vision; this is even more true of the ash of a dormouse or a field mouse, according to **Pliny**, for dormice also give birth to blind offspring. 

The **bear** <note>original: *Vrſus*</note> gives birth to blind cubs and wanders at night. **Horace** writes: 

> "...and the evening bear circling the sheepfold."

Bear's gall, anointed with that of a hyena and stirred for a long time, removes darkness from the eyes, according to **Marcellus**. 

The **fox** <note>original: *Vulpes*</note> gives birth to blind offspring and wanders at night. **Pliny** claims that those who wear a fox's tongue in an armband will not suffer from bleary eyes; it is also an effective remedy for clearing away white spots on the eye <note>original: *albuginis*</note> if you catch one alive and use its...

...you shall cut off the tongue and release the bird itself alive; then, you shall tie the dried tongue with Phoenician <note>Often referring to deep red or purple dyed thread</note> thread and hang it from the neck, according to **Marcellus**. The **Little Owl** <note>original: *Noctua*</note>, among birds with hooked claws and carnivores, does not give birth to blind offspring; therefore, an innate power is seated in its eyes which penetrates the darkness, and it sees even when the Moon is silent <note>A poetic way of saying the moon is not visible/new moon</note>. It is called *noctua* because it sees at night (*noctu*). **Varinus** and **Eustrathius** say that because of the excessively dry and thin humor of the eye, they are blinded during the day but have strong vision in the shadows. The brain of a "sea-owl" <note>Likely a type of fish or ray</note> used in a salve <note>term: *collyrium*—a liquid or semi-solid medicinal preparation for the eyes</note> takes away the defect of seeing poorly at night, according to **Rhazes**. The **Screech Owl** <note>original: *Vlula*</note> is of the same species; its gall is praised for white spots <note>term: *albugines*—corneal opacities or scarring</note>, cataracts <note>term: *suffusiones*</note>, and dimness; and its fat is used for clarity of sight, according to **Pliny**. The **Bat** <note>original: *Vespertilio*</note> takes its name from evening (*vesper*), which is when it sees. **Ovid** writes:

> *They haunt houses, not forests; and loathing the light,*
> *They fly by night, taking their name from the late evening.*
> <note>original: "Tectaq; non syluas celebrant, noctemq; perosa, / Nocte volant, seroq; tenent à vespere nomen."</note>

The ash of a bat sharpens the sight, according to **Avicenna**, and mixed with honey, it cures cataracts. The **Eagle Owl** <note>original: *Bubo*</note> is dull-witted, like other nocturnal birds, and dwells in deserted, dreadful, and inaccessible places—a monster of the night. **Pliny** promises that the ash of an eagle owl’s eyes in a salve grants clarity to the eyes. The **Cat** <note>original: *Catus*</note> gives birth to blind kittens; its eyes shine and radiate in the darkness, and they see so sharply that even in dark caverns, they behold everything as if in the light. It heals defects of the eyes and restores sight even after a year of blindness: this is done by burning the head of a black cat in a clay pot and blowing its ash into the eyes through a quill—a remedy attributed to **Hippocrates**. The **Swallow** <note>original: *Hirundo*</note> gives birth to blind offspring, as do all those that have numerous young, according to **Pliny**; it stays awake at night and completes only half its sleep, according to **Aelian**. Its brain heals inflammation of the eyes <note>term: *obtalmiam*</note> and eye defects, according to **Pliny** and **Galen**. Several birds give birth to imperfect and blind offspring, namely those small in body that produce many young, such as **woodpeckers** <note>original: *pici*</note>. The constant eating of their young increases the sight according to **Pliny**, so much so that it cures night-blindness, restores the "visual spirits" <note>A historical medical concept that a physical 'spirit' or fluid traveled through the optic nerves to enable sight</note>, and removes darkness, according to **Gordonius** and others. The **Beaver** <note>original: *Castor*</note> comes out from its hiding place at night; *castoreum* <note>A secretion from the beaver’s scent glands</note> is very effective for the clarity of the eyes when smeared on with Attic honey, according to **Pliny**. **Frogs** wander at night; the males invite the females to mate with a song, and once they have enticed them, they wait to couple continuously at night, for they cannot do so in the water, and they indulge in their embraces with great security at night, whereas they are unwilling during the day due to fear, according to **Plutarch**. Their eyes glow for a time like lanterns. The **Plinian Magi** <note>Followers of magic cited (and often criticized) by Pliny the Elder</note> order a sea urchin to be burned with viper skins and frogs, and the ash to be sprinkled into a potion, promising clarity of vision. **Crabs** wander at night; **sea turtles** also come out at night, since they never sleep in the water. Their eyes cast a glow far and wide, and since their pupils are very white and bright, they are extracted to be enclosed in gold or placed in necklaces, according to **Aelian**. The gall of turtles creates clarity in the eyes, and when smeared on with honey, it heals cataracts and all defects of the eyes, according to **Pliny**, **Galen**, and **Asclepiades**. The **Stargazer fish** <note>original: *Vranoscopus*</note> is called by the Greeks *kallyonimos* <note>original: καλλιώνυμος—"beautifully named"</note>, as if it were a fish of a beautiful name; **Oppian** calls it the "day-sleeper" <note>original: ἡμεροκοίτην (*hemerokoiten*)</note> because it stays awake at night and sleeps during the day for the sake of seeking prey; for this reason, it is also called the "night-creature" or "bat-fish" <note>original: νυκτερίς (*nykteris*)</note>. **Oppian**, singing of it, says:

> *We shall mention the "day-sleeper," remarkable for its stupidity,*
> *Surpassing in sluggishness all creatures the sea produces;*
> *All day it lies prostrate in the yellow sand*
> *And sleeps, but at night it wakes and wanders alone:*
> *Hence they also call it the "Bat-fish."*

The bile of certain animals is uniquely praised by physicians as if it sharpens the edge of the eyes and dissolves the beginnings of cataracts, such as the fish they call the *kallyonimus*, the **hyena**, and the **sea scorpion**, according to **Dioscorides**, **Galen**, and others.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of animal "signatures"—the idea that an animal's natural traits can provide clues to its medicinal uses. ->BOOK FIVE<-

# HOW SHARP-SIGHTED ANIMALS ARE EFFECTIVE FOR THE 
### clarity of the eyes. Chapter XXVII.

Just as animals with sharp sight can heal eye defects, they are also powerful for us in clarifying a dulled gaze. We previously spoke of animals that gave birth to blind offspring; now we discuss those born with their eyes open, to show how Nature uses them to grant clarity and heal ocular flaws. We shall call upon these examples to prove our proposal. The **Lioness** alone among her kind gives birth to young with their eyes already open. **Plutarch**, in his *Table Talk*, notes this among the four-footed animals with hooked claws; likewise, **Democritus** said the lion hunts by day, not by night, and possesses the sharpest vision. Its name is derived <term>from "to see"</term> <note>original: παρὰ τὸ λεύσειν</note> because of its excellent sight, according to **Porphyry**, and **Homer** writes that <term>"he gazes terribly"</term> <note>original: σμερδαλέον λεύσει</note>, which signifies a bright shine; <term>"I see"</term> <note>original: λέω</note> is the root in Greek, from which the lion takes its name, because its eyesight excels above all other animals, as **Manetho** writes in his book to Herodotus. The lion never truly admits sleep, but appears to enjoy rest with its eyes wide open. Its gall, when mixed with water and applied as an ointment, adds clarity to the eyes according to **Pliny**; **Galen** stated that when mixed with honey, it destroys <term>white spots</term> <note>term: *albugines*—white opacities or scarring on the cornea</note>.

The **Hare**, unlike the majority of cloven-hoofed animals, does not produce blind offspring. **Plutarch** said it excels most in the excellence of its senses, such as sight. **Aelian** noted it takes its food at night, though **Xenophon** believed its vision was not particularly sharp. **Pollux** claims the hare’s eyes are tireless, for it sleeps with eyes open and stays awake with them closed; indeed, while the rest of its limbs take their sleep, its eyes alone continue to see. The gall of a hare, applied with honey, clarifies the vision.

The **Eagle** hatches its chicks with their eyes open; indeed, it forces the hatchlings to face the sun’s rays. It possesses the greatest power of sight and claims the throne among birds for the sharpest eyes, according to **Alexander of Aphrodisias**. Its gaze is so powerful that, even as it hangs on motionless wings high above the sea beyond human sight, it can see small fish swimming; descending like a missile, it drags the snatched prey to the shore. It does not turn its gaze away from the sun's rays, and it holds its chicks up to the sun by its talons; any chick that blinks it rejects as not genuine, but any that turns its gaze away it casts out of the nest as a degenerate, according to **Aristotle**, **Aelian**, and **Oppian**. **Galen** recorded that eagle gall should be mixed into eye medicines. **Pliny** notes that if eagle gall is applied with Attic honey to those whose eyes are growing dim, they will fully recover their sight, and it renders the eyes most sharp; they report the same regarding the eagle's brain.

The **Hawk**, acting as a sort of lesser eagle, is born with its eyes open. The Egyptians held it sacred to **Apollo** <note>The sun god</note> because it agrees with Apollo in many ways: among birds, only hawks gaze upon the sun's rays with no effort and without turning their eyes away; they are not burdened by the journey upward nor offended by the divine flame. <term>"The hawk is sacred to the Sun-Apollo"</term> <note>original: ἱέραξ ἱερὰξ κὰι ἡλίω ἀπολλωνι</note>. Therefore, because of the brilliance of its eyes, it can be seen as sacred to the Sun. **Varinus** and **Eustathius**, in their commentaries on Homer, suggest that Apollo himself once turned into a hawk, and transformed Deucalion into the same bird. **Porphyry** reports that the ancients called the sun a lizard, a lion, a dragon, and a hawk. The Egyptians often represent **Osiris** in the form of a hawk because this bird excels in its keenness of sight, according to **Plutarch** in his book *On Isis and Osiris*. A hawk boiled in rose oil is most effective for ointments for all defects of the eyes, according to **Pliny**.

The **Kite**, like the hawk, is born of the hawk family and differs only in size. **Politian** uses "kite-eyes" as a metaphor for the sharpest vision. The liver of a kite is praised for ointments for all eye defects, according to **Pliny**.

**Vultures** are midway between kites and eagles. Of all animals, the vulture has the most far-seeing vision, such that when the sun rises in the East it can look toward the West, and from the West toward the East; it identifies the food it needs from a vast distance. For this reason, the Egyptians paint a vulture when they wish to signify "sight," according to **Horus Apollo**. It is effective for the same things as the eagle, according to **Aesculapius**. Let the <term>night-blind person</term> <note>term: *lusciosus*—someone who sees poorly in the evening or has dim vision</note> eat roasted kite liver and be anointed with it, according to **Archigenes** in Galen’s writings, and for all eye defects, according to **Serenus**, **Marcellus**, and others. 

The **Serpent** is born with open eyes: for as soon as it is excluded from the egg, it crawls and sees just like a lizard. It is of sharp sight, and "dragons" are so called from the Greek word...

PHYTOGNOMONICA, BOOK VI

...derived <term>from "to see"</term> <note>original Greek: δέρπω (*derpō*), meaning "I look" or "I see"</note>: and we have said that Apollo is called "the dragon" because of the sharpness of his vision. **Horace** writes on this in his *Satires*:

> Why do you see the faults of your friends so sharply, 
> As an eagle, or an Epidaurian serpent? <note>Epidaurus was the site of the sanctuary of Asclepius, where sacred serpents were kept.</note>

If the flesh of a **viper** is eaten cooked, it brings clarity to the eyes, according to **Dioscorides**. **Crocodiles** lay their eggs on land; as soon as they can move, they head for the water. Although they are blind in the water, they are extremely sharp-sighted out of it, according to **Herodotus** and **Aristotle**. Before the rest of its body, its eyes emerge from the depths of the water; because of this, the **Egyptians**, wishing to signify the rising of the Sun, paint a pair of crocodile eyes, and to signify its setting, they paint it with its head bowed. Its blood, according to **Pliny**, grants clarity of vision to those who apply it as an ointment and heals dimness. **Frogs** hatched from eggs are distinguished by their eyes; we have said that their ash is effective for clarity of the eyes. **Fish** are born without eyelids; they are shown to be effective for eye defects. Because of this, the gall of all fish is good for the eyes, such as that of the **sea-raven**, the **scorpion-fish**, the **swallow-fish**, the **stargazer**, the **mullet**, the **ray**, the **shark**, and in the **small fry** <note>original: *aphis*</note>, little is seen except for the eyes.

### ANIMALS WHOSE EYES ARE BLINDED AND
### grow back, and how they are effective for ulcers and scars 
### of the eyes. Chapter XXVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'E' containing a woodcut illustration of a landscape with buildings and trees.</image-desc>
IT IS a property of certain animals that, if their eyes are pierced, they grow back anew. Provident Nature has demonstrated this to us so that we might know that their blood can provide help for scars, blows, and ulcers of our own eyes. **Celsus** indicated this in his book on Medicine, saying: "If an external blow has injured the eyes, or if blood is suffused within them, nothing is more suitable than to smear them with the blood of a **pigeon**, a **wood-pigeon**, or a **swallow**." This is not done without reason, since their sight, when injured from the outside, returns to its former state after a time, most rapidly in the swallow. From this comes the saying that <term>"the place of the awl was made"</term> <note>original: *locus subulæ factus est*—an idiom suggesting that even a deep puncture can be healed</note>; that which heals by itself is restored by the parents using a herb. Therefore, their blood most suitably protects our eyes from external accidents, in this order: the swallow's blood is first, then the wood-pigeon's, while the common pigeon's is the least effective for them and for us. We have from **Aristotle’s** sixth book of *History of Animals* that if someone pricks the eyes of **swallow chicks** while they are still young, the eyes grow back and regain the power of sight afterward. It is therefore false to claim that when the chicks' eyes are lost, sight can be restored by the **celandine herb** <note>original: *chelidonia*—long associated with swallows (*chelidon* in Greek) due to the myth that mothers used it to heal their young</note> brought by the mothers. **Dioscorides** notes that swallows, like **warblers** <note>original: *ficedulæ*</note>, provide a medicine for sharp sight when eaten; **Aelian** orders live swallows to be burned for eye medicines. The chicks of swallows are blinded during the full Moon, and once their sight is restored, their heads are burned; let their ash be used with honey for clarity, for pains, for rheum, and for blows. 

But **Aristotle**, in the fourth volume of *The Generation of Animals*, immediately after dealing with certain animals that produce blind young, added: "Therefore, if someone should prick the eyes of swallows recently brought into the light, their sight may be restored." He denies, however, that sight is restored to the chicks' eyes by the mother, as this would oppose the decrees of Nature, which has ordained that the lost parts of perfected <note>adult</note> creatures do not return to their former state. But in those creatures still in the process of formation, if something is injured, it can arise anew, and the loss of a part can be repaired; for the <term>procreative faculty</term> <note>original: *genitalis facultas*—the innate power of a young organism to complete its growth</note>, which by the law of Nature is still completing the work it started, has not vanished. Acting as the architect of the form, and having found the material, it can restore it again. For swallow chicks do not see when hatched and are brought into the light "imperfect"; while the <term>procreative breath</term> <note>original: *genitalis aura*</note> still resides in the eyes that are not yet finished, it can repair those that are pricked or torn out. But this seems false to me: that this faculty was given only to certain animals by a special gift of Nature, to demonstrate to mortals what might benefit wounds of the eye and ruptured membranes <meta>catchword: could.</meta>

<summary>This chapter discusses the medicinal use of animals with sharp sight or regenerative abilities—specifically crocodiles and swallows—to treat human eye ailments. It debates the biological mechanism behind how young swallows can regrow damaged eyes, linking this to the "procreative faculty" of developing organisms.</summary>
