BOOK FIVE.

...so that they may <note>This completes the heading from the previous page: "how they are healed."</note>. The **wood-pigeon** follows after the swallow according to **Celsus**: for blows to the eye, the blood of a wood-pigeon is applied, as well as for eyes suffused with blood and for those suffering from <term>night-blindness</term> <note>original: "lusciosis"</note> according to **Dioscorides**. The **pigeon** is also effective for <term>suffusions</term> <note>Often referring to cataracts or hemorrhages under the surface of the eye.</note> of the eyes, for night-blindness, and for recent wounds by means of its own blood, according to the same author; for it is cut under the wing for this purpose, since it is more useful when warm with its own heat. It is then necessary to apply a compress of boiled honey and raw wool soaked in oil or wine, according to **Pliny**, **Sextus**, and **Marcellus**—though **Galen** refers to these as <term>subconjunctival hemorrhages</term> <note>original: "hyposphagmata"</note>. For when blows are inflicted on the eyes, bloody suffusions arise immediately at the start; then, to quell the pain, the instillation of pigeon blood is helpful, especially that which is squeezed from the tips of the feathers. Even if the **turtle-dove** is not described by some, since it is of the same genus, its pierced eyes can easily be healed, and its blood is effective for the same conditions. **Pliny** writes that turtle-dove blood is exceptionally beneficial for eyes suffused with blood, and **Marcellus** recommends it for eyes bloodied by a blow. 

But we have learned of other experiments from what **Celsus** writes, and perhaps more powerful ones for the same effects; for even the eyes of **lizards** are healed. Indeed, we read this story in **Aelian**. There is no need here for many testimonies from the ancients. When a certain man had caught a large and fine lizard and blinded it with a stylus, he placed it in a new earthenware jar pierced on both sides with small holes so that the creature would not be prevented from breathing. He also took an iron ring, which was set with a <term>jet stone</term> <note>original: "gagatis lapidis"</note>, and had engraved nine signs upon it, of which he would erase one each day. Later, when no sign remained and he opened the jar, we saw that the lizard had recovered its sight. We recognized that this happened not from any trickery of a friend, but from its own natural property. Indeed, when a lizard's eyes are blinded by old age, they enter a hole in a wall facing the East, gazing toward the rising of the Sun, and they are illuminated. This is also reported from **Isidore**, and **Pliny** said that its ash with honey is powerfully effective against dimness; its blood is good for the sight according to **Avicenna**, and its brain for suffusions. 

The lizard, says **Pliny**, enters into eye medicines in several ways. For some put a green lizard in a new earthenware jar along with little stones which they call <term>cincædia</term> <note>Stones found in the bodies of certain fish or lizards, believed to have magical healing properties.</note>, which are usually tied to swellings in the groin; they mark them with nine signs and take one away each day. On the ninth day, they release the lizard and keep the stones for eye pains. Others lay soil beneath a blinded green lizard and enclose it alive in a glass vessel with solid iron or gold; when it appears through the glass that the lizard has recovered its sight, it is released, and they use the rings against <term>bleariness</term> <note>original: "lippitudinem"</note>. Some burn a long-necked green lizard found in bean fields and use the ash to anoint the eyes at the onset of <term>watery eyes</term> <note>original: "epiphoram"</note>, and likewise for <term>glaucomas</term> <note>In this period, "glaucoma" usually referred to an incurable clouding or opacity of the lens.</note>. 

**Marcellus** adds further details: Put a green lizard, blinded with a copper needle, into a glass vessel with rings of gold, silver, iron, and amber—if available—or even copper. Then you shall seal it with plaster or close it carefully and mark it; after the fifth or seventh day you shall open it, and you will find the lizard with healthy eyes. You shall let it go alive and use the rings for bleariness, not only wearing them on the fingers but also applying them frequently to the eyes, so that the vision is transmitted through the hole of the ring. Observe that the vessel should be placed in a bright and grassy spot, and when the lizard has departed, then the rings may be collected. This should also be observed during the waning moon—that is, from the nineteenth to the twenty-fifth day—in the month of September. As long as you keep this remedy with you, your eyes will not ache. 

Sight is also restored to the **crocodile**. For it is dim-sighted in the water, but of extremely sharp vision outside of it, according to **Aristotle** and **Pliny** (following him), and **Aristotle** (following **Herodotus**), who say the crocodile is blind while in the water. There is a bean in Egypt with a thorny stem, which for this reason strikes the eyes of the crocodile, as it often encounters the thorny beans; unless they were healed by the eye's own natural power, that animal would have been created imperfectly by Nature. **Pliny** says the blood of the aquatic crocodile, when used as an ointment, grants clarity of vision and heals scars on the eyes. The blood of both the land crocodile and the aquatic crocodile heals the sight and clears scars. <term>Crocodile-dung medicine</term> <note>original: "Crocodilea"</note> is described by the same author, and **Trallianus** describes the dung of the crocodile as being effective for eye defects, suffusions, and dimness, and for use in <term>eye-salves</term> <note>original: "collyria"</note>. 

A species of lizard is the <term>spotted gecko</term> <note>original: "stellio"</note>, whose blood or dung is effective for dullness and dimness of the eyes. There are also serpents of the lizard kind, and if their eyes were plucked out, they would perhaps be restored in this way; in extreme old age they grow dim, but they restore their sight with **fennel** <note>original: "fœniculo"</note>. For the sharpness of the eyes...

### PLANTS THAT BEAR RESEMBLANCES TO OTHER INTERNAL
### organs, and heal them. Chapter 29.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'S' featuring a celestial motif with a crescent moon, stars, and clouds in the background.</image-desc>

THERE are also other parts of plants that reveal internal diseases of the body's parts and are effective for them. **Frothy poppy** <note>likely *Silene vulgaris* or Bladder Campion</note> is a small herb that is entirely white and completely frothy; it signifies the foam flowing from the mouths of those suffering from the **falling sickness** <note>original: "comitialem morbum," a historical term for epilepsy.</note>. **Dioscorides** said it heals those with the falling sickness. **Soapwort**, when agitated by the hands, produces much foam; perhaps it is effective for the same condition, but its virtue is not yet explored. **Horse-tongue** <note>original: "Hippoglossum," likely *Ruscus hypoglossum*</note> bears another leaf that is extremely sharp, much to the wonder of onlookers and as a rarity of Nature; it is established by the experiment of the moderns <note>original: "neotericorum"</note> that it is effective for stitches in the side. The **Oak**, among other growths, bears the **gall** <note>an abnormal growth caused by wasps</note>, which imitates the fibers of the **spleen** by its resemblance; its ash drunk with vinegar consumes the spleen, according to **Pliny**. The **crab** shows the chest by its shape and heals infirmity of the chest; for this reason, boiled and eaten, it benefits those wasted by **consumption** <note>original: "tabe," referring to wasting diseases like tuberculosis.</note>, according to **Dioscorides**. The **turtle** shows the same; **Leonello Faventino** mixes the flesh of the turtle into remedies for consumptives.

### PARTS OF PLANTS OR ANIMALS THAT SHOW THE
### hardness of stones, or the stones themselves, are effective for calculi. Chapter 30.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'M' featuring a scenic woodcut of a garden or rural landscape with foliage and distant hills.</image-desc>

IN MANY ways and many modes, plants show how the tortures and butcheries of **calculi** <note>Stones formed in the kidneys or bladder.</note> can be met, by demonstrating hardness in their seeds, or a resemblance to them; so also in animals, stones or their likenesses arise. As examples we shall call upon **stone-seed** <note>original: "lithospermon," or Gromwell</note>; it took its name from the seed, which produces a stony hardness that breaks calculi. **Pliny** looked upon nothing among herbs with greater wonder—so great is the beauty, as if pearls were whitening between the leaves by the art of craftsmen—such an exquisite difficulty of a stone born from a herb. It is certain that by drinking a drachm's weight of these little stones in white wine, calculi are broken and expelled. **Job’s Tears** <note>original: "Lachryma ioppea"</note> bears a seed like ferns, indeed skillfully similar to stone-seed, or rather more persistent; with the middle pierced and threaded on a string, we count our prayers <note>A reference to the seeds being used as rosary beads.</note>. It is also a well-known protection against stones in the kidneys and the **gravel** <note>original: "faburram," referring to sandy sediment in the urine.</note> of the bladder in the form of powder or decoction. Berries also grow in the middle of the foliage of **Butcher's Broom** <note>original: "rusci"</note>, with a bony kernel inside; the seed drunk in wine is effective for kidney pains and difficulty of urine, or in vinegar it breaks stones. The **Oak** for the most part produces little stones, says **Theophrastus**, and **Pliny** following him. The Oak sometimes also produces **pumice stones**, which can be an argument for us that they are clearly effective for removing calculi. There are also little stones or pebbles tied to and hanging from the roots of plants, which their resemblance demonstrates are also effective for calculi. The roots of **Sedge** <note>original: "Cyperi"</note>, similar to olives, are effective for calculi. **Chufa** <note>original: "Thrasi"</note> is a species of it. A species of **Dog’s Grass** is bulbous underneath, with many hanging globules, useful for expelling calculi. **Female Peony** casts out calculi with its grains. A type of **Saxifrage**, whose roots are divided into globules, is effective for the same. **Dropwort** <note>original: "Oenantes"</note> is for kidney stones by the experiment of the moderns. The very hard pits <note>original: "ossa"</note> of the **Medlar** are excellent for the same. In the heads of many fish there are little stones which

they are effective for breaking stones <term>calculi</term> <note>original: "ad frangendos calculos." In early modern medicine, "calculi" referred to kidney or bladder stones.</note>. They are found in the heads of wolves, sea breams, crow-fish, umbras, gulls, menas, scorpion-fish, and—though **Pliny** says they are in the tail—in mullets, grey mullets, rocklings, and tench. **Crayfish** also have round little stones in their heads, which Physicians use to expel stones; likewise **crabs**, **lobsters**, and even the stones found in **sponges**. In the liver of the **wild boar**, little stones are found, just as in the common **pig**, similar in hardness to pebbles and white; when crushed and drunk in wine, they say stones are expelled, according to **Pliny**. They say a small stone is found in the head of a **bramble toad** <note>original: "rubetæ"</note>, which must be removed using a scarlet cloth; they say it is effective against stones. I could never find one, but those they say belong to the toad, and are called **toadstones** <term>crapodinos</term>, I have seen growing in mines. The **Jew’s stone** <note>original: "Iudaicus lapis," likely a fossilized sea urchin spine</note>, shaped like an acorn and notable for its extreme hardness, crushes stones in the bladder according to **Dioscorides**. In the liver of the **wild boar**, little stones are found, just as in the common **pig**, similar in hardness to pebbles and white; when crushed and drunk in wine, they say stones are expelled, according to **Pliny**.

### TALKATIVE ANIMALS HEAL THE COLON.

->Cap. XXXIV.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' featuring floral and scrollwork designs within a square frame.</image-desc>

**TALKATIVE** animals are not subject to the suffering of **colic** <note>original: "colicę passioni"</note>, just as talkative men are not; for by their excessive chatter, the gas <term>flatus</term> from which the disease often arises is expelled. Therefore, by impressing their quality upon us, they remove such a disease. The **turtle dove** is most talkative, and not only with its mouth, but it farts while it sings from its hind parts. A creaking of the bowels is characteristic of turtle doves, and a proverb is said of those who are talkative: *He is more talkative than a turtle dove.* **Menander** mentions this proverb in the comedy titled *Plotius*, and **Democritus** also mentions in his dramatic work titled *Sicilia* that it cries out from the back part of its body, according to **Aelian**. **Aëtius** <note>OCR: "Actius"</note> said that turtle doves and wood pigeons are suitable for those with colic. The **wood pigeon** truly moans in winter for many days and at the time of the solstice. The **cicada**, noisy and constantly vocal, bursts itself by crying out: **Dioscorides** and **Galen** prescribed that cicadas should be eaten for colic. The **goldfinch** sings much: roasted or taken in food, it perfectly cures those with intestinal blockages <note>original: "iliacos"</note> and colic. The **lark** delights wonderfully with the modulation of its voice; even when shut in cages and forgetting its captivity, it hardly lets an hour of the day pass without song: we have said that the lark is effective for colic according to **Dioscorides**, **Galen**, **Aëtius**, and everyone. The **swallow** is chattering and brings aid to those with colic, according to **Marcellus**. The **blackbird** sings by night and day; eaten in food, it benefits those with griping pains, and so it is for the rest.

# GIAMBATTISTA DELLA PORTA
## OF NAPLES
### PHYTOGNOMONICS
#### BOOK SIX.
##### P R E F A C E.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'E' depicting a young figure or putto amidst scrolling foliage and flowers.</image-desc>

*NOW THAT I HAVE EXPLAINED the likenesses of plants which, through the clever work of Nature, represented the parts of humans and animals, it remains to explain those likenesses that arise from actions; soon we shall proceed to behaviors, so that we may precisely follow the division we proposed at the start. But we do not use the term "actions" as Physicians or Philosophers do—for, on the authority of **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle; he is often called the "Father of Botany."</note>, we know that plants lack actions in the animal sense—rather, we call "actions" the manner of their birth, generation, growth, and bearing of fruit. We also consider the love with which they pursue one another, shrink away from one another, or attract each other, as well as observing the times in which they are born, and other similar actions. From these, the diligent plant-observer <term>Phytopta</term> <note>original: "Phytopta." A Greek-derived term Porta uses for someone who studies the hidden signatures of plants through observation.</note> will be able to divine many of Nature's secrets. For nothing in the family of plants is fashioned rashly or in vain, but in a rare manner, with ordered causes, precise numbers, and at the opportune time and place. From the beginning, therefore, we shall look upon their origin, growth, and manner of fruiting, so that by their pure and true likenesses through which they work, we may be reminded of their powers <note>original: "facultatum." In early medicine, "faculties" or "powers" refer to the specific healing properties or virtues a plant possesses.</note>. And first, we shall begin with the seed.*

BOOK SIX.

# THAT STERILE PLANTS RENDER HUMANS STERILE.

->Chapter 1.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'P' featuring intricate floral and foliage patterns.</image-desc>

**PLANTS** all are quiet at certain times of the year, then at certain times they grow into stems, and finally emerge into flowers and fruits. The seed is the end and that final point for which the plant is destined: for the propagation of its own kind. **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC), the "Father of Botany."</note> calls the seed Nature’s most perfect gift. Nature does not show flowers until she draws out the stems, nor does she emerge into flowers until, pregnant with her own offspring, she longs for birth. When the seed provokes it, the human rod becomes stiff; the plant that is about to bear seed raises its stem, as if it cannot produce seed except by means of a stem. The flower corresponds to the monthly cleansings <note>original: "menstruis" (menstruation).</note> of women; a woman will not conceive unless the monthly cycle has appeared as proof of fertility, and likewise a plant does not show seed unless the preludes of the flowers have appeared, by which the future birth is foretold. **Aristotle** in his *Problems* states that plants live only for the sake of the seed, and when they have borne seed, they wither. Every kind of vegetable withers after bearing fruit; others, even if they cannot bear seed in their first year, perish after the seed is brought forth. For this reason, Mother Nature covers them with such great defenses and wrappings against the diseases of animals and against the weather, lest they should rot. **Alexander of Aphrodisias** <note>A Greek commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD).</note> says: "When Nature strives for the origin of seeds and the perpetual successions of following generations, she decided that the things providing that origin must be protected and hidden." In short, the proper duty of plants is to be seed-bearing.

But there are many herbs that enjoy no seed-bearing, but are expelled from the choir of the fertile. **Theophrastus** says some are fruit-bearing, others are sterile; some only grow as far as the leaves, others raise a stem and flower but promise no fruit, unless something can be fruit-bearing without a flower. **Cato** called those trees "happy" <note>original: "felices," also meaning "fruitful" or "blessed" in Latin.</note> which bear fruit, and "unhappy" those which do not. **Pliny** says those are considered unhappy and condemned by religious law which are never planted nor bear fruit. The flowering of trees is a joy, but this is denied to most, for not all bloom; rather, there are certain "sad" plants which do not feel the joys of the years, nor are they cheered by a flower, nor do they promise the annual return of fruits with a many-colored messenger.

But, good Gods, why is it that these wonders seem to come forth from Nature’s workshop, such that for many trees their lot and native condition is to be without stem, flower, or seed? These things contradict what was said by us above: that plants were produced for conceiving, nourishing, and protecting fruits. Is Nature then imperfect, so that she is proven frustrated in her work? Or does she desist from her duty? But know this: Mother Nature herself, the parent of all things, does nothing without the greatest reason; indeed, where she seems lacking and failed, there she stands more magnificent and admirable. By this omen and paradox, she warns mortals to contemplate and investigate her works; for she made those plants "eunuchs" <note>original: "spadonias, siue eunuchias."</note> so that we might understand them to be effective for preventing conception <term>atocia</term> <note>original: "atocia," a Greek term for the prevention of pregnancy or birth.</note>, for intercepting birth, and for causing sterility, so that she might turn men away from their use and consumption by that shameful lack of honor. 

We have already said in our *Human Physiognomy* <note>Porta's earlier work on judging character from physical appearance.</note> that the hunchbacked, the blind, the eunuchs, and the lame are liable to ruinous and avoidable behaviors; and the more noble the members were which the human lacked—such as the head, heart, or genitals—the more dishonest the behaviors they announced. So too in these parts where Nature is lacking in plants, in which the faculty of generation is given (among the other most necessary parts), she promises us the worst things, namely sterilities and abortions. 

But if these **Phytognomonics** <note>The study of plant "signatures" to determine their medicinal use.</note> of ours do not satisfy some nosy critic, and he desires to reduce these things to the well-known causes of "qualities," let him know that plants, by their own nature or by the spirit of a place's dryness, will produce fewer stems, flowers, and fruits. We have said that wild plants are drier than garden plants, less fertile, and fruit more sparingly. And stony and parched places produce either sterile plants or plants of fewer fruit due to the scarcity of nourishment; because moist and hollow places are more fruitful from the abundance of moisture, while those things which are dry by nature desiccate the seed and render it sterile, as the dogmas of the Physicians teach. 

But let us come to examples. **Ibycus**, a philosopher of the Pythagorean family, is the authority that the lettuce without a stem, which spreads out wide, is called *eunuchion* <note>original: "eunuchion," the eunuch-lettuce.</note>, as if it were castrated...

...and women call it **Astylida** <note>original: "astylida"; from the Greek "a-" (without) and "stylos" (pillar/stalk), referring to a variety of lettuce that does not readily produce a tall flower stalk.</note>, because it most significantly not only diminishes fertility, but if any children are conceived, it produces those who are foolish, mindless, and falling away from the natural character of their ancestors; furthermore, those who eat this vegetable continuously become very sluggish toward sexual intercourse, so that the vigor of Venus withers away within them. **Nicander of Colophon** <note>A Greek poet and physician of the 2nd century BC.</note> left it written that **Adonis**, the son of Myrrha, was killed by a boar after he had devoured lettuce. **Callimachus** adds that **Venus** hid him under a lettuce plant: by which riddles the Poets hint that its use is most contrary to Venus <note>Venus is used here as a metonym for sexual desire and procreation.</note>. **Cratinus** adds that **Phaon** was hidden among lettuces by his lover, Venus. For this reason, **Eubolus** used to attack his wife with heavy insults if she offered lettuce at the table, saying it was therefore dedicated to the feasts of the dead.

**Ferns**, both male and female, are lacking in flower, seed, and stalks, and like sad things are content with a simple leaf: neither should be given to pregnant women, for they bring about abortion; if given to others, they are rendered entirely sterile. Their powers are thought by Nature to have been added to sterility, on the authority of **Theophrastus**; indeed, those women who even step over them suffer a miscarriage.

**Hemionion**—whether you call it "mule-wort" <note>original: "mulariam"</note> because mules delight in it most, or as I would prefer, named from sterility <note>The Greek "hemionos" means mule, an animal known for being sterile.</note>—is devoid of stalk, flower, and seed. The same author said that women who take this in food, mixed with a mule’s hoof and seed, become sterile.

**Onosma** is without a stalk, seed, or flower. Its leaves drunk in wine draw out the birth; **Dioscorides** <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD).</note> said that if a pregnant woman walks over it, she will miscarry.

**Asplenon**, or **Scolopendrium** <note>Spleenwort.</note>, has neither stalk, nor frond, nor seed; it is believed to take away conception by itself, or when tied on with the skin of a mule <note>original: "stene mulæ"; likely a reference to the sterile nature of the mule.</note>; according to the same author, he instructs that it be dug up on a moonless night, so that as it is deprived of light, it might also deprive humans of offspring.

**Dittany** <note>original: "Dictamnum"</note> is without seed and flower; not only when drunk, but even when applied as a poultice, it casts out a dead fetus, according to the same source; it works so powerfully that it should not even be brought into the bedroom of pregnant women, for its very scent is effective.

The other **Savin** <note>A type of juniper.</note> lacks flower and fruit; it slaughters the living fetus and casts out the dead one, and is infamous and condemned by everyone for this harm. The same author said it extracts the birth when applied or used as a fumigant.

**Theophrastus** believed that **Epimetron** entirely lacked a flower, and **Dioscorides** recorded that it bears neither flower nor fruit; its root destroys conception, and when drunk, it cuts off the power of conceiving; it must be avoided by women.

**Maidenhair** <note>original: "Adianton"</note> is devoid of seed, flower, and stalk; **Trichomanes** has the same equal effect, and (not worthy of further comment) it moves the afterbirth and grinds down stones <note>Kidney or bladder stones.</note>, almost as much as it kills the fetus.

There are two kinds of **Cedars**: that which flowers is sterile, and that which is fruitful does not flower, according to **Theophrastus**. If the genitals are smeared with it before intercourse, it takes away the power of conceiving, according to **Dioscorides**.

**Junipers** also do not flower; some record two kinds of them: that one flowers but does not bear fruit. But this is false; all of them have a harsh appearance always, and thus the fortune of these men is "without flower": it has the same power as the cedar, according to **Pliny**.

The **Myrica**, which **Lenaeus** calls *tamarisk* <note>original: "tamaricem"</note>, the common people call the "unlucky tree" because it bears nothing, nor is it ever sown. If it is mixed with the urine of a castrated ox, whether in drink or in food, sexual desire is ended; and a charcoal made from that kind of wood, extinguished in that urine and stored in the shade, resolves the same desire whenever one wishes to kindle it. The Magi also recorded that this happens with the urine of a eunuch <note>original: "spadonis"</note>, according to Pliny and elsewhere. What **Lais** and **Elephantis** <note>Two famous ancient Greek female writers on medicine and midwifery.</note> have published regarding abortifacients is contradictory: using charcoal from the root of a cabbage or tamarisk, extinguished in menstrual blood.

**Soapwort** <note>original: "Struthios"</note>, or the "little root," does not produce seed, according to **Pliny**; it destroys the fetus in the womb, according to **Dioscorides**.

One species of **Ivy** is fruitless according to **Theophrastus**, called *helix* by **Dioscorides**; its clusters of berries, when drunk, hinder conception, and the stalk inserted into the womb extracts the fetus.

**Mandrakes** are deprived of stalks, for the flowers hang from slender stems; placed beneath, they expel the fetus, according to the same author.

**Cyclamen** also bears flowers on little stalks without a main stem; when hung upon a woman, it accelerates the birth, and is mixed into medications that induce abortion to cast out the fetus. If pregnant women step over the roots, it is judged so powerful at destroying the conception.

Very swiftly the **Willow** <note>original: "Salix"</note> loses its seed, before it feels maturity at all; for this reason it was called by **Homer** "fruit-wasting" <note>original: "ἀλεσíκαρπος" (alesikarpos)</note>, that is, fruit-destroying or seed-destroying, for it bears fruit that turns into cobweb-like down before it ripens. A later age interpreted this sentence by its own crime, since it is well known that the seed of the willow is a medicine for a woman's sterility: for taken in water, it takes away the hope of conceiving, and the excess... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "tiam," likely for "intemperantiam" (intemperance/excess).</note>

...it also restrains lust, and if taken frequently, it completely takes away the ability <note>original: "vsum," referring to sexual function</note>, according to **Pliny**. He said that the **Poplar** does not bear fruit, even if it puts forth grapes; **Theophrastus** said both varieties flower; **Dioscorides** recorded that it induces sterility if drunk with a mule's kidney. But in truth, small berries hang in clusters on long stems, which, when they have matured, turn into downy seeds <note>original: "pappos"</note>. The female **Cypress** is sterile, its cone rolled into a peak; **Theophrastus** recorded that the male has obscure seeds, while **Varro** said they are tiny. In Arcadia they call it <gloss>parthenon</gloss> <note>original Greek: "παρθένον"</note>, that is, "the virgin," because it renders people sterile: its juice is very bitter, like cedar and savine, and of almost the same kind. Among the species of **Laurel** is one called the "triumphal," said by **Pliny** to be sterile: for this reason it is called "male" by some; we read that those celebrating triumphs used this, while the Delphic variety was rejected by **Caesar Augustus**; they claim this sterile one was sent from heaven to the same Caesar; others call it "spadonia" <note>likely meaning "eunuch" or "castrated," referring to its lack of fruit</note>, with a wonderful tolerance for shade. **Dioscorides** warns that its roots must be avoided by pregnant women, because they kill the fetus. The seed of **Thyme** is deceptive and cannot be detected, mixing itself in a way with the flowers; **Theophrastus** writes that the flower is sown and thyme is born. **Dioscorides** said it drives out the dead fetus and the afterbirth. **Theophrastus** thinks that **Mint** lacks seed, for when dried and crushed, no seed ever appeared, but they do bear flowers; **Aristotle** said in his book of *Problems* that it consumes the generative seed; it does not allow milk to curdle or thicken. They say that **Mint** <note>original: "Mintha"</note> was a nymph, the daughter of Cocytus, who, when she heard that **Proserpina** was loved by **Pluto**, was indignant at that name and constantly dared to prefer herself to her, saying that if he sought the underworld, she would infest it as an enemy; **Ceres**, the mother of Proserpina, moved by the girl’s pride, trampled Mint and deformed her into mint <note>original: "mentham; idest malam herbam." A pun on "mentha" (mint) and "malam" (bad/evil or an apple-herb).</note>. **Strabo** mentions her, hinting by this name that if applied to the womb before intercourse, it prevents conception. Neither is the seed of **Watercress** <note>original: "sisymbri"</note> conspicuous, says **Theophrastus**: **Pliny** warns it should not be eaten by pregnant women unless the fetus is dead, as it ejects it when applied. But lest our speech wander too insolently through all the herbs which are "maimed" <note>i.e., lacking parts like seeds or stems</note> and have been given the power of killing the offspring, we will place an end here, thinking these examples suffice, as the mind hurries on to other matters.

## AGAINST THE OPINION OF THE ANCIENTS THAT ALL PLANTS
### are endowed with seed. Chapter VII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring a seated figure (possibly a scholar or philosopher) in a landscape, surrounded by an ornate border with floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>IT has now been revealed why the master craftsman, **Nature**, has played with the image of sterile plants; it remains to show in what little compartments the seeds are enclosed, so that their renewable fertility and permanence might be ensured. Nor does the reasoning of the **Philosophers** regarding the hot and the cold shrink from this, since, when the character of the place is not in agreement—whether regions are scorched by heat or stiff with perpetual frost—they produce "maimed" and imperfect immigrant plants. Thus one explanation is satisfied for all: for the plants, for us, and for the qualities of the land. This is the immense logic of the world's harmony, by which all things universally agree and correspond with one another. But truly, it is shameful to believe, and shameful even to report, that the greatest prince of Philosophy <note>Aristotle</note> and his pupil **Theophrastus**, along with **Dioscorides**, **Pliny**, and the other ancients—both Greeks and Latins, as well as the later Arabs—imposed upon posterity the idea that there are plants lacking their own seed; or perhaps such a small thing was either not a matter of care or went unnoticed. And so this rumor has grown so strong among us that it is most difficult to introduce anything new into the minds of men, even though there are specific places within each plant in which they conceive, perfect, and cherish their seeds. The underside of **Fern** fronds <note>original: "filicum"</note> grow hairy with a certain plumed, rusty-colored down, in which, as if in soft little bedrooms, the black, shining seeds of the ferns nod and glisten, maturing at the summer solstice; so that if anyone is able to collect them carefully—by bringing the cut branches from the roots into a house and laying them on white linen cloths—the seeds will fall out after a day, shaken off together with the fuzz. In this way, we have often been able to collect them, marvelling at the immense subtlety of Nature. In the same way, **Hart's-tongue** <note>original: "phylitis"</note>, **Spleenwort** <note>original: "asplenum"</note>, **Oak-fern** <note>original: "dryopteris"</note>, and **Wall-rue** <note>original: "filicula"</note> bear on the underside of their back certain small, sitting "worms," arranged obliquely in rows on both sides, not hanging down at all, but hairy, within which the seeds lie hidden.

240

Perhaps in the past **Dittany** <note>original: "Dictamnum"</note> was brought from a stepmotherly region <note>meaning a harsh or distant land</note> as a seed and deprived of its flowers, which is why it was believed in ancient times to lack seeds and flowers; now, however, it is brought to us gifted with seed. **Maidenhair fern** <note>original: "Adiantum"</note> bears its seed upon its fronds—a sight truly to be seen and wondered at—for the very edges of the leaves are folded, where three seeds can be seen. We have grasped this through careful observation, as we often gather it in Rome at the **Baths of Caracalla** <note>original: "Antonianis thermis"</note>, on the ruined edges of walls, and upon damp masses of masonry. Among us, the **Radicula** <note>likely soapwort or a similar root plant</note> reaches maturity with both seed and flower. The **Willow** is reported to produce seed as usual upon reaching maturity on the island of Crete, at the very descent to the **Cave of Jove**, where it is grim, woody, and the size of a chickpea. The seed of **Mint**, like that of thyme, is entangled in the spikes of the flowers; when it is perfected in summer, if the little flowers are rubbed in the hands, a tiny, reddish seed falls out, but when sown it turns into calamint, as is discussed more widely in our books on **Agriculture**. From **Mushrooms** <note>original: "fungis"</note> we have gathered seed quite well—tiny and black—hiding in oblong little stalls or furrows extending from the stem to the circumference of the cap, and especially from those that grow on rocks, where, as the seed falls, it is sown and sprouts with perennial fertility. Therefore, **Porphyry** spoke falsely when he called mushrooms and **Truffles** <note>original: "tubera"</note> "sons of the gods" because they supposedly grew without seed. Likewise, a black seed also hides in the rinds of truffles, just as in the little balls of the cypress; for this reason, they always appear in the woods where they have frequently come forth and rotted. And in places where the washings of rinds or the rinds themselves are thrown out, we have often seen them born. Nor are there lacking among the ancients those who believed they were born from a sown origin. But we have not thought it worth the effort to pursue everything; therefore, we deliberately omit further examples, especially as we have no others in mind at present.

### STERILE ANIMALS RENDER HUMANS STERILE.
### Chapter III.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' depicting a seated figure, possibly a deity or scholar, within a classical architectural frame.</image-desc>

THIS account of ours—that sterile plants procure sterility in men—is confirmed by those animals which are sterile, or which are born without seed by an unlawful order of Nature (such as from putrefaction); these retain the same power of inducing sterility and opposing conception. **Pliny** says: "Certain things are born from the unbegotten, and without any similar origin, such as **Salamanders**; nor is there a male or female genus for them, just as there is none in **Eels**, nor in any of those things which generate neither animal nor egg from themselves." There is also no gender in **Oysters** and others clinging to the shallows or the rock; however, those which are generated through themselves, if they are divided into males and females, do indeed generate something by coitus, but it is imperfect, from which nothing else may be born, such as the little worms produced by flies. This is made clearer by the natures of those things called **Insects**. The **Mule** is indeed sterile; for this reason, medicines are taken from its various parts, both to be consumed within the body and applied outside, to hinder conception and induce sterility. The Mule's kidneys are selected for this use by **Dioscorides**, the spleen by **Avicenna**, the liver by **Sextus**, the earwax and testicles by **Aesculapius**, the matrix <note>womb</note> and sweat by **Rhazes** and **Albertus**—thus its various parts are chosen by various physicians for this purpose. **Sextus** collected many sterile things. The testicles of a Mule, scorched over a sterile tree, extinguished in the urine of a eunuch <note>original: "spadonis"</note>, and bound in the skin of a mule, if hung from the arm after the menses, hinder conception. **Pliny** believed Salamanders to be sterile, and that they never appear except during great rains and disappear in fair weather, because they arise from putrefaction; according to the ***Cyranides*** <note>original: "Kirannide," a famous ancient book of magico-medical properties</note>, its heart, carried near a woman’s knees, hinders conception and menstruation to the point that they are extinguished. There are certain **Frogs** that are born by themselves, merely from the dusty sands of shores and paths being sprinkled by a summer rain. When **Aelian** was making the journey from Naples in Italy to Puteoli, he saw frogs of which the part belonging to the head was crawling and moving with two feet, while the other part, not yet formed, was being dragged along as a mass of muddy moisture. As **Ovid** says in his book of *Metamorphoses*:

> *One part lives, the other part is raw earth,*

BOOK SIX.

### *The mud contains seeds that bring forth green frogs.*
<note>original: "Semina limus habet, virides generantia ranas"; a line from Ovid’s Metamorphoses (XV, 375) describing the ancient belief in spontaneous generation.</note>

The nature of a **frog** is such that if it is pierced through the mouth with a reed, and that reed is then thrust into menstrual blood by a husband, it is said (according to Pliny) to cause a loathing for adultery. Furthermore, a stick used to strike away a snake or a frog helps those in labor. According to Constantinus, if a woman takes a frog, opens its mouth, and spits into it three times, she will not conceive for that year. In Egypt, **mice** are born from the earth and rain. Macrobius notes that near the Thebaid, when the Nile’s flood recedes and the Sun warms the mud, a multitude of mice arises from the cracks in the earth, as Diodorus reports. People are amazed by this phenomenon, as Aelianus writes, because they see the front part of these mice—up to the chest and the front feet—already alive and moving, while the back part is not yet formed but remains shapeless. Pliny also records that as the Nile recedes, little mice are found, a work-in-progress of the creative waters and earth, already living in part of their bodies while their final form is still composed of earth. For this reason, according to Sextus, the heart removed from a living mouse and hung on a woman’s arm ensures she does not conceive. According to Pliny, by smearing **mouse dung** on the pubic area, the sexual desire of men is restrained; and Hippocrates records that mouse dung applied internally can expel a dead fetus from the womb.

**Toads** <term>Rubetæ</term> <note>a species of venomous land frog or toad often associated with brambles</note>, a species of frog, are born from rot and corruption; indeed, they are generated from the ashes of a burned toad, and more are born from what is left behind. And in the province of Darien in the New World <note>modern-day Panama and Colombia</note>, according to Peter Martyr, toads are born instantly from the drops falling from the right hands of slaves while they water the floors of houses. A buried and decayed duck produces toads; there is a small bone on its right side by which sexual desire is inhibited. Macrobius said that in some places **snakes** are even generated from earth and rain; women suffer miscarriages upon encountering them. If a pregnant woman steps over a **viper**, she will miscarry. According to Pliny, the sloughed skin <note>original: "senecta," literally "old age"</note> of snakes makes for easier childbirth. The **mullet fish** <note>original: "mullus"</note> gives birth three times in its life and is sterile the rest of the time because little worms are born in its womb which devour the seed, as Athenaeus notes. Therefore, if a mullet is drowned alive in wine and a man drinks it, he will be unable to perform sexually, according to Terpsicles in the writings of Athenaeus. According to Pliny, it extinguishes the fires of Venus and helps against all sorcery involving women’s menses. There are those, like Anaxagoras and other philosophers, who believe that **crows** mate through their mouths, but they speak quite recklessly, since the mating of crows is rarely seen. According to Aristotle, their kind is not lustful, as they are not very fertile. It is commanded that pregnant women avoid the **egg of a crow**, because stepping over it causes difficult miscarriages. Little worms are born in the stalks of female **wild celery** <note>original: "apium"</note>; therefore, those of either sex who eat them become sterile. The **Glow-worm** <term>Lampyrus</term>, which is born from dew in summer, if tied to the womb of a mule, causes sterility in a woman. I remember reading that **lice**, if placed in the opening of the human penis during intercourse, prevent the woman from conceiving from that encounter.

## FERTILE SEED-BEARING PLANTS WHICH INCREASE HUMAN SEED.
->Chapter IV.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'C' featuring a detailed landscape with tall trees in the foreground, a winding river or path, and a town with towers and steeples in the far distance under a cloudy sky.</image-desc>

CONTRARY to the plants previously mentioned, the lot and condition of these plants demonstrates an opposite utility. For no one will deny that those plants which are abundantly fertile are effective, by Nature’s precept, for generating seed and for fertilizing the offspring. For just as the plants themselves are vigorous, so they ensure that the human generative process progresses. Theophrastus said there are kinds of figs, pears, and apples that bear fruit twice a year, as well as vines that bear fruit twice or even three times. He adds that the smaller the seeds, the more numerous their fertility—as seen in millet, hedge-mustard <note>original: "erysimon"</note>, poppy, and cumin—and he provides the reason: because of their small size they reach their developmental goal quickly, and because it is a simple process, it can happen frequently. They are readier for the task and more responsive to the surrounding air. Their parts are closer together since they cling to a single stalk, allowing the plant's energy to be spread into many seeds. Thus, aided by these ready and present causes, they easily dispatch and complete their work. Therefore, these seeds are more fertile than the fruits of trees,

...and legumes more than grain-bearing plants. Verannius, in his book on pontifical terms, calls "fruitful trees" <note>original: "felices arbores"</note> the oak, the Italian oak, the holm oak, the beech, the hazel, the service tree, the white fig, the pomegranate, the vine, the pear, the cornel, and the plum, because they pour forth a luxuriant abundance of fruit. The vine is of such portentous fecundity that unless it is restrained by annual pruning, it exhausts itself entirely through giving birth and dies in the process of bearing; and if the richness of very fertile soil does not support it in its weariness, it is consumed by its own fertility. Wine is effective for Venus <note>here meaning sexual desire or the goddess of love</note>, and without it, Venus grows cold. The olive is most fertile, and the wild olive even more so. It bestows fecundity on other trees as well; small branches of wild olive passed through perforated trunks bring fruitfulness to sterile trees. Palladius [writes]:

->*The sterile wild olive makes the fat olives fruitful,*<-
->*And teaches them to bear gifts they did not know.*<-

The types of wild carrot, skirret, and parsnip show copious and dense seed in their large umbels <note>umbrella-like flower clusters</note>: it is known to all that their related powers provide an incentive for Venus. Diocles and Opion believed that skirret is beneficial for Venus, according to Pliny. Cumin is of such great fruitfulness among vegetables that Theophrastus reports it grows more abundantly when sown with curses and imprecations. I believe the name is derived from *akyō* <note>original Greek: ἀκύω, "to be pregnant"</note>, as if it were a "pregnant" name. It is effective for women's conception if it is placed in the womb. Bishop’s weed <note>Ammi</note>, very similar to cumin, is thought by some to be Ethiopian cumin. Pliny records that those women who smell it during intercourse conceive more easily. Male and female knotgrass <note>Polygonum</note> have swellings under almost all their leaves, so copious that the whole plant seems filled with "offspring"; called *polyspermos* <note>original Greek: "many-seeded"</note> by the Greeks and "thousand-grain" by us. As the Quintilii report, this makes animals themselves much more fecund. Hawthorn <note>Cratægon</note> is named from *gonou kratein* <note>original Greek: γόνου κρατέιν</note>, as if to "strengthen the seed with power." Theophrastus reports it is prolific when taken with water. In coriander, the copious seed hanging in clusters is conspicuous on the many branches; it increases the "generation" <note>semen or reproductive fluid</note> on the authority of Dioscorides. Nothing is more fecund than basil. They instruct that it should be sown with curses and insults, and it will grow more widely, so that it has become a proverb: those who curse badly can be said to be "sowing basil," for those who sow it pray that it does not come up. Sophron and Demetrius Phalereus used this proverb. It stimulates Venus, and therefore it is given to horses and donkeys at the time of mating, according to Pliny. Rocket <note>Eruca</note>, especially the wild kind, has innumerable stalks and copious little horns on all the stalks; by eating it liberally, the genital seed is increased and it strengthens Venus by manifold experience. Mustard has the same virtue; hence rose seeds, with mustard seeds and the foot of a weasel hung among the branches of an unfruitful and less fertile tree, restore and fecundate it in a wonderful way. Watercress <note>Nasturtium</note> grows with perennial offspring through the rigors of winter and the heats of Syria, with manifold seeds in its stalks; it stimulates Venus. Nettles pour out copious seed in cluster-like filaments and pill-like flowers, luxuriating everywhere with an untimely growth; they provoke Venus. Lady’s bedstraw <note>Galion</note> bears copious seed in clustered tops, gathered together; Venus is excited by its root. Dock <note>Lapathum</note> is made fruitful with a fertile progeny, especially the wild kind; because of this, Africanus <note>referring to Sextus Julius Africanus, an early writer on agriculture</note> says that when hung on the left arm, it restores the lost hope of giving birth and brings back renewed fecundity. The branches of savory <note>Satureia</note> are decorated with a splendid progeny; it stimulates those flagging in intercourse, which is why they devise that it took its name from the Satyrs <note>a mythological play on words, as Satyrs were famous for their lust</note>, and other things which it is tiresome to recount.

...for according to Aristotle, both mares and pregnant women only endure intercourse: at the time of coitus, they emit from their genitals a fluid similar to seed, which many call *hippomanes* <note>original: "hippomanes"; a legendary substance from mares, often used in love philters</note>: much sought after for love-potions. Dried horse testicles, so they may be taken in a drink, stimulate intercourse, according to Pliny. To the lust of Venus <note>the Roman goddess of love, here meaning sexual desire</note>, the boar is most inflamed; the bristles on his neck stand on end, he pours foam from his mouth, he pants with a boiling breath, and burns with the madness of mating; such that if the female refuses intercourse, incited by burning stings, he either takes her by force or casts her dead to the ground with his tusks, according to Oppian. Wild sows emit that which they call *apria*, just as horses emit *hippomanes*. Boar's gall stimulates intercourse, as does the drinking of swine's marrow, according to Pliny. The sparrow is a bird so inclined toward Venus that it has passed into a proverb, *lecherous as a sparrow*; it emits seed not only when a female is seen, but even when her voice is heard, according to Athenaeus and Eustathius: indeed, it has such a surplus of seed that it may mount a female seven times in an hour, emitting copious and thick seed, according to Horus. In an hour it mates twenty times, others say three hundred times in a day. Terpsicles says those who use sparrows for food become more inclined toward sexual matters. Avicenna said sparrow eggs promote the business of Venus; Aelian and Marcellus said the same. A dish made from the heads of sparrows, especially the males, helps toward intercourse, according to Rabbi Moses <note>Referring to Maimonides (Moses ben Maimon), the Jewish physician and philosopher</note>. Quails emit seed not only when females are standing by, but even when their voice is heard; and if you place a mirror against them, the seed flows forth at their own image, which is reflected uselessly in the glass, the cause being the passion of intercourse in the mind, as is held by Athenaeus and Eustathius. While the females are nesting, the bachelor males fight among themselves; the conquered suffers the "Venus" <note>here meaning sexual mounting</note> of the victor, as Pliny notes from Aristotle. Gesner, the physician, rubs the shameful parts <note>the genitals</note> with quail fat and a little hellebore to excite the power of love; and eggs rubbed on the testicles induce pleasure, and when drunk, increase lust. Partridges are most lecherous; while the female is nesting, she does not admit the male; because of this, the males smash the eggs they find so that the female does not nest, according to Aristotle, Plutarch, and Athenaeus. The bachelors cause a tumult and join in battle among themselves; the one conquered in the fight suffers the "posterior Venus" <note>anal mounting</note>, according to Aristotle and Alexander of Myndus. Partridge meat promotes Venus, as do the eggs taken in food; Aetius and Avicenna advise those who cannot perform the sexual act to eat partridge eggs among other things. The genus of roosters enjoys an abundance of lust. Clearchus wrote that roosters emit seed not only when they see females, but even when they hear their voice; one does not permit intercourse to another male without a fight, and often there is no end to the fight until they die together. They struggle among themselves for the desire of females, and the conquered sometimes suffers an "unspeakable Venus" <note>nefariam Venerem; likely referring to being mounted by the winner</note>, according to Pliny from Trogus. But Theophrastus says the wild ones are more lustful, and wish to mate immediately upon leaving their bed. The meat of a rooster increases the substance [of seed] and adds to the genital fluid, according to Symeon Seth; and the testicles of roosters make one more robust for the business of Venus. If a mare does not endure the male, her genitals are smeared with rooster dung ground with turpentine resin; this thing kindles lust, according to Anatolius. Pliny wrote that the right testicle tied in a ram’s skin excites Venus. Ostrich-camels mate much and excrete much seed; their meat promotes intercourse, according to Avicenna. The spirit in goats is more burning than in others, their matings are hotter, and the male goat is always fervent for intercourse because of the abundance of seed; on the seventh day after it is born, it begins to mate, and although it emits sterile seed, it approaches intercourse the most maturely of all quadrupeds, according to Aelian. Immoderate in lust, while it is still nourished at the breast, it commits incest with its mother; it grows old quickly because it is exhausted in the times of its boyhood by the premature desire for Venus. In Thessaly, men drink the root of the herb which they call *orchis* <note>original: "orchim"; likely Orchis or Satyrion, named for its resemblance to testicles</note> in goat's milk to stimulate intercourse, according to Dioscorides. Deer are driven wild by the madness of a "tension" <note>tentiginis; referring to priapism or intense sexual arousal</note>; they fight for females and finish each other with mutual wounds or the danger of death. The females can scarcely sustain the most powerful thrust of the burning male because of the rigidity of the genital; while they indulge in lusts, they apply themselves to intercourse for whole days. If bulls are sluggish for intercourse, by rubbing and smoothing the shameful part and testicles of the bull with a deer's genital ground in wine, they immediately itch for Venus even unto madness, according to Xenophon and the Quintilii; which indeed happens not only in bulls, but also...

...just as in other animals, and similarly in the human race, this can occur: dried deer testicles, taken in a drink, stir up sexual intercourse with pleasure, according to Sextus <note>Sextus Placitus, a 4th-century medical writer</note>. Pigeons, because of their abundance of seed, frequently rush into the acts of Venus <note>original: "in Venerem"; meaning sexual desire or intercourse</note>; at six months of age they begin their breeding. Simeon Sethi <note>an 11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician</note> and Rabbi Moses <note>Maimonides, the famous medieval philosopher and physician</note> believed that eating them adds to the genital seed and the blood. Octopuses, having embraced one another, complete their mating over a long time; Oppian writes that they are so weakened and broken by long intercourse that their strength fails entirely, and for that reason, lying on the sand, they become prey to other fish that they previously would have devoured with no effort. They are said to provoke lust, especially the "moschatuli" <note>musky octopuses</note>.

# PLANT ROOTS LACKING OFFSPRING DENY OFF-
# spring to humans. Chapter VI.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring a serpent or dragon-like creature entwined within a rectangular frame decorated with foliate scrolls.</image-desc>
There are plants of more than one kind, but of manifold generation; the substance of the roots of some is unfit for generation. Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher known as the father of botany</note> says that certain plants are unable to produce any offspring upward from the root, such as the cypress and the pine. And others, which are dry by nature and are formed with very straight channels, cling by a single root that descends deeply: for the moisture, which is scarce, is consumed by the height of the tree because of the remarkable straightness of the channels; and because the root is straight and driven into the depths, it is granted such meager nourishment that it can barely sustain itself. For this reason, it does not produce offspring, nor does it lavishly put forth suckers <note>original: "stolones"; shoots springing from the base or roots of a plant</note>, such as the fir, pine, larch, and palm. Some count the cedar and cypress among these. There are also oily trees which reject the graftings of others and scorn the company of the rest, which weep thick resin or pitch: for even the oak has been seen to bear good pears, the plane tree to bear apples, and the pear to bear pomegranates; but in the pitch-pine and the pine, a grafted branch is said not to take hold because they weep a certain oily and fatty substance from the cut wound. Torches from the same source pour out an oily humor, and the fatness shines in them, just as very fat and corpulent people are also unfit and unsuited for procreating children; for the nourishment goes into the whole body, and no "superfluity" <note>the excess nourishment believed to form reproductive seed</note> remains for the seed. This did not escape the notice of the Observer of Plants <note>original: "Phytoptæ"; likely referring to Theophrastus</note>, hence those which rely on a single root, growing remarkably well with a healthy body and being fat, neither sprout into suckers nor bear fruit (or only sterile ones), nor do they nourish the offspring of others, such as the cypress, pitch-pine, pine, pine-nut tree, and the like. The cypress dies if its foliage is stripped and its top cut off, nor does it sprout again from there, just as if it had been burned; it produces no offspring, and for that reason it is sacred to Dis <note>the god of the Underworld</note> and was usually placed before houses as a sign of a funeral, according to Pliny. Its juice is very bitter, and it is of the same kind as the cedar and the savin <note>a species of juniper</note>, which cause *atocia* <note>original: "atocia"; a Greek-derived term for sterility or barrenness</note>. Cedar, of the same kind as we have said, both prevents conception and draws out the fetus once conceived. The smoke of pine and pitch-pine expels the fetus, according to Dioscorides. The savin lacks offspring, for which reason Pliny said it can only be born from a cutting and a branch: if the juice is drunk or the smoke inhaled, the fetus is also driven out, according to Galen. Cabbage does not sprout again from the roots into offspring, and it is false what Theophrastus said, that it produces shoots: if placed as a pessary, it ruins the fetus; its flower, placed in wool after conception, does the same.

### ANIMALS THAT BEAR FEW OFFSPRING ARE HOSTILE TO PROGENY.
->Chapter VII.<-

Animals that are not lustful and produce few offspring both weaken the power of sexual intercourse and hinder conception. Once the warmth of spring has passed, these animals are not troubled by any sexual urge <term>tentigine: a term for lustful tension or arousal</term>; they engage in mating more sparingly and live more chastely. The bull, after a brief period of lustful heat has run its course, abstains from mating by a kind of reason; he is not lustful and, according to Aristotle, never mates with a cow after she has conceived. For this reason, the Egyptians, when wishing to represent a man who is both strong and temperate, paint a bull, according to Horapollo <note>original: "Oro"; referring to the author of a 5th-century treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>. According to Rhazes <note>a celebrated Persian physician and polymath</note>, the dried, ground genital organ of a red bull, taken by a woman in the weight of a gold coin, brings about a loathing for sexual intercourse. Female turtles have an incredible hatred for their mates because mating is by no means pleasant for them as it is for other beasts; instead, it brings them the greatest pain, as the male's prickly and inflexible organ affects the female with a sensation of intolerable suffering. Because of this, they fight among themselves with their teeth, as the female strives to escape this painful union while the male pulls at her—unwilling as she is—until he subdues her by force. Their scales, scraped from the top and given in a drink, restrain sexual desire <note>original: "Venerem cohibent"</note>. Among birds, wood-pigeons <term>Palumbi: specifically the common wood-pigeon or ring-dove</term> are the most chaste; the male and female, as if bound by a marriage contract, adhere to a stable and certain union through mutual consent and the highest chastity, so that neither touches an outsider's bed. If, captured by an impure love, they cast their eyes upon another's mate, the other males sitting around tear them apart, and the females do the same to the females, according to Aelian. They are effective against lust. Martial wrote regarding this:

> *Ring-necked wood-pigeons slow and dull the loins,*
> *Let him who wishes to be lustful not eat this bird.*
<note>original: "Inguina torquati tardant, hebetantq; palumbi, Non edat hanc volucrem qui cupit esse salax."</note>

### FERTILE PLANT ROOTS ASSIST FERTILITY.
->Chapter VIII.<-

We can also predict by no weak conjecture that those plants which—either at the very base of the turf or by roots creeping far and wide beneath the earth—happily produce multiple offsets <term>stolones: runners or suckers</term> or stems through frequent and numerous spreading, are intended by Nature's providence to remind humans to care for their own propagation. Almost all bulbs demonstrate the same thing; from their roots, small bulbs compact with scales emerge on all sides into numerous offspring, propagating themselves with more and more bulbs as new offspring grow up. The "solitude" of a plant, or the lack of offspring around its roots, comes from dryness, as Theophrastus <note>an ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> says, which is unfit for generation; but the fertility of shoots comes from moisture. Furthermore, the winding and hanging nature of a root holds the proportion of many roots, because germs put themselves forward from the back of those very curves; the juice lingers longer in the contorted parts, is more thoroughly "concocted" <note>the process of ripening or maturing nutrients through heat</note>, and stays there due to the more laborious movement. In shallow roots, there is a facility of nature, both because they are "cooked" by the air and sun, and because the thin crust of the soil yields easily; when the juice flows there, it comes together more easily by the power of the Sun and gains the ability to take the form of a stem. The laurel has a winding root; the pear, plum, pomegranate, olive, and vine have long and hanging roots, and they bask in the sun through the top of the turf. The vine and the olive, therefore, possess the power to produce a numerous mass of stems around the trunk. From moderate wine comes libido and fertility; from both, so many remedies proceed for sexual desire, the womb, and conception, that you might marvel at them—whether used alone or mixed with others—and I believe no one could list them all. Theophrastus said there are palms which are called "low" <note>Dwarf palms or *Chamaerops humilis*</note>; these sprout back after being cut at the roots, with a new propagation of shoots similar to asparagus growing up every year, and such exist in Sicily...

The onion family is produced from budding, as Aristotle said "in the chapter on budding" <note>original: "ἐν τῷ παραβλαστάνειν"</note>, in the third book of *The Generation of Animals*. Around the roots, it is joined into several rootlets or kernels, and from there it grows into multiple offspring. Theophrastus says: "The roots sprout from their sides, and more are produced, as in bulbs, leeks, squills, and certain others." For this reason, Dioscorides said all bulbs stimulate Venus, as did the poet Martial:

> Since your wife is an old woman, and your limbs are dead,
> You can do nothing with bulbs other than be full.
<note>Martial, *Epigrams* 13.34; a satirical suggestion that for an impotent man, aphrodisiac bulbs serve only as common food</note>

Onion produces generative seed, according to Simeon Sethi. Pliny said garlic stimulates Venus when drunk with pure wine. We have from Dioscorides that the leek does the same, as does the "garlic-leek" <note>original: "scorodoprason"</note> which has the powers of both garlic and leek, and also saffron. Beneath the Asphodel lie numerous bulbous roots, which are often found with eighty bulbs heaped together at once, according to Pliny. They stir Venus when rubbed on with wine and honey, or when drunk, according to Pliny. The root of the smaller Arum is packed with many fibers and long, round rootlets, all of which produce stalks; it has the powers of the dragon-plant, according to Dioscorides, who says it stirs the appetite for mating.

### FERTILE ANIMALS THAT BEAR MANY OFFSPRING ARE EFFECTIVE FOR
### *Fertility and Conception. Chapter VIIII.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap letter E featuring floral designs and a bird perched within the foliage.</image-desc>
By the same similarity of Nature, hope arises for us from the most fertile animals, and a plausible persuasion for exciting fertility in women and conception, by taking, eating, or binding the womb, matrix, rennet, or brain. We shall recognize animals that are fertile or bear few offspring from the parts that nourish the fetus. Aristotle says in his book on animals that "multiparous" <term>multipara: animals that bear many young at once</term> are the pig, the dog, and the hare; "pauciparous" <term>paucifera: animals that bear few young</term> are the lion and the horse. The reason is that the former have many cells and just as many compartments for forming offspring, which they desire to be filled. Democritus asserts the same reason. Examples will be of this kind: The sow is noted for her numerous offspring, since Aristotle said she can produce up to twelve; she mates and is lustful at various times of the year. Pig fat nourishes births that are tending toward miscarriage, when applied like a suppository, according to Dioscorides. The dog is multiparous, up to twelve like the sow; she mates more often and gives birth more often, and is filled by a single encounter, which is most evident in "stolen" matings, according to Aristotle. Drinking dog's milk stirs mature conceptions; the membrane or afterbirth <note>original: "secunda"</note> that has not touched the ground brings forth the birth. The wolf, like the dog, is multiparous, sometimes producing up to ten; eating the flesh of a wolf is beneficial for those about to give birth.

Simeon Sethi wrote that if the testicles of geese are eaten, they help in procreating offspring for women. And Hippocrates, in his book on sterile women, prescribes certain medicines to be drunk with goose or sheep fat for women prone to miscarriage. Hares, while they carry young in the womb, undergo **superfetation** <note>the ability to conceive a second litter while already pregnant</note>; they have milk before they give birth, they seek mating immediately after birth, and they even conceive a new fetus while giving birth, as we have said. Dry and grind the womb of a hare and give it to a woman to drink after she has been cleansed of her menses, and she will conceive; or fry a hare's uterus and offer it as a drink regularly. Hare's blood has the same power, according to Galen in his *Euporista*. Some believe that a hare's fetus, taken from the womb, brings restored fertility to those who have ceased to bear children; however, instead of a hare's fetus, Pliny suggests giving the discharge <note>original: "saniem"</note> to the husband. **Crayfish** <note>original: "cammari"</note> lay many eggs and conceive easily, and they are effective for conception; the same must be said of the octopus.

### THAT PLANTS LACKING CERTAIN PARTS ARE MOST HARMFUL
### *to those of our own members that correspond to them. Chap. X.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial H at the beginning of the chapter, illustrating a landscape with a building and trees framed within the letter.</image-desc>

CLOSELY related to these are certain plants that are deficient in either leaf, root, or other parts; by the same logic, they are hostile and harmful to those members of our body that correspond to them. More learned physicians, who are beyond risk and know how to extract benefits and uses from disadvantages, use these plants for their various qualities, so that while the plants might tend to be harmful, they can be made to be helpful. Some examples come to mind which have succeeded most happily for us and others. **Mushrooms** <note>original: "fungi"</note>, according to Theophrastus, lack flower, leaf, seed, bark, marrow, and vein; for this reason, they offend very many parts of our body. If poisonous things are present near them, they absorb them through a kinship of nature—for instance, if there is a serpent's den nearby, a rusty nail, some rusted iron, or a piece of rotting cloth, they convert and cook down all that juice and poison into themselves, so that we see them bristling inside with black or livid parts. They produce cold phlegm and are overcome by harmful juices; taken too abundantly, they bring danger; being difficult to digest, they cause choking or stir up cholera. Galen said they possess a quality very close to being deleterious, deadly, and putrid. **Truffles** <note>original: "tubera"</note> also lack, as he says, bark, marrow, nerve, vein, stem, flower, and they rely on no roots and no fibers. It is agreed that the "fatness of the earth" is balled together into that evil. Diphilus wrote that some are found which cause choking in the manner of mushrooms. Avicenna says they are "atrabiliary" <note>producing black bile or melancholy</note> and generate humors more than other kinds of mushrooms; thus it happens that when eaten frequently, they provoke apoplexy and paralysis, and in addition, they are stubborn to digest and heavy on the stomach. Plants without leaves the Greeks call <gloss>aphylla</gloss> <note>original: "ἄφυλλα," meaning "leafless"</note>. Aphrodisaeus gives the reason: because the pores of their bodies are thicker and tighter, and their power is to constipate, which denies the growth of hair—just as we said of eunuchs <note>original: "spadonibus"</note> in our work on *Human Physiognomy*. Therefore, these plants will be harmful. The **Rush** causes headaches; the **Broom** <note>original: "sparthion"</note> bears rods without leaves: it purges violently from above in place of hellebore. Pliny says it is harmful to animals; the **Genista** species disturbs the stomach and harms the heart, according to Galen. **Broomrape** <note>original: "orobanches"</note>, growing among legumes with little stalks without leaves, chokes them, which is how it took the name *orobanches* <note>from the Greek for "vetch-strangler"</note>; added to legumes, it accelerates their cooking. By Theophrastus it is called *limodorus*. While it strives to destroy entirely, the same plant is also the *cuscuta* of the Arabs and the *cassytha* of Pliny; it is seen to be widowed of flowers, and even if it is born from roots,

<note>The opening sentence refers to Dodder (Cuscuta), a parasitic plant mentioned at the end of the previous page.</note> is born, is destitute of these <note>leaves and roots</note>, and lives on the branches of others, from which it strangles trees by hunger, and from this it takes its name <note>the Latin name 'podagra linaria' or 'cuscuta' was often associated with 'strangling' the plants it climbs</note>; for it entangles neighboring shrubs in continuous coils, and delights in wandering over the tops; it ensnares them in such a thick weave that, sitting upon the peaks, it casts down trees weighted by such a mass to the earth, or by a continuous sucking of nourishment, or by tightening its snares, it strangles whatever it clings to. It binds them as if in shackles, so that once bound they cannot easily be extricated. Added to wine, it induces a heavy drowsiness, and Mesue <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a 9th-century Persian physician</note> adds that it thins <note>reduces the swelling of</note> the spleen. Ivy also, being destitute of its own roots <note>referring to its parasitic-like climbing nature</note>, lives upon trees, creeps up them, embraces them, and strangles them. It affects the nerves, and its clusters <term>corymbi</term> <note>the round fruit clusters of the ivy</note>, if taken too liberally, weaken the body and disturb the mind; they take away the hope of conceiving and extract the fetus. Its "tear" <note>the resinous gum that exudes from the stem</note> is a hair-remover <term>psilothrum</term>; it breaks teeth and diminishes the spleen. Teucer <note>a mythical king of Troy or a famous archer</note> discovered germander <term>teucrion</term>, which spreads thin rushes and small leaves, growing in rough places, with a harsh taste, never flowering, nor does it produce seed; it diminishes the spleen. It is established that it was discovered in this way: when entrails were thrown upon it, they adhered to the spleen and emptied it; and they say that pigs who eat its root are found without spleens. The tamarisk is "imperfect," as we have said, and also destroys the spleen. The willow, mentioned above, dries up those suffering from intestinal obstructions <term>ileosos</term>. There are also herbs lacking roots, a trait given to them by Nature so that they cannot grow except upon the trees of others, such as mistletoe, polypody, and oak-fern. For we said above that roots correspond to the stomach, the spleen, the liver, and similar viscera which attract, cook, and distribute nourishment to the branches; and they affect these same members by upsetting the stomach, causing nausea, and diminishing the spleens. Theophrastus <note>an ancient Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle in the Peripatetic school</note> recorded that mistletoe grows on oak, terebinth, and other fruit trees; Dioscorides <note>a Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> said it thins the spleen. The same origins apply to polypody and oak-fern <term>dryopteris</term>, for polypody clings to old trunks, especially of oaks, and to rocks. Mesue said it harms the stomach in the digestion of humors. The same is said of the oak-fern.

## ANIMALS LACKING CERTAIN MEMBERS
->are liable to the same corresponding human parts.<-
### Cap. XI.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring floral and scrolling vine motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

BY THE SAME reasoning, passing over to animals, if we see them lacking certain members, they are opposed to those same members of ours. The more excellent Physicians, as we have said—who extract what is useful from what is harmful—wherever they see things thin, destroy, and annihilate, they use them against tumors, blockages, and growths. From this, many and excellent familiar medicines are prepared for us; and we shall begin first with the blood. Animals that lack blood put blood to flight, stop it, and destroy it. Soft-bodied creatures lack blood: octopuses <note>original: "polypi"</note> wear away the blood and expel it through hemorrhoids, and according to Pliny, they stop it. Pearls are born in shells that lack blood; they stop the menses. The purple snail is effective for the same. The frog has blood nowhere else but in its eyes, according to Oros <note>likely Horus Apollo or a similar ancient source</note>; it stops blood, according to Dioscorides and others. Likewise the gecko <term>stellio</term> for dysentery, and both land snails and slugs. The mole has almost no neck, because it is very short between the front legs; they remove all tumors of the neck. Indeed, the head cut off and pounded with the earth dug up by moles, and digested in tin boxes, deletes all things that swell in the neck, which they call abscesses <term>apostemata</term>; Pliny reports this regarding the liver and foot, and Olivarius regarding the heart. The ray fish lacks a neck: the bone from the tail (that is, the sting, for among the types of rays there is one with a sting) of the fish called the ray in the sea, provided it does not wound, is beneficial for scrofulous swellings <term>strumis</term>. Pliny teaches this should be done daily until they are cured. The frog lacks a neck, as Ovid says:

> The back covers the head, the necks seem intercepted. <note>original: "Terga caput tegit, colla interſepta videntur." From Metamorphoses, Book VI, describing the transformation of Lycian peasants into frogs.</note>

The juice of frogs boiled in vinegar abolishes quinsy <term>anginas</term> and swollen tonsils, according to Pliny. The toad <term>rubeta</term> is of that kind; boiled and applied as a plaster for those with throat infections <term>cynanchicis</term>, it helps so much that it quickly frees them.
