It explores the "Doctrine of Signatures"—the belief that the physical characteristics (or lack thereof) of an animal indicate its medicinal use—specifically regarding the neck, the gallbladder, and the feet.</meta>

->### BOOK SIX ###<-

# PAGE 249 #

->### SIXTH BOOK ###<-

**Cardanus** <note>Girolamo Cardano, a famous 16th-century Italian polymath</note> relates that he freed a man who was at the very point of death with this remedy. It destroys **scrophula** <term>strumas</term> <note>swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck, often tubercular</note> by our most certain experiment: a **toad** <note>original: "rubeta"</note> is boiled in oil until a third part of the oil is consumed and the toad wastes away; when it is turned into oil, and the skin and bones are bared, it is strained through a linen cloth. With the ointment prepared in this way, the neck should be anointed several times. The body of a **serpent** seems to lack a neck from its head to its tail; according to **Dioscorides**, **vipers** repress growing scrophula, and a viper’s noose—in which it was strangled—hung around the neck, is truly a great amulet against **quinsy** <term>anginas</term> <note>severe sore throat or inflammation of the throat</note>; it heals those already formed and prevents new ones from occurring. The **turtle** has a snake-like neck, according to **Pacuvius**; when its broth is taken as food, it dispels scrophula from the neck, which hard-boiled and smeared eggs also do. **Crabs** crushed with honey dispel scrophula; the **sea hare**, if applied and quickly removed, is effective for scrophula, according to **Pliny**. **Fish** lack a neck, and almost the greater part of them are effective against scrophula, such as the ash of **maena** <note>a small Mediterranean fish</note> heads. The liver of the **parrotfish** <note>original: "scari"</note> is for **parotid swellings** <note>swellings of the salivary glands</note>, and likewise **oysters** for the tonsils and scrophula, according to Pliny. Those things which lack teeth cure the same by destroying them. The bone of the **stingray** <note>original: "pastinacæ"</note> is without teeth, having only a rough jaw; the pain of teeth is mitigated by its spine because it breaks and draws out the tooth. Dioscorides says it is very useful to scarify the gums with a stingray spine during tooth pain; it is crushed and, when smeared with **white hellebore**, it extracts teeth without distress, according to Pliny. No fish have **testicles**, nor do animals lacking feet, whether internally or externally, except for the **dolphin** and the **seal**. Almost all are effective for inhibiting **Venus** <note>sexual desire</note>, such as the **torpedo fish**, and indeed they even destroy conception, as **serpents** do. If a **mullet** <note>original: "mullus"</note> is suffocated in wine and a man drinks it, he will not be able to attend to venereal matters, says **Terpsicles** in the works of **Athenaeus**; and if a woman drinks from it, she will not conceive. And because women prepare **love potions** <term>philtra</term> with menstrual blood to ignite passion, for this reason, the mullet helps against all sorceries and the menses of women, as Pliny is the author. **Hegesander** wrote that no mullet is carried around in the sacrifices of **Diana** because of its association with chastity. The **turbot** <note>original: "rhombus"</note> seems to lack a **spleen**, for it lies hidden among the coils of the intestines; applied alive for healing the spleen and then released back into the sea, it is wonderfully effective, according to Pliny. The **ass** lacks a **gallbladder**, as do all solid-hoofed animals; its blood and dung remove the **royal disease** <term>regium morbum</term> <note>jaundice, so called because it was thought to require expensive, "regal" remedies</note>, according to the same author. The solid-hoofed **horse** lacks a gallbladder; the blood of a foal and dung in wine removes jaundice, according to Pliny. The **elephant** has a liver without a gallbladder, yet when the part where the gallbladder usually adheres is cut, a gall-like fluid exits, according to **Aristotle**. It is situated not at the liver but at the chest, according to **Aelian**; it is beneficial for those with jaundice, according to **Agricola**. We ourselves have many times repelled jaundice with wonderful success using **ivory**, **saffron**, **wheat**, and **Aminaean wine** <note>a high-quality ancient wine</note> infused together and offered to drink every morning. The **goat** has no gallbladder, according to Pliny; its dung is effective for **jaundice** <term>auriginem</term>, according to **Galen**. In some places, **sheep** have no gall, as Aristotle relates regarding Chalcis in Euboea; the filth of their ears with a bit of **myrrh** resists the royal disease, as does their dung, according to Pliny and **Rhazes**, and their fleeces with sulfur and wine, according to **Serenus**. The **dove** is said to lack a gallbladder, as is held from **Horus**; Galen says it does not have a bladder on the liver, but elsewhere. The ash of the feathers or the entrails of **wood pigeons** up to three spoonfuls resists the royal disease. In **sparrows**, the gall is joined to the intestine in some and to the belly in others, according to Aristotle; the ash of those burned with vine-twigs in two spoonfuls resists the royal disease, according to Pliny. Animals that lack the windings of the intestines but use one loose intestine cannot suffer from **colic**; for this reason, they cure the **colon**. The **duck** has a loose intestine and is even voracious; at the sight of a duck, the pain of the intestines is soothed in cattle, according to **Columella**, Pliny, and **Vegetius**. **Ossifrage** birds <note>bearded vultures or "bone-breakers"</note> are voracious; a part of them tied to one suffering from colic frees them from the disease, according to **Marcellus**. **Doves** and **wood pigeons** are effective for colic affections. If you give the intestine of a **harpy** <note>likely a type of hawk or vulture here</note> in drink for three days, or roasted as food to the sick person, you will heal them perfectly; so also the **eagle** and that kind of family. Because **bats** have short and imperfect feet—for they are always either flying, or lying with their whole body, or clinging to buildings with the claws of their wings—when boiled with **linseed**, **eggs**, **oil**, **wax**, **bulb**, and **dung**, they remove **gout** <term>podagram</term>. Just as the **swallow** <note>original: "hirundo"</note> is capable with its feet, so it seems to degenerate in its feet, according to Aristotle; its blood eases gout, according to **Trallianus**. **Fish** lack feet. Almost all are effective for removing the pain of gout in the feet. **Birds** lack milk; none of the birds provide remedies for generating milk.

### PROLIFIC PLANTS CONDUCIVE TO CONCEPTION AND FERTILITY. Chapter XII. ###

Since we have entered into a discussion about fertile trees, before we place the finishing touch <note>original: "coronidem," a Greek-derived term for a flourishing finish or crown</note> upon it, we shall speak of the various fruits of oaks; otherwise, we would never find a more opportune place in the entire history of plants.

->In this table, we show the manifold fruits of the oak: four species of **galls**, "unions" <note>original: "vniones," likely referring to small, round, pearl-like galls</note> upon the leaves, curls, hair-like tufts, fungi, monstrosities, **agaric** <term>agaricum</term> <note>a wood-decaying fungus used medicinally</note>, and fungi around the trunk, **mistletoe** <term>viscum</term>, and similar things. Below these are hair-like tufts, crests, **bull’s horns**, and the **phallus** <note>original: "mutonem," a term for the male organ</note>, so that you may contemplate their mutual similarities.<-

<image-desc>A detailed botanical woodcut illustration depicting various growths associated with an oak tree. The primary illustration shows a gnarled oak branch with leaves and acorns, adorned with several types of oak galls (gallae), mistletoe (viscum) with its characteristic berries and paired leaves, and various fungal growths (fungi and agaricum) emerging from the bark and a cut branch stump. Below this central image are four smaller, isolated figures illustrating comparative morphology: a phallic-shaped fungus (mutonem), a tuft of hair or a crest resembling a stylized head with curly hair (cristas), a bovine skull with prominent horns (tauri cornua), and a jagged, comb-like anatomical structure.</image-desc>

The oak produces manifold and monstrous offspring with a fertile yield—from the roots, branches, shoots, and the leaves themselves—so that in the entire family of plants, none appears more prolific or more wondrous, nor any in which the kindness of the most high God shines more brightly. But there is no one of sound mind who would doubt that each of these offspring possesses its own virtues <note>original: "dotibus," literally endowments or gifts</note> and performs more than our ancestors described. **Theophrastus** <note>the "father of botany," a student of Aristotle</note> wrote that the oak, besides its fruit <note>the acorn</note>, also produces the most abundant variety of other things. **Plutarch of Chaeronea** <note>famous Greek biographer and philosopher</note> [wrote that] among wild trees, it is the most beautiful in fruit...

Della Porta illustrates how the various galls, fungi, and growths of the oak mimic animal parts, suggesting their use in remedies for conception and reproductive health through the Doctrine of Signatures.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Chapter XII of Book Six, focusing on the oak tree as a supreme example of fertility and its various "signatures" that relate to animal reproduction and health.</meta>

# BOOK SIX #

...the most excellent, the most fertile, and the most robust among the city-dwelling trees, so that birds, wild beasts, and man—the prince of beasts—might feed upon them. Antiquity believed that the oak had generated God even before humans, so necessary was its fruit to men. For this reason, the Arcadians, who boasted of being the first to rise from the earth, were said to have a kinship with the oak. It was once called an *old oak* <note>original Greek: γηρασδρυον (gêrasdryon)</note>. Hesiod used to say that the Gods granted to the just that the oak would yield fruit on its high branches, and in its middle, bees would dwell and provide honey. Socrates used to swear by the oak as if by a God; because of this ancient veneration, men made the tree sacred to God, as they first fed upon acorns from this tree for the sake of life. Italy itself is likened to an oak leaf, as the foster-child of all lands and the parent of the Gods, chosen by divine power as the queen of all nations in the whole world, equated to the most excellent and noble of all trees, according to Pliny. 

Nor should we omit the wonder of the Gauls in this matter. The Druids (for so they call their Magi) hold nothing more sacred than the **mistletoe** and the tree on which it grows. They choose groves of these trees for their own sake, and perform no sacred rites without its foliage, so that they might even seem to be called "Druids" based on the Greek interpretation of the word <note>The Greek word for oak is "drys."</note>. Indeed, they believe that whatever grows upon those trees is sent from heaven, and is a sign of a tree chosen by God himself. From this excellence and utility, the **Dryads** and **Hamadryads** were named, who were the spirits of the oak. 

But let us see what secret powers this tree can portend for us through such a luxury of offspring, with forms and figures that express the matter to some extent. Theophrastus said that the "robur" <term>robur</term> <note>a term for the hard-timbered oak</note> produces other things more abundantly than any other tree, besides its fruit. For it produces a small **gall**, and another resinous and black one, and even certain things like mulberries, though they differ by their dry hardness, though this is quite rare. It also produces another growth representing the image of a distaff, which, when perfected, imitates the head of a bull; the fruit inside has kernels similar to olives. 

And elsewhere regarding the Turkey oak <term>cerrus</term>: that which some call a "penis" <note>original: "penem"</note>, similar to branches, the Turkey oak alone produces; it is hollow and mossy, hanging a cubit in length like a long fringe of linen. It grows from the bark, not from a twig where the acorn grows, nor from a bud, but from the side of the upper nodes. It also bears another useless little ball with hair, which in the spring is stained with a juice as sweet as honey in touch and taste. It also bears what they call a *pilon* <note>original: "pilon," from the Greek for "felt" or "hair"</note>; it is a little ball, not unlike a nut, containing a down inside that is suitable for the wicks of mushroom-shaped lamps, for it burns even without oil, just like the black gall. 

In addition to these, the "wings" of its branches create little balls that sit without a stalk and are multi-colored. Indeed, some have white centers <note>original: "umbillici," literally "navels"</note>, while a variety of colors is scattered elsewhere. The middle parts are as red as pomegranate, but when opened, a bitter, rotten, and black emptiness lies beneath. It also produces a reddish little stone, but more frequently watery kernels that are white and translucent, in which "pumice-stones" also grow, hardening in the manner of a gall when they reach their proper size; these adhere to the back of the leaves. 

From the leaves also grow other coiled, compressed, and oblong little balls, turning red on the leaf; these sometimes contain flies <note>These are actually the larvae of gall wasps.</note> inside. It grows to its proper size, hardening in the manner of a small, smooth gall. The hard oak also bears a *cachrys* <term>cachrym</term> <note>a scaly winter bud or gall</note>, as the little ball is called, which has a cauterizing power in medicine and lasts through the winter after the leaves have fallen. So prolific is the hard oak that it produces mistletoe and honey, as Hesiod attests, and it is well known that the honey-dews falling from heaven settle on no other leaves more than these. It bears **boletus** and "swine-mushrooms" <note>porcini mushrooms</note>—the newest provocations of the throat—which are produced around the roots. Like other acorn-bearing trees, it also brings forth **agaric** <term>agaricum</term>, a fungus effective for antidotes. 

We have brought forward all these things so that we may consider the oak the most fertile of all trees. We have already said that the acorn is effective for matters of Venus <note>Meaning it acts as an aphrodisiac or fertility aid.</note>. Pliny relates that **mistletoe** helps women with conception if they simply carry it with them. It now remains for us to demonstrate its power for the fertility of other animals, which we judge from that "bull’s head" already mentioned, which Pliny indicates even more clearly. It is, however, very rare to find, and when found, it is sought with great religious ceremony—especially on the sixth Moon (which establishes the beginnings of months, years, and the thirty-year century for them), because it then has an abundance of strength and is not yet half-diminished. Calling it "All-Healing" <note>original: "omnia sanantem"</note> in their own language, and having duly prepared a sacrifice and feast under the tree, they bring forth two white bulls whose horns are then tied for the first time. The priest, dressed in a white robe...

# VIVIPAROUS PLANTS PROVIDE FERTILITY
## Chapter XIII

By a new and never-sufficiently praised reasoning, the supreme kindness of Nature indicates plants outstanding in fertility: those which generate animals within their fruits. These can almost be called **viviparous plants** <note>original: "viviparae plantae," meaning "live-bearing." In the 16th century, the spontaneous appearance of insects inside plants was seen as the plant "giving birth."</note>. Indeed, there are many observations by philosophers that when insects abound more than usual, the year will be most fertile in terms of crops and human births. 

Among others, we have mentioned the fruit of the **oak**. On the back of its leaves, it bears a small white, watery ball while it is tender; these sometimes contain flies inside. As it reaches its full growth, it hardens into the form of a small, smooth **gall** <note>term: "galla" (oak gall), a growth caused by wasps, which the author interprets as the tree's own "offspring."</note>, according to Theophrastus, from whom Pliny also writes. The oak also bears white, translucent, watery kernels on its leaves as long as they are soft, in which gnats are born. We have already spoken of its fertility above. 

Furthermore, our ancestors claimed a peculiar property for the larger oak galls: if those that are whole are opened, they will contain a fly, a spider, or a small worm. 
- If a **fly** flies out, it is a portent of future war. 
- If a **worm** crawls out, it signifies a scarcity of the grain harvest. 
- If a **spider**, it predicts a year of pestilential diseases. 

**Figs** also generate gnats, which emerge from the fruit of the **wild fig** <note>original: "caprifici," the non-edible male fig tree</note> when their seeds decay. The evidence for this is that after the gnats have flown away, no seeds remain inside the figs at all. There is also another kind called the "centrine," which lives idly like the drone among bees; whenever it sees insects of the other kind entering its fruit, it kills them immediately. 

The leaf also generates a gnat when the tree fruits abundantly, just as a type of small beast is born in the pods of **elms**, called "cnipes," which, when born with the figs, devours those fig-dwelling gnats. Figs increase the strength of young men; for this reason, athletes used to use them as food. According to Pliny, a decoction of them is useful for steaming women’s ailments, and according to Dioscorides, for female medicinal fomentations. 

The **terebinth** <note>The turpentine tree (*Pistacia terebinthus*)</note> bears certain hollow nut-like pods, like the elm, in which animals like gnats break out. It produces reddish "horns" resembling those of goats, in which the aforementioned gnats are enclosed, according to Theophrastus. There is also the Indian terebinth, similar to our own but with different fruit, resembling almonds; among us, these are called **pistachios**. Pliny said that the terebinth excites Venus <note>Acts as an aphrodisiac.</note>, and pistachios are frequently used to reconcile and strengthen the powers of sexual union. 

A worm is born in the **asphodel** <note>original: "albuco"</note>, which transforms into another flying, flowery animal. When the herb begins to bloom, the insect immediately gnaws through its covering and flies away, as Theophrastus says. As we mentioned from Hesiod, this plant is effective for generation. Almost all **legumes** (beans and pulses) generate animals inside them, and they are effective for the same reproductive purposes.

# ANIMALS THAT CONCEIVE EASILY AID CONCEPTION
## Chapter XIV

Furthermore, animals that conceive easily are judged to be effective for aiding human conception. We judge those animals to conceive most easily which do so not only from seed placed in the womb, but even from the **wind**. Many such cases were recorded by the ancients: in several regions, **mares** burn with such a fire for mating that even if they do not have a male, they imagine Venus <note>the goddess/act of love</note> for themselves out of constant and excessive desire (in the manner of farmyard birds) and conceive by the wind. > *And immediately, when the flame is applied to their greedy marrow,*
> *More so in the Spring (for in the Spring heat returns to the bones),*
> *They all stand on high cliffs with their mouths turned toward the West Wind,*
> *And catch the light breezes; and often without any*
> *Mates, pregnant by the wind (wonderful to tell),*
> *They flee away.*
<note>original: "Continuoq́; auidis ubi subdit a flamma medullis..." This is a famous passage from Virgil’s *Georgics* (Book 3), describing the belief that mares could be impregnated by the wind.</note>

**Varro** writes that in Spain, in the region of Lusitania where the town of Lisbon <note>original: "Ulyssippo"</note> stands on Mount Tagrus, certain mares conceive from the wind, just as hens often do; the eggs of these hens are called **wind-eggs** <term>hyponemia: from the Greek for "under the wind," referring to infertile eggs laid without a mate</term>. However, the foals born from these horses do not live longer than three years. A woman who does not conceive, if she drinks mare’s milk without knowing it and then joins with a man as soon as possible, will conceive, according to **Rhazes** and **Albertus**. The conception of quails is so easy that they are said to be filled by the wind, according to the commentator on **Nicander**. **Athenaeus** reports from **Phanedemus** that the island of Delos was called "Ortygia" by the Achaeans because flocks of quails were observed flying from the sea, as if they were even generated within the sea. **Aetius** teaches that quail fat can be used as a pessary <note>A medicated plug inserted into the vagina.</note> to stimulate conception.

The partridge conceives most easily; for at that time when it is stirred by desire, if it stands facing the male, it becomes pregnant from the breeze blowing from him—indeed, it grows heavy in the womb just from the voice of the males. If they are playful and swollen with lust, they also fly over the males; the same result can be achieved while the male himself releases a "fruit-making spirit." **Aristotle** argues against **the Ephesian**, who said this could not happen solely by "spiritual conception" from excessive longing; **Athenaeus**, **Eustathius**, **Archelaus**, **Varro**, and others say the same. On account of this, they write that if the eggs of partridges are swallowed, they cause fertility and an abundance of milk, according to **Pliny**. 

Certain vultures are born without mating; when the female is inflamed with the ardor of conceiving, she opens her womb toward the North Wind and is "compressed" by it for five days, during which she takes neither food nor drink, intent on the procreation of offspring. Their eggs are **wind-eggs** <note>original: "subventanea," literally "under the wind."</note> for eating, not for procreating, according to **Horus**. Although wind-eggs are useless in other birds, they are notable for fertility in vultures; when the South Wind or the East Wind blows, if they fly toward it and open their mouths to the breeze, the inflowing spirit of the wind fills them, according to **Varro** and **Aelian**. Hens also produce "wind-eggs" or "Zephyr-eggs," so called because they seem to be made from the wind without a male, from the strength of a swelling womb, and they are infertile, according to **Pliny**; or they conceive from the imagination of mutual lust between two females, or even from dust. **Galen**, in his *Easy Remedies* <note>original: "Euporisto"</note>, suggests a remedy: they slaughter a hen, hide a straw wrapped in linen cloth inside its anus, sew it up, boil it, and give the broth to be drunk. Mountain tortoises are filled by the wind just like quails, according to the commentator on **Nicander**. **Hippocrates**, in his first book *On the Diseases of Women*, describes a medicated plug which contains the brain of a sea tortoise, saffron, and Egyptian salt, to open the womb for conception.

**THERE ARE** also fruits which, when placed upon other fruits, ensure they do not fall or help them reach maturity; we conjecture, by a not unrefined similarity, that these are effective for retaining the fetus in women until the proper time. The **Palm** matures its fruit through **caprification** <term>caprificatio: an ancient horticultural technique where "male" or wild fruit is used to pollinate or ripen "female" fruit</term>, similar to the fig; while the male is flowering, they cut off the "spathe" from which the flowers emerge, and as soon as it contains the down, flower, and dust, they shake it over the fruit of the female. She is so affected by this sprinkling that she does not lose her fruit in any way, but preserves them all, according to **Theophrastus**; for of all trees, this one loses its fruit the most. To this end...

even **caprification** <note>original: "caprificatio"; the ancient practice of hanging wild figs (caprifigs) in domestic fig trees so that gall-wasps can transfer pollen and help the fruit ripen</note> has been discovered for this purpose: two fresh **dates**, with their stones removed and filled with the powder of the **dyer’s kermes** <note>original: "infectoris cocci"; a red dye made from the crushed bodies of the kermes insect</note> and swallowed often by pregnant women, prevent miscarriage. Furthermore, the **banana** <note>original: "musa"; likely referring to the plantain or banana as described by the 9th-century physician Serapio</note> of the same species, according to **Serapio**, is effective for stimulating sexual intercourse; it produces flowers and fruit, and then, after the sheath bursts open, the mature fruits emerge, just like a child in a fertile womb. The **fig tree** also loses its fruit before maturity more than any other tree, which is why caprification was invented. From the wild figs attached to the tree, small wasps <note>original: "culices"</note> emerge and pierce the tops of the domestic figs, which causes the fruit to endure and ripen. This is why the fig is effective for women’s health, as we have said. In some trees, **Pliny** says, "centers" are found, just as in marble—that is, a hardness similar to a nail that resists iron tools. These sometimes occur by chance when a stone is gripped or taken into the body of the tree, or even the branch of another tree. They say that stones found in this way serve as a remedy for "holding the birth" <note>preventing premature labor</note>.

### PLANTS AND ANIMALS THAT GIVE BIRTH EASILY,
### are excellent for the ease of childbirth. Chapter XVI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'V' featuring a detailed illustration of a plant with multiple long, pointed leaves emerging from a central base.</image-desc>

Those plants which produce fruit upon their leaves seem to offer a certain image of ease in childbirth, as if **Nature**, by this marvelous work, meant to stir the sleeping senses of mortals to recognize that these plants are effective for the ease of delivery and for the health of the womb. The **Butcher’s Broom** <term>Myrrhacantha: also known as Ruscus aculeatus</term>, shows very red berries clinging one by one to the middle of its leaves, in the manner of kermes dye-grains. Its root, ground with wine, is effective for purging the womb and for difficult urination. The **Horse-tongue** <term>Hippoglossum: Ruscus hypoglossum</term> has another small leaf like a tongue inserted in the middle of a leaf, as if in a hollow, among which a red berry is also set, like that of the butcher’s broom; it is given as a great help in uterine conditions. A type of **cabbage** <note>original: "Brassice genus"</note> also puts forth a small stalk above the leaf—a miracle of Nature to be admired. By eating it, women find relief through purging; if eaten raw, it expels stillborn children. Thus, from these "easy-birthing" plants, great benefit can be derived. On the **kermes oak** <note>original: "ilice coccifera"</note>, certain growths like reddish little globes are seen in the middle of the leaves by the elegant work of Nature; it has powers friendly to the heart, though its other uses remain untested.

Animals that give birth easily, and which do not suffer long delays in labor, provide humans with the ease of delivery. It is a common saying that **cats** conceive with pain but give birth without pain. **Aristotle** notes that dogs that have recently given birth will chase others away, and those in labor will often move through the levels and stairs of the house to find a spot. They provide such ease of birth that the gall of a cat, especially a wild one, can extract a dead fetus from the womb if used as a fumigant from below, mixed with the black dung of some cat, according to **Rhazes** <note>a famous 9th-century Persian physician</note>. The **Electric Ray** <term>Torpedo</term> does not lay eggs, but produces living young from eggs that hatch inside it. According to **Aristotle**, it receives these young back into itself when in fear and then releases them again. A ray has been seen with eighty young inside it. If one is caught while the Moon is in Libra and kept under the open sky for three days, it makes for easy births; thereafter, it helps whenever it is brought near. The **Stingray** <term>Pastinaca</term> does not take its young back in because of the sting on its tail, but its sting is thought to make births easy; the same is said of the **Angelfish** <term>squatina</term> and the **Shark** <term>galeus</term>. The **Viper**, though it produces eggs, is nevertheless viviparous <note>gives birth to live young</note> because of its ease of birth; yet its mere appearance can cause a pregnant woman to miscarry.

The **mare** gives birth most easily of all, according to **Aristotle**. While other quadrupeds usually give birth lying down, the mare, when the time for delivery approaches, stands up and releases the foal while standing. The spleen of a horse drunk with fresh water ejects the fetus, as does a fumigation of the hooves or dried dung, according to **Pliny**. If someone steals the eggs of a **goose** so that it cannot sit on them, it will continue to lay until it bursts, according to **Pliny**. To eject a dead fetus, **Hippocrates** suggests a "substituted" remedy: grind fresh eggshells and goose fat and apply them. All **wolves** give birth within a ten-day period. The cause of this is fabulously attributed to **Latona** <note>Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis</note>, because she was led from the Hyperboreans to Delos under the guise of a she-wolf while wandering for those same ten days. A mare that steps in the tracks of a wolf will miscarry; because of this, when the **Egyptians** wished to signify a woman who had miscarried, they would paint a mare stepping on a wolf. We have already said, following **Pliny**, that the meat of a wolf is beneficial for women about to give birth.

# BOOK SIX

## BEAUTIFUL PLANTS AND ANIMALS
### are effective for generating beautiful children. Chapter XVII.

It seemed appropriate to add to what has been said how we might be able to generate the most beautiful children; specifically, if we continually handle, eat, or keep beautiful plants with us. But let us look at some examples. The **palm** <note>original: "Palma"</note> is a most beautiful plant in the judgment of **Homer**, who compared the grace of a Phoenician girl to a palm branch. It rises with a smooth and tall trunk, all its foliage at the summit, spectacular in its beauty. Its leaves are uniform, seeming to swell and meet one another; they are firm and ever-lasting. Indeed, we do not see the laurel, the myrtle, the olive, nor any other tree of those types that are said to never be stripped of leaves, keep those same leaves; rather, as some fall away, others sprout. The palm, casting off no leaf, is always constantly adorned by its own. In Syria and Egypt, it produces dates <note>original: "balanos"</note> with such a pleasant appearance that it surpasses all delicacies and desserts. Among these "phoenix-dates," some stand out for their exceptional beauty which they call *Nicolaos*, named after the Emperor **Augustus**, who, after the most pleasant and beautiful Nicolaus <note>referring to Nicolaus of Damascus, a friend of Augustus</note>, ordained that these dates of particular beauty be named *Nicolaos*. 

The **gold-flower** <note>original: "Heliochrysos"; likely *Helichrysum italicum* or "Everlasting"</note> has an exceptional beauty of golden color; it vibrates a flashing and vigorous light to those looking at it by reflecting the sun's rays. It shows a beautiful shape of a cluster; these clustered umbels, rounded with many protruding beads and shimmering with a golden appearance, catch a long-lasting grace. Because of this, others call it the **amaranth** <note>original: "amaranton"; meaning "unfading"</note>, from which the statues of the Gods were crowned. A virgin of Ephesus first crowned the goddess **Diana** with this name. **Pliny** calls a plant *Heliante* <note>original: "Heliantē"; likely a "sun-flower" or rock-rose</note> in the region of Themiscyra and the maritime mountains of Cilicia, which has a leaf like a myrtle and a very similar flower. 

The flower of the **saffron** <note>original: "croci"</note> is of a beauty to be beheld, with filaments shining like golden blood, an intense scent, and a blue cup. It reflects the form of the most beautiful youth, **Crocus**, who, burning with love for the nymph **Smilax**, was changed into the herb of his own name. The fables of the Poets hint at nothing other than this beautiful and burning appearance of the flower. 

The **pine** <note>original: "Pinus"</note> is branched from the top, of exceptional height, with a leaf that is very thin and long, like a hair. Ancient stories tell of **Pytis**, a very illustrious girl, who was killed by a rival in love and changed into this tree. The Poets demonstrate the exceptional form of the tree not without charm through this veil of myth. 

What is clearer, brighter, and more yellow than **honey**? What is more beautiful and fragrant than **myrrh** and its tree? **Pliny** relates: They call a plant *Heliante* in the region of Themiscyra and the maritime mountains of Cilicia, with a leaf of myrtle; the **Magi** and the Kings of the Persians are anointed with this, boiled with lion’s fat, with saffron and palm wine added, so that the body becomes pleasant in appearance; therefore, it is also named *heliocallis* <note>original: "heliocallidem"; meaning "beauty of the sun"</note>. 

A remedy called *Hermesias* <note>original: "Hermesias"</note> is mentioned by the same author for generating beautiful and good children; it is not a single herb, but a composition made from the kernels of **pine nuts**, ground with honey, myrrh, saffron, and palm wine. Afterward, he orders those about to conceive to drink it mixed with *theombrotio* <note>original: "theombrotio"; an herb described by Pliny as "food for the gods"</note> and milk, and for mothers to take it while nourishing the fetus after conception; in this way, the children become excellent in mind, form, and character. 

**Quinces** <note>original: "Cotonea mala"</note> are more beautiful because of their golden-yellow color, and for this reason they are called "golden apples" <note>original: "chrysomela"</note> by the Greeks, and were called "golden apples" by **Virgil** <note>original: "Maroni"</note>. They vibrate a most excellent scent, are curled with thin furrows, and are covered in a soft down, with a rounded circularity that brings pleasure not only to the sight, but health through the scent. **Solon** mandated that a bride should come into the bedchamber having eaten a quince; not, as **Plutarch** thinks, so that the first greeting should be pleasant and not unwelcome, but so that from the first intercourse, beautiful and industrious sons might be born. If a pregnant woman eats it, she will give birth to an industrious and handsome boy. **Pliny** says: All these are now included in the reception rooms of men and women, and placed upon the statues that witness the nights. 

Among animals, the **hare** <note>original: "lepus"</note> is beautiful; for this reason, the Greeks tell the story that the hare is sacred to love. The argument for its name is that it is called *lagoos* <note>original: "λαγωὸς"</note> from *laein derkein* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ λαεῖν δέρκειν"; to see clearly</note>, from the verb *derko* <note>original: "δέρκω"</note>, both signifying sight. From this comes the idea that those eating the meat of a hare become beautiful for several days, about which **Martial** says:

-> When you send me a hare, Gellia, you always tell me: <-

Since the Emperor Alexander Severus would serve small hares at his table every day, it became a common subject of mockery that the grace of his beauty was acquired from this specific type of food. These verses survive:

# FROM THE MOST BEAUTIFUL PLANTS OUR BENEFITS, FROM THE *deformed ones our harms proceed. Chapter XVIII.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'N' featuring a figure in a landscape.</image-desc>

Lest we depart from the beauty of plants, plants also show their vices and virtues through their own "countenance." We have previously proved that a beautiful soul belongs to a beautiful body, and a monster in body is a monster in soul. It is acknowledged by everyone that a fitting and proportionate composition of limbs is assigned the greatest virtues; likewise, the deformed, the maimed, and the distorted are assigned vices and imperfections. Those most skilled in botany are advised that the similar "faces" of plants indicate whether their inner character is wicked or good. Indeed, this is perceived more clearly and more purely in plants, since plants cannot "apply makeup" to their faces <note>original: "mangonizare," a term referring to the deceptive polishing or grooming of goods by a merchant</note>, nor do they have the choice to embrace or flee from virtues and vices as a human does. 

But let us explain what we mean by a charming or an inelegant plant. The best figure for a plant is if its height corresponds to its width (or is slightly greater), and if there is a proportionate arrangement of roots, flowers, leaves, and fruits. Flowers that are perfectly colored, elegantly shaped, very pleasant, and "smiling"—so that they entice the eyes of onlookers with the greatest delight—provide us with evidence that the plant possesses the greatest gifts. Cato, speaking of the curly cabbage, says: "The curly cabbage is good in appearance and nature." 

The form of the **rose** is of such elegance that if Jupiter wished to set a King over the flowers, the rose would hold the kingdom. It is the ornament of the earth, the eye of flowers, the glory of plants, and a flashing beauty; it is the conciliator of Venus. What is more pleasing to the sight than the color that shines forth from roses? There are also other praises from the poet Anacreon. Because of its beauty, poets dedicated it to Venus:

->*Venus alone is mistress of the star and the flower.*<-

Philostratus dedicated it to Cupid. What can be seen that is more beautiful than the **lily**? A plant sought after for gardens and greenery, rising with a straight stalk, at the summit of which are flowers of untainted whiteness, arranged in striated and spreading petals, like the shape of a basket with a turned-back lip. From the center, saffron-colored stamens are brought forth, always with a drooping neck that is not sufficient for the weight of the head, from which flows an outpouring of a mild, desired, and divine scent. Because of its exceptional beauty, the Greeks called it the <gloss>flower of flowers</gloss> <note>original: "anthos anthōn"</note>. It is the delight of Venus and the "rose of Juno," from whose spilled milk the Galaxy <note>The Milky Way</note> in the heavens is seen with its starry whiteness—so that they assigned it a divine origin. It is also conspicuous in the glory of Solomon sitting upon his throne. 

The **Iris**, with its pleasant variety and colors, is a rival to the celestial bow <note>The rainbow</note>; for it paints its flower in the same way that the bow is painted in the sky by the obstruction of a dark cloud and the reflected light of the sun facing it. It is a gaping flower, and its alternating leaves are curved into the shape of a little loop. It is very fragrant in its root, not just its flower; the edges of the flower are more spread apart and gaping. It has a manifold mixture of various colors, which are usually seen across different plants but here appear in only one flower, so that it does not yield to others but competes with the rest for charm. So great is the beauty of the **olive** that Homer, when [describing] some remarkable form of a youth...

BOOK SIX

The youth who seeks to depict the olive compares it to that which shines with the joy of the earth and the clemency of heaven. The death of Euphorbus, slain by Menelaus, is compared to an olive tree uprooted by the force of winds, or a brave man to an oak. <note>The author refers to Homer's *Iliad* (Book 17), where the death of the Trojan hero Euphorbus is famously compared to a fallen olive tree.</note> And in the sacred page [the Bible], when it is necessary to recall a species, the olive is commemorated: *As a fair olive tree in the fields.* <note>original: "Quasi oliua speciosa in campis." A quote from Ecclesiasticus 24:14.</note> For it displays a certain appearance of virginal modesty; its gifts are nearly infinite, and it offers immense medical benefit. 

Conversely, what is more deformed than monkshood (*aconitum*)? Poets imagine it was born from the foam of the dog Cerberus when Hercules dragged him from the underworld near Heraclea in Pontus—where that entrance to the underworld is shown. Its flowers waste away with a deformed paleness; it kills so cruelly that no remedy has yet been found against it. What is more foul than the smell of hemlock (*cicuta*)? What is more hideous to look at? The leaves of hemp (*cannabis*) smell heavily; likewise the stinking bean-trefoil (*anagyris*): if anyone disturbs the shrub, it gives off a certain foul odor, hence the adage, *you are stirring the anagyris*, <note>original: "ἀνάγυρον κινέις". A Greek proverb equivalent to "stirring up a hornet's nest," referring to the plant's stench when touched.</note> that is, you are stirring up trouble. The leaves of the mandrake (*mandragora*) have a poisonous smell. Dogbane (*Apocynum*) grows with ill-smelling vines, all being of an inferior quality. What is more mournful than the cypress (*cupressus*) itself? A tree chosen for hanging, so that the Poets imagine it as sacred to Dis. <note>Dis Pater, the Roman god of the underworld.</note> So too the savin juniper (*sabina*) itself, born for dispersing conceptions [inducing abortion]. Poisonous mushrooms are recognized by a yellow color outside and leaden color inside, with a savage appearance and a rancid habit, with gaping channels and a lurid margin around the edge, or with a pale upper lip. 

We will add the natural cause: plants that are moist, hot, or dry have a cheerful appearance and are fragrant; but those that are cold and moist are mostly tasteless, odorless, and less edible, and because they are undigested [unconcocted], they have worse flavors and fouler smells, being contrary to human nature.

### LARGE PLANTS HAVE EXHAUSTED POWERS, SMALL ONES HAVE THE GREATEST. Chapter XIX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a figure standing in a landscape with buildings in the background, set within an ornate square frame.</image-desc>

If we remember correctly what we said in our *Human Physiognomy*, we declared that men of vast body and limbs are stupid, timid, foolish, and weak, since Nature cannot diffuse her powers into such massive limbs—setting aside those whose limbs are in perfect proportion, for they will signify less evil. Likewise, men of small body are of such hot and vehement operation that they can scarcely contain it within their own bodies. In the same way, there are plants which, although they take on a massive size, are sterile and of exhausted powers; whereas small ones, such as little roots, and those scarcely apparent to the senses, are of powerful strength. 

For in trees that luxuriate with great branches, what Nature granted to magnitude, she took away from strength, as in the pine, the fir, the cypress, and the palm; likewise the plane tree, the poplar, the Egyptian fig, and others, of which few or no powers are recorded by writers. Aristotle, in his book of *Problems*, asks why thin roots are sharp? He solves it by saying that larger ones, over a longer period of time, become more fully "cooked" [digested] and grow green. There can also be a natural cause: those things that are moist and hot grow easily but are feeble in their operation; however, those that do not grow large are dry, and are more vehement in their operation. 

Theophrastus says: those plants which are in shaded places and still air rise up tall, smooth, and more excellent; on the contrary, those which come forth in places exposed to blasts and wind, or in sunny or sparse and loose soil, turn out less so. For the increase of density prevents height, and the blasts roughen them and create knots; then, the looser, moister, and weaker ones are produced in these [shaded] places, because they cannot receive density from either the Sun, the blasts, or the cold. We have said that plants that rise in moist places are large; but those in dry, stony, and sun-exposed places are small and juiceless due to the nourishment and the situation of the sky, and for that reason are of more powerful operation—whence comes their power to act. Animals of small body are more ingenious than others of large body, such as bees, spiders, ants, and venomous spiders (*phalangia*), so that it can be seen that Nature abounded in strength where she failed in the body. Thus small herbs and seeds are more powerful in their operation, such as pepper, mustard, and the like, so that we must flee to the causes we stated in *Human Physiognomy*. In dry places, wood is contorted and bodies are small, like the Ethiopians, who with stammering

# PHYTOGNOMONICA

...are at the feet, having large bodies in moist places. City trees, which are well-watered, grow large; forest trees are dry and small. The **plane tree** <note>original: "Platanus"</note> was celebrated in the walkways of the Academy in Athens, measuring thirty-six cubits, with a single root surpassing the branches in length. Now, one is famous in Lycia for the pleasantness of its companion, a cold spring; it is set along the road, hollowed out like a dwelling with an eighty-foot cavity, and a cavern for one's feet. It has a numerous crown of foliage and protects itself with vast branches like a forest of trees, covering fields with long shadows—along with other details about its size that Pliny relates. Dioscorides said it was effective against inflammations.

The **lotus tree** <note>original: "Lotus"; here referring to the Mediterranean Hackberry (*Celtis australis*), prized in antiquity for its shade and wood.</note> was particularly sought after for homes because of the "petulance" of its branches and the very wide shade of its spreading limbs, which often leap over into neighboring houses; no branches are longer, stronger, or more numerous, so that one might say it is as many trees as it has branches. They dye skins with its bark, and it is useful for nothing except as an astringent.

The **Indian fig** <note>original: "Indica ficus"; the Banyan tree (*Ficus benghalensis*).</note> has small fruit but is spread out with vast branches, the lowest of which are curved so far toward the earth that they take root within a year’s space, creating a new offspring for themselves in a circle around the parent. Within that "fence," shepherds spend the summer, in a place equally shaded and fortified by the rampart of the tree; it is a beautiful sight to look at from below or from a distance because of its vaulted reach. Its upper branches shoot upward in a woody multitude from the vast body of the mother, so that many of them cover a circle of sixty paces, while the shade indeed covers two furlongs. The width of the leaves has the likeness of an Amazonian shield; the fruit is rare and does not exceed the size of a bean, lacking in any strengths that are mentioned by at least any writer.

The **fir** <note>original: "Abies"</note> is a huge and lofty tree, as is the **larch** <note>original: "larix"</note>; indeed, they are the tallest and straightest of all trees, preferred for the masts and yardarms of ships. The largest of the larches seen in Rome, in the time of Tiberius Caesar on the bridge of the mock naval battle, was 120 feet long and of a uniform thickness of two feet; from this, the remaining unbelievable height to the very top could be estimated by those calculating the peak. A fir tree of particular wonder was seen in the ship which, by the order of Gaius the Prince <note>Caligula</note>, brought from Egypt the obelisk now standing in the Vatican circus—along with the rest of the details Pliny relates about its vastness. From it, resin seeps out, the power of which is effective for wounds, itchy skin diseases <note>original: "psoras"</note>, and stones.

Among herbs, the **Egyptian bean**, **cucumbers**, **gourds**, and **melons** produce huge fruit, leaves, or roots, but they have few or no medicinal uses. In small herbs, however, anyone will be able to see huge powers, such as in **pepper**, **mustard**, **hyssop**, **birthworts**, **small centaury**, **rue**, **mint**, **oregano**, **monkshood**, and the rest.

## THAT PLANTS WHICH BREAK ROCKS ARE EFFECTIVE FOR BREAKING
## stones in the body, and teeth.

### CHAPTER XX.

<image-desc>Large ornamental drop cap 'D' decorated with floral and leafy scrollwork patterns within a square border.</image-desc> WE HAVE SPOKEN of the manner of fruiting in plants and the remedies that could be obtained from them; it remains to contemplate the places from which they spring, and the manner of it. For some desire to grow only upon rocks and break them by their own force, while others wish to be born upon the branches of trees; we must see what Nature portends by these likenesses. Therefore, for the dire torments of the kidneys and bladder, when those places swell with stones <note>original: "calculis"</note>, kind and indulgent Nature has granted plants of the most highly recommended gift. She has indicated this with a sufficiently ample demonstration: for with frequent and tiny fibers, these plants pierce the stones and rocks in which they grow as if with a small drill <note>original: "veruculo"</note>, or they split and open them as if with the strongest wedges.

Because of this remarkable faculty, they are called **saxifrages** <note>original: "saxifragae"; literally "stone-breakers"</note> by everyone, a name which serves as an indicator; among the Greeks they could be called **lithontriba**, <note>original: "lithontriba"; Greek for "stone-grinders/crushers."</note> as if they were "stone-drills." But there are various types in the tribe of saxifrages which are distinguished by this excellent prerogative of breaking stones in the kidneys. Dioscorides mentions one kind, which others call *saxifragon* and *empetron* <note>original: "empętron"; from the Greek for "on the rock."</note> and the Romans call *saxifragia*; it is a twiggy shrub growing in rocks and rough places, similar to thyme <note>original: "epithymo"</note>, which breaks stones of the bladder. Pliny says that **Maidenhair fern** <note>original: "Polytrichon"</note> seeks out shady rocks, the splashing of walls, and especially the caves of springs and dripping stones: it wonderfully expels and breaks stones from the body. For this reason, rather than because it grows on rocks, I would believe it was called "saxifrage" by our people. There are also many saxifrages among the moderns; one is with fennel-like leaves, longer, tiny, and sparse...

...and the seed of **stone parsley** <note>original: "petroselini"</note>, with the root of the **parsnip** <note>original: "pastinacæ"</note>, which grows among great rocks, on mountains, and in sterile sands; it is most excellent at breaking a stone <note>A "calculus," referring to kidney or bladder stones.</note>. There is also another kind with leaves like **ground ivy**, a thin, hairy stem, a bright white flower, no seed, and a root shaped like hail-stones, hanging down like that of the **lesser celandine**; a decoction of this in wine breaks kidney stones and cleanses the bladder. A third kind of "stone-cutter" <note>original: "lapicidæ"</note> is a woody shrub, twisted, with many small forks and whitish, small, oblong, sharp leaves, and a red seed; it grows on living rock, and its root lives so deeply fixed in the gaps of the stones that it can hardly be torn away. There is also the **goat's pimpernel** <note>original: "bipennella hircina," likely *Pimpinella saxifraga* or Burnet-saxifrage.</note>, named a **saxifrage** <note>original: "saxifrigię"; literally "stone-breaker."</note> because of the frequent use of its root for breaking stones and provoking urine. It grows with a face so similar to the pimpernel that you would think them the same; for it is called "goat-like" <note>original: "hircina"</note> not only because of its poisonous and unpleasant goat-like odor, but because the blood and flesh of a mature he-goat is an exceptional protection for those suffering from stones. It grows in rocks, which it splits, and for this reason it is commonly called the ***rock-splitter*** <note>original: "petrifindula"</note>. **Mountain parsley** <note>original: "Oreoselinum"</note> and **stone parsley** grow on mountains and in rocky places, which is where they get their names according to Dioscorides; when drunk, they expel stones because they possess the same power as the others. For this reason, the blood of a goat that has eaten mountain parsley and mountain masterwort is considered powerfully effective for grinding down a stone in the bladder. The **dropwort** <note>original: "Oenante"</note> herb grows in rocks; its root heals defects of the bladder, according to Pliny. The **fig** grows among walls and stone quarries and breaks them in a wondrous way; it is useful for the bladder and kidney defects, according to Pliny. **Pellitory-of-the-wall** <note>original: "Helfine, siue parietaria"</note>, so named because it grows in walls and stones, when warmed over a roof tile, sprinkled with Cretan wine, and applied to the pubic area, heals those with stones. **Stone moss**, which grows upon rocks, is effective for breaking stones by a most certain experiment. **Hyssop**, which grows on a wall, wondrously dislodges stones from the kidneys when a syrup is made from it with an equal amount of pellitory-of-the-wall water, and drunk for ten days while fasting. The **broom** <note>original: "Genista"</note> has a very long root; it grows in mountainous places and ruined walls, such that it may dig down thirty feet. Mesue <note>A famous 8th-9th century Persian physician.</note> says it benefits those with stones. The **maidenhair fern** <note>original: "Adiantum"</note> grows nowhere more frequently than on damp rocks, stony places, the edges of springs or wells, or where water splashes; Dioscorides said it breaks stones. **Spleenwort** <note>original: "Trichomanes"</note> grows in the same places as maidenhair and can provide the same benefits. **Spleenwort** <note>original: "Asplenum," or "scolopendrium"</note> grows in walls and flinty rocks; it crushes stones in the bladder, according to Dioscorides. **Goat's beard** <note>original: "Gerontopogon"</note>, called by many "stone-breaker" <note>original: "saxifrica"</note> because it is marked among the stones, has a long beard and leaves like very long hair; for this reason it was named ***rock's beard by the Romans*** <note>original: "petræ barba Romanis"</note>, and called "geranospogon" by Nicander—that is, the "old man's beard"—being very similar to the common goat's beard; it succors the defects of the kidneys and bladder. **Rock-breaker** <note>original: "Calcifraga"</note> to the Latins, or **empetron** to the Greeks, grows in seaside places, hardly anywhere else than on bare rock; a decoction in water, or ground up, it breaks stones. Those who seek proof for this promise claim that small pebbles boiled together with it are broken. There is a **fungus** growing on stones, called by some **lyncurius**, which by a wondrous experiment breaks the stone; indeed, dried in the shade, ground, and drunk while fasting with old urine, it so purges the kidneys that stones are never regenerated in them—something we have frequently experienced to the point of admiration. Herbs of this kind, which are accustomed to breaking rocks, show us by a miraculous luxury of Nature that if placed against the teeth, they break them and cast them out fundamentally.

The best physicians, who obtain benefit from inconvenience, use these same herbs if there are any teeth in the mouth that can be broken, or cast out, or if their defects must be met. **Ivy**, which bursts through tombs and walls and penetrates them, is applied to eroded teeth that need to be broken and burst, with the neighboring teeth protected by wax so they are not harmed, according to Pliny. They also seek the **gum** in ivy, which they promise is most useful for the teeth. The great **cedar** grows in mountains among rocks; the **cedar-resin** <note>original: "cedria"</note> placed in the cavities of teeth breaks them and soothes the pains. **Chameleon** grows in sloping, dry, and maritime tracts; its root, chopped and boiled in vinegar and applied while boiling with a writing stylus, breaks the teeth.

## ANIMALS THAT EAT STONES ARE EFFECTIVE AGAINST STONES.
## Chapter XXI.

Just as the "stone-breaking" plants growing in the crevices of rocks feed themselves upon their sap and are able to break rocks or the stones <note>Called "calculi," these are kidney or bladder stones.</note> in the kidneys and bladders, so too it is not far-fetched to argue that animals which feed on stones—and by their internal nature are able to crush and digest them—possess the same power. Let us now see if any examples occur to the mind from the histories of animals and physicians that might make this conjecture more certain. The **ostrich** <note>original: "Struthiocamelus"</note> digests swallowed iron; it also digests swallowed stones kept in the rumen near the reticulum, according to Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author of "On the Nature of Animals."</note>. The inner lining of its stomach, when consumed, dissolves a stone, according to Rabbi Moses <note>Maimonides, the medieval Jewish philosopher and physician.</note>. **Roosters** <note>original: "Gallinacei"</note> dissolve the sand and pebbles swallowed into their craws; for this reason, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist.</note> commands that the pebbles found in the "bladder" of roosters (meaning the belly, for birds lack a bladder) be crushed and sprinkled into a drink against stones. **Pigeons** eat pebbles and digest them because of the heat of their stomachs, as do **turtle doves**. Their dung, given in honeyed wine to those suffering from stones, causes them to be expelled through the urine, according to Galen's *Easy Remedies* <note>original: "Euporisto."</note>. **Ravens** and **crows** eat a variety of foods, including all kinds of seeds and fruits, according to Macrobius. In the bellies of crows, you will often find pebbles which they swallow and digest; their dung, placed into the cavities of teeth, breaks them, according to Sextus <note>Sextus Placitus, author of a late Roman medical work on animal remedies.</note>. Because of this, I predict they can also break stones in the bladder.

The **wren** <note>original: "Passer Trogloditis"</note>, a very small sparrow-like bird seeking its food near hedges and walls—this little animal, the smallest of all birds except for the one called the **goldcrest** <note>original: "regulus"</note>, which makes only short flights—possesses a natural power entirely worthy of admiration for crushing stones. It appears in winter and can be preserved in salt. Eaten raw or cooked in food, it heals the disease, and from its use, one is never again troubled by that affliction. Its powder achieves the same effect if it is cast with its feathers into a pot and then burned with the lid on—with constant attention being paid so that it is reduced to ash and not exhaled into the air or consumed by the force of the fire. It should be administered with a little **malabathrum** <note>original: "phyllo," a fragrant leaf used in ancient medicine.</note> or mixed with pepper to make it more flavorful, according to Aetius, Aegineta, Philagrius, and others.

## PLANTS THAT LIVE UPON OTHER PLANTS
## show how their virtues can be extracted.
## Chapter XXII.

Just as herbs grow upon stones, so they also grow upon trees. But we must investigate with diligent search what Nature wished to demonstrate to us through herbs that grow and live upon other herbs. For Nature, as we have said, when she displays something unusual against the perpetual laws of her own institution, does not do so by chance. I would have you see that she is about to display some exceptional and heavenly gift, warning you that her hidden riches are not to be hidden from you there. To us, indeed, with anxious and wondering minds as we weighed the alternatives, no better or more likely reason occurred—nor would we otherwise find a more suitable place in the whole work than this.

But indeed, it seems a paradox and a decree against the laws of Nature that plants should be able to live without a root, as if someone were to say a man could live without a mouth or a belly. But these exist in a twofold difference: some, born without seed and roots, live on foreign trees—truly an exceptional work of Nature, to be looked upon not so much for its rarity as for its appearance—such as **mistletoe**, **moss**, **lichen**, and the like. Others, embracing and entwining neighboring plants with hair-like filaments, as if with little keys <note>Referring to tendrils.</note> and supports, plunder their sap. Having found better nourishment, they abandon their own root by which they had grown and enjoy a foreign spirit <note>original: "genio"; the vital force or essence.</note>, as if not removed from their own seats, but born there...

**BOOK SIX.**

...they seem to be born, such as **dodder** <note>original: "cassutha," a parasitic vine commonly known as Cuscuta</note>. For some grow on the roots of others, a "spurious offspring," such as **cistus-rape** <note>original: "hippocysthides"</note> and **broom-rape** <note>original: "hippogenistæ"</note>; or they grow on the trunks, like **agaric** <note>a type of medicinal fungus</note>, other fungi, and galls upon the leaves; these are indeed excrementitious growths, yet they are quite wonderful and elegant in appearance. I conjecture that these plants, not knowing how to live on the dreggy, earthy sap, take their sustenance from a more purified humor that is drawn up from the bottom to the higher branches, being as it were aerial and of the greatest thinness. For the life-giving sap and vapor implanted in the tree is matured by the timely and generative suns; it rises through the hidden pores of the trunk and glides through the passages of the bark into the parasitic plant, providing a purer and more elaborated nourishment. Nor do I think these plants possess any powers other than those of the host plants upon which they depend. However, there is this difference between them: the parasites possess a subtler and more penetrating power. Just as the vapor exhaling through the siphons of an **alembic** <note>a chemical distilling apparatus</note> by the force of heat is turned into more subtle and limpid waters as it drips out, so it is purposefully done: if a patient is to be given **thyme** <note>original: "thymi"</note> or another plant that is too weak or nauseating for a delicate nature to use as medicine, a sprig of dodder pulled from the thyme should be used. Not long after it has attached to the thyme or other plants, it lives and draws the humor from them; if this is then given to the patient, the desired result will be achieved. These could be called **parasitic plants** <note>original: "plantæ parasiticæ"</note> because they always live off another’s plate. Since the dodder has no seat of its own, it lives on another, entangling the standing herbs with a numerous mane of curls. When it entangles itself over thyme, the small roots of the thyme dry up; having found more abundant nourishment, the dodder "devours" the thyme's sap through many "eyes," as if by **anastomosis** <note>original: "synastomosicē," referring to the joining of vessels or suckers</note>. Therefore, it does not have its own powers, but from the bosom of the host whose native humor it has drunk, it reflects the nature of that same parent. Thus, it reflects the faculties of the thyme, but more purified and penetrating; for this reason, Galen <note>the famous 2nd-century Roman-Greek physician</note> says it excretes **black bile** <note>one of the four humors of ancient medicine, associated with melancholy</note> more effectively than thyme itself. Likewise, near the Vale of Tempe in Thessaly, there is that which is called **polypody** <note>original: "polypodion," a type of fern</note>, and those called *dolichos* and wild thyme; and that which grows on the wild olive is called *phaulos*; while that on the fuller’s thorn is called *hypopheston*, according to Pliny. Theophrastus said that **mistletoe** <note>original: "viscum"</note> grows on the oak and the turpentine tree; Dioscorides says it grows on the oak, the holm oak, the wild pear, the pine, and the fir; Pliny says we have seen it on the almond, the chestnut, and the service tree. It possesses various faculties, especially those of the trees it sits upon. Galen says it has a mostly "aerial" quality because it lives on the more elaborated sap of the host trees. **Polypody** grows primarily on the oldest trunks of trees, and especially on oaks; for this reason, it dries out the body just as the oak does, but it "thins" <note>attenuates</note> more because it lives on a thinner sap. Mesue <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a 9th-century Persian physician</note> preferred the kind that grows on tree trunks over that which grows in the soil or on mossy stones, for the soil-grown kind harms the stomach with its uncooked humor. **Moss** <note>original: "muscus"</note> hangs from various trees; Dioscorides said it grows on cedar, poplar, and oak; Galen said it grows on pitch-pine and larch. The best is from the cedar, the poplar kind is less effective, because the cedar is fuller of strength than the poplar. In Italy, the kind on the larch is better, because it grows on astringent trees and thus has an astringent virtue; on poplars, the astringent power is weak. That found on cedar has the power of digesting and softening. **Lichen** grows on rocks just as moss grows on trees, so it might be called "stone moss." Galen said it possesses a drying and cleansing faculty because it lives on the dryness of the rock. From the middle of the **cistus** root, the **cistus-rape** <note>original: "hippocisthus"</note> sprouts as if grafted; and while the cistus has a binding power, the cistus-rape is even more binding and drying, a rival to **broomrape** <note>original: "orobanche"</note> with its fungal offspring. **Agaric** grows on the trunks of trees, especially the larch; it has the powers of the larch, the cedar (on which it frequently grows), or the oak. Galen said it consists of an "aerial substance." **Ivy**, fungi, and similar things we have mentioned are of the same condition and quality.

PHYTOGN.

...or disease, there and nearby Nature provides a timely remedy. Where there was a fault, grace was not lacking. Orpheus says of this:

> ->*The black earth itself for many-voiced men*<-
> ->*Generates both malice and the aid for pain;*<-
> ->*The Earth indeed brought forth crawling things, but over them she brought forth help.*<-

Now we shall show this in regard to locations, for we have already spoken of herbs and animals. For in those places where anything might be destructive or deadly, remedies are not far away, so that they need not be sought from afar. We shall begin with the regions of the world: for if there are any places in which a plague or some disease rages, do not doubt that they are provided with remedies. In the West Indies, everyone everywhere is seized by the venereal plague <note>syphilis</note>, and it is a peculiar evil of those islands; there, bringing no other help than the wood of the **guaiacum** <note>original: "guaiaci ligni," a resinous wood from the Caribbean used to treat "the French disease"</note>, they deliver themselves from the harms of this disease; the vice, not resisting, yields to this wood. Africa is most fertile in serpents, and there grows what is called **scorzonera** <note>original: "scorzonera," also known as viper's grass</note>, as well as spices whose use is effective against serpents. Malta <note>original: "Melitæa"</note>, an island of Italy, is most abundant in serpents, and there a stone is born <note>likely "St. Paul’s Earth" or fossilized shark teeth known as glossopetrae</note> to counter their poison. In Thessaly, serpents are produced in such numbers that, unless they were destroyed by storks, they would have forced the inhabitants to leave and migrate from the entire region; for this reason, such great honor is given to storks in Thessaly that to kill them is a capital offense. In Argos, a bounty of serpents is born; in opposition, there is a creature that fights the scorpion, so that when it sees a scorpion, it rises up against it and kills it. In the Po River <note>original: "Pado"</note>, **amber** <note>original: "succinum"</note> is produced—the cause seems connected to the location—and even today, the rural women across the Po wear amber instead of necklaces, both for the sake of beauty and for medicine, as it is believed to resist tonsillitis and vices of the throat, since a various kind of water near them infects the throat and neighboring flesh <note>a reference to goiters caused by drinking Alpine water</note>, according to Pliny. Aelian says the **sea hare** <note>original: "marinum leporem," a toxic marine mollusk</note> is born in the Great Sea; if anyone moves a hand toward it or touches it with a small stick, he perishes as if he had touched a basilisk. They say a root is born by the same sea, by no means unknown to the common people, which heals the fainting spells of one so affected; for if moved to the nostrils, it causes him to revive and be refreshed; if neglected, the disease is endowed with such robust destruction that it proceeds all the way to death. The **agate** stone <note>original: "Achates"</note> is found in Sicily, near the river of the same name; it is useful against the stings of scorpions, and with it, the plague of scorpions is extinguished. The **lion-killer** herb <note>original: "Leontophonon"</note> grows where lions are most savage toward men, and it kills them. The **oak-snake** <note>original: "Dirrhinus"</note> is born under the roots of the oak; the fruit of every kind of acorn-bearing tree, and their crushed roots, provide help against its bite, according to Dioscorides. In Apulia, a kind of spider thrives, <gloss>commonly called the **tarantula**</gloss>, whose bite is most destructive; there also grows most abundant grain in which **Spanish flies** <note>original: "cantharides," toxic beetles used in medicine</note> arise. By this contemplation, we have imagined that three or four of these given in a drink can help those bitten by it; nor did experience fail us, for the truth was discovered by making the trial. In Ethiopia, there is a people with a closed mouth and lacking nostrils, breathing through only one hole, which they draw through a reed of oats; and they use the grain of the same oats, growing spontaneously, for food, according to Pliny. At the external borders of East India, around the source of the Ganges, are the **Astomi** <note>a legendary race of mouthless people</note>, a people without a mouth, living only by breath and the scent which they draw through their nostrils from various roots, flowers, and wild apples, which the earth bears in abundance; they carry these with them on longer journeys so that the sense of smell does not lack, according to Pliny.

### THAT NATURE PRODUCES PLANTS AT THE TIME THEY ARE NECESSARY, AND FIRST CONCERNING SPRING. CHAPTER XXIV.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'U' featuring a letter intertwined with dense foliage and scrolling vines within a square frame.</image-desc>

As with places, so also Nature does not leave seasons destitute of their remedies, so that those diseases which arise at that time can be countered. From this, diligent explorers of secrets will be able to obtain a significant starting point for investigating these things, when they have carefully observed the time at which Nature is accustomed to bring things forth. # BOOK SIX.

If one were to produce a remedy after the disease had passed, he would act in vain. By considering the timing of both the disease and the plants that are born or flourish at that same time, we are led by no slight conjecture to see their effectiveness. Pliny seems to have observed this, saying: "Certain things are also born as remedies for animals, through a wealthy divinity providing protections, so that one cannot sufficiently admire the genius of the one who disposes these aids into types, causes, and times—so that they benefit some at certain hours, and nearly no day is found without its protections."

We shall begin with the start of the spring year. Theophrastus, speaking of the flowers that grow throughout the year, says: "The first of the flowers to show itself is the **white violet**; it springs forth where the weather is mild, immediately even before winter is over, but where it is harsher, it comes later. In spring, sometimes with the white violet or shortly after, the **lily** comes out, and what is called the **flame violet**; these far outrun all others used by those who make floral crowns. After these follows the **narcissus**, the **wild pomegranate flower**, and the **black violet**; among the wild plants, the **aurelia** and a type of *fremion* which they call **limonium** <note>likely Sea-lavender</note>, and the **gladiolus** <note>original: "pugio," literally "dagger," referring to the sword-lily</note>, and the **hyacinth**. The **rose** is later than these, and indeed breaks out last."

Hippocrates, in his *Aphorisms*, enumerates the diseases that usually occur in spring. In spring, indeed, there occur fits of madness, melancholia, the **falling sickness** <note>original: "morbi comitiales," a historical term for epilepsy</note>, hemorrhages, **quinsy** <note>original: "anginæ," severe throat inflammation</note>, catarrh, leprosy, coughs, rashes, white-spots <note>original: "alphi," a skin condition</note>, ulcerous pustules, tumors, and joint pains. In spring the blood increases and flourishes; the rose blooms at that time, and its flower purges the blood, which we need most in the spring. 

Melancholic episodes happen in the spring, not because they are generated at that time, but because, having been produced in winter and lying hidden in the body, they are spread by the warmth of spring, giving rise to melancholy and madness. A draught of **betony** leaves is effective against melancholy; the juice of **mallow** is also usefully given to the melancholic and the insane to drink, in a weight of six ounces. The power of **bugloss** <note>original: "bugloſſi"</note> is great for melancholic effects, when its decoction in wine is offered. **Lemon balm** <note>original: "meliſſophyllon"</note> casts out "black bile vapors" from the spirits and the blood, according to Avicenna. 

The falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note>, even if detected in the spring, is generated in winter due to phlegm born in the head, which is stirred up and spread in the spring. The seed of the **black poplar** drunk with vinegar is useful for those with the falling sickness, as it pours forth in spring. **Betony** heals the falling sickness when drunk with water, as do **plantain**, **mustard**, **squill**, **fleabane**, and the first shoots of the **white** and **black vines**. Other remedies include **yarrow** <note>original: "achillis altera"</note> drunk with oxymel <note>a medicinal drink of honey and vinegar</note>, **clove flowers**, **goat’s rue** juice <note>original: "galegæ"</note>, and **everlasting** <note>original: "heliochryſos"</note>. 

For inflammations of the tonsils, the **mulberry** is effective; **purple violets** are for quinsy. Defects of the skin are improved and leprosy is removed by **thapsia**, **narcissus**, **wild vine**, **bryony**, a decoction of **lupines**, **dock**, and **iris** <note>original: "xiphia"</note>. According to Galen, **elm leaves**, **cabbage**, **mustard**, **watercress**, **buttercup**, and **lily** are used for leprosy. For rashes and spreading ulcers, **buckthorn** <note>original: "rhamnus"</note> is applied, as are **plantain**, **gentian**, **scabious**, **hops**, and **narcissus**. Coughs are cured by **coltsfoot** <note>original: "tuſſilago"</note>, **dragon-root**, **asphodel**, **squill**, **horehound**, **wall-pellitory**, **henbane**, **bryony**, **valerian**, and **arum**. 

In spring, trees and herbs are also born which heal the diseases caused by serpents. The **ash tree** <note>original: "fraxinus"</note> is helpful against serpents: its expressed juice is for drinking, and when placed on the wounds, nothing else is found to be as helpful. So great is its power that a serpent will not even touch the tree's morning or evening shadows, however long they may be, but flees it from afar; if a fire and a serpent are enclosed in a circle of its leaves, the serpent would rather flee into the fire than into the ash. This is a wonderful kindness of Nature, that the ash flowers before these creatures emerge, and does not drop its leaves until they have hidden away. 

There is a miracle in the **dragon arum** <note>original: "dracunculi"</note> emerging from the earth at the first spring "shedding" of the serpents, and hiding itself back in the earth when they do. While it is hidden, no serpent appears; this is a sufficiently dutiful gift of Nature in itself, if it only serves to demonstrate the time of fear, according to Pliny. So many herbs, trees, and shrubs are signs, flourishing from the emergence of the serpents until they return to their dens—even if it were only the leaves of the ash, which neither grow before nor fall after. 

By the scent of **arum** when it is burned, serpents and especially asps are put to flight or intoxicated so that they are found sluggish. **Asphalt clover** <note>original: "trifoliū aſphaltites"</note>—indeed they say a decoction of the root and leaves of the whole shrub—ends the pains of those whom serpents have struck by bathing the wound. However, if anyone else with an ulcer is bathed with the water that healed the first person, they will be affected just as if they had been bitten by a serpent. Snakes flee from those carrying **dragon arum**. They also flee the scent and the bedding of **southernwood** <note>original: "abrotonum"</note>. Likewise **pennyroyal**,
