### PLANTS THAT ARE BORN IN SUMMER ARE EFFECTIVE AGAINST
### summer diseases. Chapter XXV.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'A' depicting a figure amidst winding vines and foliage.</image-desc>In summer, continuous and burning fevers occur—as Hippocrates also notes—along with many tertian <note>fevers recurring every third day</note> and quartan <note>fevers recurring every fourth day</note> fevers, vomiting, diarrhea, inflammations of the eyes <note>original: "lippitudines"</note>, earaches, mouth ulcers, rot of the genitals, and prickly heat <note>original: "fudamina"</note>. These diseases especially arise from yellow bile, which accumulates in the body during the summer season. We ought to list the herbs that draw out yellow bile and flourish in summer, for this is what Nature most specifically intended. **Aloe** gives off its juice in summer and is collected then; Galen called it the best remedy for bilious conditions. **Pennycress** <note>original: "thlaspi"</note> bears its seed in June, which draws out bile from both directions <note>meaning as both an emetic and a purgative</note>; in the same way, **campion**, **tutsan**, the **castor-oil plant**, the milky juice of the cut stem of **deadly carrot** <note>original: "thapsia"</note>, **spurge**, and the juice of **caper spurge** <note>original: "lathyris"</note>, which is extracted in summer, **wild cucumber**, **elder**, **dwarf elder**, and **heliotrope**. Likewise, the branches of flowering **wormwood** <note>original: "absinthium"</note> expel bilious humors of the belly through the bowels, according to Galen. The same is true for the herb and flower of **oregano**. For tertian and quartan fevers, three or four leaves of **bitumen trefoil** <note>original: "trifolium asphaltites"</note> are effective, as are **Saint John's wort** <note>original: "hypericum"</note>, **holy herb** <note>vervain</note>, **heliotrope**, **purslane**, and **lesser centaury**. For fluxes of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>, the juices of **gum-chicory**, **dill**, **Serapis’ orchid**, **marsh mallow**, **water-plantain**, **knotgrass**, **clematis**, **haresfoot clover**, **alkanet**, **date-palm**, the seed of the **rush**, **black poppy**, **mullein**, **sour grape**, **goldenrod**, **medlar**, **service-tree**, and **wild pear** are effective. Purslane and plantain heal eye inflammations; varieties of **pine**, **fenugreek**, dry wine in which **adder's tongue** <note>original: "ophioglosson"</note> has been cooked, and **eyebright** <note>original: "euphragia"</note> help with eye discharge. For earaches, the dripped juice of **poplar**, **willow**, **beet**, both types of **tarragon** <note>original: "dracunculus"</note>, **leek with milk**, **oregano**, **sweet clover**, **hog’s fennel**, **cleavers**, **horehound**, **hemp**, **knotgrass**, **pellitory-of-the-wall**, **henbane**, **garden nightshade**, **mallow**, and **elder** are useful.

### THAT NATURE HAS PRODUCED MOIST THINGS IN SUMMER
### to cool the human condition: and herbs for Venereal vigor.
### Chapter XXVI.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'G' depicting a figure standing in a landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc>Galen said that Nature produced moist and watery fruits in summer so that their pulp might refresh a person's internal nature, which languishes during the heat of the Dog Star <note>original: "Syrius," the star Sirius, associated with the hottest "dog days" of summer</note>. Theophrastus reported that moist things mostly sprout in summer, saying: "As for those things that sprout in contrary seasons, some assign the cause to moisture and heat; they claim that cold things sprout in summer and hot things in winter, so that each nature, suitably tempered, may be fit for each season." This is the opinion of Clidemus <note>an early Greek botanical writer</note>; and while this is not poorly stated, one ought to add the scarcity, weakness, and whatever other causes might exist. **Melon-pumpkins** <note>original: "melopepones"</note> are produced in summer; by their temperament they moisten and simultaneously cool, and they generate watery blood in the liver to restrain the heat and malice of yellow bile. Another species not only cools, but the cream extracted from its seed is usefully given to those with fever. **Cucumbers** also have a cold, moist temperament and a watery substance: if you place cucumbers of equal length next to a feverish infant while it sleeps, as if making them sleep together, the child will be healed immediately, for all the febrile heat will pass into the cucumbers, according to the writings of the Quintilii <note>two brothers who wrote a famous Roman manual on agriculture</note>. **Watermelons** <note>original: "anguriae"</note> are also of the same family:

The **gourd** <note>original: "cucurbita"</note> is of a moist and cold quality; when eaten, it is hydrating and drives away thirst, providing a moist nourishment to the body unlike all other moist foods. Its shavings are applied to the forehead of infants against the burning of the head, which they call *syriasis* <note>an ancient term for an inflammation of the brain or membranes, often associated with sunstroke</note>; the juice from the shavings helps with earaches and, when applied, aids in soothing skin burns caused by a burning fever. ->THAT HERBS ARE BORN IN SUMMER TIME FOR THE BITE<-
->OF A MAD DOG, WHICH THEN GOES MAD. Cap. XXVII.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'A' featuring a detailed landscape scene with a building or tower amidst rolling hills, contained within a square double-line border.</image-desc>

AS the heat of the Dog Star <note>Sirius, associated with the "Dog Days" of summer</note> burns, dogs are driven into a wild madness; at that time, provident Nature produces many opportune herbs by which such a deadly disease can be countered. **Madwort** <note>original: "alyssum," literally meaning "against madness"</note> comes forth in summer: when crushed in food, it heals the madness of dogs, according to Dioscorides. Galen says this should be collected under the heat of the Dog Star; it should be dried, crushed, sifted, and stored so it is not blown away, and for this reason it is called *alysson*. For the diet, Dioscorides recommends the eating of **garlic**, **leeks**, and **onions**, which flourish at that time and are dug from the earth. Aetius recommends for this purpose **fennel**, **shepherd’s needle**, **wild chicory**, **marsh asparagus**, and **garden** and **wild dock**. Avicenna uses both types of **hellebore**, **dodder of thyme**, **senna**, **fumitory**, and **deadly carrot** as purgative medicines. **All-heal** <note>original: "panax"</note> is effective against the bites of beasts that are driven to madness, as is **black horehound**. **Pennyroyal** <note>original: "pulegium"</note> protects the head from the harm of cold or heat by its scent; it is said to prevent thirst, and those who have two sprigs of pennyroyal placed behind their ears while in the sun do not suffer from the heat, according to Pliny. **Fleawort** <note>original: "psyllium"</note> flowers and flourishes in summer; the story goes that if it is brought into the house while green, it does not allow fleas to breed there. So too does **fleabane** <note>original: "coniza"</note>, which drives away gnats by its smoke and as a bed-covering, and kills fleas. Also, the root of the **wild cucumber** moistened with sea water, **black cumin** soaked in water, crushed **wild cumin** mixed with water, and the leaves of the **black poplar** and **caltrop**, according to Pamphilus. **Fennel flower** <note>original: "nigella"</note> casts out gnats by its smoke. If you place a flowering branch of moist **cannabis** near you when you are about to sleep, gnats will not touch you; they are also put to flight by the smell of **oregano** and vinegar, according to Democritus. A decoction of **elder** leaves, when sprinkled, puts flies to flight, according to Beritius. Likewise, the juice of **wild cucumber** placed in beds drives away bedbugs, as do **caper** leaves dissolved in oil, or a measure of **stavesacre**, according to Didymus.

## THAT PLANTS WHICH ARE BORN IN AUTUMN
### are effective against the diseases of that same season. Chap. XXVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'H' at the start of the chapter, set within a square woodcut border featuring a landscape with a large tree and a building in the background.</image-desc>
**Hippocrates**, speaking of the diseases of autumn, says: Most diseases occur in autumn, such as **quartan fevers** <note>original: "febres quartanæ"; a fever that recurs every third day, traditionally associated with "black bile"</note> and irregular fevers, enlarged spleens, **dropsy** <note>original: "aquæ intercutes"; fluid collecting under the skin</note>, wasting diseases, the dripping of urine, looseness and difficulties of the intestines, pains in the hips, **quinsy** <note>original: "anginæ"; severe inflammation of the throat</note>, asthma, intestinal obstructions, **epilepsy** <note>original: "morbi comitiales"; literally "the assembly sickness," so called because Roman political meetings were cancelled if someone had a seizure</note>, fits of madness, and **melancholy**. This is because at that time **black bile** <note>original: "atra bilis"; one of the four humors in ancient medicine, thought to cause gloom and various physical ailments</note> prevails, from which such diseases arise; therefore, we must prepare for its evacuation. **Black hellebore** <note>original: "Niger helleborus"</note> is in its prime in the autumn and out of season in the spring, according to **Theophrastus**. **Dioscorides** states that it draws black and yellow bile downward from the whole body; for this reason, it is prescribed for recurring and long-lasting fevers. **Epithymum** <note>original: "Epithymum"; dodder of thyme</note>, when taken with honey, excretes black bile more powerfully than other medicines; it is effective for diseases of the brain, melancholy, epilepsy, and conditions of the spleen, and it flowers in the summer. The juice of the **mandrake** <note>original: "Mandragoræ"</note>, taken in a dose of two *obols* <note>a small Greek unit of weight</note> with wine, extracts black bile through vomiting just like hellebore; the juice is extracted in summer, as is **oregano** <note>original: "origanū"</note> when drunk in honeyed water. **Pennyroyal** <note>original: "Pulegium"</note> which flowers at the summer solstice, **broom** <note>original: "sparthium"</note>, **basil** <note>original: "ocymum"</note>, and **lemon balm** <note>original: "melissophyllon"</note> also serve this purpose. For those suffering from spleen ailments, the seed of the **nettle** is a remedy, as is the root of **sowbread** <note>original: "cyclamini"</note>, a drink made of **capers**, **madder** <note>original: "rubiæ"</note>, the seed of the **stinking iris** <note>original: "xyridis"</note>, **woodbine** <note>original: "periclymeni"</note>, a decoction of **alkanet** <note>original: "anchusæ"</note>, **birthwort** <note>original: "aristolochia"</note>, and **bryony**. For epileptics, the seed of the **spatling poppy** <note>original: "papaueris spumei"</note> is beneficial, which is gathered in summer. For those with dropsy, the juice of the **wild cucumber**, **bulbs** that thrive in summer, **castor oil seeds** <note>original: "ricini grana"</note>, and an electuary of **squill** <note>original: "scillæ"</note> made with honey are useful.

## THAT PLANTS ARE BORN IN WINTER WHICH
### are effective for winter diseases. Chap. XXVIIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' featuring intricate floral and foliate scrollwork patterns within a square border.</image-desc>
**Pleurisy** comes in the winter, according to the tradition of **Hippocrates**, as do inflammations of the lungs, **lethargy**, "hail-like" eruptions, hoarseness, coughs, pains of the chest and sides, dizziness of the head, and **apoplexy** <note>sudden loss of consciousness or paralysis</note>. At this time, **phlegm** <note>original: "pituita"</note> abounds, and care must be taken that it is first evacuated. The root of the **iris**, which is dug up in winter, purges phlegm; so too does **sowbread** <note>original: "cyclaminus"</note>, which its flowers show to be flourishing then, along with **aloe**, **spurge laurel** <note>original: "daphnoides"</note>, which are green in winter, and **spurge flax** <note>original: "Thymelæa"</note> and **mezereon** <note>original: "chamelæa"</note> flourishing at the same time. **Bryony** is given to epileptics and those suffering from vertigo, as it flourishes underground in winter. For a cough, iris is effective, and **juniper berries** are most conveniently drunk; they ripen in autumn and endure through the winter, as do **cedar berries** <note>original: "cedrides"</note>. **Dried figs** cure an old cough and long-standing defects of the lungs. **Coltsfoot** <note>original: "Tussilago"</note>, which is green in winter, **wild radish** <note>original: "radicula"</note>, **asphodel**, **garlic**, and **squill** are all kept hanging throughout the winter. Indeed, hot plants are produced in winter to warm the human nature. **Theophrastus** said that those fruits produced in winter are hot in quality, for following **Cleodemus**, he believed they were generated by winter heat. Fruits that have a very hard woody pulp, or are contained in a woody partition and a thick shell, ripen late. Added to these are those with oily juices, or those that are dry fruits having little moisture. Plants that are **evergreen** <note>original: "perpetuò virent"</note> complete their fruit late; for coldness, dryness, and a heavy, earthy composition make it very difficult for them to be processed and ripened, as seen in **wild pears** and **acorns**. Because the stomach is warmer in winter, it can digest fats and items of a harder consistency. **Radish** <note>original: "Raphanus"</note> comes forth in winter and provides warmth. **Skirret** <note>original: "Siser"</note> also warms, as do the **wild turnip**, the **garden turnip**, **rape** <note>original: "napus"</note>, and both garden and wild **parsnip**. **Bulbs** are also devoured in winter, since they grow into stems in the spring.

<summary>This page discusses how Nature provides specific medicinal plants during autumn and winter to treat the diseases that arise from the seasonal dominance of black bile and phlegm, respectively.</summary>
<keywords>Hippocrates, Theophrastus, seasonal medicine, black bile, phlegm, autumn remedies, winter remedies, hellebore, iris, epilepsy, pleurisy, humoral theory</keywords>

->BOOK SIX.<-

# PLANTS THAT BLOOM REPEATEDLY, OR FOR A LONG TIME,
## *are effective against those diseases that occur frequently.*
### Chap. XXX.

If it is true, as we judge it to be true, that the use of those plants that bloom or flourish at the same time as diseases are spreading is necessary, then it follows that those which bloom twice, thrice, or many times are effective against those diseases that occur frequently and have no fixed time for attacking a person. **Theophrastus** said that **basil** <note>original: "ocimum"</note> blooms in stages, which is why it stays in bloom longer, as do **heliotrope** <note>original: "heliotropion"</note> and **chicory** <note>original: "cichoreum"</note>. The **marigold** <note>original: "Caltha"</note> has a yellow flower and springs up on the first of every month; because of this gift, it is likely named the **calendula** <note>original: "kalendula"</note>, because it is found to bloom on the *Kalends* <note>The first day of the month in the Roman calendar.</note> of all months. Hence it happens that some call it the "flower of all months." Its flower, drunk in wine, stimulates the **monthly flows** <note>original: "menses"; menstruation</note>, and also wonderfully draws out the **afterbirth** <note>original: "secundas"</note>; when dried and used in fumigations, it has been tested in six hundred dangers faced by women. **Groundsel** <note>original: "Senecio"</note> blooms for a long time; as soon as one part grows old, another and yet another is born beneath it. This happens continuously through the whole winter and spring until summer, as is held by **Theophrastus**. Among us, it is called the "flower of every month"; this herb is accustomed to stir up delayed menstruation. **Oxtongue** <note>original: "Picris"</note> blooms all year; boiled in water, it is so beneficial for women's purgings that it even draws out stillborn fetuses. **Rosemary** <note>original: "Rosmarinum coronarium"</note> blooms twice a year, in spring and autumn, but in our regions, we see it blooming almost continuously, especially where the year is more temperate; from the teachings of the **Arabs**, we know it stimulates the monthly flows. Three crops of flowers are seen in the **squill** <note>original: "scilla"</note>; its variety called **pancratium** is drunk in wine for the purpose of stimulating menstruation. **Nicander** mentions in his *Theriaca* that the **asphodel** <note>original: "Asphodelon"</note> blooms twice a year; its root, when drunk, is beneficial for the monthly flows. **Candytuft** <note>original: "Iberis"</note> always blooms and is effective for long-lasting **sciatica** <note>original: "ischiadicis"; nerve pain in the hip and leg</note>.

# THAT EVERGREEN PLANTS ARE EFFECTIVE AGAINST THOSE DISEASES
## *which can happen to the human body at any time.*

<image-desc>decorative floral ornament featuring swirling vines and leaves</image-desc>

### Chap. XXXI.

We have said that those stocks whose leaves fall produce their leaves, fruits, and seeds at fixed and opportune times; it must be added that those which are **perpetually green** <note>evergreens</note> help those diseases that can happen at any time. It was not done by Nature without reason, so that at whatever times we might need them, we can have them immediately at hand. The **pine** <note>original: "Pinus"</note> is beneficial for liver ailments, burns, and ulcers occupying the surface of the body; as a fumigant, it ejects the fetus and the afterbirth, stops the bowels, moves the urine, soothes inflammations, eases toothaches, and protects wounds from inflammation. The **mastic tree** <note>original: "Lentiscus"</note> is effective for the spitting of blood, dysentery, and bursts of blood from the womb; it cements broken bones, its decoction fills up cavities [in teeth or wounds], and it drives out urine. The **cypress** <note>original: "Cupressus"</note> heals difficulty of urine and polyps of the nostrils, casts off rough nails, restrains hernias, glues wounds together, and brings help to **holy fire** <note>original: "sacris ignibus"; likely erysipelas, a spreading skin infection</note>, carbuncles, and the stomach. **Juniper** <note>original: "Iuniperus"</note> is effective against inflammations and griping pains; it assists in ruptures, convulsions, strangulation of the womb, and leprosy. **Laurel** <note>original: "Laurus"</note> helps the faults of the womb and bladder, and the stings of wasps and scorpions; it is used for the weariness of the nerves and for stones, and it ejects the fetus. It is effective against thunder and lightning; for this reason, it ought to live always with us, to keep us safe from them. The **tamarisk** <note>original: "Myrica"</note> is effective against the **royal disease** <note>original: "morbum regium"; jaundice</note>, it inhibits [excess] urine, and is beneficial for toothaches, women's fluxes, **lice** <note>original: "phthiriasi"</note>, nits, and those who are short of breath. **Holly** <note>original: "Aquifolia"</note> cements broken bones and softens the hardness of joints; according to **Pliny**, it wards off winter lightning and sorcery. **Squill** <note>original: "Scilla"</note>, the sacred herb, **buckthorn** <note>original: "rhamnus"</note>, and similar plants live a long time when preserved, such as when hung in the home to protect it from all sorcery. The **olive** <note>original: "Olea"</note>, **wild olive** <note>original: "oleaster"</note>, and **mock privet** <note>original: "phyllirea"</note> heal holy fire, creeping, foul, and consuming ulcers, carbuncles, and torn skin...

Since the beauty of the head can be lost at any time, it was necessary for those plants that ought to assist it to be perennial, so that aid might be provided at the opportune time. Furthermore, if we may refer to the principle of similarity <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures," where a plant's physical form suggests its medical use.</note>, we have said that foliage corresponds in proportion to hair, and for the preservation of hair, evergreen plants were necessary. **Myrtle** restrains falling hair, while the **Palm** prevents the shedding of eyelashes; **ladanum**, **aloe**, and **southernwood** <note>original: "abrotonum"</note> are suited for hair loss,

# GIOVANNI BATTISTA DELLA PORTA
# OF NAPLES
# PHYTOGNOMONICS
## BOOK SEVEN.
### PREFACE.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or philosopher, amidst foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

NOW we have progressed to the characters <note>original: "mores"; refers to the innate dispositions or "customs" of the plants</note> of plants: even if Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> denies that plants possess characters, this is the third part of our classification, which we promised at the beginning. The Greeks call this **ethics** <note>original: "τὰ ἠθικὰ"; the study of character or moral nature</note>, and if these traits are more clearly discerned in animals, they are more obscure in plants and much more difficult to discover. From the characters of animals and plants, however they may be, we shall demonstrate many things for the correction of mortal characters or for the improvement of their inclinations. 

We can understand the "inclination of the soul" in two ways: one, by which it is moved toward fear, cheerfulness, sadness, and other passions of that kind; the other, by which it is inclined toward love, hate, honor, and similar feelings. Everyone admits that a person can be moved toward sadness and cheerfulness, for by the medicinal power <note>original: "medica vi"</note> in which herbs excel, the body is altered; and by this physical alteration, the soul is also moved. In this manner, Theophrastus warns that a person can be moved in mind and even alienated from reason <note>driven insane</note>, and vice versa. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author of Natural History</note> hands down a theory of immense subtlety descending from Plato, concerning the light and rough **corpuscles** <note>original: "corpusculis"; small particles or atoms</note> of things...

<summary>In this preface to Book Seven, della Porta introduces the concept of "plant ethics," arguing that the physical properties of plants can alter the human body and, consequently, influence the soul's passions and moral character.</summary>
<keywords>character of plants, ethics, Theophrastus, Pliny, Plato, psychology, passions, medicinal power, corpuscles</keywords>

--- Page 274 ---
<meta>The previous page introduced Book Seven, focusing on "ethics" or the characters of plants. Della Porta argued that plants, like animals, have innate dispositions that can be used to influence human behavior and emotions.</meta>

<page-num>270</page-num>
<header>PHYTOGNOMONICS</header>

*...with angular or round shapes, approaching the nature of others to a greater or lesser degree; therefore, the same things are not bitter or sweet to everyone. Likewise, in states of fatigue or thirst, people are more prone to anger. Therefore, this harshness of the mind—or rather, the soul—is softened by a sweeter sap. It eases the movement of the spirits and makes the channels of the body more flexible, so they do not tear as the spirits pass back and forth. Everyone has experienced this within themselves: anger, grief, sadness, and every impulse of the mind is mellowed by food. Thus, these things must be observed, as they possess medicine not only for the body but for one's character.*

*But whether plants can truly incline the mind is a question asked by many of the ancient philosophers. The greatest writer on plants <note>Likely referring to Theophrastus or Pliny the Elder</note> records that Hesiod and Musaeus <note>Semi-mythical poets of ancient Greece</note> taught that **polium** <term>Hullwort or Mountain Germander; a plant believed in antiquity to have magical and protective properties</term> is extremely useful for any serious or great undertaking, and no less for one’s fame and good reputation. He also notes that **Antirrhinon** <term>Snapdragon</term> is useful for gaining glory and the grace of life, though he considers all these claims to be mere fables.*

*We shall attempt to discover these signs in several ways. First, we must consider the characters <note>original: "mores"; refers to the innate dispositions or behavioral traits</note> we wish to change or instill in others, and see which animals possess them; then, we shall administer those parts of the plant that resemble either the animal's limbs or the animal itself. Furthermore, we will investigate which planets the plants are subject to based on their appearance—which we will provide in the following book—and from there we will deduce their powers.*

*Just as this is the most difficult task of all, so too does the majesty and the distinct markings of Nature shine most brightly within it. The **Observer of Plants** <note>original: "Phytopta"; Della Porta's term for a practitioner of his science</note> will divine far more secrets of divine providence, which are by no means to be neglected for human use and necessity. When we speak of animal "characters," we mean traits such as being lustful, chaste, greedy, talkative, silent, and the like. Nature has willed that the similarities in the parts of plants demonstrate the powers of animals; however, we must first uncover some of these animal characters.*

*But perhaps someone will object: how can anyone ever truly observe the characters of animals? Who has lived long enough in the deserts and pathless wilds of the world alongside the hyena, the rhinoceros, the **crocuta** <note>original: "crocuta"; a legendary beast often described as a hybrid of a hyena and a lioness</note>, the tiger, and the panther—wild and pitiless beasts—to be a constant observer of their ways? Who could be a tireless investigator of fish in the depths of the Ocean, observing what they do beneath the lowest rocks, seaweed, or sands, when even fishermen who spend their lives at sea hardly dare speak of such things? Indeed, if a proverb warns us that many "measures of salt" must be eaten with the men we live and associate with <note>A reference to the ancient proverb that you must eat a peck of salt with someone before you can truly know them</note> before we can truly know their inner character, how can the characters of animals become known to us, with whom we share no such social bond? To this we reply: the deception found in the human face and words is so great that our knowledge of a person’s character often fails us; it is quite different with brute animals, who, since they lack the choice between virtue and vice...*

<summary>Della Porta explains his methodology for using plants to influence human character, proposing that plant parts resembling specific animals can transfer that animal's traits to a person. He argues that animal nature is easier to read than human nature because animals lack the human capacity for deception.</summary>

## ANIMALS THAT EXCEL IN WIT AND DOCILITY ARE EFFECTIVE FOR HUMAN INTELLIGENCE AND MEMORY.

### Chapter 1.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring a figure seated at a desk or table within a room, likely representing a scholar or philosopher.</image-desc>BUT let us pass to examples, running down from the head through the other members, and first consider which animals are closest to human intellect—namely, those that excel in skill, cunning, docility, and memory—so that they do not seem devoid of intellect or reason, as *Plutarch* writes. For such creatures can easily increase human memory and intellect when those parts where the senses or intellect flourish most are administered through the medical art. These parts, as *Iamblichus* relates in his *Life of Pythagoras*, are the heart and the brain. For all *Pythagoreans* <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, known for their specific dietary and ethical codes</note> were forbidden to consume the heart or eat the brain; they were to abstain from them because they are the principles and, as it were, the seats of wisdom and life. We ourselves have adopted and recommended this through frequent and most certain experimentation. *Pliny* says that the wisest animals are those that feed on grain. We shall begin with the elephant, which seems to excel all other animals in sense, memory, and sharpness of wit. It has an understanding of its native tongue <note>original: "patrii sermonis"; referring to the language of its keepers or trainers</note>, obedience to commands, and a memory for the duties it has learned. It can dance to a beat, slow its pace to a slow sound, relax when the flute softens, and conversely, drive forward and hasten at a sharp sound. *Plutarch* relates that he marvels most at this in the elephant: that by learning and offering itself to teachers in human gatherings, they express such variety and figures in their gestures, the elegance and abundance of which human industry itself could scarcely express, nor memory easily encompass. For he tells of one in Rome with a slower wit who, finding it harder to learn certain wonderful gestures and being frequently punished with lashes, was caught at night practicing and working on them by itself. *Mucianus*, three times consul, is the authority for the claim that an elephant learned the strokes of Greek letters and was accustomed to write out words in that language, according to *Pliny*. *Nearchus* <note>An officer in Alexander the Great's army who wrote about India</note> is the authority for the fact that they learn to throw stones at a target, use weapons, and swim excellently; they are even tightrope walkers, ascending ropes and returning backwards down them. *Seneca*, citing *Aristotle*, says they learn commanded duties, adore the King, and bend their knees, and approach human wit so closely that *Cicero* did not fear to affirm that the elephant is not inferior to most men in sense and wit; and among beasts, none is more prudent than the elephant. That power of the mind remains even in the ivory, so that *Aetius* wrote that the filings of an elephant's tusk, drunk with mead <term>mellicratum: a mixture of honey and water</term>, aids the memory no small amount. The monkey is skilled at imitating everything: whatever is done with the body, if it is taught, it performs excellently and represents it in action; if taught to dance, it masters the dance; if to play the flute, it plays. *Aelian* says it can perform the duty of a charioteer, pulling or loosening the reins and using the whip at the same time; in short, if anyone trains it for anything, it does not disappoint the teacher. *Mucianus* reports that a monkey played at "little soldiers" <term>latrunculi: an ancient Roman board game similar to chess or checkers</term> with pieces made of wax, according to *Pliny*. From these observations, *Rhazes* <note>A celebrated Persian physician and philosopher</note> handed down that the heart of a monkey, roasted and dried, then drunk with old mead, sharpens the intellect. Geese are sharp of sense; *Ovid* called them "wiser than a goose" <note>likely referring to the alertness of the geese that saved the Roman Capitol</note>. *Aelian*, citing *Theophrastus*, also reports...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of "Ethics" or the innate characters of living things. Having discussed the theory in the previous chapter, the author now provides specific examples of animals whose natural intelligence, docility, or specialized skills make their bodies useful for creating medicines to improve human memory and intellect.</meta>

<page-num>272</page-num>
<header>PHYTOGNOMONICA</header>

even boys are said to have loved them. They can also be seen to possess an understanding of wisdom, for they were such constant companions to the philosopher Lacydes that they never left his side—neither in public, nor at the baths, nor by night or day, according to Pliny. Plutarch relates that when crossing the Taurus mountains, they fill their mouths with fairly large pebbles so that they might restrain the talkative chatter of their nature for a time, until they can safely slip past their enemy, the eagle, without being noticed. Aelian and Marcellinus report the same, noting that their flight—which traces the shape of the letter of Pythagoras <note>The letter 'Y', which Pythagoreans used to symbolize the fork in the road between virtue and vice</note>—is not lacking in natural wit. Simeon Sethi <note>An 11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician</note> says that through a certain peculiar property, they provide "goodness of wit" <note>original: *euthyam*, a Greek term for a well-disposed or clever mind</note> to those who eat them regularly with honey and butter; though I fear he may have been speaking of their eggs. The parrot can provide the same benefit in medicine, as is held by physicians. Plutarch believes they stand as advocates for all other animals by their very capacity for learning, since they readily offer themselves to teachers to produce human speech and articulate the voice. Pliny writes: above all else, the parrot mimics human voices; some even greet Emperors with speech and pronounce the words they receive. When a mirror is brought near, the bird is deceived by its own form and is made to appear now joyful, now grieving; it is also accustomed to kissing its human masters. Avicenna relates a story of a man so loved by a parrot that the bird grew weak and pined away whenever he departed.

Deer are also naturally clever, as witnessed by Aristotle; therefore, for those who have fallen into forgetfulness after a lethargy or other illnesses, it is most helpful to drink deer horn mixed with honeyed wine, according to Aetius. Equally clever animals are the hare and the rabbit, which share the same flesh and blood. Aelian, Philes, Pliny, and Solinus declare that hyenas possess knowledge, and especially magical knowledge. For whatever animal they gaze upon remains fixed to its tracks; and when the moon's orb is full, by standing with the moonlight behind them, they cast their own shadow upon dogs, which renders the dogs mute, allowing the hyenas to enjoy their prey as they wish. They will move their bodies close to a sleeping human or dog: if they sense themselves to be larger than the sleeper, they deprive the sleeper of their senses, eat their hands, and consume them; but if they perceive themselves to be shorter, they hurry to flee. They receive a hunter on their right side so that they may occupy the tracks already stepped in and devour the hunter’s mind, for they themselves are only captured from the left side. This is according to Zoroaster, cited in Nestor’s "Panacea": a hyena's tooth suspended above the right arm from the shoulder to the elbow resists forgetfulness; or, if the left foot and its claws are bound in linen to someone's right arm, they will not forget anything they have heard, according to Rhazes and Albertus Magnus.

The hoopoe is a most prudent bird; it smears its nest with dung so that the stench may drive humans away from its home, as noted by Aristotle and Aelian. To break open doors if they are closed, it uses a certain herb. Aelian notes it does many other things with great skill; because of this, its tongue, when suspended over a person who is overly forgetful, is effective for the memory and makes one remember what had been forgotten, according to Pythagoras. Plutarch, in his *Table Talk*, did not keep silent regarding the talkativeness and docility of the partridge. The partridge is numbered by Papyrius among the birds capable of pronouncing human speech.

->*And the partridge who reports back, joining repeated words.*<-

Athenaeus said that in Laconia, partridges are considered vocal; if their gall is rubbed upon the temples every month, the memory is awakened, according to Simeon Sethi. Next after the peacock, roosters feel a sense of glory; they command their own kind and exercise kingship in whatever house they live. They fight among themselves and sing immediately upon victory. They walk with an equally proud and high neck, their crests held tall, and they also raise their sickle-shaped tails on high. When defeated, they hide in silence and endure servitude with difficulty. If the mother hen dies, the rooster himself broods and hatches the chicks from the egg; at such times he remains silent, being clearly conscious that he is performing a womanly task, according to Aelian. Alone among birds, he looks back at the sky; he knows the stars and distinguishes the three-hour watches of the day with his song. Simeon Sethi records that the rooster's flesh increases the substance of the brain and nourishes it abundantly; therefore, it is beneficial for the mind and for a lighter wit. The same is held by Avicenna, Arnoldus, and others. The beaver is described as skillful and provident by Albertus, Agricola, and hunters; indeed, it builds itself houses on the banks of rivers with several levels, so that as the river water rises, it may ascend, and as it falls, it may descend. For it is an amphibious animal, living in both land and water. The tree which it chooses to cut for the building of its house and for food, it does not leave...

...leaves the tree until it has bitten all the way through, and when it is about to fall, it looks up with every stroke lest it be crushed unawares. Furthermore, among its own kind, if there is a stranger or one too old to be fit for life, when it goes out for wood, it places the logs upon the belly of the one lying on its back. To keep the wood from falling, so that it might serve as a vehicle, it skillfully arranges the legs between the logs, and thus draws the burdened animal back to its lodge. For this reason, according to Aetius <note>A 6th-century Byzantine medical writer</note>, <term>castoreum</term> <note>A yellowish secretion from the scent glands of a beaver, historically used in medicine</note> helps those who have become forgetful after lethargy or other illnesses, whether the back of the head is anointed with it and oil, or a dram's weight is drunk with honeyed water. 

Bears are cunning and fraudulent, so much so that they cannot be tamed even over a long period, according to Adamantius. If a person's face is anointed with melted bear fat, they will understand and remember whatever they hear or read. 

Aristotle says that cranes do many things wisely: for they seek out distant places for their own benefit, migrating from Scythia to the Nile to spend the winter, as Herodotus records. Indeed, they excel in the sharpness of their senses. When they travel, they form a triangle so as to cut the opposing air more easily; then, they lighten the course of the birds by using their wings gradually from either side like oars. If the sky grows fierce and the wind rises, they do not fly head-on or in a crescent-shaped flock as they do when it is calm, but instantly shift themselves into a <term>cuneus</term> <note>A "wedge" formation, often used to describe military ranks</note>. If they see themselves being attacked by an eagle, they stand in a circle and show the appearance of a battle line drawn up as if for a fight, which causes the eagle to retreat. In flight, by resting their necks on the backs of those flying ahead, they make their labor easy, according to Aelian, and when the leader tires, it moves to the back. When they stop to rest, the others sleep while the leader, being vigilant, signals whatever it perceives with its voice. They keep watch during the night, holding a small stone in one foot; if the stone falls as the bird relaxes in sleep, it proves the crane's negligence. There are those who report that the gall of cranes is beneficial for a failure of memory, according to Simeon Sethi. 

It is well celebrated in writings that the <term>pagurus</term> <note>A type of crab or crustacean</note> loves music and possesses prudence. Writers report that for this reason, a crab was once hung from the neck of Diana of Ephesus as a symbol of wisdom and counsel. Truly, when it sheds its shell, being stripped of its spikes and armor, it attacks no one until it has recovered a harder shell; this is greatly praised by Oppian. I speculate that its limbs confer wisdom, but its powers are as yet unexplored.

## THAT THE MOST BRUTE AND UNTEACHABLE ANIMALS PRODUCE STUPIDITY
## Chapter II.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' at the beginning of the chapter. The letter is ornate, set within a square frame, and contains an illustrative scene with a figure in a landscape.</image-desc>
On the other hand, the most brutish, coarse, dull, and unteachable animals imprint fatuity and coarseness upon a man if eaten. This is evident from the experiments that philosophers have learned regarding their behaviors and physicians regarding their powers, which they have prescribed for us. 

Among land animals, mice are unteachable, according to Pliny. Arnoldus <note>Likely Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a medieval physician</note> said that the meat of a mouse taken as food brings about great forgetfulness. Rams are of a simple and foolish wit, as is held in Aristotle's *History of Animals* and his *Physiognomonics*. The sheep kind is mindless, possessing the most foolish character among all animals; it wanders into deserts for no reason, and in the face of winter—even when it often leaves the stable and is overtaken by snow—it will not leave unless the shepherd compels it, but perishes where it stands. Because of this, the marrow of an uncastrated ram is so contrary to human nature that it abolishes the function of memory, according to the same author. The donkey is of the most foolish character, with a degenerate and stolid soul; it does not know how to yield to those it meets on the road. The camel is simple-minded, not much different from the donkey. Galen says that those who feed on the meat of camels and donkeys turn out to be like camels and donkeys in both mind and body. 

The cat is forgetful; when it goes out into the neighborhood for the sake of mating, it forgets to return. Because of this, whoever eats the brain of a male cat is nearly driven mad, for it obstructs the passages of the brain and hinders the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>In ancient medicine, these were refined fluids that carried thought and sensation through the nerves</note> from passing to the posterior ventricle; since memory is excluded from there, the person is rendered without a mind.

PHYTOGN. <note>Short for *Phytognomonica*, the title of Giambattista della Porta's work on the medicinal and magical properties of plants and animals based on their appearance.</note>

### ALERT ANIMALS MAKE MEN ALERT.
->Chapter III.<-

Nocturnal or night-wandering animals communicate their wakefulness to us; for this reason, those who desire to be alert should seek out those members in which sleep is absent. We read in the works of Psellus the Platonic scholar <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine philosopher</note> that dogs, crows, and roosters contribute to wakefulness, as do the nightingale, the bat, and the owl—and especially the head, heart, and eyes of these creatures, so that his opinion is not far removed from our own method. Hesiod testifies that the nightingale alone of all birds is exempt from sleep and busily engages in night-watches, as recorded by Aelian in his various histories. The nightingale is an ever-watchful guardian; when she warms her eggs in her breast, she consoles the sleepless labor of the night with the sweetness of her song. From this comes a proverb recorded by Varinus: *They do not even sleep as much as a nightingale*, meaning they are very meager sleepers. For this same reason, Aelian wrote that the flesh of a nightingale, when taken as food, promotes wakefulness. Pliny recorded that the eyes of crabs, when tied in a deer skin along with the flesh of a nightingale, provide wakefulness and put sleep to flight.

Stags feed at night, especially if they remain in the fields, for they fear men during the day; however, in the mountains they are caught at night, and for a long time because of the solitude. Mithridates of Pontus <note>A famous king known for his hardiness and his use of complex medicinal concoctions</note>, when he took his sleep, would entrust the guardianship of his body to a bull, a horse, and a stag, and these would stay awake for his protection. Crabs are watchful, especially at the full light of the Moon, when they come out from their hiding places at night and wander about; for this reason, Pliny said that the eyes of crabs should be tied in a deer skin. Jupiter willed that kingfishers feed at night, as Oppian says, especially around the most solitary parts of pools and rivers, so they would not be a nuisance to men. If one places the eyes of a kingfisher, wrapped in linen, under the head of one who is sleeping too much, it will drive the sleep away, according to Aelian’s various histories, which he cites from Hesiod. Swallows do not always stay awake throughout the entire night, but complete only half a sleep. Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century scientist and theologian</note> says that the eye of a swallow placed in the bed does not permit the one lying there to sleep until it is removed. 

The bat is named from "night," as we have said; the Latins call it *vespertilio* <note>original: "vespertilio"</note> from *vesper* (evening), which is when it usually flies. According to Pliny, its dried head, when tied on, wards off sleep. Others say that if you tie the severed head of a living bat <note>term: *nycteris* (Greek for bat)</note> in a black skin and place it on someone's left arm, they will never sleep until it is removed; the same is true if its heart is worn. The watchful crow also provides wakefulness; some believe that its heart, worn continuously, is effective for driving away sleep, as Fernelius wrote. The owl is named *noctua* by Festus from the time of night in which it sings or flies, but according to Varro, it is named from the time it stays awake. Although there are many kinds of nocturnal birds, this one especially took its name from "night" among the Latins. To Aristotle, it is a night-wanderer. Rhazes <note>A famous Persian physician</note> writes that when it is beheaded, one of its eyes remains open and the other closed; if the open one is placed under the head of a sleeper, he will wake up; if the closed one is placed under one who is awake, he will fall asleep.

### SLEEPY ANIMALS ARE EFFECTIVE FOR INDUCING SLEEP.
->Chapter IIII.<-

In the same way, animals that are greatly devoted to sleep are able to procure sleep for those who lack it or who sleep very little. Here are some examples: The hare is an animal much devoted to sleep; it sleeps with its eyelids open and motionless, as is held from Xenophon. From this, the Egyptians, wishing to signify something that stays open, paint a hare, since it always has its eyes open. Nicander thinks that people become sleepy by taking hare in their food, a habit Cato followed according to Pliny. Among birds, a cuckoo tied in a hare skin attracts sleep, according to Pliny. The cuckoo comes forth in spring and goes into hiding at the rising of the Dog Star <note>The star Sirius, associated with the heat of late summer</note>, as Pliny says; it is very rarely seen, according to Aelian, and hides in the hollows of trees. The pig sleeps a great deal, especially in summer, when its moisture is dissolved by heat, according to Albert. For sleep, the foam of a boar with fat in a half-pint...

...boiled down to three portions until only one-third remains and given, it is effective. Sixth: No animal is weighed down by a heavier sleep than the **sea-calf** <note>Also known as a seal.</note>; for this reason, Pliny recorded that its flipper has a sleep-inducing power and can lure sleep when placed under the head. **Hedgehogs** hide themselves in hollow trees during the winter, and Aristotle says in his *On Marvelous Things Heard* that they can endure up to a year without food; Aelian and Philes add that they feed on apples collected during the summer. If the left eye is fried in oil and stored in a small vessel, the liquid is sleep-inducing; for if it is dripped into the ear, sleep will invade, according to Rhases <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi, a famous 10th-century Persian physician.</note>. The nature of **bears** is to hide themselves before all else when lethargy approaches; before they become entirely numb and lie stupidly, they hide in their dens. The males remain hidden for forty days; for the first twice-seven days they are weighed down by such a heavy sleep that they cannot even be awakened by wounds. During this time, they become wonderfully fat from lethargy, according to Aristotle, Plutarch, Pliny, and Solinus. Rhases says that if a bear's dried eye is hung upon children, it drives away the fears by which they are troubled in their sleep. **Stellions** <note>A type of spotted lizard.</note> remain hidden during the four coldest months, according to Aristotle. Joannes Ursinus, citing Arnaldus <note>Likely Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a medieval physician.</note>, says regarding the stellion:

> Eat the heart, and so great a sleep will lay prostrate the body,
> That the hand might be cut off without pain.
<note>original: "Mande cor, & tantus prosternet corpore somnus, / Ut scindi possit absq; dolore manus."</note>

**Frogs** all hide during the winter and come forth to the waters in spring; an oil prepared from them provokes sleep, according to Mesue <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a Christian physician in Baghdad.</note>. The **hoopoe** sings in summer and sleeps in the hollows of trees in winter, where it hides without its feathers; Rhases reports that if its right wing is hung at the head of a sleeping man, he will not wake up until it is removed.

### ANIMALS THAT DREAM, INDUCING IN MEN
### terrible, peaceful, true, and false dreams.
### Chapter V.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut drop cap 'S' featuring a figure in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>
Certain animals dream just as men do. Pliny, following Aristotle, states it is evident that besides man, horses, oxen, sheep, and goats dream; for this reason, it is believed to occur in all animals that give birth to live offspring. Man dreams most of all animals. Among those things that prompt dreams is food, as we have said elsewhere, but to have eaten the flesh of these animals that dream induces dreams even more. These dreams correspond to the qualities of the animal: from **black** and **melancholic** animals come melancholic dreams; from **white** ones come phlegmatic dreams; thus come sad or cheerful dreams, false dreams from those with intemperate natures, and true dreams from those that are most temperate and consistent in themselves. And it is not only flesh taken as food, but also their skins spread beneath one. The **hare** breeds most frequently and dreams most frequently; its meat prompts many dreams. Marcus Cato the Censor used to order the sick to be fed with vegetables and the meat of duck, pigeon, or hare; for he said this was light and suitable for the sick, except that it produces much sleeplessness. Pliny notes that Cato thought people became "dreamy" if a hare was taken as food, but because its meat is cold and dry and produces **black bile** <note>One of the four humors; in excess, it was believed to cause melancholy and dark visions.</note>, as is held by Hippocrates, Galen, Psellus, Paulus, and Simeon, it can only generate sad dreams. The **monkey** is cold and harsh, and generates the worst of humors, as held by Rhases; for this reason, if its heart is placed beneath the head of a sleeper, he will see terrible things in his dreams, according to the same author. Likewise, if anyone about to sleep puts a snake’s **slough** <note>The shed skin of a snake.</note> under his head, or sprinkles his head with ashes collected from a burnt snake’s slough, he will see terrible dreams. The meat of all **birds of prey** tends toward dryness, which generates black bile in the body. The worst, however, are **dog** and **wolf** meats, which corrupt the humors and spirits because they generate melancholic and wicked imaginations in both sleep and wakefulness, according to Rhases. Aelian mentions a **marine fish** called the "hyena"; if you move its right fin toward a man lulled in sleep, you will certainly disturb him, for he will see frightening specters during his rest and suffer bitter insomnia. The **hoopoe** is a bird colored with black spots, and for this reason is of a melancholic complexion; it seeks the deserted parts of the forests and pathless regions, according to Aeschylus. It is a most filthy bird, in...

among tombs, and lingering near human dung, according to Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar and encyclopedist.</note>. Among birds, it is a friend of the night and shadows, mournful and a lover of grief. Its flesh is harsh, according to Rhases; for this reason, the blood of a **hoopoe** smeared upon a sleeping man produces demonic phantoms, according to Pythagoras. Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and scientist.</note> adds that anointing the temples with hoopoe blood when it is time to sleep causes one to see terrible dreams. The **chameleon** is of a pale color, marked with black spots—the pallor of the dead—and it changes its color frequently, reflecting whatever it most recently touched, except for red and white, as Pliny notes. Anointing the temples with the blood of a chameleon induces terrifying dreams, according to Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a medieval physician.</note>. The flesh of an **ox** causes insomnia, since the animal itself dreams; the flesh of bulls is of the worst quality, as is that of calves, but that of castrated animals is superior. The flesh of calves is moist and soft, and thus more easily digested; because they are not contrary to the human body, people used them—and bull’s blood—for prophecies. Pliny says that fresh bull’s blood is among the poisons, except in Aegyra; for there, the priestess of the earth, about to prophesy, drinks the blood of a bull before she descends into the caves. From this truth, the Poets fashion the gates of dreams: one of horn and one of ivory—true dreams from horn, false dreams from ivory. Virgil says:

> There are twin gates of Sleep, of which one is said to be 
> Of horn, by which an easy exit is given to true shades.
> The other is perfected, shining with white ivory, 
> But the spirits send false dreams to the sky.
<note>original: "Sunt geminae Somni portae, quarum altera fertur / Cornea, qua veris facilis datur exitus umbris. / Altera candenti perfecta nitens elephanto, / Sed falsa ad caelum mittunt insomnia manes." — Virgil, Aeneid, Book VI.</note>

And Sleep is depicted with a horn, and they compare celestial dreams to the horns of bulls because they point upward; terrestrial dreams, however, they compare to ivory, because on an elephant it points downward. **Lambs** provide nourishment that is hot and moist but phlegmatic; **rams** are animals of a better temperament than the younger ones, and they lack the gas <term>flatulence: internal gasses believed to rise to the brain and disturb the spirit</term> by which dreams are disturbed and become tumultuous. **Goats** are best in the summertime, when shrubs abound with the buds they usually eat. We read that among the Daunians or Calabrians <note>Ancient peoples of Southern Italy.</note>, it was the custom to lie upon skins, which they call *melotas*—that is, sheepskins—at the tomb of Podalirius <note>A legendary healer from the Trojan War.</note>, and thus be instructed by oracles during rest. Those who sacrifice to Amphiaraus <note>A hero and seer of Greek myth who was swallowed by the earth.</note>, once the sacred rites were finished, would spread out a ram’s skin and sleep upon it, seeking dreams, according to Pausanias. Of these things Virgil sang concerning King Latinus in the seventh book of the *Aeneid*:

> He lay upon the spread skins, and sought sleep.
<note>original: "Pellibus incubuit stratis, somnosque petiuit."</note>

For the flesh of many animals tends to restrain the chance phantoms and disturbed movements of the mind; hence, through countless dangerous trials, we have learned that those who lie at night upon spread ram skins have captured true dreams, and many of the ancient learned men felt the same. The many-learned Poets alluded to this secret, not because I think one should entirely rely on the omens of dreams, but rather how much natural causes can promise in times of necessity. We read in Porphyry’s <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> book *On Abstaining from Living Things*: those who wish to take into themselves the souls of prophetic animals devour the principal parts of them, such as the hearts of ravens or hawks, and thus receive the souls of these animals into themselves, which then foretell things to them like an oracle.

# PLANTS THAT DEMONSTRATE JOYFUL, SAD, FALSE, AND TRUE
## *dreams.* Chapter VI.

**S**imilarly, plants with a black flower or fruit, or those of an earthy and dry quality, provoke melancholic dreams; likewise, gassy plants excite terrifying ones, and finally, according to the modes of their quality, plants also stir up their own types of dreams. Examples follow: The **bean** has a flower and fruit of various colors, for it is either tawny, black, grass-green, or scarlet. Amphiaraus used to command those who were occupied with the prophecies gathered through dreams to abstain from beans, because by their gas they [disturb] the calm [of the mind]...

# BOOK SEVEN.

disturb the peace of the mind during sleep; for they cause imaginative and entirely tumultuous dreams, according to Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist, author of *De Materia Medica*.</note>. The **lentil** has nearly the same flower; there is no doubt that insomnia is caused when lentils with black grains are consumed in food, because they cause flatulence and the dreams become tumultuous. The flowers of **phaseli** <note>A type of bean, likely the kidney bean or black-eyed pea.</note> are multi-colored, as is the fruit; for they are reddish, honey-colored, speckled with various spots, and black. When eaten, they cause bloating and produce "brutish" and terrifying dreams, just like lentils. The **garden smilax** <note>Likely a species of bindweed or morning glory.</note> is of the same kind, with similar flowers and fruit; Dioscorides wrote that it causes tumultuous dreams. The **smooth smilax** produces a black fruit in the manner of a lupine; they say that when its seed is drunk with **dorycnium** <note>A plant often identified as a type of nightshade or convolvulus.</note>, using three obols of each, varied and tumultuous dreams appear, according to Dioscorides. **Pycnocomon** <note>A plant identified by later botanists as a species of *Leonurus* or scabious.</note> consists of a seed like that of a leek and a black or pale root; its seed, drunk to the weight of a drachm, causes heavy dreams. The **headed leek** causes bloating and tumultuous dreams through its black seed. **New wine** causes flatulence, especially the black variety, and stirs up heavy dreams. Conversely, we know that peaceful and cheerful dreams are produced by **melissa** <note>Lemon balm.</note>, which has a white flower and is fragrant and pleasant to the taste.

But the **tamarisk** <note>original: *myrica*</note> causes true dreams. We read in the *Theriaca* of Nicander <note>A 2nd-century BC Greek poet and physician.</note> that Apollo decreed the tamarisk should announce future things to mortals; for this reason, he calls this remarkable shrub a <term>mantin</term> <note>original: *μαντιν*, meaning a seer or prophet</note>. Indeed, the Magi of the Scythians prophesy using tamarisk wood; for in many places, the black varieties portend things, as Dion confirms in the first book of his *Third Composition*. In Lesbos, Apollo holds tamarisk branches, for which reason he is also surnamed "Myriceus"; and Archaeus records that once that God appeared in dreams adorned with a tamarisk branch. The Egyptians are crowned with tamarisk in the procession of Jove, as are the Magi among the Medes. But it was believed by all that the **laurel** <note>The bay leaf tree (*Laurus nobilis*).</note> is sacred to Apollo, the god of prophecy, and possesses a certain foreknowledge of future events. Claudian says:

->,, the laurel, foreknowing of what is to come.<-

For this reason, if laurel leaves are placed under one's pillow at night, they bring about the truth of dreams, a fact which Fulgentius <note>A 5th-century Latin mythographer.</note> did not omit. The commentator on Hesiod's *Theogony* also writes that the laurel is an effective aid in divine inspiration. There is a passage from Tibullus concerning the Sibyl:

> I sing truths; thus may I ever eat the sacred laurels 
> Unharmed, and may my virginity remain eternal.

And the Latin poet also said:

->,, and he bit the laurel.<-

Dionysius, in his account of panegyrics, calls the laurel a <term>mantikon phyton</term> <note>original: *μαντικὸν φυτὸν*, meaning a prophetic plant</note>, and Aphthonius testifies that the laurel is a symbol of divination; Eustathius notes that a person prophesying is often called a <term>daphnephagon</term> <note>original: *δαφνηφάγον*, meaning a laurel-eater</note>. He writes that the laurel was the crown of Apollo, which Chryses <note>A priest of Apollo in Homer's *Iliad*.</note> brought with him when coming to the Greek army, by which the gods were compelled either to retreat or approach. There are also verses added by Porphyry:

> Loosen the garlands, and sprinkle the feet with flowing waters,
> And take away the branch from the hand, the green laurels.

The commentator on Aristophanes says that priests and diviners are crowned with laurel because it is the badge of their craft.

->VINOUS PLANTS AND VINOUS ANIMALS CAUSE<-
->drunkenness, while watery ones ward it off.<-
->Chapter VII.<-

Nature demonstrates that there are certain plants that smell of wine and inebriate; so too there are animals that become intoxicated by wine, such that they can be called "drunkards." Their parts, when given to drink—especially those parts that crave wine—render a human being drunk. In the same way, things born in the water, being enemies of wine, make a person sober. We shall begin with the plants. There are indeed vinous plants...

# PHYTOGNOMONICS
<margin>Page 278</margin>

Plants that smell of wine, such as the **pear**, **hops**, **evening primrose** <note>Original: *onothera*. Literally "wine-seeker," often identified as evening primrose or willowherb.</note>, and others, seize the senses, impede the stride, slow the tongue, and bring on the vice of drunkenness. **Theophrastus's evening primrose**, which is the same as **Dioscorides's rhododendron** <note>Likely the oleander or rosebay willowherb.</note>, has roots that smell like wine; it intoxicates and tames all wild beasts. The fruit of the **mandrake** is black, with a certain flavor of wine; it induces drunkenness and deep sleep. They ascribe the same effect of cheerfulness to **elecampane** <note>Original: *helenium*.</note>, which has a very sweet and wine-like juice, if its roots are drunk in wine; they say it is the **Nepenthe** <note>A legendary drug of forgetfulness mentioned in the Odyssey.</note> praised by **Homer**, by which all sadness is abolished, according to **Pliny**. Wine is pressed from the fruit of the **lotus**; but they say it does not last beyond two or three years. The fruit is so sweet that it gave its name to a people and a land; it is so hospitable to strangers that it makes them forget their homeland, and if eaten in large quantities, it is said to represent a state of drunkenness. They tell a fable that a **Nymph** was turned into a tree of her own name <note>The water lily, *Nymphaea*.</note> while fleeing from **Priapus** who sought to embrace her, implying that **Venus** follows **Bacchus** <note>Meaning that lust follows wine.</note>. Many types of wine were made from plants. The **Adipsos** is a palm with the scent of a quince and the fruit of a caper, which **Pliny** calls the **myrobalan**; it is gathered a little before it begins to ripen, and what is left is called the **phoenician date** <note>Original: *phœnicobalanos*.</note>, which intoxicates those who eat it. Among animals, the **monkey** is intoxicated by wine, and once drunk, it is captured, according to **Athenaeus**. The heart of a monkey, roasted and dried and drunk to the weight of a drachm with old mead <note>Original: *melicratum*.</note>, strengthens the heart, increases its sharpness and boldness, and dispels faint-heartedness and palpitations, according to **Rhazes**, which are the natural effects of drunkenness. The **elephant** is intoxicated by drinking wine; **Athenaeus**, citing **Aristotle's** book on drunkenness, says the elephant is a creature calmed by drinking barley beer <note>Original: *zythum*.</note>. **Aelian** notes that for an elephant about to fight in war, a use of wine made not only from vines but even from rice is permitted; and according to **Plutarch** and **Dioscorides**, ivory soaked in beer is rendered workable for any task. **Simeon Sethi** reported that elephant bones macerated for some time in beer soften like wax; **Seneca** says that **Democritus** was the inventor of such a device. Ivory, by its own substance, strengthens the heart, according to **Sylvius**. We have seen **dogs** also become intoxicated by wine; the earwax of a dog mixed with wine intoxicates immediately, as **Albertus** reports from **Rhazes**, but in **Rhazes** it reads: if you give someone wine to drink in which ticks <note>Original: *ricini*.</note> have been infused, you will intoxicate them. The **leopard** loves wine and is captured when drunk. **Oppian** describes the method most elegantly: as soon as they notice a small spring in **Libya** where leopards usually drink at dawn, the hunters bring many jars full of sweet wine. After they have poured this into the spring, they sit nearby covered with blankets, for they can hide themselves with nothing else. The leopards, burning with thirst, approach the spring, and as soon as they have satisfied their thirst with the drink of wine (which they are very fond of), they first play by dancing, then gradually falling asleep they are stretched out on the ground; thus, sleeping heavily, they are captured with no trouble. If the scent of leopard fat is inhaled while it is roasting, it causes a spinning of the head, as in drunkenness, according to **Rhazes**. However, aquatic animals, or those that seem to hate wine, ward off drunkenness. **Wild boars** are haters of wine; the lung of a boar or a pig, roasted and eaten while fasting on that day, wards off drunkenness, according to **Pliny**. **Livestock** dread wine from afar; the roasted lung of livestock, taken beforehand, wards off drunkenness, according to **Pliny**. **Paul the Venetian** <note>Marco Polo.</note> records that the **unicorn** <note>Original: *monoceros*. In this context, likely a rhinoceros.</note> wallows in the mud like a pig; it is a wild and solitary beast. The **King of the Indians**, drinking from a cup made of a unicorn's horn, when asked why he did so, replied that this drink removes drunkenness, according to **Apollonius**. The **lion** is a wild and solitary beast; its dung drunk in wine with a measure of **wild carrot** <note>Original: *daucus*.</note> makes one loathe wine, according to **Rhazes**. **Eels** are born in the water, and if they are suffocated in wine, and anyone who indulges too much in pure wine drinks from it, he is offended by the smell and will become abstemious. The **green frog** also induces a loathing of wine among those things that live in water, if they are suffocated in wine.

# NOISY AND LOUD ANIMALS PREVAIL OVER DEFECTS
## of the voice. Chapter VIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' with scrolling floral patterns.</image-desc>

So, loud animals and those of a clear voice, being talkative and noisy, can bestow and impress loquacity and a clear voice upon a person if served to them as food, even if they were as silent and of as little speech as **Harpocrates** <note>The Greek god of silence, adapted from the Egyptian child-god Horus.</note>. A melodic animal, the **poultry cock**...

# BOOK SEVEN

...[continued from previous page] linaceus, from Cicero. Lucretius, in his work *On the Nature of Things* <note>Original: *de co.*, likely referring to *De rerum natura*.</note>, writes:

> Nay, even the rooster when he flaps his wings at night, 
> Is accustomed to summon the Dawn with his clear cry. 
> <note>Original: "Quin etiam gallus nocte expandentibus alis, / Auroram clara consuetum voce vocare."</note>

Nature created the **rooster** to rouse mortals to their work and to break their sleep, just as she created **dogs** for the daytime. **Avicenna** stated that the meat of hens brings clarity to the voice. **Elluchafen** <note>Also known as Ibn Butlan, an 11th-century Arab Christian physician.</note> said that soft-boiled eggs clarify the voice. **Galen** taught that soft-boiled eggs should be given to those who need to break up humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids thought to govern health.</note> trapped in the chest and lungs, and they are used by those whose throats have become roughened by shouting or by the sharpness of a bodily humor. **Cranes** are noisy creatures. They elect a leader to cry out while the others sleep; **Aristotle** notes that while flying, they take turns placing individuals at the rear of the line to call out and keep the flock together with their voice. When they descend to the ground, the leader cries out loudly so that all may gather and feed together; if he becomes hoarse from too much shouting, another is substituted. Lucretius refers to this:

> ...as the cry of cranes, when 
> It is scattered high in the airy clouds of the South Wind. 
> <note>Original: "...gruum, quum / Clamor in ætherijs dispersus nubibus Austri."</note>

**Simeon Sethi** <note>An 11th-century Byzantine Jewish philosopher and physician.</note> says that crane broth clarifies the voice. **Ducks** are loud and clamorous, and they cry out in flocks even while eating; following the nature of geese, duck meat clarifies the voice. **Serapio** says the same, citing **Aben Mensuai** <note>Masawayh, a Persian physician.</note>, as did Avicenna. The **swallow** is strong in song, according to **Aelian**, but it does not sing when in distress, as **Plato** says. It is a talkative bird, announcing the day by singing beforehand; as soon as they return in the spring, they seem to applaud and congratulate themselves on finding their old nests with a wonderful, varied, and almost articulate song. Its ashes, drunk with honey-water <note>Original: *mellicrato*. A mixture of honey and water, sometimes fermented.</note>, heal hoarseness. The **dog** barks, and terrifies most with its voice. **Virgil** writes:

> ...the barking of dogs rages toward the breezes. 
> <note>Original: "saeuit canum latratus ad auras."</note>

Lucretius calls their sound "yelping" <note>Original: *baubatus*.</note>. A "snarl" <note>Original: *gannitus*.</note> is a soft growling, while "howling" <note>Original: *vlulatus*.</note> is when they emit a mournful and complaining cry. **Ovid** writes:

> And in the forum, around the houses, and the temples of the Gods, 
> The nocturnal dogs howled. 
> <note>Original: "Inq; foro, circum domos, & templa Deorum / Nocturnos ululasse canes."</note>

Indeed, dogs have many voices. Aristotle, in his *Physiognomonics*, said that dogs are very clamorous and talkative; hence **Rhases** <note>Al-Razi, a Persian polymath.</note> claims that if someone drinks wine into which a stone bitten by a dog has been thrown, they will be compelled to cry out. **Bears** are rabid and noisy; while hiding, the bear sucks its feet with a certain murmuring sound. **Alexander** <note>Likely Alexander of Tralles.</note> believes the brain of bears is a poison in Spain, and the heads of those killed in spectacles are burned, under oath, because if drunk in urine it drives one to madness. According to **Pliny**, the **nightingale** produces a talkative song for fifteen continuous days and nights without intermission; it is a marvel that such a great voice exists in such a small little body, and such a persistent breath. All those qualities which human art has devised in so many exquisite pipe organs are contained within such tiny throats. They compete among themselves, and the contest is openly spirited; the vanquished often ends its life in death, its breath failing before its song. Truly, among birds, none soothes and cheers the ears more sweetly with a most delightful song. According to Pliny: if someone swallows the heart of a nightingale while it is still palpitating, mixed with honey, and carries another heart of the same bird along with its tongue, they will be sweet of speech, possessed of a sonorous voice, and will be listened to gladly. This is from the *Cyranides* <note>A famous ancient compendium of magico-medical lore.</note>. Pliny also mentions the **Eriphia** <note>Possibly a type of plant or a legendary creature associated with a kid goat.</note>; this contains a beetle in the oats that runs up and down with the sound of a kid goat, from which it took its name. He reports that nothing is superior to this for the voice. The **Calcophonos** <note>Literally "brazen-voiced."</note> is a black stone, but it gives off the ringing sound of brass; it should be worn by tragic actors, according to Pliny, because it produces an excellent voice.

### ANIMALS THAT SPEAK AT NIGHT FORCE HUMANS TO SPEAK IN THEIR SLEEP. Chapter VIIII.

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial 'N' featuring foliate and floral vine patterns.</image-desc>
**Night-speaking** birds, specifically those that are awake at night and are exceedingly talkative, can provoke humans to speak at night by placing their tongues on the chest above the palpitation of the heart. This is especially effective on women, since they are considerably more talkative, by communicating the bird's own quality to them and forcing them to reveal secrets they have committed during the day. **Examples.** The **Eagle-owl** <note>Original: *Bubo*.</note>, a genus of nocturnal bird, howls and cries at night and is rarely seen during the day; because of this, they say that its heart, placed upon the left breast of a sleeping woman, ensures that she will pronounce all her secrets, according to **Pliny**. The **Little owl** <note>Original: *Noctua*.</note>, like the eagle-owl, sings and keeps watch at night, according to **Rhazes**. If the large heart of a little owl is placed over the left breast of a sleeping woman, she will confess the good or bad things she has done. **Frogs** are talkative at night in the summer, as we have said. **Democritus** indeed reports that if someone extracts the tongue of a living frog without any other part of the body adhering to it, and after the frog is released back into the water, places that tongue over the heartbeat of a sleeping woman, she will answer truthfully to whatever he asks, according to Pliny. The **Goose**, as we have said, observes nocturnal watches, and constantly testifies to its vigils with its song. If anyone cuts out the tongue of a living goose and places it upon the body of a sleeping man or woman, they will confess everything they have done, according to the ***Cyranides*** <note>Original: *Kirannide*; an ancient book of magical and medicinal properties of stones, plants, and animals.</note>. No bird sings when it is afflicted by cold, hunger, or other distress—not even the nightingale or the swallow—but the **hoopoe** <note>Original: *vpupa*.</note> is said to sing as if mourning out of grief, as **Plato** said in the *Phaedo*. The hoopoe is persistent with its single voice in the spring. **Euax** <note>A legendary king of the Arabs to whom a treatise on gems was attributed.</note> reports that a stone is sometimes found in the nest of a hoopoe which they say betrays secrets and promotes visions when placed on the chest of a sleeper.

***

### SILENT ANIMALS BESTOW SILENCE. Chapter X.

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial 'C' with foliate decorations and a small mask-like face at the center.</image-desc>
**Conversely**, the silent animals and those with few songs, which we have mentioned, can also provide silence <note>Original: *taciturnitatem*.</note> to a human. One may connect these examples: The **wolf**, even though it is a wild dog, lacks a bark; howling is proper to wolves, according to **Varro**, and especially during hunger. A man whom they see first becomes silent; if he is anticipated by the sight of the harmful beast, even if he has the will to shout, he lacks the use of his voice, according to **Solinus**, citing Pliny and Plato. There is a **reed-frog** <note>Original: *rana calamitis*.</note> which lives among reed-beds and herbs; it is mute and without a voice. **Nicander**, in his *Theriaca*, calls this little green frog deaf and mute; they say that if this is thrown into a dog's mouth, it renders the dog mute. **Apuleius** writes: "And from the mouth of the shepherd's dog leaped a little green frog." The **toad** <note>Original: *Rubeta*.</note> is a silent animal, and even in being killed it preserves its silence; authors treat many things concerning it with great rivalry, claiming that if it is brought into a crowd, silence falls. The **chameleon** is without a voice; its tongue, when carried, makes enemies fall silent, according to Greek sources. The **tortoise** is mute, and among the ancients it was a symbol of secrecy and silence; for this reason, **Phidias** made a statue of Venus for the people of Elis which stepped upon a tortoise, demonstrating more covertly and intricately that it is becoming for women to guard the home and keep silence. I remember reading that a tortoise given to a noisy **hawk** renders it mute, though this has not yet been tested in a human.

***

### THE STRONGEST ANIMALS STRENGTHEN THE HUMAN HEART AND INCREASE FEROCITY. Chapter XI.

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial 'R' with acanthus-style leaf decorations.</image-desc>
**Robust** and fierce animals provide that same ferocity and robustness to a human, rendering them invincible by strengthening the heart and increasing the spirits. But those animals are fierce, robust, and very hot which have a small heart, because of this continually...
