# BOOK SEVEN.

...they suffer from continuous fever, those parts of which induce spirit and ferocity. **The lion** is the strongest and most noble of beasts, being so extremely hot and dry that it is afflicted by a continuous **quartan fever** <note>original: "quartana febre"; a fever that returns every fourth day, historically associated with a "melancholic" or "dry" temperament</note>, even if it seems to enjoy health; and unless the force of this disease restrained it, it would be far more deadly to us, according to **Phile**. **Aesculapius** records that those suffering from hallucinations <term>phantastics</term> are healed by the meat of a lion, if the heart is strengthened by removing the phantasms and melancholy and by gladdening it, according to **Sextus**. **Dioscorides** says that lion's fat used as an **amulet** <note>original: "amuleti"</note> protects against those lying in wait; **Pliny** adds that it seems to resist plots. Similar powers are promised from the tooth, especially from the right side, and the whiskers from the lower snout. 

A composition of the **natural Magicians** <note>Practitioners of "natural magic," the study of the hidden properties of nature</note> to render one invincible includes the tail and head of a **dragon**, the hair from the forehead of a lion and its marrow, the foam of a winning horse, and the claws of a dog, all tied together in deer-hide with alternating sinews of a deer and a gazelle. **The hawk** has a small heart, is extremely warlike, and suffers from fever. The **Egyptians** consider it sacred to the **Sun**; they say its nature consists of blood and spirits. It wages war with the **eagle**, the strongest of birds, so that even while the hawk is resting, the fowler's work is done. The meat of hawk chicks strengthens the spirit and resists melancholy and distress, according to **Rabbi Moses** <note>Maimonides</note>. Its heart, when worn, strengthens the heart and preserves the wearer. 

**The hunting dog**, though robust, has a small heart and is an extremely dry animal, so much so that it suffers from **rabies**. The **Indian** dogs are especially robust, as is also held by **Aristotle** in his *Physiognomonics*. **Plutarch** says that dogs were kept away from the gods on the Athenian island, not because they mated in the open, but because they are robust and pugnacious animals. The composition of the natural Magicians to make one unconquerable includes the claws of a hunting dog. 

There are also **dragons** in Ethiopia thirty paces in length, which they call "elephant-killers," and they carry on heavy enmities with the **elephant**. They surround it with a wonderful winding embrace, for each animal has a marvelous cleverness for its own sake. The dragon, having watched the path to the feeding grounds, hurls itself from a high tree; the elephant knows the struggle is unequal for him, and soeks to rub against the knots of the trees; the dragon avoids this, and for that reason binds the elephant's legs with its tail. The elephant undoes the knots with his trunk <note>original: "manu," literally "hand," but used for an elephant's trunk</note>, but the dragon hides its head in the elephant's very nostril, simultaneously blocking its breath and tearing at its softest parts; they are often found dead together. The aforementioned composition includes the tail of a dragon. 

And although **the hyena** has a very large heart, as **Aristotle** records, it overcomes the largest and strongest animals through its cunning and great ferocity. It hates the **leopard** <note>original: "pardalim"</note> with a hostile passion, such that if the skins of a hyena and a leopard are mixed together, the leopard skin loses its hair. Therefore, the Egyptians, wishing to signify the superior being conquered by the inferior, paint two skins—one of a hyena and the other of a leopard, according to **Horus** <note>Horapollo, author of a treatise on hieroglyphics</note>. They are a source of terror especially to **panthers**, so that they do not even attempt to resist, and anyone carrying a piece of hyena skin will not be attacked. Horus further writes that if someone wraps themselves in a hyena skin, they may pass through the midst of enemies intrepidly and without harm; hence, by Egyptian hieroglyphic reasoning, a painted hyena skin is held as a sign of fearlessness and constancy in calamities. 

**The horse** has a small heart with a bone inside it, according to Aristotle; it is a warlike and spirited animal, and very often seized by fever. The foam of a winning horse is also included in the same composition. **Ovid**, in his *Halieutica*, describes the nature of the horse:

> *This is the noble honor and greater glory of horses:*
> *For they take the palm in their spirits, and rejoice in triumph,*
> *Whether they earned the crown in seven laps of the circus,*
> *Do you not see how much more sublimely the victor*
> *Attolls his high head, and sells himself to the breeze of the crowd?*

**The vulture** has a small heart; it is a rapacious and carnivorous bird, fighting with the hawk and with every kind of bird. It can do the same things as the eagle and the hawk, but more effectively. Its claws, burnt and dissolved in old wine, then smeared over the whole body and drunk, contribute greatly to victory over enemies, according to the **Kyranides** <note>An ancient book of magico-medical properties</note>. **The eagle** has a small heart; it is a violent animal, held in the greatest honor and possessing the greatest strength as the queen of birds, spirited and proud against dragons and men...

PHYTOGNOMONICA

...any other animal fights with wondrous spirit even to the danger of death: it does all that a vulture can, but more effectively. **Roosters** have a very small heart, yet they are extremely pugnacious, haughty, and persistent in battles. Nature has bestowed a certain privilege upon them, for among birds, it alone wears a crest like a helmet, and has spurs on its feet, and spreads the feathers around its neck and throat like a mane when about to fight. When it enters a doorway, even if the top is very high, it still bows its head; this is caused by pride, lest its crest be struck anywhere. When it is the victor in a fight, it carries itself insolently, both with the prominence of its eyes and its uplifted neck, as well as with the straining of its song, and it acts like one celebrating a triumph. It is a terror even to the **lion**, the most noble of wild beasts, and the **basilisk** <note>A legendary serpent said to kill with a glance; it was a common belief that the rooster's crow was fatal to it</note> fears both its appearance and its voice; for according to **Aristotle, Athenaeus, Eustathius, and Aelian**, the basilisk dies in convulsions [upon hearing it]. Its brain increases the substance of the [human] brain and sharpens the senses, according to **Simeon Sethi**. In its stomach is found a stone called the **alectorian** <term>alectorius: a mythical stone, often described as clear or crystal-like, supposedly found in the gizzards of old roosters</term>; when carried in the mouth, it renders one invincible and steadfast, and they claim that **Milo of Croton** <note>A famous ancient Greek wrestler known for his incredible strength</note> used it in his matches to remain undefeated. Against adversaries, **Rhazes** <note>An influential Persian physician and polymath</note> advises that a rooster's spur taken from the right leg is effective. The crest of the head, carried with a grain of frankincense and a stag's horn, removes every **evil eye** and fear, and renders the wearer intrepid.

## *THE STRONGEST ANIMALS ARE EFFECTIVE AGAINST NIGHT-*
## *terrors.* Chapter XII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring scrolling vine and floral motifs.</image-desc>
There are also **night terrors** which especially afflict sleeping children, regarding which the care of physicians ought not to be slow or negligent; we have discovered through no vain conjecture that noble and intrepid animals are effective against them. The **Rooster**, as we have said, is pugnacious and fearless: the schools of physicians proclaim that its crest, when worn, works against night terrors. The **Eagle**, the tyrant of birds and mighty in war, can do what the vulture does; its beak, when worn with the tongue, renders night journeys safe and puts to flight demons and phantasms, according to **Scicus**. The **Hawk** can do the same as the vulture and eagle; it resists melancholy and distress. The **Hyena** fights with dogs and men; it is insidious and malicious, and if it lacks strength, it prevails through cunning. Against night terrors and the fear of shadows, it is said by **Rhale** that one of its large teeth tied with linen provides relief. The **Lion** is most spirited; according to the testimony of **Sextus**, its flesh frees a person from phantasms. The **Bear**, trusting in its own strength, attacks not only deer but also sows and bulls in open warfare; they exhaust them by the weight of their bodies hanging from their mouths, horns, and feet; nor is the "folly" of any other animal more tolerable in its mischief, according to **Pliny** citing **Aristotle**. The right eye of a bear, dried and hung upon children, removes from them the fears by which they are troubled in dreams. The **Dolphin** has much strength in its tail: it is very strong and fights with the *amia* <note>original: "amiis"; likely a type of tuna or Mediterranean fish</note> and overcomes them; it also kills **crocodiles** in the Nile, as Pliny relates. The crocodile is soft in its belly and has thin skin; therefore, the dolphins dive as if terrified, and coming up beneath them, they cut the crocodiles' bellies with their dorsal spines. A dolphin's tooth, when tied [to the body], removes sudden fears. The **Lamia** <note>A term often used in Renaissance natural history for the Great White Shark or similar large, predatory fish</note>, a man-eating fish, is a voracious creature armed with sharp teeth and a vast, wide-gaping maw, such that it might swallow a man in armor; its teeth, hung from the necks of children, ward off fears. **Rhazes** says that **skinks** <note>Small lizards, often used in medieval pharmacology</note> are beneficial for children who are afraid in their sleep. But the Arabs often use the name of the **crocodile** for the skink, both the land and aquatic varieties. For the crocodile is a most fierce and ready enemy, insidious, deceitful, and armed with very strong teeth. The **Salamander** extinguishes fire by its touch, in no other way than ice does; Pliny said it has such great coldness, as did **Theophrastus** and **Nicander**. The heart of a salamander, when worn, provides security from fire, and according to the **Greeks**, renders one bold against flames and incapable of being burned.

BOOK SEVEN

## **Angry animals make men angry, and gentle ones make them gentle.** Chapter XIII.

In the same way, angry animals make men angry, and gentle ones make them gentle. We call those animals "angry" which are excessively prone to every kind of outburst. The **bear** is savage by nature, according to **Adamantius** <note>A 4th-century physician and author of a treatise on physiognomy</note>. Poets call them savage and fierce. Persian bears rage beyond all madness, according to **Ammianus Marcellinus** <note>A 4th-century Roman soldier and historian</note>. **Ovid** wrote:

> What is it but a sluggish weight, and the stupid ferocity of a mind? <note>original: "Quid nisi pondus iners, stolidaq; ferocia mentis?" from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*</note>

They believe the brain of bears to be a poisonous substance, as we have said, so that it may drive one into a "bear-like madness," according to **Pliny**. The **lion** is angry, hot, and dry; its brain, if ingested, induces a stupor of the mind, according to **Rhazes** <note>A 9th-century Persian physician and philosopher</note>. The **deer**, on the contrary, is a gentle animal, devoid of anger and peaceful. Deer teeth tied with the skins of roe-deer using deer tendons make masters gentle and the powerful exorable <note>capable of being persuaded by entreaty</note>, according to **Pliny**.

## **How our ancestors settled mutual marital quarrels.** Chapter XIV.

Our ancestors thought that remedies could be provided for them from animals that were most fond of marriage, so that spouses who had become hateful to each other might be reconciled. We shall bring forward some examples—not because we believe them to be true or that we approve of such things, but so that we may reveal the reasons why they committed these things to the memory of posterity, lest we think they spoke rashly; so that from these, the mind may transcend to the greater things we intend. **Plotinus**, the greatest of the **Platonists**, reveals the reasons for these things, saying: from the fact that most animals can easily love each other naturally, they infer a reciprocal love in things between themselves; thus the efficacy of the "amatory art" was born, using certain filters and enchantments <note>The author uses "fascinationibus" to refer to charms or spells</note>, while they apply things to be touched, reconciling some natures to others, having an implanted love, and coupling one soul to another, just like those who join distant palms together. But I think these things are true only in the way that the mutual love of palms is joined by the knots of little cords. 

But let us look at the examples. **Doves** love each other so much that the female does not admit the male unless he has first kissed her, according to **Aristotle, Aelian, and Pliny**. Doves do not allow their mates to copulate with others, nor do they desert the marriage entered into from their very first birth, unless one becomes a bachelor or a widow. During the birth, the male is present and performs every duty and care; the male strikes the female if she goes too slowly to the nest and forces her to enter; when she has laid eggs, he forces her to sit on them, and they both incubate them in turn—the male by day, the female by night. They are most chaste regarding adultery, for never is the male separated from the partnership they established together, unless by death itself, nor is the female dissociated unless she becomes a widow, according to **Aelian**. But if, seized by an immodest love, they cast the eyes of lust toward another's Venus <note>Meaning toward another's sexual charms</note>, the rest of the birds sitting around them—the males indeed for the males, and the females for the females—tear them to pieces. **Aristotle, Eustathius, Aelian, Athenaeus, Oppianus, Pliny**, and other authors compete to hand down many facts about the mutual love and marriage of doves, and they read of remedies for inducing love in these authors. 

**Kingfishers** <term>Alcyones: mythical birds identified with kingfishers, believed to have such a strong bond that the sea calmed for them to nest</term> are so fond of marriage that they stay together and admit mating not just at one time, but at any time of the year; for they do not mix with any others, but live for the sake of conjugal benevolence, which befits a bride, and for the study of friendship, according to **Plutarch**, who calls them the wisest and most divine of sea animals. What doves shall we compare to them regarding the love of a husband? If the husband dies, the female, abstaining from all food and drink, mourns for a long time and wastes away. You will find many things from both birds pertaining to benevolence and against sedition and enmities. **Crows** do not establish a society rashly, yet once they have entered it, they maintain mutual faith between themselves...

PHYTOGNOMONICA

...lovingly. **Aelianus** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author who wrote "On the Nature of Animals"</note> teaches regarding marital love that they should spend their whole life in harmony with mutual love. **Swallows** love one another, and in raising their children, the male as much as the female labor with the greatest fairness. A love potion <note>original: "philtrum"</note> for love may be made from swallow chicks enclosed in a jar and roasted. But **Nicolaus Myrepsus** <note>A 13th-century Byzantine physician known for his medical compendium</note> suggests this so that a woman does not depart from her husband, and a woman may no longer think of any other man. In the bellies of swallow chicks, pebbles are found of a white or reddish color, which are called **swallow-stones** <note>original: "chelidonii"</note>; according to **Pliny**, these are suitable for the arts of lovers. **Mares** are most lustful and fond of males: they are the only animals (except for women) who permit mating while pregnant; they lack the "cleansing" <note>menstruation</note> which is as necessary to women as mating is to males, and if you prevent the females from mating when they desire it, they are driven by the furies of lust. From this comes the name given to a poison, **hippomanes** <note>literally "horse-madness"</note>, because it ignites a love in mortals similar to the desire of horses. **Columella** <note>A 1st-century writer on Roman agriculture</note> says: At the time of mating, they emit a fluid from their genitals similar to seed, which some call *hippomanes*. **Virgil** wrote:

> *From this, finally, the hippomanes, which the*
> *shepherds call by its true name, trickles slowly from the groin.* <note>original: "Hinc demum hippomanes verò quod nomine dicunt / Pastores, lentum distillat ab inguine virus" from Virgil's Georgics</note>

**Aristotle** said this was sought specifically for love-poisons. When a mare has given birth, she immediately devours the afterbirth, and also that which adheres to the forehead of the newborn foal, called *hippomanes*; it is smaller than a small dried fig, somewhat broad in appearance, circular, and black (**Solinus** <note>A 3rd-century Latin grammarian</note> says it is tawny). If someone takes this away and presents the scent, the mare is excited and goes mad upon recognizing the odor; for this reason, it is sought by sorcerers. Regarding this, **Pliny** says: A love-poison born in horses is brought forth, called *hippomanes*, on the forehead, the size of a dried fig and black in color, which the mother devours immediately after birth, otherwise she will not admit the foal to her udders; the scent of it drives that species into a madness. **Aelianus** says it has the power of alluring one to lust and exciting the flame of love, and for that reason, out of "raging envy," the mare does not permit a human to have these charms. He says shepherds know this: if they ever need to remove love-traps from someone, or if they wish to inflame them toward the passion of Venus, they diligently observe when the mare gives birth, and immediately after the birth, they cut it from the foal and place it in the mare's hoof. Thus, whoever tastes that flesh through such a trick is held most tightly by a cast-off and headlong amorous lust; they go mad and rave wildly. **Hesychius** <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian</note> wrote that sorceresses use it for love potions. **Virgil**, in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*:

> *Search is made for the love torn from the forehead of*
> *a newborn horse, snatched away from its mother.* <note>original: "Quæritur, & nascentis equi de fronte reuulsus, / Et matri præreptus amor." In this context, "amor" refers to the hippomanes growth itself.</note>

Animals that are most fond of humans are sought for erotic medicines. The **Wryneck** <note>original: "Iynx," a bird known for its ability to twist its head almost 180 degrees</note> bird turns its neck backwards while the rest of its body remains still; for just as it moves its neck freely forward and backward and twists it in a marvelous way in any direction, so it was said to move the hearts of mortals, to twist their minds, to disturb them, and to move them backward. When a human approaches, it does not flee, but rather is delighted by the sight; for such a slight reason, therefore, it is infamous in sorcery. Indeed, because it was used so anciently for philtres and amorous allurements, they used the word **iynx** to signify longing, desire, enticement, allurement, and whatever might draw the mind to love. **Pindar** <note>An ancient Greek lyric poet</note> used it as a proverb: those who are drawn to something by a vehement and powerless desire are said to be "drawn by the wryneck." **I am drawn in my heart by the wryneck** <note>original Greek: "ἴυγξ ἕλκομαι ἦτορ" (iyngx helkomai etor)</note>; **Theocritus** <note>A Greek poet of the 3rd century BCE</note> has the same. It is said that **Venus** first brought the wryneck down from Mount Olympus to men and gave it to **Jason**, teaching him the arts of incantation so that he might compel the mind of **Medea** to love him. According to the commentator on Pindar, this bird was usually tied to a circle or wheel by sorcerers—two wings at the top and two feet at the bottom—so that it presented the appearance of a four-spoked wheel. Or it was burned entirely with wax over glowing coals; others record its entrails being wound around a wheel; others used the feathers specifically from around the tail, and a bone near the chest of a **lambdoid** <term>labdoyde</term> <note>shaped like the Greek letter Lambda (Λ)</note> shape, similar in appearance to a rider's spur. The neck, which is twisted backward, is said to be useful for other things, but the whole bird is used for love affairs, stretched and revolved upon a wheel...

# BOOK SEVEN.
<meta>catchword: beta</meta>

...turned toward the name of the lover, according to **Johannes Tzetzes** <note>A 12th-century Byzantine poet and grammarian who preserved many ancient traditions</note>. The peacock loves a maiden. **Clearchus** <note>Clearchus of Soli, a student of Aristotle</note> is the author who states in *Leucadia* that a peacock loved a maiden so much that when she died, it died alongside her. It is written that the brain of a peacock is a love potion, and that carrying its heart provides favor and goodwill. The **lizard** <term>lacerta (lizard)</term> is naturally a friend to man; wherever a human is, lizards gather, contemplating the person's face with a tilted head; if you spit, they lick up the saliva—indeed, they even lick saliva when brought to the mouth—and they stand in your way as you walk, following you if you continue. If tired farmers fall asleep in a field and a snake is secretly cast into the open mouth of the sleeper, the lizard—though it is small—saves the man; when it senses the snake lying in wait, it runs all over the face and neck and does not stop until the man wakes. Because of this, **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman encyclopedist</note> writes that the lizard is among the love-charms, specifically when killed in a man's urine. The **Remora** <term>Remora (the "suckerfish")</term>, because it delays ships driven by oars and sails as if they were flying, was believed for that reason to be effective for delaying court cases and for love-sorceries. But who is more loving of man than man himself? Thus **Orpheus** and **Archelaus** write, according to Pliny, that arrows pulled from a body—if they have not touched the ground—are a love-charm when placed under those sleeping.

## ANIMALS AND OTHER THINGS BORN OF THE EARTH
## HAVING MAGNETIC POWER, PRODUCING THE SAME RESULTS.
### Chapter XV.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'N' depicting a woodcut of a man and woman (Adam and Eve) flanking a tree.</image-desc>
With a reasoning no less frivolous than it was empty, when our ancestors saw animals, plants, stones, or other things that had a certain magnetic power of attraction, they thought that this "magnetic" power (if I may call it that) was effective for love-charms, and they established a method for it. **Plotinus** <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism</note> says that magical attractions (including love-charms) occur from a certain consensus of things in their shared experiences, and by a law of acting Nature, so that there is harmony among similar things and discord among dissimilar ones. The true power of magic is friendship in the universe, and conversely, discord. Thus far Plotinus. We shall prove this power with certain examples. A certain power is granted to the **stag** to draw snakes out of caves with its breath, even when they resist, by a generous gift of Nature; for leaning its nostrils into the snake's den and breathing out very forcefully, it draws them out as if luring them with a love-charm, and brings them forth against their will, according to **Aelian** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author of natural history</note>. Having observed this wondrous power, Orpheus writes in his book on stones that a bride should wear stag horn, for in this way there will be perpetual harmony between her and her groom.

> *Leading the young girl into the chambers as a new bride,*
> *Let him bring that stone as a witness of lovely delight:*
> *Indeed, in the face of broken harmonies, he will possess them both*
> *Together through extreme old age and for all their days.*
<note>This verse, attributed to Orpheus, suggests that animal or mineral "witnesses" can heal marital discord and ensure lifelong love.</note>

As if to say, having something of the stag's horn with him, he will be continually loved by women. I suspect there is a very great love-charm in the **elephant**, though not recorded by anyone; for it draws snakes from caves like the stag, and has magnetic power. **Pliny** says: The breath of elephants draws out snakes. The elephant is also captivated by a woman's form, and growing faint at her beauty, it relaxes its mental fury, according to Aelian. One is said to have loved a certain woman in Egypt who sold garlands; and lest anyone think her a common choice, let them marvel that she was pleasing to **Aristophanes** <note>Aristophanes of Byzantium, the famous grammarian of Alexandria</note>. Pliny, following **Plutarch**, says that after the woman departed this life, the elephant—no longer possessing its former habits—was driven mad, just as humans laboring under grief, according to Aelian. Thus others have loved other women. Perhaps the poets hint at this power when they tell the fable of **Pygmalion** <note>The mythical sculptor who fell in love with his own creation</note> making an ivory statue of a maiden, and captured by love for it, obtaining from **Venus** that it be turned into a true, living maiden. He said that those wearing ivory ornaments <term>Spatalia (ivory bracelets or necklaces)</term> about their necks possess the enticements of love. ### PHYTOGN.

The **beet** <term>beta (beet)</term> attracts the **weasel** <term>mustela (weasel)</term>, a marvelous sight, as we have learned from many trustworthy sources, even if it has not yet been recorded in the writings of some of the ancients. The weasel, upon seeing a **bramble toad** <term>rubeta (toad)</term> from the trees, immediately cries out and implores for help; it descends and glides into the mouth of the toad, which waits with its mouth wide and gaping, and then devours it. There is a small bone in the side of the toad which, when moved toward water, makes it appear to boil; the attacks of dogs are restrained by it, and it procures love. Weasels also attract mice, both by entering their holes and by drawing them out, even as they themselves are attracted by toads. **Aelian** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author and teacher of rhetoric</note> relates that the Magi affirm the weasel was nursed by **Hecate** <note>The Greek goddess of magic and witchcraft</note>, because this goddess is employed in love-charms; for its entrails are suited for these things, according to **Volaterranus** <note>Raffaele Maffei, a Renaissance humanist and encyclopedist</note>.

There is also a sorcerous power in the **hyena** to stop a man, as we said regarding the remora. Whatever animal it passes by, the hyena sticks to its tracks so closely that the animal seems unable to move; for this reason, they pronounce that a magical science dwells within it, according to **Pliny** and **Solinus** <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman grammarian and geographer</note>. Its shadow causes dogs to fall silent, according to Aelian. It moves its body toward a sleeping man or dog, and if it senses itself to be larger than the sleeper, it deprives him of his senses and takes away the use of his non-resisting hands. If it turns a man to the right so as to occupy the tracks he has already made, he becomes alienated in his mind and may even fall from his horse. People have generally held the hyena in the greatest admiration among all animals, as they have attributed magical arts to it, and a power by which it allures to itself men who have lost their minds, according to Pliny. Because of this, it is said that the hairs of its snout, when applied to a woman's lips, act as a love-charm, and that the harmony of the entire household is maintained by preserving the hyena’s genitals and a joint of its spine with the skin still adhering. A hollow of the same animal bound to the left side is so potent a love-charm that if one looks back at a woman, she follows immediately—and other things which we willingly omit because they are vain. 

The hyena is like a wild wolf, and they have many things in common, such as their form, their ambushes, and other traits described by **Oppian** <note>A 2nd-century Greek poet known for his works on hunting and fishing</note>; they mate together so that **thos** <term>thoes (likely a jackal or hyena-hybrid)</term> are born. Indeed, a magical power dwells in it, for they say it takes away the voice of a man whom it gazes upon first, as reported by **Plato**, Pliny, and Solinus. They say the snout of an old **wolf** resists witchcraft, and for this reason, they nail them to the gates of farmhouses; the solid skin from the neck is thought to provide the same protection. Indeed, the power of the animal is so great that, besides what we have related, its trodden footsteps bring a numbness to horses. **Horace**, in his book of *Satires* regarding the sorceries of women, says:

> *And how they secretly hid the wolf’s beard,*
> *along with the tooth of a dappled snake, in the earth.*
> <note>original: "Utq; lupi barbam, variæ cum dente colubræ, / Abdiderint furtim terris." (Satires I.8)</note>

Furthermore, a love-poison <term>amatorium virus (amorous fluid or toxin)</term> is commonly thought to exist in the tail of this animal in a small tuft of hair, and it is said to cast it away when captured; it is not effective unless taken from a living animal, according to Pliny and Solinus. 

The attraction of iron to the **magnet** <term>magnes (lodestone)</term> is sufficiently well-known to everyone; for this reason, our ancestors said of them what **Marbodus Gallus** <note>Marbod of Rennes, an 11th-century bishop and author of a famous book on stones</note> relates:

> *She can reconcile husbands to their wives,*
> *And in turn recall the brides to their husbands,*
> *Thus, he who desires to know if his wife is an adulteress,*
> *Should place the stone beneath the head of the sleeper:*
> *Soon she who remains chaste seeks to embrace her husband,*
> *Yet not waking, every adulteress falls from the bed,*
> *As if pushed by a hand.*

For the same stone attracts from one side and repels iron from the other; for this reason, it can allure a wife or reject her from a husband, as we have said. There is also a "fleshy magnet" which attracts flesh, as **Albertus** <note>Albert the Great, the 13th-century philosopher and scientist</note> relates from **Aristotle**. **Amber** <term>succinum (amber)</term> has such a power of attraction that when it has received the power of heat by the rubbing of fingers, it can attract chaff and dry leaves, just as a magnet attracts iron. Pliny says the Syrians call it *harpagas* <note>From the Greek 'harpazo,' meaning to snatch or seize</note> because it snatches up leaves, chaff, and the fibers of clothing. It was also mentioned by the ancients to be effective for love-charms. We shall prove that Pliny's *charitoblepharon* <note>A legendary stone or substance described as "the eyelid of the Graces"</note> is actually amber.

# BOOK SEVEN.

The islands of the **Troglodytes** <note>A name used by ancient geographers for various "cave-dwelling" peoples, here likely referring to those near the Red Sea</note> are said to possess a shrub called **charitoblepharon** <note>original: "charitoblepharon," from the Greek for "graceful eyelids"</note>, which is effective in love charms. Women make bracelets and necklaces from it; it is said to sense when it is being captured, hardening like horn and blunting the edge of iron. However, if the ambush fails, it is said to transfigure into stone. The same author <note>Likely referring to Pliny the Elder</note>, among other opinions of those who speak of where it is born, says: "Asazubas is still living, who reports that near the Atlantic Ocean is a place called Cephisida, which the Moors call **electrum** <term>electrum (amber)</term>. He says that when this is warmed by the Sun, it flows out of the mud as liquid amber." Theomenes says that near the Great Syrtis <note>A coastal region of modern Libya</note> is the Garden of the Hesperides, from which it falls into a pond and is collected by the Hesperian virgins. Pselus stated it is produced in Arabia. Serapio, however, speaking of amber, says it is born under the sea, like mushrooms on the earth; it stands out above the water, is broken by the tide of the sea, and is thus captured. It is called *charitoblepharon*, as if to say "graceful eyelids," because from burnt amber comes a very black smoke, which in ancient times was used to dye and adorn the eyelashes; furthermore, if amber is yielded to, it blunts the edge of iron. It is beneficial for infants to have amber tied to them as an **amulet**, and it protects people of any age against **hallucinations** <term>lymphationes (madness or water-fears)</term>. This fact supports those who have scrutinized hidden natural properties: if you dress one person in an amber garment and another in straw, they are immediately joined together by mutual bonds <note>An early observation of static electricity</note>. **Jet** <term>Gagates</term> is of the same kind; it also attracts straw, and we suspect it is effective for the same purposes.

### THAT PLANTS ARE EFFECTIVE FOR LOVE POTIONS, AND FROM WHAT ARGUMENTS THEY DEVISED THIS. Chapter XV.

<image-desc>A decorative capital 'S' featuring a floral design within a rectangular border.</image-desc>
BUT men have imagined that plants are effective for mutual hatred and love based on far-fetched arguments regarding their form and actions. The Greeks said that **Palms** pursue each other with mutual love; they confirm that females do not bear fruit without males, as seen in groves that grow spontaneously, where several females lean toward a single male with flattering fronds. He, standing erect and bristling, "marries" the others by his breath, his very sight, and even his dust <note>A reference to pollination</note>. They say that if this male tree is cut down, the females afterward become sterile; so great is their "understanding" of Venus <note>The goddess of love</note> that the act of mating has even been devised by man, by sprinkling the females with the flower and down of the males, or sometimes just their dust. In certain fruits, there is a bony, crescent-shaped piece which, when polished, is religiously used as a charm against **the evil eye** <term>fascinantes</term>. Similar to this is what Apollodorus reports grows among the Parthians, called **Philadelphum** <note>original: "Philadelphū," meaning "Brotherly Love"</note> because its branches spontaneously embrace one another at intervals, like lovers; afterward they part, conceive, and give birth. There are also plants which, because of some similarity to our internal organs, or to amorous animals, or to some notable action, have been named "love plants." An example is the **mandrake** <term>mandragora</term>; because it has a split root, spreading like two legs, it was called **anthropomorphos** <note>original: "ἀνθρωπόμορφος," meaning "human-shaped"</note> by Pythagoras, because it shadows the human trunk and limbs. There are two kinds: the "man-bearing" and the "woman-bearing," because the plant displays the buttocks of both sexes, which it shows as distinct; the female is smaller due to the weakness of the sex. Columella alluded to Pythagoras’s naming of the plant:

->Though the mandrake, pregnant with the mad grass<-
->of the half-human, produces flowers.<-

It was once believed most strongly to be effective for love, and was called **Circea**, after the sorceress Circe, the daughter of the Sun, who discovered it. Theophrastus wrote that it was given for love when mixed with wine and vinegar, and Dioscorides reported the same from him. Similar to the previously mentioned **hippomanes** <note>Usually a growth on a foal's head or a discharge from a mare, thought to have aphrodisiac properties</note>, there is a **hippomanes herb** celebrated by Theocritus in his poems on love, in these words:

> The hippomanes is a plant among the Arcadians; after eating it,
> both colts and swift mares go mad throughout the mountains.
> <note>original Greek: Ἱππομανές φυτόν, ἐστὶ παρ’ ἀρκάσι, τῷ δ’ ἐπιπᾶσαι, Καὶ πῶλοι μαίνονται ἀν’ ὤρεα, καὶ θοαὶ ἵπποι.</note>

Theocritus took these things from Hesiod. There are those who disagree with Theocritus, saying that no such plant is found in Arcadia or anywhere else, but that it is a small piece of flesh growing on a horse’s forehead, as we have said. But Crateuas <note>A Greek physician and pharmacologist of the 1st century BCE</note> recognizes the plant, which has fruit like a wild fig, and a dark leaf like a poppy, and is even thorny; he says it is mixed into love poisons...

<meta>This page continues the seventh book's investigation into the "signatures" of plants and animals—the idea that their physical appearance reveals their hidden medicinal or magical properties. ...to be wonderfully powerful. **Asphodel**, called "hundred-headed," is so named because it somewhat mimics the likeness of human testicles. Pliny relates a marvel regarding it: that its root reflects the likeness of one of the two sexes, though it is rare to find. But if a "male" root is found by men, they become lovable; for this reason, Phaon the Lesbian was loved by Sappho <note>A famous Greek lyric poet from Lesbos</note>, a story much celebrated by the Magicians and the followers of Pythagoras. They believe that if it is sown before the gates of a house, it acts as an amulet. Dionysius also distinguished it by sex, finding both male and female forms in it. Crateuas <note>An ancient Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> related that it could end the cravings and desires of Venus <note>Metaphor for sexual desire</note>, yet when taken with wine, it excites them. **Cyclamen**, with its rounded root bulb, skillfully demonstrates the shape of the female womb. Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany" and student of Aristotle</note> said its bulb is effective for love affairs when dug up from the earth, mixed with sweet wine, and shaped into small cakes—much like wine dregs, which wipe away stains. Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and author of the influential "De Materia Medica"</note> recounts the same things about it: when added to wine, it increases sexual vigor and can even cause abortions. **Cotyledon**, or Venus’s Navel <note>Commonly known today as Navelwort</note>, produces a concave, round, smooth leaf like a vinegar-bowl or a woman’s navel; it is thick, fleshy, and succulent. Physicians call it the "navel of luxury." Dioscorides also said it is effective for love affairs. **Great Houseleek** (*Aizoum*) bears leaves at the tip similar to a human tongue, fleshy and fat, shaped in their outline like an eye. Pliny wrote that it is called <term>epigonon</term> <note>original: "epigonon," Greek for "offspring" or "that which reproduces"</note> because it is suitable for love charms.

**Lion’s Leaf** (*Leontopetalon*) produces leaves that turn white with a woolly tuft near the root. Dioscorides records that when worn as an amulet, it is effective for love. We have contemplated this root ourselves: it so resembles a woman’s pubic area growing with downy, soft tufts that we rejoiced at such an insight and similarity. Dioscorides related that **Phyteuma** is so effective for love affairs—perhaps because it bears abundant seeds in each seed-vessel, and being perforated, it would be fit for love and for bearing offspring. Dioscorides says that Thessalian sorceresses <note>original: "tribades," referring to women practitioners of magic or "female-loving women"</note> seek out both types of **Catananche** <note>Commonly called "Cupid’s Dart"</note> for love charms—perhaps because the drying leaf bends toward the ground and contracts into the likeness of the claws of a dead kite. Pliny, mocking this conjecture, says it is gathered for this use only because, when it dries, it contracts itself into the shape of a dead kite's claws. For the same reason, the *lemos* <note>A plant of uncertain identity, possibly a kind of grass</note> is passed over by him in silence. The name *Catananche* was given as if it impelled one to love by a fatal necessity <note>original: "catanance," from the Greek *katanankē*, meaning "compulsion"</note>, or as a necessary enticement of love, as if endowed with bewitching and deceptive powers.

**Staphilinus**, or the parsnip <note>Often referring to the wild carrot (*Daucus carota*)</note>, mimics a human leg or limb. Orpheus said that a love-power resides in the parsnip, perhaps because it is certain that sexual desire is stimulated by this food; therefore, some have reported, following Pliny, that it helps with conception. On the other hand, the ancients said that animals hateful to themselves and all others, and those without offspring, provide the opposite effect; for just as the sight shudders at seeing them, so they make a person hate and be abhorred by everyone. The **Chameleon**—a poisonous, hateful, and deformed animal that lives on no food <note>A common ancient myth that chameleons lived only on air</note>—is said by Pliny to dissolve love charms with its liver. Its intestines and dung, smeared with monkey urine on an enemy's door, win for them the hatred of everyone. The **Toad** (*Rubeta*), an animal foul to look upon and horrible, born from rot, was said by Pliny to end love when tied in a fresh piece of cattle hide. **Mules**, being deprived of the ability to reproduce, are also used to destroy the enticements of love (as we have said), and to cause hatred and the undermining of love. Pliny wrote that the dust in which a mule has rolled, when sprinkled on the body, mitigates the heat of love. If the dung of a mistress is placed in the lover's shoe where he can smell it, the love is dissolved, as this thing is loathsome—a fact cited by Ovid in his book *The Remedy of Love*:

> With that medication your tables smell like Phineus’s,
> Not once has my stomach been moved to nausea.
<note>Ovid is referring to the Harpies, who polluted the table of King Phineus with their foul stench.</note>

### ANIMALS OF SWIFT COPULATION ARE EFFECTIVE FOR THOSE WHO THINK THEMSELVES BOUND BY ANIMALS OF SLOW COPULATION. Chapter XVII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' set in an ornate square frame featuring scrolling floral patterns and a bird (possibly a phoenix) in the center.</image-desc>
There is a **VAIN** belief among foolish and common men that they can be easily "bound" <note>Referring to "ligatio," a traditional folk magic spell intended to cause male impotence</note> by low women so that they become impotent for intercourse; they think this happens through superstitions and whispered empty words, whereas it only arises from natural causes and...

<meta>This page continues the seventh book's exploration of natural "signatures"—the belief that the physical characteristics or behaviors of animals and plants reveal their medicinal and magical uses. # BOOK SEVEN.

The ancients wrote that such things arise from the superstitions of others; let the credit remain with them. We shall bring forward some examples and the reasons that led them to believe these things. To create these effects, they used animals characterized by slow or "bound" mating, selecting those members through which the act is completed. According to Aristotle <note>A foundational Greek philosopher and scientist</note>, animals that experience a bound and lingering mating include the dog, the wolf, and the seal; however, Oppian <note>A Greco-Roman poet known for his works on fishing and hunting</note> mentions turtles and seals. Inquiring into the cause of this, Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>An influential commentator on Aristotle</note> said that the <term>penis</term> <note>original: "coles"</note> swells during sexual use, and because the mouth of the <term>vulva</term> <note>original: "vulvae"</note> is narrow, they are joined together until the sticky and slow-moving seed is instilled into the womb. Wolves mate in the same way. Dogs turn away in the middle of mating and, even against their will, remain stuck together, according to Aristotle. Because of this, they said a man’s <term>virility</term> <note>original: "virga," literally "rod" or "wand"</note> could be "bound" <note>A reference to "magical binding," or causing impotence through spells</note>, and according to Rhazes <note>A celebrated Persian physician and polymath</note>, no binding is more powerful than this. See with what slight persuasion they were driven to write such things! The dog mates in the same way and is bound during the act; because of this, according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic "Natural History"</note>, it was believed to make one more sluggish in the matters of Venus <note>Metaphor for sexual desire or activity</note>. Regarding the seal, nothing has yet been fully explored or handed down by anyone. By the same conjecture, animals that we see have difficulty passing urine are thought to be effective for the retention of urine—so that they do not empty the bladder until they are released—just as we see every day. Dogs pass urine with difficulty and cannot urinate unless a leg is lifted; therefore, Pliny uses dog urine for this purpose, and Rhazes uses the skin of the penis. The wolf has the same property and power; hence, if any animal urinates upon the warm urine of a wolf, it will never conceive, according to Pythagoras <note>The famous Greek mathematician and philosopher to whom many mystical traditions were attributed</note>, though Rhazes says this specifically of a woman. We have already mentioned above that birds are animals of the easiest mating, specifically the **woodpecker** <note>original: "picus martius"</note>; not only because of its ease of mating, but because it "dissolves closures" and thus releases those who are "bound." The common **magpie** <note>original: "pica vulgaris"</note> and similar birds, when eaten roasted or boiled, immediately release those who are bound, as we have experienced many times.

## ANIMALS THAT BEAR THE APPEARANCE OF SHAMEFUL LUST ARE EFFECTIVE AGAINST IT.
<margin>Oppian, 20</margin>
->Chapter XVIII.<-

There are also certain defects contrary to nature to which we believe some animals are subject; and there are some which, although believed to be so by the common people, are not so in reality, for Aristotle rails against those who believe them. But Nature gave us this example to demonstrate to us that such animals are effective against this shameful and infamous "Venus" <note>Referring to perceived sexual deviancy or "softness" of character</note>. Regarding **hares**, as Archelaus <note>A Greek philosopher</note> wrote, both sexes are present in each individual, and they struggle to give birth without a male. Pliny writes that sometimes it is a male, sometimes a female; sometimes it fathers as a male, and sometimes it submits as a female. Among the ancients, the opinion was accepted that those who eat hare appear beautiful for several days. But regarding the **hyena**, it was believed to be a male in some years and a female in others; in truth, this is false. It does not possess the genitals of both male and female at the same time; what is located under the tail resembles a female's genitals but has no internal passage. Nature shows us this, as Pliny wrote—and from him Rhazes and Albertus <note>Albert the Great, a medieval scholar</note>—that the ash of the hair from a hyena's "cavern" <note>referring to the pseudo-genital area</note> smeared with oil onto those who are of a "shameful softness" <note>A historical reference to effeminacy or passive male sexuality</note> causes them to take on not only modest but even severe morals. If the hairs from the anus of a male hyena are burned and ground with pitch and rubbed on the anus of a <term>catamite</term> <note>original: "cynaedi," a term for a male who takes a passive role in sex, often associated with perceived moral vice</note>, he will be freed from that vice.

## CHEERFUL PLANTS AND ANIMALS BRING CHEERFULNESS, WHILE SAD ONES BRING SORROW.
->Chapter XVIIII.<-

There were sad plants with black fruits, flowers, and leaves which, as we have seen, induced melancholy; and there were cheerful ones which, through a kind of intoxication, brought joy and playfulness to our minds. There are also cheerful animals—namely, those that play easily and excel in clownish gestures—which are effective for expelling melancholy and inducing cheerfulness. On the other hand, sad animals induce sorrow and sadness. Nature

# PHYTOGNOMONICA

Nature gave the monkey, that ridiculous animal, a ridiculous soul and a ridiculous bodily constitution; according to Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire</note>, it can be taught any game, delights in playing, and is an animal born for play and imitation. Adamantius <note>A 4th-century physician and writer on physiognomy</note> ascribes a <term>scurrilous</term> <note>original: "scurrile"; meaning clownish or buffoon-like</note> nature and a notable talent for mimicry to the monkey. The heart of a monkey, roasted and dried, when taken as a drink in the weight of a <term>drachma</term> <note>A small unit of weight, roughly 3.4 grams</note> with old <term>honey-water</term> <note>original: "mellicrato"; a mixture of honey and water</note>, strengthens the heart and dispels cowardice and heart palpitations; according to Rhazes <note>A celebrated Persian physician</note>, by expelling melancholy, it induces cheerfulness. It is even devoured by the lion to expel its own melancholy. The magpie, having obtained a singular nature for the imitation of the voice, sometimes imitates the voice of a kid, a sheep, or a calf upon which it sits, as well as the whistle of a shepherd, according to Oppian <note>A Greco-Roman poet</note>. But as the author of *Philomela* <note>Likely a reference to a poetic work about birds</note> says:

> The talkative magpie modulates various voices in its throat,
> ->*Whatever it hears, it repeats with a scurrilous noise.*<-
> <note>original: "Pica loquax varias modulatur gutture voces / Scurrili strepitu quicquid & audit, ait."</note>

It is well established that they may die if defeated by the difficulty of a word they are trying to master; they are cheered in a wonderful way if they happen to hear that word again in the meantime, according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of Natural History</note>. When burned in a sealed earthenware jar and administered in any manner, it is effective against melancholy, according to Arnaldus <note>Arnald of Villanova, a famous medieval physician</note>. Conversely, oxen are melancholic and are cheered by no joke; for this reason, their meat generates melancholy and melancholic diseases, according to Simeon Sethi <note>An 11th-century Byzantine physician</note> and others. The habit and meat of the crow are also melancholic and make a person so disposed; and so it is with the rest, lest we dwell too long on well-known matters.

### ON THE ANTIPATHY AND SYMPATHY OF PLANTS AND
### *animals, and on the singular antipathy of plants.*
->Chapter 20.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'I' set within a square woodcut border featuring foliage and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
AMONG the behaviors of plants and animals, nothing is found more useful, and from which great and marvelous properties of things can be hunted out, than from the hidden <term>consensus and dissensus</term> <note>agreement and disagreement</note> of things, which the Greeks call *antipathy* and *sympathy*. Nothing more admirable can be observed in all of Nature than how one plant or animal dreads another, or how they are bound together as if by treaties struck between them—a thing worthy of an amphitheater spectacle when it occurs. For who could bring forth the cause of such great discord and disagreement, unless Nature promotes this spectacle to move mortals to contemplate and unearth her secrets? So that if one should dread another, the hated thing might be able to heal or repair the defect of the envier. Thus, mutual love and hatred arise from mutual and adverse forces, advantages, or disadvantages; for from similarity comes love and attraction, but from dissimilarity comes disadvantage and flight. Pliny says of this: "It shall be called the peace or war of Nature, the hatreds and friendships of things that are deaf and lack sensation, through which we may admire all these things for the sake of mankind." We provide another reason for this friendship and enmity of plants and animals than what has been handed down so far regarding the cold, the hot, and the dry; for Nature has proposed this spectacle for the contemplation of higher things and the investigation of useful ones. Certain things are made worse by the powers of their juice or odor, just as the cabbage and the laurel offend the grapevine; for they say the vine "smells" and "draws in" <note>attracts</note>, which is why when a sprout is near them, it retreats and turns away, fleeing the enemy odor. Androcides used this example when a remedy against wine was fashioned—namely, from cabbage—to be able to drive away drunkenness, since even vines flee the smell of cabbage, according to Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany," a student of Aristotle</note>. Nestor, in that book titled *Alexicepos* <note>The "Garden-Defender"</note>, writes that the cabbage is the "tear of Lycurgus," which he shed when he was tied to a vine by Father Liber <note>Bacchus/Dionysus, the god of wine</note>; Lycurgus, deterred by the severity of the punishment, had plunged himself into the sea, and from his tears this vegetable was born. Therefore, the vine and the cabbage suffer from such great discord that if this vegetable is planted near a vine in the fields, the vine itself immediately withers, or certainly its branches grow weak and waste away. Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note> records that vineyards in which cabbages also grow produce a weaker wine. The flavor and odor of wine are ruined by cabbage in the vat. The Egyptians, who are great lovers of wine, have a custom of eating cooked cabbage before all other foods to prevent the harm of wine...

### BOOK SEVEN

...stops it: cabbage juice held in the mouth for a long time restrains a swelling <term>uvula</term> <note>original: "vuam"; the fleshy part at the back of the throat, which shares a name with the Latin word for 'grape' (uva). This linguistic connection was often used to justify medicinal links</note> in the throat. So persistent is the enmity between these plants that if the uvula should fall forward due to the force of a <term>fluxion</term> <note>A discharge of fluid or "humors" within the body</note>, or hang too loosely into the throat, if raw cabbage juice is applied to the head, it immediately leaps back up into the high part of the mouth. I have quite often recalled people laboring under this defect from the brink of death with this remedy. If someone should instill even a little wine drop by drop into cabbage boiling in a pot, it will no longer cook at all, but having lost its strength, it is drawn toward ruin. Those who drink much wine, or challenge themselves in drinking contests, prefer raw cabbage before their food so they are not overcome by drunkenness.

The laurel also offends the vine, as we have said according to Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher often called the "father of botany"</note>: for this reason, when the vine’s shoot comes too close, it turns away and moves backward, fleeing the hostile scent. It also heals the uvula, as we said, for leaves boiled in three parts of water restrain the uvula when used as a gargle. The vine also hates the hazel tree; unless it is far away, the vine becomes sad and sickly. Toasted hazelnuts also heal <term>distillations</term> <note>Running of the nose or throat, like a common cold</note> and restore hair to <term>alopecia</term> <note>Patchy hair loss</note>; for those who drink more wine than is right experience baldness and premature graying. Hazelnuts contribute to fatness more than seems likely, and increase corpulence beyond belief; whereas ingested vinegar makes men thin.

Another great miracle of discord occurs: this vegetable [cabbage], by which we said the vine is put to flight, shrivels up in the presence of cyclamen and oregano. Cyclamen put into wine causes drunkenness, according to Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and author of the famous herbal *De Materia Medica*</note>, while cabbage, as we said, is effective against drunkenness. Cabbage generates a black and <term>melancholic juice</term> <note>According to the theory of the four humors, "black bile" caused sadness and depression</note>, according to Simeon Sethi <note>An 11th-century Byzantine doctor</note>. Dried oregano, drunk in the measure of an <term>acetabulum</term> <note>A small Roman liquid measure, about 60ml or a quarter-cup</note> in <term>honey-water</term> <note>original: "aqua mulsa"</note>, draws out black humors through the bowels.

An oak planted next to a walnut tree shrivels up. Eaten acorns produce gas, according to Dioscorides; walnuts given with their shells and applied to the navel soothe <term>tormina</term> <note>Severe griping pains in the abdomen or colic</note>, according to the same author. And although ivy strangles all trees with its embrace and kills them by sucking out all their moisture with its thick juice, it nevertheless offends the vine most of all. It is most hostile to it, opposes wine, and drives away drunkenness. Indeed, the nature of ivy is wonderful for testing the frauds of wine: for if a vessel is made from ivy wood and wine mixed with water is put into it, the wine flows through while the water remains, for an ivy vessel does not hold wine, according to Cato <note>Cato the Elder, a Roman statesman who wrote on agriculture</note>.

People make ivy sacred to Bacchus <note>The Roman god of wine</note>, and especially that kind which is called *Dionysia*, for this reason—indeed, the poets tell the story that the youth Citton, while indulging in leaps and dances before Father Bacchus, was cast down to the earth. The earth, extolling Bacchus with great honors, brought forth a little vine, nourished forever with youthful sprouts and leafy greenness. Nor, as many believe, does it induce drunkenness; rather, it brings harm to those drinking rather than intoxication, as is held by Triphon in the works of Plutarch <note>A Greek historian and essayist</note>. 

<term>Orobanche</term> <note>Commonly known as broomrape, a parasitic plant</note> grows among legumes and strangles them, which is where its name comes from; yet if added to legumes while they are boiling, it makes them cook more easily. The <term>antipathy</term> <note>A natural "hatred" or opposition between two things</note> between hemlock and rue is wonderful; a probable proof of this is that those gathering rue arm their hands with hemlock juice so they are not infested by ruinous ulcers from it, and rue dulls the hemlock's poison, for rue is an antidote against poison. When a weasel is about to fight a snake, it eats rue as if it were some sort of <term>alexipharmacon</term> <note>A protective remedy or antidote against poison</note>. Dioscorides notes that rue is added to extinguish the harms of hemlock; yet rue juice given in larger quantities acts as a poison, which is then extinguished by hemlock juice, so much so that they are the "poisons of poisons."

Limodorus, which we elsewhere called <term>dodder</term> <note>original: "cuscutam"; a parasitic climbing plant</note>, strangles bitter vetch by entangling it, hence the name *orobanche*. Bitter vetch, when the injury of hunger is rampant, is burdensome to the head and stomach, weighs down the knees, makes oxen <term>frenzied</term> <note>original: "cerebrosos"; literally "brainy" or "headstrong," meaning mad or light-headed</note>, and disturbs the bowels. Dodder cleanses <term>pituitous</term> <note>Full of phlegm or mucus</note> veins and unloads the body of bilious humors. The cucumber flees oil so much that if any is in its way, or if it hangs near it, it folds back on itself like a hook; this can be observed in one or two nights. The cucumber excites <term>horrors</term> <note>A medical term for shivering or cold fits, often preceding a fever</note>, while oil is effective against such horrors.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of natural antipathies, shifting focus from plants to the animal kingdom. PHYTOGNOMONICA

# ON THE SPECIFIC ANTIPATHY OF ANIMALS.
### Chapter XXI.

We shall bring forward the same examples from the animal kingdom, and we shall see that they possess the same power for remedies. The **moose** <note>original: "Alces"</note> constantly suffers from the falling sickness <note>original: "comitiali morbo"; epilepsy, so named because an attack was considered a bad omen that would dissolve a Roman public assembly, or 'comitia'</note>, and it dreads the **wolf**, so much so that as soon as it sees one, it rushes at it. A wolf's heart, burned, ground up, and taken as a drink, is wonderfully beneficial for epilepsy; and according to Pythagoras, the teeth of a canine wolf liberate a person who has been affected by the Moon <note>A reference to "lunacy" or seizures thought to be triggered by lunar cycles</note>. The **elephant** dreads the **ram**, so much so that if it is acting wild, it grows tame as soon as it sees a ram, and its fury withers away, as is held by Aelian, Plutarch, and Zoroaster in the *Geoponica* <note>A 10th-century collection of agricultural lore</note>. For this reason, it is written that the Romans turned the elephants of Pyrrhus, King of the Epirotes, into flight and brought back victory from that war by using rams. The Egyptians, wishing to signify a King fleeing from foolishness, paint an elephant and a ram, for the former flees when it sees the ram, according to Horus <note>original: "Orus"; likely referring to Horapollo, an author on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>. Because of this, an ointment made from a ram's tongue is used for **elephantiasis** <note>A disease, often a form of leprosy, where the skin becomes thick and bumpy like an elephant’s hide</note>; it prohibits its growth and makes it decrease, according to Avicenna. Also, goat's blood heals **carcinomas** <note>Cancerous growths</note> according to Pliny. For "elephant" is a name given to a type of leprosy, named for its resemblance to the skin of an elephant, with frequent spots over the surface of the body and humors, and the feet and calves swell so that they appear to have the feet of elephants; and just as a cancer affects one part, the "elephant" disease is considered like a cancer of the whole body.

The elephant also dreads the **horned viper** <note>original: "cerastem"</note>—unless Volaterranus has mistakenly translated "horned viper" as "horned goat"—according to Aelian; and it especially dreads the **dragon**, so much so that they fight to the death. Snakes and vipers provide a cure for elephantiasis, according to Dioscorides, Galen, and others. Solitary **dogs** dread **wolves**, and if they are caught by wolves, they are devoured. For this reason, if a wolf skin is worn by someone who has been bitten by a rabid dog, they will not fall into **hydrophobia** <note>literally "fear of water," a primary symptom of rabies</note>, which is a disease peculiar to the dog. The dog fears the **hyena**, for the hyena prepares many snares for it; if it circles a dog three times, the dog stays fixed in its tracks and cannot move, according to Pliny and Solinus. Furthermore, when the Moon's orb is full and the moonlight is behind it, the hyena casts a shadow over the dogs, which makes them mute and binds their senses as if by some sorcery, according to Aelian and Philes. Hyena ash is effective against the bite of a rabid dog, its liver even more so; and its hide spread beneath someone, or even its fat, helps those who are terrified of water. 

The **bear** dreads the **dog**, so much so that the bear's treachery blazes out against it, and it later tears it to pieces. Bear's gall is given with great admiration to those bitten by a rabid dog in the writings of Galen. A bear's skin is placed under those wounded by dogs, according to Aetius. **Wolves** hold **horses** in hatred, and if they follow the tracks of wolves while under a rider, they are said to be seized with distress and even to burst. Pliny says that if a mare presses upon a wolf or touches its tracks, she will perform an untiring run. Wolves provide a cure for "shortness of breath" <note>original: "anhelosis"; a respiratory distress or heaving</note>, a disease which afflicts horses most disruptively. Of all animals, the elephant hates the **mouse** the most, and if a mouse touches the fodder placed in its manger, the elephant loathes it, according to Pliny and Solinus. Whether the mouse is effective against elephantiasis is as yet untried, but a **weasel** of that genus suspended, or its ash, is effective for elephantiasis according to Pliny, Sextus, and Aesculapius. 

The elephant flees upon hearing the grunting of **pigs**, according to Horus the Egyptian; either it dreads the swine by nature, or it dreads the discordant sharpness of the voice. For this reason, when the Megarians were besieged by Antipater, they set fire to pigs smeared with pitch to disturb the Macedonian elephants and break their formation. According to Aristotle, elephants are immune to all diseases except for being sharply infested by inflammation of the gut. Furthermore, they are tortured by pain in the shoulders due to the rubbing of their loads; Aristotle says these are soothed by the application of pig's meat. Very old pig fat, mixed with lime, helps inflammations; and a ground, burned knuckle-bone taken in a drink cures inflammations of the colon and torments of the gut <note>original: "torminibus"; griping pains or colic</note>, according to Dioscorides. The **porcupine** <note>original: "histrix"</note>, being of the swine family, also cures elephantiasis. **Horses** are terrified by elephants in battle, according to Heliodorus and Marcellus. A remedy of ivory <note>original: "obur"; likely a variant of 'ebur'</note> and milk is effective for a rabid horse, according to Nemesianus. For horses go mad for various reasons, as noted by the horse-doctors <note>original: "Hippiatricos"</note>. Elephant blood is effective against **rheumatism** <note>original: "rheumatismos"; a flux of humors</note> according to Pliny, a disease from which the horse suffers greatly. To the horse kind, all things related to swine are hostile and hated: the grunting, the stench, and the breath. Toward horses...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the antipathies of animals, specifically how the natural enmities between different species provide clues for medicinal remedies. It concludes Chapter 21 and begins Chapter 22, which focuses on animals that hunt venomous creatures.</meta>

BOOK SEVEN.

For those suffering from **respiratory issues** <note>original: "pneumaticos"</note>, if you immediately pour the blood of a suckling pig or warm blood into the throat of an afflicted horse, as Pelagonius <note>A 4th-century Roman writer on veterinary medicine</note> advises, it has been found to be equally effective for human lungs. The **camel** is opposed to **horses** by a natural hatred, as witnessed by Aelian and Pliny. Cyrus, in his battle against Croesus <note>The famously wealthy King of Lydia</note>, set camels against the cavalry for this reason: the horse so dreads the camel that it cannot bear to look upon its form or endure its scent. Thus, Cyrus devised a way to render Croesus’s cavalry—which the king believed would give him the upper hand—completely useless. As soon as the battle began, the horses, smelling and seeing the camels, turned back, and thus the hopes of Croesus perished, according to Herodotus. **Asthma** is an incurable disease in horses, for which camel's milk provides relief, as it does for those who are short of breath, according to Avicenna.

The **wolf**, which strikes terror into many, is itself terrified of the **hedgehog**. If a gargle is made from the soft blood of a hedgehog and warm water, it heals a hoarse and muffled voice—a condition the wolf is said to cause just by looking at a person first <note>A common ancient folklore belief that if a wolf sees a man before the man sees the wolf, the man loses his voice</note>, according to Aesculapius. The **lion** terrifies all animals with its strength; even those that have never seen or experienced one remain stunned upon hearing its roar. Because of this, if anyone rubs their body with lion’s fat, they will be safe from all beasts. Furthermore, if a lion’s hide touches a wolf’s hide, it causes the hair to fall out, and similarly with other skins. Yet, the **rooster** is a source of terror even to the lion, the most noble of wild beasts; the rooster puts such a fierce animal to flight with its crest and its crowing. Indeed, the lion is overcome with great fear. Proclus even relates that the rooster terrifies demons appearing in the form of lions, according to Aelian and Zoroaster. For this reason, panthers and lions do not touch those anointed with chicken broth, according to Pliny. For quartan fevers, rooster testicles are prescribed as a drink according to Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus</note>, and for black bile and long-lasting fevers, they provide chicken broth according to Dioscorides—the very diseases to which the lion is most susceptible.

The **hawk** is said to be the greatest enemy of the **chameleon**; it is reported that the hawk draws the chameleon out as it flies above, and the chameleon voluntarily offers itself to be torn apart by other animals, according to Pliny. Hawk’s gall is specifically believed to correct **glaucoma** and **cataracts** <note>original: "suffusiones"</note> with a three-day application. Chameleon’s gall is believed to have such power that it heals **eye spots** <note>original: "hippochises"</note> within three days of anointing, according to Marcellus. Hawks are more prone to dimness of vision than other birds, so much so that they possess a natural remedy for this ailment: they seek out lettuce for the sake of medicine.

**Lizards** are most hostile to **snails**, according to Pliny. If you strike and cut a lizard through the middle, it knits itself back together by a silent consensus <note>A poetic way of describing the lizard's ability to regenerate or heal its body</note>, according to Solinus and Philes. Snails, in turn, heal other wounds, especially those of the nerves, according to Dioscorides. The **monkey** dreads the **tortoise** <note>original: "testudinem"</note> beyond measure; when one is seen, it is a marvelous spectacle to see with what horror the beast leaps back. Hence, if one ties a tortoise to the chain by which a monkey is bound so that it cannot escape, it is incredible to say how much the monkey is tortured, nearly fainting from fear. Monkeys drink wine and are captured when drunk, as Athenaeus reports. If someone washes a tortoise in good wine for some time, takes its blood, mixes it with that wine, and gives it to someone to drink secretly in a measure of half a cup in the morning while fasting for three days, they will see a divine power <note>likely as a cure for drunkenness or alcoholism</note>, according to Myrepsicus. There are perpetual quarrels between the tortoise and the **partridge**, the one being lustful and the other chaste.

## ANIMALS THAT BATTLE WITH VENOMOUS CREATURES
## are effective against their venom.
### Chapter XXII.

There are also animals that, through a certain antipathy, battle with venomous animals and eat their flesh; we are taught by Nature that these are effective against their venom.

**Examples:** There is a battle between **crows** and **snakes**, nor can the snake escape its enemy even by hiding in its lair. Furthermore, by a generous gift of Nature, **stags** draw snakes out of their holes with the breath of their nostrils and, once extracted, they eat them, according to Aelian. For this reason, all snakes flee from those anointed with stag's fat, and the **bezoar stone** <note>original: "lapis bezahar"</note>, which is formed from the tears of a stag, is a most effective antidote against poisons. Its rennet is also effective against snake-

...snake bites, and a skin spread beneath a person makes them safe from serpents; they are all driven away by burnt deer horn. The breath of **elephants** also draws serpents out of their holes, and the elephant bears a natural enmity toward the dragon; its fat is effective against poisons, for if one is anointed with it, or if it is used as a fumigant, the serpents must flee with great speed, according to Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author of "On the Nature of Animals"</note>. As a food, it is also a most effective medicine against the venom of serpents. Around Thessaly, there is such a great abundance of serpents that, unless they were defended by **storks**, the inhabitants would be driven out; according to Aristotle in his *On Marvelous Things*, the stork hunts lizards, *chersydros* <term>chersydros: an amphibious, venomous snake described by ancients</term>, and other pests of the meadows, and especially the *cenchrus* <term>cenchrus: a type of spotted snake whose bite was said to cause rotting</term>. Their body parts are effective against all poisons, according to Aelian; likewise, the water from its stomach acts against the plague, according to the Quintilii <note>Two brothers who co-authored an influential work on agriculture, the *Georgica*</note>.

It is said that the **gecko** <note>original: "stellione," a spotted lizard or gecko</note> is particularly opposed to **scorpions**, so much so that the mere sight of it strikes them with fear and the cold sweat of numbness; therefore, people let the gecko rot in oil and use it to anoint the places where a scorpion has stung. This is recorded by Aelian, Philes, Pliny, and Galen. The **mullet** fish captures the **sea-hare** <note>original: "leporem marinum," a toxic marine mollusk</note> and eats it; thus, it is effective against its bite. The **ichneumon** <note>The Egyptian Mongoose, famous in antiquity for fighting cobras</note>, having rolled itself in the mud of the Nile, suns itself until its back dries and hardens; thus armored, it rushes at the asp, either biting off its head or dragging it by the tail into the river after gripping it with its teeth, according to Nicander in his *Theriaca* and Aelian. Venomous creatures flee from the fat of dragons, and likewise from the musk of the ichneumon and its skin when applied with ash and vinegar, according to Pliny.

The **weasel** attacks the serpent, and the ash of weasels is fatal to the **basilisk**—the most poisonous of all serpents; thus Nature was pleased that nothing should exist without its match, according to Pliny and Solinus. Its flesh opposes poison, according to Avicenna, and is effective against the venom of serpents. The serpent is an enemy to the **pig**, which devours it; indeed, the power of the **salamander** is such that it is even eaten by pigs without harm, according to Pliny. In the mountains of Pamphylia and Cilicia, wild boars that eat a salamander cause those who eat the boar to die, according to Aelian. A pig's liver taken with wine heals the bites of venomous creatures, according to Symeon Seth; the liver of a boar also helps against serpents.

The **eagle** has a great and very uncertain struggle with dragons; it seizes them with its claws and beak into the air, while the snakes entwine the eagle in multiple coils so that they fall to the ground bound together. Florentinus, in the *Geoponica*, says that a serpent will not approach where the dung of an eagle or a kite lies, or where a fumigant is made from burnt rags. The **ibis** is called a "snake-eater" <note>original: "ὀφιοφάγος" (ophiophagos)</note> by the Greeks because it eats and fights serpents; it is worshipped by the Egyptians because it not only kills serpents but breaks their eggs and brings them as food to its chicks. When roasted, it drives away serpents and heals their bites. The basilisk fears the sight and the song of the **rooster**, which fights against serpents on behalf of the hens; its broth, when drunk, is effective against snake bites, according to Pliny, and chickens cut open and applied while still warm help with snake bites; their brains are also given to be drunk in wine, according to Dioscorides. The **turtle** fights with the serpent and is effective against the venom of the salamander, according to Nicander. The **chameleon** draws a hawk flying above it down to itself; for those who have swallowed chameleon eggs, the dung of a hawk in wine is given as a drink, according to Bellunensis. We must not omit this wonder: **shrew-mice** <note>original: "mures aranei"</note> die if they cross a "wheel-track" (that is, the mark of chariot wheels pressed into the ground); therefore, the soil from that track, when sprinkled on the bite they inflict, serves as a remedy, according to Aelian.

## ON THE MUTUAL ANTIPATHY OF PLANTS.
### Chapter XXIII.

Next follow those things which are not merely opposed to another, but are mutually hostile to each other. The **Oak** and the **Olive** disagree with such persistent hatred that if one is planted in the pit of the other, it dies. Eaten acorns cause a headache; but oil from olives is excellent for headaches. The oak constricts, while the oil relaxes. The **fern** will perish if it is surrounded by a circle of abundant **reeds**, and conversely, the reed will waste away if it is enclosed in a circle by many ferns. A crushed reed applied to the body extracts a fern splinter, and likewise the root of a fern extracts a reed splinter. Freshly crushed reed drunk in wine stirs up Venus <note>Acts as an aphrodisiac</note>, according to Pliny; the fern is an enemy to women, for it causes abortion in those who are pregnant and sterility in others.
