It renders the wearer chaste and modest, making them peaceful, amiable, pious, and devoted; it also expels melancholic terrors.

## FLOWERS OF VARIOUS COLORS AND STONES OF MERCURY
### *represent his star.* Cap. VII.

<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut initial 'P' featuring intricate floral and leafy patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>Plant flowers that display a mixture of various colors will remind you of Mercury, for in the star of Mercury there shines a pleasant mixture of all colors: the green and pale of Saturn, the rosy of Venus, the saffron of Jupiter, and the golden of the Sun. Mercury presides over memory, the brain, and eloquence. The **Iris** <note>referring both to the flower and the "rainbow stone"</note> took its name from its resemblance to the heavenly rainbow, as many colors are represented in it; in general, the iris has great use for all things: its juice purges the brain of thick phlegm.

There are also the **daisies** <note>original: *bellides*</note>, which the common people call Pearls; some have golden petals in the center surrounded by red, others are white-to-red and multi-colored, and their petals are so crowded together that they mimic silk tassels. They purge the brain of phlegm and other such things. We shall say the same regarding stones: namely, that a mixture of colors demonstrates a stone to be Mercurial and bestows Mercurial powers. First occurs the **Opal**; in it is the thin fire of the carbuncle <note>a deep red gem like a garnet</note>, the shining purple of the amethyst, the green sea of the emerald, and all these shine together in an incredible mixture. It is not unfitting for it to have as many virtues as it has colors, a fact confirmed by the consensus of all philosophers. Orpheus <note>The mythical poet, to whom works on the magical properties of stones were attributed</note> said it heals the eyes because it reflects the color of the iris of the eye. The **Nicolaus** stone is adorned with a double color, yellow and black, among others; its virtue is to make a person popular. There is one type of **Jasper** that is variously colored, which they call *polygrammos* <note>meaning "many-lined"</note> due to the various streaks of colors. The Magi recorded that this stone is effective for those making public speeches, over whom Mercury presides. The **Panther-stone** is a stone having various colors in the likeness of the animal of its name: pale, black, red, rosy, green, and purple. Its colors are to be inspected at sunrise, for then they all shine forth; you will be the victor in all the actions of the day on which you wear it. Many are the colors of the **Agate** <note>original: *Achati*</note>; you will find in it green jasper, blood-red sard, shining emerald, and the color of cinnabar. Furthermore, it has the color of bronze and of a spring apple. The best of all is that which has the tawny color of a lion, called *leontoseryn* <note>lion-colored agate</note>, interspersed with yellow, white, black, and green spots. Orpheus records that it makes a man pleasing to women and charms people with words; whatever you seek, you will obtain, so that you may return home cheerful. It is effective against the stings of scorpions, against the fire of fever, and the quartan ague <note>a fever recurring every four days, often associated with malaria</note>. Among stones, he proclaims none better for retaining the best powers of celestial influence; if Ajax had possessed it, he would have gained victory over the eloquent Ulysses, but he spurned the counsel of the Gods. The **Amethyst** gem shines through with various purples and is streaked with various colors; it defends the citadel of the brain from the siege of intoxication <note>original: *temeti*; an archaic term for strong wine</note>, and for this reason antiquity consecrated it to Mercury.

## HELIOTROPIC PLANTS AND SOLAR STONES ARE THOSE
### *that participate in his gifts.* Cap. VIII.

<image-desc>Small decorative initial 'D' with leafy scrollwork.</image-desc>We have spoken regarding how plants are categorized under the planets based on the colors of their flowers; now we shall add the **heliotropes**, which turn daily with the Sun and show the hours to farmers, even on a cloudy day. Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle in the Peripatetic school</note>, concerning those things that flower, says some seem to follow something, like the plant called the heliotrope and the thistle; for the thistle also follows the sun during the solstice, and these have in part a natural cause...

<summary>This page discusses the medicinal and magical properties of stones and plants governed by Mercury, such as the opal and agate, which are identified by their multiple colors. It also introduces solar plants like the heliotrope, which are defined by their movement in relation to the sun.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of plants governed by the Sun and Mercury. The previous page ended with a discussion of the iris and daisies. This page explores "heliotropic" plants—those that move with the sun—and their medicinal applications, particularly for the heart, adhering to the theory that plants mimicking the sun’s movements possess solar virtues like vitality and courage.</meta>

<page-num>312</page-num>
<header>PHYTOGNOMONICA</header>

...the cause is partly accidental. It is much more marvelous that the Egyptian **lotus**, its calyx, and its stem—to say nothing of the poppy—open at sunrise and are compressed at the setting of that star. Indeed, from evening until midnight, the flower’s stalk retreats into the lake so deeply that it cannot be reached even by a hand plunged into the water; then it turns, gradually rises, and returns at dawn, with the flower gaping open at sunrise so that it stands clearly high above the earth and emerges out of the waves. The cause of this has been attributed to heat or cold. For the flower is compressed by gathered and, as it were, thickened moisture, and is then deprived of the power of its own heat; it opens itself when the heat is diffused, relaxing what the cold had tightened. This should therefore be credited to the Sun. Those things which descend deeper do so out of a certain weakness and, as it were, go to ruin in the Sun's absence; yet by the gift of its presence, they grow more vigorous and emerge supported by it as if by a prop. But those things hidden in warmer and more turbulent waves recognize these turns of the departing and returning star.

No less marvelous are those herbs they call **heliotropes** <note>literally "sun-turners"</note>, which turn their leaves with the Sun’s declination. I believe this usually happens to those plants that are soaked with excessive moisture; for while they are being driven by the exhausted force of the heat, it is natural for them to be carried and inclined toward wherever the Sun, heating the moisture, provokes them. Therefore, the Sun is the author of all these things, which, by luring the moist sap to itself and dragging the leaves with it, seizes them such that as the Sun moves, they follow submissively. These are the words of <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>an ancient Greek philosopher often called the "father of botany"</note>. All species of **Serides** <note>chicory-like plants</note> open at sunrise even on a cloudy day and turn with it toward the sunset, always compressed at night and gaping during the day. <term>Pliny</term> says that those anointed with its juice mixed with oil become favored and obtain what they wish more easily. <term>Dioscorides</term> said it is usefully applied to those with heart conditions <note>original: *cardiacis*; referring to heart-related ailments</note> on its own or with barley meal, and that it acts against poisons. **Mallow** <note>original: *Malvae*</note> flowers, when the midday Sun climbs to the zenith of our sky, then gape open as if longing for the star’s radiance; after an hour or two, as if saddened by its departure and longing for it, they wither and close; for this reason, Theophrastus calls it "the hourly plant." <term>Columella</term> <note>a Roman writer on agriculture</note> describes the *moloche* <note>another name for mallow</note> in this verse:

->*And the mallow, which follows the sun with a bowed head.*<-

It is a prodigious miracle of Nature that herbs, even on a cloudy day, betray the hidden Sun, and when a cloud is in the way, they demonstrate the true seat of the concealed star by the layer and conversion of their leaves, like indicators of its course. Indeed, they more truly perform the function of a sundial, so much so that even when the Sun is not visible, we can gather the hours. It is held in high praise, and marvelous things are reported of it—even more so if someone were to swallow half a cup <note>original: *cyathum*; a Roman liquid measure</note> of its juice every day, they would be free from all diseases. The flower of the **Heliotrope** opens at the rising of the Sun and closes at its setting; therefore it is called "sun-follower" <note>original: *solsequia*</note> or "the Sun’s bride," because it wakes and lies down soothed by the twilights. Out of a certain longing for the returning star, and likewise through the day and by a certain lover's pact, it gazes at the Sun from its rising; for this reason, it is called "friend of the sun" by some. The <term>Magi</term> <note>ancient practitioners of ritual and herbal magic</note> promise much regarding this: they order it to be bound four times for quartan fevers and three times for tertian fevers by the sick person themselves, who should pray that they will untie the knots once freed from the illness, and do so without removing the herb. 

One genus of **Tithymalus** <note>spurge</note>, which they call *helioscopon*, follows the path of the Sun, and always proceeds with it toward the sunset with a bowed head, looking at it throughout the day so that its little stalk never seems to have twisted away; such is its greed for following the star. When taken, it affects the heart; hence, when it is consumed, it is mixed with those medicines that strengthen the heart, according to <term>Mesue</term> <note>an influential medieval physician</note>. The guests of <term>Athenaeus</term> said that **Hemerocallis** <note>day-lily</note> flowers wither when the Sun sets and sprout again when it rises—not that they entirely wither or fall off, but at the arrival of the somewhat chilly moist night, the flowers contract and collapse into themselves; at the next light, illuminated by the Sun's rays, they unfold and, as it were, come back to life. Modern practitioners use it, by experiment, to strengthen the heart and all principal faculties, and for those seized by fainting fits or shaken by heart palpitations. The **Lupine** also turns with the Sun and shows the hours to farmers even on a cloudy day; eaten frequently, it cheers a person of poor complexion and makes them more beautiful. **Tragopogon** <note>goatsbeard</note> follows the Sun with its flower; in a clear sky it opens, but when it is cloudy, it contracts and is closed by its calyx. It is of the same genus as the plant called **scorzonera** <note>black salsify</note>, the juice of which is given to those with heart conditions and for fainting fits...

...and for the beating of the heart and those subject to tremors; when chewed, it dispels sadness and brings about cheerfulness. The **Castor bean** (*Ricinus*), since it turns toward the Sun, has earned the name of "heliotrope" <note>original: heliotropij; literally "sun-turner"</note>: it extracts the bile from which tertian fever <note>A malaria-like fever that spikes every third day.</note> is born, just like other solar herbs. The same must be considered regarding stones. The **Heliotrope** stone is so named (commonly called *heliotropia*), which, when placed in a basin full of water and struck by the rays of the Sun, renders the Sun looking blood-red and seems to show an eclipse because of this sympathy it has with the Sun. It possesses solar virtue: it excels in prophecies, provides men with praise, grants a good reputation, and keeps them safe throughout their lives; it drives away poisons and is effective against them. Orpheus <note>Refers to the *Lithica*, a poem on stones traditionally attributed to the mythical Orpheus.</note> speaks of two stones of the Sun, both nearly divine, in which the rays of the true Sun are implanted—straight and shining—in which something like hair appears, though they differ in form from one another. He says one is similar to crystal, the other to **chrysolite** <note>A yellowish-green gem, possibly peridot.</note>, were it not for the rays they possess. These stones greatly benefit those into whom the Sun has impressed a spirit of white light, being most excellent for receiving solar influences.

## HERBS AND STONES THAT MOVE WITH THE PHASES OF THE
## Moon are Lunar. Chapter IX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' with foliate patterns and scrolling vines within a square border.</image-desc>
THERE ARE also plants and stones that grow and shrink according to the movement of the Moon. It was observed by the ancients that all things born on land and sea flourish when the Moon is waxing and waste away when it is waning. The **onion** alone among all vegetables is said to feel the contrary effects of the star, having opposite cycles of increasing and diminishing; for it revives and sprouts again when the Moon is waning, but conversely dries up when the Moon is waxing. For this reason, the Egyptian priests of Pelusium <note>An ancient city in the eastern Nile Delta.</note> banned onions from their diet. From these signs, we judge that such things provide remedies against the phases of the Moon. For those subject to the "falling sickness" <term>epilepsy</term> <note>Historically called the "comitial disease" because Roman assemblies (comitia) were suspended if someone had a seizure.</note> feel the damage of the waxing Moon, and they counter this disease by eating onions; after countless trials, this has finally been proven true. **Squill** (*Scilla*), a type of onion-like plant, is administered to those suffering from vertigo and epilepsy if a vinegar is made from it, which they call "squill-vinegar"; **garlic** is also given to epileptics for the same reason, as we said above regarding that species. Furthermore, among crops, **broad beans** (*fabae*) alone are said to fill up as the Moon waxes, though their power regarding lunar diseases has not yet been tested. **Groundsel** (*Senecio*) produces new yellow flowers at almost every phase of the Moon, which briefly turn into downy seeds <note>original: pappos</note>; it is given against epilepsy. There is also the **selenite** stone, which some call *aphroselinum* <note>From the Greek for "moon-foam."</note>, because it is found at night to reflect the image of the Moon, which increases and decreases along with the star; Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> commands that shavings of this be given in a drink to epileptics. There are those who report that in the shoulder of a **panther**, there is a spot similar to the Moon, growing into a circle and hollowing out into horns in the same manner as the moon, according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist.</note>; its fat is useful for those who suffer from vertigo if the scent is inhaled while it is being roasted, according to Pliny.

## CONCERNING LUNAR HERBS THAT SHINE AT NIGHT IN
## the Moonlight. Chapter X.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' depicting a pastoral landscape with a figure and trees within a square border.</image-desc>
WE SHALL NEXT list the lunar herbs which, because they shine at night or move according to the motion of the Moon, are said to have a certain sympathy with the Moon and are called "lunar." These are believed to be effective for the falling sickness and for fertility, because the Moon presides over fertility and generation. There is an herb called **cynospastos** <note>literally "dog-dragged"</note>, known by another name as **aglaophotis** <note>literally "bright-light"</note>; for this Greek name was given to it because of the brilliance of its light. During the day it hides among other herbs and is in no way recognized, but at night, shining like a star and quivering with a fiery splendor, it easily comes into view. Therefore, a marker is fixed at its roots, and people leave without it, for they would recognize neither its color nor its appearance by day. Once the night has passed, they return and recognize the herb by the marker, but they are careful not to pull it up themselves; for they say that one ignorant of its nature would perish. They bring a shining, hungry dog and tie a cord to the lower stalk of the herb and fasten it to the dog. They then throw meat for the dog while standing very far away. As the dog rushes toward the meat, it tears the herb out by the roots, and the dog expires. The use of the herb, among other things, is as a remedy for the falling sickness in humans, and it is recommended for defects of the eyes when the faculty of sight...

the faculty is admitted, according to Aelian. There is another plant called **aglaophotis** <note>original: aglaophotis; a legendary plant often associated with peonies or magical light</note> described by Pliny from the works of Democritus, which earned the admiration of men because of its extraordinary color; indeed, Josephus commemorates this in his *History of the Jewish War*. More recent writers call a certain herb the "Greek Moonwort" <term>lunaria graeca; likely the plant Honesty, *Lunaria annua*</term>, which bears somewhat long seeds between wide and flat pods that are like the thinnest plates. When these are mature at night, they reflect the image of the shining Moon on their smooth and splendid surface like a mirror, so that from this the name of "Moonwort" <note>original: lunaria</note> was bestowed upon it. Others say it is because the leaf, which forms a little sac on both sides in the middle and contains the seed within, shines with a silvery brightness, and that splendor glows toward the Moon like a mirror-stone <term>specularis lapis; a translucent stone like mica or selenite</term>. It has blue flowers; I hear a remedy from it has been proven against the **comitial disease** <note>original: comitialem morbum; a historical term for epilepsy</note>. Regarding the **Peony**, Apuleius says that it glows at night like a lamp, and for that reason is found by shepherds at night, and is called by another name, **aglaophotis**. If it is placed upon a person lying in a lunar fit <note>original: lunatico; someone suffering from epilepsy or mental distress thought to be caused by the moon</note>, they immediately rise as if healthy, and if they keep it with them, it never happens to them again. The **Nyctegreton** <note>literally "night-waker"</note> was admired among a few things by Democritus; it has the color of fire, the leaves of a thorn, and raises itself from the ground. He narrates it is found especially in Gedrosia <note>A coastal region of ancient Persia</note>; it is dug up by the roots after the spring equinox and dried by the Moon for thirty days, thus it glows in the nights. He says that the Magi and the Kings of the Parthians use this herb for undertaking vows, and that the same is called **chenumychon** <note>original: chenumychon; Greek for "frightener of geese"</note>, because geese are terrified at the first sight of it; by others it is called **nyctilopa**, because it shines from a distance during the nights.

### ANIMALS WHICH HAVE A CERTAIN SYMPATHY 
### WITH THE MOON. Chapter 11.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a figure in a rural landscape with foliage and distant architecture.</image-desc>

There are also very many animals that seem to have a certain sympathy with the Moon; I would dare to assert that all these are effective for the comitial disease and for defects of the brain. The eyes of **Cats** <term>aeluri; from the Greek word for cat</term> become larger and smaller according to the phases of the Moon. It is much more to be wondered at that the male cat, as Horapollo <note>original: Horo Apollini; an ancient author on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> believes, feels the changes of the Sun and changes the pupils of its eyes with the course of that star; for indeed at the rising of dawn they are stretched out, and at midday the same are contracted into a circle, and at the setting of the Sun they grow dull and darker. The Egyptians, believing that the divinity of Isis encompassed all of nature within herself, therefore joined this animal to her because it reflected certain marks and images of the Moon—by whose stellar benefit a great part of Nature stands—especially in its eyes. Many have testified that in these, according to the daily decreases and increases of the lights in the sky, the pupils in cats increase and diminish; and not only that, but at night and in the darkness they shine in the manner of that star, and—what is greatest—the cat equals the fertile and vegetative nature of the Moon with its own fecundity. The **Weasel** <note>original: Mutela</note> is a species of it, whose flesh is effective for those with epilepsy according to Avicenna; its stomach according to Dioscorides; its blood according to Galen; and the ash of its brain, testicles, and womb according to Pliny. Solinus said that **Monkeys** <note>original: Simias</note> are sad during the waning moon but adore the new moon with exultation; Pliny says that those in the genus of monkeys which have a tail are sad during the waning moon and adore the new moon with exultation. The Egyptians paint the **cynocephalus** <term>a baboon or dog-headed monkey</term> to represent the Moon, because this animal is affected by a certain sympathy during the Moon's conjunction with the Sun. For when the Moon, meeting with the Sun for some time, remains devoid of light, then the male cynocephalus neither looks at anything nor eats anything, but with its face cast down to the earth, it seems to grieve for the lot of the Moon as if she had been snatched away, and to bear it indignantly. The female, however, besides the fact that she never turns her eyes away and suffers the same as the male, additionally sends blood from her genital vessel <note>A reference to the menstrual cycle's perceived link to the moon</note>; and to this day, cynocephali are nourished in the sacred rites themselves, so that the time of the conjunction of the Sun and Moon can be known from them. Wishing to indicate the rising Moon, they paint a cynocephalus standing, raising its hands to heaven, and wearing a royal insignia on its head, because in this posture the cynocephalus seems to congratulate the Moon, according to Horapollo. The roasted and dried heart of a monkey, drunk in the weight of a drachm with old honey-water, is effective against the comitial disease, according to Rhazes. In **Elephants** there is a religion and veneration of the stars, and of the Sun and Moon as well; I understand that when the Moon is growing after the dark moon, by some hidden reason of Nature, the elephants first pluck branches from the forest where they are born, and then carry them high, then indeed they look up to the Moon and move the branches gently, just...

Ivory <note>original: Ebur</note> is administered with honeyed water, having a very remarkable power against **falling sickness** <term>comitialibus; epilepsy, so named because an occurrence during a Roman assembly or 'comitia' was seen as a bad omen, requiring adjournment</term>, and elephant liver is excellent for these same diseases, according to Pliny. Upon mating during a waxing Moon, a tiny fiber is said to grow in the liver of a mouse in a marvelous way every day until the full Moon; then, as the Moon wanes, the fibers likewise decrease, and having thinned into a single body, they gradually vanish, according to Aelian, Cicero, Lucilius, Gellius, and Pliny. The Egyptians hold the shrew-mouse sacred because its liver diminishes when the Moon is obscured. By dissecting a mouse during the silence of the Moon <note>the new moon</note>, its liver is extracted; roast it and give it to an epileptic to eat, according to Galen’s book of easy remedies. They say the rooster, at the rising of the Moon, is inspired as if by some divine spirit to act with ecstatic joy, according to Aelian. Rooster testicles are given to be drunk in rainwater, preceded by five days of abstinence, for those with epilepsy, according to Pliny and Sextus. They report that the bodies of oysters, shellfish, and all manner of conches increase by the power of the Moon, and shrink again as it wanes. Horace wrote:

->Slippery shellfish fill out as the Moon is born.<-
---

The cause lies in the Moon's own properties, which are to moisten bodies with a chilling effect and moderate color. Therefore, the Moon nourishes and governs the humors, just as the Sun fertilizes all things with his heat; for the life of all things arises from the mixture of heat and moisture, and is cherished by the tempering of both. The Sun is a masculine star and performs the role of the male; the Moon is a feminine star, soft and nocturnal, which releases moisture and draws it out, but does not take it away, as Pliny says. We have said that shellfish and pearls are effective against epilepsy. Furthermore, it is a marvel that the ant feels the phases of the star, ceasing work at the time of the new moon and working through the nights during the full moon. Indeed, the scarab beetle exerts itself for as many days as there are in a month, during which the rising Sun follows his courses; it clearly demonstrates the conjunction of the Sun and Moon, since it rolls a pellet of ox-dung from sunrise to sunset, shaping it into the image of the world. It buries this in a small pit in the ground for twenty-eight days, keeping it hidden until the Moon, circling the zodiac and returning to the period between months, falls silent; then, opening the little ball and announcing the union of the stars, it brings forth new offspring. It knows no other origin for its birth. The nature of these green creatures sharpens the sight of those who gaze upon them, according to Pliny.

## THE BRAIN OF ANIMALS, WHICH GROWS ACCORDING TO THE PHASES OF THE MOON,
### *and withers with the lunar cycle. Chapter XII.*

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'E' featuring architectural and floral motifs.</image-desc>
THERE is also the brain of certain animals, which increases and decreases quite perceptibly with the Moon, since it is seen to increase and diminish even in humans and all animals according to the lunar phases. Wise surgeons do not open the head during a full Moon, because we have seen the brain to be more diffused then, filling the entire skull. Hippocrates, in his book on the **falling sickness** <note>original: morbo comitiali; epilepsy</note>, says: In the sacred disease, the brain is excessively moist; one may recognize this most clearly in sheep, and especially in goats. For these animals are very frequently seized by this kind of disease; if you dissect their heads, you will find the brain moist, full of fluid, and foul-smelling. Plutarch, in his *Roman Questions*, reports that the goat, more than other animals, is afflicted by the falling sickness, and for that reason the ancient priests strictly abstained from them as if they were diseased. The flesh of a goat roasted on a man’s funeral pyre is effective for epileptics, as we have said. Goat brain, strained before milk is given to infants, is distilled against falling sicknesses, according to Pliny. Galen prescribes the liver; Dioscorides the milk. Sheep always have a moist brain and are seized by the falling sickness; the blood of cattle is wonderfully praised for these diseases. Elsewhere, Pliny praises gall, Serapio praises the sweat of the animal, and wool-grease <term>oesypum; the fat or grease extracted from sheep's wool, used in ancient medicine</term> with myrrh is praised for the moment of the fit. The brain of a pig is somewhat fattier, according to Aristotle, and it diminishes more than that of any other animal as the Moon wanes. The Egyptians consider the pig profane, for it seems to mate primarily during the waning Moon, according to Plutarch’s book on Isis. Against the falling sickness, the testicles of a pig are given, aged and ground in sow's milk, with a preceding abstinence from wine; and on the following consecutive days, let the patient drink the urine of a wild boar with oxymel <term>oximelle; a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</term> and a rem-

The head of a quail is moist and foul-smelling, and for that reason, it is harmful to those with epilepsy, according to Pliny. Quails were banned from the table because of the falling sickness and were usually spat upon, for they alone among animals, besides humans, suffer from it. An effective remedy for the falling sickness: grind the brain of a quail with myrtle ointment and store it in a tin vessel. Chickens have a moist brain and are seized by the falling sickness; we said above that rooster testicles are effective for the falling disease <note>original: caducum morbum; another term for epilepsy</note>. Aelian, citing the opinion of Demonstratus, says there is a fish called the "Moon" <note>original: Lunam</note>, flat in shape, small, beautiful, and of a sea-blue color, in the form of a crescent moon. It is said to be filled when the Moon is full, and to fill others; surely if you hang it on trees during a waning Moon, they dry up and perish; if on plants, they wither. If you throw its water into a well during a full Moon, the water will be constant and perennial, but during the last phase of the Moon, the water dries up.

### FLOWERS MIRRORING THE FORM OF THE SUN, AND ANIMALS

->Retaining the powers of the Sun.  Cap.  XIII.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap letter 'F' depicting a human figure amidst foliage.</image-desc>
FLOWERS exist which imitate the form and even the color of the Sun. First, the pregnant coverings of the flowers swell and show a spherical orb in place of a bud. As this opens and unfolds into leaves, it displays a radiated, circular orb through a numerous series of small petals arranged in a crafted sequence around the edges, just like little rays; they seem to counterfeit the rays of the Sun. **Heliochryson** <note>likely 'Goldilocks' or an Everlasting flower</note> seems to emulate the Sun's rays with its surrounding leaves. It is a Solar herb, and we have said it is effective for achieving glory. **Helenium** <note>Elecampane</note> has a golden, star-like flower resembling an ox-eye, surrounded by tender, oblong, radiating leaves. In its center, a hairy boss <note>original: umbo; the central knob or disk of a flower</note> stands out, imitating the Sun's orb. This should be used in moist, fresh wine to provide comfort to the mind, bring joy, and expel sadness; because of this quality, the ancients valued it highly, and some believed the Egyptian *nepenthe* <note>a legendary medicine for sorrow mentioned in the Odyssey</note> was made from this alone. They call it **Heliantes** <note>Sun-rose</note> in the region of Themiscira and the coastal mountains of Cilicia. The Magi and the Kings of the Persians are said to anoint themselves with this, boiled with lion’s fat and added saffron and palm wine, so that the body becomes pleasant to look upon. The flowers of **Anthemis** <note>Chamomile</note> have a yellow, bubble-like cluster on their stems, like a little hub in the middle surrounded by small leaves. It is called by another name, *chrysocome*, which means "golden-haired." It was consecrated to the Sun by the Egyptian sages and is considered a remedy for all fevers. **Scorzonera** <note>Black Salsify</note> also produces radiating flowers; its juice is given for heart ailments and fainting spells. **Caltha** <note>Marigold</note> has a flower shaped in a circular orb, with a conspicuous boss standing out in the center, surrounded on all sides by many-cleft rays, as if made of glowing gold. It is second to no other flower in beauty. It is added to salads for heart conditions and to sharpen the eyesight. There are also animals which, by a certain form and virtue, counterfeit the Sun; they are effective for strengthening the heart and against poisons. The **Lion** has a round face, and for that reason reflects the Sun, since it also displays a certain image of rays in the circumference of its hair, and its pupils are flashing and somewhat fiery. The Egyptians consecrate the Lion to the Sun because that animal seems to derive its substance from the nature of the Sun. First, it surpasses other animals in impulse and heat, just as the Sun surpasses the stars. The lion is stronger in the chest and the front part of the body, and it tapers off in its hind limbs, just as the power of the Sun increases in the first part of the day until Midday, or in the first part of the year from spring to summer, and soon failing, it is brought down either toward the sunset (the lower part of the day) or toward the end of the year (the lower part of the year). Likewise, its eyes are always seen to be open and fiery, just as the Sun sees the earth with an open, fiery eye in a perpetual and tireless gaze. These are the words of Macrobius. By this argument, the throne of Horus [is decorated with] lio-

The fat of this [fish], mixed with rose oil, cures fevers according to Pliny; or, the magicians mentioned by Pliny <note>original: Magi Pliniani</note> promise that those anointed with its fat will find easier favor with Kings and common people. The Hawk of the Sun, above all other birds, appears to be a living image of the Sun itself, because by a certain particular and hidden logic of Nature, it looks out with eyes intensely focused upon the solar orb. From this comes the fact that Physicians use the herb hawkweed <term>hieracio; from the Greek 'hierax' meaning hawk, as hawks were believed to eat it to sharpen their sight</term> to heal defects of the eyes. For this reason, they sometimes paint the Sun—as the author and lord of vision—in the form of a hawk. The Eagle is also sacred to the Sun, not to Jupiter as the Poets’ fiction claims, since they themselves say the eagle snatched fire from the Sun. The eagle is endowed with excessive heat, just like the Sun, and therefore it places stones in its nest so that the eggs do not grow hotter than is proper. It stares most intensely at its eggs against the disk of the Sun and forces its young to gaze at it; because of this, they say its stone <term>aetites; known as the 'eagle-stone,' a hollow geode believed to be found in eagles' nests and used in traditional medicine</term> increases wealth, and its right eye is powerful for gaining favor. It is also beneficial for fevers, according to Alexander of Tralles <note>original: Tralliano; a prominent 6th-century Greek physician</note>. The Rooster is even more solar than the lion itself, and for that reason, it puts the lion to flight; it announces the hours of the approaching Sun, as the Poets tell in their fables about Alectryon <note>original: alectore; in Greek mythology, a youth turned into a rooster for failing to alert Ares and Aphrodite of the sunrise</note>. He [the physician] commands that those suffering from fevers be anointed with the burnt and ground combs and ears of roosters mixed with oil.

-># PHYTOGNOMONICA<-

**Senna** possesses crescent-shaped pods or follicles; it cleanses the brain and all the senses of the body, and assists with all their ailments. It brings cheerfulness to the spirit, and strengthens the brain, the nerves, and the sharpness of vision, according to **Mesue** <note>Johannes Mesue, an influential though semi-legendary medieval Arabic medical authority</note>. **Lesser Moonwort** <note>original: *Lunaria minor*; likely *Botrychium lunaria*</note> has a round stem and bears seven crescent-shaped leaves attached on each side; the number of its fronds also corresponds to the number of days in each of the Moon's quarters. While its virtues are as yet unexplored, we predict it is effective for the same remedies we have mentioned. **Plutarch**, in his book *On Rivers*, writes that the **selenite herb** <note>original: *selenitem*</note> grows on Mount Apsantus near the River Trachus. He records that shepherds smear a dripping foam from this herb on their feet at the beginning of spring so that they may be safe from serpents. Through a certain absurd common belief, it is thought to release a kind of foam, from which the mirror-stone was named **aphroselinus** <term>aphroselinus; from the Greek 'aphros' (foam) and 'selene' (moon), literally 'moon-foam'</term>, as if it were hardened from the Moon’s foam; it is also said to treat the **falling sickness** <term>comitialem morbum; epilepsy, traditionally associated with the cycles of the moon</term>, from which those afflicted vomit from the mouth. Among the varieties of palms, there is one type whose fruit has a crescent-shaped and bony stone; according to **Pliny**, this is religiously polished with a tooth to serve as a charm against enchantments. There are also many and varied forms of sea-scallops <note>original: *pectines marini*</note>, among which some are crescent-shaped, and we have already said that shells are effective against the falling sickness. **Cockscomb** <note>original: *Alectorolophos*</note> is seen with crested, sickle-shaped leaves, among which a crescent-shaped pod shines forth, covered with a thin, membranous skin; **Pliny** stated that it is effective for dimness of the eyes. The leaves of the **dragonet** <note>original: *dracunculi*; likely *Dracunculus vulgaris* or Green Dragon</note> are also crescent-shaped by reason of the stem to which they cling in a curved fashion; they say it should be dug up when the barley is ripening and the Moon is waxing. It also stops the menstrual flow <note>original: *menses sistit*</note>, provided it is not touched by iron. In the **anaxarytis**—so named for that same crescent shape—a type of sorrel with horns standing out on both sides, the plant ground and applied restrains the excessive flows of women, while roasted in wine, it induces menstruation. **Arum** has a broad leaf near its base where horns stand out on both sides; in an electuary <term>eclegmate; a syrupy medicinal paste taken by licking</term>, it stimulates the monthly cycles. **Mule's fern** <note>original: *hemionitis*</note> and **hart's-tongue fern** <note>original: *phyllitis*</note> also have crescent-shaped leaves, but their virtues remain as yet untested.

->We present the spotted leaves of **Sowbread**, **Smartweed**, and **Arum** as obvious examples, so that you may contemplate the image of the spots that mar the face of the Moon.<-

### SPOTTED LEAVES OF PLANTS, SHOWING THE SPOTS OF THE MOON, ARE LUNAR. Chap. XV.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring a landscape with a tower and foliage.</image-desc>

EVEN plants, animals, and stones confess themselves to be lunar if they show spots on their leaves, fruits, skins, or surfaces. **Sowbread** <note>original: *Cyclamino*; often *Cyclamen europaeum*</note> has variegated leaves, for white spots appear on both the upper and lower sides; its juice is infused into the nostrils to purge the head. **Arum** <note>original: *Aron*; likely *Arum maculatum*, or Cuckoo-pint</note> has leaves distinguished by fewer spots; two drachms of its seeds are usefully given to encourage menstruation. The **Black Chameleon** <note>original: *Chamaelco niger*; likely *Cardopatium corymbosum*</note> varies the colors of its leaves, so that here they are found green, elsewhere whitish, and elsewhere reddish; it inhibits the flows of fluid which they call **rheumatisms** <term>rheumatismos; from the Greek for "flowing," referring to any excessive discharge of humors</term>, and cures those with dropsy. **Smartweed** <note>original: *Persicaria*; also known as Lady's Thumb due to the dark spot on the leaf</note> has a mark on its leaf inscribed in the manner of a lunar spot, which reflects the image of the crescent Moon; it has the effects of **molybdenum** <note>original: *molibdenæ*; referring here to a lead-like medicinal property</note>, for if it is bound to the eyes, the **lead** <term>plumbum; here referring to a specific eye disease or growth, likely a cataract or pterygium</term>, which is a type of defect, is removed from the eyes.

### SOLAR HERBS ARE THOSE THAT GROW UNDER THE TORRID ZONE. Chap. XVI.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring birds and foliage.</image-desc>

THERE ARE also many plants that grow under the **Torrid Zone** <note>the tropics</note> which we say are solar, just as are certain animals and stones. For the Sun thrives most vigorously there and impresses its solar power upon them; hence they are hot and dry, and they assist the heart, the sharpness of the eyes, and act against poisons and fevers. **Balsam** grows in Judea, and especially in Jericho; it is effective against the bites of serpents and venomous creatures, it dispels dimness of the eyes, and when applied as an ointment, it removes the shivers of fevers; the heart is wonderfully refreshed by its scent. Ethiopia sends **Cinnamon** via the **Troglodytes** <note>a historical term for "cave-dwellers" of the Red Sea coast</note>; it is given for dimness of the eyes and for heart ailments. **Cloves** <note>original: *Garyophylli*</note> are produced in the East Indies; they help the heart and the dimness of the eyes, and they sharpen the sight. **Cassia** <note>a spice similar to cinnamon</note> grows in Ethiopia and in the regions of fragrant Arabia; it resists the bites of vipers and contributes to the clarity of vision, along with countless other things which it would be tedious to relate. Conversely, there are plants that face the North, in damp and cold places, over which the Moon presides. An example is **hemlock** <note>original: *cicuta*</note>, whose power is exceptional in the lands of the Parthians; it is of such a chilling nature that it kills powerfully, restrains rheums, and so it is with others.

### THINGS THAT RISE UP TOWARD HEAVEN ARE EFFECTIVE AGAINST LIGHTNING. Chap. XVII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' featuring a landscape scene within the letter.</image-desc>

THESE things seem in a certain way to savor of a celestial nature. Let us reveal by reason how lightning and storms are to be countered, and satisfy those who torment themselves in the investigation of causes as to why some things are not struck by lightning. It must not be ignored that all those things which, at the time of storms and imminent lightning, rise up against the sky as if to struggle with heaven, undoubtedly resist storms and lightning. By these forms, they show that they are preparing themselves against them, or are protected by a hidden consensus; I see that even the ancient natural philosophers perceived this. For **Pliny**, speaking of the seal, says: They say that the skins of **seals** <term>vituli marini; literally "sea-calves"</term>, even when stripped from the body, retain a sense of the sea, and always bristle when the tide recedes. Because of this, being fearful of being struck by lightning, people cover tents with the skins of these beasts which they call "sea-calves," since this is the only marine animal that lightning does not strike. The Emperor **Severus** wished his litter to be covered with the hide of a seal. We have often observed that when southern winds rise up, the hairs bristle, but during northern winds, they become still; they have spoken in the same way regarding the skin of the **hyena**. For **Palladius** says: It is believed to counter hail if someone carries the skin of a crocodile, or a hyena, or a seal around the boundaries of a property, and hangs it at the entrance of the villa or the courtyard when they see evil threatening. **Philostratus** attributes power to the **hippopotamus**; for he says: Within

<summary>This page discusses plants with spotted leaves as being under the Moon's influence and details how tropical "solar" plants like balsam and cinnamon possess healing properties for the heart and eyes. It also describes how certain animal skins, like those of seals and hyenas, were traditionally believed to protect against lightning and storms.</summary>

--- Page 323 ---
<meta>This page concludes the author’s discussion of how plants and animals react to the heavens, specifically focusing on those that possess a natural resistance to lightning and storms. It transitions from the lunar signatures discussed previously to the "signatures" of protection against the elements.</meta>

<page-num>320</page-num>
<header>PHYTOGNOMONICA</header>

Bury the skin of a **hippopotamus** <note>original: *fluuiatilis equi*, literally "river horse"</note> in a field, and lightning will not strike that place. Hippopotamuses are covered in hair like calves and live in the water; though it may not yet have been widely observed, their hairs bristle upward during storms. For this reason, ship captains use them to reinforce the edges of their sails so they are not consumed if touched by lightning. Among birds, they write that only the **eagle** is not struck by lightning, which is why it is depicted as the bearer of Jupiter’s weapon <note>The thunderbolt</note>; its feathers are said to stand on end during a storm, though this is perhaps untested. Because of this, men consider the eagle alone among all birds to be divine. One may see the same behavior in many herbs, which raise their leaves and "bristle" against approaching storms.

Pliny, speaking of **clover** <note>original: *trifolio*</note>, says that it also raises itself against storms, though he does not specify which kind. **Fuchs** <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a renowned German physician and herbalist</note> says it is **wood sorrel** <note>original: *acetosum*; likely *Oxalis acetosella*</note> which, growing in shady places, announces coming storms; it raises itself against them as they approach. He and others have observed that when this herb produces many flowers, it surely portends frequent rains and floods for that year, while few flowers portend drought. Speaking of **asphalt clover** <note>original: *asphaltite trifolio*; likely Bitumen trefoil</note>, its scent is present seven times a day and lost as many times; as long as it grows in gardens, its scent becomes much more powerful when the weather is rainy or a storm is imminent, so much so that it fills the entire house with its fragrance. However, I have observed this in meadow clover and all other clovers as well; from this, I would most certainly predict protection against lightning.

The ancients wrote the same of **bryony** <note>original: *bryonia*, also called *alba vite* or white vine</note>: that it was effective against lightning. I too have observed a certain change in it during storms. **Palladius** <note>Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius, a 4th-century Roman agricultural writer</note> surrounds the entire space of a garden with white vine to protect against hail. And **Columella** <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, an influential Roman writer on agriculture</note> says:

> *Thus Tarchon, to keep away the lightning of great Jove,*
> *Often encircled his dwellings with white vines.*

Of all plants sown by hand and kept in the home, the **laurel** alone is not struck by lightning. Because of this, they say the Emperor **Tiberius** used to be crowned with it when the sky thundered, out of fear of the bolts. We have stated the reason: it raises its leaves against storms. We shall offer another reason: it seems to be most opposed to fire in its actions. Pliny adds that the laurel visibly rejects fire with a loud crackling and a kind of "disdain." Nature is wonderful in this plant; it contains fire within—for by rubbing two sticks together it kindles a flame, as we have often experienced—yet it casts out and detests external fire.

The **fig tree** is also never struck by lightning. The **bulb** <note>likely a species of wild onion or *Muscari*</note> escapes the impact of lightning not because of its small size, but because it possesses a nature that turns back the lightning's stroke. **Coral**, called "Gorgona" because it turns into hard stone, is affirmed by Pliny to resist lightning and storms. **Truffles** <note>original: *tuber*</note> have a similar gift; hence the proverb used for a person who, forewarned by his own protection against the power of omens, is said "to carry truffles" <note>original: *hydna gestare*</note>. They show a kinship with thunder, for when there are great storms and thunders in autumn, they are born then. The poet **Aquinas** says:

> *And the longed-for thunder will make for magnificent feasts.*

Indeed, the rain and tempests that are hurled down with fire seem to be the cause of their generation, as is held by Plutarch. Of a contrary nature is the **cucumber**; whenever the sky thunders, as if terrified by fear, it turns away.

Therefore, it may be printed; all the more so since everything contained within is stated philosophically and according to the mind of Natural Philosophers. <meta>This page concludes the alphabetical index of the manuscript. It covers the letters V, X, and Z, focusing heavily on the "Doctrine of Signatures"—the belief that the physical characteristics of plants and animals (such as hairiness, color, or shape) indicate their medicinal properties. The text includes references to the healing of wounds, treatments for hair loss (alopecia), and remedies for eye conditions.</meta>
